Summary: A game for those who don't care whether their farm has aliens they need to fight off, or NPCs they can romance. This game doesn't have that. It has farming equipment and a great environment for people looking for a relaxing evening or a great co-operative experience with friends who enjoy simulated farming with heavy equipment.
Hours of fun: *Varies - If you like simulators then it may well be infinite
Suggested Retail Value: $20
Graphics: 7/10
Voice-acting: NA - No voice-acting
Music/SFX: NA - Calm music on menus only
Uniqueness: 5/10
First Play-through Experience: 8/10
Replay Value: 9/10
If you have any love for simulated farming then I doubt you would regret paying up to $20 for the full version. I was introduced to the game through a friend who had put in 100s of hours and just convinced me to give it a try so I could experience what he loved so much about it. I didn't expect it to be this much fun, but it's a blast on co-op play.
After a stressful day, I can sit back and relax and handle issues as they rise. Choosing to pace myself in the game by switching it to real-time and literally doing needed chores then watching the beautiful sunset or... whatever.
Then, when I'm feeling ambitious, we both hop into our private server and divy up the tasks at hand, co-operating in beautiful harmony to bring our farm ever closer to being a mega-success.
It's hard to describe how it feels to grow a farm from humble beginnings with one small field to a booming business with dozens of fields, 1000s of tons of equipment, and a ranch boasting hundreds of animals, but I highly recommend sharing it with friends.
To help with that, the game has an incredible community. Whether you're looking to see the mods that are available, wanting to create your own, looking for a buddy to chat with while you drive the harvesters, or wanting to join a sever with dozens of players trying to achieve a shared farm (even splitting up the tasks, creating jobs, dolling out wages, the whole deal!) the truth is you'll find it all here.
I say this about few games (Skyrim readily comes to mind) but FS 2013 feels less like a game and more like a world you visit for as long as you like. Highly recommended if the above sounds interesting to you.

The short:
- Do not buy, not even on sale or for nostalgia. Save your money.
- Poorly optimized.
- Framrate and lighting issues.
- Intrusive autosave screens.
- Outdated shooting mechanics that don't age well, unlike some classic shooters.
The long:
- I would have recommended this game when if came out all those years ago, but even on sale price I couldn't justify it. If you're looking for nostalgia and a fun shooter to play, then I would honestly say save your money. I blazed through this game with little challenge (on extreme difficulty) and I wasn't creeped out in the slightest or completely satisfied with the shooting mechanics - as fun as they used to be back in the day.
- The original game is more or less playable, but the higher resolutions aren't optimized, the lighting effects flicker on and off  just enough to annoy you but not enough to deter you from not playing. It might cause some people migraines.
- The worst thing is when the game autosaves it freezes the game on a black screen for 2-3 seconds, and this is quite frequent and really breaks immersion. The original, even with these problems, plays fine for how old it is, then the expansion, Extraction Point, plays like absolute garbage; the framerate dives insansely low at many parts rendering this old♥♥♥♥♥game unplayable even on a beast rig, so I stopped and uninstalled it and probably won't touch it again. I have no idea how Perseus Mandate runs, probably the same if not worse. Look elsewhere for older games that are better optimized or have HD remakes.

My "Yes" recommendation has reservations.
The game is very solid. I encountered no bugs or crashes, and the UI, while different from what I'm used to (I've never played a Paradox game before) is relatively intuitive. The graphics are beautiful with no observed artifacts, as are the sounds (although the music gets repetitive.) The tutorial is bare-bones, and there is no manual other than the Stellaris WIki that can be accessed within the game.
I have two real beefs with the game, however: the AI-controlled sector management hides too much important info from the player, and the mid-to-late game crises are often game-endingly brutal.
In the interest of manageability, you are limited to direct control of only 5 planets. You may group additional planets into sectors which are managed by the AI. This is fine except that should you build colony ships in a starbase in one of the AI-controlled sectors, the player receives only a brief notification when the ship is ready for use. This can be critical because colony ships drain energy credits like mad until the colony is created.  Colony ships created on non-sector planets are displayed as Civilian Ships in the Outliner (a quick access menu on the right side of the screen) but sector-created colony ships are not.  If you don't handle the ship when the notification pops up, the player is forced to manually check each starbase until he locates the colony ship, which becomes clumsy and tiresome as your empire grows. Paradox should address this issue in a future patch.
The more serious issue is the inevitable mid-to-late game crisis. As your empire grows, you will encounter one or more older races which are overwhelmingly advanced and xenophobic. Just encountering them is sufficient to provoke a game-ending jihad by an insanely powerful race bent on your destruction. The frustrating part is that you can't avoid these berserkers if you expand, and if you don't expand, your empire will die. This game is just great. From the first moments, you just expect it to be a colourful platformer with RPG elements, and a reletively simplistic style, which is all there, but that's just the tip of the ice burg, and Dust offers so much more.
Without discussing any story elements, I can say dust offers an interesting experience, and the way it blends gameplay mechanics into the narrative is one that all developers should strive towards when immersion is fundamental to the game play experience. (An example of this is the first time you get silenced.) Dust also employs many common tropes of action platformers well, such as backtracking, treasure hunting, and the way in which new mechanics are taught to players.
All in all, Dust is an excellent game, and despite its length, it brings much to the table and ultimately gave me a very enjoyable time. If you are looking for a good time and enjoy platformers, Dust: An Elysian Tail will not fail to provide it.

When it was first released it was more stable that it is now, odd things happened, units disappeared but all in all we played games through to completion.
Now there isn’t a single night where the game does not lock, crash or do something that means we can’t continue.  We lost the last game when it reached the point where it would crash at the end of a specific turn, at a point halfway through the game.
These were standard galaxies played without mods.
The support we have had was always excellent and helpful but that doesn’t change the fact the game has way more content with the expansion and yet is totally unplayable.
I want to like this game. I do like the idea of this game but as things are, I hate this game, I hate the frustration it causes me and regret that the developers add content with one hand and remove features with the other (still no custom races in multiplayer since the Crusade expansion).
If you want a single player 4x game then take a look but this isn’t the review for you.
If you want a multiplayer co-op turn based strategy game then Civilisation in whatever flavour you desire is the only real choice unless the developer really starts to seriously resolve issues.

Large room for improvement, and when I mean large I mean the Devs should all sit down and talk to eachother about what's necessary to create a game and put it for sale on Steam.
It's clear that they put some time in creating it, but the amount of negative things just erases that time put in completly. Let's start with the story, it makes sense even though it's very Naruto-alike (by very Naruto-alike I mean it's actually Naruto but just different names for the characters), with just a bit of creativity you could do something better. The dialogs are down right bad, many grammatical errors , spelling errors, overall poor quality (makes me wonder if they put some 13 year old teenager writing it), once again, with a bit of effort they could have had someone spell-proof the dialogs, and it would have felt better for us players. Then there's the combat, great customization many spells, but what for? Most of the battles are downright unbalanced, most of the spells are either badly scripted/bugged (many of them hit for 1hp) or just useless when compared to others, why not cut the spell list a bit and make sure every single spell is actually useful?
Finally the thing that upset me the most, script class exceptions happening in the game, literally in-game errors that caused the game to crash, was this game tested before it was deployed on Steam? Was there a beta version? Did you receive user feedback? I bought an in-game item and was all happy, went to use it and get an error saying basicly that the game wasn't tested enough. This is not admissible, not if you want to charge people for the game.
There's much to be done for this game if there's still will to improve, and a good start up point would be to review all the dialogs and remove spelling/grammatical errors and cursing all together, followed by a revamp on the combat system.
Overall a mediocre at best RPGMaker game who strived to be good but just couldn't due to basic errors that could have been avoided with a bit more planning. 3/10

I've always had a soft spot for space 4X games like Galactic Civilization or Master of Orion, but thus far Stellaris does something that those games don't do: they make you invested in your creations. Even though you could customize races before, you don't have the degree of empire customization as you do here. You have a myriad of race appearances, flags, titles, government types, ideologies, and names to create your own unique empire.
It doesn't end there, the early game gives you many opportunities to flesh your Empire out through random events and scenarios. For example, I had one event around Turn 46 where my science vessel discovered an alien's version of "The Prince" and I had 3 choices. I could bring it back to my culture and study it, I could return it to the aliens (if I found the), or I could've called it garbage. All of those were based off the ideologies I chose in the beginning. This displayed that the developers built scenarios that did factor in your beginning choices and it makes you invested.
The end game scenarios are also fascinating. The most common ones involve a race that is like the Reapers from Mass Effect, they have come down to conquer and annihilate all the races within that galaxy. There's also moments where you could have rogue AIs taking over a section of space and other stuff like that.
I do have a few criticisms that bug me about Stellaris:
1. The soundtrack is limited and gets boring to listen to after awhile. Paradox usually makes great soundtracks  so I was disappointed they didn't bring the kind of quality they had with the Crusader Kings II or Europa Universalis IV scores.
2. The diplomatic AI is still irritating and you'll find yourself frustrated of making progress diplomatically with other powers.
3. There are no unique victory conditions outside of pure conquest and "prestige" victories. This is standard to find in the other Paradox strategy games, but if you're used to different victory scenarios from 4X games, you won't find them here.
4. While the early and late game is awesome, the mid-game can be tedious. With the forementioned diplomatic AI, the lack of a espionage system, the lack of different victory conditions, and the number of random events slowing down, you may feel impatient to get to the next scenario or the next step on your way to galactic domination. I will admit there were times I had to start over because my empire couldn't grow and the empires next to me were blitzing my borders to the point that I couldn't put up a fight.
Despite those criticisms, I would recommend this game to anyone who loves strategy games, especially 4X players. This takes a successful formula from old space 4X games and injects it with steroids. Paradox also said that they'll release the majority of new content through free patches so you won't feel the need to prepare to purchase multiple DLC packs to get the "full" experience.

OK, honesty time - I haven't beaten this game yet - I've been playing it with my 7 year-old daughter and we've both been swept up in the Don Bluth-like visuals (see: An American Tail), snappy sound design and incredibly tight gameplay.
The story is very solid, and for a gamer like me whose history goes back decades, there are more than a few clever nods to funny moments in games past.
It's frequently described as a "Metroidvania" game, and I'd say that describes the mechanics well - it's got a lot in common with Castlevania in terms of platform jumping and exploration, although it's definitely a lot more linear than either of those games for much of the adventure so far.
The other thing it does - very well - is implement a combo system like a brawler - but with weapons. Think of the original Soul Calibre and you're not too far off (although this game is strictly 2d).
So who is this game for?
For me, it scratches a lot of the same itches as Guacamelee - fun, challenging but fair platforming with great combat mechancics that are easily grasped but sufficiently deep to reward longer gameplay sessions. Highly recommended, one of my favourite games, and one I pick up and play quite often, as it's rewarding in short bursts, not just when you have hours to spend.

Airport CEO is a nice and interesting Airport management game with allot of detail, and micro management.
You start the game with an empty area with a road and some delivery spots.
Then you start to build your airport form the ground up with click and drag selection.
You employ people, and you design your airport with building blocks, and some premade modules..
The game might look simple, but you soon will discover that people will not cross the street if there is no
path across.. Your fuel trucks will not arrive until you connected the road to the airport area, and you wont get any fuel at all until you have signed a contract with a company to deliver it to you. ect.
The same goes with everything els in the game, you can employ many different type of personel from different CEO's to cleaning ladys... The CEO's have different speciality and you employ them to unlock the ability to research and use different things in your airport.
Exmaple to be able to handle lugage and load/unload you need an COO and pay to unlock technology and buildings.
Next you ahve to setup your lugage transport system including security scanners and so on.
With other words the game have many nice features and you need you will have to build and tweak and rebuild things to do them better and better. The more passengers the more planes, the more difficult the game will be when it come to logistics.
You can micro manage many things, from how many people need to be at the boarding gate, to checkin people that goes on the plane.
In the future the game will also have maintenance, and catering of food and more features than today.
So far I enjoy the game, even though it rather fast become a bit repedative..
The game is in Early access and features are missing, but for what it is woth it have great potential and i belive it will be really good in the future.
If you are the type who like to try the game now with missing features go for it and you get it cheap.
But if you are impatient and dont like missing features then you should wait.

I used to have a postive review for this game that I have since deleted. Here is why I no longer enjoy or recommend this game.
The new card system is♥♥♥♥♥♥to put it bluntly. OB64 killed the game and was the last nail in the coffin along with the many bugs and issues the game already had.
I have been an avid supporter of the game by purchasing different bonus packs and crystals and have enjoyed many an hour playing it, as you can see from my hours played. I used to really enjoy the card system that was in the game, it made it more unique to compete with games like Overwatch, LawBreakers, Battleborn and other types of hero shooter games of that nature.
It was rewarding to build my own card loadout and being able to test out my skill against other players. Everyone was on a level playing field when it came to this. Since the pay/play to win aspect was released and the format changed, you can tell how much it's gone down hill and how many people have backlashed against hirez as a company. Did they listen to feedback and complaints? Not really. They bought back 'classic' siege mode which is nothing like the classic game. It's like they worked hard on a new system and wanted to lauch it live regardless.
It should be it's own game mode and everything else should be kept the same. I don't have my loadouts anymore. I feel like my money spent on the game has been wasted. There are some things that are great in OB64, such as the new background for the champion select screen when you are in a match, and the way your character does an emote or some sort of action once you've picked one. I like the new skins and the Grohk re-work and the way he FINALLY has a new voice pack and cosmetics pack. Is this enough to make me still play the game? No.
This is it for me now. Goodbye old friend, it was nice knowing you.

Zeno Clash is a weird game.  "Weird" is definitely the best adjective to describe it.  It's an odd game with odd characters in an odd world.  The game is made in the Source Engine, but the visuals are strikingly different from other games from the same engine, like Half Life 2 or Vampire: The Masquerade.  The game is a string of arcade-esque fights with guns and fists, all in first-person.  Zeno Clash is actually one of the only games to do fist fighting correctly in first person, and it does it well.  While Zeno Clash is very short, the story clocking only three to four hours, it does have a challange mode and varying difficulty levels.  Even if it costs too much at full price, it's undoubtably worth it on sale.

I also appreciate the fact that the game is easy to mod, as I'm a big fan of modding games.
Finally I think that Stardock is one of the few developers that actually listens to and interacts with their fans, which helps make the game even better.
++ Massive galaxies, with resonable turn speed
++ Easy to mod and I do love modding
++ Making custom ship designs to conquer the galaxy
+ Fun vanilla and custom races to dominate the universe
+ Good looking engine

-/+ AI: The AI can be quite good at times, but there are some cases where it can be positively stupid. If some of those cases could be fixed, it would simply be a plus, but right now. Not really any worse than most other games out there though.
- Spelling. My pet peeve, but spelling mistakes just reduce the polished feel of the game
- The thing I miss in GC, which really made my time in MOO2 so memorable is the ship-to ship combat. In GC it's a cinematic battle based on the ship stats. I miss the tactical battles of MOO. I knew what I was getting into though when I bought it.
- Some bugs and the occasional crash. Overall, Stardock manages to fix most crashes, and I haven't had one in quite some time, however, some bugs I just decided to fix myself (Yaay for modding!)
Overall I would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the genre and I think it's a good ambassador for the genre.

Final Fantasy VIII is a great game with a solid story, great atmosphere, and fun battle system.  In this version, however, the music is mixed so badly I can't stand it.  I've seen other reviews that mention this and figured I could get over it if that was the only issue.  While it IS the only issue, it's bad enough that I cannot listen to any of the music without gritting my teeth.  As such, I cannot recommend this port to anyone who has played the original.  The music was a major selling point for this game, with all the complicated and nuanced themes that delighted the listener throughout the story and battles.  Now the tracks have been compressed and reimagined as a two channel midi nightmare that unbalances the original parts, and leaves out many more instruments that gave the music its character and uniqueness.  It turns a grand orchestral vision into a badly performed♥♥♥♥♥♥♥fest that sounds like it came out of the age of atari.  I simply cannot imagine how the person responsible for porting the sound could have ♥♥♥♥ed up more.  Seriously, it's really that bad.  Fortunately, this game came out before final fantasy characters had voice actors behind them, so you should just turn off the sound entirely, put on your own music, and enjoy the game.
Oh, and magic booster is a HUGE time saver.  Use it, abuse it, enjoy your story!

Sure, the junction system takes some getting used too (especially if you're used to the traditional MP system) and continually drawing magic from enemies can, and will get tedious, (have your GFs learn them refining abilities!)  not to mention the teen drama style story might not be up everyone's ally, but in all fairness, FF8 is a solid game with a ton of nostagia surrounding it, for me anyway.  The smooth looking Steam version is very appealing to the eyes, but the stock midi format music kind of kills the trip down memory lane for me. I mean come on! FF8 has, in my opinion, one of the best soundtracks in the Final Fantasy collection. I can understand making the game smaller in size, but the music is a key factor in the whole Final Fantasy experience.  (Nobuo Uematsu is a game music GENIUS!)  But fear not friends, get the Roses and Wine mod for oust the midis and replace them with the original PS1 music, or add some of the different songs that come included, I recomend the orchestrated Balamb Garden, Blue Fields, Boss music and Battle themes. All in all, the Roses and Wine mod is a major saving grace for this purchase, and I highly recommend it.

The makers of this game think best part of jrpgs is combat, which is always the worst part. Endlessly repeating the same things (skills, combos etc) over and over again. Even worse, this game has unseen enemy encounters with those that you can see. Which is pretty idiotic. At some point of the game even normal enemies start to have so much hp that random encounters vs normal enemies last for minutes. And you have to fight them ... a lot. Also 90% of the skills are completely useless. And with enemy hp so high even your best skills dont do enough damage. And at some point enemies will start to stunlock your whole party forever.
Also that genius who thought its a good idea that enemies can spawn from treasure chests should never make games again. Also the other thing about combat later is that only your skills that use TP[TP is another mana, only worse] do any damage. And of those only those that use all your TP (100) at one time. So combat turns into use a potion to get 100 tp, use skill, use potion to get 100 tp etc etc, and the best part is that those skills can even miss, losing all your TP.
Also there is no use fighting after one point, because enemies scale with your level. So everytime a random encounter starts you can try to run away, except from chest and visible monster (what the hell?). Most of the time the running away doensnt work and because you cant access menu or load in combat forces you to close the game and when you have to do this all the time, it really buggers your steam friends receiving constant notions that you are playing this awful game. The story is pretty nice (in a so bad dialogue it turns kinda into good way), Naw who am I kidding its bad as hell.And nothing can save it as the abyssmal combat ruins the game.
And the last thing, I've never ever wished that game would end more. But no it just keeps going and going, and splitting the party all the time forcing you with horrible party combinations and with less people easier for enemies to stunlock you to death. Theres lots of content that should have been scrapped and even cheap things like big maps with mazes and levers(are there just to make the game longer) that you need to push in correct order which you cant see as theres no map and view distance is too near. All while trying to avoid combat from invisible & visible enemies and saving everytime you open a chest, because if theres combat, you need to restart the game.
Example battle I might never win. 5 Enemies vs 1 my hero. They use 3 different stuns (stun, paralyze and ice) If any of them stun me, combat is automatically lost. You can only protect yourself vs stuns with armors that have worse stats and only protect vs 1 effect so no dice there. If I luck through one enemy turn without stunlock, I can use 1 spell, which is my best spell and it does about 500-600 damage, enemies have about 10k-15k health.
So 1/10 avoid like the plague.

Destiny Warriors is a combination of questionable plot with half of characters being idiots, giant imbalance of battles, with them spreading equally between awfully boring (because they last 15 minutes each) and impossibly hard (stun-lock before you can do anything) and the fact that developer never heard of a dictionary - amount of grammar and punctuational mistakes is overflowing.
The fact that this is an RPG maker game does not makes this game bad, no. Its developers lameness that does. OK, typos do happen, but with frequency like that, I stopped paying careful attention to plot. Lack of commas makes text hard to read and there are dots missing between many sentences making it impossible to understand what is written here and there. Note that english is not my native language but even with my little skill I can spot countless errors.
Battle balance is even worse: both enemies and characters have very big HP and very low attack. This makes killing enemies unnecessary long and dying nearly impossible. However, 25% of battles work differently: you have even worse damage, but one spell that does big damage, but enemy - it either does genocidal damage or stunlock 3/4 of your party on first move. I am writing this review as I struggle through last battle where you have ONE character at max level, which does not have any attacks that would do significant damage (except super attack which first requires drinking skill potion - to get 100 skill points for that attack, and then actually attacking, which will not happen as you will get stunned) while enemies have elemental attacks, that end your first turn by either stunning you or paralyzing. Of course, you will be dead before you can move as you can get both paralyze and stun at the same time, but they wear out not at the same time, so you get at least one of those debuffs most of your turns.
If the battle is an easy one, it will be boring. The big HP and low dmg extend battles to very long times. There is nothing else about them except that enemy lvl scales as you level up, but enemies characteristics - and that is AT LEAST agility which determines turn order and is most noticeable to this as after level up you frequently no longer attack first - grow faster. Thankfully, boss battles are of a fixed levels.
For graphics and sound - PURELY default RPG maker assets. I was unable to see anything unique in this game. The only thing that was quite good is that developer used different character faces for different emotions. Not every rpg maker game does this, so it is nice too see this small feature, especially that facial expressions go very well with a plot. But the game fails in many places, so its not really helping.
Plot is so-so. People say that its a Naruto ripoff, but I haven't watched that cartoon so can't say. But what I can say is that its too much absurd at times.
I would not recommend buying this even with 90% discount, too much bad development choices make this game true mess. But if you like CRAZY plots - you might want to check it out, but make sure that you play on easy difficulty, as last boss is still hard as hell. People say that on hard, its unbearable right from the start of the game.

This heart-touching platformer involves the story of a man who is trying to reach his lover. I still found the story quite flat, though, and find it fitted to the “Quest for love” category of games. But, I did enjoy the way the game had this goal fashioned in a way that connected both in the atmosphere, and as a novel. In each level, you are introduced with a new set of dialogue that connects to the latter. The dialogues itself explains in more detail of our character, their motives and the situation. Then there are the bits of tutorial for how to play and the key controls.
The basic “AWSD” key bindings are what you use, and the space key will re-wind time to where you will see yourself and a shadow of your past self-repeating the same actions that you did before resetting. These controls are simple and easy to follow, so kudos for that.
The environment definitely gets the most compliments. The background was rich with nature and visuals of the sky, but never to the point where we couldn’t focus on the platform and characters. It gave off a relaxing vibe. That, blended with the piano piece as the background music made it all the more atmospheric. There were also small effects: fireflies that would shimmer in the levels where it is night, and snow falling on the winter maps.
I’ve already included my comment on the audio, but as for the voice acting … it was all right. Jack’s voice was done, but the female voice actor sounded too aggressive and loud to fit in with the nature of the game. Upon hearing her first dialogue, it sounded like the voice actor was shouting in their microphone!
That being said, I still enjoyed the game nonetheless. It reminded me of a similar game, titled ‘The Company of Myself’ which was also a great game. I recommend playing Broken Dreams.

If you're a fan of Civilization, I absolutely think you'll be a fan of this game.

3) The game has a lot more depth than any Civ game I've played. Down to weapons load outs on ships, leaders for multiple research queues and ships, planet-side production and population maintenance, etc, etc
4) The game takes place in space and involves a plethora of alien species to play as or against... I really just like the setting a lot more.

What to make of Stellaris...
I'm only 23 hours into my first campaign but I can tell that Stellaris is going to have my attention for a very long time!
The good:
Stellaris is gorgeous, fairly intuitive if you're used to the 4x genre, insanely complex and constantly satisfying to play. This is a game that constantly triggers the 'reward' section of my brain with multiple concurrent researching technologies, always busy planets and exploration thats genuinely rewarding. If you get into a 4x so much that you're roleplaying in your head the whole time, Stellaris will make you a very happy player.
The bad:
Stellaris is, for lack of a better word, awkward when it comes to the user interface. It always feels to me like I have either far too much information on my screen taking up valuable space or not enough. There isn't much of a middle ground. While the gameplay in Stellaris is fairly intuitive, there are times when the user interface was so unintutive that I had to look up what to do online; the most glaring example being the correct buttons to press to finish a war.
Another issue I have with Stellaris is the transition between the Stellar and Galactic maps... I loved Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion for a thousand reasons but one of the things I miss in Stellaris that was so simple in Sins is the option to scroll out from the Stellar map to the Galactic map... Its just so intuitive in Sins but in Stellaris you have to go click a button or press a key to transition between the two. Its nit-picking, yes, but its something I missed many times during play already.
In closing, Stellaris took me on a journey across the stars that has been full of great unexpected moments of story development, exploration, gorgeous discoveries and so much more. It's worth your time if you like Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion or any of the other space 4x's... Just be ready to switch your thinking back to RTS from turn based!

Quite simply, this game has one of the best campaign plots I've ever seen. The 1960's, CIA Black Ops in Russia and the Vietnam War, conspiracies, and a diabolical political plot to topple nations... all taken seriously in a totally immersive and epic experience. The gameplay is varied, indoors and outdoors, from lush tropical jungles to intelligence headquarters buildings, in a number of different historical conflicts. No spoilers, but the whole story is about finding a hidden, classified truth that is as mindblowing as the warheads that threaten to destroy the world. This dynamic and interesting campaign is unmatched, certainly throughout the Call of Duty series, as well as all the games I've played. It may not be the newest game, but the plot is worth it, I guarantee.
Although the plot and story elements alone are enough to warrant a purchase, it is as fun of an ADS FPS as I've ever played, with decent graphics, punchy weapons, and great levels. I've played through the entire game on Veteran Difficulty, the most challenging difficulty, and had an absolute blast. There's not an overwhelming amount of collectables, and they remain found after multiple playthroughs.
The Zombies mode in this game is also great, probably better than Black Ops 2. It's not overly complicated like its sequel, and is just solid and hardy. I'm terrible at Zombies and still loved it. In one level you actually get to play as John F. Kennedy fighting zombies in the US Pentagon. Awesome? Awesome.

DOOM is often credited as the best game ever made. This is true. But, true on a deeper level than usually discussed. DOOM itself was a groundbreaking game in its day. If nothing more was done than releasing the game, that alone would have forever secured it in the pages of computer gaming history forever.
What is less often noted in reviews of DOOM is that it’s so much more than just a single game. ID Software intended DOOM to be able to be modded from the beginning. That’s why it’s WAD files are designed as they are. So that resources could be replaced and the game could be ever-expanded.
More than that, once the commercial viability of DOOM had ran its course, the source code to the engine itself was liberated under the GNU GPL; making it Free Software. Everyone who knew how to code could now tare into the very heart and soul of the software that brought DOOM to life and make it into whatever they wanted it to be.
In doing this, ID Software had made DOOM eternal. More than just swapping out map layouts, audio, and visuals; people could mod the very engine itself; as well as eventually write mods for the engine to run within the game. This was made possible because people could mod the engine. They were able to implement a scripting language within DOOM that modders could then use to add things like new enemies, weapons, and much, much more.
What this all means is that when you step into the esteemed halls of DOOM, you’re not just getting a game. You’re getting so much more. You’re getting full access to an entire engine. Couple that with the Free Software programs that have been made to edit DOOM; and you have a full software development suit.
The DOOM modding community is alive and well. It creates amazing game after game. Note I said games, not just levels or mere mods. All sorts of games. It’s been nearly twenty four years and I am still finding entire games people have created for the DOOM engine. Some new, some old; all fun.
There are people who have made it their passion to mod DOOM. They try every idea imaginable for the first person shooter genre and beyond. It is a development platform that has a massive array and tools and community support. Never have I seen a more accessible entry into making your own game in 3D space.
And, if you used only your own content, the game is yours; as the license does give you that. GPL work can be sold for a profit legally. (Note, the original DOOM wad files can not be used in this way. You have to make your own stuff or start off with the FREEDOOM wad files.)
All that said, DOOM is more than a game. It is a platform of limitless potential to the budding map maker, coder, and modder. It is the definition of ease of access, yet the very wellspring of the experimental in gaming.
Time and time again, I have seen DOOM mods that I have enjoyed more than AAA releases. I have also seen DOOM mods that have re-made AAA releases with better game play.
I will describe just a small smattering of what can be done with DOOM.
Want to play something new forever? Why not try Oblige? It’s a Free Software program that uses procedural generation to create new levels for DOOM. With this program, you’ll always have more maps to play.
Try Slade and Doom Builder to create your own maps manually. They are detailed level design tools that allow for editing in 2D and 3D. Slade can edit far more than just maps.
Want to explore deep learning? There is a DOOM engine plugin for creating Bots to play DOOM. There is even a competition that you can enter; both are called ViZDoom.
Want a great arcade shooter? Try Reelism Gold. Every game is a slot machine that rolls three mods and you try to get the most points before you die.
Want to play a bloody gory DOOM with new weapons, vehicles, and new demon attacks? Try BRUTAL DOOM.
This is the value of liberating a game engine under the GNU GPL. It allows the community to rally behind the game and make it into so much more than just one game. It allows people to make the software their own and truly make new, revolutionary, and fun things with it.
I often wonder why more of the game industry hasn’t fallowed the ID Software model. Proprietary first, then Free Software once the commercial value of the engine has ran its course. It’s the ethical thing to do. It wasn’t just the technological leaps forward that made these engines and these games so valuable to the public. It was that ID Software gave these innovations to the public. In so doing, they changed the way the public saw the software they gamed with. Software was no longer a black box that just made the game work. Software was now an open door to creativity that a community could bond together over. That’s what made ID Software games so special; more than anything else.
I also wait, in hope, that ID Software itself will continue to fallow this model. We’re still waiting for the ID Tech 5 release under the GNU GPL.
That said, ID Software has no one there that originally started the company; and Carmack was known for really pushing for the source code releases under the GNU GPL. Many have told me that with him gone; we’ll likely never see another source code release from ID. I don’t want to agree with them too quickly. But, I think they’re likely right. Were the source code releases ID’s tradition, or Carmack’s tradition? Only time will tell.
I hope ID keeps this tradition. I also hope other software development companions fallow this model. That said, we’ll always have DOOM. The original DOOM. Which, twenty four years later, is still alive and well with its modding community. A truly infinite game that is forever growing.

So as of writing this review, I just finished the game less than five minutes ago AND OH MY GOD. OH. MY. GOD. You would not believe what an adventure it was. If you don't want to read the full review, then, here it is. 9/10. Masterpiece in the horror genre. Masterpiece in the FPS-Action genre. The graphics are a bit outdated tho, as of 2015 but it doesn't disturb (atleast) me much, and would fall into the decade of half-life 2 graphics. So if you don't care about flexing your PC's muscles then it's no prob for you, but if you want to experience a horrifying adventure that will haunt your dreams for months after you had uninstalled it, then go. What are you waiting for!
ok, now let's talk more detailly about each category.
Graphics:
Yes, as I said, the graphics are a bit outdated. The game was released almost ten years ago as of now, but it does not change the story and gameplay of this game. If you have a super-hyper-mega-epic gtx 970 i7 4790k build then you can play this game on 4K ultra, and get way over 200fps. If you have a less powerful build, like say a 760 with an i5 or something like that then you won't have any problems playing this game at 60+ fps either, but still i wouldn't recommend going 4K. Also, there's plenty of mods out there to fix the lighting, the reflections, etc, but I personally prefer to play the game like it is given to me (pronounce: I was too lazy to install any mods).
Gameplay:
I remember hearing that Valve once said, that in their Half-Life series, they value gameplay over story (even tho both are important). In my opinion this game perfectly nailed the Half-Life feel and even overdid it. As we know Half-Life was meant as a Light-Horror-Shooter-Puzzle-game. Well F.E.A.R. in our case is FULL-HORROR-Shooter-with some puzzle in it. For me personally the puzzles were not that interesting (go to the furthest away room, press a button, return to start, proceed to now opened gate), but at least they added diversity to the gameplay, different from CoD. The shooting factor in this game was really good in my opinion. If you're a beginner at shooters you'll have a fun time exploding the heads of Fettel's private army, but if you're an FPS veteran like me, you'll beat the game on extreme difficulty with just enough effort for the game to seem a little-tiny bit hard at moments. Also what I really liked was the time freeze button. Loved peeking around the corner then pressing U (I binded it to U) and shooting unsuspecting troops in the head with a plasma gun and seeing them throw their weapon away and turn into a skeleton. So satisfiying. Oh and did I tell you, you can completely remove the crosshair? Definetely gonna be a plus for those who are seeking realism in games and want to try their skill. And Lastly the spooky-spooks. When I started playing it, the last time i had played a horror game was over a year ago. It literally went like this: Walk out of the car. Go inside an abandoned building. Try open the door, it falls down. got me creeped but I kept going. Walk on the second floor, and see a cloud of smoke coming my way. BOOM. A BLOODY FACE COVERING THE WHOLE SCREEN. I ran out of the building, tried to get back in the car, closed the game, started laughing at myself, told my friends so they could laugh too, started crying, and went to get icecream. After a couple jumpscares i got used to them, but still thinking it all through keeping the lore in mind will get you pretty disturbed.
And last but not least the story:
Without spoiling much, you are a marine, who got sent to remove a military commander (or something) who has gone crazy, and while chasing him you start to uncover some supernatural $hit. And a girl following and jumpscaring you everywhere. Like G-MAN but creepier. Time to time she and the crazy supernatural guy talk some creepy stuff to you in between fighting hordes of soldiers. I won't go deeper into the lore, for you to still have something to discover, but the ending... Right when I had let my guard down thinking: it is finally over, but JUMPSCARE-PLOT TWIST.
Anyway this game is a definite 9/10 and would have gotten better from me if I had bought it in the gold days of Half-Life 2, but i still definetely recommend you to play it.
P.S. Not that I want to say something bad about our great lord and savior, Gaben, but this game (or rather the collection, because you also get two dlcs to continiue the story that you wouldn't have gotten otherwhise) rarely goes on sale and is still pretty expensive then. Call me cheeky, but in my opinion 60 bucks for 3 games and dlc is a tad too much for my wallet to afford. Grab this game during the next winter/summer sale and prepare for having an awesomly creepy and creepily awesome adventure.
P.S.2 I do know I had left a whole bunch of typos and mistakes in this long-a$$ text, feel free to point them out to me and make my life easier.

I rate the game F.E.A.R (First Encounter Assault Recon): 4/5. Good.
This is a an extremely creepy game that stays fairly creepy throughout. True, this game is full of jump-scares but they are all well done. The jump-scares are not usually the loud, annoying kind but the kind which give you quiet glimpses into a seemingly other world (or rather, mind). If you take the time to look at everything carefully and listen to every answering machine message you can find the game's mysterious plot gets explained quite thoroughly as well. The controls are good, the sound is adequate and the lighting and graphics, while fairly simple and minimalistic by today's standards, are clean. The enemy types do not have a great deal of variety (though there is some and this game features the most potentially realistic looking power-armor design I have ever seen in any game).
This game is short and the plot is highly linear (which limits its replayability severely) but the story that is told is fascinating and thought-provoking while the gameplay is tense and creepy throughout. The enemy AI is frighteningly clever (far superior to Half Life 2's soldier AI) with soldiers who will flank, ambush, flush you out with grenades and often refuse to get tricked into being piled up in bottle-necked doorways. 80% of this game takes place in-doors (mostly in after-hours night time office spaces (which I think is a cool idea and is a setting I haven't seen since the early part of Half Life 1) so as a result the enemy AI (and the graphics and lighting) doesn't have to deal with as much complexity as it might have otherwise.
Much of this game reminded me of the first Die Hard movie in terms of action (due to the night-time, largely abandoned office building environment) but in all the best ways. In many ways this game's style is like an even cross between the action and environment of Die Hard I and the creeping horror of The Ring (if you can imagine it). This made for a great combination. The ending is a bit of a cliff hanger but is suitably shocking and horrific (in the extreme) while still paying homage to The Ring (which is where the game has clearly borrowed most of its horror style). The music is strange but well suited to the game but I found only 3 songs I really liked (the main opening theme and two action themes they were).

The Binding of Isaac is a Roguelike game that brings back some good old memories that only Legend of Zelda could achieve.  The first aspect of the game that will hit you, is that it seems to have been made by a disturbed mind. The story of a child  who's being attacked by his mother because God told her to and then fall in his cellar to be trapped in a total nightmare is not the kind of regular story that you will often see in video games. I must say that the story gives to The Binding of Isaac a certain charm and you'll want to laugh when you'll see the shocked face of the guy beside you while you're in the bus or the metro when he'll look at a little guy shooting tears (or bloody tears) to ♥♥♥♥♥♥-like monsters on the screen of your computer. Another amazing thing about this game is the number of different object you will find. There are A LOT of them. When you die in The Binding of Isaac, you'll find yourself always saying "one more time". Another aspect that can be an issue with some computers is that the game uses Flash. Some computers with an idle and a silent mode on their CPU might lag and sometimes random lags comes out from nowhere and that can be a pain considering this is a very small portable game that you would expect to be smooth to play with a top notch FPS.

What to make of Stellaris...
I'm only 23 hours into my first campaign but I can tell that Stellaris is going to have my attention for a very long time!
The good:
Stellaris is gorgeous, fairly intuitive if you're used to the 4x genre, insanely complex and constantly satisfying to play. This is a game that constantly triggers the 'reward' section of my brain with multiple concurrent researching technologies, always busy planets and exploration thats genuinely rewarding. If you get into a 4x so much that you're roleplaying in your head the whole time, Stellaris will make you a very happy player.
The bad:
Stellaris is, for lack of a better word, awkward when it comes to the user interface. It always feels to me like I have either far too much information on my screen taking up valuable space or not enough. There isn't much of a middle ground. While the gameplay in Stellaris is fairly intuitive, there are times when the user interface was so unintutive that I had to look up what to do online; the most glaring example being the correct buttons to press to finish a war.
Another issue I have with Stellaris is the transition between the Stellar and Galactic maps... I loved Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion for a thousand reasons but one of the things I miss in Stellaris that was so simple in Sins is the option to scroll out from the Stellar map to the Galactic map... Its just so intuitive in Sins but in Stellaris you have to go click a button or press a key to transition between the two. Its nit-picking, yes, but its something I missed many times during play already.
In closing, Stellaris took me on a journey across the stars that has been full of great unexpected moments of story development, exploration, gorgeous discoveries and so much more. It's worth your time if you like Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion or any of the other space 4x's... Just be ready to switch your thinking back to RTS from turn based!

I'll assume that you've already read the popular negative reviews as I write this, so I will reference those critiques as I have relatively few of my own.
You may have noticed a trend in those negative reviews.  Something like "I realized after 50 hours of play, I was bored."
The question right now is not whether or not this is a good game.  The question is whether you're willing to spend 40 dollars for ~50 hours of generally strong gameplay.  If this were any other dev, the answer would be a resounding "yes" from the community, but many have fallen into the trap of comparing Stellaris to it's more mature siblings instead of reviewing it as an induvidual game.
Will this game be better in a year than it is now, most certainly.  Is this game deserving of a negative review, absolutely not.  The negative reviews are reviewing this game with a benchmark, but from a level perspective, it is an excellent purchase for the pricetag that will only get better as time goes on.

A long ways to go, but this could be a great game!
I like all of the preset characters, and I also like the ability to add new characters and edit existing ones. In adding/editing a character, you can give them stat boosts or handicaps based on characteristics like strength, agility, intelligence, etc. However, past character creation the game is pretty shallow with regards to features. The controller can drop mines (which almost always kill people), care packages (which I have never seen picked up), and start "events". I have only seen two or three different types of events, and I haven't noticed anything change after the event. The characters' health stay the same, and no one is ever killed during events (in my experience).
The developers also thought of this cool little bit: Alliances. In larger games the participants will form alliances with one another if one or both run into each other unaffiliated with an existing alliance. This is a cool idea, however the extent of their alliance's function is to keep allies from killing one another when they come into contact. This is bad when the game is down to two people in the same alliance, as the gamecould go on indefinitely. Also, Allies should stick together, but here they run about randomly like headles chickens.
So here's my request: MORE FEATURES!
This game could be so cool! If the controller had more things to do aside from sit and watch the little gingerbread men run into one another. Create more options for the controller to interact with the participants. More variety in the updates screen would be cool too. Make map sizes, terrains (or at least describe the terrains that are already present, like the brown areas (Mountains?)), make it so that only Jesus can walk on water, and make the events more than just a message at the bottom of the screen.
Great job so far, really looking forward to progress and updates!

Few hours on Steam, but more on disk and on DLC, and thousands of hours in other strategy games.
Think Tom Clancy's End War, but with heavy metal, models, actors you'll say 'Hey, I recognise them!' and fun gameplay.
I'm going to start with things I didn't like so I can end the "review" on a high note, because you AND the game deserve it!!
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Things I didn't like:
- It's a bit dated: It's 2017 now. I guess I shouldn't have a stake in this, being a male, but I can't help but think of others. Using the old expectation of male gamers, they cater to this cliche too much. They refer to the player as a 'him' and 'he' all the time. No male models in the game other than George Takei, that handsome dude, and some other Japanese army characters. It makes me wonder how a female gamer might feel a bit uncomfortable. Definately a weakness here. Would have been hilarious to have some jacked dudes just towering over desks, giving you a brief on a mission.
- Skirmish options: Not enough customisation of the options in skirmish. I recall only being able to change starting currency amount, starting positions and all the factions/teams/colours stuff you'd expect from an RTS game. Having played so many other strategy games, it would have been nice to have the option to customise the experience more.
- After hours of playing, it's a little TOO simple: Like I said, very accessable to new players of the genre/series, but after a while it gets old. Build power buildings, get money, build units and attack. That's the extent of it. Whereas, popular RTS game Age of Empires 1 over here, you have to get MULTIPLE resources and you have to upgrade individual troops and climb eras/tech trees etc.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Things I like:
- Art style: The artwork for this game looks really cool. I'm a fan of the bright colours and how they instantly start defining each faction by making them visibly unique, which is also shown through in game with their units and abilities being completely diferent from each other.
- 'Bad' live action cutscene acting: 'bad' because it doesn't take itself seriously! One scene showed a Russian general and a Russian Intelligence officer giving you a briefing on the situation by video call. One of the lines was something like "The Imperial Japanaese army will thrust themselves into the soft tender regions of the USSR" or something like that and the Intelligence officer, her eyes just widen as if to say 'Did he just actually say that?'
- The music: Something that has been decent since the first Command and Conquer. The main theme itself over the years acts like a time capsule for that era of video games and like the games, evolves over the years getting more and more modern. Here it's more heavy metal. As a fan of Mastodon, I approve.
- The clear and embarrassing use of models: It's like they said 'Hey, what do gamers love?' and some other guy said 'World Wars. Heavy metal. And hot female models.' I like that this is such a clear cliche, like from a movie, because it's over the top and just hilarious. And I hope they knew that.
- Gameplay!: The game itself is simple enough for anyone to start playing. Power runs buildings, buildings can get money and produce units. But it can get difficult pretty quickly. I play on medium difficulty and some campaign missions I just barely complete, which is quite exciting to see your last two units, low health and all, at the end of a battle when the victory theme plays. One massive exhale and your onto the next entertaining cutscene. The inclusion of skirmish is great too! Plent of maps here, and all 3 factions are playable AND they have a spectator mode where you can just watch a match between the AI play out. Useful for people wanting to record some background footage or sounds, or just take a look at what they do and what everything looks like. Lots of unique units and special abilities for each faction which is essential for a game like this.
- Abilities: Every unit has a special ability or unique mode which can make it even more effective in situations. Like the telsa troopers can either electrocute enemies or completly stun vehicles. There are also abilities that you can get depending on your faction, in a similar way that Company of Heroes does. Your bar fills up as you play, you get a point, you can spend that point on an ability, like the space magnet which pulls enemy vehicles into space for them never to be seen again. "Ground control to Major Tom..."
- It's fun!
- Graphics aren't bad either!
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Have a great day.

Bought the game for the Momiji and presidential candididate emoticons, stayed for the humor.
This isn't really a game per se; it's more of a simple simulation. You take different famous people, stick them into an arena, and let them brawl to the very finish. You have very little to no input on the match itself, but you set the fighters and the match settings and then let the game begin.
The real beauty of the game isn't in the match itself, but in the Updates Log, where you can monitor the action of all the participants and see what they're doing. An update might be as dramatic as one man spearing another and killing him, or it might be as simple as someone taking a bath. However, the ridiculousness of each update provides the entertainment here. You migt see that a spiteful crow has stolen Beethoven's bread roll, or that Steve Jobs just gouged out Franz Kafka's eye. The combination of silly events and placement of historical figures allows the game to work.
However, if you're not looking for that kind of humor, but instead an actual game, where you can interact with the environment and feel like you are accomplishing something, then this game is probably not for you.

An (almost) direct port of one of the greatest PS1 games.
I'll break this up into three sections:
Overall gameplay:
Final Fantasy 8 continues the trend of the ATB gauge but with a few alterations:
Magic is no longer reliant on MP, but is stocked like an item by drawing it from either draw points hidden around the world, or from enemies.
The 'junctioning' system is an unusual beast:
It requires you to equip a summon (called Guardian Forces or GFs for short.)
Junctioning a GF allows your character to use more commands than just 'attack', such as items, magic, and the 'GF' command that allows you to call upon a junctioned GF to aid you in battle.
Junctioning also allows you to allocate magic to stats.
For instance, you can increase your physical or magical damage by junctioning a fire or thunder spell to that stat.
Weapons aren't purchased or acquired frequently, but require you instead to find weapon magazines which will list parts needed to remodel your current weapon into a more powerful model.
Weapons also allow for more limit breaks for your characters.
Most limit breaks are semi-controlable, allowing you to use certain inputs to boost damage or the like.
Summary- Very enjoyable, but the junctioning and magic drawing system may be daunting to those who aren't used to it.
Story:
You are a student at the military academy - Balamb Garden
Early in the game, you learn of the tyrannical president of the neighbouring region - Galbadia - and his plans for domination and war.
As the story progresses, you find that it goes much deeper than a president gone mad with power, and will fight to save the integrity of the world as you know it.
The main character; Squall, is a steriotypical loner. However, his dullness is counterbalanced by the colourful cast of allies that fight at his side.
Summary- Interesting story, good characters, will get you very engrossed... Until you get stuck and need to go grind, typical of most RPGs.
Port Quality -
If you're like me, and love your old favourite games, you would want them to be just as enjoyable as you remember.
This is where there are a few hitches -
If you've played the game before, the first noticeable difference will be the music quality.
It has been very dulled down from the original PS1 version.
This can be easily fixed with a mod, but shouldn't have been an issue in the first place.
The next is SFX.
For the most part, the SFX is the same, however, much of it has again been stripped and dulled down, most noticeable with the summoning animation of Quezacoatl.
Unfortunately, I can't find a fix for this and have had to just grit my teeth and bear with it.
My final gripe is that even though there is controller support, there is no omni-directional movement, making navigation difficult because you can only move in four different directionss, and the in-game tool-tips don't change their text if you have re-assigned the buttons.
For instance, if you have re-assigned 'B1' and 'B2', the game text will still read what the default setting was.
Summary- Overall port quality is poor.
The graphics and gameplay have remained consistant, but there are many issues.
These wouldn't be such an issue if they weren't so prominant.
Overall, I'd give this a game a 7/10.
It is very, very enjoyable, despite its faults.

Oh Westwood Studios, how I miss you... I was a huge fan of the Red Alert series growing up. My father and I would LAN up against bots in the first game, and I spent so many bloody hours on Red Alert 2. I bought Red Alert 3, excited at the possibilities that awaited me on that shiny new disc. And then I started playing... I didn't know why it was 3D, didn't know why it was so damn cartoony - I didn't even know Westwood had been bought out by EA, I thought Westwood had just changed. Even the soundtrack was over the top, to the point of being goofy. The entire game feels more like a straight-to-DVD movie, or more like a mobile game instead being a part of the Red Alert franchise that it's supposedly attached to.
After half a decade had passed, I saw it was on sale on Steam, and decided to give it another chance. As you can see, I'd only gotten about an hour in before I had to turn it off again. It hasn't changed from what I had remembered. Rather, I wasn't misremembering this game. I'd be extremely hard-pressed to recommend this game, even for $20. I'm not quite sure who the intended audiences for. The art direction is childlike and very cartoon-esque, but as far as I can tell, people who enjoy childlike and cartoony things don't seem to like RTS war games. Nor can I see RTS fans going for a game this slow and exaggerated. I believe there are better games out there for both sets of individuals.

Disclaimer: I was generously given a free copy of Destiny Warriors with the understanding that I was expected to review the title after spending some time with it.

The music is certainly generic but far from the obnoxious noise I’ve had to mute in some other RPG Maker titles I’ve experienced recently. You also receive a rating post-combat that can give you bonus gold and experience which I thought was actually really cool. The interface, however, is difficult to read due to an over use of pastel colors and this also makes figuring out who the active character in combat is.
It works, but it’s one of a million of these RPG Maker excretions. Do yourself a favor: if you like what you visually, go get a copy of Chrono Trigger and give it a playthrough.

I have put almost 500 hours playing Galactic Civilizations III.   Before that, I put a similar number of hours into Galactic Civilizations I and II and their expansions, dating back about 15 years.
If you're looking for a "fair" game, with all the kinks worked out, this is not it.  Galactic Civilization III has got issues, with bugs, the AI, and balance.   While it does technically have multiplayer--not really.  It takes too long to play, and it's too unbalanced.  But what keeps me going back for hours and hours is the exploration.   This is a turn-based space 4X game.  I'm obsessed with numbers, and I'm constantly competing against myself, trying to maximize the numbers in my own favor with whatever new map I get.   It has around 25 different factions you can play, plus the ability to create your own custom factions and to download others'.
What makes the Galactic Civilizations series different is the presence of the developers online, and the game is still evolving even as you play it.   The game is not really a finished product when it first walks out the door, but you get to know the devs' personalities, and they are continually changing and rebalancing the game as it goes along.   The game you play 6 months down the road is not the same game you first bought, but that means you sink more hours playing it; because it's a different game.    It's a living, breathing, changing game, but an imperfect one.    That may not be everyone's cup of tea.  But you won't know if you don't try.

A bit too early for my taste. If someone had made me play this game without telling me the title and then telling me it was called RSI simulator I would believe that.  Everything you build requires at least 3 clicks: Select, select 'version', build. Doing a few floors with different textures: +- 100 clicks.
Anyway: Basically this builds (a little) on the idea of Airport Tycoon, a game where you had an avatar that was running around purchasing items, scheduling flights, etc. This game combines the scheduling with the look and feel of prison architect. So far sounds great.
However in Prison architect you could start small (holding cell) and then there was a lot to learn to progres. In Airport CEO there currently is no progresion. Basically there are GA flights that require basically nothing (no strategic placement whatsoever) and provide you with a basic income. Then there is the upgrade to commercial flights. Now this requires some planning as you need a secure erea, a boarding desk in that area, a checkpoint and exit and a checkin desk. Once you understand that it does not matter if you construct 1 or 5 gates. This is where the real problem lies. Now as a strategy fan you want to start using your airport, hire personel, min/max the balancing and make money.
Soon you will find out that scheduling flights is a nightmare. You have to click your way through at least 20 contracts to find the best ones. Then you need to manually schedule 6-20 flights per contract. This means draggin each flight into a random slot. Again without any strategy. Just spam it. As soon as you schedule in these flights they are locked and cannot be changed. This also means no changes to the relating buildings can be made. Want to move your gate? Too bad. Want to add baggage handling? Too bad. Solution: Press fast forward, make 1.000.000 bucks and the you can continue 'playing'  the game.
The final stage adds baggage handling and larger planes. Whereas prison architect in it's early stage took me about 12 hours to 'master' this took about 3 hours. The other 10 hours I spend on fast forwarding and redesigning my airport (1200 visitors look cool, game slows down though).
Would be improved greatly by changing the whole concept of scheduling. Let some staffer do this and make it more flexible. The focus should be your ever expanding airport. This also means making expansion more expensive and adding more flexibility to change things on the fly.

This was a bit of a watershed moment for the series; hot off the success of its most realistic entry in the series to date, Square moved further toward fantasy - but unlike more recent entries, it kept a healthy dose of fantasy. This game scares many off with its potential for long grinding and its polarizing protagonist (who I love), but I name it one of my favourite RPGs, Final Fantasies, and games in general. The Steam version is as good an opportunity to check it out as any - with subtly refined graphics and no need to swap discs.

Overall, the positives of this game outshine the negatives, but I'll provide all positives, negatives and neutrals anyway.
Positives
-The Story is generally well written, is interesting and has a few unexpected twists
-Characters are developed well and all have a unique and distinct feeling to them
-TWO PLAYTHROUGHS. At the end of Chapter 1 you are given a choice. Side with 1 character or another. This changes how Chapters 2 and 3 are played, what story you experience (albeit the endings are similar, but with different twists).
-Graphics are beautiful
-Atmosphere is perfect
-Difficulty settings. There are multiple, including "dark". This makes the game harder in various ways , but gives you the opportunity to get new items.
-Voice acting
-Game didn't feel too long or short. It hit that spot where it's not so long it feels dragged out or too short where it doesnt feel engaging.
Neutral
-Mature themes. Some will hate this, others will love it.
-Optimisation. Not the greatest, but UBER SAMPLING WILL BURN YOUR PC. I stress this. The setting can lower your framerate dramatically
-Combat. I didn't mind this personally, but I know that others hate it.
Negatives
-Inventory system is poor
-Movement feels a bit clunky.
Overall, the Witcher 2 is a good RPG. Choices matter and the setting feels alive. However, do not be decieved and think that it is an "ARPG". This is NOT dark souls. You don't play this for combat.

Destiny Warriors RPG is a turn-based Adventure RPG game made from RPG Maker. It's a Naruto-inspired game mixed with Dragon Quest and Pokemon concepts. I'm quite a fan of RPG Maker games but this one disappointed me the most for quite a lot of reasons.
Pros:
+ The graphics are okay
+ The game is quite cheap
+ Has trading cards
Cons:
- Dialogues have a lot of typos.
- The story/plot is terrible. (The story is a naruto rip-off)
- Dungeons are poorly-made leading to a very repetitive gameplay. It takes out the player's interest to explore the world (should stick to only one style of dungeon design either random monster encounter or placing actual monsters on the field)
- Bad level up system. (Some characters will be used at the latter part of the game and you get to use them at level 5 when all of your characters are already level 10+. Max also gets stuck at level 15.)
- Battle System is not balanced. (All your characters have high HP but their attacks just won't get strong. The enemies' HP gets higher but their attacks also don't get stronger at all. Having a higher level only shows that you have high HP and MP)
It's hard to make a decent game from RPG Maker that would actually sell because of the lack resources, etc. This game has a lot of potential but seeing the story is nearly similar to Naruto, it actually blew out the whole experience for me. It doesn't mean that if you change some of the terms, it's already a different game especially if it was based on a very well-known game/anime such as Naruto. It's not easy to make a nice and interesting story especially for a game.
Anyway, I don't recommend this game to gamers who have played quite a lot of RPG Maker-made games but if you're a Naruto fan and you don't mind a somewhat retelling of the Naruto story under different names, then you can try this game since it's quite cheap.
Gameplay: 5/10 (very repetitive)
Story: 4/10 (Nearly same plot as Naruto with a slight few modifications)
Music: 6/10
Graphics: 6/10
Overall: 5/10

Where to begin. The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a third person role playing game, where you play as a witcher, Geralt, as you set out to clear your name and find out who framed you for killing the king of temeria. For those who don't know, witchers are monster slayers, and you'll be slaying your fair share of zombies, harpies, gargoyles, and ghosts throughout the game. Anyway, as you play as Geralt, you will be faced with a series of choices of how to resolve problems, and this is where the game gets the most interesting. I'm going to avoid spoilers to anyone who hasn't played the game, but depending on your choices, you can become the linchpin character in a political turmoil between several kingdoms and organizations. That sentence alone probably tells you that the story in this game is rife with deceit, deception, cravings for power, and assassinations.
That aside, i'll briefly talk about the the game's core mechanics. Being a third person rpg, it plays similar to two worlds, except it is much more crisp an polished in nearly every aspect. The combat consists of you using a magic spell tied to a stamina meter, a trap/throwing dagger of some kind, and your trusty sword. The sword, being the weapon used 80% of the time, has light and heavy attacks, so the combat often involves using magic to disrupt your opponents and then rolling around to find an opening in their defense before either hammering them with a combo of light attacks or a heavy attack and cycling it around. Once you get the hang of it and know how to build your character, it becomes very reasonable to take on 5+ enemies at a time, but initally the combat system is a little overwhelming and can be difficult to wrap your head around. sometimes it seems like the enemies always have their guard up, or you can't escape their comboes (one of the best skills in this game is the fancy footwork skill in swordsmanship), but this all naturally comes with time. Alchemy and crafting serve as pretty large parts of this game, but it is also completely feasable to do without them. I personally only used crafting at the beginning of each chapter to gear up for the rest of the chapter, and that was it. I made about 5 potions or so in my nearly 40 hours of gameplay, because i was lazy and it seemed like a hassle. Given, if you want to have an easier time with the game, it will definitely benefit you to take advantage of both of these options.
The only things i think this game can be improved upon is possibly the pacing at certain parts, such as long walking/running sequences or little things like animations taking too long and maybe the save/load system (it can be punishing to die as you'll have to go all the way to the last save instead of having a checkpoint system, which makes the player save nearly every 5 seconds for fear of slipping up in combat and being sent back 10 minutes). These are very minor gripes, but if you are willing to stick with the game, it can be an extremely rewarding experience as your truly feel like you influence the world (enough for me to go and make a second playthruogh and have an entirely different experience). Overall, i'd probably have to give this game a 9/10 for perfecting the role playing experience and having done a wonderful job at world building, amongst other things.

Very nice!  Strikes a good balance between complexity and depth. Leaves open a lot of possibilities and variety in gameplay styles without making you feel like you're running a min/max spreadsheet empire. The UI is also quite friendly and approachable, maybe not perfect, but generally pretty darn good.

First of all, pay attention to the rhythm tag. If you don't have good rhythm, you're probably going to suck at this game, because barring certain exceptions there is no other way for either you or your enemies to move and attack--and your enemies aren't relying on you to keep the beat.
If you find yourself blessed with a sense of rhythm, that's where the real challenges begin. First, you have to memorize the attack patterns of every type of monster you come up against, of which there are a respectable variety. Then you have to unlock additional weapons, armor, and other useful things, and you have to memorize what they all do so you can make the most of the random selection each level of each zone provides you with. You can generally only equip one of each item and up to two spells at a time, so no picking and choosing from a curated arsenal, and then each level has a time limit marked only by the duration of the song you're stuck moving to. If you failed to defeat the mini-boss before the song ended, have fun fighting it and a few minions in a small, enclosed space!
All of this is going to sound horrible to a lot of people, but if you can accept the inevitability of your repeated demise, I've found it to be fun and focusing. You get diamonds to spend between runs, which provides tangible short-term goals to keep you going on the path towards clearing all four zones, and the random generation of levels keeps things from becoming the wrong kind of repetitive. You can even be killed by the shopkeeper!
This isn't a game for everybody, but if you like working hard for your victories, catchy tunes, and having a selection of both male and female characters to play, I highly recommend giving it a shot.

Ys VI is a pretty great game.  Being the first-made of the 3d Ys games, it's a bit rough around the edges and doesn't quite match up with Felghana or Origin, but is still a great game overall, and I highly recommend it.  As with other Ys games, the music is amazing, the story is quite good and builds upon the lore from previous entries, and the gameplay is top notch.  That said, there are a few annoyances with this game that set it below the other titles.  First off, as the first 3d game, Falcom decided to include critical hits and status effects like a traditional RPG, which is something I don't feel works out too well for Ys.  Crits add an extra luck element that can either make bosses easier if you're lucky, or destroy you if you take a crit yourself.  Enemies with status effects also just feel like more of an annoyance than anything.  Another mechanic that exists in this game, which many people find to be a nuisance due to the control scheme, is the dash attack (where you tap and release in the direction you're facing and then attack) and dash-jump attack (where jump is pressed just after attack on a dash-attack).  Personally I really enjoyed this mechanic, using dash-jump as a means to travel more quickly or evade attacks, though it does take a little getting used to.  Overall, I'd say if you like Ys games or action RPGs, then this is a fantastic game and definitely worth getting, but if you're limited on money, then grab Oath in Felghana or Origin first.
