Disappointing.  Unoriginal.  Boring.
I own every Paradox Game and am familiar with their DLC practices.  Whatever.
What bugs me about this, is it's absolutely unpolished and unfinished.
It has a good start, I was enjoying it for awhile, but after about 25 hours you start to realise there's not much to do.  It really is deceiving that way, because as you're starting out it seems fun, until you start to hit your head against the numerous shortcomings.
The diplomacy is terrible.  I think it's the worst set of diplomacy options I've ever seen.  It's yards backward from EU, which wasn't the best to begin with.  I had high expectations for this, given the federations and so forth, but it's actually a frustrating mess.
For example, trading is very abstract.  As such, there's no trade fleets or trade routes that can be plundered.  There's no diplomatic option to allow people non-hostile access into your borders.  The only way to explore, once contained, is to declare war or go full alliance.
There's no espionage options whatsoever.  While interesting events with the minor species, where you can replace and subvert their population - similar things do not exist for the major players.  There's no meddling with other factions or anything interesting like that.
The AI is pathetic, rudamentary and oft times non-existant.  You can send fleets to their outer-most planets and they just let them fall.  No attempt to save anything or split their forces to deal with you, rather, just one giant doom stack and that's it.
Combat is also boring and not very original.  It makes use of doomstacks.  Once you have a doomstack you fight your opponent's doomstack and there you go.  Whomever wins that, wins.  There's no recovering from it and meh.  It's as unimpressive as it sounds.
Landing troops on planets is very simple.  You just bomb them until there's not much left, which isn't difficult at all.  There's no downside to doing that, other than a few planetary buildings/population might be diminished.  But you can change your bombing options to reduce that and it just makes the "siege" take a bit longer.
Then you land your ground troops and a very uneventful and uninspiring battle occurs, which I've always won .  In fact, my unanimous victories are not because I'm skilled, but because it's so easy and the AI is so terrible.  I'm normally quite dreadful at these games and I enjoy the challenge.
Everything here has the veneer of being fun, but when you look underneath, it's just a pretty package with something ordinary inside.
Yes, Paradox will overwhelm with DLC that will cost a few pounds in the future; however, the features lacking here are quite significant and I am not hopeful they will be properly introduced with DLC.
Was a bit of a rip off buying this now, to be honest.

* The fact, you can play DLC content if your server has the DLC, and you are not left out of game mechanics changes without it, but only events if you host a game, makes such DLCs top amongst games like this. No "Pre-Order-Exclusive Content" shenanigans, no "You don't have the DLC so you cant play in this lobby" stuff. Made me buy the DLC right after release just to know, I can still play with those who will not buy it right away! Civ, look at this.
* Networking. For the most part (occasional bugs and desyncs - which seem to be fixed fast), this game is built around the idea of network gaming.
* It's real time. It feels like round based. But it's not. So all that sweet planning, but still enough opportunity for fast action.
* Workshop: mods are multiplayer ready. And some of them add awesome additional balancing, which shifts the game away from the vanilla competitiveness.
* Min-Maxer barriers in the mechanics. Research could need more depth, but some mods take care of that - however, the card rules for how the research system works are awesome, for those who are more creative and do not just play the fastest minmax strategy from start to end. But you still can, limiting you to going the warfare route. This is how it should be.
* The style. Pseudorealistic sun systems, eve like overview map, funny stories, this game is so much at the core of what makes space games great, its astonishing. I love it, because a lot of details are very well researched, and some events hint that a lot of thought and research is behind the game. It is good, if sci-fi games are made by people actually interested in space science.
* Straight out of the box presets. This game, you got presets en masse. GalCiv3 may only beat it with its ship designer, but even there, they updated visual differences.
* When you have that desync, that never goes away trashing your savegame of 7 days consecutive teamplay.
* I whish there were also more presets for fleet styles and some influence on the battle - even if only through delayed ability switches. Again, some mods take care of that.
* Techs in vanilla were a bit too linear, they still are somewhat, but it has improved. Having a straight tech for gameplay, and some side techs for specialization is still I think improvable.
* I miss tradestations. I miss cloak. I miss more finetuned local diplomacy. Finishing a small research quest by brokering a deal for one science ship to enter some space - or similar - diplomacy could be more. It has been improved in Heinlein, but I still miss short term options. Most of the diplomacy only affects the permanent karma levels between empires. AI could need emotional relations (afraid, annoyed, interested, etc.), to achieve more local goals.
Btw. judging from the assets, cloak was indeed part of the development...
* I miss a bit of neutral zones, when all empires have their borders, space kind of feels small then. Hyperspace gets boxed in. More interaction, like even trading pops, or shared star systems, maybe border stations which hold only _one_ star in your territorry, to finely define friendly borders. And maybe artificial hyperlanes and jump gates for alliances. I still wait to the day I can build Babylon 5 embassy station and invite major civs to send their representatives... :P
* I miss the persistent after thought: the engine itself would be ideal to work on the first mmo-like 4x strategy game, with more persistant homeworlds fighting for distant galaxies.
* Game lobby is awesome, but it could need improvement, so that you can truly find games, which are still waiting in lobby, and waiting for players. I find, people are not making big enough games for this game most of the time. And there is no info which mods run.

A brilliant 4X space strategy with unrivaled depth. This game is essentially the love child of Sins of a Solar Empire and the Civilisation series. I don't personally consider myself a pro at grand strategy but THIS IS THE STRATEGY GAME I'VE BEEN WAITING FOR.
Pros:
+Huge, content filled maps.
+Challenging random events.
+Really captures the four Xs perfectly. You truly feel like space Christopher Columbus sending your science ships out to explore the void for the first time. Expanding your empire into the galaxy is so satisfying and also necessary to exploit the vast riches out there. The war system is amazing with its victory conditions. You don't necessarily have to invade a planet to take control of it. Just go and exterminate the enemy and force them to submit to your will.
+Responsive friendly AI - your alliances are actually beneficial in this game! Go forth and crush your enemy, and your friends will race to your aid.
+Aggressive enemy AI - just had war declared on you? Need to build your fleet up? Well bad news, the enemy isn't going to wait around.
+Sector system makes micro-management much less tedious than Sins.
+Can customise your ships to suit your preferred combat style.
+Gorgeous graphics as far as a strategy game goes.
+Like any grand strategy game should be, you will not finish a game on a large map in under a week.
+MOD SUPPORT
Cons:
-Minor bugs in places, particularly with some sound effects.
-Random options research system is a bit annoying for trying to colonise certain planets, you essentially roll a dice on what research you can do each iteration and choose from three options.
-Music is a little repetitive after a while, considering how long games take.
-Getting your construction ships to build on all resource spots is really tedious - I wish sectored systems would get stations built automatically over time.
-Leader deaths can be frustrating. It would help if it came up with a window asking if you want to assign a new leader to the deceased one's role, instead of having to do this manually.
-Would be useful if you could reallocate excess food to a planet that needs it more.
-No pretty trade convoys going between your planets.
-Combat isnt hugely tactical for the tacticians out there. Essentially just "strongest fleet wins". However you can overcome a stronger fleet with well-equipped ships.
BUY THIS GAME THOUGH HOLY SH*T.

It’s tempting to be brutal to ABZÛ, since it is so unrelentingly stripmall zentimental. It’s got the same motivational poster sheen as Flower and Journey, themselves mawkish little shrines to the power and beauty of positive thinking propped up with some ecobabble no doubt mined from temples deep in the valleys of mount whateverest.
The whole Thing feels like a production process and a few idée fixes, in this case inherited from notable Csikszentmihalyi-interpreter and spiritainment entrepreneur Jenova Chen. The only thing about ABZÛ that resembles art is its craft and self-importance. Unfortunately, this is a high standard for videogames to reach, so I am going to have to be nice.
ABZÛ is vaguely touching. It is very pretty. Its craft is immaculate if unambitious, and faulting it for being so goddamn Hallmark actually feels cheap and bitter, like missing the point on purpose and expecting it to be something it’s not. Even if it has a Press X to Meditate prompt and awarded me an achievement for riding a breaching whale in heaven.
Formally, ABZÛ is a cod-spiritual walking simulator with six degrees of freedom. It carries you between spectacularly decorated oases of colour and life on rollercoaster current channels, eagerly displaying its mishmash of fish, triforces, hieroglyphic lampshading and Moorish architecture. There are trappings of traditional videogame structure with progress gating and secrets, but the emphasis is on immersion over activity -- though the balance is uneven.
Cutesy minisub companions get introduced and tied to progress, then Giant Squid seems to change its mind -- first the minisub economy collapses, before unceremoniously vanishing without a trace in the second act. Fortunately, ABZÛ has a moment of clarity about midway through and remembers its mantra: I’m a swimming game. I’m a swimming game. I’m a swimming game.
It’s a swimming game. You swim and watch little softbody art deco fish school, drift and dart around. Swimming feels nothing short of splendid. Giant Squid’s water is nice, viscous and propagates motion interestingly and satisfyingly. Makes you notice how many games struggle to make movement anything more than rote traversal, revealing how locomotion is not just a hard problem but a matter of taste. Ideals.
Giant Squid executes both character and camera controls effortlessly. Moving and shaking around ABZÛ is pure videogame. It’s not punchy and visceral like Doom or exhilaratingly tense like Outrun, but it’s got that 24 carat heart of gold emblazoned with LUDUS GRATIA LUDEM.
Unfortunately, ABZÛ doesn’t trust itself to be sublime. It wants wavy, semi-transparent Hollywood spirituality. It wants not one, two or three but MANY cetacean money shots. It wants whale song. It wants moody strings too. But it needs none of these things.
ABZÛ only needs its final twist, a fine and understated realization of the expressive potential of videogames as not just vehicles for narration and spectacle, but as sensual experience. A second locomotion model, sparingly utilized, only there to remind you how ABZÛ is different and how a little difference goes a long way.

ABZU is undoubtly beautiful and highly atmospheric but that's where it stops. I would not recommend it as a game because it is more like an art exhibit. The story is way too short and linear, the amount of space you could move in is very limited, there is no danger or fear of death, the fish species sometimes do not interact with the player's movements... Pro:
Beautiful scenery, beautiful atmosphere, beautiful concept, great mix of fantasy, sci-fi, and mythology.
Some parts of the experience bring true joy and a sense of freedom.
Very good rendering of fish movement (but cannot compare with real ocean).
Con:
The game is way too short (~2h) and it not interesting enough to replay.
Story is linear and player can only move in a small defined space in each chapter.
I feel that some of the story elements (e.g. triangle factory, ancient people living with fish) are not fully explored by the game.
PC controls need a little improvement, I have trouble swimming to the direction I want and it often takes several seconds to adjust. Perhaps related to the control: I tend to get motion sickness easily from this game.

Where to begin. The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a third person role playing game, where you play as a witcher, Geralt, as you set out to clear your name and find out who framed you for killing the king of temeria. For those who don't know, witchers are monster slayers, and you'll be slaying your fair share of zombies, harpies, gargoyles, and ghosts throughout the game. Anyway, as you play as Geralt, you will be faced with a series of choices of how to resolve problems, and this is where the game gets the most interesting. I'm going to avoid spoilers to anyone who hasn't played the game, but depending on your choices, you can become the linchpin character in a political turmoil between several kingdoms and organizations. That sentence alone probably tells you that the story in this game is rife with deceit, deception, cravings for power, and assassinations.
That aside, i'll briefly talk about the the game's core mechanics. Being a third person rpg, it plays similar to two worlds, except it is much more crisp an polished in nearly every aspect. The combat consists of you using a magic spell tied to a stamina meter, a trap/throwing dagger of some kind, and your trusty sword. The sword, being the weapon used 80% of the time, has light and heavy attacks, so the combat often involves using magic to disrupt your opponents and then rolling around to find an opening in their defense before either hammering them with a combo of light attacks or a heavy attack and cycling it around. Once you get the hang of it and know how to build your character, it becomes very reasonable to take on 5+ enemies at a time, but initally the combat system is a little overwhelming and can be difficult to wrap your head around. sometimes it seems like the enemies always have their guard up, or you can't escape their comboes (one of the best skills in this game is the fancy footwork skill in swordsmanship), but this all naturally comes with time. Alchemy and crafting serve as pretty large parts of this game, but it is also completely feasable to do without them. I personally only used crafting at the beginning of each chapter to gear up for the rest of the chapter, and that was it. I made about 5 potions or so in my nearly 40 hours of gameplay, because i was lazy and it seemed like a hassle. Given, if you want to have an easier time with the game, it will definitely benefit you to take advantage of both of these options.
The only things i think this game can be improved upon is possibly the pacing at certain parts, such as long walking/running sequences or little things like animations taking too long and maybe the save/load system (it can be punishing to die as you'll have to go all the way to the last save instead of having a checkpoint system, which makes the player save nearly every 5 seconds for fear of slipping up in combat and being sent back 10 minutes). These are very minor gripes, but if you are willing to stick with the game, it can be an extremely rewarding experience as your truly feel like you influence the world (enough for me to go and make a second playthruogh and have an entirely different experience). Overall, i'd probably have to give this game a 9/10 for perfecting the role playing experience and having done a wonderful job at world building, amongst other things.

Stellaris is a real time empire builder, that seems to focus heavily on exploration. All kinds of fun stuff has happened to me so far, from finding extinct races ruins, on various planets to wild indiginous native xenos whom you can accelerate their growth, and make them a space faring vassal state, to having asteroids threaten my planets and require destruction of the asteroid. It really hits that spot of "I want to see just one more star system", perfectly.
Also, I really like the Sector generation. You can create sectors, (and infact you are encouraged to do so to avoid being penalized) within your empire to take the load off of you, and into the AI's hands. The AI can be altered, in their focus, as well as microd later as necessary, and is a welcome touch to the game to keep you focused on the unknown, rather than being dragged down into minutia.
The faction creator, is fun and easy to use, though maybe it's lacking a bit of depth compared to some other titles in the genre, and the same with the ship creator.
That being said, it's enough to be solid, give some variety in gameplay and quick enough to get you playing without pining for an hour each faction made.
I've hundreds of hours into 4x space games like Endless Space, Gal Civ3 etc, and this holds up.
Highly recommend.
The cons: There are some minor bugs, and issues that crop up from time to time. Like how you can't undo a change BEFORE confirming sector creation, for adding planets to sectors, without it costing you influence points.
Race and ship creation is a little shallow.

So, I just kinda nominated Dust for the "Woaaaaaaaaahhhhhhh, Dude" Award for December 2016 and because I never really told a lot of people what got me into the game and why I "only" got 24 hours or so here's a Review so I'll be finally free of this (not really existing) torture of questioning.
[TBH I was actually only questined one time, but please! I need a god damn story to make the Review interesting. Sooooo this totally never happend, mkay. YOU HAVEN'T SEEN A THING!!!]
Dust: An Elysian Tail is in my opinion one hell of a game. The 24 hours of playtime I've got are more or less from one sitting where I played through every Side Quest and the Main Quest right to the final boss (and stoped then, because I was literally playing for 19 hours straight). As you might can guess from that statement this game got me real good. I'm in love with the whole universe the game is creating.
But how did I get into this masterpiece of a game?
Actually I didn't really... I only bought it in the last Summer Sale, because it was every other day on my recommended list and I never really knew anything about it more than it's named Dust. And then one day I thought, f**k it, and bought the game with the last money on my steam-Acc and never regretted it.
But what is Dust?
Dust is a 2D-Sidescrolling "Beat'Em'Up" with some elements of Hack'n'Slay Titles. You're fighting with a magical sword which name I kinda forgot atm (Shame might fall upon me xD) and with your magical and totally not satirical Sidekick Fidget, A Nimbat (Please don't ask me what exactly a Nimbat is... Because I couldn't explain it ^^" ).
Throughout the game you'll get some upgrades for your Armor, Attack, Health, etc. through grinding and/or buying/building stuff that looks nice in the ingame menu, and from a certain point onwards they're kinda needed if you're not perfect with every little attack you'll use.
But this is with the genre not really a new thing to bring to the table.
In general Dust not really goes out of it's way to try the new ultimate Upgrade of Game-Controls n stuff but rather keeps it simple and on the line one might've already played. But the Gameplay and (to a certain degree) the story didn't really keep me going, but rather the Characters (that are all totally awesome, especially Fidget. I love the Sidekick that comments on a lot of things you'll do, always with a grain of Satire and Ironie. Just the best!) and the Art.
As I don't want to spoil anything from the story I'll keep shut about the characters but the Art... You're seeing that? IT'S FREAKING MARVELOUS!!! I'll just keep add with saying what most probably know, but Dust was (more or less) created by one individual (minus Voice Acting and Music if I' not completly mistaken ^^") and for that the Art is just beautiful. That's something I could put on my wall and be like, yep, that was worth it!
Not one design really stood out as being created with less interest than the others, I was kinda blown away when I saw everything ingame!
But, because I know not everyone has the time to read through my ramble on stuff that aren't technical and aren't about distinct parts of the game I'll end it hear with a short and sweet Too long; didn't read.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is a wonderful game with a really creative mind behind it. The Gameplay is like it should be and the Art and OST are ingenious. The Story though a bit cliché at some points is through it all interesting and even the Side-Quests are made so you want to go out of your way to Clear them.
While I personally found the VAs perfect for their characters some might come off as a bit ennerving (especially the Sidekick Fidget) as they'll talk through quite a lot of Cutscenes.
All in all I would recommend this game to more or less everybody. While some might find the Gameplay addicting, others will find their joy in the story and others will just look up R34 and will be happy with their lives.
So buy this definitely, when it's on a Sale! When it's Full Price it's still it's money worth (I would argue even more) but I can see why some would be turned off. 14$ isn't much but like a wise guy (probably) said: Even the Pence will be a dollar in times of need...
[Nope that last sentence is totally by me, a wise guy wouldn't have spoken about worldly topics :3)
And with that I wish all of you whom reading this a beautiful day or night and I hope I've helped you in your decision.

This game is glitchy. It is really unoptimized with many framerate drops regardless of how good your PC is. It has a mixed history that includes quite some controversy over changing their name to avoid a terrible metacritic score. It was described as one of the absolute worst games of all time. All but the last are true.
The game itself is buggy and absolutely unoptimized. It is also extremely fun, with a very large variety of weapons and quite a few different enemy dinos to take down.  The special weapons were particularly fun. It makes for a great game to jump in and shoot some dinos with friends, or even just alone. Throw up max money, buy all the cool weapons and just wreck the dino horde.
Is it the greatest game of all time? No, but it is far better than everyone made it out to be. When it was $15 this would've been a negative review due to the poor performance and that things just don't work right a good chunk of the time. But now that it's a dollar, and a 4-pack can be had for $3 (prices as of writing) it is a hearty recommendation instead. Think of it this way: A cup of coffee, an energy drink, or 4 copies of this game for yourself and friends to play. It'll provide a minimum of a few hours of entertainment, either through actual fun with the game or purposefully trying to break it and make silly things happen.

Final Fantasy VIII is my all time favorite RPG. Why? Because it's one of the first video games I ever got into, so naturally I have some sentimental value. That being said, I'll give as unbiased of a review as I can on this game.
Story
The story of Final Fantasy VIII is somewhat strange and can be hard to follow at times, but, it's Final Fantasy. I wouldn't consider any of the games normal story wise. I find the characters to be very individual and personable. While Squall does start out as somewhat cynical and brooding, you, as the player, slowly watches him grow and develop into a new person in a very natural way. Not to mention he has one of the most badass weapons ever created, though it's nowhere near as interesting as Selphie's comically large nunchaku that everyone is just kind of okay with.
Gameplay
A lot of people gripe about the system in VIII. Truth is, you aren't understanding it. If you think you have to sit for hours and draw magic from random monsters, you aren't playing the game right. Learn the system inside and out and you can make absolutely insane characters. I tested just how strong you could go, and ended up soloing most of the game with Selphie. More so, the battle system is fun, and a little bit more interactive than just hitting Attack over and over again. The GF's (Summons) are powerful, and completely infinite use, and the center of the whole system. While the animations for the GF's can be somewhat long, if that doesn't bug you, it can make for pretty epic battles visually, with respects to when the game came out. Magic works like Ammo, with no MP system, and you can obtain more through various ways. There are a lot of extra abilities you can learn as well, which can help specialize each character.
Visuals
Again, it's a PSOne game, and while the character models recieved a nice upgrade, the field took a pretty serious hit. I honestly have no idea why they couldn't upgrade everything on a PC but I'm not gonna complain too much. The art of the world is very sci fi and quite beautiful in my opinion. There is a lot of realism, which both characters and field. While a bit futuristic, it's very believable to see these towns as places that could actually exist (barring Esthar).
Audio
Unfortunately, all the music in the PC version of this game is in the MIDI format. It's not nearly as good as the original soundtrack, but if you can get over that hump, it's still the same music, just crappier quality. There are ways to patch it if you really want to, but it doesn't bug me enough to want to change it. Oddly enough about 90% of the sound effects stayed the same. There are some minor differences, most notable in Quezacotl's summon sequence, but for the most part, they are all the same. Force Your Way will forever be my single most loved video game song ever.
Bugs
So far, I haven't encountered any serious bugs. If you tab out of the game, sometimes all of the music will stop playing, which is weird. Incredibly weird. Final Fantasy VIII with no music makes for an odd and awkward experience. Everything just kind of feels... empty.
Overall
I would highly recommend this game to anyone really. Hell, I bought this game for a good chunk of people for the holidays. If you are an RPG fan, give this a shot. It might just be your next favorite.

- - - - -THE SHORT REVIEW PART - - - - -
Don't write off the classic DOOMs as obsolete, there is still plenty of fun to be had here! I'm sure you've heard or seen that enough times, though.
If you want to run around abstract playgrounds of destruction with a double barrel shotgun, this is the DOOM for you; if you want a more refined experience with SOME semblance of progressive level design and story, get DOOM 1.
Better yet, just get them both and play them sequentially!... Not that story is really super important or anything, but they're both good games, and it's worth playing both just to appreciate the differences between them.
- - - - -EXTRA THOUGHTS ON AESTHETIC- - - - -
Have you ever seen or heard something and thought that the planets and stars must have aligned to create it "just so"? I think that you see that in a lot of old games.
As far as DOOM and DOOM II go, I think this applies especially to the aesthetics of it all. Graphics capabilities at the time weren't so primitive that all the 2 dimensional art assets+enemy designs had to be over-simplified or cartoonishly stylized to make up for lack of detail, but rendering everything in 3D wasn't an option either. As you see in Quake and a lot of other early 3D titles, early 3D also had to be very simplified or stylized to work out well.
Doom kind of came out in the perfect way and at the perfect time, as it got to avoid being hindered by some of the graphical limitations on either chronological side of it while also getting to avoid more methodical conventions of development that you see in most games today.
DOOM appears to have strove for realism (at least as much as was possible then), and because iD software was iD software and the video game industry wasn't as cut and dried back then, DOOM got to be this kind of mishmash of whatever the hell the developers wanted it to be, pun intended.
You have shiny cyber-techno-future stuff mixed with old cliche satanic/spooky stuff in space as your setting, with big guns (both the fancy sci-fi and the good ol' conventional lead spewing kind), a chainsaw, and a spiked fist as your arsenal. You take this arsenal, and across this setting, you fight zombies and weird shiny-metal-augmented cyber fiends that are simply
, even as they appear alongside more classical and more obviously hellish demons, and then you have a coating of semi-realism brushed over everything to top it off.
The end result is something that just couldn't exist today.
-The limited brand of realism employed here that gets baked into every sprite (some of which were photos of models that were modified) and makes everything pop and look crisp, which really winds up becoming its own style in a sense, couldn't exist as a result of today's standard, calculated real time rendering of shaders and stuff. Even though everything that goes into todays rendering is miles more advanced and certainly was more amazing when it first came out, now its just an expected feature of everything; the coolness has worn off to be kind of unimpressive and bland in many circumstances
-The year is 2017. All big shooter games are no longer allowed to have colors in them
-The classicly hellish demons and their accompanying spooky hell aesthetic just really don't get much love anymore, do they?
-The mishmash of sci-fi and cyborg stuff alongside marbley, gothicy, candley, pentagramy, spooky hell stuff, and then mixed with sawed off shotguns and miniguns, couldn't come out of any big developer now, partly as a result of the earlier mentioned bland realism; everything has to be unimaginatively logical, so as to be palettable and consistent with everything else in the stream of industrial games that get put out by big developers. The exception to some of this is DOOM 2016, but even as it tries to emulate the original games, the demons are part of that organic, alieny kind of design thats standard fare in a lot of things these days. It really would've ruled to see Ye Olde Hooved Goat Man Demon and friends straight off of old cautionary depictions of paganism running around in DOOM 2016 just like in the classics
But rejoice, because the classic DOOM games are still around, and still kitchen ace!
(Oh, the largely
soundtrack still kicks ace too. Sorry DOOM 2016, you're beat there)

Now, I don't play a lot of horror games, mainly because most are just jumpscares and mindless wandering. This game does horror perfectly. When it gets scary, it is the atmosphereic creepiness, a bit of mental horror, and just overall dread, not relying too much on jumpscares. At times, when the creepy stuff happened, I have begged for combat.
Overall, this is a great game, it has a good plot, things that you can search for, and fun gameplay. You can run it on a decent computer too. I would reccomend this game to anyone, if they can handle it...

It looks like I have a lot of hours on this game, but that's deceptive. I keep my computer on 24/7 so my actual hours are probably 15% of those indicated.
That said, the patches and Crusade DLC are pointing this game in the right direction and it gets better with each iteration. For that reason, I can recommend it, especially when it's on sale. Still, GC3 is not perfect.
The issues I have with it primarily relate to the AI. The AI does these things wrong, among others:
1. It does a lousy job of claiming relics and exploring anomalies. In GalCiv2, the AI was extremely competitive in claiming relics and scooping up anomalies. In GC3, these elements offer a distinct advantage for the player as AI civilizations will claim only a couple of relics each at the maximum and they don't seem to touch anomalies at all.
2. AI fleets are slow and quite easy to beat with better speed, logistics (i.e. stacking) and sensor range. You can be way behind overall in tech (as you will early on at difficult settings), but as long as you focus on those three techs you can win battles. You can enter a war being outnumbered 50:1 and still win by defeating enemy fleets in detail as they plod toward your territory or stay tied to planetary or starbase defense.
3. With Crusade, you now have administrators, a finite resource, which is a great concept in general coupled with Citizens. This is a positive development, as you burn an administrator for each colony or starbase, thereby forcing you to make strategic decisions on how they are used. Where this goes wrong is in civ traits. There's a trait which allows you to colonize without burning an administrator. If your civ has this trait (I forgot what the trait is called), you'll end up being able to colonize far more planets than the other civs, which is important on a big map, less so on a small map.
Now, a player can obviate the above issues in the game set-up phase by: 1) drastically limiting or removing anomalies and relics entirely; 2) picking a smaller map size, thereby ensuring earlier enemy encounters; and 3) choosing or creating a civ that can't colonize without using administrators.
Hence, I can still recommend this game as you can compensate for a lot of the AI's faults. If Stardock is reading this, I do hope you address some of the issues mentioned.

GC3 is big robust space empire strategy game. Unlike some other modern games it's relatively conservative. The focus in on economical development and diplomacy; war is simplified and is mostly a continuation of diplomacy and economy. There's a very complex spaceship constructor but you may use autotemplates or just quickly fill ships with desirable component; or you can create your own ships with distinct look and loadout.
The base game is underwhelming. It feels sterile and more like a math puzzle than a strategy game. There was a big problem with micromanagement and lack of interesting choices.
However after patches and especially with Crusades expansion it's a completely another game now. There's little micromanagement and economy and internal politics come alive. You need various resources and this creates the need for diplomacy and way, space map becomes varied and interesting. You have special Citizens used to focus on specific tasks in economy, military or espionage. There's lots of freedom now and it feels like an interesting sandbox with decent AI. Updates make the game better and better and it's quite possible in the future we will recommend GC3 as the default empire building game you should try the way we refer to Civilization 4/5 now. It's much more economy focused now compared to other similar games - planet improvement is a complex affair and you have to mine space for resources. There's also underused morality system adding some twists to the empire management through events and forging end-game alignment-based coalitions. Tech tree suffers a little from boring technologies: there's a lot of "improved trade" or "Laser 2" techs. But at least there are many unique race-specific techs and depending on factions even basic planetary buildings are different. Combat-wise it all look more or less the same though: you chose your weapon focus and build ships as big as your tech allows, send them as far as the tech allows, unite them in fleets as big as the tech allows. There are also mercenary ships (added in Mercenaries DLC) providing some special bonuses both to fleets and planets, and you can assign commanders to give your fleets bonuses. The combat is automated, you only decide what your fleet consists of and who you fight, so no military micromanagement.
The game features some solo missions and story you won't probably care about. It's all very Star Trek-styled, the atmosphere is optimistic epic space opera. May feel a little complex but this means the skill cap is high. Devs are also proud of the engine which, in theory, supports huge maps and dozens of empires. Nice and simple faction creator is included, you can even set focuses for AI in it which adds to the personality.

Playing with the Crusade expansion. The expansion does several nice things to the base game. A few good improvements including citizens. Removing the economy control wheel was a very good decision.
My earlier review listed a few examples of the AI being very poor. Good news! WIth version 2.6, those  specific AI issues have been fixed. The AI now forms large fleets and will capture defended planets. The AI will also build starbases. However, seems the AI doesn't know how to survey anomolies.
Oeverall, the AI expands well in the early game. After a while it stalls out. Played 10 hours till turn 146 on a huge map with 12 gifted opponents. There are still a small number of uncolonized planets. My large size, ships are going speed 9 or 10. The AI ships are going at most speed 5 and are usually medium size or smaller.
Good AI is obviously of key importance for a 4x game. Why are the AI empires not progressing? It is difficult to manage food/pop. Its difficult to produce a steady supply of administrators. Its even more difficult to produce a planet with excellent research or manufactoring production. Lots of stuff to juggle.
There are also a huge number of techs to research. Believe that the AI is failing to prioritize increase of their research production. While I can puzzle out the most beneficial techs in the tree, doubt the AI can.
So version 2.6 is an improvement. However, I'm still leaving a negative review. I find that after a hundred plus turns the game becomes tedious and bland. The AI (gifted difficulty where its cheats are not insane) is not a steady challenge. No challenge and the great amount of tedium involved in playing well becomes painful.
What in the game involves a great deal of tedium? Micro managing exploration. Managing your planet builds. Managing your ship designs. Surveying anomalies. You could let the computer manage these things for you but it does so poorly. Suggest playing on the smaller maps to minimize a lot of the repetition needed.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is an action platformer game with one runner "minigame" in one of the area. This game features Dust, a man with no memories of his past life, whom meet a talking sword and a flying animal called nimbat. This game has Metroid like minimap with several connecting areas in a map. There are also a world map in addition of the area map. There are 5 chapters in total and in each chapter you will learn more techniques in order to be able to travel to more places.
This game is using a blend of 2D and 3D models with a beautifully drawn background. I love how the particles glow in the area and the lighting which made the map to look more beautiful. I also love how the dialogue animates and how the character's mouth are moving when they're talking. The character potraits look like an old child cartoon movies and has an oddly shaped head, however.
There are some anime styled short cutscenes in some areas and i think that they are very neat, although it still can be improved.
As for the UI, i can't really say much except that it is looks very pleasant, although there are some UI bugs which are related to alt tabbing, such as the mouse pointer which will be gone when you do alt tab after you open the menu.
The musics sound very pleasant in the ear. I never get tired after listening it for a long time. Honestly, i am impressed with a lot of voiceovers in this game because all dialogues in the game are dubbed, and this includes the moving character mouth i specified in the previous section before.
Firstly, i want to say that you can choose difficulty in this game. There are 4 different difficulties to choose from and you can change it mid game. I don't know what's different in each difficulty because i only played in one difficulty, but they said that the enemies will have more HP and attack and has a better AI. I myself find Tough difficulty to be not really difficult as long as you have enough HP before attacking the enemies.
Speaking of enemies, there are a lot of enemies variation in this game. The enemies are unique in each chapters and by unique, i mean that they have different attack patterns and sometimes require a different approach to beat. You will be briefed when you encounter one of them prior to Chapter 3, but there will be no guide on how to beat them after that. I have trouble in killing a summoner in a map before and it took me a lot of retries until i get used to kill it. I never had any problem defeating other enemies every since (except the red skinned guy with a blade in the same map).
There are 4 boss in the game in total, although i won't say that they are  difficult. The first boss can be killed in two combos in tough difficulty and you actually can kill the boss without losing any health in the process as long as you know  its attack pattern (there are only 1-2 attack patterns in total). They also don't have a lot of HP (except the final boss). Honestly, i feel like killing the summoner and the "red skinned guy with a blade" in a row to be harder than the boss.
This game has a semi automatic hitting system, meaning that your character will auto target its enemies at close range as long as you are in combo. You also can change the direction of his attack with left and right. Speaking of combos, there are some combos that you can use to kill the enemies, with one ultimate attack called Dust Storm which will be your main weapon. This Dust Storm can be "imbued" with magic to make it stronger. The magic will be using stamina which will recover periodically and (or) by hitting enemies. The same stamina will be used for dashing which can be done with Q (dash to the left) and E (dash to the right) by default. The dash, although can't be used to hit an enemy, can also be used as another attack pattern by adding a J (normal attack) after it, which will cause a backward slash.
This game also has an easy crafting system. You'll get blueprints from monster drops and the blueprints will specify materials that it needs to make an item and the items can be obtained by slaying monsters. The only problem is that the blueprints drop chance (especially for robe and augment slot) are quite low. I ended up raising like 7 levels and i still didn't get the ultimate robe blueprint (which is actually doesn't needed unless you aim for 100%).
There are 4 upgradeable stats in this game, which are HP, attack, defense, and fidget (magic attack). There are 15 slots in each stat which can be raised upon level up. Besides the status, there are also equipments which can help boost your stats. There are robe, augment (attack), 2 rings, and necklace slot. There are also equipments for regenerating HP and boosting XP, gold, and item drop. Although there are items to boost XP, i find that leveling up to be not that difficult. I can raise my level easily after killing a few low leveled monster in the first few areas when my level is around 50 ish (the cap is 60).
There are also two main collectables in this game: treasure chest and friends. Although treasure chest holds a random item, friends can help boost your HP by 5% permanently. You also need keys to "unlock" them; 1 key for a treasure chest and 4 keys for a friend. There will be a minigame when you're doing the "unlocking". The map will mark the areas with treasure chest, including whether they have been taken or not.
There are 6 main areas in the game which has a save point between 2-4 areas. There is also an auto save slot which will auto saving your game when you're passing through a save point. You can also do manual saving in addition to auto saving to make a backup slot.
In addition to main quests, there are 21 sidequests in total. The sidequests varies from talking to people to exploring an area. You'll also be rewarded if you finish them.
In some maps, there will be a challenge arena called Cirelian Trials. It's a speed run to go all the way to the exit and hit some lanterns on the way to reach the highest score. Although you need to do several tries to get 4 star (the maximum star), it's not really difficult to get it and difficulty settings won't really matter.
The only complaint i have is how hard it is to descend through the stairs in the manor area and how you can't continue the game after you complete it. There are some bugs concerning alt tabbing, but i think that it's tolerable and doesn't make the game unplayable.
Pros:
- 4 difficulty settings
- 21 sidequests
- "Speed run" challenge arena
- Quick and easy save points
- Customizable stats and equipments
- Easy crafting system
Cons:
- Alt tabbing bugs
- Difficult to descend through the stairs in the mansions
- Unable to continue after completing the game

Stellaris is a real time empire builder, that seems to focus heavily on exploration. All kinds of fun stuff has happened to me so far, from finding extinct races ruins, on various planets to wild indiginous native xenos whom you can accelerate their growth, and make them a space faring vassal state, to having asteroids threaten my planets and require destruction of the asteroid. It really hits that spot of "I want to see just one more star system", perfectly.
Also, I really like the Sector generation. You can create sectors, (and infact you are encouraged to do so to avoid being penalized) within your empire to take the load off of you, and into the AI's hands. The AI can be altered, in their focus, as well as microd later as necessary, and is a welcome touch to the game to keep you focused on the unknown, rather than being dragged down into minutia.
The faction creator, is fun and easy to use, though maybe it's lacking a bit of depth compared to some other titles in the genre, and the same with the ship creator.
That being said, it's enough to be solid, give some variety in gameplay and quick enough to get you playing without pining for an hour each faction made.

As a reviewer, what was I ever going to be able to add to this game's reputation? Not much.
Playing since the time it was new on PlayStation, I've long ago come to consider that you have to realize what you can expect from FF8 and then want that. If you stick stiffly to certain expectations you started with from its franchise siblings, you may not get your money's worth. I think you should get your money's worth, so as with all games and especially for FF8, see what is good and available as well as what is not good and not available, and then enjoy it when that's the sort of thing you're feeling open to.
What I personally came to like and expect from FF8 is a game of fine-tuning. You can tweak your stat numbers and aspects of your Limit Breaks, get or neglect to get various resources through cards and other means, use more and less powerful strategies. Oddly enough for all this, the game doesn't really lend itself to making challenges, yet I still respect its fine-tune-ability.
It does have a fair few missables that are hardly anywhere neatly laid out. I know it was infuriating to me those years ago that I kept discovering more and more things that I had missed. But once I had got them all, it was a prouder accomplishment than in games where I personally had had to do less work and research.
I bought the Steam version because I felt like playing FF8 and I was persuaded that I would particularly enjoy certain mods from
: a set of addons including a hard mod and the Roses & Wine music mod. I was not disappointed. I think the Steam+qhimm version I have now is far and away the best FF8 I have played.
If you have patience, I would highly recommend this game. It takes some trial and error to understand, but it is a great concept for a game and I can't wait to see what else they add-on to it!

As an avid Overwatch player, I downloaded this as bit of a "Let's see what Totally-Not-Overwatch is like". I must admit I was pleasantly surpised to see its actualy a half decent game.
Graphics are quite nice, the voice acting is actually far in excess than what I anticipated and the skins are generally quite good.
I'm not going to lie, a few heroes are direct rip offs of Overwatch but that doesnt detract from the experience.
Now I say half decent because while its well made (for beta) there are a few things that dont feel right.
1) You can only play with a full lobby. If someone leaves, the game exits to the main menu, in the queue again. This is a big one for me, as I'm used to drop in drop out seemless games. (Maybe in full release this wont be an issue). Once you have a full lobby you have to wait for everyone to load in (like LoL) which is annoying as my gaming PC shouldnt be penalised by a potato.
2) Hitboxes feel odd, and the "death replay" always looks like the enemy was barely aiming at you.
3) The team balance doesnt feel quite on point. You can have a whole team of attackers and just out DPS the enemy, which seems like a downside as everyone picks Damage or Flank (meaning everyone is lone wolfing).
4) The first 5 levels are against Bots (which the game does not tell you). It wouldnt take much to add a tooltip or note saying "Your first 5 levels will be against bots, so you can get a feel for the game and heroes"
5) Not the games fault, but no one seems to talk much. Very little (to none) in the text department and due to it being a "Free to Play" game means the headsets are usually owned by kids who feel making odd sounds and screaming a lot is the way to go.....

First off let me say that the game is in Alpha, and the Devs still seem to be very active at this point, and that is why I am giving this an overall recommended tag. Now thats over with let me go into a bit of detail, and show what I see as good (or even potential) and the bad (or frustrating).
I have built a few aiports in the game, and each time I keep hitting the same conclusions:
1) This is an airport sim, and if you are like me the details matter. The Devs have gone to the lenghts of allowing us to plot out taxiways to each stand, but then not allowed directional control of the taxiways. So planes will use what they feel like, and this always causes major log jams when you scale up the airport.
2) No directional understanding of the flight orientation, similar to above you have to build the runway, and get it working  before you can understand what directions the flights will land and takeoff in.
3) Always a big bug for me, is the fact you cannot build over a road. I know the game is 2D but they have implement a similar function with Over/Undergroung baggage belts.
4) Assinging Arrival and Departure areas, most airporst I have visited have public transport dedicated to 1 or the other, and when setting up a system to mimic this the passengers just walk to one bus stop, even if it is 1 hour (game time) to get there.
5) Rejecting old contracts is really, really boring. I go to the contracts panel to do up my next load of flights, but before I can get to the correct game day, I have to scroll through 15 to 25 out of date contracts that should just not come up when looking for new ones. I don't know how many time I delete the HWY contract, but it's a lot.
6) Baggage is still a work in progress. I have 8 ramp agents on each side, but they always seem to load less bags than the flight requires, and the planes numbers majically drop to fit the bags the lazy Ramp agents managed to load, just so the plane can leave.
7) Not all airports round the worl have curfews, and we should be able to potentially open this up, once a desired metric is met, by negotiating with the city.
8) Naming stands and runways would be awesome, and essential in scaled up airports. Also assigning certain airlines to stands would be a good addition (although not essential).
9) Trucks, buses, cars, luggage carts, all seem to be driven by inept people who cant turn at a specific point, and instead drive miles to the end of the road, do a u-turn and head back before pulling into a bay.
10) We should also be able to assign buses into a bay, as at times I have people waiting at 6 bus bays and 4 buses lined up to all park at the 1 bay no one is at. I note the Devs have gone to the trouble of giving each bus a unique company name, so why then can't we assign company A to bus stand 1, and schedule a service every 30 mins?
Don't get me wrong by the above comments, as the game is good and playable now, but for the more detailed people it will frustrate you in the short term and limit you playing time, and enjoyability as the above points and more block the game in it's current state. Lets see what the Devs can deliver over the next 3-6 months, as this game has the potential to be very good.

When I was a teen, placing in my PlayStation for the first time, I knew I would be a gamer for life.  This wasn't Sonic jumping on robot creatures or the pixelated curiosities that were the original Final Fantasy's on the NES.... This was a heartwarming journey weaving an epic and timeless tale of the human spirit.
I collect and play Final Fantasy games, and this one is my classic favorite.  The story and characters are more realistic than the previous games starting a trend in the series.  It hurts to relive the pixelated limits of 5th generating gaming, but if you can look past (as we all had to back then), you will see a beautiful 3D rendered world featuring elements from modern architecture, classic fantasy, sci fi, and steam punk.  This was one of the first multi-million dollar game productions, and it shows.  I'd love to see high-res versions of these backgrounds.
The magic draw system is tedious to play as a completionist, but it is a fun diversion for adventurers because with every enemy encounter, there is an opportunity to draw something unique you can use in gameplay.  Also, each of your party is setup like a blank slate and you strengthen them with magic you've drawn.  So, unlike other RPGs, you can create your own jobs using any of your favorite characters.  And the backgrounds, Enemies and GFs are artistically rendered, and it's easy to feel a sense belonging to this world.  For newcomers to classic RPGs, think of a large open world game like Skyrim or Fallout 3 with quests, but with a turn-based battle system.
Pro draw tips: Make every character able to draw and Mag-J if you can.  Find one weak enemy, draw with each character and hold down the confirm button.  I use Xpadder to toggle-hold it down.  If you have to draw from a stronger enemy, you can put one person on cure-duty, and I like to make Selphie weak on attack (no or weak Str-J and low level) and give her mug and put Stop on Status-J.  This is a good setup for the draw, and also a weak attack can help you bring their hp low without killing so you can finish them off by turning them into a card (which is refinable and also gains AP).  In the beginning of the game, I find galbadian soldiers (which have 4 spells) and Fish from Balamb are strong early draws.  When you convert a Fastitocalon fish to a card and refine it, you get 20 Water which is a midrange attack spell and a powerhouse on Str- J early in the game and defeating them yields 3 AP each which I think is even more lucrative for grinding than the famous cactaurs.
Also, there is a chance to play the game non-violently which should appeal to some including women and girls who may also appreciate the game's romantic undertones.  Most of the enimies are not evil minions.. They are more like nature's creatures in this fantasy world.  Gaining experience from killing is not really rewarded because the enimies gain xp as you do.  However, you can non-violently draw magic.  I have a combo team: One freezes the enemy and steals items with a weak whip attack, a second draws magic, and the third heals any damage recieved.  You can also gain the coveted AP (used for building abilities for the Guardian Forces which are like spirit-assistants in battle) by turning enimies into cards (which I like to imagine is like keeping them as a pet).
Not that this release isn't without problems.  To me, the most noticable omission is analog controls.  They were a great improvement over FF 7 and brought the more realistic characters to life.  Also, it's a shame the face lift didn't make the cards in the in-game card game, Tripple Triad, higher resolution.  I also didn't like the control customizations which don't support the triggers or the D-Pad on the X360 controller; although the extra buttons are really needed.  I used Xpadder to keyboard emulate to fix that and emulating the keyboard's "confirm" key because the gamepad one doesn't work everywhere. Unfortunately, this means setting up both gamepad and kb controls in the game's settings.  I wish I could just disable gamepad support in the menu and do full keyboard emulation.  That way, I could keep it all in one place.
In fact, first, the fact that it wasn't exactly the same as my mint condition Play Station 1 version infuriated me.  However, when I took my rose colored nostalgia glasses off for a moment, I can appreciate that it has HD 3D (although they had to preserve the original lo res background images).. and there are things you can do to achieve a more original look including lowering game resolution and checking the "original graphics" box in the settings.  Also, the high resolution character and GF profile pictures are a nice touch.  I found the MIDI music an acceptable with those nostalgic melodies, but I hear you can community patch it with original sound.  I imagine they had copyright issues with sony requiring them to use PC-MIDI effects.  Modern games tend to have a lot less music, so appreciate the themed soundtrack that accompanys you throughout your journey.
Thank you, Square, for bringing these Final fantasy games to Steam.  I hope everyone interested chips in and rewards Square with a little fresh support for these efforts.  Not everyone can collect classic consoles like I do, and very few FF fans can collect every console every FF game was originally released on.  Even for a console collector, it can be more convenient and practical to download from steam and avoid using outdated hardware (I admit: my PS 1 joysticks are getting a bit stiff d: )  Also, we have a chance to share the classics with the younger generation.  But trust me, if you can overlook the outdated graphics, the near-futuristic sci fi and fantasy atmosphere will feel modern and timeless.

Airport CEO is getting better with each alpha release. You can spend hours planning out an optimal airport layout and several more just detailing the facilites inside and out. Once I understood the logic of the staff, passenger, and aircraft motion, it was much easier to create a design that was efficient.
It appears the taxiway nodes are functioning much better now with the latest update. That was really hanging me up with aircraft getting stuck taxing off / onto runways. At one point, I had a stalemate between an incoming commercial flight and a general aviation aircraft. They just sat there for several hours (game time) nose to nose and I had to go back to a previous save. I don't believe I'll run into that again with the bug fix.
I would say the most challenging aspect is use of limited space on the map and placement of key pathways that in most cases cannot cross. For example, the terminal foundation doesn't allow for sky walks over public or service roads just yet, so the terminal needs to be all in one building.
I have not made it to baggage services with conveyor systems yet, but will need to in order to progress to larger passenger aircraft and generating more revenue. I'm still enjoying running a small to medium airport servicing general aviation and local prop plane flights.
I really like how the dev team added a real world map for airport selection and that it pulls in local city names for regional flights and more distant cities for larger flights.
I think this game will keep progressing into an excellent airport sim.

Fights took a while, especially when the monsters chose to 'guard' which didn't add any depth to the game - just made the fights longer (monsters doing 20 hp damage attacks on 2000 hp heroes).

The Witcher 2 picks up the story fairly soon after the end of the first game. It's also possible to import a save from Witcher 1 (as I did), although this only affects a few details about the world and your starting equipment.
In many ways the Witcher 2 is a big improvement over the original game. The production values are clearly a lot higher and the art and sound assets still hold up reasonably well even few years later. The writing and voice acting are pretty decent too, and certainly better than in the original game. The main quest is interesting enough and there are a lot of great side quests. The game could have used even more quests where Geralt is doing actual Witcher work, however.
The combat has been completely redesigned, and it's certainly better than in the original Witcher. It's now much more action oriented with a big focus on rolling and mobility. The controls often feel bit floaty and clunky, though, and hit detection is poorly implemented. The battles can also look pretty silly with all the rolling around.
The original game was ridiculously easy even on hard, but this time around things are better balanced. At least on higher difficulties the game provides a decent challenge overall, even if the combat becomes pretty easy near the end of the game. There are still some annoying difficulty spikes and a few encounters can be pretty frustrating. Geralt also feels pretty squishy for most of the game and is quite vulnerable when facing larger groups of enemies.
There are also some extremely poor design decisions that hurt the game. The game features a fair number of quick-time events that add nothing to the game. The menu UI is also a horrible mess and barely usable with mouse and keyboard. This was a huge step back after the great journal system in the first Witcher.
While I still liked the alchemy, I wasn't a big fan of the new crafting system overall. Having to scour the world for mundande crafting parts was a major pain at times. And having to use the Witcher medallion to highlight objects was a big annoyance as well. Luckily there are several mods that can help with these issues without really affecting the overall game balance.
On the whole I enjoyed the game more than the original Witcher, even if this second entry has a share of its own problems. I played through the game on hard and picked Iorveth's path.
The good:
- Interesting characters and well-realized world
- Great graphics, especially for a slightly older game
- Decent main quest and lots of interesting side quests
- Meaningful choices and consequences
The bad:
- Crafting is annoying, especially without mods
- Annoying quick time events
- Terrible menus and dialogs, these are a huge step back from Witcher 1. The menu UI is a major pain to use
- The ingame map is one of the worst I have seen in an RPG, especially when outdoors. There are very limited map markers and no way to add your own. Furthermore, objective tracking can often be quite misleading when targets are underground
- Mutagen system is poorly thought out and promotes mindless grinding
The ugly:
- Dice poker is even worse than in the original Witcher. In general all the minigames are pretty terrible
- No potions in combat, this felt like such a useless change. To make matters worse, there are a few boss fights that throw you into combat with no warning or chance to prepare
- The pop culture references often felt out of place, at least they were pretty rare
- The game was crashing to desktop fairly frequently, especially when reloading a save game

Fear was the system hog of its time. It was also touted as one of the best FPS titles of its time. Does it hold up to both those titles today.
Well, yes and no. Yes it's one of the best FPS titles of its time (and still an impressive shooter nowadays), no it's no longer a system hog. Let's look deeper into that.
FEAR puts you in control of Point Man, the newest member of a government team meant to combat paranormal threats. You're sent out to stop a crazed cannibalistic solider who's taken telepathic command of an army of clone soldiers. Meanwhile, there's this creepy girl stalking you through the whole thing and making people explode into meat splatters with her telepathic abilities. The whole game is pretty much you tracking down the cannibal freak, killing clone soldiers, investigating the situation's backstory, and discovering all the dirty little secrets. It's a mildly intriguing story, but i'll admit it's never really hooked me. The gameplay on the other hand...
Woo boy. This game has some of the best shooting i've ever come across, even by today's standards. If you've ever watched a John Woo film, you know what you're gonna get here. the gunfights here are cinematic, frenetic, fast-paced encounters where bullets tear chunks out of concrete, glass windows are shattered, bodies fly around like ragdolls, blood splatters, smoke emanates from gun barrels, dust clouds your vision, and furniture is obliterated. Despite the near complete lack of enemy variety (they're all literally clones), the action never gets old. All this is made even better by the smart enemy AI. Clones pin you down, shout orders to their squad mates, flank you while the others keep you in cover with gunfire, throw grenades your way, jump over ledges to avoid your bullets, run away from your grenades, take defensive positions, crawl under tables for cover, notice your flashlight, and even hear your footsteps if you don't crouch. The AI here was ahead of its time and still impresses today.
The game's also pretty scary and atmospheric too. I wouldn't call it terrifyin, but I will say it managed to give me the chills and jolt me many, many times. Disturbing hallucinations, that creepy ghost girl stalking you, chilling music, and things moving on their own all work together to unsettle you whenever you're not locked in a fierce firefight with enemies.
Like I said though, the graphics have already been eclipsed tons of times in the years following this game's release. It simply isn't all that demanding anymore. On a mid-range laptop, you can easily run it at max settings with 60 frames per seconds. The visuals themselves are very sharp at max settings, but not exactly impressive. Textures are... all right. Water effects are fairly basic. The two places the graphics are still fairly impressive are in the lighting effects and, especially, the particles. Remember what I said about how the environments just come apart when you're in gunfights? Yeah, the particle effects actually add to the gameplay here and turning them down deals a serious blow to the enjoyment in my opinion.
Overall: recommended. It's a solid, exciting shooter worth your time and money. Not for the graphics enthusiasts (though the game isn't what you'd call ugly), but definitely for shooter fans and anyone who wants to see some terrific AI at work.
Pros:
Frenetic, intense, satisying combat
Impressively smart AI
Great music and sound effects
Genuinely chilling
Not hard to run nowadays
Cons:
Visuals aren't all that impressive anymore

The Ark of Napishtim is an oddity. It’s an amazing game, but it has many flaws. It’s filled with great ideas, but it doesn’t always take advantage of them. It’s forgiving, but can be brutally unfair. The ideas of Napishtim don’t always mesh, and the resulting contradictions in balance are the result. But the ideas that do work do so extremely well.
Positives:
- Epic in Scope
- Phenomenal Soundtrack
- Solid Gameplay
- Ys Boss Battles
- Tons of Secrets
- Catastrophe Mode
Negatives:
- Fundamental Design Flaws
- Treatment of Minor Bosses
- Poor Tutorial
- Catastrophe Mode Implementation Issues
The Ark of Napishtim is an awesome game with an epic presentation. Everything about Napishtim feels huge, vast and mysterious, be it the story or the Islands of Canaan. In fact, Napishtim doesn’t just feel huge, it feels like it was meant to be bigger than it already is! For instance, there’s a talisman that lets Adol breathe underwater, but it’s barely used (far from the epic underwater coral dungeon I was expecting). Nonetheless, the world of Napishtim is beautifully crafted, and filled with a diverse variety of characters and monsters alike.
The secrets in Napishtim are amazing! Not only are the secrets numerous, many are deviously hidden. I love it! Admittedly, some things shouldn’t be secrets since they can significantly affect the game’s balance.
Napishtim’s main story, though not the strongest, is actually really good. However, the depth and weight of the history implied by the Ark itself opens new possibilities for the series. Napishtim is such a powerful cornerstone of Ys lore that it changes the nature of Ys!
The main story is an exploration of greed. That said, greed is not portrayed as a fundamentally bad thing, and is in fact shown to help bring two neighboring societies, both at odds with each other, together for mutual benefit. However, greed cannot be fully explored without demonstrating its use as a means of manipulation; both innocuous and malicious. And Napishtim does this exquisitely.
Like all Ys games, the soundtrack does an excellent job supporting and defining the atmosphere of game, but at the same time, the music easily stands on its own. One track in particular stands out to me personally; the theme for the Ruins of Lost Time. This is not because the track is necessarily Napishtim’s best (arguably). But rather because this track, more than any other, expresses the weight of Napishtim’s deep and rich history.
Of the three games based on the Napishtim engine, it’s the gameplay of Napishtim that is the most ambitious and unique. Napishtim’s gameplay is based around 3 spiritual swords, each with their own unique properties and attributes. Each sword also has two unique skills; one elemental attack, and one magic attack. I love the fact that Napishtim includes 6 abilities, especially since some of these feel very outlandish compared to future entries.
The greatest downfall of Napishtim’s gameplay is that some of the mechanics are very non-intuitive. Since the gameplay is very refined, the non-intuitive aspects would be a non-issue if they were supported by a solid tutorial. Unfortunately, the tutorial is less than stellar. Everything is crammed onto 2 pages, and most of it is self-explanatory. While non-intuitive points are described in the tutorial, the descriptions tend to be confined to 1 line of text. This critical information is so obscured by everything around it that, even if you’re careful, it’s easy to miss.
The Bosses in Napishtim are primitive compared to Felghana or Origin, but they’re not as simple as one might think. The boss designs hold a surprising amount of nuance and depth that take all aspects of Napishtim’s gameplay into account. In Catastrophe Time Attack, the bosses really shine; all major design issues that ultimately hurt Story Mode are gone, resulting in the bosses in their purest, most refined form. This, consequently, exposes their raw points; the hit detection for some attacks is a bit unfair, and the random-luck factor is unusually high. It’s worth mentioning that two of the bosses are just borderline beatable on Nightmare Catastrophe Time Attack, and only if you really know how to beat them. Napishtim’s Bosses, for what they are, are frustrating but fun, and very satisfying to beat.
I do have a nit-pick with the final boss; it’s way too easy to beat. Don’t get me wrong, it’s a fun and challenging boss. It’s just not challenging enough for a final boss.
A huge number of Napishtim’s issues revolve around how bosses are handled in Story Mode. One of the biggest issues is Healing Items. If you have them, you can beat the boss by spamming them. If you don’t, you’re effectively playing Catastrophe Mode. As far as balance is concerned, it’s impossible to account for this chasm of variability. In addition, since Magic Gauges don’t reset when a boss fight starts, Magic can also be spammed. The Magic in Napishtim is literally three powerful boost-like abilities, and being able to spam them is a huge balance-changing advantage.
It probably wouldn’t be too difficult to make Magic Gauges reset for major bosses. But this is impossible for minor bosses due to two design decisions. First, none of the minor bosses have a savepoint immediately preceding them. Second, you can flee from nearly all minor boss fights. Both of these points add severe limitations to how these bosses can be balanced, and unfortunately prevents them from being pushed to their full potential.
The optional bosses also suffer from a further issue. Optional bosses should be extra challenges that have near-zero impact on the overall balance of the game. However, most of Napishtim’s optional bosses have a significant impact on the game’s balance. One of the biggest issues in the entire game is that three of the optional bosses guard game-changing accessories, around which the end-game bosses are balanced, and the game provides no hint that these bosses even exist… Why?
There’s also a late-game sidequest that earns a single-use auto-revive accessory. It’s not part of the game’s balance at all.
The optional superboss Majunun also doesn’t quite work. As a superboss, Majunun is spectacular. But in order to properly fight Majunun, you have to grind and grind and grind... Mandatory grinding is not what Ys is about. In addition to this, the Level 11 swords only exist for Majunun, but a player might think they’re necessary in order to fight the last main bosses. The Level 11 Swords and Majunun would probably be better off as a post-game event. This way, grinding isn’t necessary to beat Majunun, and it’s clear that the final bosses only require Level 10 Swords.
I love Catastrophe Mode; I have nothing but praise for the idea. With that said, its implementation does have issues. In Catastrophe Mode, healing items in treasure chests are replaced with Capla Water, which can be sold for gold in order to buy items way earlier than intended, thus allowing two tiers of armor to be completely bypassed. This makes the early game significantly easier, but it leaves the late game open to a very steep difficulty spike. The primary function of Catastrophe Mode Capla Water, curing status ailments, is almost effectively useless due to Napishtim’s overall design. The secondary function of Capla Water, fully filling the Magic Gauges, is far more useful, but is rendered useless due to the restriction that Capla Water can only be used if Adol has a Status Ailment.
With all of these issues, can The Ark of Napishtim really be considered an amazing game? Well, yes! Napishtim changed Ys on a fundamental level, and that’s not an easy thing to do or do well. But Napishtim did exactly what was needed to make it work. And it’s brilliant for it. It definitely has serious flaws that hold it back, but its strengths far outshine its weaknesses.

Where to begin?
Well, GC3 is indeed a unique and honestly quite deep turned based 4X-style strategy-management game. It's basically the civilization series but in space.
Galactic Civ 3 is very intuitive, and user friendly, and my favorite part being the numerous customization possibilities.
Building ships in the designer, and in game is absolutely awesome, and that is the standalone thing that separates GC3 from any other similar titles, allowing the player to feel like the fleets they control are actually their own creations winning battles.
However, there is some downs...
The graphics, well, it depends. If you have a potato pc, the game will run fine (with the exception of the 3d battle sims). Unfortunately, great pc or not, the actual effects and so forth are a little... unremarkable. For me, I've found that GC3 is not about the graphics, but the gameplay.
Speaking of which.
It is what you may expect of a 4x turn based strategy-management. It's pretty easy to pick up, and can be a lot of fun. Patience is important in this game. I feel the researching is a little... cluttered and clunky.
Most games you play in GC3 will start slow, sometimes... excrutiatingly so.
If I were the developers, I personally would focus on making gameplay more immersive. Suggestions include:
-this one is big; Domestic Affairs. One immersion breaker that hurts badly in this game is that there is quite simply zero domestic events or decisions. For example, regulating trade for your own colonies, more advanced information on cities and settlements on planets, local political events such as a governer election or something of that sort- and the list goes on.
-ship construction is a little lackluster. I honestly feel that the numbers of ships that you can actually deploy over a period of time is too small. I'd imagine huge fleets of perhaps a few capital ships, but hundreds of individual fighter/bomber/intercepter type craft. It feels as if the scaling is far too small. One big hitter for me and many people is the real huge scale of space, and the density of populations and militaries.
Concluding this review, I can easily say, if you enjoy strategy games similar to Civilization, GC3 is a must.
It is a little rough in areas, such as graphics and some gameplay, but overall, I'd say GC3 is a solid 7/10.
