Greetings Everyone!   Today we go back to a classic of the RTS Genre, Command & Conquer:  Red Alert 3; a game that some call the best of the series and for the most part I agree.  However, the real question is:  Does it stand the test of time?  The short answer is, aside from a few small areas, it does!  Even today the mechanics and design holds up for the most part.  I didn’t find myself massively missing some kind of function or ability, though some of the keybindings are odd (queue commands I’m looking at you).
Commanding Satire:  The game’s story revolves around its trademark style; live action characters with silly or somewhat poorly done CG.  This is all kind of tongue in cheek with a hint of taking itself too serious in the name of satire; there are absolutely parts of cringe and I still found myself amused.  There are some scenes and some underlying ‘concerns’ for some people.  Notably the endings which have the commander being invited by the female characters in some fashion; I don’t have issue with this but some with more modern issues might have.
Lost in Time:  So there are some issues with the mechanics, many of which are very much hindsight type of problems but there are the typical pathing issues that many old games have but overall not terrible.  In addition; you get some quality of life areas that could be improved upon; namely queuing up things (looking at you Rising Sun Nano-Cores) or abilities (fly here, transform, attack, transform, come back).  For the most part I’m probably just spoiled by modern games but it does need mentioning.  Another thing that annoys me is the campaigns over abundance of naval missions…except for the Rising Sun ones which I feel I needed more (spoiler they like their boats) but I was a big fan of the unit descriptions and the overall tutorial missions; more games need this.
Glorious History:  I feel this is a game that most people need to play if they are new to the RTS scene and want to know about where the modern games come from.  However, this being a old game there is one serious annoyance and that is co-op.  To begin with co-op doesn’t exist; even if you had a friend who wanted to play you can’t the game uses the now gone Gamespy servers and not the steam one.  To make matters worse your AI commander is daft beyond recognition; so many times he was wiped out or down to just a few small buildings and I’m still sharing resources; or even worse, he’s just building infantry for what is supposed to be a naval encounter.
Overall:  I like this game; I recommend it to anyone wanting to walk down memory lane or to show a younger player the old days.  If it is on sale; grab it but I’m not sure if I’d recommend paying full price unless you absolutely must have.  But, I waited for a sale, and I encourage you do to the same.  Enjoy!

I purchased the entire Delicious franchise after watching someone play through several of the games. I played two of the games prior to playing Emily's Hopes and Fears. I expected more of the same. I was pleasantly surprised with the differences that Hopes and Fears offered.
During Hopes and Fears, Emily's daughter, Paige, gets sick with a mysterious illness. Patrick, Emily's hustband, decides to go find a mystical flower in the north that's supposed to cure any disease. Half of the game is spent around Patrick's journey. The other half is spent with Emily and Paige, who stayed at their family home. There is drama on both ends. No matter where the player is, they are going to play through time management levels in order ot progress through the game. Each level has challenges that players must do in order to perfect the game. There are challenges between levels that players can also opt into.
Pros:
- Simple controls and gameplay.
- Different locations add a lot more variety than previous games.
- Although the story is a bit ridiculous, the serious aspects make the story more interesting.
- Characters feel like they're actually worth following.
- Most achievements tie into gameplay and are easy to get.
Cons:
- Some grinding may be necessary to get some items.
- The last five levels are boring.
- Playing previous games may be necessary in order for the player to care about the leads.
Of the Delicious games I've played, this one is my favorite so far. It's a shame the story relies so much on players knowing the characters. If that wasn't the case, this is where I would recommend all players start their Delicious journey, to see if time management games are for them.

When I first came across Abzû I was taken in by three main factors; the beautiful graphical style, the vibrant colours and the excitement of exploring the ocean’s depths. Abzû is a game that puts you in control of a deep sea diver, allowing for you to travel from the surface of the ocean right down to the abyss. Along the way you’ll come across various types of fish and other aquatic beasties. Dolphins, Manta-rays, angler fish and sharks, to name a few, all of them beautifully rendered in the cel-shaded style. Abzû is very much a casual, exploration game that is both colorful and charming.
The story behind Abzû is very much like a puzzle, and I’m not talking about those one hundred piece puzzles from Ravensburger, I mean those two thousand piece map of the world jobies. It’s complex stuff that you have to work out on your own, which I think is a nice change. Although you are given some hints as to what might be unfolding, thanks to a few paintings inside the various temples you’ll visit. As you progress, the story will slowly unfold, allowing for you to piece together the information and build an idea of what’s happening. Not so much create your own story, but more build the story from what you know. I prefer not to spoil the story, especially in this instance where you want to work it out for yourself. But all I’m going to say is; it’s not what you’d expect.
Gameplay-wise there’s a whole ocean to investigate, hundreds of different fish to see and numerous puzzles to solve. Abzû presents you with different areas for you to explore, each containing various puzzles to solve, most of which are fairly straightforward. There are also several interactive objects in each area. A shark statue for one, which you can meditate at, allowing for you to see all of the fish in the current area. Then there’s also, what I call, coral circles which spawn a schools of fish, that vary on species from area to area. Lastly there are little, yellow drones, which follow you around. These friendly little robots can be used to interact with various object throughout the game and are mainly used to clear out anything that might be blocking your path forward.
As you advance through each area you may come across peculiar, tower-like structures with bodies of water on-top. Head inside and you’ll enter a weird, dream-like, ethereal plane. Here your objective is to follow the glowing route, which takes you to the bubble that has to be activated. Once activated an amazing and quite beautiful event takes place. That all might sound like complete and utter nonsense, that’s because it is, but this isn’t for pointlessness sake though, there is a much larger picture to uncover as you play.
To signify the end of each area you are met with a large, triangular doorway, which stares at you with a giant, mechanical eye. Then, once you open it, it’s on to the next area.
The controls are fairly simple, with the option of either mouse and keyboard or controller, I’d advise the later though. Why? Well it just feels, to me, a lot smoother and less clunky. This is a game about swimming around in the open ocean after all, fluidity is a key part of it.
This takes us nicely onto mechanics, of which there are a small number, but nothing complex or difficult. You can swim around freely and even perform water acrobatics, of sorts. Back-flips, somersaults and even leaping out of the water. These moments flow incredibly smoothly and are amazing to watch time and time again. By performing these tricks you are granted a temporary speed boost, which lets you to jet through the ocean at high speeds.
It can sometimes be very easy to get lost in an area, so very conveniently you have the ability to summon a handy little arrow, directing you towards the area’s end. This is usually the best thing to do after you’ve searched every possible nook and cranny of each zone, of which there are a fair few.
Moving on to graphics and sound.
Graphically Abzû is a beautifully, vibrant game, with a very pleasing cel-shaded art style, think games like Zelda: The Windwaker and Bastion, to name a few from memory. I’ve always been a big fan of cel-shaded graphics and I’ve seen games in the past make a complete shambles of the format. But Abzû makes the most of cel-shading and it shows, not to mention is blends well with the feel to the game.
Sound-wise there’s little to not love about both the sound effects and the music. The squeaking of dolphins in the distance, whale songs echoing all around and the splashing of colorful yet tiny fish, it’s delightful. These sounds accompanied by the charmingly, colourful music create an almost magical feeling.
Overall I’d recommend Abzû very highly. It’s charming and vibrant. It has a magical feel to it, without there even being magic, now there’s a first. It’s a casual, calm game where you could spend hours checking every tiny detail or performing acrobatics, (aquabatics?) or simply watching the fish. If you want something that can relieve the stresses of day to day life, even for an hour or two, Abzû is a great way to do it. There is very little not to love about this beautifully crafted game. Calming, vibrant and very enjoyable. I’d highly recommend it to anyone. Good Day!

The little bits of story and commentary and attention to the tech tree on Gal Civ 3 does make it stand out.  Infact I feel that the little attention to details on that front are probably one of the games better aspects.  There are a few rough spots in the little details that could have been executed a little differently, like when you play a 'synthetic' robot race, they kind of leave out some important information before you start.
That and I've no idea how or why you'd eat robot innards, if you are.. yourself.. not a robot..
This particular Gal Civ seems to be focusing more on Ideology, with actual perks you can pick out of a list.  As nice as this sounds, it also causes some other issues, as differences in ideology alone have been the entire reason for wars to just start up in games that I've played through.  Unless of course the Devs change that a little bit of course to maybe not be so harsh on diplomacy standings.  I do wish they had something for you at the end of an ideology when you've actually unlocked all the options.
For the first time Gal Civ series has a functional multiplayer.  At first glance it seems all good, but I do miss having simultaneous turns while I play cooperatively with my friends.  Perhaps someday that too can be fixed.
For the most part the game runs reasonably well on my AMD Ryzen system, not really having any issues there.  I do wish it was more multicore/multithread capable as larger maps and more bots do tend to make the turn timer get a bit.. well tedious.
The Addition of shipyards and pirate shipyards/bases is a nice touch, but the lack of being able to upgrade the shipyard defense wise like a starbase is somewhat concerning and the pirates are rather mind numbing after awhile as they kind of just drive their faces into the nearest item of yours endlessly.  I think I would rather have them actually have a planet now and then too, or even have the potential to take over a planet that you or a bot ignored long enough..  Even though the bots already seem to just jump to war too soon rather then threaten you, or extort you for research or resources.
Now onto a more serious matter, I've been finding some issues as I've played through the game, but all hope is not lost. The Developers are actingly seeking feedback and seem genuinely interested in fixing things still.  Just to name a few.. some in game items not rendering properly.. bots being ludicriss and down right dirty...  and map generation woes..
To be fair the map generation issues are actually a lack of planets at first.  However the game is meant to be played with random events on that do infact reveal more planets around all the stars on the map.  Which is perhaps easily forgetable when your roaming around your own cluster of stars and finding out that, realy have no planets at all.  So I would like to see some kind of options to see more planets, as it is right now I pretty much have to set them to abundant or common for the various types of planets it spawns in the options.
The other part of the somewhat negative view point on planets, is the ones that do spawn are generally a lower value as what was previously seen on Gal Civ 2, but there again is a reason for it.  On GalCiv3 the planet tiles can interact with nearby tiles using adjacency bonus, as well as their improvements.  So when you properly use adjancy bonuses, suddenly the planet feels much more versatile with less tiles in total.
- Summary -
Gal Civ 3, even though it's been out for awhile, has some good (and bad) times to offer a person that enjoys turn based strategy games.  While I do feel like they might be asking for a bit much for the game, I can safely say that even with the trouble it gave me and the bugs I encountered and reported, I did atleast enjoy it.
Finally a note for newer players, drones are really nice on this game, don't ignore them for planetary defense.

Of all the 3d/2d Ys games made, Napishtim was the first to be made, yet the last to finally get a proper PC re-release. And while most of the good stuff that people loved about Felghana and Origin is still there (as it originated there), it does feel like a first attempt.
Napishtim, as Felghana and Origin, is an action jRPG with pretty simple controls but a lot of depth. Also a lot of grind. As always for the series the music is good/great, story is simple, but somehow charming anyway and visuals are nice, despite being quite outdated. There's lots of button mashing, good timing for special attacks, occasional jumping, new items allowing to do new things and see new areas and stuff like that. It's very simple to get into and enjoy.
Unlike later games, Napishtim clearly didn't know how exactly to tackle the new perspective and controls. There are three weapons (as in other two games), yet they feel less varied and important. There are a lot of areas that feel like they are 3d versions of maps from Ys I and II, which is great in it's own way, but sometimes feels too open, too easy to lose track of where you are, hence Felghana and Origin have much tighter and streamlined maps. There are several (optional) horrible jumping puzzles that rely on a semi-hidden skill you can do, something that got refined in next two games. And there's way too much grinding at times with huge unexpected spikes in enemy damage mid area. Felghana and Origin not only did difficulty change better but also added a lot of things to make grind work, especially Origin, where you go into combo, grab healing off dead enemies (which heals you on spot) and things like that. Napishtim works in a more boring classic way and while there's no absolute bs moment like in Ys I, it still feels not as fun as it coul be.
That said, it's still a fun game to check out. It doesn't overstay the welcome, it entertains, it expands on the already interesting universe and you will have fun with it. You just might want to start with Felghana and Origin first to really get into the series.

Even if the genre isn't exactly the same, I like comparing this game to Civ 5.
The idea is that you should strive for the stars either diplomatically or martially, so that you more or less become the ruler of the galaxy. Therefore, you do the 4x'es: Xplore, Xpand, Xploit, Xterminate. You build buildings on your planets, you can terraform them, you can build stations around planets that gather resources or give research points, you can trade or you can go to war, either as the lone wolf or in an alliance.
Sounds great, doesn't it?
It does. But the problem is the 5th X: The Xecution. Trading is even worse than in Civ 5 where you had trade routes AND instant trade: Here, you don't have trade routes at all. If you remember the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor trade menu in Civ 5 with the tiny lines you had to click on and thought it was the worst system possible: Think again. Here, you have a similar list structure, that is bigger, but you have to switch tabs between offerings and demands. Also, the AI sometimes doesn't even accept presents, depite being "friendly". However, the AI does only do something when it is sure it will be accepted. So the AI builds alliances at staggering speeds, while you have to check every in-game month whether any of the AI would accept an alliance invite. Diplomacy? Feel free to estabish vastly overpowered embassies, ameliorating the standing with the other faction - until you run of of them, as you can maximally have 4 embassies.
Also, remember setting your scout to explore mode in civ 5 and never ever having to manage them again until they either get to the coast or the whole map was explored? Well, be excited by this immersive gameplay decision Stellaris has made: Get ready to manage every very single system survey by hand. Automatic exploration? Nope.
Same goes for contruction ships (the workers in Civ 5). Automation? Naaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaah. It's even more tedious as your faction's borders expand with time and planets that you couldn't previously mine become available. So if you have a Chile-Style empire (long and narrow), get ready to check all few years whether you can exploit more systems.
Reaseach is similar: Get ready to select research targets from 3 different sections (Society, Science and Engineering), which is fun until you run out of Scientists and you get a 20% malus on the research speed. The scientists themselves are Leaders: Guys you need to buy for influence because... ? Civ 5 had a similar thing by being able to buy prophets and stuff for faith points, but they were more or less optional. In Stellaris you don't get anywhere without research.
So far, we've established that the diplomacy lacks practically everything needed to be able to be a valuable way to go. Alright. Not what I would have hoped for in a strategy game like this. But then again, war can be entertaining as well, right?
Aaaand nope. It all boils down to the simple rule: Steamroll everything or get steamrolled. Remember in Civ 5, when you were furios about the tremendous defense strength a city had, making it nearly impossible to conquer a city until you had catapults? Well, this time, your planets are about the weakest things in the game. Sure, they can't be conquered in the first few minutes, but as your empire grows, it becomes impossible to defend every single planet. Big fleets are far better, even for defense, which is weird at best.
Alliances do a♥♥♥♥♥♥job of defending you btw, and the (thankfully disablable) empires starting with an advantage either love you or hate you from the first contact and then will steamroll you to death or leave you be. Seriously. You don't even have to give them a reason to attack you. They just do (similar to civ 5). The only problem then is: The AI does only do things when they are sure they can pull it off. So if they declare war and you're in ironman mode, exit the game and start a new one or give them half your empire, just so they can attack you again after the peace period runs out. It basically always is gg.
About the shipdesigning: Well, you design ships. Is cool, but as your fleets will be a blob anyways and you can't see what's going on in fights, you basically just change some stat values.
I personally didn't find the UI too confusing, but I can understand why some do: Too many tabs, too many hidden options and too much scrolling to do without clear indicators that you CAN scroll.
In the end, I'd consider it as a realtime CIV 5 in space without the hidious round times (as it is an RTS), but with every single contra civ 5 had (Really, it seems to me that Paradox had a checklist of all the bad things about CIV 5 to tick) and none of the pros of balance, trading and automations.
I'd say: Pick it up when it's cheaper than 20 bucks, maybe even as a package with the promised DLCs (that should have been in the basegame...) so you get the game it should have been.
Don't buy this barebone for 40 bucks.
TL:DR:
Buy it if you LOVED all things that were flawed in CIV 5, don't buy it if you didn't LOVE civ 5. (Liking doesn't seem sufficient to me).
/EDIT: So some patches after, the game hasn't really gotten better. There are still gamebreaking bugs (like inability to leave federations) and the Lategame is basically a stall to any gameplay and yields to doing nothing. You can now research auto-exploration (no, not a default: A research). C'mon man. It's 2016. This game loves micromanaging to much it's literally not fun to play at all if you expect a game and not an excel simulator.

If you're familiar with Ys, you know it's a very formulaic series of games. If you like the formula, then VI is a great addition to your library. It was the first game in the series(released in the US, at least) to take the series into more 3D gameplay. VII, Origins, and Oath in Felgana(remake of III) then followed suit.
Where Ys really shines, in my opinion, is in being a pretty light-hearted, mindless action-RPG. It's a great way to wind down at the end of the day, or to distract yourself when you're not feeling up to more cerebral RPG gameplay. If you want something more serious in tone, or if you want something that requires a bit of actual thought, then Ys VI(or any Ys game, really) probably isn't what you're looking for.
Gameplay is fun, but not particularly challenging unless you up the difficulty or do one of the specific challenge modes. The music is quite fitting, but ultimately forgettable; it complements the game nicely, but probably won't get stuck in your head. And the graphics are, thankfully, stylized(in no way meant to be photorealistic), so even though they are from an early-to-mid-PS2 era game, they hold up quite nicely.

UI is a little buggy still, but overall a fun game. I enjoy the mix of construction, scheduling flights, managing operations, and arranging taxiways.
Looking forward to how this will progress as more updates arrive. Seems promising.

This game is boring. Very boring.
You start off exploring the galaxy and that part is fun. But, fairly soon, you've finished that part of the game and you're into the part of the game where you're developing your star civilization. And there's nothing to do there. You get to make meaningless choices between technologies with futuristic-sounding names, and watch the AI develop the planets that you've colonized. And this goes on for hours and hours and hours. I've read that there's an epic war at the end of the game, but I've only played the game for about 100 hours, I haven't got that far yet.
There's a tile development mini-game within a game, as is traditional for Civilization-like games, but the developers decided to force you to let the AI do that for you. I don't know why the game's designers bothered to code this mini-game if they weren't going to let the players play it.
Wars with the AI are boring. You don't fight the battles yourself - that's all handled by the AI. You move your star ship fleets around on the map, trying to bring the AI to battle on your terms. If your fleet is bigger, chances are that'll be relatively easy. Then you get to watch the AI for your fleet ROFLstomp the AI for the AI's fleet. It's pretty the first few times, but after a while it gets old.
In fairness, the developers have said that there's a whole bunch of mid-game events that they didn't have time to code before releasing the game. They've said they expect to get that code added to the game by the end of June. We'll see. But in the meantime, if you like watching the AI play against itself, this is the game for you.

Fifteen years ago, I was uber hyped to play this game. Final Fantasy VII had blown my mind two years prior and I was itching for more. The game did not disappoint. Great graphics, a new magic system, an addicting card game... I was a happy thirteen year old boy. I had all the time in the world to absorb this game.
Flash forward to today and my life is not so "free" for playing sprawling JRPG epics. When FFVII was released on Steam, I bought it immediately, but never finished it. I loved that game growing up but found I just didn't have the time or energy to complete the games numerous (and tedious) side quests.
FFVIII is different.
I completed almost every side quest in a manageable amount of time (approx. 40 hours). The Junction system and the ability to eliminate encounters (if I wanted) made the game enjoyable like I couldn't believe. The characters, while sometimes unrealistic, were surprisingly relatable. The battle system was still challenging but not daunting or filled with grinding. In short: FFVIII is perfect for an adult gamer with limited time for gaming.
Last note: I still can't help but smile at the very last scene.

They also need to do some work on the pathfinding, but I can honestly say even in some multi million dollar games pathfinding can be a challenge.   Let's face it AI NPC creatures (in this case passengers) are not too bright.   Come to think of it, last time I was at the airport there were many people exhibiting the same daft pathfinding IRL.....
There is also some scalability issues with the game, and larger sized airports are quite lagfests.   That being said, it is early access and I am willing to give these guys much more time to flesh out their design.
Right now the game is fairly stable, you can build the basics, and if you keep it in the 4-6 commercial gate size with a 4-8 stand general avaition farm you should be okay with lag.   Also try to keep your designs basic as I mentioned before there are some pathfinding issues and creating dead ends and tight corners is just asking for trouble.
Bottom Line - I recommend

Price - good value for $$ imho

Oh If you are a tycoon game fan, you'll LOVE IT!... Micromanagement is the essence of this 2D simulator.
My Experience: I wont divide the points in PRO's and CON's but an over all point of view... It Has a moderate learning curve for an average gamer but you get the idea once you've invested a couple of hours in the game. You always have the aim to build the "perfect" working Airport! I, with every start learnt something new and had to start over and now after 50 hours of game time, have an airport with an average hourly income of 5k. Was able to wipe off debts with quite a bit of micromanagement. Keep in mind this is "VERY EARLY" Early access (yeah I wrote Early twice.. thats how early it is) So expect a lot of operational bugs, locked items/buttons/services while the game is progressing. Like After every couple of hours the baggage service will start delaying the planes/The planes themselves will delay even when all the services have completed and its time to take off, and Aircrafts getting stuck at the ends of runways for no reason at all! Everytime that happens you have to quit the game, save while quitting and start over. But since We know this is "EARLY EARLY Access" I can look beyond these bugs.
But the worst issue that I have faced till now is... Even with a Brilliant Hardware Set Up (3.8 Ghz Quad Core Core i5 processor/16GB RAM/SSD Hard drives/nVidia GeForce 970 GTX 4 GB *2 in SLI with dedicated PhysX Engine on one Card mounted on a MSI Gaming 7 motherboard, Once there are a lot of passengers, the game becomes so choppy that you feel like banging your head against the wall... and I play with the option of "Good Graphics" and not "Fantastic graphics" with 1920*1080 Resolution in 16:9 Ratio. So only option I have left is to play with "Fast Graphics" to keep my head cool.
I only wish that the rendering becomes better and the game play isn't as choppy as it is right now.
Expectations:
*Better AI for Service Vehicles and Fuel Trucks in the upcoming releases
*Better Management of Service Vehicles and Fuel trucks where we can tie them down to a specific area/ Vehicle Depot/ Group of Aircraft Stands of the airport so they dont spend time travelling from One end of the Map to another to service a Plane.
*Better AI for Planes to land and take off... Even when the runways are designated for "arrival" or "departure" individually, the planes get stuck at the start/end of runways facing the wrong direction!
---
Needless to say this list is non-exhaustive and will continue to grow as and when we encounter issues with different elements.
Overall... its a serious Micromanagement game which is awesome fun for tycoon gamers like me!

Final Fantasy 8 is a black sheep in the franchise. It's got a really different battle system and a weird story.
Final Fantasy 8 does away with MP and replaces it with the Draw ability! This ability makes it so you have to 'draw' magic from your opponents or from specific areas in the world in order to use that magic. Magic is now treated like an item, you can only use as many 'fire' spells as you have stocked. In order to use magic (or any ability that isn't 'attack') you have to junction GFs. These GFs are the equivilant of Eidolons from the other Final Fantasy games and can be summoned during a fight. It can be a real pain to grind on enemies to obtain magic, but fortunately, the Steam version includes a 'magic booster' which gives you 100 of a few spells.
Now onto the story. Squall is... a strange character to say the least. If you thought Cloud Strife was dull, you're in for a surprise. Squall is silent, calculating, and has more internal dialogue then external. He has issues relying on people which becomes quite apparent throughout the game. The plot of the story is weird and confusing and has led to may theories on what actually happens during the game. The beginning is a lot more normal however. You are Squall Lionheart. You are a SeeD (pretty much a mercenary) in training and are about to perform in an exam to become fully ranked. You have a rival (kind of like pokemon) and you have a love interest later in the game. After the first disk, things that border the ridiculous start to happen, although they can be completely 100% explained.
I liked this game because the farther you got into the game, the more you found yourself enjoying it. This game has, in my opinion, one of the hardest final boss encounters in Final Fantasy. The ending's pretty dope too.

Final Fantasy VII is very much a product of its time. When you look back at it, the Fisher Price people graphics look kind of embarrassing even by the standards of games that came later in the Playstation's life and the English translation was an abomination of poor grammar, misspellings and turning Barret in to a racial caricature.
That said, there is no denying that the game was a revelation upon its release and played an important role in Sony's early success as a console manufacturer. The story, while hamfisted and nonsensical in places, has a lot of heart and can still carry the player through the full 30-40 hours it takes to get through (though less if you're running through it and 80-100 hours if you want to see and do everything the game has to offer).
While my love for Final Fantasy dried up many years ago (too much self-serious melodrama and unintentional humor and not enough heart and intentional humor), FF7 is an inexpensive reminder of a happier time for a lot of people.
The Steam version is a barebones port but it runs fine on modern machines. Easily worth picking up during a Steam sale.

When I first came across Abzû I was taken in by three main factors; the beautiful graphical style, the vibrant colours and the excitement of exploring the ocean’s depths. Abzû is a game that puts you in control of a deep sea diver, allowing for you to travel from the surface of the ocean right down to the abyss. Along the way you’ll come across various types of fish and other aquatic beasties. Dolphins, Manta-rays, angler fish and sharks, to name a few, all of them beautifully rendered in the cel-shaded style. Abzû is very much a casual, exploration game that is both colorful and charming.
The story behind Abzû is very much like a puzzle, and I’m not talking about those one hundred piece puzzles from Ravensburger, I mean those two thousand piece map of the world jobies. It’s complex stuff that you have to work out on your own, which I think is a nice change. Although you are given some hints as to what might be unfolding, thanks to a few paintings inside the various temples you’ll visit. As you progress, the story will slowly unfold, allowing for you to piece together the information and build an idea of what’s happening. Not so much create your own story, but more build the story from what you know. I prefer not to spoil the story, especially in this instance where you want to work it out for yourself. But all I’m going to say is; it’s not what you’d expect.
Gameplay-wise there’s a whole ocean to investigate, hundreds of different fish to see and numerous puzzles to solve. Abzû presents you with different areas for you to explore, each containing various puzzles to solve, most of which are fairly straightforward. There are also several interactive objects in each area. A shark statue for one, which you can meditate at, allowing for you to see all of the fish in the current area. Then there’s also, what I call, coral circles which spawn a schools of fish, that vary on species from area to area. Lastly there are little, yellow drones, which follow you around. These friendly little robots can be used to interact with various object throughout the game and are mainly used to clear out anything that might be blocking your path forward.
As you advance through each area you may come across peculiar, tower-like structures with bodies of water on-top. Head inside and you’ll enter a weird, dream-like, ethereal plane. Here your objective is to follow the glowing route, which takes you to the bubble that has to be activated. Once activated an amazing and quite beautiful event takes place. That all might sound like complete and utter nonsense, that’s because it is, but this isn’t for pointlessness sake though, there is a much larger picture to uncover as you play.
To signify the end of each area you are met with a large, triangular doorway, which stares at you with a giant, mechanical eye. Then, once you open it, it’s on to the next area.
The controls are fairly simple, with the option of either mouse and keyboard or controller, I’d advise the later though. Why? Well it just feels, to me, a lot smoother and less clunky. This is a game about swimming around in the open ocean after all, fluidity is a key part of it.
This takes us nicely onto mechanics, of which there are a small number, but nothing complex or difficult. You can swim around freely and even perform water acrobatics, of sorts. Back-flips, somersaults and even leaping out of the water. These moments flow incredibly smoothly and are amazing to watch time and time again. By performing these tricks you are granted a temporary speed boost, which lets you to jet through the ocean at high speeds.
It can sometimes be very easy to get lost in an area, so very conveniently you have the ability to summon a handy little arrow, directing you towards the area’s end. This is usually the best thing to do after you’ve searched every possible nook and cranny of each zone, of which there are a fair few.
Moving on to graphics and sound.
Graphically Abzû is a beautifully, vibrant game, with a very pleasing cel-shaded art style, think games like Zelda: The Windwaker and Bastion, to name a few from memory. I’ve always been a big fan of cel-shaded graphics and I’ve seen games in the past make a complete shambles of the format. But Abzû makes the most of cel-shading and it shows, not to mention is blends well with the feel to the game.
Sound-wise there’s little to not love about both the sound effects and the music. The squeaking of dolphins in the distance, whale songs echoing all around and the splashing of colorful yet tiny fish, it’s delightful. These sounds accompanied by the charmingly, colourful music create an almost magical feeling.
Overall I’d recommend Abzû very highly. It’s charming and vibrant. It has a magical feel to it, without there even being magic, now there’s a first. It’s a casual, calm game where you could spend hours checking every tiny detail or performing acrobatics, (aquabatics?) or simply watching the fish. If you want something that can relieve the stresses of day to day life, even for an hour or two, Abzû is a great way to do it. There is very little not to love about this beautifully crafted game. Calming, vibrant and very enjoyable. I’d highly recommend it to anyone. Good Day!

F.E.A.R. nowadays is indeed outdated graphically. No surprise there. But despite its dated looks, F.E.A.R. possesses some fantastic gameplay, and firefights wrapped in a remarkably eerie, mysterious story with inspiration drawn from Japanese horror.

F.E.A.R.: Perseus Mandate is the second expansion, however, rather than continue the story you play as a different member of a secondary F.E.A.R. squad investigating a project known as Perseus Mandate during the same time-frame of the original F.E.A.R. Abzu is remarkably beautiful and has a very immersive soundtrack. I admittedly started out thinking I was going to hate it. As much as I appreciate relaxing games, they usually bore the crap out of me. I was far from bored though because Abzu had me in awe by the end of it.
Abzu is an atmospheric single player experience where you can't die or lose the game. You take the role of a diver in the vast ocean where you can explore at your own pace. There are collectibles such as hidden pools and shells, along with meditation statues that help you identify the creatures in the ocean.
There is a story in Abzu, but it's very subtle. It's not told through cutscenes or dialogue, but instead
. The story borrows a lot of elements from Journey, but it's still good nonetheless.
The store page says that controller is recommended, and I definitely agree with that.  I played most of the game on keyboard, and it worked fine but it felt a little awkward overall. Once I switched to controller the controls felt much more smooth and fluid. Keyboard works just fine, but if you have the option, I say go with the controller.
Overall, Abzu is calming, gorgeous, and a game that makes you feel powerful by the end of it. If you hate relaxing games such as Journey, you might not be swayed by Abzu. If you love relaxing games or underwater exploring, then I urge you to pick this game up right away. It may only be 3 hours, but it makes quite an impact. Just make sure you wear headphones for the best experience!

Doom is the game that basically created the first-person shooter genre.  It may not have been the first to do it, but it was the first to do it
Well, if you enjoyed Doom, then this is pretty much more of that.  While it adds a new weapon and some new enemies, I might have trouble telling screenshots from the two games apart.
The formula can be boiled down as such: You are in a maze.  You need to find the exit to said maze.  However, the maze is full of monsters who want to tear out your liver and shove it down your throat.  Throughout the maze, you can find supplies -- both hidden and in plain sight -- which will help you defeat the monsters on your way to the exit.
There's not much to it, and that's what makes it so great.  With no deep story or friendly characters to slow the pace and pull away your attention, you can focus on what you're here for: slaughtering demons.  Other single-player FPS' might seem like a step back, with their linear levels and terrible pacing.
Because of this, I'd argue that this game has aged rather well.  It's levels are well-designed, and the formula it works on is timeless.  This is a game you can always come back to, one that you can boot up to blow off steam when the alternatives just seem too exhausting and unrewarding.
This game was released years before I was born and I'm saying it's great.  That's how good it is.
The two things I'd say have aged poorly would be the resolution and control scheme, both products of this game's time, and both are easily fixed with a healthy dose of GZDoom.  Just go to
and forget DOSBox exists.
The one biggest reason one might buy Doom II over
would have to be the game's modding scene.  Thousands of mods (called patch WADs, or 'PWADs') exist for the game, and more continue to be made to this very day.  A combination of improvements in technology and many,
years of experience means some of them arguably
the original games in terms of quality, and definitely in terms of presentation.  If you're so inclined, you could buy this game and play its mods for years without ever playing the base game.  You shouldn't, the base game is still great.  But it's something you can do.
I'd recommend this to any fan of the FPS genre.  This is the grandfather of the first-person shooters multiplied by two.  Because of the simplicity of the gameplay, it doesn't seem obsolete compared to newer games of the genre.  This is a game you can pick up whenever you're not sure what to play and always leave satisfied.

Here's the thing... and the reason why I have a problem with Steam's review system in general.
There are things I like about this game that I would consider an improvement over it's predecessor. Then there are issues that I feel hurt my ability to actually play the game. I even had Crusade on my wishlist until I ran into these problems.
PROS:
Space battles look really pretty, and I enjoy watching the action everytime there is some sort of galactic conflict with my faction. The design of the faction leaders, the ship customization is on point. You could have 2 to nearly 50 or so factions in your galaxy clashing for power. The RTK player in me loves that idea! Really. I spent quite a bit of time making my own factions (as I did in GC2) and ships. In my opinion, that's the coolest idea this series has!
THE PROBLEMS I'M FACING:
Bugs. A few key things that affect this game's stability. And I'm not talking "little annoying things that don't ruin gameplay". I mean some that pretty much make a game unplayable. My biggest problem is that starbases, starships -- and sometimes  ENTIRE PLANETS will randomly just disappear (for no apparent reason). It's a strategy game. You need to be able to see what you are managing, otherwise you "overlook" them (no pun intended). You see, the game will still know these things are 'there' and behave normally on each turn. This naturally means that any enemy faction can still attack them (if they are at war with the player). This means any thing that needs working on (like planets) will still be needing improvements, etc.
It'd be one thing if the game occasionally had some funky bugs that were just annoying or something like that (Fallen Enchantress, for example has a ton of those, but the game is still playable. I would rather this game have similar annoyances than something like this). It's not just an immersion thing, it's a vital gameplay facet. One needs to see what they are strategizing. Sorry, it's just a fact.
Right now, I just can't recommend it, unless something is done about this. Trust me. I really do want to recommend this game, but not in the state it seems to be in now. :(

I've been a fan of Stardock Games for some time now--going all the way back to GalCiv 1 and as a rule, they put out a good product and Gal Civ 3/Crusade is no exception.  The developers are very good about listening to player feedback and responding and have done much to fix earlier teething problems.  We seem to be in something of a renaissance as regards 4X/Grand Strategy space games with Gal Civ III, Endless Space II, Distant Worlds, Stellaris, and other titles all jockeying for players' time--and I think that's great.  Each of these games are fine games in their own right and each offers something different for a play experience.  What I like most about GalCiv III/Crusade is the sandbox mode where you can create your own civilization or play with someone else's and tell your own story--the only limitation is your imagination.  I do admit to having problems wrapping my mind around the Ship Designer--I see all these terrific designs on Steam, but when I try to make my own, they come out like Lisa Douglas's hot cakes (gotta be a Green Acres fan to get that one) .  I like the concept of citizens and administrators and the diplomacy system is most definitely a game strong point for me. This game is boring. Very boring.
You start off exploring the galaxy and that part is fun. But, fairly soon, you've finished that part of the game and you're into the part of the game where you're developing your star civilization. And there's nothing to do there. You get to make meaningless choices between technologies with futuristic-sounding names, and watch the AI develop the planets that you've colonized. And this goes on for hours and hours and hours. I've read that there's an epic war at the end of the game, but I've only played the game for about 100 hours, I haven't got that far yet.
There's a tile development mini-game within a game, as is traditional for Civilization-like games, but the developers decided to force you to let the AI do that for you. I don't know why the game's designers bothered to code this mini-game if they weren't going to let the players play it.
Wars with the AI are boring. You don't fight the battles yourself - that's all handled by the AI. You move your star ship fleets around on the map, trying to bring the AI to battle on your terms. If your fleet is bigger, chances are that'll be relatively easy. Then you get to watch the AI for your fleet ROFLstomp the AI for the AI's fleet. It's pretty the first few times, but after a while it gets old.
In fairness, the developers have said that there's a whole bunch of mid-game events that they didn't have time to code before releasing the game. They've said they expect to get that code added to the game by the end of June. We'll see. But in the meantime, if you like watching the AI play against itself, this is the game for you.

This is the game, originally released for PC in 2003, which started the "modern" phase of the Ys series, with polygonal environments and a more complex gameplay, with the ability to jump and do attack combos. The original version was released only in Japan, but it got ports for PS2 and PSP which came to the West. I read bad things about the game's performance on the PSP. The PS2 version, on the other hand, has everything polygonal (in PC / PSP all but scenery and important bosses are sprites), which is nice, and voiceovers for the dialogues, which by the little I've heard is not at all nice... Now, over 10 years later, XSEED released a western localization of the PC version on Steam, with some improvements such as support for widescreen.
Compared to the other two games of the series in this generation which I played on Steam, Ys: The Oath in Felghana and Ys: Origins, Napishtim is the one that adopts the most traditional style for a JRPG. Many NPCs, many dialogues, many events, much coming and going, a broader sense of exploration, relatively large inventory with manual item usage, etc.
Felghana then simplified things. It was only one town that was pretty much just a hub between dungeons. Combat and exploration had systems that encouraged advancing quickly and not wasting time. Origins then completely focused on action and was practically a dungeon crawler interspersed with small cutscenes.
Returning to Napishtim, graphically it is exactly equal to Felghana and Origins. featuring polygonal environments which are simple, but clean, having a nice visual style and very well animated sprites for the protagonist, NPCs and enemies. In the dialogues, nice anime-like portraits with a visual style that I really enjoyed. As one might expect from a 2003 game made natively for PC and only slightly improved and updated, it runs smoothly in 4K@60fps in a modern card. The game has a bug in that eventually the sprites will glitch and turn into a lot of geometric shapes flashing on the screen. Fortunately ALT + TAB solves this.
The sound follows the series' tradition: Excellent. There are two or three songs in the game that really stood out for me, but all of them are at least good and nothing gets irritating.
The game's story is simple, much along the lines of the series. It has its twists, but nothing that is very impressive or makes you care too much. The central plot is self-contained, but both minor and major events have some connections and references to Ys I and 2 (and therefore Origins, although this was released later), so playing those games before can be helpful to make the most out of it, although this is not necessary. This is not a long journey, but it's noticeable that the staff had a certain dedication and attention to detail, such as the fact that all the dialogues of all NPCs change after every event that advances the main story.
The way the situations and events elapse and how they fit in the exploration reminded me a bit the first Ys. Except that unlike it where basically half of the game is the final stretch, here when the really important events begin to occur you discover that you are practically at the last boss' door. It's something I've noticed in some other games and is not the kind of pace that suits me.
It reminded me of the first game also for the fact that some levels are the difference between you being unable to scratch an enemy and it being unable to scratch you. The game controls your progress by gradually reducing the XP enemies give as you level up, but this doesn't mean grinding isn't important: Some situations and bosses are somewhat difficult and both levels as equipment upgrades, which cost a time-consuming to get resource, are important. But the difficulty is somewhat balanced by the fact that you have an inventory with a variety of healing items that stack in groups of up to 9.
I really liked the game and it is very high on my list of favorites in the series, I just don't know exaclty in what position.

The Witcher 2 is a great game for it's combat system, setting, characters, and general RPG elements, to put it short it's a great game with few flaws, a solid 8.5/10. Now to go into detail.
Pros
-Great combat system once you get past the learning curve.
-Setting is a breath of fresh air and isnt overwhelming if you've played any other game with a similar setting.
-Geralt can pull of the ponytail look.
-Item system was done reletively well, what i mean by this is that you werent getting better items almost every 5 seconds, and it also didnt starve you from new gear. so you take passion in finding the best gear for yourself, or just use what you find and not pull your hair out because you cant do enough damage.
-Quests require you to be a normal human being and provoke you to talk to people about your quest, and to see if they can either help you or further it. This is very refreshing from the good ol fassioned: OKAY HERES A MAP MARKER GO GET IT BOY! mentality that many RPGs do today.
-Plot can still be comprehended by some one who hasnt played the previous game.
-Game is pretty well good looking, especialy for the time of wich it was released.
-The money system is done well, you can still save up and buy the shiny sword, but you cant just grind at one point of the game and be rich for the rest of your life.
-Game saves, loads, and acts overall pretty fast.
-took me about 30 hours to beat this game while taking my time, this game is woth the money for the time you will spend in it.
-Booty, you figure out wich kind im talking about.
Cons (not alot)
-Game crashed multiple times during my playthrough, resulting in me losing about an hour total in catching up to my progress, make sure to save every now and then and you should be fine. just dont depend on the auto save.
-Story was strong at first, but lost gravity the longer the game went on.
-occasionally slow loading textures and frame rate drops, EVGA SSC 960 I5-4460 8gbs RAM
-Dwarf told me how he wanted to ♥♥♥♥ in a dark cave, and proceeded to call his wife a cow.
In summary, a great game! Crazy cheap during steam sales,  definitly buy if your into RPGs and ponytails.

Enemies tend to use cover and I like how they communicate with each other and act on the orders they are given via radio, but there are only like 5 different types of enemies and the maps don’t change much either. In the end you are just wishing for it to end, because you’ve visited that same place (or at least a very similar one) just in the last mission. As you can expect, the graphics are old and what is supposed to be its greatest feature, its story, is really not that much interesting until the last bit.  By that time, however, you have probably guessed the ending and the only exciting thing about it is making sure you were right the whole time.
Oh, and seriously, they could have come up with something better than: “We’ll regroup later, you go alone first” in every single mission. Gets tiring pretty soon. Other than that, the slow motion mechanic is quite cool, but don’t expect the game to scare you too much. I don’t know. In most cases I probably wouldn’t recommend playing it, but since it’s not too long and it was quite a game back in its day, I suppose it couldn’t hurt to give the game a try. Just be ready to experience a really repetitive game until the very last stage.

I was pleasantly surprised by this title having honestly had low expectations for an 8 year old title at the time of purchase. It is not without it's imperfections when looked at from a modern perspective but much effort was made to make the game focus as much on the horror aspect of the story as it dod on the action and neither disappoint. A true survival-horror game often slowly fills you with dread and giving the odd jump-scare to race your pulse, something CAPCOM has since forgotten for their Resident Evil games in favor of aggravating quicktime nonsense and over-the-top silly action, but I digress.. FEAR has no such failings although the action doesn't disappoint, the bullet-time game mechanic which is familiar to those who've played Max Payne games makes the gameplay so much more fun and for a near-decade old game I was mesmerized by combat AI that was far more advanced than I'm used to seeing and wasn't surprised to find out it was revolutionary for it's time. Al lin all a great survival horror with a slightly greater emphasis on the action than the story but that's not a fault in how it was presented.

I just stopped playing this game before writing this review, and unfortunately I can't recommend it due to the steering. It's unresponsive and clunky. What I mean by that is this: you'll be in the middle of a big spoon curve, or coming out of a tight turn, and you wanna stay on that good line by evening out your steering at a spot that sets you up to get where you're looking to be on the track. But the game gets in your way. No matter how lightly you tap the thumbstick, your car will steer heavily in that direction. This results in out-of-control fishtails if you're aggressive in trying to correct the issue, or a trip into the grass/gravel/wall if you try to let it even itself out. There's very rarely any middle ground, and when I did nail it, it felt like luck, like the binary steering system just so happened to have a "notch" that put me where I was trying to go. This is an issue regardless of stability control or braking assistance settings, as I tried it all four different ways.
It's not as noticeable with less powerful cars, but the more powerful the ride, the more glaring this issue becomes. The AI doesn't seem to have this problem. About the only way to consistently avoid it is to hit the brakes, slow to a crawl, then creep around the curve, at which point the AI either blows by you or rear-ends you.
Considering this is a game about the joy of driving cars, and the driving part of it is so flawed, save your money for something better. Even at $5, I regret my purchase.

TL;DR - The Grudge + The Raid + ONI = FEAR

With GalCiv 3, we get the buggy, low feature release - and then get to pay for improvements.  Nope, there are PLENTY of other game companies more deserving of my attention that make better games while being less focused on a blatant cash grab.
I give this game an aluminum ranking - that means you should crush it like a cheap beer can and discard it.

This game is boring. Very boring.
You start off exploring the galaxy and that part is fun. But, fairly soon, you've finished that part of the game and you're into the part of the game where you're developing your star civilization. And there's nothing to do there. You get to make meaningless choices between technologies with futuristic-sounding names, and watch the AI develop the planets that you've colonized. And this goes on for hours and hours and hours. I've read that there's an epic war at the end of the game, but I've only played the game for about 100 hours, I haven't got that far yet.
There's a tile development mini-game within a game, as is traditional for Civilization-like games, but the developers decided to force you to let the AI do that for you. I don't know why the game's designers bothered to code this mini-game if they weren't going to let the players play it.
Wars with the AI are boring. You don't fight the battles yourself - that's all handled by the AI. You move your star ship fleets around on the map, trying to bring the AI to battle on your terms. If your fleet is bigger, chances are that'll be relatively easy. Then you get to watch the AI for your fleet ROFLstomp the AI for the AI's fleet. It's pretty the first few times, but after a while it gets old.
In fairness, the developers have said that there's a whole bunch of mid-game events that they didn't have time to code before releasing the game. They've said they expect to get that code added to the game by the end of June. We'll see. But in the meantime, if you like watching the AI play against itself, this is the game for you.

There is just enough here to enjoy to the fullest and be done about the time you finish the game itself.
If you are looking for something easy, funny, and relaxing to play for a night or two after work or school, this game can certainly fit the bill depending on your sense of humor. It's not as good as the other 3D Ys games (Oath in Felghana and Ys Origin), I'm going to be honest about that. This is due to it being the first-ever 3D Ys game, and even though this is a remake, it still carries a lot of the unfortunate baggage of the original, in the form of brutally difficult boss fights (which you are expected to survive by having a lot of healing items on-hand) and some required grinding. But it could be worse, and the grinding is only -really- bad at the very end of the game, where you *need* to get one of your swords to max level to do anything more than chip damage to the final set of bosses, which requires 100,000 emel. You get that much, but you probably need to spend it on your armor first, so you still need to get 100,000 by grinding in the final screens.
That aside, it's still an enjoyable game and a good remake of another installment in the Ys franchise. A single run on Normal that missed only a few items but saw the majority of the content took me 10 hours - so you might want to wait for it to go on sale first unless you intend to replay it. To that end, it does have multiple difficulty levels and 'catastrophe mode' which is truer to the other 3D remakes where healing items can't be carried around.

Pros:

cons:

What do you get when you take a first person shooter, give it great guns, atmosphere, level design, a suspenseful plot, and spooky psychological scares? You get FEAR.
FEAR (First Encounter Assault Recon) is a typical first person shooter at a glance. You move from point A to point B, gun down some baddies, flick a switch here, blow up that, turn a crank there, pick up ammo, etc. What makes it unique is the horror implemented into it. Between sessions of mowing down replica soldiers, you are treated to creepy dark places in buildings, officers, sewers, and even a research facility. Images of Alma and Fettel haunt you as well as what appear to be flashbacks along the way. Corridors fill with blood, specters appear out of no where, and voices or strange signals come in from unknown origins. Throwing you away from the run and gun style and then putting you into tense progression then throwing you back into the gunfights makes for an awesome receipe that likes to really play on your emotions.
Aside from the awesome weapons, the game has really nice story flow. You chase after Paxton Fettel, but along the way, you get side-tracked and have to complete other objectives such as rescuing hostages, investigating areas, linking up with team members (hopefully) and getting the hell out of nasty situations. Along the way, you'll fight mind controlled soldiers, specters, drones, stealth soldiers, and even a few mechs and heavy suits. When you're in the horror parts of levels, you'll get incoming transmissions from unknow origins and may see or hear things that can make you jump if you haven't played through or forgot they were there. It tends to play more on the A aspect of horror as opposed to the B, but there is some B there.
Combat and gameplay is simple for a shooter with two really awesome perks. You have boosted reflexes (which, in addition to your health, you can increase the meter of finding boosters) that slows the world around you allowing you to gun down soliders easier. You also have a jump kick and slide attack, very uncommon for many FPS which usually use melee as hitting someone with your gun in common practice. Second, the AI learns your play style presenting a really fantastic challenge. I tested it by starting off as a run and gun, get in there, shoot me all you want I'm coming for you style to where I saw the AI hiding or retreating to different cover often. Other times, I played it safe, hid behind crates and walls, leaned, shot, duck and cover. Eventually, the enemies were flanking me, doing pincer attacks, and coming at me hard to fish me out. Every time I changed tactics, the AI did the same for next time. It gets me wondering that if the intentional breaks in the action to move to the more horror parts of the levels was for that purpose, to recalibrate the AI. Regardless, the transition from spooky to run and gun and vice versa is sheer genius.
There are two major issues I have with this game, however. One is that it's short. I can get through this game in 6 hours, less if I put more time into it. This game came out around a time where these games were becoming faster, easier, and designed shorter sadly which many FPS post Half-Life 2 tend to be now. I can understand that Multiplayer in an FPS is more popular now then Singleplayer, but outside of a game's story, I love to play Single first to get a feel for the game's mechanics and style and practice with the weapons first before I go in and totally embarass myself until I get used to it. The second issue with this game is not really a huge one, but it's still there. I really wish that the AI would support you and join you, even if for brief moments. You do sometimes link up with squadmates or joint op teams (Delta mainly), but either something happens to them, you get derailed from your path, or you watch them do scripted routines and they tell you to go do something or find someone. At least it's not like in Doom 3 where you're praying you link up with Bravo, but the reality is you know you never will and you're alone. The linear path I could complain about, but this isn't the type of game meant for exploration and the atmosphere at least immerses you into the game so that can easily be overlooked.
Overall it's a great game that has the same formula you'd expect an FPS to have with its own nice little contributions. It's no Half-Life, but it's unique, exciting, and scary enough to keep me returning when I'm in the mood.

This is the first time I've written a review but this game has given me a reason to finally write one. Dust: An Elysian Tail is by far one of the best indie games I've ever played, if not one of the best games I've ever played in general. The combat is very responsive and fluid. The story is very engaging and manages to keep you interested from start to finish. The animations are very good and manage to look flashy while not being over the top. The story and writing is very well put together and it feels very natural. The voice acting is also really good.
The only "cons" that I can think of, which are more just nitpicks than actual problems, are that the game in total is around 15 hours long but for an indie game that's pretty standard and you never feel bored the entire time you're playing. Another con is that the mouse and keyboard controls aren't the best. I'm not saying they're bad, it is possible to play this game soley with mouse and keyboard but I found that the game felt better when using a controller.
There aren't any real problems with the game. The game runs smoothly at all times, it never crashes or anything like that and there aren't any game breaking bugs that I could find. You will encounter the occasional item getting stuck in a wall but it's nothing to be worried about.
I highly recommend this game and give it a 10/10.

What really makes 'The Binding of Isaac' a good game though isn't one individual element, its how it all ties together so well to match up thematically bringing together a really compelling experience. The dark overall themes, the random levels with unknown monsters and power up that always keep you on your toes, the music and art design ensuring that you know this is a giant metaphor for a trip through the seven layers of hell. At the end of the day though I know that the 'The Binding of Isaac' isn't for everyone, if you like retro games like Contra then you should get this otherwise stay away because the very reason that makes this game good (a perfect side scrolling shooter true to the genre) is the same reason that people will hate it. Its a matter of taste and you really should be taking some of the blame if you have no idea what you like and don't like by now.

: XSEED Games, Marvelous USA Inc.
I'll try to keep this review as spoiler-free as possible.
==========
Ys is one of the oldest action RPG series, and quite possibly my favorite RPG series ever. The first game was
in 1987, and since then numerous titles have been released, and some remade a few times for other consoles and handhelds. They are still being developed to this day, with a new title having been recently announced for the Playstation 4 and Vita.
The Ys series chronicles the adventures of Adol Christin, a young man with a zest for adventure and an uncanny knack for being in the right place at the right time. Currently we only have 4 Ys titles on Steam, with Ark of Napishtim being the 6th installment. First released for PC back in 2003, it was later ported to the Playstation 2 in 2005, and the PSP in 2006. Ark of Napishtim was the first English release of the series since Ys III: Wanderers of Ys. An English translation of the original PC version was released here on Steam on April 28th of 2015m with some enhancements and added features. The Steam release is hands-down the definitive version of Ark of Napishtim.
==========
Ark of Napishtim is a hack and slash action RPG with some light platforming elements. Controlling Adol Christin, players are able to freely move around the world, jump, and attack enemies. The game takes place on the Canaan Islands, after an attack on Adol's ship forced him to sail into an unknown region and into a large storm. This resulted in Adol being thrown off his ship and washing ashore in a new mysterious land.
Progression is story and exploration driven. As you explore each new area, bits of story are revealed through dialogue and events. You will also find treasure hidden all over, some of them granting new abilities or allowing you to explore areas you were previously unable to. Pieces of equipment, as well as healing items and accessories, are also hidden in treasure chests. To save your game you need to find a Spirit Monument. Touching one will completely heal you and cure any status ailments. Typically great areas to grind EXP and gold are the areas near Spirit Monuments.
Adol will eventually have access to three different swords with magical properties, each based on a particular element: Fire, Wind, or Thunder. These can be upgraded over the course of the game using Emelas Ore, which is dropped by enemies in small amounts. Upgrading your swords unlocks new traits for them, such as increasing their attack power, unlocking special elemental magic, or increasing magic regeneration. Upgrading your swords is the best way to strengthen Adol against the challenges he faces, so make it a point to collect as much Emelas Ore as you can.
One of the best things about Ys titles are the boss battles. Every boss is a screen-filling affair, requiring careful movement and precise strikes to bring down. The boss battles are easily the most exciting parts of the game.
One of the new features added to the Steam release of this title is Catastrophe Mode, which means you will not be able to stock up and use healing items freely. The game will play more like Ys Origin or Oath in Felghana, with healing items being used automatically when you pick them up! Couple this with Nightmare difficulty and you have one
of a challenge ahead of you.
The other new feature is the inclusion of a special item called the Wing of Alma. This enables you to warp between all found Spirit Monuments. This saves you SO much time it's unreal. In older releases you would literally had to backtrack through many areas, using the Wing of Alma you simply select the Spirit Monument and you're off!
==========
Ark of Napishtim got a slight upgrade in it's looks department. Utilizing DirectX8, the game looks much better than it's previously releases. Smooth animations all around, from Adol, enemies, and even bosses. Every sprite is very sharp, well designed, and highly detailed. Perhaps the best thing about the game are the environments. The land, water, the skies, dark caves, and ancient ruins all look fantastic.
==========
Ys is known for its musical scores, and Ark of Napishtim is no exception. Every track is amazing. From the boss theme to each different area's own theme, the music is really second to none. I wish there were soundtrack editions here on Steam for us to buy, as I would buy every single one. Physical collector's edition Ys releases usually come with a soundtrack disc, so I don't see a reason why Steam users can't have a similar option available.
As for sound effects, you have your usual Ys sounds. Attacks, footsteps, monsters...all have viable sound effects. They sound great, especially swinging the different swords and using the elemental magic.
==========
Perfect 60 FPS all across the board. No lag, stuttering, slowdown, framerate drops, or random crashes. The game literally ran without a single hitch. Flawless.
Ark of Napishtim has full controller support, and is the recommended way to play the game. My only gripe is with one of the 'hidden' abilities: Dash Jump. To do it, you have to move in a direction and press the jump and attack buttons at the exact same time. I am able to do it properly maybe 40% of the time, and never when I need to. There is a guide available that uses a script to make it a lot easier, but I have yet to try it as I prefer to try and master the technique myself.
==========
A fantastic re-release of a fantastic game, Ark of Napishtim is a fun and exciting action RPG that fans of the genre will love. If you have not played a Ys title before, you owe it to yourself to buy Ark and all the other titles on Steam. If nothing else it'll show Nihon Falcom and XSEED Games that we want more Ys on available here on Steam!

Having played the other Ys installments and this game being the foundation for Origin and The Oath in Felghana, The Ark of Napishtim came as a godsend. After the dark ages resulting from Kefin: The Lost City of Sand, Falcom went to make another installment to restore their reputation, and they came back in a fiery way.
The story is actually okay, but not really the main focus. The story mostly consists of a traveler, Adol Christin, finding himself washed up in an island surrounded by a Vortex, and having to solve the mystery of the island's ills. Along the way, he comes across legends, the history and mysteries of the island, and eventually becoming a sole hope against events manipulated behind the scenes...
Combat consists of fast-paced sword fights, and the boss fights provide plenty of challenge. One consideration of difficulty however, is that most boss fights become more a war of attrition. For those who thought the game STILL was not difficult, the option exists to play Catastrophe Mode, which removes the stockpiling of recovery items. And like the other games, grinding is prevalent, which may be a turnoff, but is very necessary to advance through the game. Expect to spend a lot more minutes or hours just to get that one level or sword upgrade just to give you an edge in boss fights.
The music, as always, is the selling point of Ys, and it does not disappoint.

Recommended, with certain caveats.
Ys VI is the first, and arguably the least of the 3 games which have similar gameplay; Ys Origins and then Ys Celceta being the other two, and I would recommend them in that order over this if you are new to the series. Napishtim is not a bad game, but it's let down by flaws that the later two would fix.
Combat in all 3 is fast and furious, almost like pinball in a way, as you plough into creatures and mow them down left and right; Unlike the original Ys, you manually control your own sword here, and a pad with autofire will be a blessing to cut down on repetitive strain as you hammer away. The speed of the game remains high throughout, even during some rudimentary but fun platforming, and the bosses as always are closer to a bullet hell shoot 'em up than a platformer.
The first problem though is that the plot is not tight enough to guide you from boss to boss, and you'll spend enormous amounts of time getting lost without resorting to a walkthrough; this is not the fault of the localisation, which Xseed have performed to a high quality as always, but simply because the game follows it's old 8 bit ancestors in having little room for text in game, and plot specific way points that could be anywhere within the dungeons you've already cleared.
This leads to the second problem in that items are scattered about in some quite obscure places, which on the higher difficulties (my first play through was on Hard) will prove vital; in particular it's possible to miss one extremely useful item by accidentally advancing the plot onwards, where as others are hidden in what you might take to be just background images.
And then there is the spawn of the devil known as Dash Jump: To activate this you need to move in one direction, stop, then simultaneously move that direction again whilst pressing both attack and jump at the same time. Maybe it's my old man reactions now, but I never once managed to pull this off manually, and resorted to a Hotkey macro to automate it. And some of the items you desperately need require this to be done multiple times. Later games would drop this entirely and replace it's usefulness with other magical powers, but here you need it, and it's enfuriating.
Having said all of that, the game is still fun, and I would recommend it to anyone who loved the first or last Ys games. To those new to the series, start with Ys Origins first.

I've been following the game since I discovered it over a year ago now and it's probably been my most anticipated game ever. I love what the devs have done here and the constant flow of updates following the early access release shows how much they are investing into this. I've played 14 hours of it so far and to be honest, it took me about 6 tries to make my first "proper" airport that I didn't mess up in one way or another, but I enjoyed learning the ins and outs of the game throughout.
The game concept and mechanics are great and I do not agree with some negative reviews saying it is impossible to grow the airport. Building a commercial airport right at the start is only really possible on easy mode or using loans, however you are able to only start with a tower, runway and a GA stand. This will earn you money, which can then be invested in increasing GA capacity, adding fuel services (which you are not required to have, but adds to profits) and later building a terminal and start introducing commercial flights. The game isn't without fault and there are many "easy" fixes that can be made, such as GA planes not arriving from South Africa when your airport is located in Europe. There is also the question of replayability and it will be interesting to see if anything will be done on that aspect of the game. The devs have said that Steam Workshop implementation is in the plans and I honestly can't wait for that, especially if they make it easy to add new objects, new planes/airlines or even new mechanics to the game.
Detail is king in this kind of game and from what I have seen so far, this game is going in the right direction and I can't wait for the future. There is so much potential here and I hope the developers keep doing the amazing job for which I and countless of other people are incredibly grateful for. I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tycoon or prison architect type games and especially anyone who has a particular interest in planes in general.
