Remember when you where a teenager? Perhaps you are one, and that is why Final Fantasy VIII is a hidden gem, concealed by the fact, hype and fans of 7 & 9.
Final Fantasy VIII is in many ways like other FF's, its set in a huge explorable world upon which, a situation arises, threatening its existence, companions are gathered along the journey to prevent it. But what 8 has done is extraordinary although it has to be said, unappreciated. This fantasy is through the eyes of a teenager, Squall, dubbed a Leonardo Dicaprio look-alike misery guts. Which is without doubt true, and possibly a strong reason why so many detest this game, living-reliving the life of a teenager in a world that is the closest to this one than any other FF game beyond 7. Effectively taken place in a Garden (school/college) where the students are trained to be become functioning members of an elite group of soldiers known as SEED. Ok not exactly a clever or exciting plot at first glance but this is only the beginning of something overlooked. Everything about it has that youthful learning element to it, such as the SEED tests as a means of gaining regular income, testing your knowledge of enemies, magic and general surroundings, you participate in field exams where you are graded accordingly on time, battles, attitude, spirit etc. oh and you're not aloud to buy a porn mag because you're to young.
Like all successful square games, it begins slow but picks up the pace by new events, addictive mini games and tugs on your heart strings with a puppy love storyline. Clearly, gamers have taken one look at the indifferent main character they must control and shake their fist in disgust that they aren't a mysterious mercenary, fun loving optimist athlete or a womanizing thief with a tail. I'll admit there are moments in the dialogue where you get annoyed at the ignorance of said character, such phrases like "go talk to a wall" are aimed at someone spilling their emotional guts and "whatever" occurs repeatedly followed by "....." making Squall an essentially unresponsive cold jerk.. what he wants you to think.. however the time I played this, I was of a similar age, disposition and could defend 'some' of his actions. As time wears on though, more light is shed as to why your guy seems so hormone ridden, a past frequently visited in game that should be cherished to understand. Ahh but Square likes messing with you and cant resist a sub-plot, cue Laguna (main), Kiros & Ward, three laughable soldiers in the Galbadien Army (who later become a threat to SEED) running around like headless chickens on a journey of old, with Laguna the exact opposite of Squall - a moronic happy-go-lucky journalist. This change of setting and character can be greeted with relief or reluctance as it occurs when things are about to get interesting.
Battles are both improved and altered with the addition of a new "Draw" system, abstracting magic from creatures and specific points in the world, and simpler nice touches like summoning times with button bashing and chance (due to low health) involved with limit breaks. GF's or Guardian Forces (that's summons, eidolons, aons to you an me) are introduced in a brilliant new way, instead of merely stumbling across them all the time, you must battle them or draw them from powerful boss's. All of which is overawed by this games surroundings. When a place has a name like Fisherman's Horizon you know its gunna be weird.. in a good way. Towns like Deling resemble London with an array of shops and structures like Big Ben. Dollet seems like an old French town with cobble roads and 18th century architecture, even the score fits thanks to the genius that is Nobuo Uematsu. I could write a thesis on how spectacular the soundtrack is but I'll just say look at the soundtrack itself for reviews. Such is the realism of the setting but don't be fooled, around the 3rd disc you'll stumble across the city of Esthar, a gigantic technological wonder the size of a continent.. then you wake up as a writer in a rustic village called Windhill, magic. Shame that such an innovative, well designed game is largely considered poor, when really its similar to all the others. It still has the apocalyptic doom threat, it still has a global scourge of an adventure if you're into doing things properly. There's the giant airship that takes you there. SPACE, 7 went into space for a few minutes, 8 goes there for a while and conjures up some of the most cinematic and thrilling events that square couldn't come up with on earth, so much so they put in a song with vocals and as you know that's a special almost rare treat. Plus you can play cards with cactuars on em!

Okay, so I'm clearly biased on this one, have finished this a dozen times or more, 100%'d it, what have you. This is a JRPG from the PS1 era, it features turn based combat, a winding storyline and RPG style equipment and leveling. You play a group of eco terrorists bent on destroying a world controlling corporation who have found a way to tap the planets life force to fuel their powerplants. The real world parallels are obvious and gee could you even have a big name game made by a AAA publisher these days where the main character is a terrorist bombing civilian targets? It would be a bit risqué. Regardless the story moves forward quickly with aliens, rocketships, dolphin riding and so, so much more as the plot unravels across the 3 discs the game originally came on.
-great plot, believable characters who grow over the game, genuine "oh ♥♥♥♥" plot twist moments
-solid mechanics, cool spell system
-amazing soundtrack and solid sound design all over
-some cool graphics sequences (junon anyone?)
-the amount of hidden stuff to find
-huge game that will take you a while to get thru
-some sweet minigames
-Has some pretty adult moments, and mostly executes them in a mature way
-hasn't aged super well, it's amazing the characters are as expressive as they are with the primitive character models in use (no one has mouths for instance)
-JRPG trappings. Some moves have long animations attached to them, after the 50th time seeing the KOTR animation you will be sick of it. Even small things like the battle start animation are a bit slow
- a bit easy, unless you impose limits on yourself to make it harder. Which doesn't seem to have been anticipated by the devs.
So yeah, it's a bit old and clunky but this is a classic game in every regard and the storyline holds up even today. If you haven't experienced it yet and you like RPGs then you really ought to give it a try. Tthis is in my top 5 favorite games

Abzu è uno di quei titoli che non vanno approcciati come un videogioco qualunque, o si rischia di non apprezzarlo appieno. Io per primo ho fatto l'errore di prenderlo all'inizio in un’ottica complezionista, pensando solo al a finire i livelli (e, lo confesso, agli achievements). Mi sono bastati pochi minuti immerso nel suo florido oceano per capire che stavo sbagliando tutto.
Abzu è un viaggio, un’esperienza visiva e sonora nella quale siamo trasportati nel corpo di un misterioso nuotatore, che attraversa i fondali marini e il Grande Blu in una missione mai presentata e mai espressa. Non c’è una storia chiara, e purtroppo si arriva spesso alla fine della prima run senza un’idea chiara di cosa sia successo.
Fortunatamente non è la trama il punto forte di Abzu, ma il suo oceano. Ogni area di ogni livello è un ecosistema mozzafiato in cui flora e fauna marina navigano indisturbate dalla presenza del protagonista, permettendoci di perderci nella danza di pesci e creature marine che ci circonda. Tutto è transposto graficamente in modo semplice ma chiaro, e ogni pesce o creatura viene riportata in modo realistico, sia nell'aspetto che nel comportamento. E' inoltre possibile osservare la fauna da determinate statue da meditazione, che ci permettono di vederle dalla loro prospettiva e ci forniscono il loro nome scientifico.
Muoversi in questi habitat marini è possibile grazie a dei comandi semplici che richiedono giusto il primo capitolo per essere appresi con dimestichezza; questo, unito all'assenza della classica necessità videoludica dell'ossigeno rendono il nuoto in Abzu piacevole e rilassante.
Abzu è un gioco che può essere tranquillamente finito in un paio d'ore, ma consiglio caldamente a chi vorrà provarlo di non fare il mio stesso errore; consiglio di giocarlo attivamente, in un momento tranquillo e con le cuffie, per apprezzare a pieno ciò per cui è stato creato.
Abzu is one of those titles that should not be approached as a standard videogame, or you may not appreciate it properly. I made the initial mistake of taking from a completionist point of view, thinking only about finishing the levels (and, I admit it, the achievements). It took me a few minutes submerged in its flourishing ocean to understand that I was doing everything wrong. Abzu is a journey, a visual and sound experience in which we are transported into the body of a mysterious swimmer, travelling through the the Big Blue in a mission never presented and never expressed. There is no clear story in it, and  unluckily for the players the first run often ends without a clear idea of what has happened.
Fortunately, it's not the storyline Abzu's strong point, but its ocean. Each area of each level is a breathtaking ecosystem where marine flora and fauna swim undisturbed by the presence of the protagonist, allowing us to lose ourselves in the dance of fish and marine creatures that surround us. Everything is transposed graphically in a simple but clear way, and every fish or creature is reported realistically, both in appearance and behavior. It is also possible to observe the fauna by certain meditation statues, which allow us to see them from their perspective and provide us with their scientific name
Moving in these marine habitats is possible thanks to simple commands that require  just the first chapter to be learned with confidence; this, coupled with the absence of the ever-present oxygen necessity, makes swimming in Abzu pleasant and relaxing.
Abzu is a game that can be safely finished in a couple of hours, but I strongly recommend anyone who wants to try it not to make my mistake.
I would advise to play it actively, in a quiet moment and with headphones, to fully appreciate what it was created for.

Oh, you were looking for reviews for this game? Then you have come to the wrong place. Oh, you were looking for a recipe for cabbage rolls? Then you've come to the right place!
Ingredients:
1 pound ground chuck 2 eggs, beaten 1 small onion, chopped 2 3/4 tablespoons regular rice, uncooked 1/2 teaspoon salt 1/4 teaspoon pepper 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder 1 large cabbage 1 medium onion, chopped 1/2 cup shortening, melted 1 (1-pound) soup bone 1 (14 1/2-ounce) can whole tomatoes, undrained and chopped 1 (8-ounce) can tomato sauce 1 cup plus 2 1/2 tablespoons firmly packed brown sugar Dash of sour salt.
Step 1
Combine ground chuck, eggs, 1 small chopped onion, rice, salt, pepper, and garlic powder, mixing well. Set aside.
Step 2
Turn cabbage, core side up. Using a sharp knife, make an incision across the base of the outermost leaf. Gently peel away the leaf. Repeat this process until leaves can no longer be removed without tearing.
Step 3
Make additional incisions around the base of the next outermost leaves. Place cabbage, stem side up, in a colander. Pour boiling water over cabbage until leaves can be easily removed. Repeat procedure until all leaves have been removed.
Step 4
Place 1 tablespoon meat mixture in the base of a cabbage leaf. Roll leaf jellyroll fashion until the mid-section is reached. Fold left side of leaf inward, and roll up remaining length of the leaf. Carefully stuff in the open end, using fingertips. Repeat with remaining meat mixture and cabbage leaves.
Step 5
Sauté remaining chopped onion in shortening in a large Dutch oven. Add soup bone and tomatoes; stir gently.
Step 6
Alternate layers of cabbage rolls and tomato sauce over sautéed onion and tomatoes. Do not stir. Add water to cover. Cover and cook over medium heat 30 minutes.
Step 7
Add brown sugar and sour salt; stir gently. Cover and cook over medium heat 1 hour. Uncover and cook 1 hour.
Step 8
Remove cabbage rolls from cooking liquid, and place on a warm serving platter. Serve immediately.

I've been following the game since I discovered it over a year ago now and it's probably been my most anticipated game ever. I love what the devs have done here and the constant flow of updates following the early access release shows how much they are investing into this. I've played 14 hours of it so far and to be honest, it took me about 6 tries to make my first "proper" airport that I didn't mess up in one way or another, but I enjoyed learning the ins and outs of the game throughout.
The game concept and mechanics are great and I do not agree with some negative reviews saying it is impossible to grow the airport. Building a commercial airport right at the start is only really possible on easy mode or using loans, however you are able to only start with a tower, runway and a GA stand. This will earn you money, which can then be invested in increasing GA capacity, adding fuel services (which you are not required to have, but adds to profits) and later building a terminal and start introducing commercial flights. The game isn't without fault and there are many "easy" fixes that can be made, such as GA planes not arriving from South Africa when your airport is located in Europe. There is also the question of replayability and it will be interesting to see if anything will be done on that aspect of the game. The devs have said that Steam Workshop implementation is in the plans and I honestly can't wait for that, especially if they make it easy to add new objects, new planes/airlines or even new mechanics to the game.
Detail is king in this kind of game and from what I have seen so far, this game is going in the right direction and I can't wait for the future. There is so much potential here and I hope the developers keep doing the amazing job for which I and countless of other people are incredibly grateful for. I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tycoon or prison architect type games and especially anyone who has a particular interest in planes in general.

School Bus Fun is too complex for a child, too childish for an adult, too fast for a service industry game, and too random for a resource management game. Yet somehow it’s still fun to some degree.
School Bus Fun is a service industry game (the sub-genre started by Diner Dash), where your goal is to use your car to transport an increasing number of children to their local school. With this theme and graphics, one would assume this game is made for children to train their memory and help with their hand-eye coordination. While School Bus Fun indeed does all those things, maybe it also overdid it a notch.
As usual in these games, there are over a dozen “customer” types with their increasingly complicated needs. As the game progresses, it gets a lot more difficult meeting these demands in time, especially when there are two cars to control simultaneously. It can get so hectic that even an adult could feel overwhelmed.
Also, unlike most service industry games, the children appear randomly on each attempt. Beyond adding an unneeded level of difficulty, this can result in stages where it is impossible to get the top score without a few resets.
I know it seems I’m only complaining, but the game really is more difficult than it looks. Still, it can be fun, when not frustrating, and may keep you around long enough to reach the seemingly ridiculous 10 and 15-hour achievements.

is an interesting, casual, puzzle game that will test your time-management and logistical-planning abilities.  It is a truly casual game, and even at the end levels it will be easy to “pass” each level; however, to get 3-stars in later levels can be quite a challenge and will require perfect planning and execution in real time.  It is a very basic game, with little depth; but it is a great game for situations where you want to play something that isn’t overly immersive and is easy to put down.
The idea of the game is to pick up children and drop them off at school.  The mechanics are very simplistic.  The game boils down to logistical puzzles that will require you to figure out the optimum paths to take to earn the most points.  You do this by clicking on icons as they pop up on the screen in real time, while being sure to adhere to auxiliary rules that influence your score.  As the game progresses, different types of rules are added; this makes it increasingly difficult to get a 3-star rating in later levels.  Simply “passing” the levels by reaching the par score remains rather easy.

There isn’t much else to say about

Oh boy, oh boy, oh boy. It's here, it's finally here. Well, it's been here for a few months now, but still - WE GOT YS: THE ARK OF NAPISHTIM!
See, when I first found this game (and this was the one that got me into the series), I was immediately hooked on it. I played it on Ps2, loved it and kept playing it on newer saves, harder difficulties. It's such an awesomely fun game. Years later, when I first joined Steam, I came across a sale of Ys games. I was overjoyed... until I found out this game wasn't in the library. So I played some of the others, enjoyed them some, but nothing compared to this game. So when I saw I could finally buy it, I pre-purchased it. And the day it went live, I played the hell outta it. A few months later, I decided to write this review on it, because I'm kinda lazy like that.
So, in Ys: The Ark of Napishtim, you play as Adol the Red, a renown swordsman who saves his crew from a terrible seastorm, only to be thrown off and swept to the sea, washing ashore on a beach where he is found and rescued by 2 young women from the Rehdan clan. You learn about them and their turmoil with humans who live on the other side of the island, you do some adventuring, some exploring, lots of killing and even more dungeon-delving.
Ys is a platforming action-RPG, in the simplest terms. It's got a serviceable story (clearly dated, but still fun), the graphics here are dated as well, but it's ripe with nostalgia for Ys fans. And if you're new to the series or wondering what this game is about, my advice is to just buy the damn game, if you're into similar games (Legend of Zelda comes to mind, though it's nowhere near as expansive.)
I got about 12 hours in my storyline, but I did a lot of backtracking, a lot of grinding and you will, too. Understand that, towards the end, you WILL want to grind up and get yourself ready for some epic boss fights. The game has some really good ones that will make you use all your skills and sweet moves, like Dash Jump and Magic Charge!
Man, I can't get enough of this game. I think it's time I start another New Game and jump right back into this one! DEFINITELY RECOMMEND! (though, I'm not 100% sure what the hell the DLC is I have in this game).
I'll be fair and say there are some cons to this game. Sometimes, enemies can be very cheap. Sometimes, what to do next isn't 100% clear. But those things don't detract from the core fun of the game. If you're never sure what to do, explore - you'll figure it out :)

Really good game, not yet tweaked 100% right, but guaranteed to get there.
Pros:
- The multiple endgame crises. You may remember these from Crusader Kings 2 (The various hordes that invade Europe later in the timeline). I'm not going to spoil too much, but in Stellaris they provide a lot of story that almost every other 4X or Grand Strategy game completely lack. I very much enjoy these RPGish elements. Fallen Empires are a part of this as well. Threatening dormant super powered ancient empires that can only be taken on with end-game tech? Yes please!
- The race designer. Seriously, this stuff is great. Endless Space did this right as well, but Stellaris expands this into typical Paradox directions. Great for replayability, great for strategy, great for role playing.
- The visual design, aliens, ships, the galaxy, the UI, all look gorgeous. Scientifically gorgeous.
- The weapon and defense system, while still under some balance scrutiny, is great. It's not 100% rock paper scissors, and the 20% that isn't provides all the difference. It's a game of poker, of strategy, it even reminded me of magic the gathering deck building. It's great.
- The research system is ingenious. You get a few randomized options of stuff you can research next, and this forces you to make interesting decisions. It isn't so much that is hampers you, it switches up the order in which you get the different great stuff. In some games, you'll be better at colonizing early, in some game you'll get flak early, and in every game, your opponents tech will be different from yours.
- Every anomaly you research has a story, and there are rewards that stick around making a difference till the end of the game.
- The resources are also well designed. I like the way you energy credits are a monthly upkeep. You constantly switch between building a up stockpile, expanding generation capability, and running a deficit to boom.Your combat fleet is a large part of the upkeep, as is your mineral and research generation, and this creates an interesting balance between militarization, economic expansion and research.
Cons:
- I had a lot of fun with my first playthrough, more will follow, but the game isn't as finished or as polished as many other games on release. It's good, not early access, not beta, most game systems are good, but there is clearly still some work needed. I think Paradox is using a different approach to releasing, that is cheaper and in the end manages to actually create a better product. They release a game at 85% power, and then grow it to 130% power using the power of interacting with their customers. Please note that 15% of this 130% is most likely going to be reasonably priced DLCs with good content that I'm probably going to be getting on sale. I'd rather have a game that slowly grows to 115% (for free) or 130% (with DLCs) power than a game that is quickly dumped by it's developers only to be replaced by a completely redeveloped full price sequel that may very well be worse than the old game. I mean, seriously, Total War: Rome 2 and the new Masters of Orion was some ♥♥♥♥ed up♥♥♥♥♥♥that can not be forgiven (While they cost MORE). Crusader Kings 2 however was so amazing it may very well be qualified as a narcotic addictive substance in the near future.
- Time consuming.

The black sheep of the Final Fantasy series, Final Fantasy VIII is a game that divides opinion to this very day. Is it good? Is it bad? Does it make a lick of sense? Is Squall a sexy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? No one entirely agrees on an answer to any of these questions (except for the last one, the answer of which is YES), but I have my own take it. FFVIII is perhaps the most underappreciated games in the entire series. Much like how FFVII deconstructed JRPGs that existed up to that point, FFVIII deconstructs the wave of RPGs that followed in Final Fantasy VII's wake, mocking their tropes and characters, while at the same time telling a very unique story. FFVIII follows Squall Leonheart, a student at Balamb Garden, a military academy that trains SeeDs, a mercenary force designed for one purpose: to hunt down and destroy Sorcerresses. Squall is probably my favorite lead character in a Final Fantasy game, and that has one clear reason: he's realistic. Unlike Cloud or Zidane, he isn't a teenager who can somehow fight the forces of darkness without sweat: he's a flawed person, broken by a crappy childhood and a dehumanising education that taught him how to kill. In essence, he behaves how a real person would in his situation. Over the course of the game, we're treated to a near-constant internal monologue that tells us about the struggles he faces internally and how he deals with them. He's a great lead. The rest of the cast is more mixed, with high points being Irvine, who often reflects Squall, and Laguna, who's chipper attitude is a nice respite from the grim tones of Squall, and low points being the annoying and fairly useless Zell, the bland and boring Quistis, and the game's dumb villain, Ultimecia. The plot itself is also a bit of a mixed bag, with some really good moments offset by some really dumb ones. The battle system is a clear departure from the rest of the series too. Rather than levelling up your characters to build stats, instead, stats are built by "junctioning" magic to various stats to increase their parameters. This is a great system, one ripe for experimentation, hampered by one thing: Drawing. Magic works like items in FF8: once you use a charge, it's gone. The only way to get magic early on is by painstakingly drawing magic from enemies: an incredibly tedious and boring prospect. It's rectified later once you get access to card refinement, but it's still a hassle. Speaking of card refinement. this game comes with a very entertaining trading card diversion called Triple Triad, and it's a blast. Simple, quick, yet endlessly addictive.
So, that's Final Fantasy VIII. Honestly, I love it, and it remains one of my favorites of the series. However, it's a very flawed game, so chances are, you may not like it. However, approach it with an open mind, and I think you'll enjoy what lies in store.

I was recommended this game last year around Halloween by a friend. I checked the game out and seemed like a quirky game I would enjoy. I bought the game and was playing it during its "prime" which only consisted of 2-3 full games around peak hours. If you were lucky you would find 1 full game around night time. The player base was very small to begin with. The Devil's Bluff team chalked it up to struggling advertising and couple that with being (and remains) overpriced for what the game was.
The game initially was how the Devil's Bluff team intended the game to be. It was a mystery who the Devil was and you would only hear whispers or rumors while passing other players finding their clues. "The devil is male/female, the devil is _____, etc". The devil player would genuinely try to keep their dark secret, usually attacking players who are split from their teammate then returning to human form. Nothing was more scary than your teammate turning into the devil before your eyes after collecting a few clues together. But after so many games the Devil players saw no reason to ever return to human form. It became the "norm" for the devil to immediately transform as soon as the game started and begin slaughtering everyone for an easy win.
Most people would agree that a 1v11 game is widely unfair, so the 1 man out (devil) would need to have some slight advantages. The Devil player was more than well equipped to dispatch players with ease. The devil player was faster and stronger than the other 11 players combined. Even if all the players banded together to stop the devil at the start the devil would still win. Human players had no real defense against the devil besides slapping/knocking him to the ground (no damage) and running (he will catch you quickly) or "juking" him which involved enter and leaving rooms or stairs. 2-3 attacks from the devil would knock you out of the game unless another player revives you before your death timer hits 0. Most devil players would just camp around a few downed players yelling for help and then slaughter their would be saviors. The devil had a unending devil form and a secret room which allowed him to view and teleport to rooms of his choosing. The devil won a vast majority of the games unless a team was quick enough with their clues.
Clues were not very randomized in location or order of sequence. When you first started playing the game you really had to think about the clue and what room or item it is referring to. After a few games you quickly noticed clues seemed almost like an ordered set; clue 2 will be in the kitchen, clue 6 will be in the sewers, etc. Players quickly only had to read the first few words in a clue and knew what room and where the clue exactly was. Devil players hardly had any incentive to collect clues or help their teammate because while the devil camps downed players they drop clues(if you don't have that item) upon their death. Although other players could pick them up but it was unlucky they were not guarded by the devil. So a Devil who never collected 1 clue could still win by clues by killing players who collected their clues.
The community was vocal about addressing the clues and devil and had many discussions about different changes that could be implemented or changed. We wanted the game to be better for everyone because it was unique game. Players wanted more clues and they also wanted clues to have a more randomized order. They also wanted the devil to have a timer or cooldown to be in devil form so his reign of unending power wouldn't seem so unfair. The Devil's Bluff team RELECTUNLY implemented some of these changes; mostly involving the devil. I'm not sure which team member it was but I remember the patch release post where he basically called the community a bunch of cry babies so they changed the devil. I was disgusted how this team member mocked and treated players who wanted to improve a game they enjoyed. I was completely done with the Devil Bluff Team or the game at that point. However, I wanted to see the changes; I logged in afterward and the devil had a decreasing strength timer the longer he remains in devil form the weaker he becomes. Sadly, after this change it did not seem to bring anyone back to game and it became barren. Oh, you were looking for reviews for this game? Then you have come to the wrong place. Oh, you were looking for a recipe for cabbage rolls? Then you've come to the right place!
Ingredients:
1 pound ground chuck 2 eggs, beaten 1 small onion, chopped 2 3/4 tablespoons regular rice, uncooked 1/2 teaspoon salt 1/4 teaspoon pepper 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder 1 large cabbage 1 medium onion, chopped 1/2 cup shortening, melted 1 (1-pound) soup bone 1 (14 1/2-ounce) can whole tomatoes, undrained and chopped 1 (8-ounce) can tomato sauce 1 cup plus 2 1/2 tablespoons firmly packed brown sugar Dash of sour salt.
Step 1
Combine ground chuck, eggs, 1 small chopped onion, rice, salt, pepper, and garlic powder, mixing well. Set aside.
Step 2
Turn cabbage, core side up. Using a sharp knife, make an incision across the base of the outermost leaf. Gently peel away the leaf. Repeat this process until leaves can no longer be removed without tearing.
Step 3
Make additional incisions around the base of the next outermost leaves. Place cabbage, stem side up, in a colander. Pour boiling water over cabbage until leaves can be easily removed. Repeat procedure until all leaves have been removed.
Step 4
Place 1 tablespoon meat mixture in the base of a cabbage leaf. Roll leaf jellyroll fashion until the mid-section is reached. Fold left side of leaf inward, and roll up remaining length of the leaf. Carefully stuff in the open end, using fingertips. Repeat with remaining meat mixture and cabbage leaves.
Step 5
Sauté remaining chopped onion in shortening in a large Dutch oven. Add soup bone and tomatoes; stir gently.
Step 6
Alternate layers of cabbage rolls and tomato sauce over sautéed onion and tomatoes. Do not stir. Add water to cover. Cover and cook over medium heat 30 minutes.
Step 7
Add brown sugar and sour salt; stir gently. Cover and cook over medium heat 1 hour. Uncover and cook 1 hour.
Step 8
Remove cabbage rolls from cooking liquid, and place on a warm serving platter. Serve immediately.

The Binding of Isaac is a dark and disturbing game by any measure. I have friends who are not even religious who are offended by the callous depiction of many sacred themes in this game. I am not such a person. This game uses heavy religious themes, themes of heaven and hell, life and death, birth and abortion. The story the player is told at the beginning is all the more disturbing because we have seen such mental illness happen in the news, perhaps experienced it ourselves. Many items in the game are used to reinforce this idea, some to expand upon it. What happened to Isaac's cat? What happened to his brother? His father? His favorite toys? When you pick up your cat's rotting torso as an item, the answer is all too clear.
The game itself is a randomly-generated dungeon crawler along the lines of the original Zelda on NES: go into a room with possible exits to the north, south, east, and west, and kill whatever enemies you find therein and avoid the traps. Once defeated, the exits open and you stave off your fate for a little longer. Every floor features a boss, all of which reflect the themes listed above,
the biblical ones. If you dislike sacrilege or the horrors of mental illness, or if fighting enemies that look like babies in embyonic fluid sacs puts you off, perhaps you should avoid it, otherwise I heartily suggest this game.

TL,DR: Highly recommended, buggy but fun and engaging and surprisingly replayable, and since it is only in alpha one can be confident that it will only get better as bugs are resolved and gameplay expanded.
First, it must be said from the get-go that this is a buggy game -- it's still in alpha, so you are forewarned -- with very poor documentation about game elements and how they function. Certain areas are pretty straightforward -- we've all been to an airport after all, so we all pretty much know what we're supposed to do -- so the lack of information isn't always so crucial but certain areas, in particular the entire baggage handling chain --are needlessly fussy, overly complicated and poorly documented, as well as downright bugged.

The whole baggage handling functionality is a nightmare to figure out, and even once you have figured it out, it is no easy task to sort problems out, modify it and make it reliably functional. You have the sense that the devs said, "OK, all the other stuff is too straight-forward -- let's make baggage handling onto a nightmare to bring this to the next level," and so baggage handling is the Achilles' heel of an otherwise quite enjoyable game, and will annoy you to no end as suddenly all your flights are endlessly delayed because of a misplaced bag that's gone off the edge of the playable world.
At a certain point and far too soon, some major bug closes out your expansionary ambitions. Planes will just decide to sit at one end of the runway for whatever reason and you have no way to clear them, and the devs have simply not yet addressed the problem and added a timeout forcing take-off, and so your game is now over whether you like it or not. In fact, this and other buggy, inscrutable endgames is how every game inevitably ends, making Aiprort CEO pretty frustrating in its present state. Nonetheless, it is a lot of fun along the way and we can only expect that as it matures these bugs will be ironed out, gameplay expanded (there are lots of placeholders indicating it will) and the game will come into its own.

Like other entries in the Ys series, YS VI: The Ark of Napishtim has fun action RPG gameplay, albeit with somewhat level-locked gameplay like typical Ys games. The music's entertaining, memorable, and motivational. What separates this one from the others on steam is that Adol has the ability to jump. It's mainly used for combat, with the downward thrust move being a very common requirement to kill certain enemies. Adol also gets a number of other moves, including a triple combo, sword-specific attacks, an upward whirlwind attack, and a somewhat difficult to execute lunge attack. Top it off with sword-specific magic spells and you have a huge upgrade from previous Ys titles.
The storyline is also pretty strong -- it's not as story rich as Nihon Falcom's The Legend of Heroes franchise, but there's a lot more going on as you unravel the mystery of the archipelago you're trapped on. As is common with Ys games, there are few towns and overall few people, but more emphasis on individual character. Even throwaway NPCs have unique avatars and behaviors, and regularly have something new to say. It's one of those RPGs you may find yourself running around talking to everyone (even twice) after completing a dungeon.
Like other Nihon Falcom games, you get so many save slots that you probably won't need them all. So you're free to save before pretty much every gameplay or story moment and revisit it at any time. More games should be doing this.
My complaints about this game are really minor. Like a lot of these ports, there are occasional graphical glitches on the edges for widescreen users. (which is almost everyone as of 2015) The lunge attack is infamously hard to execute, which is only an issue since it's attached to a long jump which is used to get certain treasures. Finally, I twice got a glitch where the sprites and/or particle effects would just go crazy and had to restart...but haven't had any crashes yet. Both glitches happened when entering a new area and fortunately a save point was nearby and usable. Xseed has had a good track record with stability with all their ports, so this is only a minor blemish.
Go ahead and pick up this one. Enough people pick this up and we'll be sure to get Ys Seven ported over as well.

Really good game, not yet tweaked 100% right, but guaranteed to get there.
Pros:
- The multiple endgame crises. You may remember these from Crusader Kings 2 (The various hordes that invade Europe later in the timeline). I'm not going to spoil too much, but in Stellaris they provide a lot of story that almost every other 4X or Grand Strategy game completely lack. I very much enjoy these RPGish elements. Fallen Empires are a part of this as well. Threatening dormant super powered ancient empires that can only be taken on with end-game tech? Yes please!
- The race designer. Seriously, this stuff is great. Endless Space did this right as well, but Stellaris expands this into typical Paradox directions. Great for replayability, great for strategy, great for role playing.
- The visual design, aliens, ships, the galaxy, the UI, all look gorgeous. Scientifically gorgeous.
- The weapon and defense system, while still under some balance scrutiny, is great. It's not 100% rock paper scissors, and the 20% that isn't provides all the difference. It's a game of poker, of strategy, it even reminded me of magic the gathering deck building. It's great.
- The research system is ingenious. You get a few randomized options of stuff you can research next, and this forces you to make interesting decisions. It isn't so much that is hampers you, it switches up the order in which you get the different great stuff. In some games, you'll be better at colonizing early, in some game you'll get flak early, and in every game, your opponents tech will be different from yours.
- Every anomaly you research has a story, and there are rewards that stick around making a difference till the end of the game.
- The resources are also well designed. I like the way you energy credits are a monthly upkeep. You constantly switch between building a up stockpile, expanding generation capability, and running a deficit to boom.Your combat fleet is a large part of the upkeep, as is your mineral and research generation, and this creates an interesting balance between militarization, economic expansion and research.
Cons:
- I had a lot of fun with my first playthrough, more will follow, but the game isn't as finished or as polished as many other games on release. It's good, not early access, not beta, most game systems are good, but there is clearly still some work needed. I think Paradox is using a different approach to releasing, that is cheaper and in the end manages to actually create a better product. They release a game at 85% power, and then grow it to 130% power using the power of interacting with their customers. Please note that 15% of this 130% is most likely going to be reasonably priced DLCs with good content that I'm probably going to be getting on sale. I'd rather have a game that slowly grows to 115% (for free) or 130% (with DLCs) power than a game that is quickly dumped by it's developers only to be replaced by a completely redeveloped full price sequel that may very well be worse than the old game. I mean, seriously, Total War: Rome 2 and the new Masters of Orion was some ♥♥♥♥ed up♥♥♥♥♥♥that can not be forgiven (While they cost MORE). Crusader Kings 2 however was so amazing it may very well be qualified as a narcotic addictive substance in the near future.

I've played every Ys game so far except the Ys V and Ys Strategy. Ys VI was actually quite enjoyable. I'd say my only complaint is that it was actually pretty short. Admittedly it got even shorter due to an improved warp fuction included in this version.
If you played Felghana, you'll be very used to this overall, including the pacing of the story. The combat is also pretty much the same idea; in this particular game though, you have different swords that you switch between. Don't be intimidated by the thought of some swords working where others don't. They're all effective (on Normal difficulty at least), but have different levels of strength. Where they're different is how you swing them, their innate ability (once unlocked), and their magic (the first upgrade for each sword).
Bosses aren't so bad (again, if on Normal).  If you're rushing through the game, you'll run into the problem of being underleveled. In other games this might only be a minor setback with some strategy. In Ys games, especially this one the game, even on Normal, is going to pretty much force you to grind. While I can't remember my exact level at the time, I can tell you that it was low to the point where I did zero damage to the second boss in the game. Only occasional criticals would even damage him, and those were for very little damage. Loaded the file again, went back and leveled up four or five times, upgraded my swords in the process, then challenged the second boss again. I could damage him for more than I was critting for previously when I did zero damage.
Travelling is bearable now. In the original, there was a ton of backtracking by comparison. The map seems pretty big at first, but once you near the end of the game, you really notice just how tiny it is. Similar to Felghana, but I think even that was bigger than this.
Controls are okay. If you're using a controller, it might take some time to get used to. You can change the bindings, but only in the configuration outside of the game.
They're okay. Just like in Felghana you have these do-nothing characters everywhere in towns you should ignore. There's always a few of these NPCs capable of rewarding you under certain conditions. As far as truly notable or important characters go, there are a couple you'll likely not recognize unless you're a fan or well informed. If you've been playing every Ys game that has been localized, you'll be fine. You'll only really end up wondering who the unfamiliar characters are that Adol seems to know, but you can figure out when they met, since it's just filling in the blank.
The truly important characters don't seem important enough in the big picture. Probably the most important character you'll meet early on and by the end you'll come to realize how little they even do. Meanwhile the other characters, even ones that could be considered minor, practically drive the plot. Yeah, it's a good thing when you think about it. But after taking in everything you notice how insignificant they were by comparison. Even a character I'm certain is the third or fourth most important character in the game is brushed off to the side. He only ever provides one important bit to the story and the rest of his appearances except maybe one other scene are literally unimportant. I could go on and on, but I'm sure you get it. For me personally, this was the weakest part of the game.
People actually love these games for the music. Really most games made by Falcom anyway. I'll tell you right now that the music in this game is not the greatest. I'm sure people will disagree with me, but I feel there's only two themes in the game that're great.
, which is pretty short-lived and the one most everyone can agree on,
. The rest of the tracks are very underwhelming. Memorable, but most are underwhelming. I can compliment the fact that the tunes really match the environment they're played in. That's probably the greatest strength of the soundtrack in this game.
I feel this game is still pretty good considering when it was originally made. If it has any real shortcoming it's probably the short length of time needed to beat it. Hardcore players craving difficulty will probably like the harder difficulties you can play on, including a feature that makes the game feel closer to Ys Origin. Check it out if you have a chance.

I've played nearly 8 hours of this game. The concept is great, but the gameplay doesn't actually match what the trailer or description convey. If you're looking for a deception game like Town of Salem, Werewolf, or BSG where you want to find the secret traitor, you will be disappointed. If you're looking for a scavenger hunt racing game where sometimes you stray and try to tackle someone instead, you will enjoy this.
It is not an 11v1 game: it is a 2v2v2v2v2v2 game where one of the teams is lucky enough to have a faster character that can kill you. The devil is not the "1," because he can still win with his partner. Also, the trailer says things like "betray" and "deceive," but the current win condition encourages the devil to cooperate with his team member. There is no incentive to betray at all. And no, I don't mean "there is an incentive to betray but it's more strategic to cooperate"; I mean there is literally 0 incentive to betray. Because of this, it's not really part of the gameplay.
It's still fun, but the gameplay experience is very different than what the trailer and concept description would have you believe. It's not like Werewolf or Mafia or any deception game, really. I'd liken it more to The Ship (which is cheaper,  has a larger player base, and bots to play against even if you can't find a lobby).
I do think it's worth the $5 I paid for it, but it's not worth $15, especially if you can't play during the scheduled times in the discussion or if you don't have enough friends to guarantee a game. Also, there were so many bugs found within the first month of release that it really felt like I was paying to be a part of a beta instead of paying for a full game. A lot of them have been fixed now, but it's still disappointing that there hasn't been a dev update since December of last year.

The Witcher 2 is an unusual combination of exceptional and mediocre. The attention to detail, visually and audibly are above and beyond the standard of most games released in its time and even to this day. Despite being 5 years old now it still works as a visual benchmark which runs circles around many modern triple AAA games. The world and story design are exceptional, making a tangible and other wordly setting real in a way few rpgs can hope to achieve. The character animations are also exceptional, making the usually repetitive dialogue format of long form rpgs(i.e. where two characters stand in place dispercing large proportions of information) engaging by having a sizable bevvy of preset character animations which make all the characters look and feel more natural. Even once you realize what all the preset gestures and actions are they still do a great job since they are varied and naturally timed enough to the dialogue beats that they manage to convingly make life like what is something usually most games as large as this never have the time to do.
Tragically with all that said, the Witcher 2 is an overwhemingly mediocre, if not outright bad game. It seems clear that the RED engine was the labour of love for this game, because the rest of the whole "game" aspect of this video game feels like such an afterthought. It's clear that CD Project wanted to do something more ambitious this time around for the 2nd entry and created a more real time combat system. However, instead of a simplistic but functional combat minigame like the previous entry we have a real time combat system which seems broken and must have went completely untested for whether or not this combat is actually enjoyable.
You have a roll dodge and block function, as well as a combination of light and heavy attacks, as wells as spells and throwable items.The ability for these damage avoiding functions to be useful need to be unlocked, which only make them barely helpful once done so. The greatest problem is that the player can only block while standing still, which is suicidal for reasons I'll get into later. The attack moves have a randomized set of animations every time you press the attack button, which is certainly good for looking cool, but not so good for having reliably predictable attack moves every time you press the button. The game also uses an auto targeting system in which the player may only attack towards the highlighted enemy rather than where the control stick/mouse is pointed towards. You have the option of hardlocking onto a single enemy, but even if you do not lock on at all the game still cycles a cursor based on where the player character is facing, which means you can frequently end up leaping towards an enemy opposite of where you are pointing the camera or control stick.
All of this could be mitigated if the combat is balanced around this finnicky system, but the scenarios in this game could best be described as "cluster-♥♥♥♥s" from the word go, and from there it only changes to "occaisonally more manageable cluster-♥♥♥♥s" as you obtain necessary upgrades which make the player less crippled. Ignoring whether you enjoy upfront difficulty, this game has little variety in the kind of encounters or gameplay scenarios presented. Every fight is Geralt being placed in a small boxy area with dozens of enemies, in which you have little room to navigate or plan anything. Frequently the game will force Geralt to walk up to the enemies first to trigger a conversation, and then proceed to have you start a fight on top of dozens of enemies, many of which are usually attacking before the game has even finished fading out of the cutscene. If you play this game on the higher difficulties all of the enemies will also be damage sponges who can kill you rapidly, which no amount of leveling will ever fix.
The potion mechanic, a major aspect of the series, has been signficantly gimped as the player can no longer drink them midfight, a bizarre downgrade from the previous game. Since this game is heavily narrative based, it can be difficult to predict when significant battles will occur, which means the player must quicksave frequently to be ready go back and drink potions once they are enlightened of future events. Even then, since dialogues are so frequently intersperced through gameplay, and is taking place in real time, you can frequently find that even when you drink your potions as late as possible that by the time the dialogue is finished the timer on your potions has gone up. Many of the most important battles must be fought without potions, but it doesn't really matter, because another downgrade is just how insubstantial potions now are. They barely increase your health or your damage in a way which makes their prescense felt to the player so they almost might as well not be there.
Everything in this game seems designed to aggrevate the player, by design or accident. Despite the expansive world this game takes place in the player will be penned into these archaic MMO style pens, which are very cramped yet maze like, which will feel big only in how often the game forces you to tread back and forth through them in order to complete a conversation. The sidequests are repetitive after thoughts. There is a needlessly complicated crafting system, which is very time consuming but also useless as better equipment will either be given to you at set plotpoints or can be found exploring. Checkpoints are infrequent, but when set will always be set just before large proportions of dialogue rather than right after it. In trying to 'modernize' the series more, they chose the worst aspects of modern 3rd person games, including forced stealth segments in a format not built for it, and infrequent but unforgiving quicktime events.
The most famous aspect of the series, the intricate morally relative interactive narrative, is still intact. The game is still above standard in writing for a video game and the player will still get to make moral choices which have consequences down the line. Unlike the first one though, there are a lot less choices to make. While the choices that are there certainly do make a difference, the first Witcher had many more self contained quests complete with their own moral conundrums. The Witcher 2 it seems was barely able to get its core story done in time, as later parts of the game seem rushed and unfinished, with the final boss encounter being an info dump of important information before squaring away. Part of this might be because the game is the middle sequel, but knowing that CD Project will design the 3rd game, much like this one, for newer players to not needing to know much of the specifics of the previous game in able to jump in, I can't help but feel like the events in this game won't amount to much of a difference.
CD Project is clearly a very ambitious developer who shoot for big goals. With the Witcher 3 it seems that CD Project were finally able to create the Witcher game they always wanted to make, their first two games being interactive blue prints to the grand opus they always aspired and worked towards making. Despite me not enjoying the first two Witcher games, I find myself liking CD Project more with each game of theirs which I play, enjoying in a sort of masochistic way watching their advancement as a developer. If there's any failings in the first two Witcher games, it is only out of ambition outpacing execution,  which is more to be said for them than for the modern AAA developers who create cookie cutter games poorly and lazily in order to make a deadline for their yearly sequels. Despite my  negative experiences with the first two Witcher games I will continue to look forward to look forward to what CD Project comes up with next. Thank you for taking the time to read this.

This is an excellent strategy game. I couldn't be more happy with this game.
Its custom ship building combined with technology specialization allows for some highly customized gameplay, which lends well to creating a varied experience for strategy gaming.
If you've played Galactic Civilization 2 and wished it was 2 players, this is definitely not a let down. If you were/are a fan of Sid Meier's Civilization, this game is very much in the same vein. The moral choices, and custom race creation allow for some excellent flavor for the world.
Combat is much like combat in Sid Meier's Civilization, a victory is 'randomly generated' based on the stats of the ships/fleet participating in battle. Basically its an odds based system, stacking high damage and defense can guarantee victories. However the game has 3 types of offense and corresponding defense which allows specifically tuned ships to beat much stronger ships simply by focusing the correct defenses/offenses on ships/fleets.
Building your ships is limited to their 'capacity', with each piece be it a; defensive/offensive, propulsion, life support system, etc, taking a piece of that capacity. The more complex a ship, the higher the maintenance and manufacturing cost. Customizing ships and controlling your money, influence (culture), and research generation is where your typical 'meta gameplay' techniques come-in, like any strategy game.
Like any complex game you might get the odd freeze/crash etc, so remember to save. Other than that it's pretty bug free and game design flaw free.

I would not recommend this game to the general player.
One caveat being that I would recommend it to fans of loot/collecting/clearing, as this is obviously meant to be the driving force of Dust. It is a completionist's wet dream. Don't come here looking for a fulfilling story arch, truly engaging characters, or a big amount of variety in combat mechanics though.
The music of Dust is phenomenal, with great battle and fantasy themes serving to enhance the entire game and its atmosphere. The backdrops and scenic color palettes are also fantastic, giving the game a very artistic and welcoming look. Dust has some great level design and is a bunch of fun when chaining large combos and hacking tons of enemies to pieces at once, though the combat truly begins to grow stale and uninspired over the length of the game. That's about it for its more pleasant qualities.
The story itself isn't anything to write home about, and honestly it didn't progress in a manner which caused me to care for any of the characters or their fates. It simply wasn't satisfying.
With regret I must say that Dust does not have anything to really drive most players to keep playing. The only reason I personally kept pressing forward until its resolution was because I had already invested so much time and effort into beating it on a tough difficulty as a challenge. I suggest playing on such a difficulty if you want to curse your existence.

Not a bad game; it's been a very long time since I played a game that could be called an airport tycoon simulator.
My main points of criticism right now are that the game seems to be having trouble on a high-end CPU with no more than 600-700 AI agents in play, and that the game tends to require an occasionally frustrating amount of micromanagement. Additionally, the simulation seems to have trouble working properly if you accelerate time while there's a lot happening. For example, if you have a complex baggage system, bags may stop moving at accelerated speed (causing some obvious issues). Finally, the game seems to have been developed with ease of development in mind, and not necessarily user-friendliness. Players are told what the AI pathfinding is thinking, but not clearly notified of some major issues with the airport.
In terms of desired features, I'd like to see multi-level designs, like most airports have, as well as for multiple secure zones to be stabilized. Both would go a long way towards making airports more realistic.
Parking for passengers would be an interesting feature as well.
Otherwise, the game is relatively stable, and a good deal of fun.

What's a legendary scarlet-maned vagabond to do?  Washed up in a magical storm-encircled archipelago uneasily shared by pretty beastfolk and human castaways, Adol the Red must once again take up arms against ancient relics of the Eldeen gone loco.  The story, while it does take its time to get rolling, is classic Ys goodness and contains a lot of juicy bits about ancient Atlas.
As the first 3D Ys game, I expected it to be a bit rougher than
or
-- and it was, but chiefly in this regard:  the boss battles.  They are a little too sloppy and clippy, and most of these bad boys (and girls) believe in saturating the screen with so many projectiles that you can't help getting hit no matter your skill.  For this reason,
You don't need them in the slicker later entries, but you'll have a lot less fun if you don't take advantage of them here!  Don't be a cowboy.  You'll be a grumpy cowboy.
The character designs are really nice and the graphics are pretty good for such an old polygonal game.  There are two villages full of brightly hued people who may initially seem surly, but all of whom have a heart of gold deep down (this part is a requisite for Ys and I'll admit, sap that I am, that it's one of my favorite non-gameplay aspects).  The levels themselves are well-drafted, with some nice platforming sequences scattered throughout.  With only the boss fights leaving something to be desired,
is a darned good game, recommended to action RPG-lovers and required for Ys fans.

Having just completed this game, I can say without a doubt that it is one of the more challenging platformers I have played in my time. Despite some ragey moments, the game was very much a positive experience for me. I enjoyed the level design, Pixelated Cupcake did a lot with a little, as he constructed engaging stages that always helped the player grow.
What you'll find in this game depends primarily on what you are looking for. Do you want a rage game? If so, this game will definately scratch that itch, not by being unfair though, simply by being brutal in what it demands from you in terms of execution. Do you want a precision platformer? Again, this game will give you that experience, if you are willing to forgive the occasional glitch. Do you want a game that guides you? This game does indeed guide you, it just does so by punishing your failures and nominally rewarding your successes.
Basically, if you are seeking a platformer that will test your mental abilities as well as your reactions, then you should certainly give Hyper Box a try. Don't expect much in the way of unfair deaths, but don't expect to be able to skate by on luck either.

Another excellent Ys game from Falcom, with another great translation from XSeed. Ys VI grabbed the Zelda-esque gameplay from the Japan-exclusive Ys V, and made it 3D, and improved it in many ways.
Visually, Ys VI uses a strange Donkey Kong Country-esque rendering style for the character sprites, which hasn't aged that well, in all honesty. Unlike the PS2 version, which used polygons for the characters, the PC version of Ys VI doesn't, nor does it reflect equipment changes on Adol's model, which is unfortunate, but easily ignored.
The music is the usual high quality, catchy, upbeat tracks that Falcom is known for, with a fair amount of stand out tracks. Sound effects are what you'd expect, sword swipes, monster growls. The PS2 version's voice acting is not in this version, for better or for worse.
As stated earlier, Ys VI uses the Zelda-like action style from Ys V, unlike Ys I, II, and IV. Much like 'regular' action games, you have buttons for attacking, with a combo depending on which of three swords you have equipped, a jump button, your 'magic' button, and an item use button. The item use button stands out here, as the ability to stockpile and use items wasn't in the other two Ys games of this style, Oath in Felghana or Origins. This, with the right amount of health items, makes Ys VI rather easy, if you choose to use the items. But you don't have to! XSeed added in a brand new 'catastrophe' mode, that removes the ability to stockpile or buy healing items, instead making them instant-use when you pick them up on the field. Instead of health items, a store will now sell permanent stat-growth seeds. This, obviously, radically changes the game. Also new to this PC version is the ability to fast travel between save points, which is very welcome.
The story is more or less what you'd expect from an Ys title. Basic enough, just there to give protagonist Adol Christin a reason to save the day and adventure.
Ultimately, while not as good as Ys: Oath in Felghana, Ys VI: The Ark of Napishtim is still better than Ys Origin, though all three are very easily recommended.  Now, XSeed, Ys Seven and Ys: Memories of Celceta PC ports when?

Good: Great early to mid game.  The best "sim" aspect of any 4x space game.  Micro-managers wet dream.
Bad:
1. Diplomacy is horrific.  Early to mid it is worthless.  Late it is nearly impossible move a faction one way or another.
2. Combat is very simply early to mid almost so much so that it is boring.  Late combat is nearly impossible.  During the late stages when you have 10+ core sectors and you are part of a federation your navy is huge.  Probably around 50k+.  If your federation fights another alliance/federation that is of equil footing, just forget it.  You will get plastered.  Not because their fleet is bigger but because the computer just moves faster.  Not just thinking, their ships just move faster.  Now you might be thinking that is why my computer allies are for right?  Wrong.  Your computer allies does basically one thing when you as a federation/alliance go to war.  They all come to your biggest fleet and just follow you around.  I don't know if that is design flaw or intention but it sucks.  The computer fed/alliance is sending ships to like 10 to 15 systems all in small batches with landing forces.  As soon as they see your big fleet they jump and scatter.  It is IMPOSSIBLE to catch them.  I believe the intention to this tactic was to promote defense stations as they have FTL scramblers.  But at this stage a fleet that huge will blast that station and when your bigger fleet pops in will run and scatter.  Super frustrating.  It is an impossible endeavor to protect a large empire.
3. You cannot win a large map.  Victory conditions are 40% of inhabitable planets or complete domination.  600 stars = forever to conquer 40% let alone complete domination.  Even if this was doable (and I suppose several months of play time and you theoretically good) the combat system makes it impossible.  One big war and you are done.  There is no coming back from that.  The war will last forever because of their "warscore" method.  It would be an insanely long war.
I know this sounds pretty bad.  I am bit emotional because I just had my long game just get wrecked due to the combat system.  It is a great game, but right now they need to address some key late game issues.
If you have the money try it out.  If you are a little tight on funds wait a few months.

It seems every month several of these minimalist precision platform games are released onto Steam. Some of them are actually very good games such as Hyper Box but there comes a point where even being very good stops mattering because the market is flooded full of them.  With a saturated marketplace the most important thing that a game in this genre needs to be able to demonstrate is innovation. What makes it different than other games in the genre? If there’s no point of differentiation then a game will get lost in the crowd. You’ll have your early adopters and then you’ll hit the point where you’re nothing but a blip on the longtail. Unfortunately, I believe that Hyper Box will end up as another one of those blips on the long tail.
For starters, the game instantly reminds me of Russpuppy’s The Deletion. While there is definitely some differentiation between the two games they play somewhat similarly – more than just being in the same genre – but Pixelated Cupcake’s game is darker in its scheme. Both games are very good at what they are trying to achieve but a consumer who has the choice between the two probably only has the later release date of this game as a reason to purchase this over the other. However, even that may work against it if the consumer is aware of both titles because the older game has had greater opportunity for review and is a dollar cheaper.
But as I said this game does hit the mark. It is difficult as good games in the minimalist precision platform genre need to be but more importantly the game play is addictive. It very quickly becomes a one more turn type of game. Unless you are some sort of gaming god the chances of you dying multiple times perhaps even hundreds of times trying to complete the levels is seriously high. But you’ll want to battle on and unlock the unlockables within the game. They truly feel rewarding when you do because of the amount of hard work you’ve put into the game to get to them.  The only downside is that the game becomes repetitive but that is another thing to expect with the genre.
In all, I can recommend this game if you’re not burnt out on the genre. There’s not enough new to warrant a purchase if you are but expect a solid game that is what it wants to be.

While I certainly didn't know what I was expecting when first trying Stellaris, given Paradox's track record in the grand strategy arena, I figured I'd give it a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Now, I've played other sci-fi space colonization games (Endless Space, Civ: Beyond Earth, Sins of a Solar Empire, etc.) and often I feel kinda lost as to what to do, given the scale of some of these 4Xers. Stellaris, however, makes it easier to breathe in the vacuum of space, letting you have control not only over your fleets (from design, style, and equipment to technology you can salvage and research from some wrecks) and buildings, but the ethics, political views, and objectives of your species. Will you play a hive-mind race of fungoid invaders or do you envision yourself as the Earth's latest global leader as a prime minister or a despot? And with the mods already out as well as in the works (some of which include Star Wars and Warhammer reimaginings), there's no telling what new frontiers you'll be exploring next.
While like other Paradox games where players are left mainly to determine their own objectives, spurred on by missions and side quests, I have two minor complaints: the lack of a clear end goal (namely through the removal of prestige as a game mechanic/score to compare against other nations), and the lack of random decisions (at least, there seems to be less of them than prior Clausewitz-based games, but Stellaris' definitely have more detail and compelling storylines that want you craving more to read). Regardless, give it time and someone will probably fill in those gaps so as I said, I'd consider them very minor at most. You'll be too busy trying to manager your off-world colonies and defending the borders of your interstellar empire to notice anyway.

The Witcher 2 is an unusual combination of exceptional and mediocre. The attention to detail, visually and audibly are above and beyond the standard of most games released in its time and even to this day. Despite being 5 years old now it still works as a visual benchmark which runs circles around many modern triple AAA games. The world and story design are exceptional, making a tangible and other wordly setting real in a way few rpgs can hope to achieve. The character animations are also exceptional, making the usually repetitive dialogue format of long form rpgs(i.e. where two characters stand in place dispercing large proportions of information) engaging by having a sizable bevvy of preset character animations which make all the characters look and feel more natural. Even once you realize what all the preset gestures and actions are they still do a great job since they are varied and naturally timed enough to the dialogue beats that they manage to convingly make life like what is something usually most games as large as this never have the time to do.
Tragically with all that said, the Witcher 2 is an overwhemingly mediocre, if not outright bad game. It seems clear that the RED engine was the labour of love for this game, because the rest of the whole "game" aspect of this video game feels like such an afterthought. It's clear that CD Project wanted to do something more ambitious this time around for the 2nd entry and created a more real time combat system. However, instead of a simplistic but functional combat minigame like the previous entry we have a real time combat system which seems broken and must have went completely untested for whether or not this combat is actually enjoyable.
You have a roll dodge and block function, as well as a combination of light and heavy attacks, as wells as spells and throwable items.The ability for these damage avoiding functions to be useful need to be unlocked, which only make them barely helpful once done so. The greatest problem is that the player can only block while standing still, which is suicidal for reasons I'll get into later. The attack moves have a randomized set of animations every time you press the attack button, which is certainly good for looking cool, but not so good for having reliably predictable attack moves every time you press the button. The game also uses an auto targeting system in which the player may only attack towards the highlighted enemy rather than where the control stick/mouse is pointed towards. You have the option of hardlocking onto a single enemy, but even if you do not lock on at all the game still cycles a cursor based on where the player character is facing, which means you can frequently end up leaping towards an enemy opposite of where you are pointing the camera or control stick.
All of this could be mitigated if the combat is balanced around this finnicky system, but the scenarios in this game could best be described as "cluster-♥♥♥♥s" from the word go, and from there it only changes to "occaisonally more manageable cluster-♥♥♥♥s" as you obtain necessary upgrades which make the player less crippled. Ignoring whether you enjoy upfront difficulty, this game has little variety in the kind of encounters or gameplay scenarios presented. Every fight is Geralt being placed in a small boxy area with dozens of enemies, in which you have little room to navigate or plan anything. Frequently the game will force Geralt to walk up to the enemies first to trigger a conversation, and then proceed to have you start a fight on top of dozens of enemies, many of which are usually attacking before the game has even finished fading out of the cutscene. If you play this game on the higher difficulties all of the enemies will also be damage sponges who can kill you rapidly, which no amount of leveling will ever fix.
The potion mechanic, a major aspect of the series, has been signficantly gimped as the player can no longer drink them midfight, a bizarre downgrade from the previous game. Since this game is heavily narrative based, it can be difficult to predict when significant battles will occur, which means the player must quicksave frequently to be ready go back and drink potions once they are enlightened of future events. Even then, since dialogues are so frequently intersperced through gameplay, and is taking place in real time, you can frequently find that even when you drink your potions as late as possible that by the time the dialogue is finished the timer on your potions has gone up. Many of the most important battles must be fought without potions, but it doesn't really matter, because another downgrade is just how insubstantial potions now are. They barely increase your health or your damage in a way which makes their prescense felt to the player so they almost might as well not be there.
Everything in this game seems designed to aggrevate the player, by design or accident. Despite the expansive world this game takes place in the player will be penned into these archaic MMO style pens, which are very cramped yet maze like, which will feel big only in how often the game forces you to tread back and forth through them in order to complete a conversation. The sidequests are repetitive after thoughts. There is a needlessly complicated crafting system, which is very time consuming but also useless as better equipment will either be given to you at set plotpoints or can be found exploring. Checkpoints are infrequent, but when set will always be set just before large proportions of dialogue rather than right after it. In trying to 'modernize' the series more, they chose the worst aspects of modern 3rd person games, including forced stealth segments in a format not built for it, and infrequent but unforgiving quicktime events.
The most famous aspect of the series, the intricate morally relative interactive narrative, is still intact. The game is still above standard in writing for a video game and the player will still get to make moral choices which have consequences down the line. Unlike the first one though, there are a lot less choices to make. While the choices that are there certainly do make a difference, the first Witcher had many more self contained quests complete with their own moral conundrums. The Witcher 2 it seems was barely able to get its core story done in time, as later parts of the game seem rushed and unfinished, with the final boss encounter being an info dump of important information before squaring away. Part of this might be because the game is the middle sequel, but knowing that CD Project will design the 3rd game, much like this one, for newer players to not needing to know much of the specifics of the previous game in able to jump in, I can't help but feel like the events in this game won't amount to much of a difference.
CD Project is clearly a very ambitious developer who shoot for big goals. With the Witcher 3 it seems that CD Project were finally able to create the Witcher game they always wanted to make, their first two games being interactive blue prints to the grand opus they always aspired and worked towards making. Despite me not enjoying the first two Witcher games, I find myself liking CD Project more with each game of theirs which I play, enjoying in a sort of masochistic way watching their advancement as a developer. If there's any failings in the first two Witcher games, it is only out of ambition outpacing execution,  which is more to be said for them than for the modern AAA developers who create cookie cutter games poorly and lazily in order to make a deadline for their yearly sequels. Despite my  negative experiences with the first two Witcher games I will continue to look forward to look forward to what CD Project comes up with next. Thank you for taking the time to read this.

Having completed the Steam version and PS1 version back to back, here are a few things I noted:
- The button layout can be confusing in certain sequences if using a controller, for example; telling you to press B2 or B5 as instructed, requiring you to remember your controllers personal button layout.
- All polygons look much better in this version, obviously, but it often clashes very unnaturally with the low res backdrops.
- A lot of the ported-to-midi music is noticably worse than the original, some peices sounding broken and off key
- Character portraits look a lot nicer and more detailed in Steam version.
- The gameplay seems to have been sped up by about 25%, which makes the frame rate APPEAR smoother, although animations still seem to be quite choppy. Particularly makes battles and traversing the world map seem much smoother!
- Various scenes will load much faster, ie; card battles and the startup screen, which is a big quality of life difference!
- 360 degree movement doesn't work by default, only 8 direction. I'm not sure if this can be modded.
When all is said and done, I personally prefer the original PS1 version, but if you don't have access to it, this version is not a bad option either. Hope this was helpful. :)
