Final Fantasy VIII was the point where the series reached a whole new level, thanks to small changes like the focus on the romantic story elements and the more realistic character design. The Steam edition includes a few additional features over the old PC release, making it one of the best ports of the game so far, recommended for old fans or newcomers who would like to experience one of the gems of the golden age of Final Fantasy.
Final Fantasy VIII was sort of a trailblazer when it came out. This was the first Final Fantasy game where we said goodbye to the traditional NES/SNES era cartoonish characters in favour of a more realistic design, and where the romance plot-- which is normally a secondary or tertiary storyline in similar games-- is promoted to be in the focus.
This won’t turn FFVIII into a romance/dating game, far from it: your main task is still to save the world/universe from the ridiculous-haired main villain. To do so you’ll have to gather friends and allies, explore much of the planet, and of course slowly discover a rich backstory told in two separate timelines, which will eventually (with a little guess work) uncover one of the most confusing, yet best-written stories of the genre.
Gameplay-wise FFVIII is a bit of an odd one out in the series with the large amount of gameplay changes it features. Although a lot could be said about these, the length of a Steam review simply cannot hold this much information, so let’s just say that some of them, like the expanded Limit Breaks, are favourably looked upon and work well; while others, like the junction system, were met with great opposition and never returned in later games.
The Steam version can be considered a well enough port of the original PlayStation release, with a bunch of really nice technical features, including better display compatibility and more user-friendly controlling. Sadly, like the Steam version of Final Fantasy VII, it features a subpar version of the original PSX music tracks, the same ones that were used in the original PC version.
Overall, the Steam Edition is Final Fantasy VIII may not be the HD remake lot of people still want, but it is a good port of an excellent game, well worth of owning and playing, even if you have the original PSX disc somewhere.

The Binding of Isaac is, at first glance, is disgusting, and at times a little silly, but undeniably fun. If you played Two sessions as Issac, that might be the end of it. But give this game a little time, a little effort, and you'll start to see the real depth that lies within. The Binding of Issac does proceedurally generated dungeons right: The room you enter may not always be a challenge, but depending on what items you have at the time, and what transpires after you take a mystery pill, or make a deal with the devil, can compleately change the the flow of gameplay and sometimes, ruin your chance at victory (I speak from experience). The Binding of Issac is one of a handful of games of our generation that is inherantly fun; Playing it is just, fun. It doesn't matter if you win or lose, if you find the one item you so desprately need or not, at some point, none of that matters anyore, and I find myself saying "I didn't win, but I had fun getting to where I died". And when you look back at the death skreen filled with every item you've collected, you see the choices you made, or how close you came and it inspires you for next time, because every game starts with a blank room, reminding you of your controls, and every run hold potential for greatness.

Do yourself a favor: If your a fan of permadeath, and proceeduraly generated games and pick this up as soon as you can.

NOTE:There are some issues with this game on steam. It freezes on startup by default, but you can fix it by going to the community guides. Or you could replace the dosbox with your own or even use a mod called gzdoom which again you can find in the community guides. My review will be based on the game without alterations and was done by confuguring dosbox manually.
The sequel to one of the most influenal games ever made, takes what the first one laid down and makes it even better. Graphically not much has changed, but there seems to be more effort put into wall designs so it has a bit more variation. The rooms also can get quite a bit bigger than the first doom, and the levels can last longer too but the same quality level design is still there so I almost never got lost(and the map still helps if you do). It also cranked up the number of enemies you fight at once.
You only have one new weapon(super shotgun), which seems disapponting at first, but I never felt limited at all. Every weapon has it's place and adding too much more would probably lead to certain weapons being useless. There are many new enemy types and all of them are fun(I did find the pain elemental to be tedious at first, but once you know how to take care of him he fits right in) and the sound design adds new sounds and tracks that in many ways are even better than the first, they just stick out more to me. The controls remain the same as the first but they do have you use dashes more in the levels, which really works and leads to some cool sections to play through. There are plenty of new levels to enjoy, filled with secrets and even hidden levels, and all this gives the game great replay value.
I talked about the lack of a new final boss in episode 4 on the first game, and they made up for it here, as the last boss is great and deserves the name final boss. I did notice that they use teleporters much more in this game and this is fine, though one or twice I got killed by an enemy that knew I was coming or was behind me. But doom fans say this is better that the orignal, and it is. Everything that worked in the first was done even better here. And that's saying a lot since I loved the first doom. Aside from the few things I nickpicked I really felt satisfied with this game. Get it without hesitation.

Having accumulated 18hrs of gameplay and having in mind this is early acces - prealpha stuff
# There's no real sense of progress, other than General Aviation, Commercial requires you to straight up use most of the items in the game just to get going which means there's no feeling in progress or rewards with new items/functionality which is the base of every tycoon game out there and it makes sense, that's the whole point of the genre so not sure how long you can go in to this game with this model of advancement.
# There's quite a few game-breaking bugs.
# Some mechanisms are infuriating and provide no real explanation on what's wrong / how things work (i.e. baggage and all that goes with it).
# You could have all the staff, vehicles and installations in the world, you will still have delays because what can only be described as a delay in the AI itself.
# If you want a sandbox mode, you can either select Sandbox mode or you can simply build a lot of small stands and set them to GA (General Aviation). Parking fees alone will give you all the income you'll ever need.
# Optimization is non existant, be aware, anything bigger than a small-ish airport will cause your FPS to drop way to low. I want to say this is understandable this early, but I'm also worried. If the base game is this poorly optimized, then it isn't going to get a hole lot better (look at Banished for example, same problem, was never trully fixed and End-Game was horrible because of this).
Now you may be wondering why this is marked as possitive review. I'm just giving you the negative aspects of what's otherwise, a fun game and well-worthed the asking price. For now I will not play anymore until it's matured a bit more but I look forward to that happening.

When this game was originally released in the Windows XP days, I imported it in a box from Japan and found a dialog patch so I could play it -- I wrote an email to Falcom to request that they allow me to purchase it, and they actually made it happen for me. I'll always love them for that. I'd never imported anything like that before, but that's how exciting I considered this evolution of the franchise to be, and based on experience I knew that it would never see our shores in any official capacity.
However, I was wrong, and was delighted to see eventual releases on both the PSP and the PS2.
Neither of those versions were pure, though -- the PSP had dramatically down-sampled textures and really long load times between scenes, while the PS2 version swapped out all the in-game character sprites for 3D models that didn't convey the charm of the 2.5D original. I had an "I'll take what I can get attitude," and was still grateful.
But to see a fully translated official port released on Steam is a real dream-come-true for me. I couldn't be more excited to play my old favorite, and this release does not let me down -- it's the perfect balance; all the original content is here, and none of the art is lost, but it sure does look cool on today's higher-resolution screens.
At the same time, the game is now considered "low spec" enough that it would run gorgeously even on a Windows netbook. It's the perfect hardcore Action RPG to take with you on the go. I only keep a couple games installed on my machine at all times and this is one of them. Very pleased that this publishing arrangement was reached so that the original version of this awesome game could finally be released outside of Japan.

A great RPG game, full of fantasy, battles, great music, a great story and much more. Whether you're after nostalgia like me, a newer entrant to the series who hasn't played the older games, or someone who just fancies a new RPG, then I can recommend this. If you've played Ys: Oath in Felghana or Ys: Origins and liked them, you'll definitely like this one. The gameplay is like the last two (though this game was the one that inspired those title's gameplay mechanics) and there is a lot of action, item finding, gold/xp/emel grinding, and silly, but insanely deadly hidden bosses.
- Gameplay: This game is a fun action-based platformer. Again, if you liked Oath and Origins, you'll like this. That said, Oath and Origins were based off of Ys 6's gameplay, so those games did perfect what Ys 6 tried to do.
- Graphics: This game definitely shows its age (it was made many moons ago) and a lot of it is a mix of 2D and 3D sprites/models/maps. Its not bad looking, but it could look better.
- Content: I would say it does not have as much as Oath or Origins, but it has enough to satisfy you and give you some hours worth of entertainment.
- The story itself isn't too bad as it will pull you in and keep you interested, much like the other Ys titles.
The one thing I really wish this game was Alma's Trials as those dungeons were fun and it did help with the level grinding, especially after level 50. I am glad, however, we were spared the awful voice acting of the PS2 version, lol.
All in all, this game is a pretty good game. Ys 6 got me into the series when I played it on the PS2. I'm really glad people are porting these titles to Steam. The Ys games are basically hidden RPG gems that have provided me countless hours of entertainment. If you are looking for a fun action RPG that will satisfy your inner platformer/grinder and/or you liked previous Ys titles, pick this game up today!

Final Fantasy VIII was the point where the series reached a whole new level, thanks to small changes like the focus on the romantic story elements and the more realistic character design. The Steam edition includes a few additional features over the old PC release, making it one of the best ports of the game so far, recommended for old fans or newcomers who would like to experience one of the gems of the golden age of Final Fantasy.
Final Fantasy VIII was sort of a trailblazer when it came out. This was the first Final Fantasy game where we said goodbye to the traditional NES/SNES era cartoonish characters in favour of a more realistic design, and where the romance plot-- which is normally a secondary or tertiary storyline in similar games-- is promoted to be in the focus.
This won’t turn FFVIII into a romance/dating game, far from it: your main task is still to save the world/universe from the ridiculous-haired main villain. To do so you’ll have to gather friends and allies, explore much of the planet, and of course slowly discover a rich backstory told in two separate timelines, which will eventually (with a little guess work) uncover one of the most confusing, yet best-written stories of the genre.
Gameplay-wise FFVIII is a bit of an odd one out in the series with the large amount of gameplay changes it features. Although a lot could be said about these, the length of a Steam review simply cannot hold this much information, so let’s just say that some of them, like the expanded Limit Breaks, are favourably looked upon and work well; while others, like the junction system, were met with great opposition and never returned in later games.
The Steam version can be considered a well enough port of the original PlayStation release, with a bunch of really nice technical features, including better display compatibility and more user-friendly controlling. Sadly, like the Steam version of Final Fantasy VII, it features a subpar version of the original PSX music tracks, the same ones that were used in the original PC version.
Overall, the Steam Edition is Final Fantasy VIII may not be the HD remake lot of people still want, but it is a good port of an excellent game, well worth of owning and playing, even if you have the original PSX disc somewhere.

The definitive version of Ark of Napishtim, if only because XSeed made all the save points warpable and also the added a game mode that makes healing items work like they do in the other Ark engine trilogy games.  It doesn't have the Alma Trials from the PS2 release but the warpable save points go much further in making the game more enjoyable to play.
That said, Ys VI certainly shows its age as the first 3D Ys game, as Oath and Origins improve on basically everything that Ys VI tried to do; not that Ys VI is a bad game, but it has some clear flaws.  One of those was a lot of backtracking that is made moot in this version with the introduction of an item that you get about two hours into the game that lets you warp to all previously visited save points.  This removes a lot of unnecessary frustration and backtracking.
Some other problems include really weird level/enemy scaling.  Ys games have always been level dependent, but Ys VI takes into another level, as most areas will have enemies that can easily wreck you at first, but after a couple of levels, you'll be wrecking them.  It's a super-fast turnaround with little subtlety. In my playthough of this, I reached the second boss on like level 14 or something with a level two sword and literally couldn't damage it.  The game's action is fast-paced and fluid, and you level up quickly if you're considered underleveled, but you ♥♥♥♥ed up the level scaling somewhere when this kind of thing can happen. Bosses are rather uninspired compared to the other Ark trilogy games, and Limewater Cave is probably the worst dungeon in a Ys game.  Dash-jumping also is a pain that was abandoned after this game.
Onto the positives, even though the gameplay is a bit behind Oath and Origins, it's still fast-paced and has a good feel.  Most of the gameplay is just jumping around and hitting♥♥♥♥♥♥with your sword and is relatively simple but it's satisfying beyond the sum of its parts.  Adol moves fast, swings his sword fast and it just feels right.
It's a Falcom Sound Team jdk soundtrack so you know it rules, though it's one of the more unmemorable ones.  The story and characters are generic, typical Ys fare.
This review comes off as sort of negative, but I mainly want to highlight Ys VI being the predecessor to Oath and Origins and that you should adjust your expectations accordingly.  If you have only played the Ys games on Steam, go into this knowing that it's the foundation the next two games improved on in every way.
In short, a fast-paced, flawed action game that XSeed did a great job handling and worth a look if you have any interest in action games or other Ys titles.

There really needs to be a star system.  I am going to say no but just barely.
Good: Great early to mid game.  The best "sim" aspect of any 4x space game.  Micro-managers wet dream.
Bad:
1. Diplomacy is horrific.  Early to mid it is worthless.  Late it is nearly impossible move a faction one way or another.
2. Combat is very simply early to mid almost so much so that it is boring.  Late combat is nearly impossible.  During the late stages when you have 10+ core sectors and you are part of a federation your navy is huge.  Probably around 50k+.  If your federation fights another alliance/federation that is of equil footing, just forget it.  You will get plastered.  Not because their fleet is bigger but because the computer just moves faster.  Not just thinking, their ships just move faster.  Now you might be thinking that is why my computer allies are for right?  Wrong.  Your computer allies does basically one thing when you as a federation/alliance go to war.  They all come to your biggest fleet and just follow you around.  I don't know if that is design flaw or intention but it sucks.  The computer fed/alliance is sending ships to like 10 to 15 systems all in small batches with landing forces.  As soon as they see your big fleet they jump and scatter.  It is IMPOSSIBLE to catch them.  I believe the intention to this tactic was to promote defense stations as they have FTL scramblers.  But at this stage a fleet that huge will blast that station and when your bigger fleet pops in will run and scatter.  Super frustrating.  It is an impossible endeavor to protect a large empire.
3. You cannot win a large map.  Victory conditions are 40% of inhabitable planets or complete domination.  600 stars = forever to conquer 40% let alone complete domination.  Even if this was doable (and I suppose several months of play time and you theoretically good) the combat system makes it impossible.  One big war and you are done.  There is no coming back from that.  The war will last forever because of their "warscore" method.  It would be an insanely long war.
I know this sounds pretty bad.  I am bit emotional because I just had my long game just get wrecked due to the combat system.  It is a great game, but right now they need to address some key late game issues.
If you have the money try it out.  If you are a little tight on funds wait a few months.

Yet another shore to wash up on, yet another maiden to rescue, yet another dark god to kill, yet another Ys game. Of all the ones released on Steam, this is my least favorite. Ys games have always been grindy, but this is a step above. I grind, and I grind, until I'm only just strong to beat the boss, then I grind some more and now I can 2 shot bosses with magic?
The feeling of getting stronger in Ys is a numbers game. Do you do 0 damage, and the enemy does 200? Find a new gear and level up three times. Now your damage numbers are equal. Level up a few more times and now your numbers are 200 and that old monster does 0. It's always been this way, but skill only matters at that mid point where your numbers are equal. You
defeat monsters that are a level above you, and vice versa for monsters you're a level above. Games shouldn't offer you weapons that require huge grind investments if, once you get them, you're too high leveled for any boss the game throws your way. My higher numbers shouldn't completely overwhelm the previously unkillable boss, just make it marginally easier.

While I certainly didn't know what I was expecting when first trying Stellaris, given Paradox's track record in the grand strategy arena, I figured I'd give it a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Now, I've played other sci-fi space colonization games (Endless Space, Civ: Beyond Earth, Sins of a Solar Empire, etc.) and often I feel kinda lost as to what to do, given the scale of some of these 4Xers. Stellaris, however, makes it easier to breathe in the vacuum of space, letting you have control not only over your fleets (from design, style, and equipment to technology you can salvage and research from some wrecks) and buildings, but the ethics, political views, and objectives of your species. Will you play a hive-mind race of fungoid invaders or do you envision yourself as the Earth's latest global leader as a prime minister or a despot? And with the mods already out as well as in the works (some of which include Star Wars and Warhammer reimaginings), there's no telling what new frontiers you'll be exploring next.
While like other Paradox games where players are left mainly to determine their own objectives, spurred on by missions and side quests, I have two minor complaints: the lack of a clear end goal (namely through the removal of prestige as a game mechanic/score to compare against other nations), and the lack of random decisions (at least, there seems to be less of them than prior Clausewitz-based games, but Stellaris' definitely have more detail and compelling storylines that want you craving more to read). Regardless, give it time and someone will probably fill in those gaps so as I said, I'd consider them very minor at most. You'll be too busy trying to manager your off-world colonies and defending the borders of your interstellar empire to notice anyway.

NOTE:There are some issues with this game on steam. It freezes on startup by default, but you can fix it by going to the community guides. Or you could replace the dosbox with your own or even use a mod called gzdoom which again you can find in the community guides. My review will be based on the game without alterations and was done by confuguring dosbox manually.
The sequel to one of the most influenal games ever made, takes what the first one laid down and makes it even better. Graphically not much has changed, but there seems to be more effort put into wall designs so it has a bit more variation. The rooms also can get quite a bit bigger than the first doom, and the levels can last longer too but the same quality level design is still there so I almost never got lost(and the map still helps if you do). It also cranked up the number of enemies you fight at once.
You only have one new weapon(super shotgun), which seems disapponting at first, but I never felt limited at all. Every weapon has it's place and adding too much more would probably lead to certain weapons being useless. There are many new enemy types and all of them are fun(I did find the pain elemental to be tedious at first, but once you know how to take care of him he fits right in) and the sound design adds new sounds and tracks that in many ways are even better than the first, they just stick out more to me. The controls remain the same as the first but they do have you use dashes more in the levels, which really works and leads to some cool sections to play through. There are plenty of new levels to enjoy, filled with secrets and even hidden levels, and all this gives the game great replay value.
I talked about the lack of a new final boss in episode 4 on the first game, and they made up for it here, as the last boss is great and deserves the name final boss. I did notice that they use teleporters much more in this game and this is fine, though one or twice I got killed by an enemy that knew I was coming or was behind me. But doom fans say this is better that the orignal, and it is. Everything that worked in the first was done even better here. And that's saying a lot since I loved the first doom. Aside from the few things I nickpicked I really felt satisfied with this game. Get it without hesitation.

F.E.A.R. First Encounter Assault Recon, is a first-person shooter (FPS) survival game developed by Monolith Productions (known for such games as Shadow of Mordor and the Condemned series) and published by Vivendi back in 2005. During its time, it was one of the most graphically and system intensive game overshadowed only by the release of Crysis (1) two years later. F.E.A.R. features a unique game play mechanic which makes use of what it calls the 'Reflex' ability or more popularly known to players as 'slow-mo'.  It also features advanced enemy AI, and a story that blends Japanese style horror with intense FPS action in a single gaming experience.
The F.E.A.R. Team was sent in to investigate and eliminate Paxton Fettel, a psychic military commander who, using an army of clone soldiers known as the Replica Army, started an uprising against Armacham Technology Corporation (Umbrella Group of Companies). The player takes on the role of 'Point Man' (whose real name was never revealed), a new member of the 'First Encounter Assault Recon' (F.E.A.R.) Team.

Short review: It's Killing Floor with dinosaurs and I absolutely love it.
Longer review: Despite a bumpy start upon release and many updates, this game was developed into something great. You essentially fight wave upon wave of dinosaurs while obtaining credits (in-game currency). Using credits to purchase player upgrades, weapons, vehicles and useful items. Some gamemodes include a generator you must defend and other objectives.
Nothing really feels over-powered but you will notice that player weapons seem a little more powerful than vehicle weapons. I really only use vehicles to turtle myself and/or as a light defense for the generator. Player vs player battles can be fun but it's easy to take someone out with even mediocre weapons.
My only real negative for this game is vehicles are way too squishy to larger dinosaurs. A tank takes no more then 3-4 hits before being destroyed and yet can take dozens of hits from smaller dinosaurs before being destroyed. In a way, I appreciate it because it forces you to compromise. I'm all about compromises, it keeps things interesting. See? The only negative I have about this game I honestly turned it into a positive. Overall, I had a lot of fun.
You'd think flying dinosaurs would be annoying and impossible but they're well balanced.
Similarly to Killing Floor, every new experience level gives you a small reward like spawning with upgrades, weapons or items. A max level player can spawn with a full loadout of weapons and upgrades. Useful for higher difficulties so obtaining experience and gaining levels is actually worth your while. It's not terribly grindy either, you can reach level 25 in a day. Level 70 is max level.

Despite a 3rd chapter that drags, some frustrating grinding walls, and (occassionally) excessive loads of dialogue, the game's narrative and voice acting, beautiful musical score, artistic graphics, and sliky smooth controls more than make up for it. The combo game is easy enough for beginners to grow accustomed to its mechanics, and it has fantastic depth for those who want to thrash their enemies w/ the most optimal combos. The only concern would be the parry mechanic; think of it like Metal Gear Rising's, only not as offensively dysfunctional. It's more the window being confusing than anything else, and I think they should've moved the parry frames a bit earlier. Oh, and Fidget is literaly over powered. Definitely opt to level her up. Combat isn't the only thing you'll do, as there's plenty of exploration in this metroidvania, along with a healthy dose of light puzzles and platforming, all of which are enhanced by Dust's gradually growing movelist.
The graphics are flat out gorgeous; each frame is beautifully hand-drawn by Dean Dodrill: a sign of true passion. The framerate is pretty smooth, and all the visual effects are spot on. The camera feels a bit too close however, but this never really led to anything detrimental gameplay wise. The soundtrack was created by HyperDucks, and they sure knew how to craft a beautiful and emotionally charged score. From the melodically tense Abadis Forest to the peaceful Blackmoor Mountains, your ears will be pleased throughout.
The narrative is strong, w/ great characters and voice actors. Dust himself has an overdone billing, but his personality and growth is noteworthy enough to keep one engaged. Fidget is a strong companion, and despite some annoying tangents, her perky attitude is a welcome addition to the party. Most other characters (even the talking sword) are up to snuff, and only help to flesh this game out, w/ none of them detracting any points. I just wished there were more of those fantastic animated movies, as the overly abundant info dumps using texts are made even more tedious when compared their sparingly-used superior.
But none of the issues I highlighted are enough to hold Dust from being an affordable gem, one I think any fan of the genre should play. $15 is a steal.

Good lord, do I ever wish I COULD fully recommend this...  Unforuntately it was made by people who felt games like Super Meat Boy and Darkest Dungeon were made for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  Ive had to re-write chunks of this review multiple times because I honestly can't quite sort my feelings out on it.
The basic premise is awesome: you play one of a cavalcade of characters (nearly all of the non-default characters serve to add another layer of challenge to runs) in a turn-based Rouge-like affair: 12 floors divided into 4 zones, with a boss at the end of every 3-floor zone.  Pick up weapons, armor, rings, charms, spells and consumables as you go.  The twist is that everything is synched to the BGM of the level; the game is played entirely with four direction buttons (the game even has a mode for use with a dance pad), with combinations used to activate spells and items, and attacking happening automatically if an enemy is in range.  The timing is pretty forgiving, although getting thrown off can result in a failure cascade and simultaneous inputs can prove to be fiddly depending on what you're playing with.
In essence, the entire experience is a bit like a free-style DDR session where you have to out-dance a parade of monsters.
All of this is set to a dowright awesome soundtrack; the three 'main' heroines each get their own remix of the various themes and there isn't a single song in the whole game that doesn't work perfectly for the zones they overlay.  You can also substitute in your own soundtrack if you want to as an added bonus.
The sound design is unfortunately not quite as exceptional; sound cues work well enough but a number of monsters have downright obnoxious audio cues (I'm looking at you, every-variety-of-Spirit).  It isn't likely to be enough to throw you off of the infectious groove of any given floor, but it still seems worth mentioning.
The entire package is rounded off with better-than-it-needed-to-be story and better-than-it-has-any-right-to-be voice acting.  That's' not to say it's a great story, but its servicable enough to complement the core gameplay.
Sadly, this is where the nice things end: the game's difficulty curve is somewhat ♥♥♥♥ed.
The entire game is predicated on each monster having a particular pattern to its movenents, with a particular sequence of moves that best serve to handle it.  If you don't handle your approach properly there is a good chance you'll take damage, and unless you've managed to find a good armor set and/or a lot of life increases you can only really take two or three hits before you die.
Zone 1 has nothing but enemies that can be dealt with very easily as long as you're paying attention.
Zone 2 has a few slightly trickier opponents like wizards that pull you towards them (but almost never in a way that would cause you to immediately take damage) and stationary AoE damage mushrooms.
Zone 3 is where things get complicated: monsters that move every 3 beats and leave trails of damaging coals/slippery ice, monsters that can't be hurt unless you've been right next to them, monsters that move every turn, and a noticably higher density mitigated by the fact that the levels are made to generate with a lot of wide open spaces.
Zone 4 is, to put it bluntly, hell.  All of the monsters are individually pretty easy to figure out individually, but they come at you in swarms that make it extremely easy to deal with the wrong threat first, get blind-sided by wall-spiders/traps, or wind up diagonal from one of the suicide-bomber gremlins that inexplicably move diagonally just to make them that much more obnoxious to deal with.  This could still be managable if you had a lot of space to work in like in Zone 3, but Zone 4 consists of small interconnected chambers you have to dig your way between.  While there is usually a way out of these waves, if you make even one mistake you're going to take a hit, possibly a pretty serious one.  And you have less than half a second to come up with a plan of action.
And all of this is before what the Devs decided to set up as 'challenges'...
I think my personal 'favorite' is The Monk.  They COULD have done the reasonable thing and made the gold deal damage. Instead, they made gold insta-kill you.  Now, not only do you have another thing you have to factor into your already-complex moment-to-moment decision-making (step on the gold and die!) but you have to fight the instincts that countless hours of practice will have inevitably ingrained into you or fail on the spot.
This becomes even more of an issue because of Aria.
The game fully expects you to play as Aria to finish the story.   She has one hitpoint (and the small mercy of getting a potion at start), can't get a longer-range weapon than the dagger, and takes unmitigatable damage if you MISS A BEAT.
All of this culminates in the fatal flaw of the game: it doesn't know what it wants to be, a rythm game or a dungeon crawler.
A rythm game is at its best when one can get lost in the music and let their actions flow naturally.  Necrodancer's enemy design actively punishes trying to do this at later levels.
A dungeon crawler with complex enemy patterns and a low margin for error BEGS for enough time to at least consider one's approach.  Necrodancer's rythmic elements demand that you act inside of half a second lest your enemies tear your throat out when the beat comes.
Trying to do both results in an experience that is much more painful than it needs to be.
It's a shame, because the game is immensely enjoyable when it isn't being unbearably frustrating.   I can only recommend if you have a lot of patience and can deal with a neverending string of failure; otherwise you'd be better off staying away.

Another solid entry in the Ys series on the PC courtesy of XSeed.  This time players are treated to the first entry that utilized the engine found in Oath in Felghana and Origins, respectively.
While some of the mechanics are dated compared those two titles, this game is still very memorable in its own right.  3 different, upgradable swords with different abilities that also aid in exploration of the islands you're marooned on enhance the combat appeal, and there are plenty of treasures and relics to find throughout the game world.  Speaking of, the islands of Canaan have a wonderful feel to them and add some great ambiance to your adventuring.  The music is also nicely tuned to match the areas you're in and get you in the mood to explore.  I do admit that while some of the tunes in this game are not as catchy to me as in the other games, they are still very well done and indicative of classic Falcom composition.
Add in the fact that this game (along with most other Ys titles) can run on a toaster of a computer, and you have a solid entry that should attract any JRPG or Action RPG fan.  Highly recommended!

-Replayability is thin, no Alma's Trials

Stellaris is a beautiful 4X strategy game set in space. From the graphics to the soundtrack, it's artistically superb. When I first launched the game, I found myself staring at the scenery and units in amazement just as I did with Witcher 3. The detail that went into the games presentation is astounding. Once you overcome your wonder and delight enough to actually start playing, you truly feel as though you're at the helm of a fledgling interstellar empire taking its first steps into space. You're excited, and you're curious. If you're like me when you set up your first game, you'll make sure to choose humanity as your race, and purposely pay no attention to the appearances or descriptions of any other: you'll want to be surprised. As your first survey ship leaves your home system, you'll wonder what awaits it. You know you're not alone, but where are they, and what're they like? The immense depth you've already seen so far has inspired the highest expectations in you. You know only that they'll be interesting and unique. Suffice to say, you won't soon find yourself disappointed, but I won't spoil it for you.
As the game progresses, you might find that Stellaris isn't a game without problems. The signature Paradox Warscore system throttles progress through conquest, leaving the game's pace best suited for only the very most patient gamer. Luckily a few campaigns and a handful of conquered systems later, you'll find more efficient strategies for handling warscore, and the pace will seem more reasonable. There's three beginning methods of propulsion to choose from in the game, such as warp, and those other methods can be frustrating to counter. Your adversary may bypass your border defenses entirely and appear instantaneously at the center of your empire, where it could theoretically raid you with impunity, attacking your stations then moving onto the next system before your warp ships had the chance to respond to the first. This isn't a circumstance in which there's no answer, but it can and will be frustrating, especially at first. Once you do catch up with the attacking fleet, its likely to simply retreat rather than allow you to destroy it. Makes sense, but it also makes annoying. You're gonna be chasing fleets of raiders around the galaxy before you know it: They attack, you intercept, they retreat, they attack, you intercept, they retreat, ad infinitum, or so it might sometimes seem.
Is Stellaris worth it? Yes, absolutely, beyond any doubt. Will the mechanics designed to artificially lengthen and otherwise forcefully shape the game frustrate you at times? Yes, absolutely, beyond any doubt. Buy Stellaris now, and envelop yourself with the beauty and elegance, the depth and wonder, the mundane and vexation. Be amazed. Be annoyed.

I honestly love and hate Final Fantasy VIII at the same time.  I love the Draw ability but I hate that you’re punished with lower stats for using magic you’ve Drawn and Junctioned.  (Maybe percentages would have been better?)  I love upgrading weapons instead of buying/finding new ones but hate the lack of armor and the fact that monsters level with you.  I love refining magic and items from other items and making lower magics combine into bigger items, but turning monsters into cards to turn into items was somewhat tedious.  I love the music and the character designs, but by GOD I want to slap each and every one of them.
The plot runs all over the place and reminds me of those assignments in writing class where you write a paragraph and pass it to your left.  You’re mercenaries, you’re assassinating a political figure, you’re a soldier in the past, you’re dealing with the moon and time travel...  perhaps a better translation would help.  It just feels disjointed and thrown together.
As an older teen/young adult I felt Squall was a whiney, unsympathetic character.  Quistis was manipulative, Selphie cute and cliche yet harmless, Zell had SOME character development, and Irvine?  Screw him.  If you KNOW you’re going to freeze on a mission to save your home you better ask someone else to go!  And sharp shooters do NOT work alone, I hate that trope.  I didn’t like Rinoa but I didn’t hate her.  As an adult I thought I’d play the game again, and I understand Squall better, but I pity him now; poor kid’s got PTSD.
Would I recommend this game?  Sadly, no.  It’s just too tedious for me to play though so much I can’t stand to get to the parts I do like.  I’m not going to tell anyone not to play it, though.  Lots of people love this game for legitimate reasons, and more power to them.  It’s not a horrible game, just one I didn’t like.

Short review: It's Killing Floor with dinosaurs and I absolutely love it.
Longer review: Despite a bumpy start upon release and many updates, this game was developed into something great. You essentially fight wave upon wave of dinosaurs while obtaining credits (in-game currency). Using credits to purchase player upgrades, weapons, vehicles and useful items. Some gamemodes include a generator you must defend and other objectives.
Nothing really feels over-powered but you will notice that player weapons seem a little more powerful than vehicle weapons. I really only use vehicles to turtle myself and/or as a light defense for the generator. Player vs player battles can be fun but it's easy to take someone out with even mediocre weapons.
My only real negative for this game is vehicles are way too squishy to larger dinosaurs. A tank takes no more then 3-4 hits before being destroyed and yet can take dozens of hits from smaller dinosaurs before being destroyed. In a way, I appreciate it because it forces you to compromise. I'm all about compromises, it keeps things interesting. See? The only negative I have about this game I honestly turned it into a positive. Overall, I had a lot of fun.
You'd think flying dinosaurs would be annoying and impossible but they're well balanced.
Similarly to Killing Floor, every new experience level gives you a small reward like spawning with upgrades, weapons or items. A max level player can spawn with a full loadout of weapons and upgrades. Useful for higher difficulties so obtaining experience and gaining levels is actually worth your while. It's not terribly grindy either, you can reach level 25 in a day. Level 70 is max level.

ABZU is a deep dive into colorful tranquility.
The narrative in ABZU is vague at best.  As you make your way through the deep, you'll encounter odd ruins of shining tile, smooth stone, hard edges, and stark steel.  By the end of the first chapter, it will become very clear that not everything beneath the waves is what you might expect.  What's more, the first chapter itself hints at the origin of what brought this world to ruin in a very clever way; long before players are expected to start piecing things together.  Ultimately, the details of the story are up to interpretation.  Bits of nature conservation, redemption, and even spirituality permeate the world.
Making its mark in the genre of games that are less about play or challenge, and exist as a means to experience a world; ABZU is a calm game to be played at your leisure.  The act of navigating the world is smooth and simple.  On the whole, swimming feels wonderful.  The diver does have a nasty habit of righting himself if upside down though, which can completely reverse the direction you're trying to input.  A simple boost system allows players to tap the boost button three times in a simple rhythm to accelerate their speed significantly for a short time.  Interestingly, for a game centered on what lies below the waves; pockets of surface water can often be spotted dotting the ceiling of kelp and stone.  Boosting up through these turns into graceful little leaps and arches like a dolphin chasing a boat.  Alternatively, you can tuck and roll through the water, spinning forwards or backwards; left or right.  Larger creatures of the sea can be latched onto, giving you rudimentary steering abilities while on their backs and their own little dances and boosts.  Some can even leap the surface with you in tow or at their side.  Progression is achieved through light exploration as you find small buddy drones to clear coral blockades, chain spools to open doors, and even underwater fountains that clear your way.  For the more exploratory minded; hidden coral spots can be discovered.  Activating these unleashes a new type of life into the local environment; adding even more diversity to the bustling clouds of fish all around you.  Meditation statues allow you to move the camera from fish to fish, examining them up close and revealing their name.  The only drawback to what should be a meditative experience is the absolute uselessness of the controls for swapping between fish.  Which fish you'll cycle to next is completely random and not necessarily even a different type than what you're already looking at.  So if you want to examine that neat looking Bonnethead Shark, you may find the experience of getting to him more aggravating than serene.  Further hidden in each chapter are three Ammonite shells that give a special reward if you gather the full set.  All told, your journey to restore the ocean life below will only run a couple of hours and is easy to complete in a single go.  A couple extra hours can be spent searching for shells and coral caches, though some are hidden in quite obscure places.
This is where ABZU sometimes literally shines.  Its depiction of underwater ecosystems is unlike anything else video games have shown before.  Eschewing photo-realism a much simpler and artistic depiction; fish, crabs, jellies, and plant life numbering in the thousands barrage the player with color and fluid movement.  Kelp sways and stretches dozens of yards toward the sky.  Schools of fish hurriedly convene into a mesmerizing vortex of scales and sheen.  Cavernous rock stretches down into a deep blackness just begging the brave to illuminate the deepest reaches of the sea with their flashlight.  The busy visuals are supported by a wonderful score of classical instruments.  A great emphasis is place on harps, wind, vocals, and the occasional synth to portray the more modern of the ruins.  The constant slosh and churn of water completely surrounds you at all times.
ABZU is a triumph in world exploration video games and is a spectacle in its own right purely for the level of activity it renders in each scene.  Every area is art in motion.  If you're looking for a comfy game to sit back and relax, this one is for you.

The domestic chicken is descended primarily from the Red junglefowl (Gallus gallus) and is scientifically classified as the same species.[19] As such it can and does freely interbreed with populations of red jungle fowl.[19] Recent genetic analysis has revealed that at least the gene for yellow skin was incorporated into domestic birds through hybridization with the Grey junglefowl (G. sonneratii).[20] The traditional poultry farming view is stated in Encyclopædia Britannica (2007): "Humans first domesticated chickens of Indian origin for the purpose of cockfighting in Asia, Africa, and Europe. Very little formal attention was given to egg or meat production... "[2] In the last decade there have been a number of genetic studies. According to one study, a single domestication event occurring in the region of modern Thailand created the modern chicken with minor transitions separating the modern breeds.[21] However, that study was later found to be based on incomplete data, and recent studies point to multiple maternal origins, with the clade found in the Americas, Europe, Middle East, and Africa, originating from the Indian subcontinent, where a large number of unique haplotypes occur.[22][23] It is postulated that the Jungle fowl, known as the "bamboo fowl" in many Southeast Asian languages, is a special pheasant well adapted to take advantage of the large amounts of fruits that are produced during the end of the 50 year bamboo seeding cycle to boost its own reproduction.[24] In domesticating the chicken, humans took advantage of this prolific reproduction of the jungle fowl when exposed to large amount of food.[25]
It has been claimed (based on paleoclimatic assumptions) that chickens were domesticated in Southern China in 6000 BC.[26] However, according to a recent study,[27] "it is not known whether these birds made much contribution to the modern domestic fowl. Chickens from the Harappan culture of the Indus Valley (2500-2100 BC), in what today is Pakistan, may have been the main source of diffusion throughout the world." A northern road spread the chicken to the Tarim basin of central Asia. The chicken reached Europe (Romania, Turkey, Greece, Ukraine) about 3000 BC.[28] Introduction into Western Europe came far later, about the 1st millennium BC. Phoenicians spread chickens along the Mediterranean coasts, to Iberia. Breeding increased under the Roman Empire, and was reduced in the Middle Ages.[28] Middle East traces of chicken go back to a little earlier than 2000 BC, in Syria; chicken went southward only in the 1st millennium BC. The chicken reached Egypt for purposes of♥♥♥♥♥♥fighting about 1400 BC, and became widely bred only in Ptolemaic Egypt (about 300 BC).[28] Little is known about the chicken's introduction into Africa. Three possible routes of introduction in about the early first millennium AD could have been through the Egyptian Nile Valley, the East Africa Roman-Greek or Indian trade, or from Carthage and the Berbers, across the Sahara. The earliest known remains are from Mali, Nubia, East Coast, and South Africa and date back to the middle of the first millennium AD.[28] Domestic chicken in the Americas before Western conquest is still an ongoing discussion, but blue-egged chickens, found only in the Americas and Asia, suggest an Asian origin for early American chickens.[28]
A lack of data from Thailand, Russia, the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa makes it difficult to lay out a clear map of the spread of chickens in these areas; better description and genetic analysis of local breeds threatened by extinction may also help with research into this area.[28]
South America
An unusual variety of chicken that has its origins in South America is the araucana, bred in southern Chile by the Mapuche people. Araucanas, some of which are tailless and some of which have tufts of feathers around their ears, lay blue-green eggs. It has long been suggested that they pre-date the arrival of European chickens brought by the Spanish and are evidence of pre-Columbian trans-Pacific contacts between Asian or Pacific Oceanic peoples, particularly the Polynesians, and South America. In 2007, an international team of researchers reported the results of analysis of chicken bones found on the Arauco Peninsula in south-central Chile. Radiocarbon dating suggested that the chickens were Pre-Columbian, and DNA analysis showed that they were related to prehistoric populations of chickens in Polynesia.[29] These results appeared to confirm that the chickens came from Polynesia and that there were transpacific contacts between Polynesia and South America before Columbus's arrival in the Americas.[30]
However, a later report looking at the same specimens concluded:
A published, apparently pre-Columbian, Chilean specimen and six pre-European Polynesian specimens also cluster with the same European/Indian subcontinental/Southeast Asian sequences, providing no support for a Polynesian introduction of chickens to South America. In contrast, sequences from two archaeological sites on Easter Island group with an uncommon haplogroup from Indonesia, Japan, and China and may represent a genetic signature of an early Polynesian dispersal. Modeling of the potential marine carbon contribution to the Chilean archaeological specimen casts further doubt on claims for pre-Columbian chickens, and definitive proof will require further analyses of ancient DNA sequences and radiocarbon and stable isotope data from archaeological excavations within both Chile and Polynesia.[31]

ORION: Prelude. Previously known as Orion: Dino Horde, and previously known before that as Dino Beatdown. It's a nifty little FPS about...well, the mass killing of dinosaurs.
The name changes, despite what the developers will claim on their forums, are repeated attempts to avoid their perpetually low metacritic scores.
Each iteration of this dino slaughter game is merely just a shameless repackaging, in an attempt to shed it's horrible metagamer score. Perhaps neither here nor there, but it does give you an idea of how dishonest this publisher is willing to be to ensure the game continues to sell.
The game has a glaring lack of polish, tends to run at very low framerates, even on powerful machines, and has the nasty habit of crashing...repeatedly, for no apparent reason.
Notably, some people only rarely experience these crashes, but for many people, the game is rendered unplayable. And of course, when you're not crashing, your friends are disconnecting.
Playing through a single match of any appreciable length becomes rather difficult.
Pair that with the repetitive music and downright embarrasing voices the humans feature, you get the distinct feeling that there was a notable lack of love going into the visuals and sound in this game.
Seriously, though. The voices are reminiscent of an athsmatic in a bathroom with seasonal allergies and a horrible headcold. (Looking at you, support class! If you call me "homey" one more time...)
Notably, the lag and the crashes and the disconnects are issues that have persisted for me and my friends over a year, since the game was called ORION: Dino Horde.
If you are among the lucky people who can play this game without crashing non-stop, then I suggest you immediately stop to thank your lucky stars.
The game features a variety of modes, but most modes involve slaughtering dinos. (There are a few that allow you to play as dinos.) The game contains 3 classses of humans you can play as, support, assault, and recon. (Think of a clunkier version of Tom Clancy.) While assault is fun to play as with his jetpack, and the recon is nifty with her invisibility, the support class wins hands down, with his ability to heal himself and others....to an extreme degree. He can tank just about anything with his healing gun.
Even though the support class is massively overpowered, playing the game as any other class is quite difficult.
Between massive dinos that create unavoidable earthquakes, or even bigger dinos that merely swallow you whole, ORION exists on a strange difficulty spectrum.
So long as one uses the support class, and uses the turrets on the backs of the vehicles you can ride, the game seems relatively easy. If you, like me, decide to explore what else the game has to offer, you'll run back to your support class/turret combo relatively quickly, as you find that the world of dino horde is quite a cruel one indeed.
In short, Orion: Prelude, under any name, is a glitchy, laggy, poorly thought out PVP shooter/dino killing game/dinos vs humans, that attempts to excuse its mediocrity with a low price point.
Considering the legions of pvp shooters out there, you're probably better off picking up any one of those and leaving this one be.

This review is for Galactic Civilizations 3 Gold, which includes the Crusade expansion. It is important to make the distinction between GC3 and GC3 Crusade, a related, but different game.
TLDR: GC3 Crusade is the game that finally made me forget that I also have Master of Orion 2 installed on my PC. Currently it is my favorite 4x space game. Its complexity, constant ‘upgrades’ and such, infinite replayability at a ridiculously small price are hard to miss points to anyone looking for such games.
First impressions: a very complex 4x space TBS, in a permanent ‘early access’ (NOT in a bad way) state of development. What does it mean? It is a great, very enjoyable game, and the developers are in touch with the community and open to suggestions. They constantly add or improve features, based on the feedback from players. The game you play this month may be quite different from the game you played a couple months ago. All these free patches, alongside the paid DLC which never stops coming, make things very dynamic and although some players might prefer a more ‘stable’ or ‘definitive’ version of the game, I, personally, much prefer this approach. So, it is open to debate, but I, for one, give it two very enthusiastic thumbs up. Paid once, get to try multiple versions of the game and the fun never stops. There is always something new to discover or try, and they are not arbitrary changes, but they try to approximate what the community desired.
Top 10 things I like:
1.	it is turn based
2.	it is a 64bit modern game, allowing the policy of changes I mentioned before; nothing seems too complex for its engine to handle, no wishes seem unlikely to become reality
3.	unique in 4x space gaming planetary surface management
4.	unique in 4x gaming civilization and combat units designer; and I mean ‘designer’, not ‘customization’
5.	unique in 4x space gaming modularity of systems, as complex and interactive as the ones found in games like Civilization (one of the very few games that define the standards for 4x gaming)
6.	procedurally generated tech tree, based on player’s civilization design
7.	complex resource management systems and choices, allowing a vast variety of valid strategies, according to circumstances and player’s preferences
8.	fairly adequate diplomatic mechanics, which not that many 4x games feature
9.	space combat may not allow manual tactical control, but the strategic level is very good: the way you choose to conduct your research, general development of the civilization, diplomacy, your ideological choices, unit and fleet development, espionage – everything has something to do with the outcome of your wars; victory in a fleet to fleet confrontation is only the final act of a well orchestrated process leading to that combat situation
10.	the developers are not shy when it comes to DLC; some of this downloadable content has a dramatic impact on gameplay, it isn’t just decorative stuff
What I miss in this game:
1.	Did you ever want to play a 4x game featuring huge empires, allowing you to play for months and build extraordinary civilizations? Well, this game is not it. Not yet. Although it can accommodate insane/ludicrous galaxies, the gameplay mechanics and the user interface make the attempts at playing on such scale futile. Everything beyond a certain size is both boring (just more of the same) and frustrating (the management of your assets becomes a nightmare).

- Graphical the lighting source (moon, sun) not matching up with the ground shadows much of the time...they can be different by 90 degrees.

You play a character named Dust and you’re suffering from memory loss. You partake in different quest to find out the truth about yourself.

In Airport CEO its your job to build and manage an airport from scratch. You plan and build your foundations, roadworks, manage your Staff, plan for Security, CheckIns and well everything what makes an Airport. If you played any other airport building/managing Game before (e.g. SimAirport) you pretty much know what to expect, but with one exeption, AirportCEO has a great focus on realism. Lets get into the Pros and Cons about ACEO
Pros:
+ great timesink.
+ Funfactor is really high (if you are into management Games)
+ really great developer feedback (alot of early bugs and crashes have already been fixed.)
+ realistic (but not so much that it gets annoying)
+ attention to detail (not only graphics)
+ great level of control over your Airport
+ alot more to come in the future (this is Early Access)
Neutral:
~ graphics (to be honest i like the graphics and art of ACEO but its nothing special. Its 2D, its simple but not ugly)
~ price (for an EA game with this amount of content and detail the price is fair)
~ some minor things are missing but promissed to come soon
~ the UI (its not bad but it definitely needs some more work to be done)
Cons:
- performance could be better (first performance Patch is already out, so they are working on it)
- steep learningcurve (you will need some time to get into the game and fully understand how everything works)
- the lag of a propper Tutorial. (there is one but it's hidden and it is not the best one, but the Devs promissed to work on that)
Remember this is Early Access bugs, glitches are to be expected but trust me the Devs a really working on it, so far there was a Patch every day since the release to EA. Alot more content is also to be axpected. For short, if you like management Games, you are into Planes and Airports, and you like to otimize your work AirportCEO is great. For 15,99 you can't really do anything wrong and you will have a great time of Fun with ACEO and more to come in the future

Let me start off by saying that I love the concept of this game, and think it was a great idea for Paradox to venture out into the 4x genre. With that said, I really hope they learn from their mistakes and build on this product.
There are some negative reviews here that emphasize that DLCs will make this game better. While this is true, there are still A LOT of infuriating bugs in the game that makes one wonder, "did they ever beta test this?"
- Example: in your UI, on the right side, you have Military Fleets and Civilian Ships listed. Sometimes when building a Colony Ship it won't show up under Civilian Ships, and depending on how your multitasking, you may forget about it for months (in game).
What's more frustrating is the game's features. I'm not going to give voice to the choir on Diplomacy because other negative reviews have already touched that.
- As someone who likes to war, I loathe how there is no rally points for Spaceports. When building ships, you can't automatically send them to another destination upon being built. This makes trying to manage resources and ships a HUGE burden when battling other nations.
- Another big one for me is hotkeys and quick navigation. You can quickly "go to" ships and other events, but it only takes you directly to a Solar System view. I would like to do the same in the Galaxy view. In my opinion, this makes hotkey and gameplay feel less fluid, and can be annoying when your always pressing (Q) to zoom in on an object in a solar system, then immediately pressing (E) to enter galaxy view. If you know 4x games, I think you can realize how dizzy this would make you feel. They try to fix this with sectors, so that you don't have to manage those resources closely, but sometimes you need to go back and double check that your sector's AI is managing Planet resources effectively, because many times it doesn't. This also begs the question, that if you make sectors in the first place to prevent too much Solar System viewing, why don't you have a "go to" hotkey in the Galaxy view? Very confusing.
- Empire Tab, under Planets and Sectors, should also display the Solar System name in which the Planet resides. For beginners this can be frustrating trying to find a Planets in your UI with no Solar System name listed.
There are many other issues with this game that I have not listed, which is why I don't recommend it, FOR NOW. 4x games should feel less clunky than this game. However, I think with a lot of patches, and DLCs, they can turn it around. Paradox if you read this, in the future PLEASE, PLEASE, PLEASE undergo intense Beta testing. Many of these issues were noticed immediately, and could have easily been brought to your awareness prior to launch.
I hope a few months later I find many of the issues resolved. And to be honest, even with all it's issues, I still like the game and will probably continue to play it.

Beginning Comments: I don't have a whole lot of hours in it yet due to the lack of playerbase (Not the game's fault, I think it just swooped in under the radar), but this game has an awesome concept. The devs gave everyone who played the beta a free key, and they delivered, so I promised I would still buy a copy (for a friend) if they stayed true to their word, so I did as well. No regrets.
About the Game: Hide and Seek. Scavenger Hunt. Clue. A dash of Murder? Who can you trust? Your teammate? The other 10 players? Yourself? No one. You must not trust anyone with your life as it will be short-lived if you do so. You're spawned in a mansion with your teammate and 10 other players, one secretly being the Devil, and you must complete the ultimate scavenger hunt to free yourself from this haunting chase.
My personal Suggestion(s): 1. Open mic is a great idea on paper, but the only downside aside from the obvious mic spam from some users is the lack of ability to communicate with others you're already in a group chat with. Perhaps the ability to mute yourself in the game? I know that degrades the experience in a way, but I'd hate to be chatting normally to friends, but be techincally spamming in others ears within proximity.
2. I know this is trivial, but maybe a lobby idea where we can see other player's names? I figure that'd be useful if you have friends joining off of you.
3. If more maps are planned for the future, I'm psyched for that. Nothing wrong with the current mansion map of course, but it'll get stale after an extended period of time.
My Rating (So far): 8/10. The concept is original and creative, the pre-release setup the developers had gave me faith in the game's future. Kudos to the devs for being involved from the get-go!
Final Comments: This game has great potential within it, and has some dedicated, friendly developers behind it that made me think to myself: "I wanna buy this game." I already had the idea of buying it in my head before I even did any real research on the game; the concept looked that good. I hope all goes well as the devs continue to work on this game, and I hope more people find out about it as the current playerbase needs a slight boost.

I just recently purchased this game again on this steam account, I have the Complete collection on another PC, and have played this game for thousands of hours since it's release date, as well as other RTS series like Starcraft, AOE, Empire Earth however this is one of the Greatest RTS games I've ever played, though personally not as great as C&C: RA 2, which to me was the most enjoyable, but currently is not supported through Revora's online Multiplayer* system.

The game is well designed, with Land Air and Sea Combat, Good diversity between factions, unit promotions, unit microskills (activatable abilities), Support Abilities (Faction based abilities available to you).

If you are not familar with playing RTS in online multiplayer, especially during the 07-11 era when the RTS E-sport scene was at its peak then do not get too upset if you go over to Revora your first few times around and you get crushed, they do have some great people over there.
Great Soundtrack (Hellmarch is amazing), Good UI, Challenging AI, lots of maps, and a lot of Youtube content if your looking to see the game played before you make a purchase.
If you are new to RTS games, or are a long time RTS fan who never played RA:3 I suggest you do, I also personally suggest you play RA:2 if your able to play LAN games or are satisfied playing against the AI.

The gameplay itself is good, the sound effects and voice acting are also good, the in-game music and cut-scene-ish effects help delivering a great atmosphere. The graphics are somewhat dated by today standards, but are not bad. GOOD THINGS: Good gunplay and tense environments. Enemy AI is heavily scripted, but in a fairly restricted corridor shooter that's not a bad thing. Enemies will try to flank you, throw grenades around the corner and rush you in groups. They also have call-outs depending on the situation (when there are 1-2 left in a group they call for reinforcements, for example [no, reinforcements don't actually show up]). Decent variety of weapons, and none of them felt like you would run out of ammo for them if you use them appropriately.
BAD THINGS: Visuals are obviously a bit dated with some lower-res textures (and almost Wind Waker level fire animations) but certainly holds ujp well enough to be playable. Game had almost comically obvious shifts between scary time and shooty time, so I almost always knew what sections would or wouldn't hold enemies. The "scary" bits are all jump scares, and I actually felt the tenseness of sneaking around combat sections trying to get the drop on enemies to be far greater than anything the scary sections had.
All in all, a pretty solid shooter. Took me 8 hours on a blind run on the highest difficulty, so not too big a time-sink. I do recommend going with the highest difficulty you can handle (but make sure to quicksave often if you're on the highest diff, you can drop in seconds if you walk in the open without realizing enemies are there).

An unusual & amusing game where you throw items into a fire and watch them burn whilst trying to work out combos of things to burn from cryptic clues. It's much better than it sounds. Recommended.
You spend the entire first part of the game with a view of a fireplace where you can drag items and drop them and right click to produce a flame that can then be used to light (some) objects in the fire place.
You purchase items from a catalog, further items become available as you purchase different items and extra catalogs can be purchased once all the items from a previous catalog have been purchased and you have completed a certain number of combos. You perform a combo when you burn certain things together at the same time.
Purchased items are then delivered to your home and appear as boxes on a bar underneath the fireplace. There is a cool down time before you can open the box and drag the item onto the fireplace, although you can use up cards which drop from time to time in the fireplace to reduce the cool down to zero. You can only store (& so purchase) a set number of items at a time.
Cards always drop when you find a combo for the first time. There is a list of cryptic clues to combos available and as you find each combo it is crossed off. A lot of the fun of the game is trying to figure out what items are part of combos.
Once the items have been destroyed in the fireplace coins also drop (more than you paid for the item) and you can collect these.
As well as purchasing items & catalogs coins can be used to upgrade the space used to store items so hold additional items.
Letters also appear "randomly" in your item slots. These offer cryptic clues to the background story, request certain items be sent or deliver additional items.
The way the things burn in the fireplace is roughly realistic so some physics simulation is involved. There are interesting items like planets which have their own gravity, bombs which explode etc.
At the start of the game you have given hints to explain the game mechanics but to be honest its pretty simple and easy to pick up.
There comes a point when the game fundamentally changes and you leave the room with the fire and get to wander around a small town in an adventure style game. To be honest I found this less interesting and only spent half an hour or so looking round before finding the point to finish the game and doing so.
Progress is saved when you exit and it's possible to have multiple game progress saved.
All in all a surprisingly entertaining game, which my 3 year old loved sitting on my knee and watching, getting very excited when letters arrived & pointing out the things he wanted me to burn .. Hmm thinking about it now maybe I might regret this later in his life ..

.

you have access to lots of vehicles (around 160).

Races (+)

missed drifting and drag race from NFS Underground?
they are back in this game! more realistic and a lot harder though!
you need to learn to tune your cars to get to that millie second which makes you the winner.
Game Performance (-)
---------------
Crashes, low FPS issues and freezes are common.
Sound (-/+)
---------------
music mostly is horrible, repetetive and boring (depressive?) but the sound effects and car sounds are realistic and great.
overall (+)
---------------
this is a great game. replayablitiy is high due to difficult challenges and there is a still alive multiplayer and competition going on.

The visuals age fairly well, but the audio is a little spotty: a few great tunes mixed in with some less than impressive ones.  Not the classic its predecessor is, but still a game worth playing.

tl;dr 7/10, AI Sector Control bad, AI Fleet Control meh, AI Diplomacy bad, early-game feels fresh but lengthy, mid-game meh, late-game lengthy and meh.
Performance: Stable. I've experienced no crashes to date. In late-game with galaxy nearly completely mapped and populated the game will tend to 'pause' when time is set to "Fast/Fastest", but after a few moments it clears itself up and progresses normally.
AI Sector Control: What the ♥♥♥♥. So if you give a freshly colonized planet to Sector Control, the AI will avoid populating and building on food tiles (to speed up population growth) and even pull population off the colony capital tile to put on energy/mineral/research tiles corresponding to the Sector priority (Energy, Minerals, Research). This means fresh colonies in Sector Control grow slower than a 10 year olds beard. Even worse, if you build up a colony to your idea of optimal and then hand it over to Sector Control the AI will start replacing the buildings EVEN THOUGH that option is -not- selected in Sector Control.  Total ♥♥♥♥ing mess.
AI Fleet Control: While for the most part it's "fine", I have encountered situations I like to call "Hot Gating", in reference to the Battle of Thermopylae. Whereas even though your fleet may outnumber/outpower an enemy fleet, and your ships are set to aggressive behavior, they will 'at times' rotate only 1 or 2 ships in to weapons range against the entire enemy fleet. Those 1-2 ships will then get wiped the ♥♥♥♥ out, and your fleet will send in another 1-2, and another, and another, and another, until you're attrited down to nothing despite your initial overwhelming force. As if there was an invisible wall in the middle of space that only allowed you to send 1-2 ships in to their doom. I've seen this happen with not 1 fleet vs 1 fleet, but 4 fleets vs 1 fleet. And the 1 fleet just attrited the other 4 down.
AI Diplomacy: Just forget ever being able to have 'military access' to another faction's space, even if you're allies in a war.  It's fine if you want to set up phony wars with factions far away from you, with friendlies in between.
Early game: I like the concept of surveying and finding anomalies, the investigating of alien entities, finding pre-sentient species, or pre-space factions, initiating event chains. However, most of the event chains that I have initiated through anomalies must be bugged, as they rarely reach resolution.
Mid game: At this point you've mapped about as far as you can go before being blocked off by other factions' space, so it's just colonize, expand, and research until you get to late-game.
Late game: This is where you take on the ancient Fallen Empires, or the Sentient AI rebellion, or the extra-galactic scourge invasion, uplift a few species....or just go ahead and conquer the rest of the galaxy. No big deal.
Research: It's 'decent', but I feel like by the time you reach late game where you face galactic threats there's not a whole lot of teching-up left to do, and not a whole lot of variety.
So, yeah, I give it a 7/10. It's got some work ahead of it, but I have confidence that Paradox will succeed.

As far as I'm concerned, this is a very poorly done console port. The keyboard keys are bound to impossible keys, in game mechanics aren't optimized to PC, and the AI is poorly done, not to mention the fact that the game crashes often on high graphics.
Before diving into issues, i want to dive into a major issue with this game: The long, unskippable in-game movies that can't decide which volume they want to be. For starters there's the intro movie, that gets incredibly loud, and is only skippable after all the logo's displayed. These don't read into your personal volume preferences though, and are extremely loud, which is especially annoying when you play with a headset. Then, there's introduction videos that introduce you into a certain "event". These can be cool, but you need to be able to skip them. If you're hyped up for a race beforehand, a 2 minute long movie can only get you out of that hype. The fact that you actually have to delete the movies out of your data map, is a ridiculous thing in it's own. Now that that's out of the way, on to my major flaws with this game.
My first issue with this game is the horrible standard controls that the game asks you to use. This would be with the arrow keys, and the insert / delete button to shift gears. And yes, you use the up arrow for throttle. A controller of sorts makes the game easier to handle, even though this also isn't perfect. You can control in-game fully with a controller, but as soon as you enter any menu, including the pause menu, you are forced to use the keyboard. Especially when in-game this is a very poor point, given that you have to sit ready with your controller already in your hand, before pressing either the enter or escape button on your keyboard.
My second problem lays in the fact that a lot of the in game mechanics aren't optomized for pc. Left and right scrolling through the main menu goes with the arrow keys, while sub menu's always go with either U and I, or J and K, depending on what you want to do. The customization mechanic is sensitive beyond believe, and isn't, like most of the game, controllable with a controller, making it virtually impossible to line stickers up. Most of the engine / steering upgrades are standard, and it is clear that EA has it's favorite cars that are being favored. Some of the works cars (which are supposed to be the maxed out performance cars) are so horrible, that it's impossible to control on a circuit.
Finally, the poor AI. I find myself having to reset the track about 15 to 20 times, especially at the beginning,  to be even able to race in a fair matter. More often then wished, i find way too many cars bumping in on me, and spinning me out of control, making it impossible to even have a fair chance at winning. When I instead try to do the same, the cars seem to be magnetized to the track, and are unable to even get off. It's like bumping into an almost static object, sending you spinning, or even flipping out of control, but AI driven cars are completely fine. The most that the AI will do for you, is try and steer about half a meter clear from you, so that you can try and clear a corner. But more often then not, they still bump into your back and send you spinning.
That being said, I don't think the game is entirely just bad things. There are some positives, the cars generally look awesome, and there is some fun to be had in multiplayer, or attempting to break the AI in a race. If you are successful, it's definitely worth the effort, and you could get some laughs out of that.
I wouldn't say the game is worth the full 20 euro's that are currently charged, but wait until it's on sale sometime. 5 Euro's is about what the game is worth, in my opinion.
