One of the few great gems on the PSP originally ported from various other systems that still kept its charm as one of my most favorite action adventure, dungeon crawling, hack and slash games of all time! For those coming from the PSP/Vita era who missed out on this or Oath in Felghana, it retains a jump system that further expands combat past the simple slash-slash-dodge-special attack-swap party members-repeat system, given you take control of solely Adol himself.
This game's deep exploration makes it one for many secrets and vague linearity to plot progress. Yes, I still get lost sometimes taking that left fork instead. Each area contains various monsters of certain levels which are a challenge if not impossible for Adol in his level infancy. This is what shapes the game's level system. The combat is a fun grind for money and EXP to move up the ladder.
Combat is developed with a 3D aspect in mind. Given, Adol wields a sword and shield, where damage is avoided if certain enemies attack on the shield side. Not only is there a good amount of items and equipment to procure throughout the journey, there are also combat mechanisms that more modern remakes of Ys games lack. The jump system. This deepens the exploration of the game with more platforming than guessing which tunnel is the wrong path and backtracking. It also welcomes a jump attack and dropping attack mechanism that helps in combat with a variety of damage dealing maneuvers. Combat aside, this game revolves Adol's journey of collecting magical swords, each with it's own element and moveset. This is the core combat mechanism of The Ark of Napishtim.
Following Adol's journey in searching for these swords, he meets very memorable characters. Some of which people in the latter games on the PSP and Vita are simply left to accept that they exist. Have you ever wondered who Geis is and how he met Adol? He was never always allied with Adol. This is the game to play. (Another shout out to origin stories is for The Oath in Felghana, where it describes Adol's meeting of Dogi from Dogi's friends' perspectives as well as his iconic blue scarf).
Other than a solid story of our amnesiac red head adventurer and his combat prowess this game features a memorable soundtrack and nostalgic pseudo-modern pixel art and beautiful portraits of characters to keep the game attractive.
Xseed has finally ported this to PC with much appreciated features like teleporting between Save Points (obviously to prevent people like me to still get lost in this vast world! LOL)
Final note to new player of this game, save before the last area on another slot! Once you've entered the Ark, theres literally no turning back and once the game ends they dont take you back, so you'd be stuck in that final area in that save state. Xseed probably fixed this with the save point warping, but just a heads up just in case you still want to mess around in the overworld. :)
Most of all ENJOY THE GAME!

An ancient evil computer awakens, and it's up to Adol to hit it until it dies with his trusty swords of plot magic. You join Adol on another exciting adventure as he washes ashore the Canaan Islands within a fictional equivalent of the Bermuda Triangle after his survives yet another shipwreck, as expected of Ys openings.
Ys VI the Ark of Napishtim is the first Ys game of this engine; Oath in Felghana and Origin are the sequels that came after it, despite Felghana taking place chronologically before VI and Origin taking place hundreds of years before Ys I&II. Because this is the first game of this engine, you might feel that the gameplay is less refined than its two sequels of the same battle system. Even if Ys VI is the first game of this engine, the combat is still satisfying with its three elemental swords having different attack style and may even require finesse to master. Wind sword Livart requires successful button press in certain frames to spin Adol right round like a record baby like Felghana and Origin's Wind magic (just referring to Yunica and Adol's Wind magic). Fire sword Blirante allows you to charge your swipes for powerful flame waves. Lightning sword Erricil has you mashing buttons for a thrusting attack that lets you penetrate even the sturdier foes like a certain frog boss you'll fight later. Fans of previous Ys games and fans of action games in general will love this game.
Can't have a Falcom game without awesome soundtrack, and Ark of Napishtim delivers. Enjoy listening to the smooth Ultramarine Deep as you fight a certain disgruntled, butthurt, and jelly black-haired rival in Mythos Path, Mountain Zone as you trigger your PTSD flashback as you dash past exploding balls in Grana-Vallis Mountains, and Ruined City Kishgal as you explore a technologically advanced underground ruin.
For those who have never played a Ys game, this is a great start as you will appreciate the gameplay refinements in the sequel Ys the Oath in Felghana and Ys Origin. For veterans of the series you will love the game because it's more classic Falcom goodness before they joined the anime cliché-brigade with Sen no Kiseki. For those who play it already, buy this game anyways to convince Xseed we want more Falcom games localized for the West. Give this game a shot. You won't regret it.

This game isn't too bad, and I know I say this with a very low gameplay count, but it isn't THAT bad. I definitely think that this game has improved, although I hadn't played the older versions, hearing it from other players, it seemed to evolve a ton. The developers seem fun, seeing as they called their old game "the worst game ever", which is always nice to have good developers. I bought the fourpack for my friends, still haven't given all of them away though.
Let's start with the graphics. When I first launched the game, the title screen was okay, and then I joined a game and the graphics seemed a little... strange, not too well done. Then again, I'm used to ARK graphics, which is most likely why. As I went deeper into the game, I ignored the faulty graphics and I think it's still enjoyable.
Onto the gameplay. When I started up the game, I went into a server to see what everything was about. Wow, I never thought I'd be so confused - I went into a random gamemode, chose to play as a Dilo, and had no clue what I was doing. I started spitting everywhere and a human crawled up next to me and blew me up. That was that for that server, so I went into the Survival gamemode with a few other players. Man, that was certainly a plus. The survival gamemode is fun, waves of dinosaurs of all types, and it's decently challenging when you have everyone come after you. It took me about 5 minutes to get the hang of it (which I am a fast learner, sometimes), and all was good. I followed my teammates to see what was going on, shot dinosaurs, killed a pteradon. Overall, the gameplay I've had so far has been decent.
Honestly, this game is good and all, but don't have high hopes. But then again, for $1, the price of a can of coke, this is worth it, definitely. Sure, there may be glitches, the gameplay may be wonky, the dinosaurs kill you every two minutes, but if you manage to look past its faults, Orion: Prelude is a wonderful game. I'd rate it 7/10.

This is a follow-up review to The Ultimate DOOM. Also don't let the hour count fool you, I played DOOM II as well as Final DOOM through the first game due to an external launcher and a source port.
DOOM II: Hell on Earth is a first person shooter and the sequel to the smash-hit DOOM, released on September 30th 1994 as the 'retail version' of DOOM as the original was only available by mail order, nearly 10 months after the first game. While a sequel in terms of continuing the story and events of the prior game, along with expanded elements, the engine technology remains the same and the gameplay unchanged. DOOM II therefore could be thought as more of a glorified expansion pack than an actual significant leap in the series, but it did introduce some important changes to the formula of the original that are worth covering.
The story continues shortly after the events of DOOM, with the one man army space marine who thwarted a demonic invasion on Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos, as well as traveling into the bowels of Hell itself and overthrowing the source of the moon base attacks. With the last monster slain and the Union Aerospace Corporation a mess but still afloat despite the strong setbacks, you would return home after a well-earned leave as a war hero with a reputation as being the toughest son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ in the known galaxy. It was a hard fight, as you were the only survivor, but it seems the situation is finally under control. Landing back on Earth from a drop pod you secured, you open 'er up and take a look around: the city ahead of you is on fire. What in Hell happened here? Carefully getting out while brandishing your sidearm you notice a field of refugees fleeing from the hellish inferno that was once a bustling metropolis. They're all shrieking in terror from something racing behind them. You get a bead on the attackers, their movements awkward, voices animalistic, as they mob those too weak and slow to escape, greedily indulging in a ravenous frenzy of blood and death. The screams of the fallen chills you to the bone, it sounds all too familiar from what you heard on the radio back on Phobos. Bravely rushing you blast the troublemakers into gory shreds with your pistol and investigate their remains: they appear to be human, but they're all messed up looking and their mouths are filled with mangled flesh.
You can feel it, it's starting again, just like Phobos. First they take ordinary people over, turn them into cannibalistic freaks who kill without a conscience, and then the real horror starts, as beings from your nightmares pour forth from the other side. But now it's on Earth. The invaders are everywhere, billions are dead, the lucky ones are killed on sight, while others were transformed, but a very small few are still alive and fully human. The smart ones got together and came up with a plan, saving what's left of your species via enormous spacecrafts, which would carry the remaining humans into space, safely away from our ruined world. Unfortunately, Earth's only ground starport is on lockdown due to the monsters. They've constructed some kind of a demonic force field, a flame barrier over the port. No ships can land or leave. You've got to figure out how to bring it down at once, as the pathetic remnants of Earth's forces are suffering major casualties, unable to penetrate the attackers at the starport. If you win, you might be able to disable the barrier so that the ships can leave, and Homo sapiens are no longer on the endangered species list. If you lose, that's it, humanity's history. You join up and assist your remaining comrades in the killing fields, but despite your best efforts they continue to drop like flies, and eventually there's nobody left, no one left but you. Standing at the mouth of the starport, you hear familiar hissing and growling echoing through the steel corridors ahead. This time it's personal!
In the tradition via a demand for more, DOOM II brings new and deadlier monsters, a new and powerful weapon, a new pickup, and a plethora of new textures and music tracks across one large thirty-two level game, two of which are hidden, split into three sections via text intermission screens. 'The Starport', 'The City', and 'Hell'. The seven new monsters include a chaingun toting possessed former marine, the less strong but no less deadly Hell Knight who is ultimately just a recolor of the Baron of Hell, series favorites like the morbidly obese Mancubus who packs serious firepower, the highly mobile and missile-launching Revenant, the Lost Soul-belching Cacodemon-like Pain Elemental, the spider-esque Arachnotron who shares a strong resemblance to the final boss from DOOM but now packs a plasma gun, and last but not least the extremely dangerous Arch-Vile who not only have an incredibly powerful attack but also have the power to bring fallen demons in battle back from the dead. In addition to your original arsenal you will acquire the series legendary 'super shotgun', a double-barreled sawed-off killing stick that can tackle all demons new and old with relative ease, but also chews through twice as much shotgun ammo and is slower to reload as a result. A new artifact from the other dimension, rare and very powerful will grant both maximum health capacity and full armor protection, definitely something you'll need if you're going to put an end to the Earth invasion.
Visually the game is the same as the previous, highly detailed sprite and texture work, having aged incredibly well. The sounds for the new monsters are just as terrifying as they are memorable to this day, and the new soundtrack by veteran composer Bobby Prince is still effective at conveying DOOM's atmosphere and gameplay.
My criticisms are more personal than they are commercial. I don't like nearly as many of the maps in DOOM II as I did in the first game. Sandy Petersen, a level designer who had worked on the second and third episodes in DOOM created a vast majority of the maps in DOOM II and his style is a love it or hate it kind of deal. I didn't mind most of his prior work but here there can be some downright dreadful, ugly, too gimmicky or simply boring maps on offer here. I much preferred the creations of John Romero and American McGee, as Sandy's levels are a real mixed bag. Other complaints include there being a lot less usage of color, with too much grey and brown over the course of the game, and the texture set for DOOM II while not a bad set of textures in itself, being highly versatile in the hands of skilled mappers from the community, doesn't do a good job at portraying realistic Earth-based settings with places like cities and neighborhoods being far too abstract for their own good. Lastly I didn't care for most of the new music, save for a few good tunes, most sound either strangely and comically upbeat or just barely scraping by existence with absolute boredom in their instrumentation, which doesn't translate well to the often frantic gameplay. Lastly, the final boss, while very different from what you'd usually see, is really lame in execution.
At the core however DOOM II is an extremely important continuation of the first game and thanks to the alive and well community enjoys the greatest volume of maps and mods available unlike the original. The new gameplay elements are highly polished, expertly balanced, and only add to the DOOM experience as a whole as opposed to departing from it like some game sequels tend to do. Therefore it comes without saying this is a fundamental improvement, mapping for the base game itself aside. Let the obsession begin. Again.

So just a few things to point out.
This game in my opinion is not a horror title, but just very bizarre and surreal at points. The level design and pacing follows a cycle of fighting and bizarre story elements. It repeats this cycle as well.
The weapons are nothing really to boast about, as they're quite generic and uninteresting design-wise. Bullet time however seems to balance this factor out and make fights interesting. Mind you, this game doesn't ♥♥♥♥ around with difficulty, as weapons HURT and a horde of enemies will kill you fast if you're not paying attention. Some parts can be exceptionally difficult first playthrough, but you can overcome it if you figure out what you're doing.
Graphics-wise, this game has not aged well at all. The texturework and models look extremely bland nowadays, and the lighting is nothing to brag about either. As for environments? They're pretty nice, so I can't complain.
One of the things about this game that is really good is that it approaches a situation differently than most linear FPS titles. A conflict will most likely not be like the last, and that's enough to keep me hooked.
Pick this up when it's on sale or if you wanna have a good time, I recommend it.

A tough 2D platformer that struggles with pacing, and sometimes feels more like a chore than playing a game.
Video Review:
This game is fun for a little while, once your past about the first stage and boss, you spend the first few levels in a new area enjoying the new mechanics, then those mechanics get taken to insane levels until playing this game is more like creating your own death montage on the fly.
Nothing wrong with that, one of my biggest problems, is that the later levels don't tend to add much other than just the same mechanics introduced earlier, but harder versions of them.
After about half way in each area, I found myself exiting back to the map to see if I was almost at the boss, to which I'd realize I still had 5 or 6 levels left and would reluctantly start playing again to reach the next boss.
Synopsis: A difficult platformer, with a nice art style, cute little robot pal, voice acted bland storey that gets a bit boring after a few levels in a new area until you reach the boss and play the next few levels in the next area, rinse and repeat.

REALLY fun game to play, especially if you can get into a game of 8+. Don't let the 11v1 stuff fool you! If you or your partner are the devil, you BOTH can win really easily. The devil goes out and attacks while the other teammember does the hunt until it's just those two. Then you can finish the hunt and win. Up to you though, devil can just go solo and win it himself/herself.
Big tip: It's damn near impossible to capture the devil solo, so you definitely need a group around to help. Problem is, only the person that starts the capture gets credit for it. All involved should get some sort of credit for taking down the devil.
The scavenger hunt is pretty easy to handle, it'll tell you roughly where you could find the item in the first part of the clue and what the item is in the second part, the second part not really being necessary since you're looking for something different from the usual surroundings.
SLAPS! Slaps are really useful in the game vs players. You can get a few off while running out of the starting area, letting them continue the slapfest while you're on your way to the first clue. Also, you can slap players in a direction and, if set up right, into traps.
When the devil starts killing, keep an eye out for what characters you AREN'T passing. You can use that as deduction as to who the devil is and avoid them.
If more people can start playing it, definitely worth buying, you can get a lot of laughs from playing and get to communicate with the other players with voice chat.
Edit: To the creators: pressing k to use sometimes has an annoying delay, like when I'm trying to escape from the devil and running up and down stairs to slow him/her down. When I'm able to go up/down stairs or through doorways, I need to when I press the button, not mash it until I go through.

When I just started playing, Necrodancer seemed like an interesting little roguelike with a unique control scheme. And yes, it is a roguelike, not a roguelite: it ticks off all the requirements of the genre other than text graphics.
I wasn't particularly good at it. I failed a lot, died a lot, missed most of the beats -- but playing it was still fun, the soundtrack was great, and I kept at it. Gradually, I became better. What I once thought impossible, I can now do with my eyes closed -- literally, in some cases. And even with hundreds of hours in this game, there are still challenges I haven't done that I think of as impossible. I'll still keep at it, of course.~
Now, Necrodancer became my favourite game of all-time. No other game gives you so much satisfaction of getting gud. There are so many layers of challenge here, so many ways to play the game -- both very difficult and very easy -- and even after you've played for many, many, many hours, you can still feel yourself progress: actually progress and get better at the game, discover new things, new ways to do things, instead of simply upgrading your character like so many other games have you do.
I can't recommend it enough. If you get it, I also recommend redefining the default controls: there's no reason to have to press two keys to perform one action, unless you want to.
The replay system is broken though, which is a huge shame.

I was surprised by ABZU.  A lot of indie games fall flat pretty hard.  ABZU is an esoteric, casual, atmospheric "walking" (diving) simulator.  A few hidden objects to find, but mostly the game is an audio/visual journey as you swim through schools of nicely detailed fish (but, unlike spearfishing games, the point is not to kill them).
Hard work went into polishing the games minimalistic elements.  For me it ran extremely smoothly in 4K, the graphics, while simplistic, gave a solid viewing experience.  The orchestral soundtrack blends in well.  The developer advises that a controller is needed, but I found KB&M to be superior (it always is), and the PC gamers trusted interface works well enough.
Because the genre is an esoteric one, this game might not be for everyone.  Most games of this sort also happen to be poorly exectuted, not so here - the developer achieved what they set out to do.   I am not sure this is worth the full $20 price they're asking, but you could pick this up with a bundle and if you like these kinds of games, you won't be disappointed.

This game is every bit as good as the very highly rated Binding of Isaac. But let's break down why it is.
First of all, let's talk visuals. The sprite work is equal parts cute and badass when it needs to be. Everything is brightly coloured to match the disco ambience of the game and the floor lights up in time with your movements, which is a nice touch. Characters and monsters are expressive, dancing along in time to the music. The game is also very easily moddable with any graphics package, if you are so inclined!
As for the sound, Danny Baranowsky returns from his famously fantastic work on The Binding of Isaac and Super Meat Boy, and he isn't alone. Familyjules9x, a popular guitarist who enjoys making videogame covers on youtube lends his skill to easily match Danny in his energy. Other stand out musicians include Chipzel, who i haven't heard before but are also top tier. In the extremely unlikely event you'd rather listen to something else, the game will automatically generate beats in a level for any MP3 music in your collection. We're talking the best soundtrack i have heard in a rhythm game period. The beat is prominent and easy to pick up in the vast majority of the tracks. Creatures in the game have audio tells to alert you of their presence and what they are doing at that time, so that with practice you will be able to avoid some threats without actively looking at them. Voice acting is unexpectedly well done, as i didn't think it would fit the retro feel, but i am glad i was wrong there.
The gameplay is where the game shines even brighter, believe it or not. It's your standard block by block traditional roguelike game, but you can only move on the beat of the song. If you miss the beat, you wont move. All of your AI enemies of course have perfect timing. However, with practice, they will slowly become more predictable to you. Every enemy in the game has a distinct movement pattern and consequently a dance that you can learn to perfectly counter them. At first enemies have very simple movement patterns, that get more complex with every zone. The difficulty scales beautifully. Did i mention there's local co-op?
This section is about difficulty and how it is handled. First of all, i personally would recommend a dance mat. Not only is it more challenging, but i haven't found a more fun way than this game to exercise. Primarily, difficulty ramps up in the form of the complexity of enemy behaviours along with the BPM slowly ramping up too. You will need to make more complex decisions, faster and execute a response faster as things move along. You will all the while be unlocking new tools, features and bonuses to help you, though you will be counting on your skills primarily. In addition to this, theres a huge number of characters and modes that can make things more punishing or interesting as you get better. One feature i neglected to look at until now is Bard Mode. This character can move at *any* time, the enemies moving after him. Yes, this makes the game far far easier, but what it is, is a tool to learn areas, enemies and weapons more effectively for when you are playing properly and it's extremely useful.
What else can i say about this game? It's easily in my top ten. You are in for some serious fun and if you play with a dance mat, it may even have a very positive impact on your health! I don't think anyone can ask for more than that!

Unfortunately I cannot recomend this game. Its promissing, the devs seems to really make an effort to do a good game but at the current state its unplayable.
- You need to manually schedule every single flight for the rest of your life. When the flight comes, board and goes its over. You need to re-schedule again. Talk about annoying!
- Forget about playing without asking questions on forums and other places. The game gives zero clear messages. You will never know what icons or messages means. Besides the complexity the game also adds spam to make you even more confused. Even being patient and reading everything things happens without any explanation.
- There is a beep that I still don't know what it does. You have 3 notification icons plus 1 beep. Its a horrible UI. The notification icons also blink even when no notifications exist. The menu has so many submenus that I always click several times to find what I want. There are also shortcuts but its not for everything.
- You can only schedule 3 flights per gate per day. I guess that is how the devs figure out to limit the activity and not make the game lag. In Sim Airport you can put at least 10 flights per gate per day.
- Flights fully boarded just wait at the gate and say its delayed for no reason.
- PAX is confused and don't move. That can be solved inside the airport with TVs (figured that out by myself as the message of the game seems to be translated from another language - makes no sense). But PAX confused outside will be confused outside forever because there is nothing you can do to guide them.
- Several minor bugs that needs to be solved by saving and reloading or destroy and reconstruct (not talking about changes of game version). I start a new game every patch. Still no help.
- Zero help on what each employee is used for. You hire them to see what they do and most of the time they just do nothing. They also don't move around when needed and get stuck.
- The game has extensive tutorial that somehow leave you in the blank most of the time. In Sim Airport you have zero tutorial and still can figure out everything by yourself. That is what I call a well designed game. And don't say SimAirport is not complex enough, because it have everything this game have and more. (Fuel system, baggage system, Speakers system, food, bathrooms, ticketing, security, everything).
- PAX walk through walls! So what is the point of everything?
Since I don't know where this game is heading I cannot recommend it. If I need to manually schedule flights, if I cannot define how long the aircraft stays in my airport or the flight stays on ground for 2 hours 100% boarded this game is really not worth it.

While it is not one of the most popular Final Fantasy games with most people, this is my favourite title so far. A lot of the things that many felt let Final Fantasy VIII down are, in my opinion, what makes it so great. The unique junction system, different to any other Final Fantasy, is brilliant. The concept of having stocks of magic is a little off (how.... exactly?), and grinding to get those magics can be a struggle but it makes you appreciate them a lot more, especially when to be the most powerful you can be you have to have stocks of the most powerful magic in the game. But then if you use that magic, your junctioned stats will get less powerful. So then you have to weigh up what matters more. Many couldn't get used to the junction system, but I found it just as easy as the materia system from FFVII.
The music is brilliant, some of my favourite music in any of the games. Also some of my least favourite... But that's a hit and miss with all the games. But honestly, some of the music had it nailed down.
The story is excellent. A lot simpler in concept than FF7, but a lot more character driven than other titles. This is where most people either decide on their love or hate for the game. I personally love the storyline, think it's much easier to relate to than other main characters through the series and the characters are more real. Although Squall, as a main character, has to be the most emotionally unavailable person in history.
I would recommend this game to everyone if I could, but I understand you may not like it as much if you're as hooked on the styles of the other games.

If you enjoy challenging platformers like Super Meat Boy or comedic platformers such as BattleBlock Theater, I would definitely recommend Super Robot Jump Jump.

One of the best games ever. It would be unfair for me to criticise this release for not including a great source port like GZDoom and it relying on DOSBox, given that issues with licensing can prevent even free software from being included (and the true value of the game comes from its fan-made resources - both in improving the core experience, and in providing new experiences with original content).
While I have a slight personal preference for The Ultimate Doom, this game has it's own great new features, including the introduction of the Super Shotgun, new enemies (most of which up the challenge), larger maps and enemy numbers, and more levels (unless you count Thy Flesh Consumed in Ultimate Doom).
I highly recommend this game. As with most other reviews, my low hours in-game are due to the use of GZDoom as a source port. Doom 1 & 2 are timeless classics. I've personally played these for many years and always find myself returning to them. You see, unike many other more modern games, classics such as these are simple and memorable enough to warrant coming back to.
Despite not being overly scary, given the older graphics, it's in the gameplay itself that the scares can come from. Even after all these years, and in having memorised pretty much every secret, level, and monster and item placement (at least on Ultra-Violence), there are times where I still jump in surprise - unlike other more linear modern games, the majority of enemies are present on the map that you're set to explore, an some monsters have a habit of roaming through the map should they hear distant gunshots. It is this factor that can at times make for new experiences, particularly in Doom II, where maps are much larger and the monster count is higher, increasing the prevalence of these moments.
Given it's place in history, and coupled with available fan resources, I heartily recommend this game. Revisit a tme when shooters had more emphasis on exploration and pure action, rather forcefeeding narrative and slowing down gameplay with forced slow periods of waiting.

Isaac comes to in the upper level of the basement and you, the player, must guide him through the dangers that lurk below. The UI is very similar to what you’d expect from an early Zelda title. You have three heart containers. Three counters keep track of your amount of coins, bombs, and keys. The dungeon layout is shown on the upper left and your current items are listed next to your heart containers. You start out with only your tears to fight off the grotesque creatures of the basement. Each floor of the basement is littered with a slew of enemies, chests, items, a treasure room, and a boss room. Upon entering a room, all of the doors will lock until every enemy in it has been defeated. You can blow open a door, but it will cost a single bomb. Useable items can often be found in chests, but are also dropped from enemies. These could be tarot cards, pills, or some other miscellaneous item. Where as the tarot cards have a specific use, pills have random uses. These range from incredibly useful to potentially harmful, so consume them at your own risk. Treasure rooms are marked by their gold outlines, and within them lies a single power-up. These power-ups can increase your speed, change your projectile type, increase your max HP, etc. Some power-ups are weak and their effects can leave more to be desired, while others can be complete game changers and turn the tide of battles in your favor. They’re creatively designed and include some pretty outlandish things like a pair of high heels and even dog food. They also change your physical appearance, and seeing as they stack infinitely, this can result in some pretty hilarious or gruesome appearances. As you progress throughout the game, Isaac’s exterior begins to reflect the hell that is the basement. There are a plethora of bosses and they all battle in different ways. Defeating a boss will open a trapdoor to the next level, and between each floor of the basement a cutscene plays that shows Isaac having a nightmare, often of him being publicly embarrassed. The cutscenes, although oddly humorous, add little depth to Isaac’s character as it can be assumed that the events he worries over never actually took place, seeing as some are pretty over-the-top, such as one where he dreams he was being pooped on by a group of people. The final boss is no other than Isaac’s mother. And even after you’ve managed to beat her, your adventure still isn’t over. There still remains another set of levels and a whole mess of enemies, secrets, items, and power-ups to find.
Through and through, The Binding of Isaac is a bonafide roguelike in every sense of the term. Every dungeon is randomly generated, resulting in no two runs feeling exactly the same. You’re given simple controls and absolutely no tutorial of any sort. Like any self-respecting roguelike, this is a game of trial and error, and it isn’t afraid to hand you your behind on a silver platter. The staggering amount of enemies will force you to adapt to any situation, and you’ll find yourself dying often before you’ve learned most of the enemies’ maneuvers. Bosses deal a lot of damage fast and some will even spawn smaller enemies around themselves. Even after you’ve learned the behavior of every enemy in the game, you’ll still find yourself dying quite often. Useable items and power-ups add variation to the gameplay and the tactics you’ll use in combat. With the unbelievable amount of depth found in the seemingly simple game, The Binding of Isaac produces an experience that becomes insanely addictive and rarely feels stale, even after dozens of hours of playtime.
The Binding of Isaac’s visual presentation is something straight from the mind of a madman. Its art style is sleek, simple, and endearing. The various brown hues of the basement stand apart from each other, enhanced by the excellent shading, but they’re just pieces in a whole that create an immersive and beautiful environment. The story is primarily told through Isaac’s drawings. It’s all nice and cutesy, that is until you actually walk around and see the dreadful conditions of the basement. A myriad of deformed and bloody enemies stalk the rooms and each seem to spout blood like a fountain upon dying. There are these worm-like enemies that actually look somewhat adorable, until they charge at you with their fangs bared, trying to eat your face off. Piles of poop lay scattered on the ground. The changes that accompany the power-ups can be humorous, but others completely change the way Isaac looks, essentially turning him into one of the monsters that he faces. The fact that you aren’t alone suggests that you aren’t the first to face the wickedness of Isaac’s mother, and the possibility that the enemies could be related to him makes the adventure even more cringe worthy. In some dungeons you’ll find a room in which you can purchase items in exchange for coins. Each of these shops feature a hanging Isaac-lookalike, their faces twisted with expressions of despair. It’s an enthralling visual endeavor that shocks you from the start and carries out its dark themes with precise execution.
The Binding of Isaac’s soundtrack aims to emphasize the same contrast brought about by the art style, and it manages to do so quite well. The music is slightly upbeat and detracts from the hopelessness that Isaac feels as he wanders through the basement. At times the music speeds up just a bit and the volume increases, ramping up your adrenaline at the same time. There is a slight feeling of loneliness in the unknown created by the soundtrack, and this is where it slightly fractures the contrast and actually melds with the setting. Enemy and projectile sounds are squishy in nature, but impactful overall. The contrast between the game’s dark themes and relatively uplifting music is genuinely interesting and adds another layer of depth.
Despite its numerous references and tie-ins to other forms of media, The Binding of Isaac does plenty to set itself apart from the pack. There are some really laughable moments in the otherwise grim depths of the basement: there’s a certain enemy that will scurry away from you, whimpering as it tries desperately to flee; of the hanging Isaac-lookalikes in the shops, one of them has a huge grin on his face; some of the items and power-ups are just meant to make you burst out laughing, like Mom’s Pad – a useable item that makes all enemies in a room retreat for several seconds. Also, it raises some very serious questions that most games wouldn’t dare ask. It ventures into often-untraveled territory by challenging our understanding of organized religion, mental illness, and child abuse. These are very touchy subjects and it’s admirable to see developers who aren’t afraid to speak on them.
The Binding of Isaac proves to be a unique and addictive adventure. Its humor is welcoming and its roguelike nature results in an unbelievable amount of replay value. While it may look simple at first, there is a surprising amount of depth to be found. Its endearing art style and aesthetically pleasing soundtrack is welcoming, while its dark themes are perfectly executed in the story and character designs. More than just a fun game, it questions what we as a society perceive to be norms and challenges us to think differently. The only real downsides to the game are the lack of characterization on Isaac and the slight capitalization on nostalgia. Aside from that, it’s an incredible game that should be played by anyone who enjoys a solid roguelike – or just a good game in general – because it stands head and shoulders above its competition in the genre.

I came across F.E.A.R. while looking for papers on artificial intelligence to reference for my Master's thesis. Even a decade after release, the AI stands out as being the smartest I've ever fought: enemies are programmed to find cover and reposition themselves based on the player's current position, which leads to them flanking and circling behind the player, or throwing grenades to flush you out.  In short, they act very much like humans, and when you hear them freak out after you've wiped out half the squad or realise they're the only one left, it feels pretty awesome.  The well-designed levels help too, as enemies rarely have only one way to approach you, allowing firefights to remain tense.
That said, F.E.A.R. isn't just a tactical shooter with great AI. It could be described as a first-person-shooter written as a horror movie. The horror here doesn't really rely on jump scares, although they do show up, but overall it relies on atmosphere and being generally creepy, with randomly banging doors and unnerving sound effects. Some levels have few enemies - on occasion, there are none at all - and some parts will lapse into reality-warping hallucinations caused by a girl in a red dress. Even after playing through the game a few times, and remembering where these parts occur, I found it quite hard to
spam bullets - if I even had a gun at that point.
Finally, a note about the expansions. Extraction Point is set after the events of F.E.A.R and uses the same player character, but has a greater emphasis on horror and is even creepier. Perseus Mandate takes place during and just after F.E.A.R., places you in the shoes of a different character, and gives you some different (and tougher) enemies, but other than that is pretty much the same. These are offically not part of the series canon, which is a pity, because they are well-made expansions and definitely worth playing.
Overall, I consider this one of the greatest FPS games ever made, and highly recommend it.

Playing this game, even after so many years, is being an absolute blast. Especially now when comparing the rig I had back in the day, and this now where the game is going smooth at locked 60 fps, and being played how its creators have envisioned.
Besides, other memories are tied to majority of my friends, who were like "Dude, this sick s**t... I'm not even... I mean what the... This little girl, and.. dark and... I just couldn't. Start>>>uninstall after 10 mins in..." I don't know but, personally, I didn't find it THAT scary. Maybe I'm weird, or maybe I had Doom3 in the year before, where it trained me well with its cheap-as* tricks with monsters spawning behind your backs,  who knows.
So, yeah, the game is called F.E.A.R. Nice play of words which also stands for First Encounter Assault and Recon, special unit made for investigating and battling paranormal activities. You were just transferred into it, nameless protagonist referred simply as "Point Man", a dude whos inhuman reflexes earned him his place there, which are presented in-game as a slo-mo, or bullet time. Previously seen in Max Payne games, but found a great place in a FPS game as well.
With the help of unknown forces, Paxton Fettel, a psychic commander (also a canibal who enjoys human flesh...) escapes from his confinement, and has a command over a whole battalion of telepathically controlled military clones. Its up to you to stop him, and investigate the ties with the Armacham Corporation, and the little girl known as Alma (who's ghostly presence is here for scary moments), while collecting the pieces of the puzzle by advancing through the chapters and listening to the voice messages or hacking computers.
Majority of the game you'll spend battling Fettel's Replica Forces, or occasional Armacham security personel, which doesn't make much of a difference, except for the different models used. Of course, its not some scary experience unless you are playing alone (the lesson which FEAR3 maybe didn't learn), so you won't see any use of your FEAR colleagues, or DELTA Force companions. You may arrive with some of them at the scene, but soon you'll venture alone to pull some switch, just to find them lying in pieces in the lake of blood after getting back...
Action in this game is just stellar. Awesome sound design, fires and explosions are looking amazing, particles and sparcles bursting around when highly destructable terrain comes under fire, holes leaving on concrete surfaces (this game is just rich with those) bursting in dust coulds when fired upon, grenades shaking ground and causing nearby light sources to blink, or enemies to lose the balance (if not killed by those),... There's a variety of weapons and grenade types, but my personal favorite is the SMG. Effects and sounds this weapon is producing are so sweet, its such a shame that I have to stop shooting sometimes to reload it. Out of ammo already? But I don't want to use anything else... Oh well, whatever works, I guess.
AI is still better than what 99% of other games can muster. Enemies are even reacting to your flashlight, and as soon as they spot you their first reaction is diving into closest cover available. Heck, if there's no cover at all they'll make it by turning the furniture, or try to block your way with those. If you flank them they'll try to minimize the effect of it by running backwards to the next available cover while still shooting at you. In fact, Replicas are even more scary than Alma's freaks (which you'll face occasionaly every 30 mins of hard boilled action). Nothing causes a jump scare like stumbling upon them around the corner, or surprisingly after opening some door. Is he going to shotgun my face? M I going to eat his foot or his grenade? Fighting 3 of them without using slo-mo grants you quick death, even with full body armor and health (moderate difficulty level). Slo-mo serves like a cheat mode which gives you the edge over them. How much AI is smart you can see by activating the slo-mo, they immediately figure out that they are screwed over while yelling "Oh shieeeee...", or "Oh fuuuuu..."...
They love throwing grenades so much. Camp in the cover for too long and you can be sure you'll eat it. He is falling down, but ba*tard still managed to throw one down to your nose with his last breath. Boom, back to checkpoint. God help you if you forgot to quicksave since checkpoints are so far away, nothing kills your mood to play further like these things. But AI isn't perfect by any means. You can clearly hear your footseps since you are threading like an elephant, but they can't, so you can just walk to them and melee if you see their backs. Sometimes they are killed by their own grenade for hitting accidentally a part of some fence (physics in this game goes so far that even rocket launcher projectiles are colliding mid air, including with bullets). At least they can taste their own medicine sometimes, and so can you when your own grenade explodes in your face for being shot mid air with gun fire.
Their reaction to your shots is very realistic, followed by sounds of every bullet hitting their body armor. But while they are "dancing" under fire they'll still try hard to hit you or shoot you, depending on your stance. You'll also have issues with aiming yourself when being shot at. Pretty much everything you can do to them they can do to you. Melee attacks in this game are very deadly, especially your own jump kick which will one hit every regular unit. There's also a special type of cloacked clone combating without any weaponry.
Graphics are very detailed even by today's standards, special reward goes to the shadows and their relationship with light sources. They are often overused, hiding low textures here and there. Shadows are so deep you have a feeling that shooting will leave holes in them. There's no much of variety in level design, very linear game full of offices and concrete surfaces. Still, there are some hidden spots, and snooping around pays off for finding reflex and health boosters, while backtracking is mostly minimized. You can see your whole body including legs, and when using variety of melee attacks, while sounds which your equipment is producing while moving/fighting are giving a better feel of weight to the whole thing.
There's not much to say about multiplayer since its servers were shut down long ago, while music is almost non-existent and plays occasionaly during larger fights, or longer nightmares caused by Alma.

I've played this game for almost 50 hours now, and I have to say, you shouldn't buy it.  There are enough small problems that—as much as I want to play—make the experience bad.
The first sign of things going wrong was when I finally managed to complete my first run as Cadence.  It was an _awesome_ run, and as soon as I finished (and watched the credits) I wanted to replay it.  Problem is, for some reason, my moves weren't saved properly.  In the middle of level 1-3 of the replay, Cadence suddenly started acting all wrong, and got stuck.  It seems that this has been reported before, and from what I can tell there is no fix.
And, since it doesn't seem possible to name individual playthroughs, it's probably been lost forever.
I eventually got to playing as Aria, and I've found it has become almost impossible for me.  I've gotten as far as 4-3, but so much of it appears to be because of the RNG: Because of the level's layout, and the enemies that get put down.
At that point, when (for me) it becomes more about the RNG than about skill (because I don't think practicing is gonna help), it no longer becomes fun.
So now, the only thing which brings me back is All-Zones Mode, and the Daily Challenge.  And All-Zones Mode in particular exposes two big issues.
First, in All-Zones Mode, when you die, you have to start back at the beginning.  That's understood, but you start at the beginning of a _new layout_.  The old layout is gone forever, because there is no way (that I know of) to find out what seed was used for a particular All-Zones Mode run, or (for that matter) for the day's challenge dungeon.
I would be willing to give up my leaderboard opportunity, in exchange for being able to re-start the run at the start of level, so that I could try again.  But that opportunity doesn't exist.  There is a way for you to face off against an individual, single enemy or boss, but that's not what I want.  I want to be able to go back to where I failed, to see if I could do it better.  But I can't do that.
To add insult to injury, the loading screen has recently started reminding me that there's a DLC available.  I _know_ that there's a DLC available, and I do _not_ want to buy it, so it would be awesome if you could please stop reminding me about it!
So, no.  Just no.  I've given it what I think is my best try, but I don't see any way to get better, so now it's become like a gambling addition, and I need to stop.
All that said, you should definitely buy the soundtrack.  It's totally awesome.

This was a replay for me, having first played FEAR some years ago. I had fond memories of the game and thought it time to revisit it. I’m glad I did. The game has a wonderfully spooky and tense atmosphere and outdoes many more recent titles in this respect (it still startled me on several occasions). The graphics are pretty good given the game’s age. It comes from the era when FPSs were commonly set in research facilities, abandoned factories, and office buildings, and this lack of diversity in the environments is one of the game’s weaknesses. As is the lack of humour -- there are no laughs here. But the game’s strengths lie in the atmosphere and in the combat. There is a palpable sense of apprehension as you sneak along the corridors under the flickering lights. The AI is crafty and the combat is always fun, especially when using the slo-mo, or bullet-time, ability, which is flawlessly implemented. If you like a good old-fashioned FPS with loads of atmosphere and plenty of exhilarating combat you can’t go far wrong with this classic.

This game has a lot of depth and provides a good challenge. If you are looking for something mindless, this isn't for you.

Obviously, this game is in early access right now. This means that bugs and issues arise that have the potential to limit a persons ability to play the game. In comparison to other early access releases on Steam, I would say that ACEO has had one of the best early access releases I have ever seen. Kill Everything On The Screen: X, Y, X, X, X, Y, Mash B, Hold Y
Single-Target DPS Pump: X, X, X, Down + X, Repeat
The Good:
Art Assets - environments, splashes, music, etc. are among the best I have seen in this genre
Exploration - regions are distinct and visually impressive. It is exciting to unlock new ones.
Combat Feel - this game has exceptionally responsive/impactful animations/effects for attacks
The Bad:
Combat Depth - it seems tricky at first, but the first combo listed above will win every battle.
Stat Management - you don't make many choices; your character just gains power over time.
Subtle Telegraphing - telegraphs are too fast and subtle. parries/rolls are underpowered.
The Otherwise Noteworthy:
This appears to be intended as a kids game, though I (age 22) found it perfectly enjoyable. Some people might want to be forewarned about the following:
- Everybody is a furry
- Your companion has a mild case of squeaky-anime-girl-syndrome
- The story might come off as 3deep5me
These can all improve/damage your experience in accordnace with your mindset.

This is one of those games that is so good that you cant figure out why there aren't more players. I know it just released, but seriously this should be selling like hotcakes.
It's an asymmetric 1v11 game. All twelve players are on a scavenger hunt. One of those players is also the Devil.
The players go around the house in teams of two solving different sets of riddles in order to find a clue. Once all of the clues are found the scavenger hunt is won. Players take turns slapping each other silly in order to delay progress or defend themselves from the actual devil.
The disguised Devil player, who can ditch his disguise and transform into the Devil at any time, can win by eliminating all of the 11 players, or by winning the scavenger hunt himself. While transformed as the Devil, he has a much faster walking speed, and a high damage melee attack replaces his slap.
Players have a capture meter, that when full allows them to leap and initiate a spacebar mashing "brawl" with the Devil/suspected Devil in disguise in an attempt to capture him and end the game. 1v1 the Devil is afaik impossible to capture, but other players can also leap into the brawl and join in the button mashing to increase the odds of capturing the Devil. The downside to this is that if a player missed the Devil and hits another player a brawl will start with them instead and it cannot be immediately canceled.
The map is a multi-story mansion complete with garden, tea room, mausoleum, sewers, torture chamber, evil laboratory, the usual stuff mostly. It is also outfitted with secret doors and passageways, dumbwaiters, traps, and hiding places to help you accomplish your goals. Players who are not the Devil can still use traps to hurt other players or the Devil himself.
The game features proximity-based open mic chat to facilitate communication with teammates and spying on rivals and/or targets. This can be muted but it is not recommended as a majority of the gameplay takes place through this communication, and there is no typed chat in game. Players can trade information about what they know about the Devils identity, lie about it, or keep it to themselves, which opens up some interesting gameplay strategies and opportunities.

The Swan Princess and The Dire Tree is the 11th game in the Dark Parables series.  Though stand alone, for anyone who has been following this series there are omages to the previous games (Rapunzel #7 and Goldilocks #10 come to mind immediately) and adds even more history to the Prince James (Frog Prince #2) saga. (For those who care the 1st Swan Princess, Odette, was one of the Prince James' (Frog Prince) 5 wives.  Also Ross Red (Prince Ross Red) is the fraternal twin of Princess Snow White, now Queen Snow White also known as the Snow Queen (# 3), who was also one of Prince James' 5 wives.)  I do so enjoy a series that keeps their overall long term story straight and without plot holes. But enough about the series as a whole.
Storyline: As soon as the flying 'Seed of Life' from the Dire Tree (omage to Yggdrasil, Tree of Life) germinates it is stolen by the Black Swan, a title giving to a Swan Guard traitor in the Swan Kingdom on Dire Island. (Swan guards are the lifelong protectors of the Goddess Flora and the Dire Tree.)  The whole Swan Kingdom and the entire island of Dire is now facing utter destruction since the 'Seed of Life' used in a life regenerative ritual by the Goddess Flora now can not be performed unless returned. Huge lava filled cracks are appearing all over the island and the present and 6th Swan Princess has sent for aid.  That aid comes from the Master Tailor (omage to a fairy tale), who can literally sew the earthen cracks shut with his enchanted "sword" which looks like a sewing needle, and you, the player as the Fairy Tale Detective.  Your task find the traitor, the Black Swan (once Head of the Swan Guards) and the flying 'Seed of Life' then return them both to the Swan Princess.  The situation is not as it seems, appearances are deceiving and everything changes when the Goddess Flora dies. (Chapter 2).  The mission then becomes find out what is really going on, the reasons behind everything and of course, saving the Swan Kingdom from annilihation.  That is part of the job description after all, Fairy Tale Detective.
The Game:  8 chapters plus 2 bonus chapters.  Intricate storyline that has all the plot twists of a corkscrew with magic, mayhem, intrigue, treachery and murder.  And I still call this a family friendly game.
Fast travel map with things to do highlighted with a star. Pastel color pallette. Built in strategy guide. Four game modes: Casual, Hard, Insane and Custom.  No hand holding in this game, and at times the clues are a bit obsure, if not missed because the dialogue disappears way too fast.  Personally I recommend Casual for all the little sparklies that are hard to see anyway and the hints on the fast travel map.  No reason not to play on Casual.  There is no achievement for playing on Hard mode.  There are  no hint penalties unless in Hidden Object Puzzle (HOP) and no skip penalties.  The in-game achievements are same as the Steam achievements.  There are even trading cards.
All achievements can be earned in a single playthrough, and if any are missed (except the parables) during gameplay (including the collectibles) they can be picked up through the Extras menu.  All Hidden Object Puzzles (HOPs) and mini-games can be replayed in the Extra menu.  There is a mini-game called Souvenirs where the player goes back through every scene in the game and looks for a single item (watch for cursor change, if the item is not immediately apparent.) The Extra menu includes art concept, wall papers, music, video, etc.   The main game screen includes buttons for achievements, parables and collectibles so the player can keep track of their progress without leaving the game.
One of the newest features of the game series is the 3D elements.  This feature is quite prominent when opening smaller boxes.  Also they have stirred away from the traditional morphing/ghost objects and made their morphing objects (which morph into a flower) their parable pieces.  The other extra hidden find, the collectibles, are tiny acorns with wings on both sides.  Some of these can be quite tough to find.  (Did I mention that built in strategy guide that so happens to have at the end the location of all parable pieces and acorn collectibles.)
Gameplay: A smooth blend between point and click, problem solving, HOPs, and puzzles.  Nothing is contrived, all four of those elements appear where they should.  Point and click to adventure about, problem solving when a task needs to be done, HOPs when looking for or needing a specialized object like a key and puzzles on anything that locks or opens usually.
The problem solving bits can be a bit obsure at times and chase about on the fast map.  But it does not happen often  and the clues are there.  Just be very observant, click on everything, and look for cursor changes.  Some places are rather small in out of the way places or seemingly unimportant places like a brazier at the top of a staircase.  Everything is very logical in the story progression and what one would normally do if presented with the same type of situation in real life.  And yes, keys are the only thing that open locks. (Though the "key" may not necessarily be a standard type of key.  Gems are used as keys.)
The HOPs are pictures unlike the usual list finds.  These types of HOPs are standard for this series.  Basically some object has been disassembled into pieces and the HOP consists of finding all the pieces.  The game will automatically assembly the pieces when finished.  The pieces are divided into three different sections, so as the pieces of each section are all found that part will assembly itself.  When all three sections have assemblied, those three pieces will assembly into the completed object and go into inventory.  Once the mind accustoms itself to this, the HOPs can become very easy.  Nothing is unfairly hidden, though some pieces are half hidden behind other things or obsured in some way, and the size or color can change slightly.  Color changes are generally due to "poor light" or "shadows" in the game scene.  For example the game scene is heavily shaded by trees and slightly in creviss.  Every item is drawn according to these light conditions.  Though in this game finding the mosaic pieces on the mosaic itself was a challenge. It was like looking for jigsaw puzzle pieces on the jigsaw puzzle itself.
The puzzles are varied, diverse and something NEW.  There are several types of mazes including a vertical tower maze, sliders, rotators, a jigsaw puzzle, a tangram, a recipe, logic puzzles, matching and a NEW type of puzzle my friend mickmane called a logic connector.  I would call it a math logic connector or even a circuitry puzzle.  These puzzles are found on the rune pedestrals.  How they work is there are numbered dice (the amount of connections allowed) scattered all over the board and to solve the player must connect lines to every die for that amount of connections.  Seems simple when hearing it explained, looks daunting when seen, and logic is the name of this game.  And it is NEW.  After a lifetime of puzzles, I have never played this type of puzzle before.  Thumbs up!!

F.E.A.R. is an abominational failure of a horror game wrapped around one of the most stylish and satisfying first-person action shooters ever made. It's never scary (maybe shocking, definitely spooky, but not scary), but the horror atmosphere lends a terse, exciting atmosphere to it that's rarely found in its contemporaries, going only to further boost the fun of gun combat that is among the cream of the genre's crop.
Skeletons, psychic soldiers, seeping pools of blood and wild hallucinations all feature, as well as cannibals and The Grudge/The Ring, but they don't really ever frighten so much as spook. It's more akin to a theme park haunted house (or, day I say it, a Hideo Kojima title); it's surprising and strange, but behind every sincere scream is a laugh, because none of it is dangerous - it's mere window dressing. But it is a fabulously entertaining window dressing - it means that the horror gore has been ramped to 11 - so you have weapons like, say, shotguns that blow enemies into mist, or rail guns that decapitate heads and leave them pinned into walls. Also, bizarrely - and fantastically - the combat includes a fairly robust and stupidly ridiculous melee system, with flying bicycle kicks and sliding kicks all available at the press of a button, as well as a slo-mo bullet time ability. It controls less like a horror shooter and more like The freaking Matrix, and that's absolutely a positive.
It might not be scary (and for a game called "F.E.A.R." that might be a bigger problem than I'm making it out to be), but my god. The gunplay is superb, the enemy AI is just cunning enough to be a challenge while just stupid enough to not be an annoyance (it's not quite a "tactical" shooter, but it has that kind of grounding to its gunfights). It's chunky and powerful, but it isn't slow-paced, and the level design is freaking fantastic. It all combines to create a genuinely satisfying and wholly entertaining shooter, and the horror, while absolutely failed, adds an enjoyable twist to the formula that means the game rarely feels familiar. It's just a really great FPS, and if you like first-person shooters, I'd say this is one you need to play. Everything in it adds enough spice to it that the flavour is... well, it's not wildly divergent, but it's satisfyingly unique. There's nothing else quite like it, even its sequels, so, yeah. Huge thumbs up from me.

Water, water everywhere so lets all take a swim!
ABZU is from the art director of the award wininng game Journey, except with one major difference THERE'S WATER!!
This game is art in its puriest form, as ABZU relies heavily upon its visuals and atmosphere, this is done very effectively as you swim in calm waters and reefs near the surface with the sun glistening through the water bringing colour and ambiance to your surroundings to diving deep into an abyss where light is unable to reach, to create an omnious environment as you explore further into the game. And it all looks beautiful.
Much like the game Journey, there is no distinctive narrative as ABZU's story is more open to interpretation, which creates further emphasis on the artistic aspects of the game without making it feel overly pretentious. ABZU is more to do with the experience and exploration which makes it a very soothing game to play. The exploration is done pretty well as not only do explore the different environmnets that you encounter but they also incorporate smaller forms of exploration. Little Inferno is a charming one.
If you had any previous experience with World of Goo, you should know exactly what to expect out of this little piece's flavor and aesthetics. For many small games, there is a point where, for the sake of keeping up with the challenges the gameplay introduces, the player's mind effectively strips away the colorful facade of it, revealing the core mechanics to be yet another twist on an ages old arcade, which it is perceived as from there on. Here, that's hardly the case.
Then again, the complexity of Little Inferno's gameplay is somewhere between that of Clicker Heroes and a bubble wrap simulator. Yet, given how deeply satisfying the look and feel of this trivial process proves, and how the occasional story shards keep popping up at just the right moments, this simplicity manages to give birth to some mesmerizing immersion.
The visuals are freakishly grotesque and disarmingly adorable at the same time, and the beautiful soundtrack contributes overwhelming emotionality to the process. Invest in it just a bit, click away the build-up, and you find yourself at the story's climax, gasping for every little final detail like a revelation.
Little Inferno is a cozy place to be. The flames will consume you whole. But that's okay.

First off, yes I got it for free through a key give away. But I paid for all the DLC so were even Stardock.
This game is like Civilization but in space. You tend to get a lot of that "1 more turn!!" syndrome going on with it. So if you're a fan of Civ you'll like this game a lot.
The AI actually makes sense for the most part. It'll act based off the personality type of the civ. So a malviolent civ is more likely to declare war on you than a benevolent civ. There are exceptions but it tends to hold for the most part. When they attack they will also do so intelligently, they won't send 1 or 2 ships against your fleet of 15. They'll send transports to invade your worlds so if you don't defend you'll end up losing them. They swarm their colony ships so you better be faster than them to the good worlds.
Trade is clearly defined by a bar in the trade wind. It would be nice to add in the ability to threaten or convince a civ to take a deal that is unfair in your favor. Right now they'll only trade if its even or leaning towards them and the AI tends to be really greedy. And they'll offer trade deals heavily in their favor even though the bar appears even. So if you start to mess around with their demands from you the bar will adjust showing the lop-sided deal.
Lots of editing tools to build your own ships and civs for it. With that a really active workshop community if you just don't have the time or creativity to build your own ships. I fall into both categories. And if I'm not mistaken there are more modding tools that are in the works.
I know there are bad reviews and some of them I've read are from people who've played the 2nd one. I've never played the second one but this game is fine for me. But if stardock has a fourth one planned, and actually reads this, the one thing I would want is to be able to controll the fleets in combat instead of being a spectator. Sort of Total War style ship combat but with spaceships.

This game is not about perfectly recreating how cars drive in real life, it's about the driving experience. Races are intense. You feel the engine, you feel every bump in the road. If you cut off an opponent in a corner, he will notice and the next time he is in front of you in a corner, he will try to cut you off. This game is what it says: "The most immersive racing video game experience to date".
The helmet camera is an extra step in this immersive experience. This is the only racing game I know where you actually play the driver, instead of the car. You don't look straight ahead all the time, you look into the corners. My only complaint with this camera is that it sometimes rotates too much, especially when approaching a sharp corner. It also restricts your view quite much, which wasn't a problem for me, but if it could be for you, there is always the other camera's: in front of the car and third person behind the car.
And just a note: this game isn't really playable with a keyboard. Get a gamepad (or a racing wheel), otherwise the input lag is unbearable.
If you want true realistic racing, then look somewhere else. If you want something even more fun than that, an intense racing experience, this game delivers.
Update: After posting this review, the game started crashing at the loading of most races, at a point where it is unplayable. I have tried reinstalling, verifying and all sorts of tricks, but the crashing does not go away. Until I've figured out how to fix that, I sadly cannot recommend this game.
Update 2: For some reason, a few days waiting seems to have completely fixed the crashes. To my knowledge I haven't changed anything, so unfortunately I cannot help if you have a similar problem. However this means that, although warily, I can recommend this game again, yay!

Stellaris is not perfect. The UI is still, even after a few patches, a bit clunky for someone who hasn't weaned themselves on an earlier Paradox title to get used to. The AI is not terribly bright, particularly when it comes to moving fleets. Victory is achieved exclusively through military hegemony: you either make every starfaring race your vassals, wipe them out, or claim the majority of the habitable worlds in the galaxy.
Despite its flaws, Stellaris is still a lot of fun to play, and has a lot of room to grow. Paradox have brought together some of my favorite features from other games, both from other 4X space games and Paradox's other titles. Its diplomacy system is very similar to the one in Europa Universalis. It has a first contact system that is very reminiscent of the one in Sword of the Stars, where you can never be certain if an unknown alien ship is going to be hostile or not. Stellaris also has Grand Menaces that can really shake up a stagnant late game, much like Sword of the Stars. The ability (and in fact it is necessary once your empire starts to really grow) to automate "sectors" under the rule of leader characters also gives the game a tiny bit of a Crusader Kings 2 vibe, especially when those sectors begin to get unruly.
By far my favorite part of Stellaris, and what truly sets it apart from other entries in the genre, is how I end up talking about it. I won't tell someone about how I couldn't win a war until after I advanced my ground combat tech; I'll tell them about how my squishy fungus people were so miserable at ground-fighting that I had to develop artificial intelligence and build legions of droid soldiers to fight my wars for me. I won't tell someone that robotics technologies let you construct pops that don't have penalties on worlds that your species can barely inhabit; I'll talk about how the advent of independent robots allowed my empire to colonize and exploit worlds that were beyond our abilities before, as we seeded entire worlds with billions of AI-controlled robots to mine worlds with prohibitively harsh climates. I won't say that I lost the game because my reliance on AI techs meant that an event triggering an AI rebellion was beyond my means to put down. Wow, this is going to be hard for me. First I am a huge fan of Paradox games. I've been playing them since the first EU came out. Unfortunetly, the game is just plain borring. Don't get me wrong, there is a lot of potential but the game just seems unfinished. First, despite having a computer well above the recommended specs, late game just drags to the point of being unplayable. Then there is the AI, which doesn't seem to ever do anything. Even when the AI is far superior then I am, they will never attack or do anything to interact with my empire.
The biggest let down is the end game. After surveying half the galaxy the game just becomes a micro-managing nightmare. Don't get me wrong, Paradox games are known for their high levels of detail, but this is different. There are never internal conflicts or special events in late game. You just spend you time upgrading power plants and mines every time you tech up. Eventually you dwarf the other nearby empires and spend most of the game chasing down their fleets who refuse to engage.
I feel like this game is waiting for some big patch to make it fun. I know Paradox is big on patching their games and usually does a great job of making content worthwhile. However, this is the first game from them that has left me feeling let down. I want this game to be good, but it just isn't.

Well, without putting too fine a point on it, this game has gripped me like no other game this year. It's been a long time since I was as enthusiastic about anything as I am about Stellaris.
From the moment I started playing, I was hooked. My first empire was a collection of racist, collectivist insects that came to dominate the spiral arm they were born on within 150 years. Then I managed to♥♥♥♥♥♥off a Fallen Empire, who promptly destroyed all of my ships in a very one-sided war. Everyone else I'd annoyed with my earlier expansion (and constant genocide...) decided to jump in and take me to pieces like hyenas at a carcass.
I had a few more non-starter games where I was crushed before the century was out, (protip: if you don't feel like having this happen, you can turn 'advanced AI starts down and lower the chances you'll start next to someone big who hates you for existing) but then I decided to roll chill science-y space lizards.
Now, this is where I have problems with the game in its current form. It was easy from an RP perspective to knock out the empires around me who wanted me dead and burned, but once all of them were gone and I had nothing but nice neighbours, there was pretty much nothing to do. Some of them would have joined an alliance with me, but for some reason that reduces your influence per month, which I needed for lots of things. The rest of them pretty much didn't want anything to do with me. I couldn't travel through their territory with my science ships because we weren't allies, and we couldn't be allies because I needed the influence/they weren't up for it. Which left me having to declare nonsensical wars just to be able to spread out a bit.
There's a lot been said about how the diplomacy side is lacking, and I think that's probably the root of my problems. The other stuff, (strangely scaled UI, combat looking really strange, no map filters) I could either live without or mod in, but not having anything to do in the mid-game is not really something modders can fix.
I'm pretty confident PDX are going to support Stellaris for a long time, and I doubt they'll leave things the way they are for long, but I guess it's a bit of an oversight to have the middle portion of the game have almost nothing to do in it. Especially considering the endgame crises are excellent (if they fire properly) and early game is serious fun.
Should you buy this game? That depends. I've put nearly 100 hours in since release, and I don't regret it. As a reader of classic sci-fi, an ex-40k player and a keen fan of Paradox Interactive, I'm probably going to be a little bit biased. This is essentially an early Christmas for me.
However, the polish just isn't there. If you're on the fence (and you probably are, if you're reading this review) I'd advise you to wait a few months before you dive in, or maybe wait until a sale. If you're not too bothered by the things I've mentioned above and are as massive a science fiction fan as I am, you should just buy it already.

I tried to put time into Witcher 1, but it seems like that installment was stricken with the same First-Start problems that you'd find with the first Assassin's Creed and Mass Effect games. The first one, while being a solid base for what was to come, still was crippled with annoying and shoddy work.
This game makes up for it.
While it still has issues with a few bugs, it's not nearly the unpolished mess that the first Witcher fell victim to, and none of them are game-breaking. The visuals are much more striking, and while there's more than enough time to explore a given area, it still has a strong plot that promises a great deal of good things to come. Relative to the first, this game sheds the overwhelming MMO feel that pervades the original, making it the game I really like to play.
Combat revolves around careful timing and the right use of skills, and even at the start I was much more satisfied with the fight when I finish off one opponent, knock another back with a magic blast, then do a small hop to attack a third who was trying to charge in. It kinda harkens a little to the combat you'd see in Assassin's Creed, but the use of magic, bombs, and traps really puts it in its own niche.
Characters and dialog are done much better than before. Ultimately, the first one always seemed to fall flat, not quite bringing things to life for me to really get me into the story like I should. Not here. The voice actors emote, and the conversations are much more organic and have me engaged enough to put some thought into my replies.
The graphics got a huge boost, which is to be expected, I imagine... but it does more than the first ever did. Environments are diverse, varied and engaging, and definitely shed the 3/4ths view that added to that MMO-feel in the first game.
If you're a casual gamer with an interest in the series. Start here. I imagine that there are nuanced details that will slip past because they were involved in the original, but this is the more engaging experience, and I'm pretty confident that a few internet searches can cough up the relevant background detail the first game brings.
