This game got its' hooks into me good.  The action both draws reverently from the classic metroid-vania formula, while adding a unique edge and kineticism.  It's great to swoosh around destroying folks like a big blue tornado,  Great combat system, although the challenge tapers off a bit towards the end if you enjoy hunting down the prime goodies.  The story really stands out as well.  You can tell that someone cared very much about telling a sweeping fairytale, and the voice acting and animation do a great job of drawing us in.  There are a good many surprises here and there, and it dips its toe into some pretty mature conflict and subject matter.  To that end I think it could have gone a bit further and added in some moral ambiguity.  Duality is a theme, but they seem to have no qualms with clearly identifying the right and wrong sides.  That being said, the whole package; the music, story, animation, pacing, explorative spirit round this out into a fantastic little game.   16 Hours all told, and I managed to 100% most things without feeling bogged down by sidequests.  Oh, and the nods to other indie games (as well as a delightful Castlevania II reference) are a welcome addition.

Doom II is by all accounts a great game, it's fast paced, fun and requires skill and problem solving to play. It's much like the first Doom that way and feels more like a big expansion pack to that game instead of something unique. However, I was not as impressed by the level design in this one. I'm not saying it's not good, I just feel it relied too much on cheap gimmicks rather than intelligent design a lot of the time.
What I mean by that is that a lot of levels tend to throw too many unexpected threats at you with no prior warning causing you to die even though you haven't actually done anything wrong. Ambushes that you have no chance of surviving unless you know exactly where to turn, what enemy to shoot and what gun you should shoot him with. The result is either endless frustration by having to start the level over without your guns or save scumming your way through the game. Maybe some people like that type of design but I'm just not one of them.
But despite that I still think the game is great and I highly recommend it if you haven't tried it.

I still remember buying this game soon after its  release to find out that my computer at the time could not handle it, so i never ended up playing it, untill now. FEAR has always been one of those "bucket-list" type of games for me. Well, its about 10 years later, I have a decent PC for todays standards, and luckily I saw this on sale for a whopping $2.50 cents. After completing the game, i've come to the conclusion that overfall, FEAR is a very good game. Here are some pros and cons of this game:
The Pros:
Story: The story in FEAR reminds me of an action movie along the lines of something like Predator. The game itself is not scary by any means, nor is the movie Predator, but what they both have in common is that there is an over all suspensful horror-like atmosphere going on of the uknown threat that is present, powerful, and devouring everything in its path. I like the fact that there is a huge build up story wise, as in they don't explain everything in the beginning, infact pretty much nothing is explained in the beginning. Only by progressing in the single player game do you get an understanding of whats going on. So many games nowadays, escpecally horror ones, throw the plot and monsters at you right away, well not FEAR. There is quite a build up story wise,  Infact the last half hour had me on the edge of my seat.
Enemy AI: AI was certainly above average. Enemies would retreat, flank, wait for back up, swarm you. Pretty impressive AI for its time. They would even notice your flashlight in a distance.
Lighting: This game made great use of lighting. By todays standards it's alright, but its certainly one of the best points of this game.
Small funny moments: When i least expected it, i'd come across something in FEAR that was rather goofy or funny. Despite how minor this would be, it felt fresh and i welcomed it. In a straight up♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants horror game this would might feel out of place. But in a Action-Thriller type game like this, it fit very well into the story.
Soundtrack: The soundtrack was good, like something you'd hear in an action movie from the late 80's or early 90's. (and not the cheesy synth-type of action movie music, but like something from Aliens or Predator).
- Combat: The flow of combat was good. Sneaking sometimes benefited a scenario. Sometimes guns a blazin was good. It was way more involved than some generic twitch based cover shooter like call of duty.(that comment was mostly aimed at the newer COD titles) . Oh and the Slow-Mo Bullet time feature is always a plus.
The Cons:
- Some story elements i thought were really stupid, like the fire hallucinations. It felt extremely mediocre. Other aspects of the story felt very cliche and I got the "whatever lets move on" attitude from it.\
- Enemy Variety: There is absolutely no variety of enemies in this game. You are fighting nameless clone solders the entire time, once in a blue moon you'll come across a guy in a mech suit or heavy body armor.
- The subtitles are useless
- IMPORTANT: In the beginning i came across some instane stuttering in this game. after some research i found out it was related so some HID devices in the Device Manager. I pretty much had to uninstall every one for this game to run smooth.
- There is some minor platforming in this game and it feels very clunky. Completely the opposite of something  polished such as half life 2.(which came out the year before this I believe).
- this is kind of my fault, but i didnt realize till halfway through the Office complex that some phones had answering machine messages on them, which expanded on the over all story. Kind of wish the game made it a little more obvious cause the phones just blended in with everything else.
- Im not saying this game needed more color but damn is it gray. Kind of gets old after awhile.
In Conclusion: At times FEAR was great, at times it was mediocre, but most of the time , it was very good. It looks dated, but its still a very solid FPS that is worth a playthrough. I'm not entirely sure if it was worth the 10 year wait for me to play this, but i don't regret my playthrough, and i certainly recommend this game.

I can't say much on the nature of the game, since I don't have a lot of hours on it yet, but
seems to be  a rather charming version of
. You're tasked with the duty to find treasure and scavenger clues while keeping in mind that, within the mansion walls there are 11 other folks, one of whom is the Devil. The randomly assigned Devil is out to, you guessed it, kill you and it is the scavenger hunters duty to either win the hunt or be the hunted.
...
The mansion is quite large, so there is definitely a ton of map to explore. Even in the little amount of time that I've played, I know for sure that there is more to the map than meets the eye. You're able to run away from other players, hide in various barrels and crates, and traverse through secret passageways and set off remote traps. This keeps up the tension between players, while also offering a nice way to relax and mess around with friends.
The graphcis are, simply put, adorable. You can't really go wrong with these small cartoony characters dressed up in Halloween costumes. They are also quite refreshing: not everyone wants smooth graphics at the sacrifice of amazing gameplay.
offers both decent graphics with decent gameplay. Win-win situation.

Devil's Bluff is a simple game which proves to be very fun and easy to get into.
I got a free copy playing the beta and thoroughly enjoyed my time spent with it. It's just a fun, care free game you can really sink your teeth into and easily spend anywhere from 15-30minutes playing a single match, hitting the rematch button after every round until it's well into the early hours of the morning.
In Devil's Bluff you play as a survivor or the "Devil"/Murderer. As a survivor your goal is to find out who the devil is, capture him/her to win the game or finish the treasure hunt before everyone else. The role of the murderer -- or devil -- is randomly chosen at the beginning of each match and his goal is to kill everyone else or be the first to collect all of the treasure items.
Survivors basically roam around the map in teams of two with six teams(Making it 12 players a match) trying to find each piece of treasure based on the clues given to them. The idea is to work together, collect the loot together and try, if possible, to find out who the devil is and capture him. The devil can transform from a survivor to the devil freely and has a long, heavy attack to kill other players with. However there are tell-tale signs as to when the devil is near and when the devil is out of disguise. Faint music will play in the background and you'll hear distinct, heavy footsteps as he approaches.
Communication is important in this game. There is no text chat which makes having a microphone very important as the game consists of proximity based communication. It works really well and is done in a very smart manner. Voices will be muffled when players are on the other side of a wall or just out of hearing range which adds a level of dept to the gameplay and a certain amount of strategy as there are literally dozens of hiding places in any given area for players to hide in and use to access certain parts of the map.
The gameplay consists of roaming around the map trying to figure out riddles or clues for your next piece of treasure all the while trying to figure out who the devil is and also trying to avoid him, hoping he doesn't find and kill you. He could be the person you've been in a group with the entire game, he could be a person you trusted and welcomed into your group or he could be some random player no one ever sees until it's too late.
The game is a lot like the old WarCraft III custom maps Murder at the Mansion, Werewolf, Vampirism, The Thing and, to an extent, Dark Deeds(Minus the base building) except a standalone product which will hopefully expand the genre.
The game should be €15 on release but I would definitely say it's well worth it due to the amount of fun you'll end up having and the many hours you'll get out of it. It's a very
game in a sense which adds to its replay value and fun factor. There are some problems with it such as some features missing or some annoying control bugs but none of them really stop the game from ever being playable. For one there's a lacking feature in the fact you can't join a game that's already started, not even to spectate or queue up for it but apparently it's something the developers are aware of and will fix in a later patch. The controller/keyboard bugs are annoying but they won't get in the way of playing the actual game. For some reason you can use your controller in-game yet you can't use it in the main menu screen(Or it randomly works) but in-game using a controller sometimes results in the controls being split between controller and keyboard, specifically when bashing your space bar to counter a fight or revive the controller equivalent doesn't seem to register in-game(Total shame because I hate mashing my space key -- It makes WAY too much noise). It could be a rebind issue which thankfully the game allows for fully on both KB&M and controller.
A definite 8/10 with marks(Right now at least) deducted for lacking some features and a few bugs. A really great game and well worth buying if you're at all interested in the Murder Mystery genre.

-The game has a lot of permanent upgrades that let you start each run with more health, get more coins per drop or start with a better weapons.  Those upgrades help soften the difficulty of this rogue-like and make things more fun and less punishing.

Cons:

- Difficulty spiked too high for the 3rd part of the story mode.
- The game has a lot of replayability but I didn't find much of it appealing.

I purchased EuroTruck Simulator 2 last year on sale for $6 and surprisingly, it was a pretty fun game.  I took a shot on a similar deal with Farming Simulator 2013 and what was really surprising this time about the game was that as your farm grew and you gained more fields, it became more like a real time strategy game where you worked to make your farm as efficient as possible while ensuring that your crops were harvested, manure collected and delivered, sheep shorn, chicken eggs rounded up, hoppers filled, etc.  It became even more challenging when you raised the bar on yourself by increasing the time scale.
Pros were that farming is relaxing and you get to drive big machines.  Strategy play gets difficult as you expand your farming operation which leads to more challenging game play.  It's a sandbox, so you can do whatever you want and you have to be careful since you can loose a load of pallets off your trailer if you try to shortcut across some rocky areas.  Likewise, I found myself trying to use two separate tractors to free my riding lawn mower from being high centered on some poor kid's exercise trampoline he had the nerve to leave outside in his yard.
Some cons for me were the lack of an integrated music player like in Euro2.  Instead I found myself singing the chorus to Craig Morgan's "International Harvester" song over and over again as I putted down the road of middle America on my Amazone mower at a whopping 6mph!   The other con was the inability to customize paint jobs or logos on the equipment as well as the lack of proper signage for the drop off points around town.  Took me forever to figure out that the flour mill wasn't the train station even though there was a train
No frickin' sign stating FLOUR MILL.
Overall, for $6, you can have some fun being a farmer believe it or not.

Disclaimer: I have roughly 80 hours in this game prior to someone buying it for me on Steam, because I forgot to remove it from my wishlist. The 7-8 hours I have on record are not the full extent of my experience.
I love this game.
The game uses only a single CPU core to calculate everything. There's a lot of things to calculate. It's a realtime 4X game, after all. This on it's own would not be an issue, however, it does severely limit the amount of things you can process without it slowing the game down to a crawl.
And it does. Often.
Currently, the game has several crippling performance issues, caused not only by it's engine not having proper multithreading, but several problems from the game's AI, such as sectors shuffling pops endlessly. Which, by the way, the devs promised to fix by release. They didn't.
Currently, on my system that far passes by the requirements, I can only play the game at about 20 frames per second, with the game's simulation speed slowing down to at least 1/5th of it's speed. While the game is definitely not unplayable, playing on Fastest in the endgame pretty much results in playing it on Slower. Core 5 is taxed 100%, while all other cores are entirely unused.
The only way I could get this game to function at a reasonable speed is by overclocking my CPU to over twice it's capacity, up to 6.8GHz (!!!), however, unless you're cooling your system with
, this is not feasible.
Do not buy this game in it's current state, if you can't put up with this. I can, and I'll suck it up, because I love the game that much. But goddamnit, I can't recommend it to anyone.
Note how I have not actually talked about the game itself. Have you played a Space 4X? You've played Stellaris. The genre is slim pickings, and quite frankly, in the current state of the genre, Stellaris is the most well designed one in terms of theme, aesthetics, and gameplay.
But it runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥ And it probably will continue to do so, until the devs finally decide to retire this old, awful engine, and make one from scratch that can actually multithread.
If you can stomach this, play it. If you can't, stay far away.

In my opinion, there's just too much that's lacking that doesn't allow me to give the game a thumbs up. A lot of negatives have been highlighted and explained thoroughly in other reviews but these are the ones that really frustrate me the most.
1.
: I really dislike this system. You can initially control 5 planets at the start and the cap increases when you research technologies. As you control more and more planets, you have to delegate control to Sectors, and Sectors have NO CAP WHATSOEVER ! Doesn't it sound very weird in the 1st place ? If I can't manage 10+ planets myself, I will naturally delegate control to the Sector AI, but why must you force players to give up control ?
2.
: This is another part of the game that's done poorly IMO. There are 3 categories of Technology trees, namely Physics, Society and Engineering. However, what you can actually research is purely RNG-based. 3 random technologies (4 after researching a Tech) are given as options after the previous tech was researched and there's actually no planning whatsoever involved. You've just gotta pray the Tech that you actually want will appear as an option. This is actually very frustrating especially for the Engineering tree where weapons are researched. Most of the time the weapons I've researched are barely used at all just because I'm forced to pick the lowest cost Tech to have another roll on RNG for the next batch of Tech options.
3.
: IMO this part seriously needs a revamp. Often times Alliances means nothing to the player other than slowing down a player's galaxy conquest. In order to declare war on others while in an Alliance, you have to get approval from the other party and most of the time they will reject your proposal. Similarly while in a Federation, you can declare war non-stop without needing any approvals while being the LEADER, which means EXTREMELY LONG downtime between wars whenever you're not the Federation leader. On the other hand, if you go solo, you have to go 1v5 or 1v10 often since everybody else is hiding in a Federation.
and the list goes on and on....
This game will probably be improving on its various lacking parts in the foreseeable future. For now though, it's not worth it.

I've played NFS: HS (Road Challenge), PU (P 2000), HP 2, MW '05, MW '10 and this - a true NFS fan, that is.
Pros:
- Physics, realistic loss of traction at high speeds (aye, I've also driven a real car at high speed and lost traction, so I would know).
- Lots of interesting game modes.
- Lots of interesting tracks, specifically I like how this game doesn't do cheap stuff like track mirroring or obnoxious night time ice skating to bump up difficulty. I also like how some tracks have several variants with common bits.
- No catch-up! You actually get what you deserve as far as I can tell. Difficulty is dynamically adjusted in the beginning of each race according to your performance but never mid-race as it used to be.
- Graphics are stunning, camera options are good and make a lot of sense (e.g. two different in-cockpit cams with different settings).
- Background graphics because no flux were given :D
- Lots of settings for the car*
- No DLC ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, existing cars are all good enough to beat the events, your friends and even clock some serious records.
Cons:
- Loads of CTDs and sound bugs. For me the source of CTD persists over the CTD, e.g. if I was playing track A with settings XYZ and it crashes, it's gonna crash with track A and XYZ no matter how many times I restart the game. Then again, it fixes itself if I play A with settings XCV or if I play track B.
- ...loooong intro videos, yet to look into disabling them. This would be tolerable if for not so many CTDs.
- General handling settings. I play with KB and like many people have mentioned, there's a lot of input lag. This, however, is not a true con, because you can always disable the "stabilising" setting:
=> Edit DampeningEnabled="1" string to "0" in vehicleset_pc_custom_[controller name here].xml
Also the default settings for tuning are very very loose and unresponsive at times, do not forget to edit.
- While settings are plenty (see pros), the poor default settings force you to make your own. There are a lot of settings there and the explanations for each setting are decent at best - a bit of a learning curve to get them right and you'll need to tap into actual tuning guides for real world cars to get the most out of your ride.
- Lamborghini Murcielago LP640 is a Limited Edition only car by default. There are guides to unlock LE cars and events, though, but it's a bit of a nuisance and you'll need to edit the master .exe to achieve this.
TL;DR: To get everything out of this game lots of fiddling with game files, game settings and car settings is involved. For this reason I'm going to give 9/10. Otherwise a brilliant, brilliant game.
EDIT: This edit is two years after the original review.
Changes from my perspective:
- The game no longer CTDs...that often. I have reinstalled the game on the same platform but new install of Windows 7, so not much should have changed.
- Bought a racing wheel, yay!
A wheel definitely helps with some of the rear-wheel drives since it's easier to control the amount of turning than it is with a keyboard. Especially the McLaren F1 and BMW M1 became really pleasant to drive.
Settings are still plenty and wide, most of the suspension settings and angles I've learnt to work with but the exact nature of some settings is a mystery to me. I understand them from a literate background but sometimes the car isn't terribly responsive.
For most parts I still do agree with my review, though, so if the game is on sale it's a good buy. It's still the best simulator from the NFS series, for whatever that counts.

This is an incomplete game.
Paradox likes to release a lot of expansions for its games and charge people for the improvements. That's fine with me, as it keeps a game like Crusader Kings II relevant so many years after release.
This time, though, the base game is so bland that I cannot recommend purchasing it. It will probably take a handful of expansions and a lot more money than the game's base price to make this an interesting game to play.
The major problem is that after the exploration part of the game, there isn't much to do. Your neighboring empires will get angry at you for no reason, so you'll be spending the rest of the game either appeasing them or conquering them. That's it.
The fun part of the game - the exploration part - becomes a little boring after the third playthrough because it's exactly the same as your first and second playthrough.
And that's Stellaris' real problem. Each game plays out exactly the same way. Your choices don't really matter. Events and stages are all on rails.
If you want a game where you build an empire that actually feels like a representation of your choices, get Civilization 5. If you want the game to be in space, get Distant Worlds: Universe.
Stellaris is a generic game that will probably ending up being a money pit via expansions.

I tried to put time into Witcher 1, but it seems like that installment was stricken with the same First-Start problems that you'd find with the first Assassin's Creed and Mass Effect games. The first one, while being a solid base for what was to come, still was crippled with annoying and shoddy work.
This game makes up for it.
While it still has issues with a few bugs, it's not nearly the unpolished mess that the first Witcher fell victim to, and none of them are game-breaking. The visuals are much more striking, and while there's more than enough time to explore a given area, it still has a strong plot that promises a great deal of good things to come. Relative to the first, this game sheds the overwhelming MMO feel that pervades the original, making it the game I really like to play.
Combat revolves around careful timing and the right use of skills, and even at the start I was much more satisfied with the fight when I finish off one opponent, knock another back with a magic blast, then do a small hop to attack a third who was trying to charge in. It kinda harkens a little to the combat you'd see in Assassin's Creed, but the use of magic, bombs, and traps really puts it in its own niche.
Characters and dialog are done much better than before. Ultimately, the first one always seemed to fall flat, not quite bringing things to life for me to really get me into the story like I should. Not here. The voice actors emote, and the conversations are much more organic and have me engaged enough to put some thought into my replies.
The graphics got a huge boost, which is to be expected, I imagine... but it does more than the first ever did. Environments are diverse, varied and engaging, and definitely shed the 3/4ths view that added to that MMO-feel in the first game.
If you're a casual gamer with an interest in the series. Start here. I imagine that there are nuanced details that will slip past because they were involved in the original, but this is the more engaging experience, and I'm pretty confident that a few internet searches can cough up the relevant background detail the first game brings.

There's a lot more to Little Inferno than meets the eye, but let's start with the basics. Do you like to burn things? If, like me, your answer is YES!, then the Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace is for you! Additionally, if the idea of squashing and/or burning spiders appeals, then this product is also for you. If neither of these hold long term appeal, never fear - you can collect coins and purchase products (to burn and begin the process again). Everyone enjoys purchasing digital junk! Not you? Well, what about progressing through catalgoues and collecting GOLD STARS? And COMBOS. What about combos? Everyone likes combos!
It's this commentary that makes Little Inferno great - it has something to say about the state of games, about itself, about you. Yes, it is a ridiculous game, but you'll get more than you bargained for from it - or at least you should.
So, how does Little Inferno actually play?
Well, it's best described in three easy steps:
Step 1: Burn items.
Step 2: Collect coins.
Step 3: Purchase items.
Rinse and repeat.
But I'm not a pyromaniac. What's the point?
The point is to burn your way through catalogues of items to unlock new catalogues of items to burn. If you're a completionist, you can get gold stars on all of your catalogues. If this (understandably) isn't enough, there's combos - these are likely what you'll spend most of your play time on. These are Little Inferno's puzzle aspect. From the title of the combo, you have to work out which items to burn together to achieve the combo. This gets a bit trickier towards the end when you have multiple catalogues of items to choose from. That's about it for Little Inferno's gameplay. As for the /point/, well, you'll have to find that out for yourself.
But, as much as there is more to this game...
10/10 - would spend a day burning fake items in a fake fireplace again

Devils Bluff is one of the funnest Cartoon styled Hide and Seek games with a twist that I've ever played. This unlike other games in the Hide and Seek genre gives the hiders something else to do other than just hiding or killing the chaser. It lets you answer cryptic clues to find treasure which is way fun. However, this is one of the funnest Hide and Seek type games I've played, like everything nothing is perfect and there are still a few areas which could be fine-tuned which I will elaborate in my Pros and Cons.
Pro's
♦ Amazing Death Spectator Mode (Lets you easily view another living player including the Devil)
♦ Nice Help Menu (This is very detailed and a nice way to teach the game without having a full on Tutorial)
♦ Epic Graphics (Each Character and the Map is soo detailed and stunning, just amazing)
♦ Eargasmic Sound (The Characters, Map Sounds and Music all fit in soo well with the theme of the game)
♦ Nice Number of Premade Servers based on Skill Level (This is nice as it allows x number of games to quickly start based on skill level without having to create your own and find your own people to fill it)
♦ Dedicated Servers are Lag Free (I've played a full 12 person match, no spectators and not had any lag)
♦ Open Microphone Technique suits the game (Many people complain about the fact the Microphone is open. However, with it being open it adds a whole new level of stealthyness to the game that most other games don't have)
♦ Game Concept is awesome (It's a Treasure Hunt cross Hide n Seek, nothing better than this)
♦ Gameplay is really fun with Randoms and or Friends (No matter who you play with, you're going to have fun)
♦ Developers are really friendly and helpful (This is really good as they respond to issues quickly and even play matches with you)
♦ Cryptic Clues are the right balance of difficulty (This is good as they are not too easy to decipher and not too hard)
♦ Can easily Stream to Twitch via Main Menu (This is great as all you have to do is login to Twitch with your API etc and you can Stream it)
♦ Nice balance of traps and hiding spots (Literally there is a hiding spot or a trap where ever you need them without there being too many or not enough)
♦ Stunning Map (Heaps of well detailed and set out rooms, hiding spots and what not that make the map look stunning)
♦ Many ways for the game to be won making strategy a key part (Devil can kill everyone, Devil can die, Players can pick up all the treasure, Devil can pick up all the treasure, Devil can pick up some of the treasure + kill someone in first and steal their treasure and thus win. Therefore, it requires a lot of strategy and teamwork to win)
♦ Price is decent for the amount of fun you are going to have (For the amount of fun you'll have it'll pay for itself)
Cons:
♦ Controls can't be re-mapped in game but can be remapped via the Devils Bluff Configuration Menu before starting the game (This is a weird inconsistency as the Controls Menu doesn't change to the new Controls in the Input Menu)
♦ Basically controls can't be fully remapped (As the game has many random controls, not being able to set ones you want or would be better suited to is annoying)
♦ Characters are only skins (Would be good if each character had a unique bonus, aka could see further, run faster, be heard less etc. This would make the Character Selection Process more worth it as at the moment there is no benefit from picking one character over another)
♦ No way to tell the difference between a Public Match and Private Match Created (As far as I can tell a Public Match isn't listed anywhere and neither is a Private Match. Plus, both created matches have no password, so to join both all you'd need is the title. This isn't bad but it makes having a checkbox saying "Public Match" pointless)
♦ No way to quickly invite someone to your game via Steams Friend List (This is annoying as they have to load the game, click find and type in the name)
♦ Eventually people could just memorize the clues and find the items each match (Not certain to how many different clues there are, but it seems like this could eventually happen if people played enough as there is only one map)
♦ Can create a Public or Private Game with no name (The game shouldn't let you progress in creating without a name, as the only way to find and join a Private/Public game is by searching the game name)
♦ If the game becomes 1v1 can take ages (This happens because the game map is quite large and it can take forever for the Devil and the Player to find each other which can be annoying)
♦ No way to tell how much Treasure someone has found (This is annoying because you never know how close a team is to winning)
♦ Easy to pick up and pass time with as you can have a game or two and just close (Even though it's hard to predict the time frame of a game, if you are bored and want to kill a few hours... this game works perfectly as you can easily start a game with minimal wait time and just play right away)
Other Points:
♦ I found the Controls for keyboard and mouse to be great (I only used Keyboard to play and Mouse). However, as I stated some people may want to re-map controls which you really can't do and there is an inconsistency with some help menus telling you different controls/buttons that don't do what they say they do. Other than this I found controls to just work and be easy to use.
Overall, even though there are a few cons, they are only minor points which could be fixed to help improve the game. Therefore, as the Devs are one of the friendliest I've met, the gameplay is smashing and the fact you are guaranteed 100% of the time to have a laugh and enjoy your game with or without friends... then I recommend you pick up a copy of this game.

I played Shift 1 and instantly fell in love with the game - I couldn't wait to get shift two... especially when the price dropped :)!
I would say out of all racing games there are and even compared to Grid : Autosport, I have to give the cake to Need For Speed Shift 2 on this one. Just an absolutely beautiful racing game. Very enjoyable to drive, drift, turn, race, crash, and cutting off other drivers to take the lead.
The visuals are stunning. Seriously, what else do you want from an automotive game? This is 2014, we're all expecting decent graphics by now.
The game play more importantly is what makes this game stand out from other racers. Sure this isn't the classic NFS where you run from police, but this NFS is more simulation based and can make your heart skip when taking a turn. There are suggestive arrows on the track to tell you how fast to take a turn, however they are suggestions may I remind my reader. They change accordingly to your speed but I feel once you get the hang of how a car handles you don't quite need to rely on them heavily. The tracks are a perfect length and I haven't run into any races that I've dreaded (meaning those races that you have to race for 10-15 minutes at a time). Tracks are also nice, challenging, fun, and some turns just really get you into the game. I've never been a gamer to turn my controller for racing (or any games for that matter) and this was the first game where I felt that displacing my controller may do something (it doesn't but that's how immersed I can get playing). The small drift and loss of wheel control when taking major turns is impeccable. If you do over do a turn and end up hitting the wall, your screen goes hazy and gray to simulate impact. This I do not find annoying but rather amusing and realistic. Damage to your car is also pretty spot on.
RATING : 8.3/10
This game get's a solid 8.3/10. Why the extra .3 over my solid rating of 8? The game modes, the UI, just how it was all put together just makes it so nice.

I gave this game so many tries, and everytime I'd get annoyed at the stupid AI. After seeing how all the recent releases for racing games all seem to be major dissappointments, and NFS: Prostreet being pretty much unfixable, I came back to this game. I decided to stick with the game. In my previous review I gave it a thumbs down because the AI can get incredibly annoying..you'll be slowing down on a corner and the AI hits you and sometimes makes you spin out. I know Im not going slow because a lot of times I'll be up on my opponents bumper. But after a while, you learn how to avoid AI and keeping your space. Then it gets to be a pretty fun game. There are some pros and cons, some of them kinda conflict with each other.
Pros:
-There are different divisions of ranking for cars. This prevents you from farming races over and over until you have a super fast car compared to the competition, and you wipe the floor with them. Ranking works depending on what the car is initially, and then any performance mods you make. This includes things like tires, brake pads, clutch upgrades, turbochargers, engine swap, etc. Forcing you to put more thought into your car build rather than simply buying the most expensive stuff available.
-Engine swaps. No, you cant put a LS1 engine in a Miata. What you CAN do is something like
Take a Toyota Corolla AE86, swap in the V6 Supra engine. Swap in a 20b 3 rotor engine into an RX-7, RX-8, or even a Miata. So they have to generally be from the same company. Not all cars have engine swaps available. I was able to put the NSX V6 engine into an S2000. Since Acura is Honda.
-Manual transmission option. Something devs dont seem to get that many people want nowadays.
-Pretty nice car variety.
-Gorgeous graphics, for its time.
Cons:
-Annoying narrator. Too upbeat. Thankfully you can mute him in audio options. Set dialogue to 0.
-The different divisions and ranking does have a negative to me, and that means you cant do things like take your classic car like my 20b Mazda RX-7 up against modern cars. Or my Skyline powered Fairlady 240z.
-Physics at time feel a bit dated. But it is an old game. Doesnt mean I dont enjoy it.
-As I said in the intro, AI does sometimes ram you off the track. I could be nearly done with the race, finish line right there, taking this tight hairpin turn, and some AI goes too fast around it and sends me flying off course. Then 3 cars get ahead, and Im no longer in the top 3.
-Customization is really limited. Yes, no one is going to see your car but you and maybe a few people, but the possibilities with customization took such a leap backwards. NFS: Prostreet let you choose between so many vinyls, and rims. I could spend such a long time just customizing cars in Prostreet, but theres not much at all to do in Shift 2, its almost pointless.

Devil's bluff is a scavenger hunt game with up to six teams of two.  One player is randomly selected to be the Devil which gives them some extra abilities, namely killing other players, and an alternative win condition.  There is a bit of a learning curve to the game with the mansion layout/passageways and scavenger hunt riddles but it feels extremely rewarding to master these things.
The random nature of the scavenger clues makes the game highly replayable.  I was one of the earliest beta testers and the game hasn't gotten old for me.  Figuring out the safest v fastest to the next clue keeps it very engaging.
The mansion itself is gorgeous and extremely favorful; filled with secret passageways, traps, and hiding spots.  There is ingame chat that is proximity based so it can be important to be quiet when trying to hide.  Nothing raises the tension more than hearing the wolf howl that signals the death of another player.  I forsee this as the next big party game for LP collabs and streams.

In my opinion, there's just too much that's lacking that doesn't allow me to give the game a thumbs up. A lot of negatives have been highlighted and explained thoroughly in other reviews but these are the ones that really frustrate me the most.
1.
: I really dislike this system. You can initially control 5 planets at the start and the cap increases when you research technologies. As you control more and more planets, you have to delegate control to Sectors, and Sectors have NO CAP WHATSOEVER ! Doesn't it sound very weird in the 1st place ? If I can't manage 10+ planets myself, I will naturally delegate control to the Sector AI, but why must you force players to give up control ?
2.
: This is another part of the game that's done poorly IMO. There are 3 categories of Technology trees, namely Physics, Society and Engineering. However, what you can actually research is purely RNG-based. 3 random technologies (4 after researching a Tech) are given as options after the previous tech was researched and there's actually no planning whatsoever involved. You've just gotta pray the Tech that you actually want will appear as an option. This is actually very frustrating especially for the Engineering tree where weapons are researched. Most of the time the weapons I've researched are barely used at all just because I'm forced to pick the lowest cost Tech to have another roll on RNG for the next batch of Tech options.
3.
: IMO this part seriously needs a revamp. Often times Alliances means nothing to the player other than slowing down a player's galaxy conquest. In order to declare war on others while in an Alliance, you have to get approval from the other party and most of the time they will reject your proposal. Similarly while in a Federation, you can declare war non-stop without needing any approvals while being the LEADER, which means EXTREMELY LONG downtime between wars whenever you're not the Federation leader. On the other hand, if you go solo, you have to go 1v5 or 1v10 often since everybody else is hiding in a Federation.
and the list goes on and on....
This game will probably be improving on its various lacking parts in the foreseeable future. For now though, it's not worth it.

This is an incomplete game.
Paradox likes to release a lot of expansions for its games and charge people for the improvements. That's fine with me, as it keeps a game like Crusader Kings II relevant so many years after release.
This time, though, the base game is so bland that I cannot recommend purchasing it. It will probably take a handful of expansions and a lot more money than the game's base price to make this an interesting game to play.
The major problem is that after the exploration part of the game, there isn't much to do. Your neighboring empires will get angry at you for no reason, so you'll be spending the rest of the game either appeasing them or conquering them. That's it.
The fun part of the game - the exploration part - becomes a little boring after the third playthrough because it's exactly the same as your first and second playthrough.
And that's Stellaris' real problem. Each game plays out exactly the same way. Your choices don't really matter. Events and stages are all on rails.
If you want a game where you build an empire that actually feels like a representation of your choices, get Civilization 5. If you want the game to be in space, get Distant Worlds: Universe.
Stellaris is a generic game that will probably ending up being a money pit via expansions.

Fantastic game. The combat system gives a real sense of power. Dust is powerful, and you feel powerful as you absolutely destroy hordes and hordes of enemies using all kinds of combos and various elemental powers. That isn't to say the game is a breeze though. If you're not careful, you can actually die surprisingly fast.
Apart from having an amazing combat system, the game visually looks gorgeous. Though admittedly the cutscenes graphically look worse than the standard gameplay, which can be a awkward at first. This was a game made almost completely by a single person, so the quality of the cutscenes suffers as a result. They aren't unbearable, but it can be offputting if you're not expecting it.
The story is overall pretty good. Maybe a bit generic, but it hits all the key emotional points that it needs to to be memorable. I know a lot of people are annoyed by the sidekick because her voice is annoying, but honestly I wasn't bothered by it too much.
Other than that, I would say that the combat becomes a bit annoying later on, as a large number of late game enemies you encounter are capable of blocking your attacks seemingly mid-combo. This is probably my actual biggest complaint, as it hinders what the game does best, its combat.
I listed out a bunch of negatives, but make no mistake. This game is extremely solid. As far as metroid-vania games go, I would place this game up there with games like Ori and the Blind Forest. Has some flaws, but the other aspects about the game more than make up for them.

The premise of just throwing stuff into a fireplace to light it on fire doesn't really sound like a great game.  Throw in a few puzzles and now you've got something, but still not quite something great.  The sole point of this game is too find combinations of two or three items that fit a description on the list of combos.  For example, the Bike Pirate combo obviously needs you to burn the Bike and the Pirate, but others are not quite so easy.
This is basically the game of Doodle God, but instead of unlocking new elements, you're just unlocking new junk to burn.  The game is moderately enjoyable at first, but the combo-finding rapidly loses its interest.  You also need to burn the same items over and over again just to grind and unlock the next catalogue of items, which further adds to the lack of enjoyment. This really is a fantastic social oriented game and it does require a microphone to play it properly.
Players basically find themselves paired up and placed in a rather sizeable mansion consisting of different floors, outer grounds and various hidden passages.
The game is basically a treasure hunt assisted by the various clues that are provided to the player. The first team to find all their loot wins the game.
....Yet there is more.
One player is a devil in disguise and his goal is to murder all the other players whilst trying to hide his identity lest the other players gang up and capture him. The devil, when transformed, is very fast and powerful and especially dangerous to players caught alone, yet it vulnerable to players in groups.
Players have to choose whether to focus on the clues and treasure hunt which leaves them more vulnerable to the devil or stay with others which will dilute their loot search time. Teams can also be much more effective in gathering the loot if they split up but that also leaves them much more vulnerable.
Players also have to consider whether they wish to share the Devil's identity should they find it out. They could even decieved other players and pretend it is someone else in order to sabotage another teams treasure hunt or break the trust between team mates.
The mansion itself is very interactive with peep holes, hiding places, traps and secret doors. Good players will learn the mansion and utlilise it effectively.
Another fantastic aspect to the game is the music. When a player transforms into the Devil a forboding tune acompanies the Devil where he/she wil go and this really sets the atmosphere in the mansion and puts the other players on edge, ya better hide. The other compositions in the game are also very fitting and a few are quite catchy.
I highly recommend this game for people who find the above description compelling. The game certainly is niche and won't please everyone. it is not a shooter and it is not first person. It is what it is and the developers have produced a very polished and playable product that I think is well worth looking into and supporting if it is your kind of thing.

A light-hearted title, Farming Simulator 2013 provides an extremely simplified overview of life as a farmer.  The setting is based in Europe, but some of the names (e.g, International Harvester) are familiar to us Americans.  There are tutorials to help get your feet wet, though they leave a little to be desired since many of my questions about gameplay went unanswered.  Yourstarting equipment is basic at best and you have access to two small fields.  Pick your crop (wheat, barley, or canola) and get sowing!  Several hours later (fortunately, there IS a game-time speed control option) your crops are ready for harvest.  Hop in your combine, pipe it out into a tipper, and unload into your silos until the time is right for selling!  Now, go work your field and get it ready for the next crop sowing.  The process is fairly simple, but there are many logistical and efficiency-based changes to be made.  Your equipment will need to be upgraded, you will buy more and larger fields, and then there's the element of livestock to be considered...  It's a fun game for those who are into simulators.  The controls are not nearly as robust as polished titles such as EA's "The Sims", however Farming Simulator is a very enjoyable money grinder.
To my knowledge, there is no "winning" objective.  You simply continue to grow your farm and see just how large of a farming mogul you can become.  There are no limits- as long as you can project manage your way to more and better equipment and maintain the upkeep for it.  Proper management skills will keep you moving from one task to the next:  sowing, fertilizing, harvesting, cultivating, plowing new fields, delivering loads to buyers, working silage, keeping the livestock tended, moving equipment between fields, and so on.
There is also a multiplayer aspect available at no extra charge.  You may host games for up to 16 players or join others at will.  There appears to be an open field of mods to be downloaded or developed at your leisure, though I have not personally delved into that facet.
In summary, if you catch this title on sale, it's worth considering!

Rather belated I want to review this game, as it deserves your attention. So in what follows I do apologize for my own lack of reviewing skills.
As you can see on my profile I put 1000 hours into this game, maybe more. I am not a traditional gamer, having taken a long pause from them. So this review will not have comparisions and may be of most use to those who have not gamed allot (or played 4X games). Fortunately for me, games came back on my radar due to a work thing, and I decided I should play one to see how far they had come during my hiatus.
Being a bit of the analytical sort, I did allot of research before settling on GalCiv III (I also bought Talos Principle for "couples" gaming with my girlfriend, but another story).
And a bit more about me (because I think this may help), I deal a bit in life with strategy stuff and some of the overarching themes you can see in GalCiv III. Thus I was likely to be pretty demanding. I wanted the strategic element, and depth, and difficult choices and tradeoffs.
The game pretty much had me hooked at the get go. It is immersive and hours or even whole nights disappeared. The learning curve can be harsh and unforgiving. I expect there may be some who give up, but I would say you should relish this... the game is very learnable if you are willing to adapt. Personally, I like how it lets you take control of so many aspects. Some may see this as micro-managing, and you can automate some parts of the game, but if you want the full experience AND to excel then take control of every aspect of your civilization. Manage your planets, design your own ships (rather than use defaults), think about your research path, plan ahead, anticipate war and move the timing and place of battle to where it most benefits you. Hell, I took notes and sketched maps! Not to scare those away who do not like this - as I said there are other options - but other reviewers may be best suited to sell this game to such players.
This all said, you will see reports of bugs and balance issues. First, that is how modern product development has to work... you could wait a decade for a game with perfect code to be released and the user's would still find the flaws.
What matters is how the developers respond, and the Gal Civ development team is on top of it for both big fixes, as well as rebalancing and general game improvements. With the release of the Crusade expansion pack the base game will also get some improvements as they will be using some elements of the newer expansion to improve the base game.
To touch on that briefly, I do recommend also Crusade. Should you buy it all together or first try the base game then Crusade? Well, if you buy the base game and play it 1000 hours, then when you buy Crusade it will be like a new game almost. This alienated some people, others liked it. All your strategies from the base game will not work in Crusade. I liked relearning, and the strategy element is even deeper in Crusade I would say... though with less community guides and info on all the little details, but details that in the end can lead to war and defeat, the learning can be harder. Missing one resource because you did not acquire it somehow and did not think it mattered, and you may doom your civilization. You can figure out what you need though in advance, but you need to think about it, and weigh its import, because resources are more scarce in Crusade.
Personally, I would get them both together, and a couple DLCs.
Hope this helps some of you in your decision!

Final Fantasy 8 is one of the more overlooked entries in the series. Talk to fans of the franchise and you will generally find that opinion is neatly divided on both gameplay elements and storyline. The easy to abuse Junctioning system and J-drama high-school esq plot will not appeal to everyone, but are worth experiencing if you are in anyway a fan of Final Fantasy or jrpgs. The music however is like having an entire casio keyboard ground up then forced roughly into your ear canal. Whilst the recent HD remake of Final Fantasy X had its score rearranged and brought up too our refined modern standards, with this game Square Enix seems to have taken the opposite approach and ‘de-made’ its soundtrack back to era before the original game was even created. The original PC release of FF8 featured the same MIDI chip tunes used here, possible to save space, however in 2014 I would expect the quality to be at least that of the console version from 15 years ago. Unfortunately I consider this to be a fatal issue. One of the key attractions of the Final Fantasy series has always been its music. It’s a core aspect of every game in the series and one which Square Enix’s marketing department defiantly recognises. So if you are going to go to the trouble of adding these extra features (the Japan only ‘Chocobo World’ mini-game is fully welcome) is it not worth polishing up one of the games major selling points whilst you are at it? It’s like putting sprinkles on a cupcake but not bothering to brush off the ants. In my mind the addition of an achievement system is not enough to outweigh ear wrenchingly poor music in any game, especially Final Fantasy. Unless you really really like achievements or have had your ears shaved off by a murderous barber, seek this game elsewhere.

When I first saw this game it caught me off guard with the whole side scrolling RPG adventure style, I bought it and played through it from start to finish on hardcore on my first playthrough, it was quite fun with the small flawless challenge. You could die just as easy to enemies as you could kill them, I had my fair share of deaths as well as victories. But I can't deny how beautiful this game is. The unique worlds and weathers that comes with it, biomes and new challenges all around the corner. Characters you can grow to love and hate. You feel feel emmersed in this game as you can't help but feel like Dust. You're thrown into this strange world with no memory or clue as to what's going on or what you're doing. And with a gentle little shove from Ahrah, you're well on your way into a journey around this glorious landcape. I love it's simple yet facinating design and exploration. You can explore places that has NOTHING to do with the main quest line, just to feed that inner adventurer in you or do a good deed. I'm honestly surprised by the amount of potentioal in this game despite being locked in a side scrolling dimension, it still manages to show off so much. It's incredible how well they combined all the genres into this one massive scape. Exploring this beautiful world that surrounds you, filled with details and epic particles. While fending off foes along your journey. You grow close to the characters in this world and really notice the unique traits and personalities. Which makes it so much more emotional for you as you continue onwards. I highly recommend this game to anyone who's looking for a challenge, adventure or simply just want to enjoy the beauty some things can offer. The experiences I had from this game will be some I will never forget, I will carry them with me til' the Life Thread calls. And I hope anyone else who sets out on this journey will come to love and hate it as much as I have! Farewell for now though, dust to dust, ashes to ashes.

I really enjoyed the game "despite" the gameplay issues I mention below. To be honest the atmosphere simply sucks you in and the mix of platforming, combat and RPG works out quite well.
- A game with a signature mechanic which looks and feels very, very cool.
- A good amount of combat and platforming. The latter becomes increasingly trickier.
- Stunning graphics. Basically all of them are hand-made.
- Great music and voice acting is well-done.
- Cliché story (homage to retro games) with a good twist.
- A good mix of serious and cheesy/funny dialogues.
- RPG Elements such as customizing your different pieces of armor. Upgrades are available throughout the entire game.
- Very gamer-friendly mechanics. No material grinding or unnecessary backtracking!
- Talking to NPCs is literally rewarding as each dialogue grants exp - and often a side-quest.
- Opening treasure chests is fun as each of them requires you to beat a mini-game.
- Completing the game grants you a rather unique reward!
- Many Easter eggs and references to older games.
- Gameplay... is the biggest issue as the combat becomes very repetitive.
1) Spamming two moves is not only the strongest, but also the most-exp-earning move in the game.
2) The main character doesn't learn any new combat moves.
3) Later on in the game, most of your regular moves will be blocked, so we're back at 1).
4) Intermediate and chapter bosses don't feel that much different from regular mobs.
- "Normal" gamemode is not challenging at all, even for average players like myself. There is no difficulty spike. I'd recommend playing it on a harder setting from the very beginning.
- 1 mandatory BS Indie game secret (which the game openly admits with a cutscene).

It's one of the games you wish you could have a "Meh" button to click in order to express how you feel about the game.
Don't be mistaken, it is a solid game. When you carry the Command & Conquer franchise, however,  the expectations are different.
This franchise was one of the leading names in real-time strategy and held strong for a few years despite having major opponents on the market such as Total Annihilation, Age of Empires and, last but certainly not least, Starcraft. Then came Electronic Arts and their desire to expand. They wanted quality brand names quick and easy to augment their grasp on the video game world and it turned out whoever was in charge of Virgin Interactive at the time thought it would be a good idea to help them in their quest by selling them Westwood Studios, the guys who made the Command & Conquer franchise famous worldwide. Now, I wasn't part of Westwood and the same probably goes for whoever reads this, but it does seem Westwood wasn't the same as soon as it became part of EA. This would be one of the many examples of how big video game corporation somehow often find a way to destroy a great studio and/or franchise. When EA decided to effectively terminate Westwood, it had nothing to do with the Westwood of the old days. As a matter of fact, apparently, not even a single pre-EA Westwood employee was remaining.
But enough for the history lesson, let's talk about the game.
In the previous Red Alert games, the game would have you focus on collecting ressources. In this one, it rather emphasizes on unit control and practically abandons the mining dynamic. In the older games, your collectors would travel across the map in order to get the minerals. In RA3, the mines are inside your base area. That means you'll probably always collect your minerals no matter what happens on the battlefield. This downgrades the game right from the start. Because of this, there is a profound strategic element that is taken away from the game. In most RTS game, ressource collecting is crucial and therefore you have to act quickly in order to collect as much as possible. Now, you barely have to think about ressources. Even worse: collectors don't bring as much ressources as they used to. You will more than often find yourself lacking the sufficient funds needed to actually do something on the battlefield. It's obvious that this was done because the team behind RA3 thought it would be a good idea to slow down the game a little so that it would be easier for newcomers. Big mistake.
Red Alert 3 wouldn't be part of the series if not for the over-the-top units. They are relatively well-balanced in most cases. Unfortunately, since the game is built on slower ore mining, you won't be able to produce many units and send an entire platoon towards the battle unless you camp for an extended period of time. You'll often find yourself rolling your thumbs, waiting for that soldier, tank, ship or plane to come out of the building.
There are many units taken from the previous Red Alerts and you sometimes feel like the creative minds behind this third opus got lazy. If you were familiar with the franchise, you quickly notice that the whole game is even more colorful and wacky than before. Clearly, they also were told to reduce violence and to appeal to a younger audience. Turns out the game ends up being extremely cartoony even for a Red Alert game.
There's also, like all the other Command & Conquer games, a huge amount of cinematics with real actors. And there are a lot of well-known names there. You wonder how much money was spent on the game versus the casting for the cinematics!
Solo campaigns are relatively entertaining. There are scripted events which can be frustrating. For example, you will build a base according to the current enemy's location. Some time later, the map expands and another enemy pops out from an area you weren't expecting to exist. I mean, you're a commander and the fate of the world is in your hands. Can't you get your intel team to give you the bigger map right away?
The AI is not very smart. In campaigns, it will participate in scripted events by doing scripted unit movements. Other times, it will just send predictable "squad" attacks that you will, the vast majority of times, crush easily. Sometimes I wonder if the "hard" difficulty simply means that the AI gets more minerals than usual and thus can produce more units. Personally, I never saw a "change of behavior" from the AI besides seeing it sending more units faster. For example, they don't seem to target specific buildings in your base like a normal human player would do. If I saw a player with a lot of turrets, I'd target the power plants and so on... But the AI doesn't do that. So, yeah, the AI is dumb. Of course, the same can be said for the skirmish game mode with one or multiple AIs, but then again, the computer has never been very good at Command & Conquer and the same can be said for other RTS games anyway. It's no big deal although you'd expect that - when it was released - they would've found a way to make it more challenging and less mechanical. Too bad that the online multiplayer part of the game - where you could get real challenge - is dead, but I guess that, somewhere out there, there's a community of Red Alert fans who managed to solve that problem.
Overall, even though I've been mostly negative, the game is good. Not great. Good. It's not as satisfying as Red Alert 1 and 2, but it still, somehow, holds the flag despite being the worst of the franchise. There are worst RTS games out there, trust me.
On a side note, I've always prefered the Soviets ( I always enjoyed their dirty, in-your-face attitude, weaponry and buildings ) but I must admit that the Allies have the best girls once again... Why, God, why? Maybe I should use a time machine too to fix this issue... Or maybe I could go and shake hands with the EA CEO. ;)

I first bought this game on a whim, immediately wondering how and why I could buy such a thing, and experienced buyer's remosrse before I even installed it. A farming game, really? The reality is, though, that this game is way more fun than it really has any right to be. I actually searched for a reason, and it occurred to me that every kid had a farm set growing up, and this is basically that on steroids. The game presents a good sized world that you can immerse yourself in pretty quickly.
The gameplay is very well done, with integrated XBox 360 controller support that requires minimal tinkering. The tutorials are informative while remaining short enough to get you into gameplay quickly. The main thing I like about the gameplay, though, is unlike most simulators, the game's finance system gives me tangible goals that keep me playing. When I got out of the tutorial and started on my very first field, I was having a ton of fun with the different implements (again, this game is really just a toybox of large machines). But when I threshed, cultivated, and planted a new field, I was wondering what to do. Do I just sit there and literally watch the field grow? Thankfully, the game includes a mission system that keeps you busy between plantings, so you always have something to do.
The other thing that really strikes me is the insane level of detail the game has. Animals in the game are rendered well, have fluid movement, and add a nice sense of atmosphere while being useful to core gameplay. The cars driving on the roads are surprisngly varied and have a level of detail they really didn't need for this kind of game, but it shows some level of commitment on the part of the devs. The people walking down the streets also are way more detailed than you'd expect from a simulator game that's mainly focused on the technical aspects of farming.
This is a game I'd definitely recommend to others to check out, even if you're not a hardcore simulator enthusiast. It's very accessible and surpisingly fun to play.

First, I get that this is Early Access Alpha.  What is there now shows nice graphics compared to that other "airport" game.
It seems to me that there is no easy way to start ANY airport. In other words, unlike other sim games where you can start with something small and grow, I don't see that's the case here.  Certainly this game has a lot of similarities with Prison Tycoon and even Another Brick In The Wall.  But what this game lacks is no clear way to build up.  You have to build EVERYTHING at the same time... like RIGHT NOW.
You have to lay the runway, the taxiways, the stands, the roads, and then the other type of roads - the service roads, but not before you separate them with that guard rail security shack thing, and you need a tower which doesn't appear to do anything, and then don't forget to add the bus stop and car dropoffs, and hire people, and the executive staff which unlocks contracts which you need to build the fuel, because without fuel nothing you built previously is going to make any difference, and of course the terminal with endless other check ins, info, you get it the picture.
This all devolves into building everything at once, hiring everyone, checking all contracts, etc.  In other words there is no natural progression of the game as a tycoon game, once it's all unlocked because IT IS ALL NEEDED there is no tycoon game left.  You're left with a sandbox.
Sure you get to schedule airlines, and stuff, but for the most part by the time you have a working airport, the simulation is DONE!
IMO, the game would have been vastly better to allow a working airport sooner with less cumbersome need for every aspect.  It could start as a small airstrip that allows private planes into a small terminal with minimal or no need for baggage handling, a smaller and simpler fueling system, and just less stress of running baggage from checkin to the baggage bay and then back to a carousel (which you have to build yourself out of more conveyor belts).
There is no "growing" experience in the game.  You don't get to discover things along the way.  Everything is sort of thrown at you in a sandbox fashion and you have to build and unlock everything right away just to get to the "airport" part of the sim.
If the DEVS had spent time understanding how to "build" the anticipation of a true tycoon sim game this would be an awesome game, but it seems that everything is required or you have nothing... it's all or nothing sandbox.  It's boring after a couple of hours. And that brings my last point...
A successful sim game is one that engages the player not just for a short time but for a long time with small rewards along the way, with finding what works and what doesn't, customizing things (floors and seat colors are about the only thing you can customize).  A good sim game allows the player's fun and anticipation to grow as the game grows.  AIRPORT CEO does none of that IMO.
Lastly, I understand there is still work being done on the game and it is not fninshed.  I cannot imagine what else they could add to the game to keep my interest in playing it.  What additional items can be added to cusomize the airport or to grow it or make it vastly different.  I think most airports will end up looking pretty generic as there are limited items and ways to add pieces that make it work.
Due to it's very limited replayability - at this time based on what is available - and the fact that you have no growing curve in the true tycoon sim game style and have to build everything, I DO NOT recommend the game at this time.  Without a fully vetted sim "growth" the game is completed early on and just becomes repetitive.  I wish that the DEVs address what is planned in terms of making the game replayable such as:  procedurally generated terrain and starting points, ability to grow airports differently (without requiring all items at the beginning), some way to connect airports to other player created airports, more parts lilke glass walls, different types of restaurants or eating areas, etc.

This game at it's current state (0.21.10) is playable, but, as expected from early access, has some bugs. However, the two man team of developers, who to my knowledge have never released a game before, have been very active. On release weekend, they were pushing bug fixes for the game multiple times a day. I believe they have built an excelent platform for an indepth, realistic sim game, for future.
The game so far features some of the basic features that one would expect in an airport sim. For example, you can buld your passenger terminal complete with check-in desks, security stations, toilets, baggage carosels, boarding desks, shops and restraunts, just to name a few core features.
You can then place down your taxiways, your runway, an ATC tower, and few plane stands, and you have completed the basics of your airport. In addition, you can go further, and add fueling services to your airport, as well as a baggage system, that can become very complex if you want it to be.
You sign some contracts with a contracting company to build the airport, a fuel supplier, some shops, and a few airlines, and the airport is fully functional.
This game's competition, Sim Airport, in my opinion, not as good as this game, as it feels a bit lacking in game features. My opinion, is that anyone looking to buy a game in this genre, doesn't have to look any further, as this game is also cheaper than Sim Airport.
There are still a few problems with this game, I have to admit. There are some optimization issues as the moment, but you have to remember that this game came out four days ago when I was writing this review. Currently, there seems to be an issue with how the game deals with rendering the airport terminal. This means that when you have the terminal on your screen, even if it's empty, the game will lag. This doesn't seem to be too bad on smaller airports, but once you get to building airports with multiple (about 6 for me) large gates, the game begins to have some FPS problems. These problems will get ironed out eventually, im sure, but for now it is an issue that is causing me some problems.
I know that the devs have a lot of plans for this game, and that they intend to bring this game out of early access sometime in the future. I really look forward to seeing what this game has to offer, and would definately reccomend purchacing this game.
TD;LR:
-Good, playable, game right now, with more features to come.
-Has a few bugs, along with some optimizaition problems, but will get better in the future.
-Better than Sim Airport.
I'll try to keep this as updated as possible as updates come out.

I must have played this game fifteen times now and I still enjoy it every time I play it. The combat is tight, the sound is top notch, the guns feel powerful and are fun to use, and the AI gives you a nice challenge. This review is for single player only, because gamespy no longer exists, and you cannot play the multiplayer section of the game anymore.
I'm going to split this up into a few distinct sections because there is a lot to talk about in this game.
The game came out right when first person shooters were getting popular again, and it shows heavily in the design. There are obvious influences of Half-Life 2, Doom 3 and Halo/Halo 2 across the board, but it manages to combine some of the better aspects of each of these games together into a cohesive product. You have limited weapon slots and health kits, but it takes the route of giving you slow motion and allowing you to store the health kits to modernize the gameplay aspects.
The graphics style and technology has aged fairly well, and has a distinct "Doom 3" look to it with sharp shadows, dark environments and fairly rough polygonal models, but still manages to capture what the developers were going for. Texture resolution is fairly good, and there are a lot of fine details that you can pull in if you look around. I really love the bullet decals and the way they utilized parallax mapping to make it look like chunks of the wall are missing. It comes out very natural.
The environments are not very varied and it shows that the engine was not well optimized with open areas, leading to the feeling of wandering through endless corridors without much variety. They tried to spice things up by changing locations every so often, but this is one of the bigger complaints you'll find with the game. Most of the events take place inside warehouses, office buildings, and the occasional "sewer".
The sound in this game is top notch. Weapon sounds are sharp and booming, and compliment the visual look of the weapons perfectly. Enemies and allies are all well voice acted and have a large number of lines they can pick from situationally. The music is well produced and compliments the scenes taking place within the game, leaving you immersed but helping to hype you up for what is going on. The environmental effects fit well, and none of the sounds stand out as feeling off or out of place. Even the spooky scary sounds have their place, and feel well integrated. Monolith has always excelled here and this game is no exception.
The weapons are fun to use and feel powerful, both in your hands and in those of the enemies. The shotgun is easily one of the most satisfying weapons I've used in a game in a long time, capable of literally blowing people to a fine mist at close range, and cutting them into chunks at moderate range. The penetrator shoots massive metal spikes that will nail people to walls in the most insane poses. There are also akimbo pistols.
Combat is intense and thrilling, and when combined with the startlingly good AI and the slow motion it just comes with you feeling like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ while still being challenging and fun. The developers said they wanted it to feel like the opening scene to Hard Boiled, and they were 100% successful, sparks, dust and debris everywhere. With how reactive and varied the AI can be during a fight you get a decent amount of variety out of the fights.
The game has fairly good pacing, and a reasonable difficulty curve with various little spikes of difficulty scattered through to keep things interesting. Monolith knew that combat wasn't interesting if it was all you did, and so added in a bit of exploration and toned back sections to let you recover from the high intensity fighting. The game expects you to begin using your weapons more effectively, and to use the tactics you've learned and the environments to your advantage, so you never feel like things quite settle down.
I want to give the AI in this game a special mention, because it is particularly well done. Combining a dynamic squad system, flanking tactics and staggered reload pinning techniques, the AI is surprisingly lifelike. It has a fairly advanced sense system, and the individual enemies have a brain of information they retain and can share using verbal call outs, and will often react to stale information in surprisingly realistic ways. Each enemy can be scared, demoralized and manipulated, leading to unique behaviors. The only problem with this is that combat is typically too short to see a lot of this behavior emerge unless you are at a higher difficulty level. It shows that the developer put a lot of love into the AI.
This game is supposed to be scary, or maybe just creepy, and it is usually successful on the first play through. With a clever combination of supernatural powers, disturbing imagery, jump scares and sound hits, you're kept on edge. The sometimes predictable scares lose their impact as the game goes on,, but there is still plenty to love about the game even without this aspect. If you absolutely hate scary games, this is not for you.
I strongly suggest that you at least give the game a try if you enjoyed one of the games that helped to shape this game(Half-Life 2, Doom 3, Halo). For the price, it's hard to go wrong. If on sale, it's even harder to go wrong!
P.S. The expansion packs for this game will likely leave you wondering where the magic went. They don't have the same polish or enjoyment factor. The review is focused on the main game only.
