So, I bought this game for Playstation on release day. I am as big an RPG fan as they come, and always have been. But I hated it. Squall and Edea were the only characters that seemed interesting to me. I found the draw system to be an abomination. I didn't enjoy 45 minutes of "stocking" every new spell you come across. The junction system itself is nice, allowing a decent amount of customization. But to get good results you just had to spend way too much time just drawing out spells from your enemies. I love how the GF abilities work. But the draw system... It was just so terrible. I never finished the game. Bought the PC version a few years later, thinking to give it a fair shake. But, all the glorious music (some of the best in any game) was now MIDI, the pre-rendered backgrounds looked blurry and low-res, and the gameplay was reduced to like a quarter of the screen. Needless to say, the PC release just made it worse.
But now, this. This is the third time I have purchased this game. And finally, it's no disappointment. First thing you should
do is download the Wine and Roses music mod. It removes the crappy MIDI music, and replaces it with orchestral versions, OST versions, and all-around better sounding versions of all music in the game. The end result is pretty much the best sounding Final Fantasy game ever. One thing FF8 always had going for it was the music, and WaR makes it perfect. The character models far surpass any previous version, it can now be played in full screen, and it seems the pre-rendered backgrounds have had some cleaning up. So, not only is it the best sounding, but the best looking of all versions of the PS1 Final Fantasy games. (I find the Ultima edition of 7 to be rather unattractive, and prefer the unaltered PC graphics.) It looks far better than even FF9 on my PS3 with HD and smoothing. The looks and sounds of the game are just perfect.
The Magic Booster seems to be a divisive element. I don't know why. You don't have to use it, if you enjoy the draw system. I have never met or heard of anyone who enjoys the draw system, but if that's you then don't use the Magic Booster. It's that simple. The rest of us, who have better things to do than spend three days drawing basic "fire" and "cure" spells, will have no reservations about eliminating the tedious early game stockpiling. The addition of the Magic Booster takes this game's only real serious flaw and shaves the rough edges off it. That's all. It's not like it hands out Ultima spells or anything. It just gives you a good base to start with, so you can hit the ground running instead of crawling.
As for the characters, and the story, I have to say I have warmed up to some elements I didn't care for in past releases. I couldn't stand Zell's personality back in the day. He seemed like an unlikable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. But, now I voice his character in my head with the voice of Goku from DBZ, and I like him. His aggression and childishness are a lot easier to swallow when I think of him as naive and boisterous like Goku, rather than like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jock as he is portrayed. Selphie is a joke, and Irvine is just MEH. But Squall, Rinoa, and Quistis are great characters. The story is less "in your face" than most Final Fantasy games, but I find the sorceress element very appealing. A very interesting antagonist indeed, especially when you consider Siefer's role.
In short, if you could never look past this game's flaws before, this might be your time. Do yourself a favor and install the Wine and Roses mod, and you will find yourself looking at this game in a whole new like. A warm, bright light of nostalgia. It's like playing it for the first time, and NOT being disappointed like I was with previous attempts.

Summary:
Currently the best space 4X game for fans of the genre. The AI in this game is very good. Design of the name is in the name of AI – if something would be too hard for AI, it is not implemented.
The Crusade Expansion takes the series to a new level and is a must-have. Your every decision will matter, economy feels much more intuitive yet at the same time harder to master.
There is tons of content you can get cheaply that really make the game even more fun and variable, if you tire of base game. The overall immersion is deep, it’s really hard to end a session.
You will like this if you liked: Galactic Civilizations 2, Mater of Orion 2, Civilization 4, Civilization Alpha Centauri
Game play:
The game is a successor to Galactic Civilization 2. The Vanilla game is a bit dull compared to GalCiv2. You should buy the DLC Crusade. Most of the other DLCs are also recommended.
The game plays well and intuitively. Attention is put to remove micromanagement. Replay ability is very high.
There are multiple paths to victory and you write your own story in each game – you have to make decisions.
The base game is clean of bugs.
AI:
Design of the game is such that allows the AI to fully understand the game and play on equal footing. Up to normal difficulty AI gets no bonuses. After that it gets flat bonus, but never cheats.
It can have multiple personalities and it really can challenge you even on normal – equal footing game.
Variability:
The game is modable, I download a lot of content – custom races (that includes their personality), ships designs.
Due to random factors and decisions you make, each game is guaranteed to be different. You will have to adapt as you go.
Galactic lore
There is some lore and some campaigns. The campaigns are varied, but shorter than in GalCiv2.
Art:
Notably good music. User interface is average-good. Visually adequately done, but I mostly play from galactic view and in general I am not graphic-demanding player.
The difficulty curve :
Civ games and 4x games have always steep learning curve. This game is intuitive and you will get into it fast. But to master it will take time. I think you can get into this game fast as a newbie on easiest difficulty and go on about building you galactic civilizations. If you win too easy, push it up. I am a seasoned player and I am far from playing on top difficulty.
DLCs:
Crusade – must have
•	is a must have. Economy is improved, micro is reduced, citizens add whole new aspect of gameplay, population improved, expeditions
I also recommend these, in following order: they add good concepts and variability to the game, the immersion is much better:
•	Galactic Civilizations III: Crusade Expansion Pack
•	Galactic Civilizations III - Precursor Worlds DLC
•	Galactic Civilizations III - Mercenaries Expansion Pack
•	Galactic Civilizations III - Lost Treasures DLC
•	Galactic Civilizations III - Mega Events DLC
•	Galactic Civilizations III - Revenge of the Snathi DLC
•	Galactic Civilizations III - Altarian Prophecy DLC
•	Galactic Civilizations III - Rise of the Terrans DLC
It’s really just best to buy the -42% bundle, even though 2 of the DLC are questionable.

They have clearly chosen simplicity over game experience.
Everything has been reduced in scale.

The worst part now is that all race specific and unique structures require rare resources to contruct. If your Arcean Empire can't find any Xanthium then you don't get any Arcean specific stuff. Same for every other race. You need extremely rare resources to build anything that makes your race unique.
Even with the random map generator "resources" turned all the way up this is still insane. Honestly about 3/4 playthroughs you will not get access to a resource that is crucial for your species.

If you can't get to elerium then your ships don't get lasers or shields.

No Thulium? Then nothing but basic sensors all game. Forget advanced technology infrastucture.
Like missles? I did too. Hope you have alot of antimatter.
The main thrust of this being that all resource placement is random, so you can be utterly crippled right from the start.
And since you wont get race specific things most of the time, all the races feel vaguely the same now.

Excellent game and I am excited for the updates!
NEGATIVES: It takes a couple of hours to begin to actually understand what you are doing, even with the tutorial. And the tutorial is actually detrimental to your gameplay after the first hour or so. Shut it off and then hit the interwebs while you play, if you still are confused. That will be a much better experience. I do not like how dry the Event text is and we do need some more Events.
POSITIVES: Talk about addictive! I would suggest you play the game for the first time on a Friday night because the next few days will be a blur  :)  You will make tons of mistakes and get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked...and you won't care. Levelling up your leaders is satisfying and it gives you added incentive to explore, do battle and develop your colonies.

I really enjoyed the game "despite" the gameplay issues I mention below. To be honest the atmosphere simply sucks you in and the mix of platforming, combat and RPG works out quite well.
- A game with a signature mechanic which looks and feels very, very cool.
- A good amount of combat and platforming. The latter becomes increasingly trickier.
- Stunning graphics. Basically all of them are hand-made.
- Great music and voice acting is well-done.
- Cliché story (homage to retro games) with a good twist.
- A good mix of serious and cheesy/funny dialogues.
- RPG Elements such as customizing your different pieces of armor. Upgrades are available throughout the entire game.
- Very gamer-friendly mechanics. No material grinding or unnecessary backtracking!
- Talking to NPCs is literally rewarding as each dialogue grants exp - and often a side-quest.
- Opening treasure chests is fun as each of them requires you to beat a mini-game.
- Completing the game grants you a rather unique reward!
- Many Easter eggs and references to older games.
- Gameplay... is the biggest issue as the combat becomes very repetitive.
1) Spamming two moves is not only the strongest, but also the most-exp-earning move in the game.
2) The main character doesn't learn any new combat moves.
3) Later on in the game, most of your regular moves will be blocked, so we're back at 1).
4) Intermediate and chapter bosses don't feel that much different from regular mobs.
- "Normal" gamemode is not challenging at all, even for average players like myself. There is no difficulty spike. I'd recommend playing it on a harder setting from the very beginning.
- 1 mandatory BS Indie game secret (which the game openly admits with a cutscene).

When you first play Stellaris, it's like having intercourse with a hooker. It seems great and you can't believe you could get so much pleasure and excitement for the low, low price of $40.00.
1.) In the early game, Stellaris entices and teases you with a galaxy that is just begging you to explore it's most intimate and private parts. You send your little men to impregnate fertile planets, research techonolgy to aid in the development of your species' colonies and military, and then fight a couple of wars with aliens that don't share your political views (or because they wouldn't give you station rights in their space). So, in a nut shell, you spend the first twenty hours of the game spreading your empire's seed all over the galaxy's dirty face. Stellaris also boasts great writers that clearly know their science fiction. For instance, Stellaris wears little ringworld shaped piercings on its (censored) like a stripper would. The ring world, rarely featured in Science fiction these days is an invention by Larry Niven, a sci-fi writer whose ringworld is rarely featured in its entirety in videogames. There are many other subble sci-fi techs that are little references to many more sci-fi books and television shows. Also there are nice easter eggs strewn throughout the galaxy, such as an earth that has a chance to be a tomb world (basically a world ravaged by nuclear holocaust*see Fallout for more info*) or in the middle of WWII, or even infested by sentient cockroaches. So, needless to say, Stellaris does very well to entertain the player for the first twenty hours.
2.) However, like most $40 dollar hookers, Stellaris' features and encouters become predictable. By the mid-late game things slow down. You've conquored, and/or, made peace with the galaxy, and you're left there reasearching technology to develop more efficient colonies that will sustain an economy that can afford to sustain a huge military that will never see combat. Yes, there are the "crisis" situations, such as the invasion of the Tentacle Hentai monsters who come from the Gamma Fallopian Galaxy with the sole goal of violating the privacy of the Galaxy's Japanese School Girls, and the robotic rights revolution but these are just minor set backs. Most of these can be overcome easily by the strongest empire that was supposed to be swayed by the afore mentioned crisis. In addition, even in the midst of a♥♥♥♥♥♥monster invasion, other empires that hate you aren't willing to unite to stop it. If you're playing single player, every AI in the universe is a helpless little baby, and you're the only adult who can solve the situation. Your enimies will find no reason to team up with you to stop the *instert event here* and will merely shrug you off. This seems very unrealistic, and in the events of a galactic crisis, one would think that every species, no matter how different, would want to band together for the sake of school girls virginity. Also, Stellaris has very little late game features that set it apart from the early game. Even though the empire has the ability to produce massive fleets with unheard of techonogical prowess, there are still using little rinky dink mining stations. It's like paying for the "happy ending" only to reach the point just before climax. You can't build your own ringworld, or even a dyson sphere to harness more energy to build a bigger space fleet. To construct these massive super structres would be a huge step forward for the game and could potentianally add a bunch of other late game crises that are even more entertaining to deal with. An espionage system where other races could infiltrate your planets and sway the ethos of your pops to get them to side with another race would be another tough thing to deal with, especially for free thinking democratic government societies.
3.) Stellaris Multiplayer is like a 3 way with a $40 hooker, i.e. nearly endless possibilites. Where single player fails in unprodictablilty, human nature corrects this. The game becomes infinatly more interesting as you can't predict how the human empire's you're playing with will react. Crisis situation become more realistic as well as humans will actaully ban together to take on a threat like the Unbidden (and unlike AI empires would allow you to build wormhole generators in their space so you could aid in the battle).
tl;dr Stellaris is a good game, but as of now, is only worth about $30 dollars. I've read in numerous reviews that paradox releases DLC content to supplement their games like CK2 and EUIV. This means that Stellaris will stop working the streets and upgrade to the highlife of a $400 hooker one day, but until that day comes, we're merely left with a single hand job that gets old after the second or third round. 9/11, would purchase and play once but would like to recieve more content.

is a Metroidvania style platforming action-RPG in which you play as the protagonist, Dust, accomponied by sidekick Fidget on a mission to save Falana and it's inhabitants from General Gauis' wrath. The game was almost entirely made by Dean Dodrill (the creator) alone. He handpainted the games' visulals and vistas, wrote the story alongside Alex Kain and programmed the game himself.
I played the game on the normal difficulty setting using a keyboard and a mouse and spent about 16 hours completing all the levels and collecting all the collectibles. I made short notes about what I felt was positive and negative about the game. The following are the positives and negatives of my experience of the game.
- You start you adventure with a descriptive tutorial in which you learn the basic controls. The tutorial also features the     beginning of the story and is almost perfectly integrated into it.
- The game has smooth and solid platforming. Special skills are aqquired as the story progresses such as,
, which help you platform better and visit places which you couldn't get to early in the game.
- Platforming is also quite challenging and there are many terrain based puzzles you need to solve to get to some platforms. There are many different types of barriers and obstacles and you often need to find alternative paths or make calculated sacrifices to health to overcome them.
- The game also has a strong RPG aspect to it such as collecting materials for crafting different items, completing main quests and optional side quests and grinding for XP.
- The graphics are really good in the game. The backgrounds are all handpainted and animated meaning they change dynamically as you platform and move. There are different terrains, weather conditions and day cycles which makes the game very immersive and atmospheric.
- This is also an action game in which you need to learn different combos to defeat your enemies. The combat animations are smooth and satisfying. You see different animations while executing different combos which is really important.
- The story is well-written and I personally like how it developed. There are also several reccuring themes and plot twists in the story. There is flow in how the story progresses.
- There are many different characters in the game, each with unique backstories and motivations. Doing quests for these charachters enhances the experience of the game and makes it more fun. Some characters make hilarious jokes.
- The voice acting is phenomenal and one can see the effort put into it by the actors and the director. I watched some uncut youtube videos in which the voice actors recorded their dialouges and man they were funny.
- The sound tracks was made by HyperDuck Soundworks. It is really good. My favourite is the "Abadis Forest" track.
- There are many types of enemies, each with unique traits and charachter models depending on their locations. There is also a learning curve as each type of enemy has it's own combos and attack patterns.
- You can level up from XP by defeating monsters and completing quests. The level cap is 60 as of writing this review. Going up a level rewards you with an ability point which can be used on four different traits such as attack, health, defense and Fidget's magic power.
- There is no enemy scaling and the combat becomes very hack and slash after you obtain decent weapons.
-
- Some characters lacked sidestory and contextualization. I really enjoyed Fidget for example but would have liked more of her lore etc.
- There is no way to obtain some items, except for them randomly dropping from enemies. It was frustraiting grinding and waiting for these random drops, as someone who likes to max their charachters in games.
- There were some minor bugs I encountered and I had to restart the game once due to the screen getting stuck. Apart from that the gameplay was smooth.
Dust: An Elysian Tail has a solid story, combat, platforming, soundtrack and other things it advertises. The game is well optimzed and polished. There is flow in the gameplay and the game has replay value and potential. I would recommend buying this game for an enjoyable 15+ hours experience.

"Little Inferno" has been out for a few years now, but I only just encountered it as part of the Steam 2016 summer sale. It's quirky, weird, and oddly engrossing. You're a kid with not much, but you do have a magic fireplace and a directive to burn stuff because it's apparently been snowing forever outside. Everything given to you can (and should) be set on fire, and fortunately you can do this just by pointing at it (holding down controller or mouse button as appropriate).
I'll be honest and admit it was the two preview videos on the Steam store page which caused me to have to buy the game. I just couldn't not. It's like being inside an episode of Ren & Stimpy.
As you burn stuff, it produces coins which you can then use to purchase more items to burn, and as you buy more items, it unlocks more catalogs of stuff to buy. (Bit of a consumerism message in there, I should think.) The only real challenge sometimes is figuring out all of the various combinations of items which, when burned together, produce bonuses and little achievement messages. (I'll give you one obvious combo: Pirate toy + boat.)  At times, you receive letters from people -- Miss Nancy, who apparently runs the Little Inferno program. A girl in the same predicament as you. And a weather guy in a balloon. (Yes, you burn their letters, too.)
After you've burned everything you can burn... well, let's just say the ending is pretty good. Not so sure the game is worth the original list price unless you have more than one person in your household, but it is absolutely worth the price when on sale. At least I thought so.

But the levels are never the same, you can change what will show up in them by collecting diamonds and using them to buy things from the lobby shopkeepers, and every time you forget a dragon's pattern (or a bat's lack thereof) or do something dumb with a black skeleton, you're only losing a couple minutes of work. It's the easiest thing in the world to try again, just one more time, until finally the game gives you a blood rapier and heavy plate in a chest and you're blazing through the boss fight before you know it, feeling your heartbeat speed up until it almost matches the music.
THE MUSIC. In my opinion, the music is the best part (with the storyline a very close second, lore nerd that I am) - it's half the point, after all! Even if you never plan on playing, go listen to the soundtrack. Seriously. Go crank up The Wight to Remain (4-3) or Konga Conga Kappa (King Conga) or FamilyJules7x's Trial of Thunder (5-3, from the DLC) or Virt's Deep Sea Bass (Coral Riff) or Vamplified ([REDACTED for DLC spoilers]) or...really, just find the soundtrack somewhere. I cannot recommend that bit of NecroDancer enough.
Now to see if, having gotten my start with this incredibly awesome game, I can actually play any other roguelike without the beautiful, brutal simplicity of a beat to stick to...

Still one of the premier first-person shooters of all time. The shooting mechanics are in-depth and satisfying, with the slow-mo ability adding an intense, if unoriginal, tactical advantage. Beyond the gameplay, this still remains one of the best horror and story-based games as well. The scare-tactics are a bit "in your face" compared to some recent gems in the field of horror, but it still has a deeply disturbing atmosphere and a low-key ambient soundtrack adds to the tension.
The story is a sickening descent into the horrors unleashed by mankind's wickedness, the desire to play god, and monsters who destroy their makers.

F.E.A.R. was the first horror game I ever played all the way through. I recently revisited it since I picked them all up on steam. And I got to say it holds up. Unlike most modern horrors, that show you horrific creatures mauling people or torturing them, F.E.A.R. takes a different approach. At times you almost forget that you are playing a horror game. You spend a lot of your time in office buildings and research labs encountering soldiers trying to kill you. It feels like a standard FPS game. But they sprinkle horror elements into the game throughout. Whether it is from the unerving quiet of the offices, or from glimpses of people who vanish or rooms full of blood, you are quickly reminded that something is not right.
The FPS gameplay is solid for a game of its time. It feels reminiscant of Half Life. I recommend playing this game on the higher difficulties. This not only increases the horror of the game due to tension of ammo and health supply but also makes the game more of a challenge. F.E.A.R. has a slow motion ability that you can use for a short amount of time, and it recharges over time. On easier difficulties, this makes the game a breeze. On harder difficulties, I found myself saving it for when I truly needed it. I recommend checking out
for some tweaks to all the games. I had to increas the FOV for it. It looks a tab weird at first, but nothing that takes away from the game.
The F.E.A.R. series will always be in my short list of horrors I recommend. Definitely worth picking up if you havent played through it before, turn of the lights, put on the headphones and have at it.

This is a re-release of the original PC port from 2000.
In terms of gameplay, original glitches and exploits are still here. The game itself however is not fully representative compared to it's PlayStation version, read below for more info.
- Cannot use dpad or triggers (bumpers work, but not triggers.)
- Due to lack of triggers, clicking the thumbsticks is used to escape from battles.
- Original game has rumble support, this does not.
- Very playable, but does not perfectly emulate the PlayStation version.
- No mouse.
- Not all keys are bindable.
- Binding other keys like Enter, Tab, CTRL, Spacebar, etc. is possible but requires trial and error.
- Playable to a certain extent.
In-game control prompts are also buggy with misplaced buttons or displaying the keys NONE if you manage to bind certain keys like tab, enter, shift, ctrl, spacebar, etc. This will lead to certain sequences like entering passwords for the train napping sequence being harder than usual and possibly lead to a game over screen.
- Can be played in a higher res compared to PlayStation version.
- Models do not look as jagged compared to PlayStation.
- Character models are much more sharp in this version and look decent for a PlayStation title.
- FMVs (while compressed) have aged pretty well.
- Game battles are locked in at 16FPS, world map at 30FPS.
- World map framerate is good, but looks HORRIBLE with blurry textures.
- Pre-rendered backgrounds while upscaled are very pixelated.
- Would recommend playing on a TV or a Window for those that do not like pixels.
While the game has a "widescreen option" I would highly recommend playing the game in its original 4:3 aspect ratio with your regular screen resolution, playing this game in widescreen will only stretch the image and make it look worse.
Edit: The world map looking horrible is due to a glitch that reduces the textures to it's lowest quality when bringing up the menu, going into a battle or a town fixes this. I have also noticed a major FPS drop when summoning the GF Eden and going up against the final boss. My PC itself meets the requirements and should not be an issue.
This game DOES NOT have the original PlayStation soundtrack and uses the original PC Midi mix which does not compare to the original PlayStation soundtrack, would HIGHLY recommend using third party mods to fix this as it is very easy to find and implement. Some original sounds are changed or missing but not a major distraction.

Is the game fun? - yes.
Should I buy it? - if you like turn based 4x this one is a must and the best one currently on the market (imho).
The Crusades expansion has pretty much nailed all the issues I had with the game.
- The race creation is probably the most robust (and rpg like) that I've seen in a x4 game (and I've played most of them).
A slew on new race types and abilities in addition to the traits tree all which combine to create a unique race (and determines what techs you can research).
Want to create a time traveler synthetic cyborg race or a silicon based xenophobic warrior race, done! And in game your decisions define you Ideology which further adds to how your race evolves.
- Ships Creator - With tons of parts you can build almost any type of ship or modify any of the existing ones.
- AI - One of the best I've seen. 64 bit and uses all the cores on your processer blah blah.
- Gameplay - This is one of the biggest and best changes Crusade brings to the game.
Want to build tall (small number of powerful planets) or try and grab as many planets as you can and build them up later, you can do both.
The new Citizen system gives you a citizen every 10 turns to train in various skills. Want to buff your research? Train a citizen in research and you can either assign him/her to give a small faction wide increase in research or assign them to a planet to give a larger planet wide increase. You can do this for production, manufacturing, banking, espionage and so on.
Have you caught on to how deep the game gets?
- Size - No 4x game is more customizable. You can create small quick games all the way to mammoth marathons with randomly generated 500X500 mapsets filled with up to 90 different major races plus minor factions! And thanks to it's 64bit multicore tech the turns are still fast.
- Mods - Want to turn your game into the Star Trek universe with ST races and ships? Modders have you covered. Want to download custom made races to play or play against? There are several hundred or more on steam for you to choose from.
- More to come! StarDock has some big plans, including fleshing out politics, elections, protectorates, etc and several more campaigns.
- You're still here? Buy the game already =)

I just want to point out a couple of really nice things they accomplished with making DDE.
1)They made it more of a challenge.
2)They made it cross-platform.
3)They made it run on just about anything imaginable.
4)They made it to where you cannot cheat (online of course) like you could in DD1
5)In some ways, they made it more fun.
6)They made it to where you get all the DLCs that you have to pay for in DD1, in DDE
I'd like to get all you naysayers out there, to really look at this game for what it is.  Not for how "DD1 is better than this" point of view.  I'll admit, DD1 does have some things that are better, like the private tavern, and the various level item drops.  But there are several things that DDE has that DD1 just didn't.
And what I hope more people will do, is not trash one game because another that is like it is better, but instead, look at that game alone and figure why it is good, or why it is bad.  That may be a dying hope though, because most of you seem to be on the bandwagon and you may be riding it with too much pride. Heh

GalCiv III feels like an amateurish, one-man-team's attempt at creating a 4X game as a final project for a programming class, rather than the finished product of a multi-million dollar company. Apart from game breaking bugs, like AI turns hanging indefinitely and fleets becoming an 'InvalidObject', the FEEL of simply interfacing with the game is fundamentally unsatisfying. Simple things like the overt lack of feedback when you click on buttons, queue up research, finish research, upgrade ships, or honestly do anything just leaves you sitting there asking yourself "Did it do it? Did it go through? Did it work?", whatever "it" may be. Or the utter lack of ability for the game to deliver to the player critical information, like WHAT was the planet of mine that was just invaded by enemy forces? All it shows is a splash screen with the word "DEFEAT". WHERE was the enemy fleet moments before this happened? WHY was I in no way informed of enemy units in by boarders? HOW were my planet's defenses overcome by the invading force? ...The entire game just feels like it was designed by someone who already knew the intricate details of the game, so didn't see fit to create a system to deliver information in an intuitive, aesthetic way for anyone who wasn't on the dev team (like their entire customer base, for example). And honestly, one the worst parts is that the game is a near complete clone of GalCiv II, as if the dev team simply wasn't interested in innovating, and instead opted to create a carbon copy of the game's predecessor. I could go on, but there's no reason to.
tl;dr:
The game is amateurish at its core and fundamentally unsatisfying to interact with, and poor at delivering to the player very basic information.
Note: This is based on GalCiv III + Crusades DLC, so no, the DLC didn't save this game.

First time writing a review, but I felt the need to warn others.
Was really intrigued by this game, as it hits all of my soft spots: 4x, space, etc. It looks awfully pretty, like a strategy version of Elite: Dangerous.
However, that's the end of my list of positives. If a game is a series of interesting choices, then this is not a game. Every part of it, from building and colonizing planets, to exploration, to combat, feels rote and superficial. You simply set up stations near resources, upgrade your level 2 mines to level 3 mines, build more corvettes, and wait for the queues to finish.
Combat is laughable, even after this recent patch. There's no reason to build anything other than corvettes, the basic ship. Tech upon tech adds complexity in the form of military stations, defense platforms, larger ships, etc, all of which are fairly useless. You simply build a corvette swarm, click on the enemy, wait for them to explode. Whee.
Other empires look fun, but are basically identical, with ethics providing a thin veneer of personality. Think Civ 5 AI, but without unique abilities, aggression, or anything else worth talking about.
A lot of hype was built around anomalies and exploration, but 90% of the anomalies I found simply unlocked a resource or gave me a research boost. No choices, nothing interesting. Even the flavor text was repetitive by my second game.
Ultimately, this has the depth of a $5-10 strategy game, with the blatant intention of filling in the gaping chasms with paid DLC and expansions. I feel conned out of my $40.

This has probably become one of my favourite Metroidvanias on Steam (along with Valdis Story)! Not something I'd hold as the hallmark of game design, but the combat is so good that it makes playing the whole game really fun, despite being somewhat monotonous, otherwise.
Valdis Story is a very methodical metroivania with a pretty deep combat system (with combo-cancelling, lot's of timed dodges and parries, etc.) and tough, pattern based boss fights that you really need to try to learn and pay attention to learn the game, and it's incredibly satisfying when you do!
Dust: An Elysian Tail, on the other hand, is very loose. You fight dozens of enemies at once, if necessary, but your attacks are very large and throw enemies all over the place, making you feel like a badass! Fighting these many enemies at once is really satisfying, if not a bit too chaotic to be challenging (in a fair way).
The crux of it is that your sword attacks have a rather wide range, and you have the ability to suck enemies in. With that, plus a helpful magic, you'll easily manage dozens of enemies, racking up combos of 1000+, at times.
In short, you're like a ♥♥♥♥ing tornado. With fire/lightning at the center.
And that's enough, surprisingly enough. The combat is very fluid and looks awesome!
Most of the game will be you tearing throw many enemies at once. However, there are different enemies, some of which can be tough, and require more attention, and parrying to defeat. Which helps a lot to keep things somewhat fresh!
The most disappointing thing was the boss fights. They're mostly really easy. And I was playing on the highest difficulty. On the whole, the game is fairly easy, if you take your time to explore and learn how to deal with different enemies. Only one of the bosses was somewhat hard to me, requiring a few tries, making me switch my tactics a bit.
The game had one frustrating element, which was the environmental hazards, in some places. These do a ton of damage, often killing you in 1 or 2 hits... But, otherwise, the game was very fair.
With one exception (graveyard), checkpoints were very kindly placed, so you never lose much progress on death.
The game as a lot of other features, like a crafting system, and fairly wide equipment system, leveling up, etc. etc. These all worked pretty well, giving you several options to tackle your progression, but they couldn't really be a focus for any player. They're there to support the combat and keep the progression up, nothing more.
As a metroidvania, especially regarding the abilities you gain, it wasn't spectacular (well, the abilities weren't very interesting), but the exploration element is very present, and in a good way!
The game has side-quests that cannot be completed when you first get them, making you go back to the places you've been to after you get more abilities and... have grown overpowered. Going back to previously hard areas and feeling like a God is ... well, it makes you feel like a God. (The leveling system is exponential which explains how much more powerful you get after each area)
There are several references to other games, which are nice, and lots of treasure and blueprints to help you get stronger.
The map system is also very generous, telling you the screens where you've missed something with an icon so you can easily check back later and know more or less what you may be missing.´
I don't want to write much more about it. The game is beautifully drawn and has some nice screen effects (distortions, for the most part), with one of the most fun combat systems around. So definitely give it a go!
Not the most challenging game, so try Valdis Story if you're looking for a more difficult game.

Warning: this is a "could be good" labelled as a no. After beating the first zone after 35 minutes of gameplay I feel like this is a game i should like but i just don't.
It's a very traditional fogue lite in that you spawn in a dungeon, fight enemies, die, spend currency to make the next run slightly better, and then play again. However this is the first rogue lite i haven't been able to get into in a very long time.
Maybe the game requires too much coordination, every step you take you want to try and line it up to the rythm of the music so i found myself spending huge chunks of time just starting at the bottom of the screen trying to time my actions to the beat. This meant i wasn't really paying attention to what i was doing and constantly ran into enemy attacks that would have been really easy to beat without the intense time pressure. The game really pushes the time mechanic, if you're too slow the game will skip one of your movements and give you enemies an extra chance to move. The game encourages you to play very quickly and rewards players who do, all of which is to the strength of the unique core mechanic the game has. It sounds like a recipe for success on paper but i just got frusterated and wanted to quit, a feeling all rogue lites give me eventually but with this game is came after the first few runs. Maybe i'm just tired of the try-die-repeat formula, maybe i just need to get comfertable with the unique movement, and maybe in the future i'll pick the game up and really enjoy it.
For now i found the games core mechanic hard to get used to and after beating the first boss i'm just happy to put the game down. I do not recommend Crypt of the necrodancer.

After completing F.E.A.R.3, which is one of my top favourite Co-Op games, I wanted to find out how it all started, so I picked up the first game in the series.
The graphics are old, but still decent on highest settings. It doesn't hurt the gameplay. The battlesystem is nice, with great AI behaviour, though enemies are a bit more challlenging than in F.E.A.R.3. It takes 3-4 shots before you are killed on normal difficulty. So, you should be really careful. But with slow-mos and covers it's managable and, leaving those piles of corpses behind you, makes you feel like a mass murderer.
There are a lot of surprises in terms of enemy spawning, which adds up for a nice challenge. You don't get bored, because as soon as you get used to enemies and start to think "meh, this is too easy", something new pops in, requiring you to adapt to the new level of difficulty.
There is not much of a story in terms of dialogues and cut-scenes. But what you have is a rather direct experience, and the story reveals itself, as you advance through enemies and levels. The sound and special effects adds up nice tension to the gameplay.
So, as a result, you get a really good semi-horror first person shooter with a nice polish. I recommend it to all players, especially, if you have played and like such games as Return to Castle Wolfenstein and F.E.A.R.3.
EXTRACTION POINT expansion: F.E.A.R. at its best. Includes more paranormal content and horror elements, engaging in very, very tense, almost psychologically tormenting, yet addicting gameplay. The enemies are more difficult, too, ranging from regular soldiers to armored units, mechs and phantoms, that will slice you up in no time.
PERSEUS MANDATE expansion: after completing Extraction Point, it will feel like a casual game. In this game you play as Pointman from the second F.E.A.R. team. There's not much of horror in this game, the focus is on different guns. Still, it is a satisfying game. 3 unlockable bonus missions included (kill all the enemies in the clinic; survive the arena; and sprint trough enemy lines).
My overall rating: 9/10
Note. There are many players saying that F.E.A.R.3. ruined the series, because there wasn't a lot of horror in it. But I liked F.E.A.R.3 better, because you could play with two characters and there is a co-op mode in it. Sure, the first game is more emotionally involving, but just a bit. It's not a big deal from me. And who gets scared by a video game anyway?

I only discovered The Witcher due to the extensive media buzz aroudn the third. Not wanting to leave empty handed during the Summer sales I decided to see what the buzz was and picked up the second for £2.
First impressions are good, the game looks like it has a massive world and story to discover with graphics that suit the scope it aims for. It's nice to feel early on that I'm not missing out by not playing the first game, picking up the basics as I go, learning a bit about the main character Geralt as I play.
For an older game the graphics are brilliant, showing Skyrim up for what period pieces should look like when money is spent wisely. The game runs at high settings on my machine, the ultra for the first time seem to run awfully, though I'm hesitant to just blame the game rather my PC showing it's limits finally. The landscapes are fantastic, big broad views and draw distance keep the world wide open. Character models look great though the voice acting sometimes drag it all down into parody territory.
However the controls, combat and UI are just short of disgusting. The layout of the buttons is annoying on keyboard, using Alt to aim while trying to cycle to 'R' or 'E' to parry and press the mouse button to attack, he's not the quickest at reacting to the key presses so it becomes tiresome fast. Switch to a controller and discover the preset key bindings are barely configured, these can't be changed in game so you have to exit if you want to correct them. The fighting itself is slow and calculating, opting for a more realistic approch with two main options to fight, strong attack or light attack. Then there's powers to be used, traps/ranged attacks and an option to attack after a parry. It feels like everyone had an idea on what the Witcher fighting should be like and no ones ideas were shot down.
Walking feels cumbersome and janky, it works but there's something odd about it. Perhaps it's the camera that doesn't really attempt to follow the character in any decent fashion, often gifting you the view of the back of a bush while you struggle to fit a small army. There's no jump feature either so the world has a very linear feel, restricting you to a set level.
The UI is horrible at best, an entire screen filled to the brim with all kinds of options, inventorys and menus. There's no realy layout scheme that makes any sense, compared to Skyrim or other RPG's that utilise all of it's features in a nice easy to view way. Crafting, levelling up, sub levelling up and this weird power menu and another power wheel where you can take a nap or quick view your weapons all feel like over kill, you don't need to add that many features. I honestly can't be bothered to learn it all, I want to immerse myself in the world not get bogged down trying to earn my degree in Witcher menus.
Overall, this is much more beautiful than Skyrim ever was and the story is engaging. However the actual gameplay drops this title into Two Worlds territory for me. Absolute ambivelance I'm happy to part with £2 for.

Far worse is the tendency for the game to hang mid-turn On the last game I bothered to pursue in any length, I was in the middle of a war in which the tide had just begun to turn in my favour. The turn stopped on the Altarians. So I waited. And waited. Went to make a coffee. Apparently, the Altarians were still thinking about it. I was actually able to start a completely different game, play that for a bit, and switch back to Galciv and the Altarians were STILL thinking about it. Tried loading a save game. Same problem. And it's not the only time that's happened.
So far, I don't think I've actually completed a map. I get angry every time I play it. Every single time. I keep giving it another chance because the core game (when it actually works) is actually really, really good. But, until it's fixed, I can't recommend it.

Like all strategy games it could use a slightly more realistic diplomacy, needs more tradeable commodities and better sector management --- all easy fixes though I doubt diplomacy will be improved, bad (or should I say questionable) diplomacy just seems to be a constant for almost all strategy games.

After playing Stellaris what I would call a decent amount I feel like I can shed some light on how the game functions. It's a lot of fun the first six or so hours of every game exploring systems, colonizing planets, meeting new empires. However, after that short period of time begins the long drawn out "build a fleet, attack someone, defeat them, repeat" about fifty times. The AI is extremely docile and besides one kind of government I've never been declared war upon. The way to win is simple own 40% of the colinizable planets or take over or ally with every single empire. There's no tech victory, or "I have 10 empires as friends" victory. The game forces you to attack other empires controlled by the AI that simply sits there and does nothing exciting. Eventually even exploring is impossible because you become blocked in by other empires that will always refuse to allow your ships into their borders no matter what you try to give them. The game is fun though, I've put almost 100 hours into it already and will probably put in a few hundred more. However as the game sits now it feels empty and lacking with Stellaris being hailed as the best grand strategy game of the decade it's definitely dissapointing. I'd reccomend it but not for $40.

It's EA so has bugs for sure. I've had issues with contractors stopping moving and passengers somehow getting in to areas they shouldn't and then getting stuck, these being about the 2 biggest i've experienced. Beyond these, which I have confidence will be ironed out with time, the game is great.
It has a Prison Architect style approach to building the airport but I think with slightly greater depth. The contracts system and employee management add a dimension to this game that's missing from PA as well as greater pricing and budgetary control. It's simple and deep both at once. Content wise it is a bit light at the moment, you're limited to small airfields really and can't expand land or build large runways to host the biggest planes (at the time of writing) but I know the latter is in the works.
Bug fixes are coming out pretty much daily at the moment and they're active in the forums addressing bug reports so I have confidence the devs care and will give this game the attention it need to grow into a great tycoon/ management game in the near future.

Everyone knows this game and there's nothing I can say that hasn't been said already.  So, I won't waste time giving a magazine-level review of every aspect of this game.  I remember when I was in middle school and first "discovered" Final Fantasy.  I had been renting "Final Fantasy III" (SNES) for years, on and off, and eventually our NES/SNES household got a PlayStation, thanks to my little brother.  One of the earliest games I played (After Breath of Fire III) was this.  I remember the night I bought it.  It was a Monday.  I had a Boy Scout meeting and had bought the game beforehand.  I couldn't wait to get home and play.  The graphics were awesome, and I loved the almost cartoony polygons in game and the semi-realism in combat.  The story gripped me, and I loved the LIMIT system.  For the first time in my life, I played a multi-disc game, a story so big it needed all that space!
This was also the first game I ever played where I accidently beat the game.  Wandering around at the end, I went past the "point of no return" and instead of turning the system off, I just kept playing to see if I could win.  I did.  I was treated to a semi-ambiguous ending which left me wondering "Where did those other guys come from?"
Aside, I loved all the characters, and the fun of having secret characters.  And even though I was the only person I know of who didn't care a thing about (you know who)'s death, I was still drawn in by the fun story.  (Honestly, I just don't care so much for "healers" in game when anyone can heal, and I liked Sephiroth a whole lot more...)
I cannot recommend this game enough!  We have no excuse now.  PlayStation, download on the PS3 or 4 store, original PC, Steam download, download from Square's website, PSP, phones...  Buy it.  Play it.  It's in my top 3.

Gorgeous but strangely unengaging.
The lack of a neutral button has proven a serious detriment to the validity of reviews on the very fringes of acclaim and this is no exception. Dust is a gorgeously made labour of love but it feels very lightweight in every aspect. Storyline light, design light, gameplay light. Lots to snack here but not much nutrition. Every aspect is perfectly functional and well made but lacking depth and I didn't feel any incentive to go deeper.
While the personal drive of the single developer is admirable the limited scope does show in the finished product. Graphics alone do not make a great game so I felt the same kind of detachment from the characters and their world that I felt for similar games like Odin Sphere that likewise excelled in style but never really draw you in emotionally or even with bare function.
Dust isn't bad but personally I can't recommend this game to anyone because everything here has been done before but better and more engaging. I know that "bored" is the least descriptive, helpful and insightful emotional state one can express but that was alas my main reaction, which I find curious because I like every part of this game individually (or rather in other games) but not the game as a whole.
If you like anthropomorphic animals (the cast is cavity-inducingly sweet) and the world of Dust you will get the same kind of enjoyment by watching a let's play on youtube as you would get from playing it.

Review for Little Inferno
Now this game is something special.
The game is simple,basic and in general and easy game. There is no objective,you are not being timed. You burn toys and eventually other items. You do so to get coins to buy more things to burn. You basically just sit there beside a cozy fire infront of your computer.
So the game introduces you to a set of charachters early on, making you not feel so lonely. These charachters give you comfort and will not dissapoint you. The main charachter introduced in this set would be sugar plums. Now she is something special, she will keep sending you mails, and you soon become friends that keep sending eachother items to burn. Now the other charachter is Ms Nancy she is the head of a corporation called Tomorrow corporation, the maker of the Little Inferno fire place. Now she will introduce you to the shop system. And the last charachter would be The weather man. He gives updates on the current situation outsides and gives you a rough idea on what is happening outside and why you should make your fires to keep cozy.
The simplicity adds many hours added to your play count. Beside the fact of not being timed, you have all the time in the world, find all the combos, a system to keep the player puzzeled and entertained.
The game isnt perfect of course. The simplicity does make the game worse in some ways. The game is short but furfilling.
You will feel satisfied when you finish, due to the atmospheric and intriquing ending of the game.
Talking about atmospheric the game has a fantastic artstyle which you have never seen. This game,with its artstyle, will keep you cozy,calm and intriqued. The mails that you keep getting sent will keep you company and will make you feel like you arent alone in this heartless cold world, that seems to have no hope. Now there is a bother in this game, the wait times. Without doing the combos, which you should if you have time, the game will be a long game with wait times that last to 6 minutes. Now the good news logging off would save your progress and save the time , atleast it did for me. Now the ending. The ending is introduced rather slowly. Sugar plumbs will slowly push you towards the end, explaining what has happened to her, will happen to you. The last catalog was her end and you know this as you progress through the game. Now the ending requires you to know the items you send to her over the course of this game. But surprisingly this isnt a hard task, at all. You will remember the items, unless certain conditions. Just due to the unique charachter that she poses to be. The end ties up all the loose strings and as said will make you feel satisfied.
I would if I had to rate this game give it a 7/10 Its not something fantastic that would add TONS of replay value. But it is unique and has kept me on my toes, making me pay attention to every damn detail.

Ah, F.E.A.R. What can I say? Well, it's an excellent game that offers some solid shooting mechanics and the occasional spook. The spooks, although few and far between (this actually works in the games favour) are very effective and really add to the games already deep and eerie atmosphere. The shooting is just so well done with each gun having a nice punch to it not to mention the slow motion is very, very well implemented. The huge amounts of blood, bullet casings and smoke particles left after an intense fire fight really just look awesome and help give the game a truly cinematic feel (Ubisoft, start taking notes). The excellent shooting coupled with fantastic atmosphere and marverously well executed scares make this game action horror done just right (Capcom, also start taking notes). The story is actually quite good in F.E.A.R. Not excellent or mind blowing but pretty good granted that you don't already know the whole plot before playing which is kind of  a hard thing not to know in the modern gaming world. The music in this game is also very good. Like really, really good. It's mostly comprised of this breathy and low fi sounding music which works beautifully with the games already strong atmosphere. The enemy A.I is also very good with the enemies talking to each other and working together to try and take you down which can, at times be quite challanging. However there are some parts of F.E.A.R that really don't hold up so well. The level design is sometimes slightly maze-like and other times quite linear. F.E.A.R. also has quite a lot of frustrating backtracking which really does break up some of the tension. There also isn't much enemy variety in the game. You got shooty guy A, shooty guy B, guy with gas mask and teleporty ablities and some robots. That's about it.
Those last points aside, F.E.A.R. perfectly combines elements of action and horror to make for one hell of a game and one of my personal favourite games, let down only by it's slightly frustrating level design and lack of enemy variety.
F.E.A.R.
Final Verdict -
83/100

Looking back, it's not the masterpiece that I thought it was, back when I played it on PS1. After replaying it thrice, I realized that the whole thing ends up being an intentionally addictive and time wasting game with many flaws.
-The characters are mostly 2 dimentional and forgetable (the main character has the charisma of a soggy french fry and is very, very unlikable).
-Some scripted pauses are tedious to endure (Lucky for many, there is a fast forward button that comes in handy every time)
-The fact that you need to draw magic (up to 9 units every turn, if you're lucky) by grinding it from enemies, until you've maxed them at 100 each, or until you get around it by using GF abilities, adds HOURS to the game!
-The game kinda makes you junction depletable magic to your stats, therefore penalising the use of most magic spells.
-Even Chocobo World ends up being a tedious minigame that will have you wasting hours on the premise of gaining just a few items usable in FF VIII (Not that I was expecting much from a pocketstation game).
-This isn't a dealbreaker for me, but the music quality has suffered a noticeable downgrade, and there have been many complaints about it.
(SPOILERS... kinda)
-The love story between Squall and Rinoa seems forced and contrived, and yet, the whole game revolves around it.
-Don't want to play triple triad? go on... you'll just miss on a bunch of swell items, items that are necessary to beat late game monsters like Ultima and Omega weapon, that otherwise are a pain, if not downright impossible to beat without.
-You gotta wait your sweet time to finally be able to drive the garden arround and explore the world, and you gotta wait even longer to get your hands on that shiny ruby red Ragnarok (and therefore being finally able to scout the entirety of the globe).
I won't recomend this game, since there are better games in the FF franchise, buy it only if it is on sale or if you're a diehard FF fan.
None the less, this old rascal still holds dear to me. and maybe that's saying something.

Issac is really a hard game to recommend, the game is rather grotesque even if the cartoonyness helps bring it back down some. The religious tones of it can be off putting even if they are done in a semi satirical way like Issac does.
What really saves Issac is its gameplay, the game starts out with very bare bones gameplay, think of it as original Legend of Zelda on NES but only the dungeons and the dungeons were always random, throw in a good helping of cartoon gore and a naked hero and you got Issac. As you play the game more, either dying or winning. more items in the dungeon become available, new monsters, new characters and new features. Its a game that evolves with how much you play it for quite some time before you'll run out of new stuff. and that I believe is what Issac's best move was, because its really simple game, but it keeps evolving with you with more content that gradually unlocks so the game stays fresh for a really long time.
The game is very cheap and its add-on wrath of lamb adds a very substantial amount of content to the game for its price. In all this a very solid rogue-LITE experience.

The Witcher 2 is a great RPG where you make a lot of very important decisions that have an impact on the story, some major, some minor.
The story is the game's best part, and can be quite overwhelming at times. I would definitely reccomend reading up on and/or recapping the events of the first game before playing this one or you could get quite lost at times. You play as Geralt, who is a Witcher, and is a great protagonist and overall character. The plot, storyline, characters, monsters and dialogue are all plentiful and very well done throughout.
For a game that is 5 years old, the size of the game and the visuals are impressive. You get to experience 3 different large open worlds throughout the game (A different open-world for each chapter of the game basically). You dont get to go back once you leave, so instead of it being one massive open world it's basically 3 smaller, but still plenty large open worlds. The game is visually appealing and I experienced no major graphical or FPS issues throughout my playing time.
The gameplay is good, nothing special, but way better than the first game. You have two swords, one for dealing with monsters/undead, one for dealing with humans and you can switch between them anytime. You also have 5 magical abilities at your disposal. You can craft potions/elixirs to give Geralt a boost in certain areas for the alotted time, and oils to increase your weapon's stats for a short time. Additionally throughout the game you craft gear and weapons and can buy recipes and then craft everything mentioned above, runes, potions, oils, armor, weapons.
*** SAVE YOUR GAME OFTEN because the autosaves aren't that often and you can lose a lot of progress at once if you dont manually save through out. You can save at anypoint not in combat by simply pushing one key (F5), so please do so! ***
The only criticism I'd have is if you die or fail at certain points, you have to re-watch cutscenes/go through long dialogue. There was one fairly difficult fight where I had to reclick through dialougue 9-10 times.
I really enjoyed this game, and can't wait to finally start The Witcher 3 now that I am all caught up. To anyone who is thinking about skipping this game and just playing The Witcher 3, I would definitely not reccomend doing so, as this game was great and definitely worth the time and money, especially when on sale, its a no brainer.

So, I decided while I'm downloading Total War: Warhammer I might as well do something productive with my time.
That lasted about thirty seconds before I started to think about space travel.
So in the spirit of recklessness with my life, let's take the time to review Stellaris!
So first things first, I have to say I'm pretty much giving this a not recommended because it feels... Wanting. Horribly. Where to start, where to start?
While I was never a fan of customization, it was actually very pleasant in this and the system seems balanced enough to create your own little race of warrior sociopaths to conquer the universe through aggressive negotiation or even more aggressive negotiation. Lovely! Well... Not entirely. I have to admit there is an issue with the traveling system, which I'll explain later, because it's more relevant in two paragraphs.
When you start, there is plenty of options in research and development. You could explore systems, expand borders, research and develop a fleet with high-end weapons! (Trust me, I was actually ecstatic when my fleet power tripled over an upgrade.) As you meet races, they either like you or not like you in a more natural way than some games-- Looking at you, Civilization 5-- and actually do react to your actions as a whole. You conquer, they tend to band together. No big deal!
Now since were on the subject of interaction through weapons of mass destruction, we will go right to it then. It is for certain quantity over quality. A fleet of three battleships that are technologically superior and have more firepower than a group of corvettes is actually less effective. I'm a little iffy on this since I would imagine a group of Man-O-War ships would go down to a modern destroyer, but I digress. I kind of eat my shoe though when every upgrade I find myself sitting there and waiting (Oh god the waiting in this game, fastest is not fast enough.) on an entire fleet to upgrade which will take ten minutes. By then I'm chewing on my shoes and praying that something happens that speeds it up, but something never comes. Now, a major glaring issue with the combat system. This war-score sounds good on paper... In practice, you make me want to stab someone's eyes out.
Let me explain it for you. War score determines who is the victors in a figurative victory-victory tug of war. You're winning if your numbers go positive, and if they reach a 100, then you win altogether and the terms for your victory are honored. Vise versa for your foe if numbers go negative. Sounds good, right? Sounds like, "Oh so this means I can be beaten down, but maybe get my revenge later since I won't lose everything right away."
Hahaha... No.
I destroyed a space station, battled it out with the enemy's main fleet which was basically their entire navy until they were forced to retreat with 1/4th left that were falling apart, and captured their homeworld.
Now explain to me why the HELL is it that war-score of what I just earned is easily overruled by them destroying a few of my mining stations over uninhabited planets?! It may be a viable tactic in war to shoot the enemy in the foot by damaging their resources, but guerrilla tactics by a few raiding starships should not be equal to complete conquest by planet and by planet.
Speaking of raiding. This is when the travel system shows itself as broken. I usually picked hyperspace because ♥♥♥♥ it I ain't no lazy♥♥♥♥♥using warp and I don't have the patience to try (Or really, the patience for this game to get around to try it.) the wormhole travel. Warp speed itself is supposed to be slower, but you aren't limited. Good for new people. Hyperspace, you have paths to take as you move your fleet, supposedly faster. Wormholes is the mode of travel in which you use some type of wormhole generator or some-such to move ships instantly around the galaxy.
But late game, it doesn't really matter since everyone's mode of transportation becomes equal except for the wormholes! It's nothing short of bothersome when you are at war and someone uses warp drive to jump wherever they want into your territory. (Dear god they have telepathy or something, because they somehow always know where my main fleet is.) Then they do some of that raiding stuff by destroying whatever they can to make the war score go up, and then♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the moment a real fight shows up.
This mixed with the lazily handled war-score mechanic is disgustingly annoying. I was enjoying the game until I started to notice the cracks and lines...
Now the waiting. Dear god the waiting. Ship upgrades, research, economy, building, establishing a colony. There's a point when you stop being able to grow, being able to do anything.
Then this sector mechanic comes in saying, "You can divide your territory because if you don't, your economy will start falling apart. It's good because if you divide your territory, you can't do anything but direct it from five hundred feet away to either give you a certain amount of resources, or what they should focus on. And yes, the governors will be slow as ♥♥♥♥ in development. But this also gets rid of micromanagement. AREN'T WE NICE?!"
Lovely, thank you. I appreciate the sentiment, but there's one thing that you're forgetting.
"What's that?"
Micromanagement is what I have when I spend the entire goddamn game WAITING.
"Then maybe you should research to make it so you don't have to wait so long to build/research/upgrade-- wait what are you doing?"
I am getting the shovel, because you are going to dig your own grave out back.
Okay, maybe I pushed it a bit there at the end. But honestly the waiting was painful. Even goddamn launching a land invasion army to fight was waiting, and not even a small little visual to make it pleasant was there. Not even a small war game to play... While if Stellaris had more to offer, I'd be more worried about everything else than playing a little war game.
My consensus can be summed up in this way:
Stellaris is a one night stand that was an absolutely gorgeous looking that night, and that was quite fun to go out for fun then take home for a ♥♥♥♥ until the sun rises. I have been playing Paradox games for some years now, and despite being a very loyal fan and supporter of their historical grand strategy game series, I have generally followed the "wait until a couple expansions" rule of thumb with their games. I purchased Stellaris because it was the first new franchise from Paradox in some time and was looking for a new strategy game outlet.  I am not a sci-fi game fan for any genre and I am aware of the varying states of polish associated with new releases.
That said, this game is out-of-the-box fun.  The exploration component remains a consistent element of the game well through mid-game and depth of different component systems; from ship design to technological progress to diplomacy and planet planning and developement are all well thought out systems and well executed.  There is sufficient enough differences betwen the pre-start choices of ethics and species talents to create an asymetical feel from one species/empire to another.  The procedural generation of the worlds is not overly balanced, which present frustrations (e.g. not enough minernals near starting star systems can be a real drag on early game building capacities) but it also prevents cookie cutter, scripted opening strategies and pushes the player to adapt to the strategic map as it is unveiled.  This keeps you thinking from game to game and evolving new approaches to handle complex and emerging landscapes.
Overall, despite being a new release without supplemental dlc to flesh our and refine, this game in its current state stands as one of the most complete and deep vanilla Paradox games I have played to date.  I am enjoying it now and look forward to watching it continue to evolve.
Well done, Paradox.  Your commitment to releasing games in a finished state is changing perceptions and your willingness to take the risk associated with launching a new franchise appears to be on its way to paying off.

I remember when I was in middle school and first "discovered" Final Fantasy.  I had been renting "Final Fantasy III" (SNES) for years, on and off, and eventually our NES/SNES household got a PlayStation, thanks to my little brother.  One of the earliest games I played (After Breath of Fire III) was this.  I remember the night I bought it.  It was a Monday.  I had a Boy Scout meeting and had bought the game beforehand.  I couldn't wait to get home and play.  The graphics were awesome, and I loved the almost cartoony polygons in game and the semi-realism in combat.  The story gripped me, and I loved the LIMIT system.  For the first time in my life, I played a multi-disc game, a story so big it needed all that space!
This was also the first game I ever played where I accidently beat the game.  Wandering around at the end, I went past the "point of no return" and instead of turning the system off, I just kept playing to see if I could win.  I did.  I was treated to a semi-ambiguous ending which left me wondering "Where did those other guys come from?"
Aside, I loved all the characters, and the fun of having secret characters.  And even though I was the only person I know of who didn't care a thing about (you know who)'s death, I was still drawn in by the fun story. I cannot recommend this game enough!  We have no excuse now.  PlayStation, download on the PS3 or 4 store, original PC, Steam download, download from Square's website, PSP, phones...  Buy it.  Play it.  It's in my top 3.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a wonderful experience of a Side Scrolling Hack N' Slash game, and I'm here to tell you why.
The game starts off with you playing as Dust, a... furry (?) who woke up in the middle of the forests who dealt with amnesia, and is awfully confused on whom he is, and is confronted by Fidget the Nimbat, and Ahrah the Sword. You set out on a perilious journey to discover Dust's past and face all kinds of wicked monsters across the world.
The game features extremely satisfying and smooth combat despite it being limited to 2D, yet, it plays so well.
The game's combo system works by pressing two buttons, one for slashing, and another for extra combos. You gain new abilities, most likely to help you in enemy confrontrations when you play more of the game.
The game world is absolutely lovely and beautiful to look at, as well as the scenery you come across. It is quite expansive, as you head out to new areas to explore the world.
The combat can sometimes get repetitive and tiring after a while, as the fight mechanics do not change, but the game can make up for this with it's wonderful speed and fluent style of gameplay, that happens so quickly. It is very awesome.
The difficulty is not in any way lacking, unless if you have mastered the combat to the extreme, as it allows you to pick which difficulty you would prefer, easy, moderate, or hard.

There are many characters and side quests to tackle on if you do not want to try and finish the main game's storyline, as they give you time to explore the world for secrets, treasures, and quests to start on your own time.

The game allows you to craft new items to your liking that has stats you'd generally prefer to have and use, such as armor, sword buffs, pendents, rings, etc.
Dust An Elysian Tail may seem short to some who've played and decided to go on a quick speed-through, but it is a fun experience nevertheless and I suggest buying at full price to support the developer 100%, since a lot of love andeffort to making this game. Kudos.

Warning: this is a "could be good" labelled as a no. After beating the first zone after 35 minutes of gameplay I feel like this is a game i should like but i just don't.
It's a very traditional fogue lite in that you spawn in a dungeon, fight enemies, die, spend currency to make the next run slightly better, and then play again. However this is the first rogue lite i haven't been able to get into in a very long time.
Maybe the game requires too much coordination, every step you take you want to try and line it up to the rythm of the music so i found myself spending huge chunks of time just starting at the bottom of the screen trying to time my actions to the beat. This meant i wasn't really paying attention to what i was doing and constantly ran into enemy attacks that would have been really easy to beat without the intense time pressure. The game really pushes the time mechanic, if you're too slow the game will skip one of your movements and give you enemies an extra chance to move. The game encourages you to play very quickly and rewards players who do, all of which is to the strength of the unique core mechanic the game has. It sounds like a recipe for success on paper but i just got frusterated and wanted to quit, a feeling all rogue lites give me eventually but with this game is came after the first few runs. Maybe i'm just tired of the try-die-repeat formula, maybe i just need to get comfertable with the unique movement, and maybe in the future i'll pick the game up and really enjoy it.
For now i found the games core mechanic hard to get used to and after beating the first boss i'm just happy to put the game down. I do not recommend Crypt of the necrodancer.

I bought this game as part of a bundle with the much more realised EpiStory (which has some great graphics to boot). The multiplayer is completely dead, but it could be a bit of fun with friends. However, this game has some huuuuuuge balancing problems.
There are a few game modes where typing speed isn't sooo important, but if one player can type at 100wpm and one player types at a max of 55wpm, there's no question who is going to win - even if the 55wpm player is, say, better at coming up with words in 'Creativity' mode or has faster instincts. There is one mode where typing speed isn't a significant factor but can still decide matches - Reflection. It's variant, Tug, is still largely decided by typing speed. I just don't see any way this can be much fun with the lack of balance.
Competition against the AI falls into two categories: way too slow, or impossibly quick, to the point where it is impossible to do things earlier than the AI. It isn't all that much fun even when the AI does match you because the match feels empty.
Typeracer is, unfortunately, way more fun.
I played it for about an hour and I don't think I'll ever touch it again. It definitely isn't worth the $2, and I'll go into exactly why with some more brutal comments as this review draws to an end.
TypeFighters is a poor realisation of a great - but largely impractical - idea. A game that uses typing as its main game mechanic? That's so cool! Typeracer is great and all, but it's not that much fun when the only game element is competing for the top 20 scores of the hour. It's just a singleplayer typing test where the results are compared against other people, and the closest it comes is to 5 people doing the same typing test at the same time. That's *almost* like competitive gameplay, but it's still way too separate. Typeracer is an ego trip - I've wanted a multiplayer typing game where there is both skill and speed involved for a long time. TypeFighters is the exact kind of game I wanted to love, but it's just gets boring too fast.
There are a bunch of modes, but once you've played them a few times, you've played them to death. There's some definite creativity here - I particularly like Tug & Reflection. If only they worked practically. Much like TypeRacer, the competition is still too separate because of the disparate typing speeds between players. It's just too imbalanced for it to be any fun, and there's no depth in the singleplayer to make it worth buying.
