I remember when I first bought this game at Best Buy. I rushed back to my college dorm to play it and proceeded to freak out to the edge-of-your-seat gameplay and creepy atmosphere. This was before I knew about Steam. I was not able to buy physical copies of the DLC and I was really bummed about that...until I saw they were included with F.E.A.R on Steam! I paid full price for F.E.A.R just so I could get those DLC and I am glad that I did.
F.E.A.R. came out in 2005, and it really has aged. However, the gameplay and the story more than make up for the older graphics. The combat is intense, forcing you to fight through tons of soldiers by yourself in order to reach your target. The AI can be pretty annoying sometime since they can figure your tactics, and also freak out when they have realized you took out an entire squad. There is strong language throughout the game. The gore can be intense. Carnage and blood is everywhere and not just from bullets. After the firefights, Alma shows up.
The story that surrounds Alma is the reason I recommend this game. This is what I feel sets this game apart from all other FPS's. You have military combat gameplay team up with a seriously creepy and supernatural storyline. It's a terrifying combination. She may be inspired by The Ring and countless other scary movies with little girls with black hair, but she is so original, you won't have any trouble singling her out as one of the scariest forces in video games. FEAR ALMA.
Now for the DLC. They are not necessary but they are fun to play. Both are similar in length. Each one took me six hours to complete. They are not considered canon but you do learn some interesting things about the Perseus Project and Armacham.
This was a great game to play and it got my psyched for the sequel, Thought I have not played an extensive list of FPS's, I believe that this one stands apart for merging a military FPS with psychological horror.

Looking back, it's not the masterpiece that I thought it was, back when I played it on PS1. After replaying it thrice, I realized that the whole thing ends up being an intentionally addictive and time wasting game with many flaws.
-The characters are mostly 2 dimentional and forgetable (the main character has the charisma of a soggy french fry and is very, very unlikable).
-Some scripted pauses are tedious to endure (Lucky for many, there is a fast forward button that comes in handy every time)
-The fact that you need to draw magic (up to 9 units every turn, if you're lucky) by grinding it from enemies, until you've maxed them at 100 each, or until you get around it by using GF abilities, adds HOURS to the game!
-The game kinda makes you junction depletable magic to your stats, therefore penalising the use of most magic spells.
-Even Chocobo World ends up being a tedious minigame that will have you wasting hours on the premise of gaining just a few items usable in FF VIII (Not that I was expecting much from a pocketstation game).
-This isn't a dealbreaker for me, but the music quality has suffered a noticeable downgrade, and there have been many complaints about it.
(SPOILERS... kinda)
-The love story between Squall and Rinoa seems forced and contrived, and yet, the whole game revolves around it.
-Don't want to play triple triad? go on... you'll just miss on a bunch of swell items, items that are necessary to beat late game monsters like Ultima and Omega weapon, that otherwise are a pain, if not downright impossible to beat without.
-You gotta wait your sweet time to finally be able to drive the garden arround and explore the world, and you gotta wait even longer to get your hands on that shiny ruby red Ragnarok (and therefore being finally able to scout the entirety of the globe).
I won't recomend this game, since there are better games in the FF franchise, buy it only if it is on sale or if you're a diehard FF fan.
None the less, this old rascal still holds dear to me. and maybe that's saying something.

Issac is really a hard game to recommend, the game is rather grotesque even if the cartoonyness helps bring it back down some. The religious tones of it can be off putting even if they are done in a semi satirical way like Issac does.
What really saves Issac is its gameplay, the game starts out with very bare bones gameplay, think of it as original Legend of Zelda on NES but only the dungeons and the dungeons were always random, throw in a good helping of cartoon gore and a naked hero and you got Issac. As you play the game more, either dying or winning. more items in the dungeon become available, new monsters, new characters and new features. Its a game that evolves with how much you play it for quite some time before you'll run out of new stuff. and that I believe is what Issac's best move was, because its really simple game, but it keeps evolving with you with more content that gradually unlocks so the game stays fresh for a really long time.

The Witcher 2 is a great RPG where you make a lot of very important decisions that have an impact on the story, some major, some minor.
The story is the game's best part, and can be quite overwhelming at times. I would definitely reccomend reading up on and/or recapping the events of the first game before playing this one or you could get quite lost at times. You play as Geralt, who is a Witcher, and is a great protagonist and overall character. The plot, storyline, characters, monsters and dialogue are all plentiful and very well done throughout.
For a game that is 5 years old, the size of the game and the visuals are impressive. You get to experience 3 different large open worlds throughout the game (A different open-world for each chapter of the game basically). You dont get to go back once you leave, so instead of it being one massive open world it's basically 3 smaller, but still plenty large open worlds. The game is visually appealing and I experienced no major graphical or FPS issues throughout my playing time.
The gameplay is good, nothing special, but way better than the first game. You have two swords, one for dealing with monsters/undead, one for dealing with humans and you can switch between them anytime. You also have 5 magical abilities at your disposal. You can craft potions/elixirs to give Geralt a boost in certain areas for the alotted time, and oils to increase your weapon's stats for a short time. Additionally throughout the game you craft gear and weapons and can buy recipes and then craft everything mentioned above, runes, potions, oils, armor, weapons.
*** SAVE YOUR GAME OFTEN because the autosaves aren't that often and you can lose a lot of progress at once if you dont manually save through out. You can save at anypoint not in combat by simply pushing one key (F5), so please do so! ***
The only criticism I'd have is if you die or fail at certain points, you have to re-watch cutscenes/go through long dialogue. There was one fairly difficult fight where I had to reclick through dialougue 9-10 times.
I really enjoyed this game, and can't wait to finally start The Witcher 3 now that I am all caught up. To anyone who is thinking about skipping this game and just playing The Witcher 3, I would definitely not reccomend doing so, as this game was great and definitely worth the time and money, especially when on sale, its a no brainer.

To start this off, I would like to say that I have loved paladins, and am somewhat sad that I have not played more of it. Also, as this game is free, it does have micro transactions,which might turn some people away from it,but it is not pay to win. Yes, there are things you can buy to help you out in the game, but the things you can buy can also be earned in game through enough work. Players who pay can get newer and cooler skins, but it doesn't help them to win. Every 5 days (I believe, it might be every 7 though.) You can earn 50 diamonds through daily gifts, and lots of gold. Hi-rez actively updates the game, adding characters and skins, as well as buffs and nerfs, by what the community wants. You can get a boost to gold and exp by playing in a group, so paladins encourages players to play with friends. There are a few different modes, as well as a casual and competitive options. You can also test out maps and give feedback. There is no single player campaign though,but I'm sure that the multiplayer is still fun. Some negatives are that people can buy essence and diamonds, which can help you easily customize your character(there are loadouts that are made up of 5 cards, and each gives you a special perk) so you will have to grind for the essence while they can have it from the start. Putting the TL;DR at the top: I don't know why you're reading recomendations, instead of buying it. Go buy it. Now. I've bought 8 copies so far, and may buy another 4 pack. I've not regretted it. Ever. Disclaimer: I've only ever played PvE mode, so everything I say here reflects this mode. I've heard PvP is good, but PvE is just too fun to quit. Broad Description: Does shooting raptors in the face with a magnum in slow-mo, and watching their head pop and their body stumble to the ground sound fun? Buy it. Does driving a tank down a vertical cliff side (does take some learning) and using the cannon to knock a T-Rex's block off sound fun? Buy this! How about punching a triceritops to death? Or mowing down flocks of flying pests with a 250-round-a-minute hand-held gattling gun? Or maybe you'd like to spam grenades? Not your thing? Rockets. No? LASER CANNON. No? EXPLOSIVE BOW. The list goes on and on. The AI is simple at first, but as you turn up the difficulty, and face the bigger dinos, you might start to see some surprising moves. I can't recomend this game enough, even if it was $10, I'd still recomend buying it, it's that good. Details: The 2 PvE gamemodes that I play (there are others) Survival: Simple enough: 10 waves, with 3 side objectives. You have a generator to defend, and a spot to buy weapons and augments. Good for a quick game (lasts 10-40 minutes, usually around 30). Conquest: Like 3 survival matches strung together, almost. You have 30 waves with 9 side objectives. This is split up over 3 different generators, with 10/3 on each one. Every base has a weapons and augments area, but 2 of the 3 also have vehical shops, where you can buy anything from and air bike to a 5 person party tank, or a VTOL. This one is more fun for experementation, because of the massive quantities of in-game cash you build up by the end. I've actually built walls and/or card houses using tanks. Took me like half an hour, but it was totally worth it. Usually lasts close to an hour There is a level up system, which gives some awesome stuff when you get higher up, though every levelup gives something nice. Sometimes there's a few glitches, though the VAST majority of these are harmless and funny, such as a dead stegosarus suddenly deciding to do front flips. STILL updating, though I'm not sure what the patches are for, as I'm always too impaitent to read the patch notes when I could be playing Prelude instead. Feels very similer to how I think Halo feels (only watched videos, never played the game myself), but with dinos. Community is very friendly, chatting with them ('t'? might be 'u') will usually be very helpful if you need help with the controls, or a trex that decided you looked tasty. Complete control list (for PC): LMB - Fire gun RMB - Aim gun or spin up v - Mele t(might be u) - allchat shift - sprint c - toggle crouch if clicked, roll if held at the same time as a directional key wasd - standard movement space - jump e - use/interact k - drop 1k credits on the ground l - drop weapon z,x,f - quick message keys g - grenade ctrl - class special ability (jetpack for assult class, medigun for support and invis for recon) tab - stats screen esc - menu Probably some Im missing EDIT: Some I was missing: 1-Primry weapon, and adrenaline weapon. Hit again to cycle through choices. 2-Secondary weapon. Hit multipult times to cycle through choices 3-Pistol. Same cycling as the last two 4-Item. Only one at a time, purchasable in Weapons>Items. Ammo and health packs do not count for the slot. 5-Teleporter. Teleports you to your current generator. Has a short cooldown. Remember: most of these controls can be changed in the options menu.

Shift 2: Unleashed is as good as Need for Speed: Shift was bad. Bold statement as Shift 1 was widely praised for splitting the franchise and moving into the racing sim genre, breaking away from Need for Speed’s arcade roots. But it wasn’t quite there. Shift 1 was a prototype for the formula, testing what worked and what didn’t. What definitely didn’t work were the physics and handling. Floaty, unresponsive and still clinging to the series traits. An EA inclusion more than Slightly Mad Studios, as the UK developers were definitely capable of more precise and realistic handling based on their earlier GTR games.
However, the cockpit view was an absolute blessing and Shift 2: Unleashed drastically improves the handling to match the visually stunning cockpit view.
Gameplay
Shift 2’s cockpit view is the best and most visceral experience I’ve ever seen in a racing game. Not only is it highly accurate and detailed, the cockpit also features amazing effects. Wing mirrors shake at high speeds, vision is blurred at those speeds, the dashboard is reflected on the windscreen, shifting, handbrake and pedal actions are all intricately animated, dirt flicks on to the windscreen, rubber and gravel ‘marbles’ hit the undercarriage and wheel arches and high speed crashes cause violent shaking, temporary loss of vision and heavy breathing from the driver. Also the option to have a helmet camera further emphasises the impact as well as the precision as the head sways towards the corner direction for added realism. The third person camera offers the chance to view the detailed cars from behind but it doesn’t offer the connection the player has with the car as the camera is a bit too floaty, I like that word, making it hard to aim for the apexes.
Luckily, the improvements in handling have made it much easier to point a car at an apex. Turning off all assists, except ABS and Automatic (c’mon now), produces the most rewarding driving experience in a racing game. Throttle control is vital as well as judging the braking zone and corner angle all to get the best exit creating intense racing. Immersion can be broken however by the slightly over-aggressive AI drivers who have no problem PIT manoeuvring you off the track or blocking you on straights. A little more Jenson and little less Pastor would’ve made a less frustrating battle for 1st. This is tied to the fact that Unleashed doesn’t have a rewind feature made popular by Codemasters and now prominent in the Forza series. Thank God though, as racing intensifies in the latter stages making it a white knuckle ride to the finish line without a safety net.
Career progression is improved above and beyond Shift 1’s silly star system as well as the XP rewards being based on good driving rather than awarding careless racing. Videos by real-life racers and drifters such as Vaughn Gittin Jr. introduce each racing category and you are provided the opportunity to learn and hone the skills before heading out on track. Need for Speed fans are also given extra cash and cars for their dedication to the franchise, which helps save up cash to buy their dream cars. Unlike Shift 1, to race a car in Hot Lap mode, you have to buy the car in career mode. Perhaps unfair, but it gives a real incentive to finish gold in every race and manage the cash in order to afford the cars you really want. Helpfully, cars can be sold for the price bought making it easy to sell the lower-powered sports cars necessary for a category in order to save for a hypercar.
The car list is smaller than GT5 or Forza 4, but it ignores the unnecessary hatchbacks and endless Nissans of the GT series. The cars here are focussed racing machines and monstrous production cars all with beautifully detailed interiors and exteriors with moving airbrakes and wings. Not included are any Ferraris but the Porsche selection more than makes up for it. The diverse variety of tracks features all the greats such as Suzaka, Silverstone and Spa as well as an interpretation of the Monaco GP circuit.
Technical
The sounds are loud. My headphone volume was at 50% most of the time and sometimes lower at night. The cars sound great though and the noticeable differences in sound from the cockpit view to behind the exhaust demonstrate the attention to detail that Slightly Mad paid. The graphics are impressive not just the cars but also the track surroundings, including helicopters and planes flying over whilst racing. Night racing is also a welcome addition with tactics having to alter and slight apprehensiveness when approaching blind bends. The ability to turn off HUD whilst in-game is also a brilliant addition as you can have the lap times and positions when you need them and turn them off to not obscure the view without breaking the flow of the race.  The framerate could be improved though as modding was the only way to uncap the 30fps limit.
Verdict
Turn off assists. Stick it in cockpit view and go RACE.

Shift 2 Unleashed was a solid racing game and the first one I've played to completion on career mode of 100%.  While I would recommend this game, I do so with some caveats, which I will list in the cons.  The most important point people need to know is that controls have to be customized heavily, I used an Xbox 360 controller for windows and the stock settings were awful, however I followed some guides online and tweaked a couple ini files and was good to go.  Here is the guide that was helpful for me setting up controls:
Pros:
- Lots of races
- Good variety of cars
- Most cars look great and have great interiors
- AI makes mistakes on occasion, even knocking themselves out of the race
- AI will bump into you more if you start driving dirty
- Difficulty Levels and driving assists really let you tailor this into either a sim racer or arcade, I like it closer to sim but not all the way there and played with no damage, driving assist line, medium AI, elite handling mode and all driving assists turned off.
Cons:
- Crashes (not the kind you'd expect, in my 75+ hours I've probably had about 30 crashes to desktop, sometimes losing progress, particularly maddening on endurance races).
- Ignored/Lost progress bug.  I noticed this when doing the last drag races, often times the race results screen would show up twice and I would lose all my progress and have to repeat the series, very annoying but after 3 tries on each of the last standing mile races I was able to get through.
- Challenges like the modern A invitational can be difficult because you are provided with a car and not able to tune it for the track (makes for a frustrating experience at times).
- "Cut the track" bugs.  Perhaps I'm misinformed but on a few tracks if you go too wide on a turn (understeer) into the grass and then come back to the same turn it would say "you've cut the track!".  I call BS on that, I thought cutting the track was when you took a shortcut through a turn on the inside grass, not the outside.  This was infuriating on one particular track where following the ideal race line would put you into this situation on purpose, even with just two wheels off.
- Other general bugs, none of the "videos" unlocked even though I completed the career stuff for them.
- Not enough levels, Max level in game is 20, after that you keep earning experience but it goes nowhere.  I hit level 20 by 45% career completion.  Why build levels in at all when they end that soon?
All in all, this was a fun experience and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys a racer that helps bridge the gap between simulation and arcade.  8 / 10

I think it is time to write a review.
This is likely my favorite game of all time.  It combines brilliant music, good pixel art and highly difficult roguelike elements with the unique challenge of rhythm games.  Runs can be short enough to race with friends, and the online racing community is a fantastic group of people (races are organized external to the game - sadly there is no online multiplayer).
The game provides a variety of items so from one run to the next you will often end up with an entirely different build, and it takes a lot of time to get practiced with every build.  There is also the challenge of playing low%, taking no items at all and trying to clear that way.
The game provides some challenges that can take thousands of hours to have a good chance at completing - unlocking Coda is one enormous milestone (which I only recently passed) and beating a run with her is an even more difficult feat.  That said, the difficulty is rarely the game giving you impossible situations, but instead very difficult ones that test your ability.  I almost always look back after I die and realize the mistake that cost me that run, be it a silly decision or a matter of reaction time.
The DLC adds 4 new characters and some new modes which are generally fun but sometimes not as balanced as the standard All Zones Mode.  It also adds a new zone with new enemies, and many new items.  The changes made by the DLC do a good job addressing some of the balance issues with the base game, but the DLC also adds some items that are arguably quite overpowered.
The game is quite easy to mod if you are interested in changing the gameplay, either by altering enemies, items, or any aspect of the graphics.  Hopefully in the near future we get access to the source code for more modding power.

I can't rightly tell you how I've spent nearly 60 hours on this game. Content-wise, it's not actually that deep--with only four "zones" and a few characters to give it variety, but the core gameplay concept is good enough to last for a while, especially as a zen veg-out game.
For the uninitiated--this game is a basic dungeon crawler with a twist--everything, including you, can only move on a beat, which transforms it into something like a turn-based game with a surprisingly fast rhythm. That alone is very entertaining during the first hours of gameplay when you're going through the zones, getting used to the controls, trying out characters, but it's good even after you've exhausted the basic content. The gameplay lends itself to good, zen-ish veg-out sessions, which is only improved by the fact that you can add your favorite tracks and songs to the game.

Putting the TL;DR at the top: I don't know why you're reading recomendations, instead of buying it. Go buy it. Now. I've bought 8 copies so far, and may buy another 4 pack. I've not regretted it. Ever. Disclaimer: I've only ever played PvE mode, so everything I say here reflects this mode. I've heard PvP is good, but PvE is just too fun to quit. Broad Description: Does shooting raptors in the face with a magnum in slow-mo, and watching their head pop and their body stumble to the ground sound fun? Buy it. Does driving a tank down a vertical cliff side (does take some learning) and using the cannon to knock a T-Rex's block off sound fun? Buy this! How about punching a triceritops to death? Or mowing down flocks of flying pests with a 250-round-a-minute hand-held gattling gun? Or maybe you'd like to spam grenades? Not your thing? Rockets. No? LASER CANNON. No? EXPLOSIVE BOW. The list goes on and on. The AI is simple at first, but as you turn up the difficulty, and face the bigger dinos, you might start to see some surprising moves. I can't recomend this game enough, even if it was $10, I'd still recomend buying it, it's that good. Details: The 2 PvE gamemodes that I play (there are others) Survival: Simple enough: 10 waves, with 3 side objectives. You have a generator to defend, and a spot to buy weapons and augments. Good for a quick game (lasts 10-40 minutes, usually around 30). Conquest: Like 3 survival matches strung together, almost. You have 30 waves with 9 side objectives. This is split up over 3 different generators, with 10/3 on each one. Every base has a weapons and augments area, but 2 of the 3 also have vehical shops, where you can buy anything from and air bike to a 5 person party tank, or a VTOL. This one is more fun for experementation, because of the massive quantities of in-game cash you build up by the end. I've actually built walls and/or card houses using tanks. Took me like half an hour, but it was totally worth it. Usually lasts close to an hour There is a level up system, which gives some awesome stuff when you get higher up, though every levelup gives something nice. Sometimes there's a few glitches, though the VAST majority of these are harmless and funny, such as a dead stegosarus suddenly deciding to do front flips. STILL updating, though I'm not sure what the patches are for, as I'm always too impaitent to read the patch notes when I could be playing Prelude instead. Feels very similer to how I think Halo feels (only watched videos, never played the game myself), but with dinos. Community is very friendly, chatting with them ('t'? might be 'u') will usually be very helpful if you need help with the controls, or a trex that decided you looked tasty. Complete control list (for PC): LMB - Fire gun RMB - Aim gun or spin up v - Mele t(might be u) - allchat shift - sprint c - toggle crouch if clicked, roll if held at the same time as a directional key wasd - standard movement space - jump e - use/interact k - drop 1k credits on the ground l - drop weapon z,x,f - quick message keys g - grenade ctrl - class special ability (jetpack for assult class, medigun for support and invis for recon) tab - stats screen esc - menu Probably some Im missing EDIT: Some I was missing: 1-Primry weapon, and adrenaline weapon. Hit again to cycle through choices. 2-Secondary weapon. Hit multipult times to cycle through choices 3-Pistol. Same cycling as the last two 4-Item. Only one at a time, purchasable in Weapons>Items. Ammo and health packs do not count for the slot. 5-Teleporter. Teleports you to your current generator. Has a short cooldown. Remember: most of these controls can be changed in the options menu.
Bad quality, but still, it's good enough to play. Needs a graphics update. I don't know.

This is an excellent and deep airport simulation. It gives you all the flexibility you need to build and manage your own airport that you can locate anywhere in the world. Flgihts go to and from real cities. Aircraft have needs. Passengers have identies and actual boarding passes. They also have luggage, and when it is checked, they have a luggage tag too. And needs as well - such as bathrooms, shopping, food and drink.  Beautiful design, you almost forget thst this is an early access title. Already feature rich and deep, and the developers roadmap shows that there is so much more to come. I highly recommend this if you love true airport simulation game experience. There is a learning curve, but it is fun to learn and once mastered, amazining easy.  It is the sim city (old school style) of airport building and the airport tycoon simulation I've been waiting years for.

In the dafault/vanilla portion of this game it can get really repetitive real fast. The maps are small when comparing it to other popular open world games and after a small amount of time both standard maps can get travelled real fast. It's not really a simulator at all, it's very arcadey. The Titanium Edition DLC offers a lot of high-detail models and new features which look amazing, but the eye candy loses it's charm after a short while. But what really makes this game is the mods. This game is 1000X better once you get into modding. The gameplay becomes more realistic as well as the machinery and maps. Downloading new texture packs for this game will really boost up the flair of how everything looks making it visually stunning if you download the right ones and put them together. The modding community for this series is very much alive and thriving even as far back as Farming Simulator 2009. Lots of great mods for tractors, combine harvesters, tools, implements, cars, trucks, etc are available. Without the modding component of this game, it would get old real fast, but I still can't stop playing this game with all the new free mods you can get and download that keeps this game fresh all the time. It has an extremely fair price and even comes with Giants Editor where you can make your own maps and machinery. A lot of skill is needed, but learning the basics is easy. I give the default/vanilla portion of this game a 6.5/10, but with the modding components, a 9/10.

After Galactic Civilization II: Twilight of Arnor, I was so happy with the franchise that I was SO glad when I saw that the same people (in theory) were developing a new entry (Galactic Civilization III).  I was thoroughly disappointed when it came out.  And I just tried playing it again, thinking that I might have just been in a bad frame of mind when I tried it the first few times.  I was wrong -- this game sucks great big green rocks through a soda straw.
Buy GCII:Twilight of Arnor and play THAT.  Leave GCIII on the shelf, and you'll be much happier (spending hours clicking "turn" and waiting for SOMETHING that you can do to get somewhere is not my idea of fun).  There are reasonable paths to a "win" in GCII, but the only path to a "win" in GCIII seems to be through near infinite clicking.  The ship design is strictly cosmetic -- there's no improvement in the base game over the customizations available in GCII.  The tech trees are suffiiciently restrictive (both in what can be accomplished and WHEN they can be accomplished) that specialization and approach are almost meaningless concepts.
All in all, play GCII and leave GCIII to the drones who will likely buy it based solely on the good design of GCII.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a wonderful take on the standard "Metroidvania" formula. You have a large world map that you can openly explore (or travel around with nifty waypoints) much like in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. Throughout your adventure you'll visit a variety of different locations, level up your character, and meet a variety of different characters. While the voice acting is satisfactory at best, the combat, graphics, and soundtrack are all phenomenal.
The first item that must be discussed is the art style. While it's not as active and vibrant as other 2D games (like Rayman Origins or Rayman Legends) it still is beautiful enough to hold it's own. Everything has a hand-drawn look to it and the animation is fantastic.
Combat is another area where the game excels. You're given a talking sword as your main weapon but receive several upgrades and combos to fool around with so combat doesn't get stale. Having the option to counter enemies in a 2D game is always a great addition as well.
Getting 100% for this game wasn't particularly difficult. Most are story related and there are a few missable achievements if I recall but nothing too difficult. Overall it was a very fun game to 100% and quite satisfying as well.
I would highly recommend Dust: An Elysian Tail to any Metroidvania fans or 2D side-scrolling fans in general. It's a fun game that looks great and plays very well.

Dust: An Elysian Tail starts off with a very simple concept, yet it stands up to what it promises.
Speaking of the gameplay, it's platforming mixed with action fighting.
The fighting system is rather simple, you have a few skills need to learn to use in the right combination and situation considering the hazards around you and the enemies you're facing. Especially on higher difficulties, you really want to know what enemies can stagger after how many hits, or when you need the energy to dodge instead of using Fidget attacks. Knowing your surroundings is mandatory as you need to manage your movements while fighting. The attacks and combos are limited, but that means you have less to work on, and you need to make the best with what you have.
The platforming parts are fun, but they can get really annoying, especially on higher difficulties: Playing Hardcore from the start, I found myself loading and repeating the same sections lots of times, since the damage the obstacles deal are increased with difficulty. I guess it's my fault for making a mistake if I land on a spike, but when I find myself in front of unpredictable hostacles, I can't really be blamed, since the lack of regular pattern just made me jump towards my own death, or sometimes you'll find yourself stopping a jump in midair to avoid that obstacle falling on other ones (Like Mudpot mushrooms and Mountain icicles). Another annoying thing was the trials: fun challenge, but a restart option would have been nice since you need an almost perfect run to get 4-star ratings, instead of having to clear the whole course just to get another shot at it.
The classic RPG-styled system for EXP, gold and items is nicely managed. Except for the huge boost you get from almost-end game items, the character build up speed is just right to keep a good challenge if one doesn't stop grinding at the first obstacle. The only problem I could find is that you'll need to buy usable health items even if you're in a town, where there could be a classic inn to fill up your health bar (I found myself buying from the town store after clearing a dungeon where the only damage I got was from the last rooms, usually containing bosses).
The game experience in general is quite astonishing. There are some clichés here and there, but the storyline and ambience are what really got me.  Trying to understand who the protagonist is during the main quest, how he behaves, Fidget, the rising climax towards the end of the storyline really got me glued to the screen. The variety of landscape, ambients, enemies, and weather are simple yet effective addictions to an original art style. Some sloppy animation during cinematics, but consindering what I just said, it's not a big deal.
Intriguing storyline after the amnesia cliché starts developing, Fidget, exciting gameplay, original art style, Fidget, variety of characters and landscape, Fidget... If you have the chance, give it a go, you won't regret it. I'd say a solid 9/10

F.E.A.R. is one of the best horror themed FPS's to come out of the past decade.  Intense gun battles, unique story, and a superb atmoshpere make it an unorthodox blend of genres that delivers a precedent-setting experience.
The First Encounter Asssult Recon (F.E.A.R.) is a U.S. government special ops group specializing in the investigation of paranormal events.  Players embody the "Point Man", a faceless, nameless protagonist as he is deployed on his first F.E.A.R. operation.  During a briefing, it is revealed that defense contractor Armacham Technology Corporation (ATC) has a small problem.  A man named Paxton Fettel, with the ability to telepathically control an army of clones, has seized control of ATC's headquarters.  F.E.A.R. is sent to apprehend Fettel at another location, but he mysteriously evades capture.  What follows is a game of cat-and-mouse between Point Man and Fettel, interrrupted with paranormal phenomenon and disturbing visions involving a little girl.  Point Man pursues Fettel undeterred and in doing so, learns more about Fettel's origins and uncovers a project that ATC is attempting to conceal with alacrity.
The expansion known as Extraction Point follows Point Man after the conclusion of the main game as he tries to escape his new conditions.  In Perseus Mandate on the other hand, players inhabit a sergeant in a second F.E.A.R. team (deployed at the same time as Point Man's) to another ATC facility.  Both of these expansions provide more lore to soak up but the only canon events in the F.E.A.R. series occur in the base game according to the creators.
F.E.A.R. is played in first person but unlike some FPS's, Point Man's body is fully rendered (meaning if you look down you will see his feet).  This is important due to some of Point Man's abilities explained later.  Movement is fairly slow, but it makes you feel as though you are wearing a ton of gear.  Point Man can peak around objects lending to his tactical training but he also has a unique skill.  At the push of a button, players can enter "reflex time", essentially bullet time allowing Point Man to deal with impossible odds.  These enhanced reflexes also allow Point Man to execute elaborate melee maneuvers such as slide kicks and leaping kicks (where seeing your feet is helpful).  Thus combat is often a blend of bullet time shooting, peaking around corners for kills, and melee attacks.  The Replicate forces (Fettel's army) have extremely cunning AI though, forcing the player to adapt quickly.  Enemies will flank, use explosives to flush you out, and kite you to death if you try to rush them.  Enemies communicate with one another, reporting losses and calling for reinforcements along with other situational dialogue.  Fettel throws everything he has at you: heavily armored foot soldiers, "Watchers" that use guerilla tactics, and even unmanned mechs.  To deal with these threats, Point Man can carry up to three weapons, making your loadout choices very important.  Guns are not scaled in F.E.A.R., so your starting equipment works just as well as weapons found later in the game.  That being said, weapons run the gambit from the usual stock to unconventionals like lazer rifles and particle weapons.  The game will take you anywhere from five to ten hours depending on difficulty.
Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate both introduce unique weapons and equipment, however core gameplay reamains the same.  Extraction point only lasts a few hours but Perseus Mandate is almost the same length as the base game.
F.E.A.R.'s lighting is some of the best I've seen in gaming.  Your flashlight has to recharge after using it for a certain amount of time so there are moments in the game where you almost scare yourself.  Going down completely dark hallways is always nerve wracking.  Explosions shake overhead lights that react realistically, fires have heat distortion, glass shatters satisfyingly, and enemies ragdoll and dismember depending on where and how they are injured.   Voice acting is very good, and music is appropriately creepy or intense depending on the situation.  But, the reason this game is lauded is because you never know how it will scare you.  Walking around empty office buildings is creepy enough, but you never quite know what's around the corner.  This was the designers' intention, to make a game that was unpredictably scary, rather than just jump-scares cubed.  The result is a game that does not feel formulaic in its approach to horror aesthetics and one that will often surprise players with its use of special effects.
F.E.A.R.  is remembered as one of the best marriages between horror and the FPS genre of gaming.  Paced excellently and with some challenging shooter segments, F.E.A.R. may just change your opinion about what makes a great FPS truly great.  I'll never climb a ladder the same way again.

I came into this game thinking it would be a run-and-gun type of game. I was completely wrong.
The AI in this game is absolutely brilliant.
Every encounter is a challenge.
You have to be prepared for an encounter at all times.
You have to form a strategy quickly for each encounter and execute it without mistakes or you will die.
You have to use slow motion for each encounter or you will die.
Enemies don't just run at you, you have to draw them out of cover or try to flank them (which is impossible sometimes).
The levels are designed very well, leaving you with minimal cover and putting you in awkward spots where it is very difficult to advance on the enemy.
The weapons are well balanced and very fun to use.
This is an excellent FPS if you're looking for a challenging game with an interesting story. I highly recommend it!
P.S. Logitech devices make this game perform very poorly. It's something about the polling/report rate of their mice. So you have to disable the Logitech HID's in your device manager and everything should run great!

The second and probably last Shift game to come by Slightly Mad Studios.
It is very similar to Shift but also very different.Graphics/Performance
The graphics on Shift where great for a 2009 game and the same follows for Shift 2. They are similar but slightly better compared to Shift especially on the vinyle quallity. The surroundings on the track are not the greatest but it is hard to notice when you are gunning it down the track at 180 MPH. The car detail is very nice and the paints look very pretty. For me at least the game runs fine but every once in a while when starting a race it gets ♥♥♥♥ing slow for a few moments and goes back to normal. Other than that it performs great on my PC. I'd give it a 9/10 on graphics/performance for a game from 2011.
Gameplay
Well for one the gameplay is totally different from Shift. They took the realisim up a notch on the way cars feel and handle compared to Shift. Drifting has also been made way different compared to Shift and is actually quite hard for most people. Overall the game is probably 2 times as hard as Shift was. The customizing like in Shift sucks just the same with no paintable wheels and hardly any vinyles to apply thus making it impossible to make your own liveries. This makes me feel forced to use the pre made liveries that look bad IMHO which leads me to just paint my cars metallic blue and be done with it. The vinyling system was definatly improved since Shift but they removed a great number of vinyles and made 90% of them only one colour. The AI can be annoying at times especially on small, tight tracks as they will push you out of their way in a hairpin making it almost impossible to win. I'd give gameplay a 8/10 only because of the crappy vinyling system.
Overall
Overall this game is fun and challenging making it very entertaining for me. Nothing beats blasting around the Nordschleife in a 1986 Toyota Corolla AE86 with over 800 HP. If you like racing simulators, buy it. If you like cars, buy it. If you like drifitng, buy it. If you want your Vette to handle like a Lotus and be fast, I'd run and never look back.

Big fan of Galactic Civilizations II, which I played to death. When Galactic Civilizations III released, I bought it immediately and tried to furiously get into it, but I just couldn't. Too much was the same and a lot of things felt clunky, like the constructor spam for starbases. So after a few dozen hours I found out I wasn't really enjoying myself anymore and I quit playing.
When Crusade came out and I read that it really changed the base game, I gave it a shot. Unfortunately, after a few hours trying, it still doesn't click for me. Stardock changed a lot of things and some are definitely improvements, like eliminating the need to spam constructors to build up starbases. However, the experience is still not streamlined enough. Galactic Civilizations, inclusing Crusade, feels too much like I am playing a Civilization game in space. And it doesn't really work for me anymore.
I have been playing a lot of Stellaris this year, and although far from perfect, it is a better game. When playing Stellaris I feel like I am running a galactic empire. With Galactic Civilizations III this galaxy feels small and cramped. Especially when playing with the suggested amount of civilizations for the galaxy size. In Galactic Civilizations III I also get spammed with little choices, like research, buildings, citizens, ships, etc... but in the end it feels rather inconsequential and tiresome.
Unfortunately, I just cannot recommend this game anymore. Get Stellaris instead. It's the better game and Paradox will probably be improving it for years to come (though it of course means paid DLC).

Obviously our current state of technology requires the ability to type.  Sure there are applications that are do voice to text very reliably.  Still though the need to be able to type is super important.  I’m 27 and I learned to type when I was 6/7 so I’ve been typing for nearly 20 years.  Why then would I play a typing game? Haven’t I already mastered typing?  Well yeah, I know full well how to type, just like 99.99% of you out there reading this, BUT practicing on occasion is a really good way to keep your skills honed.  Seriously, if I practice typing by using a typing test or game like this one I can keep my WPM reliably in the 65-70 range w/ 98% accuracy.  If I don’t practice and just use my normal day to day typing as “practice” my wpm will fall to around 40.
So what you ask? Well the faster I type the faster my work gets done.  What does this have to do with Typefighters?  Practicing typing can be really stupid and boring but having something to do really breaks up the monotony.  Basically all you do is write sh!t.  Whoopty doo.  Having a game to play while you practice really helps.  Typing of the Dead is another game to practice typing w/ but of course it’s implemented like crap and is only partially functional.  Coming across Typefighters has been great! Not only is it a fun way to practice typing but it also has multiplayer.  I have 4 employees that work under me and i’m “team leader”.  What do my employees do? Writers.  So to help both myself and my team get better I’ve had everyone install this and it’s fantastic.  Yes it’s just typing but having an engaging way to do that typing makes all the difference.  This is a great game for teaching anyone how to type or more importantly practicing and honing your skills. One of the coolest features (though it took me a minute to figure out) is how you interact with the menus. You type everything.  Wanna exit? Type E X I T.  Yeah it’s dumb but I really enjoyed that feature.  Please, do yourself a favor and grab this game.  It will make you a better typist while not boring you to tears.

Now, one thing I really hate, it has lots of unnecesseary micro. Not only is the game full of hard counters so you have to order around units so they wouldn't get owned by their counters while concentrating their fire onto weakest targets, pretty much every unit has it's own gimmick special, be it a special attack or alternative fire mode, so the amount of unnecesseary micro is unberable. Red Alert 2 kept it way more simple, and if unit had several firing modes you wouldn't need to switch between them, meanwhile here it's not even Starcraft or CoH levels of micro. Worst offender is the new third faction, Empire of the Rising Sun. They have probably the most of alternative modes due to sizeable chunk of their force being transformers like a machinegun mecha that switches into a fighter and such, and you can't switch back for some time like you get with, say, Starcraft 2 vikings, so it's rather annoying.

The campaign is short, like the previous CODs, about 10- hours. It's not a sandbox and there are many QTEs. Overall it's still a good experience but the replaying potential's poor.
I won't say much about the Multiplayer mode since I don't play it much. From what I've seen, it's mostly like the previous versions with new maps and new options in the same style.
The zombie maps are good, two basics: Kino Der Toten and Five. Both are good, Five will have you survive in close quarters. "Dead Ops Arcade" isn't really a zombie map but a 2D like shooting mini game.
The four DLCs are expensive for what they bring: about $15 each even though they're getting older and older. Buying them when there's a -50% firesale is a good deal.
Ascension and Call Of The Dead are fine, Shangri La and Moon are really hard (mostly in early rounds for Moon, then it's easy).
The easter eggs are hard too, especially on Shangri La where four players are required, and Moon's normally requires to complete first COTD and Shangri La's easter eggs too (or have at least 1 player in the party who completed both easter eggs, or possibly 1 player with COTD's ee and another with Shangri's ee).
The last DLC Rezurrection pack is really worth buying if you haven't played the previous zombie maps from CoD 5 World At War (though these maps are free on CoD 5 WaW). These maps are back with BO weapons, Mule Kick and Monkey Bombs. Last but not least, the Wunder Waffe does not zapp the Juggernog anymore on Der Riese.
The gameplay is different in the sense that zombies won't stop/glue you anymore when you touch them, so that's rather a good point. But what disturbed me the most is the way zombies now shout: 1 zombie alone can make several shouts at the same time (??!!!), unlike CoD 5 WaW where 1 zombie could make only 1 shout at a time (sounds logic since a zombie doesn't have more than 1 mouth...), so you could use the sound of the game to be a better killer (at the end and the beginning of a round, you could feel - or hear - how many zombies were left or spawning on the map, which was extremely helpful. It used to be possible to locate a zombie with the sound it made, especially when one was coming in your back, but now you can only rely on what you see because the map is overwhelmed with shoutings). So this huge advantage is lost.
Next I don't like the way knifing has changed since CoD 5 WaW: knifing from a short distance was possible, the character was charging into the nearest zombie. Now in BO the character will still do it, but it's more or less random, so you really have to go in front of the zombie by yourself. Sometimes the character will even charge even though you didn't want to do so, and that may lead you into a very bad position...
Using bindings is still possible fortunately, but this requires to edit the config file before launching the game (no in game console, this has been patched). Cheats are still working in solo, maybe infinite ammo too in coop and provided you're the host. The "give all" cheat has been tampered with and will actually take all your points and guns. I like the "noclip" code just to take a tour and visit the map.
Now on to the drawbacks:
the worst thing, in my view, is the DRM. There's NO way to play zombies solo offline. So what if I want to play zombies solo, say in the train on my laptop? Or if my ISP has a breakdown? That also means that when the BO servers are shut down, we will have no way to play zombies, even in solo, ever!
Edit: there are 2 workarounds I know. The first and fastest requires however to start the game online, then once the map is loaded, cut your connection.
The second and most efficient workaround is to simply bind a key to a map:
bind KEY "devmap MAPNAME"
Kino = zombie_theater
Five = zombie_pentagon
Ascension = zombie_cosmodrome
Call of the Dead = zombie_coast
Shangri-La = zombie_temple
Moon = zombie_moon
Nacht der Untoten = zombie_cod5_prototype
Verrückt = zombie_cod5_asylum
Shi No Numa = zombie_cod5_sumpf
Der Riese = zombie_cod5_factory
Dead Ops Arcade = zombietron
For example: bind F9 "devmap zombie_theater"
Another disastrous point is the inability to "restart" a game when hosting a private server. The host must end the game, wait for the game over screen, then load back to the lobby, and load once again the same map. Abominably awkward!!
There's a workaround: by binding a key to "fast_restart". It makes really no sense that this option is disabled.
Black Ops 1 also marks the shift from the publisher to focus from PC to consoles: now PC players just get ports from console versions. That means the end of the golden age for Call Of Duty on PC since mods and custom maps aren't allowed anymore. Look at the old Doom or CoD 5 World at War: people are still playing these games thanks to the ability to create custom maps and play mods. That's what keeps people playing these games, sustain a player base and gives all sense to "personal" as in personal computer. No wonder the BO1 zombies player base has been shrinking more and more.
Following this trend to go "consolish", the next thing that I dislike is the server system: you can not open a public server anymore but only a private server where only your friends (and recently met players) may join. So unlike CoD 5 WaW, it's not possible anymore to kick awkward random players and / or have them to abide by some rules, like no stealing, advise everybody to reload before taking a Max Ammo etc. (There's a workaround if you want to be the host and avoid those kids killing the server after going down: the first player in the lobby is the host. A better suited name for this would be Farming Simulator Arcade: this simply is not "simulation" enough. After being surprised by the excellent Euro Truck Simulator 2, I was expecting sort of the same experience, only with cows and grain instead of long nightly drives through Germany. And with multiplayer! But I was let down…
To be fair: the game can be fun, especially on a LAN with some friends, country music on the speakers and a bottle of Jack to pass around. And the models of the farming machines are pretty nice and detailed as well. However, many things simply are a let-down or maybe wasted potential. For example, the rear mirrors are not functioning, essentially making it impossible to play the game first person when driving. And don’t get me started about the dreadful physics engine powering it all: you will encounter gravity defying bouncing farming equipment at regular intervals (and pray those will not get stuck in the scenery). Also, there are no real management options: you can hire some dumb helping hands but that is about it. Even an ancient game like Sim Farm had this. And speaking of Sim Farm: why is there no option to actually upgrade the farm itself (beyond the buying of extra fields).
Hopefully future versions will fix some of the issues I had with this game, since there is some great potential here. But for now I cannot really recommended it, unless it’s really cheap in some sale and you have some friends to enjoy it with.

Little Inferno is a toybox game. There aren't any set objectives, there aren't any rules, just pick up your toys, throw them into the fire, and burn them. Ultimately that is the premise to the entire game however there is more to it than that.
You begin with a small number of toys available to order from a catalog, and you can unlock more toys in that catalog by earning money, and you earn money by burning toys. The more toys you burn, the more you can buy, and so on and so forth. You can only 'hold' so many toys in your inventory at one time, however you can increase the size of your inventory by spending some of your money which makes the game a little easier as you progress.
There are numerous other toy catalogs that you can unlock playing the game, but to do so you also have to work out combinations of toys to burn together from combo names which are given to you. Making combinations of burning toys will not only unlock catalogs it will also give you stamps, and these stamps can be used to reduce the time it takes for your toys to arrive once you have ordered them from the catalog - these stamps are invaluable when you get to ordering toys from the very last unlockable catalog as some of the delivery times are around 4 minutes, and this does start to feel like a long time to wait particularly when your toy goes up in a smoke in a number of seconds.
There is a story throughout the game which isn't particularly obvious until right at the very end, and I won't include any spoilers here as I think it needs to be played to be experienced. I found it quite moving, and the whole experience very enjoyable.
This game is fairly short - I managed to complete it in 3 1/2 hours, but I hadn't worked out all of the stamp combos, and I'm actually already keen to go and play it again so I can work the remaining ones out as some combo names are quite cryptic (whereas some are blatantly obvious).
This game is £6.99 on Steam and this is a lot of money for a short game, however I do think if you connect with the gameplay and the story there is scope for replay-ability, and certainly once you've unlocked everything you can just leave it as a 'toy' in itself to pick up and play whenever you fancy burning something on-screen.
Little Inferno is simplistic, it looks great, it's fun, it's challenging, it's polished, it's thought-provoking. I really didn't expect it to be as good as it was. I thoroughly enjoyed it from start to finish, and would definitely recommend giving it a try. It's something that can be played in one sitting, or something you can come back to, either way it's definitely something that should be experienced.

This game in comparison to other racing games, particularly Forza and Gran Turismo on the consoles, is rather low on car variety and has less tracks as well.

This game provides that ♥♥♥♥ing masterpiece that is Need for Speed racing enviroments, soundtrack, and being able to do exactly what they want to do in each game - shooting for realism this time around, it came out in a FANTASTIC way, allowing you to adjust every setting to go from basically being an arcade racer to being a full on simulation with full support for external wheel/shifter/pedal controllers of every sort (Logitech G27 in my case). The graphical style is outstanding, and I say that because without the use of extreme filters and such like Need for Speed Rivals for example, it still pulls of a rather impressive appearance if a bit dated (It did come out in 2011, after all).

Is Drive to Hell shoot'em up? Twin stick shooter? Bullet-hell? Actually, its more like a mix of all of them, plus a bit of driving game with a crazy storyline. Yeah, story is about aliens invading the Earth and you - some driver shooting the hell of them. Oh, and I'm gonna spoil it, you will me meet a big alien boss at the end of the game ;).
Drive to Hell has all elements what makes this genre so immersive - solid gameplay and good balance. Shooting is satisfying and the interesting part of gameplay is that it enforces player to pick and use different power-ups, because they are freaking powerful, while the main gun, in most cases, is weak and requires much more effort to succeed. Varied enemy types adds up to a great experience. As I mentioned, balance is suprisingly good, normal difficulty is suitable for anyone, while higher difficulties and survival mode really test your skills, but in a good way and is never impossible.
Gameplay feels good and features many cars to choose from, which can be fast, but without much of firepower or a complete opposite. Completing levels with good score earns money, which can be used only for different cars. Length is just right, there are 5 levels with 5 waves each and a boss at the end of level. Along with 4 difficulties, many achievements and survival mode it can easily immerse for at least 5 hours. For such a low price its amazing how meaty the game is.
What really separates Drive to Hell from others shoot'em ups is graphics. Its made with Unity engine and features very crisp colors, which makes it so easy to notice every enemy or bullet.
Well, there is some some problems too, coop mode works, but it can be hard to make your controller work, also music and sound effects lacks variety.

Typically, my recommendation is dependent upon whether or a videogame exceeds my expectations. Went I started Drive to Hell, I wasn't expecting much if any quality. Devils just destroyed this guy's favorite hangout, so he's gonna get revenge. I mean...really? That's just totally gag-worthy. Also when the title screen has "Like us on Facebook/Twitter/Other Networking Sites!" I begin to wonder why I even installed the game. After all, idlemaster works as long as a game is in your library.
But, I played through the game a few times, and it's legit.
Drive to Hell is a vehicular twin-stick shooter. You're on a highway (to hell) and devils approach from every direction. Some simply home in on you, others circle around the screen, and some prefer to harass you from the sides. Also since you're in a vehicle, your mobility tends to be limited. Most of the play-field either slows you down, or is blocked off entirely. Twin-stick shooters tend to get claustrophobic, so one where you have maybe 1/3 of the screen to actually work with gets pretty ridiculous.
While shooting everything that moves is fine, you also have to consider your vehicle. There are a handful to unlock, all with their own strengths, weaknesses, and special abilities. While you can drive a heavily armored tank, you'll find that it is slow, and its bulk makes weaving in-between bullets a bit too difficult. Alternatively something light and weak is liable to be much smaller and more maneuverable. The special abilities can be anything from a bullet-absorbing shield to proximity mines.
It's also important to look out for weapon and item power-ups. Weapons are just that, more powerful (but temporary) methods for bringing death to minions. Items are a bit different, since they can held onto for the right situation. This might be a good reason to choose a heavier vehicle, because they can carry more items. Being able to crack open a shield or a bomb when the situation gets out of control is really handy.
That's pretty much the extent of it I believe. Even though there are boss-battles, this isn't the type of game where you have to memorize patterns or develop strategies. Choosing the right vehicle for your play-style and your reflexes will get you very far. There are four difficulties though, and the later settings can get really intense. Thankfully, the difficulty doesn't do anything cheap, like force one-hit kills on you, or make it so you can't continue after dying. However, if you're the type that plays for score, you can't take damage at all, because it'll kill your multiplier. All in all there's a good difficulty balance for every kind of gamer.
Drive to Hell gets my recommendation because it exceeded my (admittedly low) expectations. I'd even go as far to say as I'm pretty impressed with it. Once I got over my initial "What is this hunk of.." reaction, I discovered that this is a solidly-designed game with satisfying controls, playability, and even a touch of depth. My only real complaint is that there are some annoying foreground objects that block a good portion of the screen. This hasn't led to any deaths (yet), but I've gotten hit once or twice. Otherwise this game is pretty decent, you might want to give it a try.

This is a beautiful combination puzzle game. The goal is to figure out which items in your ever-growing catalogue you have to combine in order to get the combinations that the game asks for. The art is beautiful. The puzzles are mostly relatively easy. Some puzzles have several sensible solutions, but the game only accepts one, so some guessing and trial and error is necessarily involved. The art is beautiful, and the story is also nice. The game is relatively short. Figuring out all the puzzles myself and completing the game in this way took me slightly more than 6 hours. If you don't want to find all the combos, it can be finished in maybe 2 or 3 hours.

I tried to like Stellaris, I truly did. However, all things considered, the Ankle deep diplomacy, the imbalanced poorly executed  civilization management system, the one sided incredibly overpowered AI, all that Stellaris boils down to is a paper thin pretty picture. The exploration is fantastic, but it ends there. as soon as you have the misfortune of encountering another intelligent society, kiss your pretty little empire good-bye.
All AI races within the game follow no logical pattern. They will declare war on you at the drop of a hat no matter your current relationship with them while roundly rejecting every single attempt you may make at interaction. Would you like to form an alliance? +180 opinion towards you? NOPE, rejected. Trade technology for the greater good of us both? ABSOLUTELY NOT! Can we at least trade minerals? NO, UNACCEPTABLE! Then you get invaded by an empire with a 2 planet economy matching you 1:1 for production power.
My breaking point was spending over 100 years as a technological isolationist, I was CONSTANTLY under attack by everyone and their dog. Never took land (because that is a negative influence bonus) just defended myself like the nerd in high school. Finally manage to get 4 neighboring powers to over 200+ opinion of me, and you know what they did? Allied to the bug people to my flank who have attacked THEM before and then, even with the fact that alliances must VOTE for a war, they raise their guns and JOIN FORCES against me.
Avoid this game at all costs, it's all show and zero real initiative or effort. Do what I didn't and save your money for a game that has earned it.

Late game isn't a grind anymore because someone will end up running empty.

This is basically a text-based RPG that tells a revisionist history of colonial Congo, in which the Congolese rise up and overthrow the King of Belgium. (Picture
in text form, stripped of verbal pizzazz, and with Leopold II taking the place of the fuhrer).
I'll concede upfront that it's not a particularly good
The basic mechanic involves clicking on various villages, recruiting any of the locals that feel like joining your army, and then attacking whichever colonial official is labelled "Very Easy" at that moment. (The game calculates this automatically, depending on how many soldiers and weapons you've got with you at the time). The battles themselves require a bit of quick-thinking resource management, as various options pop up while the two sides trade attacks. Increase your defense, or call in reinforcements? Make yourself invulnerable for four rounds, or take a chunk out of your enemy's stamina stats? This is pretty much the only part of the game that requires any degree of skill, and the lack of clear instructions meant that it took me an hour or so until I realized that I was even supposed to be making some of these choices at all. Once you get the hang of it, though, the game becomes incredibly easy (probably mind-numbingly so for some players).
There's no animation or sound effects to accompany any of this, just a mournful classical music loop that gets pretty annoying after awhile. However, the game is just short enough (1-2 hours) that I didn't get bored, though that's probably due to the fact that I'm a history nerd with a soft spot for a good colonial uprising. I particularly enjoyed the way that the victories snowballed into each other, with your army becoming larger, more and more villagers joining your side, and the momentum of inevitable victory beginning to take hold. (None of this is really communicated by the game; my imagination had to do the work). The final battle against Leopold himself is totally ridiculous, but also catharctic: who
want to take some revenge for Congo's historical suffering, if only through a cheap Steam game?
is a curio, and probably won't be enjoyable unless you've got a particular interest in both colonial history and experimental video games. I'm gonna go out on a wild limb here and guess that's quite a niche market -- but it also happens to be one that I squarely belong to. So it's a "thumbs up" from me, and a bit of a warning to everyone else.

After the success of DOOM, id Software decided to develop a sequel, which is pretty much the same as the first game, but with a few new enemies, which, unlike the original demons, require a little more strategy and attention from the player's part. The Super Shotgun was also introduced.
The main difference between DOOM and DOOM II is the level design. John Romero, DOOM's main level designer, didn't work too much on DOOM II, and as a consequence the levels are really different. They aren't better or worse, it all depends on what you think.
And finally the soundtrack. Instead of being a fast paced metal thing, it's more... atmospheric let's say. Again, if it's better or worse depends on the person.
Personally, I like more the first game, gameplay and soundtrack wise, but I can't say that this isn't a really good game.

I only played one hour of this at the time I'm making this review and despite the short playtime I foresee playing this more in the future. The premise is simple, why make a typing game be convoluted. I'm not saying Typing of the Dead is bad, or god forbid the games of our childhood that we were told to play in class. No those were all good on their own, but there's something so blissfully simple about this game that makes it exciting. It's like the typing version of "You Don't Know Jack." It has multiplayer implemented very well upon release. Not many small games get the "Join Game" functionality right on steam, but this one has it down so it's easy to get your friend to hop on board with you and compete 1v1.
Speaking of competition, there are SOOO many different game modes, from connect 5, tug of war, to even just who can make the most words. There's always variety and you can always swap game modes in between matches. You can customize your matches to crank up the difficulty so it's fair.
You can even CREATE YOUR OWN LIST OF WORDS. I know, it's crazy, but say you wanted to just play a full game with nothing but curse words, you can do that. Albeit you have to type those words in by hand or find some website to rip the words from, but there's always some way to customize your experience. Just last night my friend and I jotted down a list of dank memes for our word bank to choose from for each game mode and had a blast!
For only 2 bucks...well $1.50 right now, I can't recommend this game more. Just sell a few steam trading cards or one of those stat trak fedoras you got from CS:GO and get typing!

This is an odd game, if you can't tell.  It's not a choose-your-own-adventure.  It's not an RPG.  It's basically a browser-style clicky game that runs in Adobe AIR, or like a time-management game where you click as fast as you can to keep tasks from overwhelming you.  It tells the story of Belgian atrocities in the Congo in the early 20th century, although it uses fictional characters and events to do it.  Your goal is to win battles by choosing "battle cries" and spending "hero points", basically managing about three choices constantly in real time while the losses of your troops and the enemy troops are displayed.  Besides the battle cries and hero points, success depends on picking up rewards for defeating village bosses or for amassing enough men or weapons, setting your battle stance, and keeping morale high and fatigue low.  This sounds more complicated than it is, and none of this comes with graphics other than some basic background images.  Battles play quickly, allowing you to retry immediately if you lose.
There is a small amount of strategy involved, but the game reports your chances before you choose a battle and it autosaves, so you really just click until you win.  You have to beat 11 bosses, but you can choose more if it helps you acquire people.  Essentially you just play the "very easy" battles until there aren't any more, then the "easy", then "fair", then "hard".  Actually I missed some rather obvious choices early on and still beat the game in less than two hours without restarting, just retrying.  If I had done it right, I may have never had to fight a battle rated "hard".
The game is redeemed by the story, which is fairly well-written in English by an apparently Brazilian developer.  There are a few typos or instances of strange grammar, but the actual text is not terribly long anyway.  The game could be improved, of course, even for what it is.  For example, I accidentally clicked past one of the Sir Arthur Conan Doyle quotes and had no way to re-view it.
Anyway, if none of that turns you off, get it cheap (I got it in a bundle) and try it for an hour and a half.  For what that's worth, I'm glad I played it.

A rogue-like, rhythmic-based dungeon crawler about a traveler whom mysteriously wakes in a cavern of music and monsters.
The main quest follows the plot of a village girl named Cadence. She heads out in search of her missing father Dorian, against the wishes of her uncle Eli. Upon some digging one night, Cadence collapses into an opening chasm, briefly knocked unconscious until the wandering NecroDancer traps her life, her heart, into a rhythmic beat. Stuck in the crypt, she ventures forward, continuing her search deeper into the catacombs.
The ultimate goal is for players to traverse each zone with the tools given to you with your character. As they continue deeper and deeper into the caverns, they have to adjust and work around obstacles, monsters, and items, while keeping in sync to the beat.
Admittedly, the game proves a challenge for beginners; the game provides a basic tutorial of how some things function in the game and some training for specific monsters, such as slimes, skeletons, and ghosts. In the base game, you have the opportunity to play between ten different characters, each with their own set of rules and restrictions that add to the challenge of each dungeon. Crypt's soundtracks are all beautifully composed and the pixel art is quite an aesthetic. There is much of a story that can be explored in the game as well; every completed zone provides more in-depth backstory to the world of the NecroDancer and further explains who is exploring the crypt from the beginning. Lastly, the bosses are fun and a joy to encounter in the game.

Despite being very interested in the subject and having high hopes for this game I can't recommend it.
The gameplay itself is forgettable and repetitive: Go to each territory, recruit whomever is ready to join you and fight the enemy. Always picking the weakest enemy guarantees that you will win. There is no character development or any choice, aside from who you recruit and fight.
There is no dialogue with the other characters, they will just give you a quote (which is sometimes cut off mid-word at the end as if there is a character limit)
But then again this game, like other games from Locomotivah is not about gameplay, but about the story and about reflection. So does it deliver on this front?
Well, as stated before I was pleasantly surprised at seeing the title but my excitement was replaced with worry as soon as I saw the protagonists name as Miala is not a Congolese name. It made me worried about the research behind the game and unfortunately this worry proved to be justified.
None of the Congolese names are actually Congolese, they range in Culture from Southern African to Western African and anything in between. This made it very hard for me to get into the game, as I never got the idea that I was anywhere near the Congo, the Belgian names were reasonably accurate though.
You get virtually no background information before you get started and even if you click on "learn more" there is very limited information, including a 5 book Bibliography of which only one is from the past twenty years.
I also find it strange that one of the locals would compare Leopold II's riches to Rochefeller in one of the quote's. What would they care about Rochefeller? The story about Miala himself, which progresses whenever you kill a district commander, is also rather classic and unimaginative. And why in the world did the writers feel the need to
Anyway, to summarize: This game is a shallow execution of an interesting topic.
Pro's:
+ Interesting topic
+ Attempt to bring a lesser known part of history to attention
Cons:
- Poor immersion
- Very limited roleplay
- Hardly any strategy
- Sometimes text is cut off
- some spelling mistakes

Positive things first: Good intent in the story and selection of topic. Yet the game leaves the impression that the historical issue was only scratched on the surface. The choice of the actual gameplay mechanic, which is quite simplistic (build up army, fight, repeat, repeat, watch your fatigue) and that of the protagonist seem both quite out of touch with historic realities.
I might have rather played a text adventure as E. D. Morel in the «Congo Free State Propaganda War» or anything from a western perspective that touches well documented reality, than as Miala, a fictional very vaguely defined native African rebellion leader in his early twenties. Spoiler:
.
The gameplay almost exclusively consists out of grinding through battles and increasing the strength of your army by beating the easiest opponents first (conveniently labeled «very easy»). The Campaign is beatable in under 30 minutes, probably always in under an hour. Once you figured out what does what in the very abstract fights, it's pretty much impossible to lose the game if you stick to the easiest opponents first. Since there is no variation or obvious alternate endings, the game itself doesn't offer any new content or difficulty in repeated playthroughs. It seems to be strictly linear.
A lot of good chances were missed here and the lack of media other than text is astonishing, no explanatory maps, no short general introduction into the history of colonialism. The game itself transports no feeling of the horrors, only facts. One might want to read Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" or (re-)play Spec Ops: The Line (which is very loosely based on Apocalypse Now and Conrad's Book) and just imagine the setting being transformed to the Congolese jungle, to compensate for that.
But for anyone who starts playing this and eventually learns on elsewhere about the topic and in the process probably gets lost in Wikipedia, I can still only recommend the game and hope for a better more extensive revisit to the topic at large in the future.
