Hello all and welcome to my review of Stellaris. This game is a 4X strategy game with an aerial (top-down) view where the object is to conquer the universe. I will try my best to give a non-objective view of the game for someone interested in playing it.
The first thing I would like to say about this game that no one ever mentions with 4X games is that this game is a strategy game, not a tactical game. I mention this as strategy and tactics are two totally separate things. Strategy is the planning, coordination, and general direction of military operations to meet overall political and military objectives (or ‘long-term’). Tactics implement strategy by short-term decisions on the movement of troops and employment of weapons on the field of battle. Another way to put it is “Tactics is the art of using troops in battle; strategy is the art of using battles to win the war”. There are games out there that include both tactics and strategy, but Stellaris is not one of them. As long as you accept this before you begin, you won’t judge this game unfairly.
Your race has both a cosmetic and practical element. Cosmetically I won’t go in too deep here as people’s taste and opinions vary, but there are many options to choose from in how your race looks, the naming conventions, and the look of your ships. Practical elements include racial traits (Are you strong/smart/charismatic?), ethos (What do you believe in?), and government (How do your beliefs define your people). Government can be changed in-game, racial traits can be ‘adjusted’, and ethos stays where it is for the most part. Government is also directly related to ethos, and some government types are specifically included or excluded based off of your race’s ethos.
You can play and win in multiple different ways, but the win condition is conquering-based (‘control X planets’ or ‘defeat all other races’), and not ‘tech-based’, ‘objective-based’, or ‘resource-based’ as many other 4X games have. In this game, tech, money, and resources in general are means to an end and not the end themselves. Having a strategic advantage (be it tech, money, resources, diplomacy, etc) in this game is important only if you exploit it. Most of this game focuses around two things; your ‘core’ systems (5+, depending on government and tech), and sectors (areas given to a governor to control with a small return given). You only manage your core, which is fairly simple but has strategic elements, so you don’t have to spreadsheet your way to victory nor auto-play the game either. The tech-tree is based off a 'weighed' system giving you three options over three different areas, with more common tech's having greater weight then rare or dangerous techs.
Pro’s:
-Good variety of racial options, both functional and cosmetic (maybe some more traits)
-Balance between different traits, ethos, and government; no ‘weak links’
-Simple but fun ship customization, planet management, sector management
Con’s:
-Interface isn’t difficult but it’s not intuitive either.
-Races are not aggressive when it comes to expansion
-Non-existent tactics; combat is viewing only
Recommendation:
I recommend this game if you want a strategy game with a simple but robust tech tree, planetary system management, and race customization. This game has its faults; it needs a boost to the AI in terms of aggression and utilization of technology and resources. Just remember that this game focus on strategy and not tactics.

A rogue-like, rhythmic-based dungeon crawler about a traveler whom mysteriously wakes in a cavern of music and monsters.
The main quest follows the plot of a village girl named Cadence. She heads out in search of her missing father Dorian, against the wishes of her uncle Eli. Upon some digging one night, Cadence collapses into an opening chasm, briefly knocked unconscious until the wandering NecroDancer traps her life, her heart, into a rhythmic beat. Stuck in the crypt, she ventures forward, continuing her search deeper into the catacombs.
The ultimate goal is for players to traverse each zone with the tools given to you with your character. As they continue deeper and deeper into the caverns, they have to adjust and work around obstacles, monsters, and items, while keeping in sync to the beat.
Admittedly, the game proves a challenge for beginners; the game provides a basic tutorial of how some things function in the game and some training for specific monsters, such as slimes, skeletons, and ghosts. In the base game, you have the opportunity to play between ten different characters, each with their own set of rules and restrictions that add to the challenge of each dungeon. Crypt's soundtracks are all beautifully composed and the pixel art is quite an aesthetic. There is much of a story that can be explored in the game as well; every completed zone provides more in-depth backstory to the world of the NecroDancer and further explains who is exploring the crypt from the beginning. Lastly, the bosses are fun and a joy to encounter in the game.

It's relatively rare that I bother writing a negative review, but this seems warranted due to the current, inexplicably high positive review rate, low price, and alarmingly high number of purchases I'm seeing on my FL. Basically, it seems worth warning people off from this.
I wanted to, erm, not hate this game, shall we say... but...
It really is quite terrible. Despite being a very fast typer, I have trouble mustering the typing energy to even elucidate why.
Perhaps that's because I am afraid of spending more effort writing a review than it takes to make a game as simplistic and terribly flawed as this.
In that sense, I speak as a programmer and a connoisseur of typing games.
So, I'll just quickly list out a bunch of the problems here:
There's (almost) nothing here for fast typers like myself. The game just doesn't scale. Doesn't show enough words on the screen at once (except the stream mode, which, due to its lateral movement, is too hard to visually follow; Lines mode is ok, and maybe projectiles mode in multiplayer, but that's about it).
The whole concept of multiplayer as executed here is fatally flawed. The only way this would ever be remotely fun is if the two players were almost exactly matched, and how likely is that? Not very, considering the huge range of typing ability that exists. The game tries to inject other elements besides just typing speed, but doesn't really succeed, imo. It's just awkward.
The "matchmaking" doesn't even exist as far as I can tell in the modern sense of the word. I think what the dev meant by this is... a server list. Yeah, a server list. But, even on launch day when steam stats say ~70 people are playing, I couldn't find any open games. It also supports direct IP, but then you'd have to fiddle with ports. From what I read on the forums, it sounds like you have to fiddle with ports to even get the non-direct "matchmaking" to work. There's no instructions on that, and maybe I'm wrong, but, whatever.
You can play against AI, but the AI just types words randomly at an EXACT speed. That kind of makes sense, but it's just not fun, especially since, at least for faster typers, their performance against AI especially will be down mostly due their ability to recognize words quickly after they appear (the AI starts typing immediately with no delay), and to not get tripped up by "weird" words that the game throws at you.
Similarly to "matchmaking", yes, the game has steam leaderboards, but they're, erm, silly, shall we say. Mostly they just track number of games won, which isn't well correlated with skill or anything. Then there's other stuff like a leaderboard for the highest difficulty AI opponent won, but that's just a multiplication of the two variables you can set for the AI, and there's pretty cheesy ways for even inexperienced typers to win against the hardest setting, so that, too, is awfully silly and pointless.
There's a variety of other more specific flaws like not being able to cancel out of typing a word you accidentally started - sometimes it's even hard to quickly figure out which word that is since you weren't already looking at it. The lines mode, one of the more interesting ones, has screwy graphics that make words hard to see quickly, which is again, a must for fast typers, if nothing else.
The word list is... bizarre. You are given a lot of very weird, obscure words, and lots of random proper nouns, and... roman numerals. It seems to randomly choose between categories of words, so a large proportion end up being proper nouns, and a surprisingly large percentage seem to be roman numerals... how did that ever seem to be a good idea?
There are, of course, no real graphics to speak of.
On the positive side, it's cool that the menus can also be operated via typing (though not entirely original), and the overall feel of the typing is slick and responsive. The general concept is interesting, but interesting ultimately doesn't matter if the execution is inadequate.
So, sure, this is kind of an original idea (at least, I'm not aware of another game that has this kind of direct, mano a mano typing gameplay), but who would this appeal to?
Well, I guess it just might be sort of fun for two friends that don't type very fast and happen to type at very similar rates - so I guess if you fall into that narrow category, then go for it, but otherwise steer clear.
Or, you can try it for less than 2 hours and see for yourself and then just grab a refund like I'm about to. EDIT: or, you can find the free version around elsewhere (I think it's the same except for the server list feature).
There plenty of better/good/decent alternatives for typing games out there. Even if you've played them all and are desperate for variety, this is unlikely to satisfy you in any way. For example, choose Epistory for a generally nice, well rounded typing game on Steam, or Typer Shark for a more simplistic yet challenging typing experience. For a real time competitive game, try Serpentine online (basically a Tangleword/boggle clone), or hi-games for pure, real time typing speed matchups.

I like the game a lot, it has a fair to wide variety of dragons/weapons you may choose from. Each dragon/weapons has its own unique attacks, however, I will complain that I don't feel certain dragons/weapons are balanced out in a fair way. The game has 4 different maps, and a voting system for which map you would like next after a 25-30 minutes time period. Some maps seems to be a bit laggy, and the servers are down (for multiplayer) sometimes, which can be frustrating, but it's a pleasure to play versus your friends, rivals, and even enemies. Runes also make this game interesting, allowing your dragon to gain small buffs that overall make a huge impact the more you level up in battle. This adds a nice complexity to the game, allowing you to easily twist and turn past a few of your dragon's/weapon's weaknesses, or to allow you to try and make it slightly less of a weakness. The rating system is a nice feature, making so you don't play against newer players, adding challenge, but also making it so that they don't get creamed and can learn a few steps at a time of how the game works.
While the game is no longer in developement, I think it'd be nice if it was.
One last thing, it would be nice to have a way to gain more crystals (the currency in the game) other than buying the titan pass, which gives you 4x crystals, but only for 1 year. I think making it so you can gain crystals in a faster manner (with either the titan pass's 4x crystals no longer working or if you can't/haven't gotten the titan pass). I've heard complaints about not getting very many crystals after a match, making it so you must grind (which is very annoying) Singleplayer or Multiplayer. With the game no longer in developement and the fact it has "died" a quite a bit, people think the $25 for the titan pass is no longer worth it.
I do really enjoy this game though, and I myself don't want to give up on it. Hope the devs decide to go back to it and give it a little more love  <3

BLUF:  This is an early access title with some bugs, an excellent foundation and tremendous potential.
Overall, this is an interesting, in depth look at airport aviation management.  There are very obvious places where this game will grow to expand upon it's current concepts.  With its alpha release, AirportCEO has been immediately updated multiple times to address multiple expected alpha bugs, most of which can be resolved with a save/load.  The game does lack expansive replayability as an airport franchise can't be explanded outside of one save.  My #1 improvement would be to add an overarching 'grant' system that gave players long term goals to help shape and reward airport development in addition to the tutorial system.  Beyond that, being able to 'sell' your airport and start a new one with greater funds would foster rewarding replayability.
Pros:
-In depth look at airport management
-stable alpha (contradictory, I know)
-rich in aviation detail
-a strong foundation on which to build
-active devs
Cons:
-alpha bugs
-early end game/minimal replayability
-steep learning curve lacking adequate tutorials/guides

Few other games can compete with Final Fantasy VII's epic story. You will fall in love with the characters and be fascinated with every facet of the game's perplexing story. The mysterious and vague philosophy written in allows the story to be interpreted by the player while still maintaining a strong plot. especially the tear-jerking plot twist at the end of Part 1. The game's charm makes you want to explore every corner of Gaia, discovering every character, limit break, and materia. The active battle system and materia system set new precedents for how RPGs should be played and allow versatility and customizability on a whole new level. Although the graphics now look cute and simple, this game has held up in every other aspect for almost twenty years now. While some argue Final Fantasy VI is the best, no other Final Fantasy game has touched the hearts of gamers as much as this one. Final Fantasy VII was a masterpiece when it released in 1997 and still is today. Desperately await the remake but make sure to pick this one up first.

Stellaris starts strong, putting you in charge of a pre-made race that populates the new game screen, or more interestingly, one of the many combinations that can be made to make your own unique race or variety of human, with various traits and ethics and bonuses from government forms.
The early-game is very much exploration and colonisation, with a variety of alien life not of another empire and the various event mechanics put to good use in anomalies that pop up as you survey. There are others that occur, tied to your colonies either through the previous anomalies discovering something or their own, seperate unique chains. Anomalies can range from everything to a resource or research boon, either on the planet or to your stockpile, to out-right changing some world's biosphere's or sending you to discover the secrets of a precursor race, something full of lore that kept my attention through many ingame decades.
The tech tree is "randomized" with a "card" system that draws 3, or more depending on certain techs or government types, cards, allowing you to choose from a selection of techs. You'll eventually see most of the techs - but some are tied to certain ethics and will never be seen whilst playing an opposing one, while others are rare and can take many a shuffle to re-appear. The tech tree also continues beyond actual techs, to minimally rewarding "buff" statistics. This system is a good compromise between meaningless stat buffs, a randomized tech tree, and a straight up "plow through this in the most efficient way possible". The tech system as such gets a solid thumbs up from me, but others may get frustrated by the random nature of it. This is complimented by a debris system where destroyed ships and stations add techs - don't forget to scroll the tech cards to see!
The mid-game is where Stellaris begins to lose some of its glamour. The galaxy fills with empires and many a time, you're cut off from exploring. There are still a few events, typically colony ones, here and there, but it becomes a period of saturising your own territory and often war for wars own sake. Personally, I like to fill this time with uplifting - a process of technological enlightenment for some of the planets in the galaxy that start with their own, pre-ftl  or spaceflight civilizations (how cool is that?!) and a few rare worlds with pre-sentient races that require genetic modification. This part of the game is particularly weak, and some of the flaws in the systems meant to ease micromanagement falter.
The late-game becomes a traditional game of jockeying for power, with wars now serving a purpose of dealing with real rivals and threats that the mid-game doesn't quite seem to give. Most importantly, the true end-game crises begin in 2 flavours. The game has 3 end-game crises, that I won't spoil, that really shake things up, providing they don't stall out against a Fallen Empire - the other "end game". The end-game crises can wipe out old rivals and new friends alike. Don't underestimate them if they end up on your door and you're not prepared. Sadly due to the Fallen Empire mechanics currently crises can suffer if forced to push through one of these.
Fallen Empire's constitute the other, ever-present problem. Coming in four varities with differing views on the galaxy, each knowable by hovering over their "attitude type" in the diplomacy screen and from experience of them telling you exactly what they dont like - typically followed by the hammer. They exist from the start of the game and represent the apex of technology, though they have the full tech tree researched, they don't research any further than that. Provided you don't evoke their wrath, build up and take them on for valuable worlds and, if you're lagging behind in tech but adept at strategy and tactics, scanning their debris can offer you a leg up.
At this point, the galaxy is what you make of it and imagination and roleplay help. Stellaris features victory screens, but seem to be largely pointless.
There are lots of little things and systems inside the game I havn't touched upon here that I would encourage you to seek out and enjoy, particularly special systems that spawn, systems such as slavery and, of course, genocide, though you know, be nice! Even with all my time in the game, I'm still uncovering new things and experiencing new events and new emergent stories.
Also, you can have an actual Earth with the proper texture, what's not to love? Oh, and if you're aliens.. Sol is out there somewhere!

Pros:
-A Strong Start, with fun customization leading to your own, unique characterization, particularly as you explore and pull back the veil.
-Damn pretty for a Clausewitz game. Most of the game is wonderful to look at.
-Lots of little touches and in particular some of the events and anomalies add atmosphere
-Fallen Empire's offer a unique twist to the galaxy
-Tech and debris offer an enjoyable overall system
-You can build robots and give them rights.
-End-Game Crises shake up the late-game galaxy.
-A fantastic emergent storyline that arises out of these systems can lead to great ~roleplay~ if you care for that.
-Multiplayer is incredibly stable.
-Game is stable in general.
-Moddability.
Cons:
-Sector AI is wonky and the AI in general can be wonky.
-Galaxy can become static, though this is largely due to the game seeming to love to fill it with pacifists, a minor deviation from this pacifists for all makes things much more violent - and even pacifists go to war. It's a problem I've not noticed but one I know occurs.
-AI is slow to expand. It doesn't weight certain colony techs as high as a player would and consequently takes it's time. It will, however, do so en masse in time.
-A few minor localization bugs and one rather moderate multiplayer bug I've found, though it doesn't affect stability.
-Combat a little wonky and brawly.
-Slaves can't currently rebel, making this broken if you min-max that route.
-----
I've mentioned a few of the flaws in this as we've gone through. Critically, mid-game suffers from not being fleshed out as the early game, nor with the threats posed in the late game. This is being somewhat addressed by the upcoming 1.1 patch, and should be treated accordingly.
Some say the universe feels a little lifeless without civilian traffic and such - this is hopefully being made an addition in 1.3, but is not "critical".
The 1.1 patch will also address a number of small AI issues, and larger ones related to sector management. Personally, I've noted lots of minor niggling flaws that I essentially could argue as being "inefficient" - and so I just let the sector AI do what it wants, but understand the problems others have.
One major stumbling block is currently how end-game crises are treated as "wildlife" and not at war with AI empires, allowing things such as the "at peace" fallen empire fleet respawn to occur, thus preventing the crises from knocking them out, as well as how the AI empires in general only react to the end-game crises assaults if they are actively threatening important worlds. This is hopefully being fixed, for the latter, in 1.1.
The mid-game slump is also due to be addressed by the 1.2 patch, with further flavour and life added in 1.3 - you may wish to hold off on your purchase till 1.1, if not 1.2.
Stellaris is a solid game, and despite its flaws and small bugs, though sometimes numerous, are all easily redeemable. Critically, none of the problems seem to be with the core mechanics and more with execution and the always tempermental AI.
Currently, a lot of mods address issues and add new gameplay. This is a blessing for the moddability and future of the game - but also a remark on how some dislike the combat, so go in with eyes wide open.
This is easily a recommendable purchase, but for those who want a "cleaner" experience I do advise waiting until 1.2. 1.1 if you can forgive a slower mid-game.

F.E.A.R., lembro que joguei ele em 2005 qdo foi lançado mas não cheguei a terminar. Tinha achado legal pacaraio, mas com cenários meio repetitivos. Resolvi tirar a poeira do jogo e ir até o final e ver se minha visão do jogo mudava.
Ao contrário de jogos como Doom 3 e Half-Life 2, graficamente o jogo não envelheceu bem. A engine não é legal. Deus Ex 1 com Unreal Engine envelheceu melhor, e a sensação é que FEAR foi lançado em 2003, ou algo assim. Sombras duras e ambientes escuros demais te forçam a usar uma lanterna que ilumina só a curta distância. Sons ambientes são processados de forma estranha também, e o jogo no geral é bem silencioso.
Na época ele competiu com Quake 4 e a grande vantagem dele, q deu toda a atenção, foi a Inteligencia Artificial. Ela é♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ela faz bom uso do level design q em áreas de batalha possuem mais de um caminho, te deixando tenso sobre onde olhar, te forçando a jogar de forma mais tática. A IA é capaz de te flanquaer, pular catwalks, parapeitos e até janelas quebradas, usar cover e lean pra se proteger dos seus tiros enquanto atira, e as vezes só colocar o braço pra fora da cobertura pra atirar.♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ainda to pra ver IA melhor em jogos FPS.
Combate é dificil e você toma muito dano com pouco tiro, e o jogo equilibra colocando sempre muito medkit e armor em locais de combate. Isso meio que quebra a surpresa de certos combates pq vc passa numa área com esses itens e sabe q a coisa vai ficar preta. Eu preferiria que o jogo tivesse equilibrado melhor os danos e colocado menos medkit. Por outro lado, quando você passa de um combate e não precisa usar medkit nem repor seu armor você se sente♥♥♥♥♥♥e q sua tática foi boa.
A história é interessante e ao mesmo tempo não. Eu não curto o quase plágio do filme O Chamado (q eu curto bastante) com a história da menina, mas no final das contas ela até q se desenvolve de forma interessante apesar de bem previsível. O jogo te dá uns sustos legítimos, principalmente nas expansões. Acho que tomei mais susto aqui do que no Outlast.
Level Design é bom, o q ajuda a IA a funcionar, pois áreas de combate geralmente tem dois caminhos. Mas o cenário se repete muito. Você passa muito tempo dentro de um prédio onde é tudo muito igual. Corredores, escritórios, copas, mais corredores, escritórios... Sem muita variedade. Nas expansões isso melhora muito.
Sobre as expansões: a primeira, Extraction Point, é continuação direta do jogo original, acaba sendo um pouco mais do mesmo, e prolonga um pouco a história do jogo que é meio curto. Foram 8hs pra terminar o original e mais 5 pra terminar a primeira expansão.
A segunda, Perseus Mandate, é bem melhor e na minha opinião obrigatória jogar se você curte o jogo. É uma história paralela muito bem encaixada com o original, mostrando eventos sobre outro angulo. As vezes lembra um pouco Half-Life, q ele se esforça pra ser, mas não chega a tanto. Foram mais 8hs de jogo que valeram muito a pena. Além dos cenários variados, eles melhoraram um pouco o engine com o lance das sombras cruas, e aqui os ambientes são um pouco mais claros e a sombras mais suaves.
Se você curte FPS e tiver o jogo empoeirado e não tiver terminado ainda, jogue, com as expansões. Se jogou o jogo original, jogue as expansões, pelo menos o Perseus Mandate.

Dust: An Elysian Tale is one of the best side scrolling action platformer out there! It features a great story, some rpg elements and some metroidvania style upgrades! You control Dust on his quest to find who he is and you are accompanied by 2 quite colorful characters, the blade of Ahrah, a sentient artifact sword that has a serious and mentor-like character and that you use for combat, and Fidget, the guardian of the sword and a comical character overall, she will make you giggle quite many times!
Firsts things first! The visuals are marvelously pleasing, an eye candy of sorts! The animations for both Dust and the enemies feel fluid and clean making combat a good feature instead of a filler through the story parts. The sounds and music as well as voice acting are right on point making the game an even greater gaming experience. To add to that the story is really compelling as you will find yourself, quite many times, in a spot where you will want to play just a bit more to uncover the next part. To add to that it’s the type of the game where I didn’t want to finish, as the gameplay, along with the story left me with a void when I finished it.
The main features of the game is its combat and exploration. The combat can be as easy or as demanding as you like, as the games difficulty affects this aspect only. Easy difficulty will result in enemies dying easily and doing less damage as well as you healing at check points, while higher difficulties can result in certain enemies being able to kill you if you don’t counter at the right time. Generally you have your base attacks and combos that you can do with Ahrah, and with Fidgets help you can unleash a powerful duststorm that will serve as your aoe attack. Small and normal sized enemies, besides bosses, do not require any special approach. However bigger enemies, like rock giants and trolls, can be a threat! Shield wielding enemies are immune to frontal attacks and since they will always face you, you need to counter their attack in order to stun them. While stunned all enemies take a lot more damage, so countering does feel rewarding no matter the enemy!  If you want that extra satisfaction from this game, I recommend higher difficulties for your first playthrough.
As you progress the game you will earn experience and upgrades for your skills. Experience is gained from completing quests, main or side, talking to characters and by killing enemies. Additionally while you kill enemies you can chain hit them, resulting in a combo meter, after the combat ends you will get additional experience depending your combo meter! Each level up will give you a stat point that you can use to increase 1 out of 4 base stats. Attack, Defense, Health and Fidged (yes she is actually a stat too!). The first 3 are obvious to what they offer, Fidget on the other hand increases the potency of your aoe, the duststorm. Personally this was my favored stat as I used duststorm a lot and because you will find gear that sadly overshadows the increase one skill point adds to that stat.  Also as you venture the lands of Elysium you will encounter certain shrines that will either augment a skill or give you a new one, skills like sliding or climbing are in this category. Finally after each major boss you will get an upgrade for duststorm, giving Fidged a new element for it! The cool part of this system is that you get to visit older areas, that were previously had an exit out of reach, to find secrets or easter eggs and the challenges! The challenges are hidden rooms with speedrun courses. You do not have to ace them to get the reward but if you like the challenge you can try get those 4 stars! All these are marked to your map, so you can see each areas completion and where is something hidden, the twist is, that besides that info, you do not have detailed map of each area, so you need to explore it yourself!
The controls are easy to grasp and fully customizable, keyboard or controller. Having tried both I did not find a more favorable, it depends on your playstyle!
The only negative of the game is its crafting feature. Throughout the game you will find blueprints for gear that once you gather the materials required you cab craft. However quite many times the vendor offered the best version for a slot or even after making a good gear for a slot, inferior gear and blueprints dropped. Generally I did not get to use the crafting system that much since I rarely got an actual upgrade.
Overall, Dust: An Elysian Tale is a great game, and a game that definitely is worthy of its price! I recommend it with my eyes closed!

Isn't as addictively fun as Red Alert 2 and Yuri's Revenge, but, you know what? It's still fun, and it's different enough from other CnC games (in a good way, unlike CnC 4) to stand out on it's own. Like, there's a pretty interesting balance between naval and ground combat that doesn't make either feel like an afterthought, and the campaigns, while campy with pointless fanservice and mindnumbing writing, offer diverse scenarios.
Now, one thing I really hate, it has lots of unnecesseary micro. Not only is the game full of hard counters so you have to order around units so they wouldn't get owned by their counters while concentrating their fire onto weakest targets, pretty much every unit has it's own gimmick special, be it a special attack or alternative fire mode, so the amount of unnecesseary micro is unberable. Red Alert 2 kept it way more simple, and if unit had several firing modes you wouldn't need to switch between them, meanwhile here it's not even Starcraft or CoH levels of micro. Worst offender is the new third faction, Empire of the Rising Sun. They have probably the most of alternative modes due to sizeable chunk of their force being transformers like a machinegun mecha that switches into a fighter and such, and you can't switch back for some time like you get with, say, Starcraft 2 vikings, so it's rather annoying.
Units in general are pretty cool, even if there are some familiar ones like Natasha Volkova not only sharing the cyborg's from Red Alert 1 name but also being pretty much Yuri's Revenge Boris crossed with GLA's Jarmen Kell. IFVs are exactly the same too, but they are light ATVs and not paper-thin armored vehicles now. Tesla Troopers, despite having an AoE paralysis alt-fire mode, are exactly the same slow knuckleheads as before. The more unique units are alsothe more bizarre ones, say soviets have APCs that instead of deploying troops fire them out of a circus cannon just to have them land with parachutes, Allies have helicopters equiped with freeze and shrink rays (the first just paralyse and weaken affected targets, meanwwhile shrink rays make units punny, squishy, squeaky-voiced but also fast), and Empire has anime schoolgirl psychics, katana infantry, obligatory mechas and even more obligatory ninjas!
Now, visuals! Units are absolutely cartoony and bright, which is forgiveable considering general tone, but Soviet aesthetics are attrocious. They have some sweet designs like Sickle, but their heavy armor and structures are butt-ugly and look more silly than threatening. Some structures even have those Kremlin towers slapped on, like in RA2. Except it worked in RA2 because red brick buildings with towers did look like Kremlin, and RA3's towered soviet buildings look like turtles with erection! One thing that's actually gorgeous is the sea, which makes sense considering you get as much naval action as ground. Oh and soundtrack is great. They had Klepacki write only the Hell March but this other composer seems to be talented, too.
Other stuff worth mentioning: there are no permament upgrades you research like in Generals or CnC3, instead you get experience points in battle that are then redeemed for special abilities and upgrades, which can be quite a game changer. Also there is co-op but to be honest considering the fact campaign isn't really difficult while playing on your own with a dim-witted AI companion, I wouldn't expect it to be a challenge for two players, plus most of the time it's just "Player 1 takes on ground forces, Player 2 takes on naval forces". Uprising standalone expansion has some actually challenging missions but ironically lacks in co-op functionality.
Overall I could recommend this even for die-hard CnC fans, unless they're not fond of dense and campy setting or hate micro, and it's definitely a must-try for anyone interested in an enjoyable and accessible RTS.

ABZU can be described as a third person short experience on sealife with some twists. In other words:
+Amazing ethereal atmosphere, that really draws you into the peacefulness of the sea
+While the graphics are not very detailed, they're innegably beautiful and full of personality; they give this game some much appreciated eye candy
+Great soundtrack by Austin Wintory, acclaimed composer whose works include the music for Flow, Journey and The Banner Saga 1 & 2; it's soothing, smooth and greatly contributes to the game's overall peaceful atmosphere
+While it isn't necessarily the focus of this game, there's also some interesting lore to piece together, and some collectibles to recover around the levels
-As for all the "experience" games like this, ABZU is extremely short. Even without hurrying too much I had completed the game and seen around 80% of what it has to offer in a handful of hours; depending on your inclination towards these games, of course, it can have replayability
-Again, this goes as a given for all the games like this: the gameplay is basic at best and a mere accessory at worst, but the controls to swim are still comfortable enough to not hinder your enjoyment of the game
While i consider ABZU a stylish, successful take on the genre from Giant Squid, i can't ignore that it could very easily be summarized as "Journey underwater" and dismissed because of it. It is extremely derivative, even if Journey isn't available on PC it's hard to ignore its impact on this niche of games. Yet, i still think ABZU is an experience worth playing through. A delicate, relaxing game that will give you a couple of hours of relax and still make you stare in awe at it several times for the sheer beauty of some scenes. A must buy if you like its genre.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of The Kings is a game which is able to devour you for days and you still won't have enough of it after finishing. The game noticeably focuses on storytelling and explicates everything to the detail so even the most curious and demanding players get their money's worth.
The famous witcher, Geralt of Rivia, lost his memory and slowly remembers what had happened. On his way he has many options what to do, how to respond or react, but still everything revolves around a mysterious slayer of the kings. This assassin might be the key to Geralt's past. Geralt's path is completed by a wide range of cutscenes which complements already thrilling story.
✪ Detailed story and background
✪ Breathtaking cutscenes
✪ High quality graphics
✪ Large scale of possibilities
✪ Elaborate 3 branch talent tree
✪ Complex background could be chaotic for new players and takes a while to understand who is who and what is going on. On the other side players can simply ignore parts which are not directly connected to Geralt.
✪ Combat system is something I personally didn't enjoy much and had a problem to cooperate with. Still it's something players get used to.

Gameplay: Gameplay was fun. Standard beat em up idea with offensive buttons. J to attack, K for special (pretty much just dust storm) and L for magic. I found this got dull kinda quick though, as you never expand your inventory of combos and soon your just playing to do as much damage as you can, flying across the screen. Still, for as simple as it was, kept me entertained for 90% of the run until they stop giving you magic upgrades. Platforming can be a bother though as there are spots in the beginning you can't reach with a lot of upgrades, and I personally don't like backtracking. Main things I feel could have made this better is the inclusion of a block button to give the player time to think how to defeat an enemy, which would be helpful for some of the enemies towards the end, and maybe a run button to make backtracking go by faster. Overall, I'd say 9/10.
Graphics: I found the art pretty good while in combat, but when you stop to actually look how Dust walks, or how the enmies move, it seems kinda unnatural and silly. But you hardely ever see this since it always feels like your fighting. Cut scenes look ok, taking a cartoonish style to them. Was uneasy with the anthropromophic choice as some characters did look weird jumping in, but it grew on me. What didn't grow on me was the lips syncing. For some reason whenever a character talks via cutscene, there mouth kinda flaps unnaturally? It's hard to explain, but it bothered me the whole way through the game, Still there are parts of this game which look gorgeous and have you take a moment to appreciate the world you are in. Overall 8/10.
Sound/Music. Oh god the music! I love tracks with some depth and length to them. Fight music gets you pumped, and the serence tracks calm you. I find it truly amazing that at times, I wasn't sure if a track repeated itself while in an area, and if I did, I didn't care. By far one of the best things about this game is the music. Sound was good all around and have no real complaints, though the companion characters voice may irritate some at first who don't like the Navi pitched voice. Overall, 10/10
Story: Story was good. Nothing super new, but I enjoyed the ride nonetheless. There are parts where its kinda predicitable, but even at those moments, it did tug on the heart strings. The lore of this world feels pretty vast, and makes me feel there could be potential succesors to this game with mention to other legendary items that are not seen. Jokes in this also keep the air light hearted and happy to balance out some of the later down feeling themes of the story. Overall 9.5/10
Final Note: This game was a blast. It lasted me 6.5 hours, and I probably could spend another 2 hours if I wanted 100%, but sadly 9 hours is the max I can see someone playing this and experiencing something new. But if you want a good single player experience that you can finish on a weekend. This game is great and would highly reccomend it, even at full price. Overall 9.5/10

First off, don't be fooled by my low amount of hours here on Steam with this game, I have done 2 playthough's when I owned it on the Xbox360.
This is a really good racing game that sits between not a full on arcade racer, but also not a full on sim racer. For me, it is a good balance between the two. I absolutely loved the first Shift and eagerly awaited this sequel. IMO, it did a good job of expanding and improving the many greats about the first one, while still managing to up the ante and introduce some new things. One of the biggest improvements individuals will notice after playing the first one is the way you upgrade the performance of the vehicles. If you've played Forza 3/4, then this type is oh so familiar to you.
There is now a much wider range of performance options instead of the tried and true Tier 1, 2, 3 formats. In this you are granted with pretty much any aspect of the car you could think of upgrading and giving them all to you off the bat, the strategy is finding that sweet spot balance of parts to give you the edge, without going over the performance rank (A, B, C, D etc.), which is what races are locked to, or going over your budget.
The physics are neither the best, nor as detailed as games like Forza or GT, but the damage and handling models are pretty stellar IMO. As I said previously this is not a full blown Simulation racer. This game is pretty deep as far as modern racers go these days so that’s good and I expect the average person to get a good solid 30+ hours out of just the single player career alone.
The AI in this game is quite comical sometimes and makes for some random comical relief. I normally play all my racing games in the highest of difficulty and even on "Hard" you will sometimes not too uncommonly see an AI opponent going full throttle in a straightaway and not even brake for the oncoming turn, leaving him careening off the track and slamming into the wall at high speeds leaving an explosion of parts and glass flying everywhere, or slamming into you or another AI opponents read end at full throttle, causing them (or you) to make like a space shuttle into the barricade. Sometime's I think they program to AI to do such nonsense to show off the physics engine haha!
However, this is nowhere near a perfect racer by any means and comes with its laundry list of faults that is for sure. Some of the most annoying are: The randomly crazy handling, grazing another driver often leaves you defying the laws of physics, by careening you off the map or putting you into an uncontrollable spin even tapping an opponent in the right spot at relatively slow speeds and at times wired input lag. This also happens just grazing a wall or similar object, which will leaving you scratching your head at how just barely scraping the wall at 40 MPH, sends you into a uncontrollable 1080 degree(3 rotations) spin...
Aside from that, the drifting in this game is absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ no thanks to some of the issues mentioned above and thankfully you can just skip that portion of the game entirely, other than the tutorial you are forced to do. Shift 2 still suffers from the dumbed down money system where after a few levels you have more money then you know what to do with and can max out every car you buy with ease, this kills some of the "I worked for this" feeling, or struggling to get that next little upgrade to give you more of an edge.
Shift 2 no longer has that "Obviously best car in the class" problem that was in the first Shift where there was that one car that was leaps and bounds better than the rest of the cars in that class as far as performance went. With the addition of a horde of new cars, quantity of cars and classes and the Performance Index system, there is now a whole new level of strategy in picking and choosing the best cars and parts to suit your gameplay, while still staying in the Performance Index rating.
In the end this is a decent console port with everything else being truly satisfying. Good deep racing scene with multiple disciplines, sometimes seemingly endless amounts of races, character leveling system, good customization esp. for performance parts and The graphics which I know most put a lot of emphasis on are decent, not as good as say Grid 2 etc., but still good eye candy in Ultra settings.

I did not play a lot, I do not hide it. Yet I feel like I have played enough to give my impressions on this game.
What I noticed first was graphical issues. Some textures seem to me missing whatever quality / resolution I am using. Maybe this will be fixed later, maybe this did not happen to other people, but on my side it does. This isn't game breaking but it did not gave me a good feeling at first, I'm afraid.
Looking at the different solo missions available, it is quite obvious that dragons and titans is about playing it again, again, and again. Playing a few memorable missions is something I would like to do, but, please, don't make us play 15 times the 10 missions of every act. This does not make me want to keep going. Sure, there are rewards awaiting you if you are patient enough to accomplish this, but I don't feel like it is worth it.
The controls are pretty okay to me. Right click to move, left click to attack. It has auto aiming so you can move around and attempt dodging fireballs and stuff while breathing stuff at others. Every playable character has its regular attack, different from the others, and its active skill. You can equip a weapon to gain two more active skills. Gold isn't used to buy stuff but when returning it to your team's horde you get experience points.  I liked things being this way : simple, allowing you to play right off the bat without wasting your time setting up the perfect build.
I'm coming back to the farming / grinding thing : everything can be bought at once with the titan pass as well as the next year's new weapons and mounts (I have no idea is this is still worth it from now on... I don't know how fast things are being added) or one by one with real money. And, god, this is expensive if you don't take the titan pass. Or you can grind, and grind, and grind to get enough gems (the in-game currency) to buy a pack of three mounts that can be mounts you already possess ! You apparently can upgrade them if you have x times the same tier of a mount's type but I still did not went to this point.
There is an annoying "bug" where there is an "attention" pop-up seemingly wanting to tell me something... But it is empty and there is no way to get rid of it, forcing me to quit and relaunch the game. This is pretty annoying when this always happens after around 20, 25 minutes of gameplay.
To sum it up : a pretty easy MOBA to get in with little work to put in builds. If you want to get new stuff, buy it or grind a lot. Since it's free to play, giving it a try will not hurt anyone. I just hope you won't get the few annoying things I got while playing.
I am recommending this to people who know nothing about MOBAs and would like to know the very basics of what it is. I find LoL and Dota2 quite harder to get at first so this game might be a good start.
Cheers !

Now, this is a 2 dollar game, so while i do make some allowances in regards to it's "minimal" graphics, i still find the game to be a barren landscape of...words. But thankfully, the game has words and typing aplenty in a pretty decent multiplayer as well as a surprisingly good Ai with a reasonable set of customization options considering it's price.
The various game modes work to lesser or greater extents, but all of them do full fill a different take on the whole "type words faster than your opponent" thing.
It's fully a niche title and it's full game play is visible from the get to, and while it does have some strategic components to it, it still boils down to "type faster than player 2"... which is fine.
for the price, it's hard not to recommend the title if you, in any way, are interested in some scrabble on steroids.

Summary:
Positives, negatives, and in the middle of the two:
+ A few new maps, some from the community.

+ New currency system. This is one of the few good ideas they had to be honest.
+ Gear is phsyical. Equip it and it shows. You can make it invisible if you want, you just need to buy the ridiculously cheap invisible armor from the tavern keeper.
+ Ability to dye items. This is good since you can make the weapon fit with your overall look.

+ Physical dye. Work towards making your character unique!
+ All classes and characters unlocked. Well that's nice. Another good idea.
- No steam workshop for mods. Just microtransaction ideas for items people submit. Sad thing? No one submits anything. That's . . . Just sad. Why did they think people would help with this if they hate it so much?
- No local multiplayer with a controler, and a rather dumbed down singleplayer thats nearly impossible.
- Microtransactions for emotes and hats. I think this is a slap to the face since they wanted it to be like TF2 or any other social game we see with a vanity system.
- Difficult to level. Extremely slow leveling speed.
- Level 60 cap.
- Gear is divided into levels of 8. Honestly, did they REALLY just think that was a feature that was a good idea? Now it's even HARDER to get past the easy maps. It's now nearly a REQUIREMENT to jump on a survival game built by a high level. God.
- Skins are all unlocked at the beginning. All of them. Even ones that were unlocked by getting an achievment.
- Pets given at the start include the cube everyone used as advanced currency before . . . Big slap to the face again. It stings that none of the starting pets can be upgraded or even be useful.
- Very low enchantment/upgrade limit. 16 upgrades max?! That's insanely dumbed down, making it EVEN MORE IMPOSSIBLE for new players! Now they can't upgrade their low level gear with the gold they EARN.
- No more minion units. ♥♥♥♥ing. Genius. I mean, theres no real reason we needed those, right?
= New system that involves the requirement to have played that map or unlocked it in order to play a server with it.
Now the rant. Oh boy.:
. . . Why did I think this game was good when I was playing it, is the question. I mean, I played it because it's DD and I can't afford every single DLC and content pack for the original. I hoped this was going to be the same or at least like it, but it turned out I'm not the only one upset that it's entirely different. Oh no, it turns out, everyone agrees. It's sad to see that 'Mixed' score on DDE, then look at DD1+DD2, and see 'Very Positive' on both. Just utterly sad; the people who remade DD were probably entirely different devs than the people who made it. Otherwise, the qaulity check is long overdue and Trendy needs to try to seriously reconsider the 'rebalanced' idea.

The video game Little Inferno is quite simple and self explanatory. It is easily manageable by almost anyone. Especially to those whom do not consider themselves to be great gamers, and or don’t have much experience with video games, much like myself. Although, I did find the game to be accessed with simplicity, it was not until I figured out what my actual goal in the game was. In the beginning I found myself overwhelmed and confused. I could not figure out if I’d move forward from the place I had been stuck at for hours. Once I actually figured what I was doing I actually enjoyed the game it was a bit of a challenge. The purpose is to create combos and accomplish finding all ninety-nine of them until the player can finally conquer the game. What I loved most throughout playing the game were the sound effects each time I accomplished to create a combo. It was like I had a tiny cheerleader rooting for me on the side. Yet, what I would’ve appreciated more from the game would be better graphics. It appears to me that the icons where designed for infants which made it uninteresting at some points for me as the player. Overall, I rate this game a 7/10. I probably wouldn’t play this game a second time, but it is something that I think my younger nieces and cousins would definitely be entertained by and enjoy.

I don't like to really comment much on other peoples' reviews... however, what are people moaning about?
This game has been realeased as Early Access... I can't understand why people are moaning that the game has bugs, etc!!! It's an Early Acess release for crying outloud... it's supposed to be incomplete.
Now to the actual review...
This game is simply great!
So great that even though you may find it frustrating at start by the minimal guides/instructions given... but once you start building and playing you will understand that it is actually part of the fun of it all.
If the game was simply easy then it would just be boring.
Plus, the Developers have been doing a great job of tackling peoples suggestions and most of all whenever someone points out a 'bug' they will work on it as fast as you blink and before you know it a new alpha version has been released tackling all the issues brought to light thus far.
Yes, building isn't easy and as intuitive as one would personally like it to be. But if you allow yourself to have a laugh by doing mistakes and trying to correct them and by engaging with the discussions and the Devs then you will quickly find yourself addicted to Airport CEO before you can say a word.
Currently you can either follow the regular path and start a campaign style mode to the game with a few difficulty levels setting to choose from.
Or, if you are like me and like to Sandbox it... then you will have an absolutely huge canvas to work with.
Building is fun... from every small detail like zoning, getting taxiways together, etc. But wait until you start getting into the management aspects of the game and it will really blow your mind.
From hiring, firing, getting contracts and managing them, the flight scheules, the shops and cafes... so much to play and dwelve into that you will spend hours laughing just as quickly as shouting outloud at yourslef for the latest mistake you've managed to make!
Even though, at this stage of the game release, I am still experiencing sound issues, difficulties getting the baggage systems to work perfectly, the luggage onload and offload as well as understanding some other mechanics of the game... I have had almost 20 hours of absolute addictive fun with this game and just can't seem to turn it off (unless when I really have to).
So yes, at this stage this is my review and perhaps I will have to edit it later... but for now and the way the game is currently at, I would have to say 'BIG THUMBS UP'.
Thanks to the Devs for the amazing hard work :)

Pros: Story, Gameplay, Graphics, Sound, Controls
Cons: Horror, Repetitive, Multiplayer
Though a bit telegraphed, F.E.A.R. does have an interesting narrative to unravel.  Gameplay is solid; enemy AI is much better than most shooters nearly a decade later.  Most modern systems can handle the game at maximum graphical settings, an often overlooked advantage.  The sound and voice acting is excellent.  Controls are good but not quite thoroughly refined (e.g. no hold-down aim).
Unfortunately, F.E.A.R. is not particularly frightening, especially to someone wanting to be scared.  The gameplay and environments become a bit repetitive after some time.  Finally, multiplayer has long since shut down.
Overall, F.E.A.R. manages to create a little fear without abusing jump scares or monster closets.

So what have I learned regarding the vast reaches of space.
Boring... black, empty, desolate, void of any interesting features. Perhaps this is somewhat realistic... after all, from a personal stand point, I do not believe there are other habital systems outside of ours. The odds appear against it.
But this is my universe, and I want something in it other than endless black empty circles interspersed with resources I will probably never use as I can't find enough habital systems to make it worth my while.
And anolmalies... they live up to their name. Finding one is a truly anamolous experience for they are few and far between.
And this is on max abundant settings, can't even imagine what other settings might bring.
These are fixable problems, mere balancing issues. Along with, for example, the numerous text oversights such as mercenaries whose values have obviously been changed, but whose script has not caught up so you really can only guess at the true value of mercernary ships.
On the other hand, does such poor attention to detail portend favorably for a future where the game has been so completely overhauled it is no longer recognizable.  Stardock has a wonderful history of breaking their games. Fallen Enchantress was at one time a favorite of mine before patches and overhauls made the game litterally unplayable. Could this new direction eventually pan out... maybe... some folks seem to like the new citizen system, but I find a dull bit of busy work that adds little to the game. Personally I liked the sliders... made my economy easy to control so that I was left with the freedom to attend other details... such as interacting with what was then a vibrant universe. When I get a new citizen I care nothing about him. He/she/it is little more than a place holder for some buff of some sort, nor do these so called citizens have any distinguishing characteristics other than names and an arbitrary gender. More over, tying them to  a ten turn generation rather than population growth is an arbitrary and curious decision. I could have just as many of these 'citizens' rather I remained on my original planet (probably not a bad option considering how empty the universe is) or expanded to the far reaches of space.
In short, this expansion is poorly tested and implemented. Could there be an eventual game here? Perhaps... Unfortuanately Stardock has shown itself adept at breaking more than they fix. Time will tell. Until then there are better places for your gaming dollars...

Spent a lot of my time on this game, so I think I am eglible for a review...
This game was first released for playing only through Facebook, and those were the days the game actually shined. There was a (relatively) decent amount of players of all kinds and from all around the world, and also updates were applied on a daily basis... It was easy to lose your entire day to playing Dragons And Titans.
After about a year after it came out, Wyrmbyte made a Facebook > Steam transfer which seemed like a happy deal for a lot of enthusiastic players, but also made the Facebook version less and less playable, gradually. In the first days of the Steam version there was a lot of lag since they didn't separate players on Facebook from the ones on Steam, but that wasn't as much of a problem as the Facebook version being unplayable.
That said, the playerbase halved, since a lot of players were only people who enjoyed quickly logging into Facebook and having a quick game before going to work/school/lunch/...funeral?, and didn't have the time or will to go through the hassle of installing the Steam version.
After a year of basically Steam-only DnT, the playerbase started to shrink even more.
Since there was a lot of raging and reporting other players (clear example of a MOBA community huh?), the devs of the game decided to try and make the 10yr olds playing happy:
- basically added aimbot, removed any skill required
- removed map selection
- allowed more than one number of same dragon or weapon selected in the same team
- removed microtransactions and added a macro (some would think that'd be good but oh boy how wrong those would be! Christ it's supposed to be a F2p, and with unlocking EVERYTHING for the buyers for a year, while also making them earn 4X THE XP AND CRYSTALS (currency) it doesn't really thrive to remain f2p friendly.) The macrotransaction also nullified all your microtransactions from before, so despite the hundreds some had spent, they had to pay 20$ to get what they already payed for.
- made buying dragons and weapons random, no possibility of picking
- started adding new dragons and weapons on almost a weekly basis, but those were just so unoriginal and you could see the uncanny resemblance not just with some features from other games, but also copies of other DnT Dragons, with changed names!!
- there was even an ARAM map which they at some point decided to make more child-appealing, so it just became ... AM (all middle)?
...
To summarize, if you're looking to play, consider this:
PROS:
- free

TL;DR: I was honestly disappointed. Following on Paradox's trend, it might be good in 3-5 DLCs, but right now, avoid. Also, I hate that they advertised it as a Grand Strategy game in space. It's a barebone 4x, at best.
Long version:
Paradox excels in Grand Strategy. Diplomacy, family, relationships and general "human" interaction. Why was almost all this removed from Stellaris? There are cookie-cutter/forgettable rulers that you allocate in charge of planets and researches. They have no life, relationships and are there to grind xp, or deleted if they have bad traits. Zero attachment.
Semi-random research tree. I hate this so much. In one of my first playthroughs, I didn't feel like getting the colony ship right away, so I got the power plant tech that needs a specific resource. After capping my planet (2-3 hours) and researching about a dozen other techs, I have yet to see the colony tech. Got trampled by a hostile empire.
Scouting is mindless. Just send your fastest ship (usually the military) in a spiral and only scan systems with habitable planets. This makes most planets pointless and a huge time sink to survey at the early game.
Anomalies are far too random. How many 5-star scientists have you lost in 1-star anomalies that you had under 5% of failing? I lost count.
AI easily exploitable. Build embassy + send two or three energy + wait 2 years = BFF.
Early game is lonely. Takes far too long to reach any workable relationships with any race.
Mid game is grindy.
Neutral enemies (clouds, crystals, etc) are even less appealing than Civ's barbarians. They don't have bases or any real reward upon defeat, aside from some % in tech advancement. Not to mention the difficulty is all over the place. Drones are too easy, crystals are impossible until mid-game. Terribly annoying if you have NPC fleets stationed in the system right next to yours, defending resources. Cripples early game.
No main quests. A standard for 4X games in the last few years is to have a storyline or quests to follow, to spice up your adventures and give you objectives when you're done allocating your pop. Here it feels too "open" (in a bad way). Here you just have minor quests for detectice sources of clouds or developing a specific tech from mining drones. It's missing the main story questline for the race, or something to do to "win" the game (reach center of galaxy and do X, discover the origin of race X, etc).

This game was my childhood. It was my first ever major RPG, and I barely knew English when it came out, and I was very young when playing it for the first time on the PlayStation. So much so that I couldn't even get past the first 15 minutes without getting stuck on a ladder.
It didn't matter though, as I've played it alongside my childhood friends and it was quite the experience, moving the game back and forth between our houses as we'd manage to crack through a certain section the other side couldn't, as time and knowledge of the language progressed, so did our progress with the game.
I consider Final Fantasy VI amongst the best in the series. The game needs no introduction. Its fast-paced, futuristic style just sucks you in as you play it, having top of the line graphics at the time, for 1997. It's almost 20 years old, and although the overworld blocky sprites of the beginning of the 3D era do look dated, it's still charming to me to this very day. The Full Motion Video cutscenes, especially in certain key points of the story, were jaw-dropping for the time and those still look great.
While I don't consider the plot of the game as ground breaking as I did when I was seven years old, I do have to say that although there are a few plot holes here and there (which the Compilation, with later spinoffs tries to fix), it's quite enthralling and curious.
I've recently been replaying this old favorite of mine, trying to see if it was simply my nostalgia glasses or if I still find this to be a good game. More importantly, if the Steam version was any good. Yes, and yes.
The Steam version has the original MIDI soundtrack from the PS1 version. There are so many good tracks in this game, and the fact that this version has the super quality soundtrack is a blessing.
There are achievements to give you some motivation if you're replaying this and actually want to show that you've beat that last optional boss, and while I haven't used them or even find a reason to, because this game is actually really easy as far as JRPGs go, cheats.
I was going to hold off on this review until I 100%'d this game, because I felt like I owed it to myself to do it, but with the recent Steam Awards, I've just had to nominate this for "The Test of Time" and decided to write this one earlier than expected. If you even want to slightly alter the difficulty or graphics, it can be modded.
If you've never played this I'd say wait for the PS4 version because that'll most likely impress you more, but for veterans like myself, have no fear, this game is exactly the same game you've enjoyed all those years ago, and I suspect will return to every now and then. It's a classic.

Stellaris is the newest, until June 6th that is, from paradox interactive that takes us to a stellar journey to space. It greets you with a splendour and invites you to explore the randomly generated galaxy for at least 50 years in the campaign when things tend to fall flat.
The early game is absolutely amazing. For a first time developing a 4x paradox nailed the exploration part of yet they failed at expansion and exploitation. The strategic  resources in the game aren’t really that important. Not to wage a war over. Mainly because the galaxies you fight in are so vast.
And for a development studio where painting maps is a real goal Stellaris can make it so tedious to wage war and the peace mechanics are engaging enough that I find myself at the opposite problem of EUIV as I don’t want to wage war.
The late game event, since 50 hours in two different campaigns that got to the end game I got the same event, are interesting but still broken since the AI won’t do anything about it themselves, the diplomatic bonuses mean that the galaxy suddenly becomes more static and the reward for beating the is mediocre at best.
Yet I played 50 hours of this game and enjoyed most of at least. When I go out I spend more and spend more time not enjoying it so I would still recommend the game. It might already be cliché to say patches will fix it but it seems it will. Paradox listens to its fans, for the most part anyways.

The game that encouraged me to pursue a career in computer graphics and software engineering.
At the beginning of the 90s John Carmack and John Romero made a press-release to inform the public of the greatest game ever made. It would be a 3D world with rooms at different altitudes, the most complex lighting in any game to date, filled with hundreds of enemies and running at a blazing fast speed. A small team of guys pulled this off and revolutionized the games industry forever. Where most entertainment is subjective in quality, DooM represented a solved problem: it is so tight in its design that you can not improve it by adding or removing anything.
Except these guys improved on the original base game with DooM 2. A ton of new enemies, the super shotty, and another 32 levels of incredile variety - from "Gotcha" to "Barrels o' Fun" DooM 2 is still engaging today in a way that most modern FPS can't hope to achieve.
If you are in the mood to shoot some bad guys, and you don't want any of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that comes with modern game design (regen health, aim down sight, cutscenes, hints, etc) DooM 2 is the cure for the itch. About 10 seconds from executable to shooting an imp in the face, DooM 2 respects your time while offering a surprising level of challenge on the hardest difficulties.
Buying this game grants you the game files and a dosbox executable to immediately start playing without any fuss. However, you can drop that DOOM2.WAD into one of hundreds of free source ports (doomsday, chocolate doom, zdoom, etc etc) to play with modernized graphics and online multiplayer. Further, you can download one of the thousands of mods (yes, including Brutal DooM) and level packs that people are still developing to this day.
"Check this box if you received this product for free". I have probably bought this game about 10 times since the original set of floppy disks. It comes in so many bundles, has been ported to so many consoles, and is wrapped with games like DooM 3 BFG. I can safely say I will be playing DooM 2 for the rest of my life.

I used to own the non-steam version and played the game quite extensively. I recently had a bit of craving for a good story driven RTS that's just a bit of silly fun so I bought the game again via G*2*A. I have just in one sitting played for about 2.5 hours straight with the new steam version I purchased. The game has a great campaign and the cut scenes are fun to watch if you don't mind some cheesy acting but I think it has been clearly done like that on purpose to give the game a B grade movie feel.
Coming back to this game nearly 5 years on I have to admit the graphics fully cranked look pretty good considering it's age. I'm also finding a lot of features that bring some quality of life to controlling the game. Setting up way points with the alt key. Attack ground to kill units not in vision, units that can be tabbed through via type when all selected at once and lastly unit abilities.
The game encourages expansion and feels fast paced a little like a more shallow version of StarCraft 2. I read some reviews about balance especially with the ERS but I have found from playing RA1,2 and 3 in the past there is always stength and weaknesses for each side and using them correctly helps immensly. I briefly checked out some of the maps and they seem fairly balanced to allow for the strenght and weaknesses of each faction.
I'm going to try and start some multiplayer with the newer C&C Online in the near future. Overall the game is great for its age and I think the game has a fairly solid campaign with fun cut scenes good variance and over the top acting which from around RA2 started becoming its distinct style.
I recommend this for a cheap story driven time sink.

Galactic Civ 2 was renowned for having some of the best AI in strategy games. That is not really saying much because good strategy game AI is really hard. One factor in that is the time it takes to really understand the AI and how it competes with the player. The end result is like Gal Civ 1, Gal Civ 2 started mediocrely and as time went on with patching and polishing, in response to player feedback, it got better and better until it reached the pinnacle of the genre.
Unsurprisingly Gal Civ 3 is much the same story. At launch and at the launch of every new major game changing DLC, everything is broken. Parts don't fit together right and the AI does dumb things that it will take days of playing to notice the impact of. The game also allows creativity on the players part to the point where new ways to cheese the AI are constantly discovered. But over time the dev's work on it, iron out the mess and at the end of each evolution, you get something that really stands out as remarkable.
You will be really hard pressed to find another strategy game where the AI tries as hard as it does to beat the player intelligently as it does in the galactic civ series... Unless a new expansion just came out, in which case it's as dumb as the rest of them. The rest of the time however, the AI makes its moves with purpose towards its end goals. It watches you and its other AI opponents and always keeps an eye on the victory conditions. Whenever someone else gets close to any of them and stealing victory from it, it collectively makes moves to intervene. 
Going for a diplomatic victory? The non-diplomatic civs will try gang up on the weakest member of your coalition and share tech and resources with each other to try to bring down your alliance piece by piece. If you are closing in on a technological victory everyone will turn and jump on you to try to stop you crossing the finish line. Your allies may be more subtle about it, simply funding and supporting the more war capable races... But no one is happy to let you seize a victory without them. Or at least that describes Galactic Civ at it's best, which is often not at.
Welcome to the modern era. Where games are funded and kept alive by regular DLC additions (paid or otherwise) and everything is constantly changing. It must be a nightmare from a dev's perspective. It's bad enough you have to fix all the ways a new piece of DLC breaks the game balance. You also have to consider every combination of the game where players are missing DLC. The only solution is a lot of playtesting and in a grand strategy game, playtesting the balance changes of a single feature takes thousands of hours. It's probably for this reason I've never seen Galactic Civ product launch without serious underlying issues that aren't immediately apparent.
There is more to it than that though. Stardock often runs open betas for their products and they pay careful attention to all the feedback and still to this day I have never seen them launch a product with the issues brought up in the beta addressed. They seem to run on a rigid schedule where they scramble to get all the critical blockers dealt with by launch day and then call it good enough and just let it loose, they can get to the rest of mess somewhere down the line and then look at all the new feedback. This means that most of the day one feedback is issues they already know, yeah yeah we'll get to it. To their credit, they WILL get to it eventually. Here on steam in the age of early access, we are used to these kind of rough launches from various indie devs and that seems to be the elephant in the room.
Despite everything Stardock, to this day, still operates much as indie devs do. They have much larger teams and budgets and thus work on much larger products. But the games still come out feeling like some garage game designer pet project rather than an AAA product because that is just how the company is run. That comes with all the hang-ups of them being too close to the product to see the flaws and the horrible "that issue is to complicated for now, just put it on the backburner to deal with later" mentality that comes with having to meet deadlines but knowing that being your passion project you will still be working on it and can come back to fix those issues once the deadlines have passed. Being one of the most well funded indie studios on the planet just means they keep slogging and working on grinding issues down at solid pace until it sparkles. That is really why I can recommend their products, it takes a while but once they get to that point, they shine.
Galactic Civ has all the love poured into it of indie title and all the resources big a studio behind it. There are a lot of speed bumps on the way but the end product is the best of it's kind. At the end of its lifespan, Galactic Civ 2 had no worthy competitor. It was the top of the class, king of the hill, hands down champion of the genre.  Galactic Civ 3 is much the same game but with everything shined up and a million quality of life improvements mixed in (all praise the mighty tooltip!) and more content sprinkled on top. It's more user friendly, new-player friendly and easy on the eyes.
The DLC is a mixed bag in terms of value for money. Some of it is just aesthetic fluff, some of it is real game changing new feature content. You really will have to go through DLC one by one yourself to decide what appeals to you to get your monies worth. The core game however is a rock solid purchase. It gives you almost endless potential to creatively play the game in a style that suits you and rising to meet your expectations of it. Just don't jump in and expect everything to go smoothly the day a new expansion is released.

Having played this previously on XBox 360, I was looking forward to this being my racing game of choice on my return to PC gaming. Whilst the graphics are nicer, everything else about this game seems so far to be inferior to the XBox version.
First of all the game refused to run via Steam, and I had to create a shortcut for the desktop and run it as administrator. OK, fair enough, that's just PC gaming.
But the real problems started once I began racing, where I found the controls (using the same 360 controller I had used on the console) to be sluggish and unresponsive, almost as if there was a delay. I've been playing the Next Car Game recently, and there the controls were snappy enough.
Where the cars in the 360 version felt like they were a part of you, in the PC version they feel remote and unconnected. Even worse, in the chase view the car appears to vibrate at times, almost like it's doing a belly dance! WTF? I needed to use the chase view because in the first person views the delay or stodginess of the controls meant that I didn't have any real idea of how the car was responding. At least in chase view the car bears some relation to the road.
I tried setting up the responsiveness in the options menu, but even with the sensitivity at 100% there wasn't enough response until the stick was fully extended, and then there was often too much. This made it almost impossible to hold the racing line, and the car veered crazily all over the place.
I'm not a newbie to racing games, but this game made me feel like a novice!
This was a real disappointment to me, and I could not in all honesty recommend the game.

Mostly this is an light exploration and journey game where you swim around, look at sea life and scenery in a sort of fantasy world, uncover a few secrets, and wrap it up in under two hours. There's a story that's told, but it's mostly through implication and not through narration, so don't expect any definitive answers. Though there are extras to find and cheevos to get, they seem almost antithetical to the spirit of the game itself. I kind of wish it had either leaned harder on the exploration aspect or cut out the "easter eggs" entirely, but that's only a mild rebuke.
Overall, I enjoyed my time with it. Bear in mind it's not a game in terms of challenge, it's more of toy or visual story than something where you worry about interaction. Though you'll ride some animals, flip some switches, and avoid some hazards, nothing gives you a game over and threats are minimal.
It's kind of what I wanted old Genesis game Ecco to be all along - a game where you explore and experience the ocean - instead the challenging sidescroller that was. While it's not a profound game, it's a nice game to relax with for about the length of a movie.
