Beware this game is not for everyone.
I give it 6/10 and here's a few interesting things about it.
The game feels like a Halo 1 mod. The locations, the power armor, the weapons, most of it's design choices. You could pretend you where playing master chief and you'd feel somewhat at home.
There's a reason for this beyond the art style. It's because many of it's game resources where lifted or “stolen” from Halo 1. I've played Halo 1 for 5 years give or take and I've really got to know the game, it's physics, it's weapons, maps, everything.
Playing Orion: Prelude I saw a warhog, then I saw the exact same animation when you get off the turret. Then I saw animations from using the melee button from guns. You also realize for a new game it sure looks like it came out in 2001 same as Halo 1.
I had no idea this game was a kickstarter, and it's a perfect example why I've never supported a kickstarter and probably never will. (including paid Early Access).
The number of things they say in the Kickstarter and it ends up just all being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Even the in game shots look nothing like this game when you play it. Just watch the video and then compare it to screen shots and videos of the actual game. They promise things like a deep lore, etc. I'm sorry this is just a Horde mode game, and a easy one at that.
The game itself is lots of mindless fun, but so many other games do everything this one does better. There is no sense of challenge, you can easily go on a mountain and shoot all the dinosaurs out of range. You have many weapons and augmentations you can buy to make turn this game into Very easy mode even on medium settings. I can't say for the higher settings.
The game does lack polish. Things like getting stuck in graphics, warping dinosaurs, unpolished animations, etc. When I said it feels like it's a Halo 1 Mod, it sure does due to it's unfinished quality.
The creators are already on their sequel so I wouldn't expect this one to be polished, they probably learn that from EA games.
In itself the game can be lots of mindless fun, but don't expect anything amazing, just like a cheap mod, it's fun to try out, but rarely better then the original.
A few annoyances;
One thing I'd like to point out, you know how in Halo 1 the sniper rifle leaves a white trail, well in this all the bigger guns seem to, so after a while you only see cloud lines and not your target so well. Then you got rain on your screen, you know the dripping water, I was never a fan of this. And in this game it's constant. There are a number of things that make it harder to see your targets but it's mostly just annoying and pointless. Especially then it's raining on your screen in third person view.
I bought this game for 1$, I would be willing to pay up to 2$ but no more. If you want a good horde mode game I'd say Killing Floor tops this hands down.
This is the type of game you have fun messing around and shooting easy targets, but you'd probably never recommend it as anything worth wile. Not♥♥♥♥♥♥ but not great.

Overall, it is an awesome game, and even better if you actually know what's going on.

While The Witcher 1 was a big first and successfull attempt to bring the world and feel of adventure of Witcher books to the video games, Witcher 2 wanted to up the quality. Tell an even better story, look better, play better... Which might've worked if not for all the issues this game had during the development, issues that are felt throught the rather messy experience The Witcher 2 is.
They did succeed in making it look better, obviously, but the look actually aged a bit worse due to the colour filtering choices and the fact that for all the looks it achieved, the world feels smaller, more cramped, more boring to look at. Not everywhere, of course, act 2 has few locations that look nice and the opening scenes can be impressive, but most of the game just looks like a mess of drab colours.
It tells the story in a more interesting way, but the story itself is less interesting. It has more nuances, it has some very exciting global implications on the game world and choices feel more natural, are provided in a more personal way. It does bring even more wit and humour from the books, it evolves the characters. And it is the very best thing about the game. Although, it seems, that in Witcher 3 most of the choices are invalidated by events out of your control anyway. Oh and if you do play for story - just go with Iorveth. While Roche path has some pretty interesting (and also mostly invalidated in TW3) choices, all of Act 2 and most of Act 3 will be extremely boring, as Roche gets the most boring locations, quests and dialogues in his path, seemingly mostly due to the fact that this path was developed last.
As for the gameplay... If you play on Normal, it's not bad. If you try the Full Combat Rebalance 2 mod it might make some things more interesting. If you play Dark mode or something like that, then don't try the FCR2 mod... Actually, just don't play Dark mode at all, or any other higher difficulty. Despite some attempts by CDP RED to make gameplay fun, gameplay is mostly pretty frustrating and is either simply not fun, or in some cases maddeningly broken. A lot of ideas, with recipies, crafting and such are just a mess (and Dark mode only "benefits" depend on those). In addition, all those small animation limitations, you encounter everywhere and things like that make The Witcher 2 to be not a particularly fun game to play.
But the story can be worth it. And was for me, twice. Just, don't expect to like anything else.

One thing that was nice about the earlier Call of Duty installments was that you had an opportunity to become familiar with your hardware (weapons and equipment), because you got to use it a lot, and in different scenarios. You tried the different weapons, discovered your favorites, and learned to acquire them and play missions your way.
Black Ops doesn’t let you do that. Through the campaign, you never have anything long enough to become familiar with it, or attached to it.
Once Call of Duty moved away from legitimate battles in the second world war, and into the realm of fiction, they felt compelled to add more story. In Black Ops’ case, I kind of wish they hadn’t. The story exists, but I never found myself caring about it or the characters. That made the mandatory, super-long cutscenes even more irritating. And the long dialogue sections right before a stealth section with no save points. After being forced to listen to the same speeches so many times, I grew resentful.
The mission objectives were also iffy. I would get stuck on some parts, fighting indefinitely, not knowing what I was supposed to do, or shoot, or run up to and “use”. I found the campaign, overall, to be tedious at best, and frustrating at worst.
Nominated for "The “Test of Time” Award" ;)

Despite the not-so-subtle acronym, F.E.A.R is actually a fairly strong title. As a Horror-style game from 2005, is it worth playing?
As a game from 2005, it may be a little dated for modern gamers. Yet, despite being old, it isn't unbearable, and sometimes it's outright good. Dynamic lighting is something even modern games lack, yet FEAR manages to make a lot of atmospheric design choices that make you overlook the actual quality of the graphics. The level design, use of shadows, and the sound all make up for a dated look.
Speaking of sound, the audio in this game is often fantastic. Bullets rip through the air, footsteps can reveal enemy positions, and the 'horror' moments of the game are made all the more tense because of the audio.
Does it work as a horror game?
Unlike a game such as Amnesia, FEAR is a horror game where you are armed and capable of defeating potential menaces, which reduces the amount of raw tension usually present in horror titles. In fact, it would be more accurate to say that it is an FPS game with horror elements, much akin to Dead Space. If you enjoyed Dead Space, FEAR is very similar, with slightly less emphasis on Sci-Fi and a little more on the modern paranormal. FEAR also crosses territories with Half-Life in terms of look, feel, and storytelling; combat is often done in narrow halls, yet they are not so constricted that something cannot sneak up behind you, or that there isn't a different angle to attack from.
The game's difficulty is also somewhat irregular, though not necessarily in a bad way. At normal difficulties, enemies are easy to rip through, but can return the pain quite well. A bad grenade, a turn taken too fast, or being snuck up on can leave a player with a third of their health gone in an instant - and that's on the normal difficulty. However, smart use of the character's "Slo-mo" power, attentiveness to surroundings, and smart use of the game's more powerful weapons (proximity grenades are excellent for covering your back and alerting you to a flank) will make the game seem easy to the point where the player will not take damage for long periods of time. Since difficulty can be changed in-game, you are free to set it to hard (or very-hard), but normal will be enough for most players.
Are there jump scares? Yes, and they will shock you into wasting your ammo, I guarantee it. However, with only one or two exceptions, most of them are harmless to the protagonist; trying to predict them just makes you more tense. Both the severity and frequency of cheap scares go down near the mid-game though, allowing players to focus on the action and the brief bits of story (though I have to admit, some of those scares were fun in retrospect).
If you want a more modern, darker Half-Life 1 and you enjoyed the kind of tension Dead Space offered, FEAR is probably right up your alley.
Ah! One more thing; there is an FPS issue for those using Logitech mice/keyboards. Go to your Device Manager and switch off anything labeled "HID-Compliant Device." Don't touch anything that doesn't say exactly that. There should be guides to help you if that's not enough. But yes, if you're wondering why your shiny new computer isn't giving you crisp FPS on a game from 2005, that's why.

Here is an example of why I will give this game some time before I play again. They haven't implemented one way roads. Shockingly fantastic. I installed it just looking for sort of a janky aging shooter to mindlessly walk through but from the very first level F.E.A.R. blew my mind.
I think this game single handedly caused my mind to divide the term FPS from Modern Military Shooter. I don’t know that I have the insight, experience or the articulation to explain it, but these older games really are different than modern shooters. And in my opinion, it was for the better. One of the very first things I noticed was how spectacular the texture work was in FEAR; some of the objects even trumped objects I’ve seen in recent AAA releases. The lighting also must have been something to behold when it first released. All the light sources in FEAR are dynamic and interact with the environment and with your character, casting shadows which enemy AI are amazingly aware of. The first time I heard a guy say “Hey! I think I saw a shadow over there!” while I was walking past a lamp in the next room, my mind literally shut down in disbelief. I actually have to play FEAR the way that I pretend I have to play MMS games and it is everything I’ve been looking for in a FPS game.
I’ve always told people I don’t like shooters. What I’ve actually meant is that I don’t like modern military shooters. FEAR has shown me that I really do love FPS, it’s just that no one does it right nowadays.

They don't call it F.E.A.R. For nothing.
(If you're too lazy to read this review, just buy the game).
FEAR is a first-person shooter game that swaps between throwing baddies with guns at you, to throwing a scary little girl and some really frightening hallucinations at you. This game made me deathly afraid of ladders for the entire playthrough, from just one hallucination early on.
Basically, the story is a little goofy and feels goofier when all the characters take it so seriously, but you are a member of the "First Encounter Assault Recon" task squad (nevermind that Assault and Recon are two entirely different things) and are assigned with bringing down a man named Paxton Fettel, who is a psychic commander to a secret clone army (I said it was goofy) and out of nowhere an evil little girl ghostie-goo is haunting you and killing people. Despite it's goofiness, the story gets better as it goes, and ends up becoming really awesome.
The gameplay is broken into segments of exploration and light puzzle solving, to crazy fun combat, and getting the poop scared out of you by the mysterious ghostie girl. The exploration and puzzles aren't really anything new, if you've played Half-Life 2 it's like that, but with none of those dumb see-saw puzzles. The scary moments are, well, scary and well done, however they begin to get a little predictable near the end of the game, but for the first 70% of the game people will disintegrate around you, you'll be teleported to different locations, and the little girl will try to kill you, and you'll be scared. Not horrified, but scared and probably asking, "What the #@^%$?," multiplie times. Where the game truly shines though is in it's combat. The combat is fast paced and brutal, and bullets tear chunks out of walls and objects and spray particles into the air. A simple office shootout becomes mayhem as dust fills the air as shrapnel flies off walls, computers explode in bright flashes of light, and paper flutters around the air as enemies hunt for any sign of you, whether it's your flashlight or a sound you make in game. And these enemies are smart, they have the best AI I've seen in a game. They constantly hunt you down, flanking and calling orders to each other, quickly detecting you if you get to close  to their field of vision, spot your flashlight, call for reinforcements. This makes it feel like you're fighting a true army of highly trained soldiers and makes the combat shine, as each individual fight will play out completely different ways each time you play. You also have a bullet-time feature which you can trigger whenever you'd like, and it turns any combat situation into the lobby scene from The Matrix. Bullets cut through the air, leaving little ripples behind them, dust slowly explodes from damaged walls as you and your enemies shoot and jump kick each other to death in slow-motion. It's incredibly fun, and gives you the killers edge you need against the intelligent AI, and also ties into the story nicely.
The game was a real blast to play through, and when things become a little too boring it introduces new things, such as hallucinations that will try and kill you, or invisible, wall climbing ninjas that will make you jump and scream and spray your bullets wildly. When these newer features get old (the ninjas never do, there were too few of them actually), the game gives you one of the best video game finales you will ever see.

It's a three way fight between Mr Sulu, Frank N Furter and the dude from Brazil and you're issuing the orders!
Westwood's legendary C&C franchise hit it's high point with this one, beginning just before the climax of Red Alert 2 the Soviets rewrite history by going back in time and eliminating Einstein (oh the anvil of irony) in order to remove the Allies' technological advantage but, in the process, birth a new superpower, the Empire of the Rising Sun, and thu the War of the Three Powers begins with a japanese invasion of the USSR.
Gampelay wise this is pretty much the same Red Alert goodness but with the extra unit/superweapon powers added to C&C3. The Red Alert series has always added more emphasis on Air/Naval power so they took the next logical step and added seaborne bases as well was making a number of units amphibious (Empire probably wins on that score with the amphibious tank though) but C&C is one of the few game series that believed in "If it ain't broke..." (at least until they did break everything in C&C4...) and Red Alert 3, for my money is the best in the franchise. However Gameplay is largely irrelevant here, the true value in this game lies in it's story and cast. It's as cheesy and stupid as hell as the previous C&C games but that is what makes this series so damn good, especially since Red Alert's lighter tone compared to the gloomy post-apocalyptic Tiberum series allows for what can only be described as bacon-ribs levels of ham acting and it is glorious and what better way to highlight the magnificence of this than getting Tim Curry to be your villain for the evening, this man and J.K. Simmons actively compete to see who can devour the most scenery as the Soviet Premier and U.S. President respectively whilst George Takei provides a subtle but still pretty cheesy performace as the Emperor of Japan. Add to this Johnathan Pryce's slightly bewildered Supreme Allied Commander and Randy Coture and you've got yourself the best cast in C&C history.
If you want a game thats just sheer pleasure and over-the-top fun but still retains a tried-and-true formula that worked right up until EA screwed it up to bury the franchise to concentrate on ten thousand unecessary sports titles then this is the game for you.
Oh, and one thing... Man-Cannons... that is all.

Dragons and Titans. Let's talk.
I saw this game, saw dragons, and thought "Well, why not try it out. It's free so let's see what it's about." And thus learned this is what a MOBA is called. For what it is, if you have no experience with any MOBAs it really is good. It's a great "Get your feet wet" kinda game. Hell, I spent over 850 hours playing it so it must be good right? Right?! Well, frankly, if there was a "neutral" button, I'd put it. If I had made my review a year ago, it'd be an absolute thumbs up reccomendation. As of now, I can't. It pains me to say it because this game is boat loads of fun. Was, I should say...
First, let's discuss how you begin: You start off with the tutorial, and afterwards get a dragon egg pack. There are like, 30 dragons and the egg packs are random. You could get x3 of the same dragon, x3 support, x3 damage, or just x3 crap dragons you suck at. It's 100% random. You can get more egg packs for 5,000 gems which are the currency in game, but it takes a while. The first egg pack you get is free. I've heard stories of people starting out with x3 support dragons which suck for a new player. But again. Random.
So, if you start out with dragons that are support or dragons that just arn't your playstyle, etc...you're going to have a tough time starting out. Did I mention 5,000 gems takes a while to get?
Sure you can buy individual dragons, with REAL money, but....do you if you JUST are trying out a game?
RNG aside, you start out now. There are 4 acts for the main storyline for single player, single player for the 4 MOBA maps, co-op vs ai, and pvp. You can only play the first act as the others are locked until you pay 20$ for the Titan Pass. I never got it. Payed for a few dragons though when they had a sale though.
Alright, now for game play. You can choose a dragon and weapon combo. Some are better than others and are overused in PvP but that's besides the point. Each dragon/weapon has two abilities, some passive, others active depending on the weapon/dragon. Traditional MOBA however.
You also have Runes which in truth are the main game changer. You have rune pages that you can customise for your game style. Each rune can be upgraded, but...RNG TIME! You need x3 t1 runes OF THE SAME to upgrade to t2, and x3 OF THE SAME t2 runes to upgrade to t3. How do you get t1 runes? A random t1 rune pack for 250 gems! And there's a super difference between a player with a rune page full of 15 t3 damage increase runes to a player with no runes, even if they have a same combo.
Oh, and each pvp match gives you about 30-100 gems on average, with 100 being the cap. Co-op gives 20-40 and single player about 10-25. So, those 5,000 needed gems start looking harder and harder to achive. Sure the Titan Pass increases your gem income per match but....20$.
Dragons are similar with you needing x3 t1 of the same dragons for t2, etc. But with random dragon egg packs....
Weapons can be fordged to be better using reagents you find in game so that's easy to do. You get more weapons for 2,500 gems...but it's a RANDOM weapon pack that you MAY easily get more of the same weapon if you're unlucky and more than one weapon is 100% useless.
But through all this it's a super fun game! It's engaging, you WANT to upgrade your dragons...you WANT to succeed for fun! So why not the reccomendation thumbs up?
Well, let's discuss why I stopped playing. Remember when I said that Runes can make or break a game? I would have a full rune page of damage runes mix with T2/T3 runes and deal so little damage it's pathetic. Then randomly, mid match (Sometimes never) I suddenly deal massive damage. With a page full of Cooldown runes, I notice my cooldown's aren't getting reduced. Then suddenly, mid match my cooldowns half they were.
My rune pages weren't always active. So, I send in a ticket like normal people and figure I'll stop playing for a while till it gets sorted out.
That was a year ago. No comments back.
Also, there were no updates to the game in over 6-7 months.
So, while it was (And is if the bugs don't kick in) a super fun game, until the bugs get worked out, I don't see much more redemption for the game.
Perhaps in due time I can update this and say it's back in business. But right now, it pains me to say...
No.

Hey to all my fella players of the realm. At the moment of writing this review I have 378 hrs of gameplay and I've been playing Paladins since patch thrity-some, so I'm a bit experienced you could say! So I'm gonna explain this in full detail and I hope you read this completely.
It goes to the very beginning when I installed Paladins, I had this issue when I press Tab (which should show all players' details) I couldn't see a few players' listed!! This becomes more annoying if you are playing as a healer who should know everything (such as loadout, legendary, etc.) about ally Front Lines who are supposed to tank against the enemy, on the other hand, if you can't see your ally/enemy listed, you won't be able to see their respawn cooldown or health bars as well! The interesting part is it's been 20 patches my friends and I have this problem but they don't bother themselves fixing it.
Time to hold your horses! It was the first problem! The second is competitive mode (It's ranked mode and way too serious). It's entirely broken! Since some players troll pick champions or go afk in mid-game, in this situation you can report that specific player. But wait a minute, does it make any difference? NO! To make sure, I started trolling like 10 matches and I'm sure at least 30 players reported me in the same day, I can confirm NOTHING happened to me, not a single warning, not a temporary ban, NOTHING! That's why every single Paladins player will tell you it's full of trash people. It's not! Support team just don't ban those who are, so you keep playing with them over and over.
It's quiet common these days... You start a competitive match and your team is about to win but suddenly you drop out to main menu like you never started a match at all! In result you won't gain any ranks. That happens when someone drops a hack which is why we call it "Drophack". This is a solid way to avoid loosing ranks for players who are about to defeat! That's beside those timings servers are overloaded and all players are lagging as hell.
That's it. I waited a long time since I decided to give negative rating, hoping devs might be concerned and try to fix them. But guess what, they added even more skins! so YAAAY :/

I am a huge fan of RTS games. I love many types of strategy games. Of all the Strategy games I habe played I would put this in the top of my list for sure. I have only been able to log in 52 hours into the game, yet I still have only scratched the surface. This game to me is a great blend of two of my favorite Strategy games. Total War and Civ.
I like how the economy is set up in the game. I think it has a good balance. What I mean by good balance is that it is not incredibly easy to have a surplus of materials, while in the same sense it is not terribly hard either. By adding the rare materials that give you a great boost in your economy was a good idea. It also adds a reason to fight over certain solar systems as well. It keeps you from just sitting back and racking up resources until late game.
The amount of content the game has is really compelling as well. There are tons of different technologies you can learn to better you planets, you defenses, your military, etc. Also there are a ton of different races and traits to choose from.
The ability to customize your own civilization is fantastic. The traits keep you balanced as well. By not allowing you to do certain things within your own goverment makes it a little more difficult when conquering other civs.
Those are a few of the reasons I think this is a great game. The only con that I personally would like to be changed is the combat. I dont feel too involved in the combat. It doesnt capture my attention. I like to be more involved in my battles like I am in Total War. I do understand not every game and its combat will be like Total War and that is fine. I would just like to be a little more involved then just click a whole fleet and watching them fight a different fleet. Maybe that could be supplemented by adding the ability to control the armies that invade planets.
Overall I think this game was worth every penny and any fan of RTS/Strategy games should play this. It is alot of fun.

In truth I wasn't sure what to expect from 'Stellaris'.
I've played RTS games such as 'Company of Heroes' and turn-based games such as the 'Civilisation' series before and somehow this game manages to merge the best of both worlds. It does this by combining the real-time (though pausable) orders system with a massively in-depth command and control element, not to mention the massive technology research trees that go from usuing simple thrusters on your ships to navigate your system to FTL-drives for inter-galaxy travel.
This game takes a while to get into, but it does have an optional tutorial system built in that will explain what each screen does, and introduce you to many of the deeply-involving facets of the game. Its by no means an EASY game to get into - you aren't going to be taking over the galaxy within the first 10 minutes, but if you can afford to put time into a game such as this, I feel you'll find it deeply rewarding. I've only spent ~5hrs with it so far, and I certainly enjoy it.

This game is amazing. As I chug ever closer to the hundreth hour of playtime, I wonder. Why does THIS game in particular hold my attention so much? Well, you see, this game is a randomly generated rougelike permadeath romp through your basement as you drown your opponents in tears. You are on the hunt for your mother who tried to sacrifice you to whatever voice she heard in her twisted mind. Pure gaming bliss. Even more reason to play this game is the sheer amounts of items that will alter your journey. Ever wanted to vomit bombs? How about vomiting bombs that make a rotation around you and ultimately deal more damage to you than anyone else? How about launching missiles from the sky to rain down upon your enemies? How about shooting lasers from your mouth? If any of this sounds fun at all, (other than the whole bombs redirected at you thing) you should pick up this game. It's pretty cheap to boot!
Unfortunately, there are negatives. Like I said before, some item combos can screw you over. Also, since this game runs on flash, it will lag. A lot. There are more glitches than you can count, all of them unpatchable due to flash's limitations. But does this mean it's a bad game? No. Not at all. This is one of my top ten favorite games of all time, and I can't even describe the replayability of this game. The variety that this game will bring to the table is astonishing. If you're looking for a way to waste lots of your time, this is it. By the way, don't pick up the DLC until you know what you're doing. ABZU is a weird little title, which I think should be experienced by everyone.
Story:
ABZU is not really a story driven game, it's more of a visual experience than anything. This game reminds me of Journey ( which was made by people who worked on ABZU) where the visuals are there to tell you a story and everyone will have a different meaning. To break it down in the simplest way I can the game puts you in the shoes of a diver who explores the depths of the ocean. You explore underwater temples and other places which I won't spoil here.
As I said this is not a story driven game in any way, so don't expect a story going in. However I have to say that the journey you take through the game is so good it's worth it even if you want a story in your games.
Graphics:
ABZU is one hell of a game to look at. The visuals of this game are drop dead gorgeous and are a treat. All the environments are vibrant in color and are incredibly pleasing to the eye. It's easy to get lost in the environment looking around at the beautiful wild life and how amazing everything looks. The design of this game is top notch and is almost wort the asking price alone.
I can imagine playing this game on a 4K screen on a couch is a mind blowing experience which is something I would like to try one day, the graphics themselves provide quite a relaxing experience.
Audio:
Audio design in this game is wonderful. Most of the musical tracks are amazing and set the mood perfectly. It goes from somber to creepy to fit the mood of the situation. Apart from the music the only things you hear is water noises and that's about it.
Gameplay:
ABZU is not really a gameplay heavy game. All you do is swim and sometimes solve really easy puzzles, which is basically follow wires to a device and turn it on. Most of the game you go from point A to point B and that repeats until the end of the game.  There are some secrets to find, but apart from that this game is really basic, but that's not a bad thing.
Verdict:
I wanted to keep this review short, because there's not much I can say about this title. ABZU is definitely an amazing game, but I would suggest waiting for a sale as the game is way too short ( took me an hour to finish the entire game) to actually pay full price for, but once it hits a sale this is a must own, without a doubt.
Final Rating:
9/10
Pros:
+ Amazing visuals
+ Great soundtrack
Cons:
- Too short

I must admit to being rather disappointed by this game when i first bought it, so left it gathering dust for quite a while afterwards. However, after enjoying the original NFS: Shift for the umpteenth time i decided to give this another try... and i'm glad i did.
In many ways this is more of the same, only with a new, rather cluttered layout and inferior graphics (sadly). There are more cars (a LOT more) to choose from, more circuits, more events... and i'm pleased to say the engine sounds are every bit as good as they were in the original. But one of the changes didn't agree with me. I really don't like the default helmet cam view, and i can see it being off-putting to a number of people, so changing it back to the same cockpit view as used in the first NFS: Shift game was essential. The other major change is one that initially i didn't like, but now i'm finding it great...
Upgrading your car is no longer as simple as it was in Shift. Now as your car is upgraded, it's performance rating increases, and as it increases it is possible that it is no longer eligible for the class that you are still racing in. I'll use my current car as an example. The Audi R8 is a Class C car with a performance rating of 920. If that rating reaches 1000 or more, it becomes a Class B car, and can no longer be used in Class C events. This means you have to be careful when choosing your upgrades, do you go for top speed, acceleration, or handling... or only a slight improvement in all 3? This means you have to think about your upgrades carefully. Thankfully you can sell all upgrades (and purchased cars) back for the same price you bought them, so if the upgrades you've chosen aren't working out for you, get rid of them and try experimenting with different ones. This means it's no longer as simple as just slapping on every single upgrade for your car as soon as you can afford them... chances are you can afford far more upgrades than you can actually fit while remaining in your racing category. This also has the benefit of being able to keep your favourite Class C car, but giving it the performance to genuinely compete in Class B, maybe even Class A, races.
The pure racing arcade game is no longer quite as mindless as the first Shift game... and i personally think that makes this a great game that is well worth buying.

Final Fantasy 8 was the last one in the series I had not played/beaten. My favorites are 7 and 9, but I figured I needed to give 8 a try because it was from that same era.
The story did not stick with me like 7 or 9 did. Squall was a character I eventually connected with, but things really take a wild turn after disc one. What initially seems like a simple quest to defeat the sorceress turns into a jumbled time-warping mess of confusion. All of the information is bombarded to you at random moments, while the characters never seem too surprised at how ridiculous their situation is becoming. The game flies around areas too quickly, so you never really get comfortable with your surroundings. You rarely ever go back to places you visited earlier in the game (besides Balamb Garden).
It took me hours of reading different websites explanations of the story just for it to make sense. Even after beating the game, I was still left wondering what really happened. I didn't have a great sense of accomplishment, because the ending leaves you more confused than comforted.
It still had the great CGI moments, and the ending (while confusing) was beautiful to watch.
The World Map is something I always looked forward to in the older Final Fantasy's. That moment when they give you freedom to explore wherever you want, hopefully finding some secret optional dungeon or little town. Final Fantasy 8's world map compared to 7 or 9 wasn't quite as good. It looks big on the surface with 5 major land masses, but these continents really don't have much on them.
The 'Draw' magic system was okay with me. Of course, I was used to the MP system, but drawing magic was a nice little change. Tons of different spells to draw from enemies made battles more creative. It took me some time to learn how to junction properly. At the start of the game I was thinking to myself "this is annoying why can't this be more simple?" but as the game progressed I understood it well.
The Card game was something I wasn't interested in at first, but when I learned of all the items and benefits of playing, I decided to give it a shot. I played alot of cards during the first disc, but once I got farther in the game, I found it to be more distracting than enjoyable. All the rule changes made it extremely tough to win, and I'd find myself restarting the game after losing a card match too many times. I managed to beat the game and get just about every item I wanted without spending much time playing cards at all.
I've always liked doing the small secretive side quests that are a constant in FF titles. FF8 had a few, with the Underwater Research Lab and the Centra Ruins being the only 2 that were really unique and rewarding.
Overall, it's a quality game, with most of the classic features you'd expect from the FF series. I do think they over-complicated the story which alienated me from feeling quite as engaged. I could never connect with the characters peril or satisfaction because I never quite understood what was being accomplished. It's worth a play for someone who's a Final Fantasy fan.

It's loudly trumpeted that this game has been in development for two years - and I'm sure everyone here knows it, with delay after delay from Apoapsis. The delays were earmarked with "bug fixing", and I fully admit that I said at the time that I wished they hadn't delayed it, but put it out with bugs in early access.
I'd like to take the opportunity to revoke that statement. I have been proven wrong. At the time, I was under the impression that the bugs that were being referred to were reasonably minor: after all, after 2 years in development, we were all excited for something new, different to SimAirport, say.
In its current form, I find this game to be completely unplayable. The baggage system is completely broken beyond belief - I have baggage going round on invisible carousels forever because their passengers have already left. Pathfinding is a mess - planes crash into each other, people walk in the middle of roads, construction workers refuse to enter certain areas of the airport. Sprites turn incorrectly, or not at all. Planes sit on the runway, unable to find a gate, despite three being available. People stand outside security exits, unable to move. Virtually no tutorial, especially if you start the game in sandbox mode. The list goes on, and on, and on.
Now, if this game is playable for you, great! All the best with it, I hope you find it great fun. I'm fairly sure I speak for many people in this community, however, who feel extremely let down by this release. I held off on buying SimAirport to wait for this release, but I think I'm going to take the plunge now, because this simply hasn't worked out.
In a few months to a year, this could be a great game. But right now, it's nowhere near ready for even a pre-alpha, in my opinion.

Ah, Dungeon Defenders Eternity! We have a love hate relationship. I love the game, but I hate how addicted I become during my hardcore sessions!
This is a tower defense and RPG hybrid that could almost be called a reverse MOBA.
There are many lanes, crazy map layouts and plenty of heroes to choose from, but the goal is the same no matter what: Protect the crystals. If a single one is destroyed, it's game over.
The general idea is to build tower defenses like any other tower defense game and defend the crystals, but the formula has never been done like this outside of Trendy's Dungeon Defenders series.
The entire game is played from a third person perspective, and during combat, you can run around and fight enemies much like a hack and slash RPG, all while gaining experience points to level up, find awesome loot and become one of the few elite heroes that can destroy anything without any trouble.
If you like tower defense games and you want to try a new spin on the genre with many new layers, give this game a shot! You likely wont regret it!

I am a huge fan of RTS games. I love many types of strategy games. Of all the Strategy games I habe played I would put this in the top of my list for sure. I have only been able to log in 52 hours into the game, yet I still have only scratched the surface. This game to me is a great blend of two of my favorite Strategy games. Total War and Civ.
I like how the economy is set up in the game. I think it has a good balance. What I mean by good balance is that it is not incredibly easy to have a surplus of materials, while in the same sense it is not terribly hard either. By adding the rare materials that give you a great boost in your economy was a good idea. It also adds a reason to fight over certain solar systems as well. It keeps you from just sitting back and racking up resources until late game.
The amount of content the game has is really compelling as well. There are tons of different technologies you can learn to better you planets, you defenses, your military, etc. Also there are a ton of different races and traits to choose from.
The ability to customize your own civilization is fantastic. The traits keep you balanced as well. By not allowing you to do certain things within your own goverment makes it a little more difficult when conquering other civs.
Those are a few of the reasons I think this is a great game. The only con that I personally would like to be changed is the combat. I dont feel too involved in the combat. It doesnt capture my attention. I like to be more involved in my battles like I am in Total War. I do understand not every game and its combat will be like Total War and that is fine. I would just like to be a little more involved then just click a whole fleet and watching them fight a different fleet. Maybe that could be supplemented by adding the ability to control the armies that invade planets.
Overall I think this game was worth every penny and any fan of RTS/Strategy games should play this. It is alot of fun.

In truth I wasn't sure what to expect from 'Stellaris'.
I've played RTS games such as 'Company of Heroes' and turn-based games such as the 'Civilisation' series before and somehow this game manages to merge the best of both worlds. It does this by combining the real-time (though pausable) orders system with a massively in-depth command and control element, not to mention the massive technology research trees that go from usuing simple thrusters on your ships to navigate your system to FTL-drives for inter-galaxy travel.
This game takes a while to get into, but it does have an optional tutorial system built in that will explain what each screen does, and introduce you to many of the deeply-involving facets of the game. Its by no means an EASY game to get into - you aren't going to be taking over the galaxy within the first 10 minutes, but if you can afford to put time into a game such as this, I feel you'll find it deeply rewarding. I've only spent ~5hrs with it so far, and I certainly enjoy it.

This game is one of those where, now that I get a chance to dive into it, I wish I had done so much, much sooner.  I've played so very, very many roguelikes/lites/whatevers over the years, and of course many games in a general sense.  This, honestly, may be one of the greatest of all of them, which isnt exactly something I say lightly.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is two things:  A turn-based roguelike, and a rhythm game.  The core mechanic is that the "turns" pass with the rhythm of the song being played.  On each beat, you make a move, and enemies also make a move.  This creates a game that is actually very fast-moving and active.  You must constantly be doing stuff, as if you skip a beat, or if you screw up the timing on one, Bad Things will tend to happen (depending on who you're playing as).  For most characters this involves your coin multiplier dropping to nothing (which can cause any Obsidian equipment to become weak), and maybe certain items might vanish.  For a couple of others, they just outright die if you screw up even once.  The rhythm mechanic is the absolute core of everything in the game.  Not only do all of the game's mechanics and design aspects revolve around it, but it's also a huge part of what makes the game so very, very fun. Two genres that appear to make no sense together are fused regardless, and the result is just stunning.
The good thing is, you dont have to be a master at music games to play this.  Necrodancer doesnt require the hyper-exact timing that most rhythm games do.  Dont get me wrong, it's still easy to screw up, but this is a game that anyone can get into.  Even the way the rhythm works... with many music games it's this chaotic pile of interspersed notes flying at you in various patterns along with the music.  In Necrodancer, it's an extremely steady beat. It's displayed at the bottom of the screen constantly, but almost immediately you'll find that you dont have to look at it.
However, that doesnt mean it isnt tough to deal with in other ways. One huge aspect that goes along with this is the fact that you MUST make some sort of movement on every beat.  You cannot simply stand still; that'll cause the aforementioned Bad Things to happen.  So you must either move, use an item, use a spell, or dig at a wall, on every single beat.  This constant forced action goes along well with the whole dancing theme of the game, but also adds alot to the challenge.  It can be difficult to place yourself into the right position to deal with the myriad foes that will attack you from all angles.  It does create a high learning curve... at first you're going to die over and over and over again simply due to this aspect, which could mean frustration.  But once you get used to it, it just WORKS.
Not that it'll ever get easy, mind you.  The game's difficulty ranges from "difficult" to "completely absurd".  Much of this has to do with not only the core mechanic, but the enemies you'll face.  Every floor is absolutely stuffed with monsters.  And these monsters arent the ultra-simple traditional sorts that simply walk at you and deal damage.  Every individual monster type has a unique pattern and special abilities, and learning those behaviors and traits is the most important thing when it comes to your survival.  Some enemies are simple:  skeletons for instance only move every other beat, and they raise their arms up on the beat before they do move. Easy to understand.   Others are much more confusing to deal with.  The infamous Red Dragon for instance has the ability to fire a blazing deathray to the left or right; it'll always try to do this if you are on the same horizontal line as it is, and you get exactly one beat to get out of the way of this extremely damaging attack.  Skeletons may not be so bad, but that dragon is the bane of many players and requires great care and special techniques to defeat.  The good thing is, enemy behavior is very easily understood, very well telegraphed, and NOT stuffed with RNG (with certain exceptions, but even those can be understood in a way), yet these facts absolutely do not detract from the challenge they produce.
Fortunately you have all sorts of different weapons and items to use.  The game's combat system is fantastic, and one of the reason for it is the weapons.  Each weapon has a "hit pattern" where it can damage tiles in front of you.  The basic dagger only damages the tile directly in front of you as you attack.  A longsword however can hit two tiles away.   A whip on the other hand has that very short range, but also a huge straight spread to the side.  Every single weapon type is useful in some way, and every weapon type comes in a variety of interesting flavors, as do other types of equipment.  For example, obsidian items base their power on your coin multiplier.  Blood items do things with your health.  Glass items are very strong but shatter if you get hit.  There are many item categories, including shovels that let you dig at walls, and torches that not only increase vision range but let you see THROUGH walls, making "hidden" rooms a major aspect of the game.   The items in the game are all sorts of fun to use, whether they're equipment or spells or whatever.  They are very, very well thought out and usually easy to understand.
However, the game isnt always so easy to grasp.  Shrines for instance can be very confusing in terms of exactly how they work.  Many times you'll run into a new one, try it out, go "WTF?" and then die horribly, not because the effect was bad, but because you had no clue what to do with it.  Other quirky mechanics like hidden shops, or the extremely varied effects of each different character (and there are MANY characters) can take awhile to really get the hang of.  There is alot of depth here, but that also means alot to learn.  This is NOT an easy game, and chances are, it's going to take you quite some time to beat it even once.  But it has features to help you learn... lots of such features, actually, something hardly any roguelikes ever do.  It makes it easy to practice against specific foes or test things out.  It even has a full level editor and Steam Workshop support.  There is so very, very much going on here (and even more if you get the fantastic DLC).
Overall, it's a very difficult game (and the difficulty just keeps going higher, and higher, and higher, as you continue to play it), yet one with neverending replay value, and one that I honestly just never get tired of. It also has the very, very rare quality of doing everything it can to help you learn in a non-frustrating way (heck, one particular character turns it into a TRULY turn-based game, letting you experiment and learn without having to worry about the rhythm, and he's unlocked from the start).  It's just plain FUN in a way that very few games truly manage, with a level of quality that is also rarely seen.  Every single aspect of it ties together to create something truly amazing.  Even if you have a hard time with it at first, stick with it:  It's absolutely worth dealing with that brutal learning curve.  This is something you dont want to miss.  I've reviewed many games on here... but this outdoes nearly all of them.  It's that good, in my opinion.
Oh, and did I mention that the soundtrack is absolutely incredible?  You can use your own songs, too.  Good things, in a game where the rhythm is everything.

Skylar & Plux: Adventure On Clover Island is the flagship game for new developers Right Nice Games. The game is a 3D action platformer, and a love letter to the PS2 era of 3D platformers. The game borrows from a number f sources, with fast, momentum based movement and melee combat, in the style of Jak and Daxter (Even borrowing animations from the first Jak and Daxter game). The game also borrows moves from Ratchet and Clank with it's jet pack moves, and Prince of Persia with it's time stop ability and time puzzles.
I found the game to be just the right length for the asking price, although it was a bit too easy, and lacked decent enemy variety, I still found myself greatly enjoying the freedom that the quick paced gameplay and interesting geometry allowed for. I also very much enjoyed the time slowing mechanic, it made me very nostalgic for Playstaion demo discs.
All in all, I'd give this game a solid 6 out of 10.

I'm going to premise this review with the bad qualities first. Even though I feel like there are more bad qualities than good, I'd still recommend this game any day.
| Game Length |
-- This game is SHORT. Even if you actively look for all of the cages, your game time might be 4 hours at the most. According to Steam, I beat it in 2, though it's probably on the edge of 3.
| Difficulty |
-- There is no increase in difficulty. Sure, there are some difficult spots. The tree takes a little bit of mental energy with the sliding puzzles (which I personally think is a poor choice in puzzles), and when the volcano is bursting, you do have to think on your feet. But that's about it. In fact, I think the volcano is even easier than the tree. It literally gives you a giant metal ball that lets you create mass destruction. While it is enjoyable to use it as a bowling ball and mow down a bunch of enemies, it absolutely tanks any amount of difficulty. I'd definitely classify this game as a 2/10 on the Difficulty Scale.
-- As an addendum, creative thinking is a bit shot because Plux is constantly out there like, "Hm... I wonder what would happen if you did this." He even does that in the later parts in the game!
| Artistic Style |
-- Alright, let's get to the good style. This game is good on the eyes, even when you're in normally-boring areas, like the desert. Plus massive bonus points for the comic book-esque cutscenes. Though sometimes I wish that there'd be more "panels" during the cutscene. Some of the scenes focus on one shot for far too long.
| Characters |
-- And ending on my favorite part of this game, the characters. Perhaps this is a unpopular opinion, but I really love that these characters are silly and perhaps even "generic". But Plux was fun, despite being the typical Navi character. And CRT and Bob make this wonderful villain duo. CRT is kinda like the evil version of Cave Johnson from Portal 2. A sense of silliness and sarcasm, but also this bold nature. I like how intense he gets after you open up the Siphon.
For those who are reading this part, if you need something simple and easy to play, then yes, play this. It's fun and charming and worth checking out. But if you just want to see the colorful palettes and maybe hear some of the dialogue between the characters, then perhaps watching cutscenes on Youtube would be more up your alley.

Excellent fun. Incredible depth in terms of staff and contracts, a familiar building mechanic (if you've played games like Prison Architect and Rimworld), and a great deal of complexity in regards to management of day-to-day operations await.
I've been eager for this game for months now, and it hasn't disappointed. The polish has a little ways to go, and it could certainly use more features (right now there's no "large" planes; mid-size regional craft are the biggest you'll get), but I have complete faith that it'll get what it needs in time.
Why? Because the developers, a pair of guys with full-time jobs, chose the launch date with extreme care, and have been on call since the first moment of release to keep up with bug reports. Something like six or eight updates have been released in a 24-hour period, and in addition to fixing bugs, they're also finding time to add quality of life features (optional edge scrolling and tooltips for worker stats, for example).
I've never been so impressed with a developer as I am with Apoapsis. I strongly, strongly recommend the game if you're on the fence. It is complex, though, and right now the tutorials miss a couple little things, so be ready for a little trial and error! But that trial and error is actually part of why I find the game so fun. It's very rewarding when things finally get rolling, you know?
If you're still not sure you want to commit, Katherine of Sky on Youtube has a several-hour video in which she learned the game while playing. There are also introductory videos by the developers on the official Youtube channel. Check those videos out if you want to know more before buying.
But yeah, definitely recommend. TWO ENTHUSIASTIC THUMBS UP. As well as both big toes, and I'm working on teaching my cat to raise her thumbs as well.

The first few hours are pretty great; exploring, getting all sorts of interesting pop ups from your scientist...the research system is innovative and I like it. Well that's about the good part...
After you run into some other empires, you'll soon learn that diplomacy is basically non existent. No really; don't expect much from it, since it's just (plain) mathematics, which most of the time you cannot influence enough...Factions that like you early on; those will be your friends. Factions that dislike you; this will not change much, not enough to become allies. Think you can do defensive alliance? Think you can join up to go to war to the same rival? Think you can actually trade for some energy/minerals? Well think again!
Allies suck either way; since the only thing they will do is follow you strongest fleet. Yeah really; that's ALL they will do, regardless of ANYTHING that is happening around them. Some enemy jumping into their home-system, just 1 jump away from them? Nope; not gonna defend it!
You thought there were interesting battles? Well perhaps in the future. But for now; you cannot do ANYTHING, you cannot tell your guys to hold a point (dont move), nor to attack the heavies first, nor...well you just cannot do anything.
And wait for the joy of battleships...see the AI is not smart enough to reduce speed when moving a sector...so your strongest ships will arrive after the rest of your fleet is already annihilated.
Colonies, sectors, planet management. I mean really; have Paradox not taken a look at any other 4X space games? Sectors suck so hard; the AI is just...well basically stupid. There are so many things missing; like the inability to transfer food from sector A to sector B. What use is a mining sector, if the minerals (surplus) cannot be transported from it?
What baffles me is how you create an galaxy with so little interaction. Not for a second does it feel alive. It is just conquer this enemy; conquer that enemy; alliances and federations are flawed and thus pointless. There are so many thing missing gameplay wise; I could write pages on stuff that seems so obvious, that Paradox must have known...and they still brought out this game and sold it for 40,- euros. That is just rather ♥♥♥♥♥♥; call it alpha access if that's what it is!

This is a cautious recommend.
Like most Paradox games there is a ton of possibility waiting to be unlocked by piles of DLC. I don't know if they do this on purpose or just throw a half-baked idea out there and see where the players ask for things to be filled in later. The ability to create a race is neat but doesn't seem to make much difference that I've seen since you can pick any type of race and the traits which create the modifiers are available to any race whether a cat person or a fungus person.
The AI players are incredibly passive and their war strategy boils down to making a huge fleet and launching it at you. If you can beat that giant fleet you win every time and they will just spend the rest of the war sending ships at you piecemeal as they complete them and you can just go planet to planet picking off the enemy where you want. The AI is also quite happy to surrender after a few setbacks I've yet to see one fight to anything like a proper ending.
You are allowed to conquer only so many planets after that limit it goes to the AI controlled sectors that the AI can't properly manage you will be reduced to tears as you watch how poorly a job the AI does with your conquered/colonized planets.
Ship designer is pick parts A,B,C and not nearly as awesome as the designer in Galactic Civilizations.
Diplomacy is worthless and the AI basically greets you when you discover them and then ignores you until war is declared.
Okay enough complaining what doesn't suck?
The random events are pretty neat.
Your colonists will gradually evolve on their own forming new factions or even literally evolving into distinct races on their own and leading to infighting which will destroy buildings or lead to race wars costing countless lives.
The research tree is clever you pretty much get the same techs each game but they are unlocked in different orders so you can't just rush the same techs every game since some are offered earlier or later (even MUCH later) than others each time.
You can replace your people with robots that will happily toil on ice covered worlds without complaining like your lazy organic subjects do.
You can move populations from planet to planet or launch a genocide to purge less cooperative factions or races you've conquered that don't appreciate your rule. Bird people not digging your fungus despotism? Kill 'em all. Replace them with robots.
There is much to like but much that is awful or not quite there if you want a fully fleshed out alternative to Galactic Civilizations (my benchmark for space 4X goodness) this isn't it. In time I think this game will give Galactic Civilizations a run for their money but at this point it is a "meh". A good "meh" but still a "meh".

I like this game.  It scratches several itches I have when playing games.  System building and interaction being the primary.  This is intricate, at the beginning, as the systems are not explained well enough in the tutorials.  The UI doesn't help you much either - it is not intuitive to me.
BUT .. when you finally (4th attempt) get the luggage systems working.  When you finally, destroy the gun-toting bags that the peeps try to smuggle on the planes.  When you optimise the landing of 4 seperate airline companies across 5 gates using  a single baggage hall feeding 5 different baggage claim areas.  When the taxiways don't get clogged up (again) with the aircraft following simple rules that I, as the architect didn't understand.  When you done all that, my son, you can call yourself a Airport ARCHITECT.
This game is Airport Architect - every single bit and piece you need/want to build you do it yourself - by hand.   I don't think it is Airport CEO so much.  Perhaps it's the lack of strategic decisions that a CEO would make that is the problem for me?  I don't see any CEO deciding where a rubbish bin should go in the entrance hall (2 squares or 3 squares away from the door)!.  No, I only know one CEO, in my real life - my boss, and he would not be doing this, but he would be asking me, as his senior architect, to draw up the building plans and ensure they follow standards and rules.  Building regs, Aviation rules, that sort of thing.  The CEO I know would likely be in some strip club while I was drawing those plans up for him, not standing over my shoulder clicking the mouse to position some sidewalk.
Perhap the depth of CEO'ing will come later in patches/releases?  I confess I haven't seen the roadmap at all.  But, if they fix the crankiness - which they will in this early access release feedback - people are not slow in coming forward when they hit problems and the devs are responding quickly too it seems with bug-fixes.  Perhaps it was that bug-fix they did yesterday that finally allowed my airport baggage system to work exactly as I had planned it?   I like to think I overcame the difficulties the devs have added to this game, with their poor instructions and lack-lustre UI, with my smarts though.
Yeah, Airport Architect, is scratching that itch quite nicely.  Hope it keeps developing in a positive way.
Mods!!  I want to see mods.  Now, where's that roadmap?  :)
[EDIT: it's been 7+ days of EA]
Well, the game has got better and worse with each patch, and there have been a number of those.  So I'll continue to praise the developers for their responses there.
However, I am criticising the developers for not releasing a roadmap of the future path to release.  I don't know how long that will be.  I do not know what will be included in that release.  I do not know what the developers longer term aspiration for this game are - AirportCEO 9.0, for example.  I don't know what longevitiy this game can have without the commitment from the developers.
Sum Up:
If you like building structures and systems from items drawn on a 2D architectural canvas then this is the game for you.  However, that game should be called Airport Architect.
If you like a game that challanges you in business planning and tycoon-em-up then this is not, currently, and probably long term either, the game for you
If you like certainty in the future then this game is not for you - but you knew that aleady as it early access
Still recommended though

Yesterday was Christmas day and I was 6 years old again. I woke up at 7am to an email from Steam "Airport CEO is now available in Early Access on Steam!". Excited and still a little hung over from the night before I stumbled out to the lounge, logged onto Steam and splashed out the best $17.09 I've spent this week. Ten minutes later, surrounded by a litany of snacks and suitably cold beverages I hit 'Play'... and Airport CEO booted up in all its glory. And then it froze.
Airport CEO is a great game for an Alpha. There are bugs, there are oddities and there's a reasonably steep learning curve (took me far longer than I care to admit to learn that holding CTRL delete's zones, rooms etc.) but there's also so much potential and two great developers who really care about their community. Within the first 24 hours there were 5 hot patches full of fixes. I've bought a fair few EA's and so far this blows them all away in after sales support and updates. I've been eagerly awaiting this game since it was announced two years ago, having spent my younger days playing the likes of 'Airport Inc'. I even purchased 'SimAirport' a few months ago hoping that it would fill the void and while that too is a great game, it feels more childish and casual when compared with Airport CEO. Even simple things like Queue management are more polished than ‘SimAirport’ which really shows the level of research and quality control that Apoapsis have already put into this game.
Yes the replayability is currently limited, some features don’t yet work (like the Graphics or Sound Options) and the décor options are severely limited but give it a few months and some great community mods and this game will be up there with the likes of ‘Prison Architect’.
When a game is an important part of your life memory, it means it's masterpiece.

TL;DR: Great game. The updates have made this into an actual MOO2 killer.
-- Full Review --
Stellaris is a real-time 4x game, similar in concept to Sins of a Solar Empire, but closer to MOO2 or Civilization in depth of gameplay. In a lot of ways it surpasses MOO2 in terms of depth and realistic feel.
You start with a pre-designed or custom-built race on a single planet, and try to conquer the galaxy with them. However, this game does a much better job of simulating actual empire management than other similar titles. As your empire grows, your people can split into various factions, and you need to keep them happy or they may rebel and form their own empire. Also, there is a small limit on the number of planets you can manage manually. The others have to be assigned to a 'sector', which is essentially an AI-managed group of planets. This is a great mechanic, because it takes the tedium out of the late game, something that other games have struggled with.
When creating a custom race, you choose the species (mammal, bird, fungus, etc..) which doesn't affect anything but appearance. Then you choose the home planet type and ethos, which is kind of like your race's philosophy. Ethos affects a lof of things in the game, and so is very important. Thankfully all of the choices seem pretty well balanced. You can then choose a government type, which is limited by your ethos. Finally, you can choose traits, which give you bonuses or penalties, using a point system. While the traits you can choose are much more limited than MOO2, the combination of traits, ethos, and government makes a wide variety of races possible.
Research is handled similar to MOO 1, in that you are given a selection of techs to choose from for research. Ones you don't choose usually show up later, so you don't normally lose anything by not researching them immediately. The selection of techs is somewhat dependant on your ethos and government, with techs that would appeal to your racial type being more likely to appear. There are also rare techs which you may or may not have available, and techs which can only be obtained by killing enemies and researching the debris, similar to MOO2.
The game features not only enemy empires similar to yours, but primitive (i.e. pre-space flight) races that you can study, exploit, or uplift, and fallen empires, which are high-tech empires that have passed their prime and are now basically stagnant. (Similar to MOO2's Antareans, but not immediately hostile.) The fallen empires are generally neutral unless you make them mad.
There is a quest system that is called 'Special Projects' that requires you to do certain things in order to receive a reward. Usually it's just moving a science vessel to a particular planet and doing some research, but there are other more complicated (and interesting) project, such as investigating a precursor race. These are mostly optional, but have nice rewards. And some are necessary in order to communicate with other empires.
The systems all seem to be fairly well balanced, and the game never seems to bog down with nothing to do. There's always another star to survey, another planet to build up, or another enemy to fight.
One of the nicer additions with the latest patch was Unity, which acts similar to Culture in the Civilization series. Accumulate enough of it and you can unlock special bonuses in things like Exploration, Prosperity, Diplomacy, or Domination. These specializations can help guide your empire into the play style you prefer. Diplomacy allows you to create federations (alliances) with other empires, so that you stand united against common threats. There is even a federation victory condition, so you can win the game even by staying a small empire, if your federation is strong enough.
One of the things that may throw off players is the war system. Unlike most 4x games, you can't just go to war and start gobbling up planets. This game features a system where you have to set war goals, and fight the enemy empire until they concede. War goals may be ceding planets, liberating planets, ending slavery/genocide, or just humiliation. After a war is won or lost, the empires involved have a forced 10 year peace treaty, so you won't be able to conquer large empires quickly. The ability liberate planets is a nice addition for pacifist empires. It basically carves off a part of the enemy empire into a separate empire that is friendly to you, which means you can vassalize them or invite them into your federation. It's a dirty political trick that fits very well into the game.
One more thing that is interesting is end-game crises. These are world-altering events that usually happen later in the game, that have the potential to wipe out all of the players. One example is an invasion force of extra-dimensional beings that eat all sentient life. These end-game crises are deadly if not handled properly, and can add some spice to the late game.
Other features which I won't dwell on:
- Leaders (civic and military)
- Slavery
- Vassalization
- Terraforming
- Scientific anomolies
The DLC add giant space-monsters and mega structures, but I haven't tried these so I can't comment on them.
The only down side I can say is the time it takes to complete a game. These games are marathons, not sprints. They take even longer to complete than a game of Civilization, so be warned that it's a huge time sink. In fact, I haven't even completed a game myself. But a lot of that was due to the poor state of the earlier versions of the game. With the latest patch, I hope to actually finish a game soon. :-)
I highly recommend this game to any 4x junkie. It's the best one I have ever played. After all these years, someone finally came up with a game that can equal (or even beat) MOO2.

Garry's Mod is not a game, it's a sandbox that can be made into a game much like bottlecaps made into a game when you and your friends have nothing to do, so as you may expect, many aspects are quite crude and rudimentary. Some mods or mini-games require assets from other Source games which you need to own; otherwise they appear as error messages on screen and you can't see the textures/models. The community is not as great as you think; therefore good friends and know-how in tinkering with mods is important to enjoy this sandbox tool. Even when this is on sale, I would advise you to think twice about this purchase, and be sure to fully understand what you're getting when you buy Garry's Mod.

This is a very fun little indie game where you spend ingame money to buy items to burn to earn ingame money to buy more items to burn.
There's a short and cute plot which takes a small fairly dark turn as it wraps things up.
You play as a young boy living in a world where everything is snowy and freezing cold, he uses a "toy" called The Little Inferno Fireplace which is advertised as something to keep people warm and safe. Throughout the story your neighbour, a little girl with a fireplace of her own sends you letters and items to burn. The fire looks and sounds great and it's very satisfying to burn things.
You can even pick a photo item which lets you pick a picture you have saved on your computer to burn.
There's very little in terms of gameplay besides burning items, and replayability is low. But there's a very therapeutic/calming sensation just watching the crackling fire with quiet all around you.
Well worth the low price if you like games like this.

This game is one of those where, now that I get a chance to dive into it, I wish I had done so much, much sooner.  I've played so very, very many roguelikes/lites/whatevers over the years, and of course many games in a general sense.  This, honestly, may be one of the greatest of all of them, which isnt exactly something I say lightly.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is two things:  A turn-based roguelike, and a rhythm game.  The core mechanic is that the "turns" pass with the rhythm of the song being played.  On each beat, you make a move, and enemies also make a move.  This creates a game that is actually very fast-moving and active.  You must constantly be doing stuff, as if you skip a beat, or if you screw up the timing on one, Bad Things will tend to happen (depending on who you're playing as).  For most characters this involves your coin multiplier dropping to nothing (which can cause any Obsidian equipment to become weak), and maybe certain items might vanish.  For a couple of others, they just outright die if you screw up even once.  The rhythm mechanic is the absolute core of everything in the game.  Not only do all of the game's mechanics and design aspects revolve around it, but it's also a huge part of what makes the game so very, very fun. Two genres that appear to make no sense together are fused regardless, and the result is just stunning.
The good thing is, you dont have to be a master at music games to play this.  Necrodancer doesnt require the hyper-exact timing that most rhythm games do.  Dont get me wrong, it's still easy to screw up, but this is a game that anyone can get into.  Even the way the rhythm works... with many music games it's this chaotic pile of interspersed notes flying at you in various patterns along with the music.  In Necrodancer, it's an extremely steady beat. It's displayed at the bottom of the screen constantly, but almost immediately you'll find that you dont have to look at it.
However, that doesnt mean it isnt tough to deal with in other ways. One huge aspect that goes along with this is the fact that you MUST make some sort of movement on every beat.  You cannot simply stand still; that'll cause the aforementioned Bad Things to happen.  So you must either move, use an item, use a spell, or dig at a wall, on every single beat.  This constant forced action goes along well with the whole dancing theme of the game, but also adds alot to the challenge.  It can be difficult to place yourself into the right position to deal with the myriad foes that will attack you from all angles.  It does create a high learning curve... at first you're going to die over and over and over again simply due to this aspect, which could mean frustration.  But once you get used to it, it just WORKS.
Not that it'll ever get easy, mind you.  The game's difficulty ranges from "difficult" to "completely absurd".  Much of this has to do with not only the core mechanic, but the enemies you'll face.  Every floor is absolutely stuffed with monsters.  And these monsters arent the ultra-simple traditional sorts that simply walk at you and deal damage.  Every individual monster type has a unique pattern and special abilities, and learning those behaviors and traits is the most important thing when it comes to your survival.  Some enemies are simple:  skeletons for instance only move every other beat, and they raise their arms up on the beat before they do move. Easy to understand.   Others are much more confusing to deal with.  The infamous Red Dragon for instance has the ability to fire a blazing deathray to the left or right; it'll always try to do this if you are on the same horizontal line as it is, and you get exactly one beat to get out of the way of this extremely damaging attack.  Skeletons may not be so bad, but that dragon is the bane of many players and requires great care and special techniques to defeat.  The good thing is, enemy behavior is very easily understood, very well telegraphed, and NOT stuffed with RNG (with certain exceptions, but even those can be understood in a way), yet these facts absolutely do not detract from the challenge they produce.
Fortunately you have all sorts of different weapons and items to use.  The game's combat system is fantastic, and one of the reason for it is the weapons.  Each weapon has a "hit pattern" where it can damage tiles in front of you.  The basic dagger only damages the tile directly in front of you as you attack.  A longsword however can hit two tiles away.   A whip on the other hand has that very short range, but also a huge straight spread to the side.  Every single weapon type is useful in some way, and every weapon type comes in a variety of interesting flavors, as do other types of equipment.  For example, obsidian items base their power on your coin multiplier.  Blood items do things with your health.  Glass items are very strong but shatter if you get hit.  There are many item categories, including shovels that let you dig at walls, and torches that not only increase vision range but let you see THROUGH walls, making "hidden" rooms a major aspect of the game.   The items in the game are all sorts of fun to use, whether they're equipment or spells or whatever.  They are very, very well thought out and usually easy to understand.
However, the game isnt always so easy to grasp.  Shrines for instance can be very confusing in terms of exactly how they work.  Many times you'll run into a new one, try it out, go "WTF?" and then die horribly, not because the effect was bad, but because you had no clue what to do with it.  Other quirky mechanics like hidden shops, or the extremely varied effects of each different character (and there are MANY characters) can take awhile to really get the hang of.  There is alot of depth here, but that also means alot to learn.  This is NOT an easy game, and chances are, it's going to take you quite some time to beat it even once.  But it has features to help you learn... lots of such features, actually, something hardly any roguelikes ever do.  It makes it easy to practice against specific foes or test things out.  It even has a full level editor and Steam Workshop support.  There is so very, very much going on here (and even more if you get the fantastic DLC).
Overall, it's a very difficult game (and the difficulty just keeps going higher, and higher, and higher, as you continue to play it), yet one with neverending replay value, and one that I honestly just never get tired of. It also has the very, very rare quality of doing everything it can to help you learn in a non-frustrating way (heck, one particular character turns it into a TRULY turn-based game, letting you experiment and learn without having to worry about the rhythm, and he's unlocked from the start).  It's just plain FUN in a way that very few games truly manage, with a level of quality that is also rarely seen.  Every single aspect of it ties together to create something truly amazing.  Even if you have a hard time with it at first, stick with it:  It's absolutely worth dealing with that brutal learning curve.  This is something you dont want to miss.  I've reviewed many games on here... but this outdoes nearly all of them.  It's that good, in my opinion.
Oh, and did I mention that the soundtrack is absolutely incredible?  You can use your own songs, too.  Good things, in a game where the rhythm is everything.
