F.E.A.R. has plenty of flaws. The levels in the first half are samey, featuring dull and bland-looking industrial environments that aren't helped by its aged graphics. Mission objectives are uninspired. The scares wear off quickly, especially when they happen while you're looking in the wrong direction. Story is meh. Frankly, the only positive thing about the game is the combat, and the combat alone is what makes this game a classic. Bloody combat, vicious weapons, impressive enemy AI and cool visual effects make each battle an event to look forward to. Include the slow-mo ability and the battles become a thing of beauty: Grenade distortions rippling through the air, the vicious "thump, thump, thump" of your assault rifle, enemies dying in glorious sprays of blood, seeing a Replica sailing stylishly through the air after receiving a flying kick...
In short, F.E.A.R. has some of the most impressive FPS combat ever, and you should definitely experience it.

I tried to hop on the "2D indie metroidvania" bandwagon after Ori and the Blind Forest. Dust: An Elysian Tail was on the list, and while it looked very promising at first, after a short while it became clear that this game lacks polish, variety and quality in some aspects. It's nothing that demolishes the experience but neither is it fair to say that this game is perfect. It has obvious flaws. It's basically developed by just one man and it took almost 4 years, which is extremely impressive! But instead of covering so many aspects alone (inventory system and such), maybe the developer should have focused on most important things? Instead, this game is "a little of everything", it just works, but it's not working so good that it should have 95% positive reviews.
With all that in mind, I'd say I recommend this game (considering you are aware that it's a cartoon inspirated game), but there's an issue which affects my experience - broken depth perspective (more info on this later).*
-The artstyle is nice, the scenery looks great at times, but not always - the quality varies a lot.
-The music is fine, sometimes inspiring, but can be repetative.
-The combat is literally same thing all over again (AOE Spam&Slash). If you don't like the combat, the game will be really boring.
-The controls, while they make it possible to reap&tear through the enemies even while mid-air without any problems, are somewhat questionable. Blocking done with the base attack button, by just holding it? Without any "blocking" animation so you don't know if block is engaged?
-Voice acting is somewhere in between AAA and indie games. The emotions are well expressed, clear pronounciation.
-The writing is funny, whether or not you will like it depends on your taste. This game likes to break the 4th wall.
With all that in mind, I give it 7.7/10, which is high considering that I didn't give any game a score higher than 9.6 (because nothing is perfect). If you are into the theme and enjoy the slasher sort of combat, grab it. If you have doubts, take your time.
*A huge issue I have with this game is sort of distorted depth pespective, the space perception is broken which can be seen while moving, or simply by judging objects' sizes. Objects which are supposedly closer to the viewpoint are moving as fast as some objects which are further away. This doesn't affect the gameplay, it just messes with my sight, a lot! This is subjective, this issue exists in many 2D sidescrollers. I guess I can get used to this, but right now, I can't play more of the game just because it gives me a light headache. Even though it's a decent game which actually deserves a positive review, this issue is enough to give the game a thumb down, and I believe it's fair, considering that this game is somewhat overrated already.

I have so many positive and negative feelings about this game. Overall I am scoring it positive - this is one of those reviews where if I could say "Maybe" instead of "Yes" or "No" I would.
As described in many other reviews Skylar & Plux is an homage to Ratchet and Clank. Those games you slaved away at during your childhood and adolesence. Personally I could never get into Ratchet and Clank whilst growing up (except for Secret Agent Clank damn what a game) but, I enjoyed every short lived second of Skylar & Plux. As a result the gameplay is very similar. Exploration of envrionments, platforming, puzzling and battling enemies.
Sadly the game is incredibly short. As you can see from my game time (two hours as of writing this review) you can breeze through the story of this game quite easily. I have not collected all of the ingame collectables I am missing roughly seven at this point however, that process would not increase my overall game time that much.
The story of the game is simplistic and beautifully executed. I am not going to go into detail about it. But it is fun and relaxing. Relaxtion seems to be a key theme whilst exploring Clover Island. Amongst the chaos of battling hordes of RoboPuppers and dodging homing projectiles; the scenery is gorgeous. I was very apprehensive about how well the Unreal 4 engine had been used at the start of the game but, I was quickly set straight when exploring the first ecosystem of the island.
Overall is this game a worthwhile purchase. Absolutely. You are not going to find the next Ratchet and Clank, Banjo Kazooie or Psychonauts here. But you will find a game overflowing with potential. With enough support Skylar & Plux could become the next platforming pantheon. It appeals to so many demographics, the voice acting and writing is hilarious, heartfelt but most importantly it is real. The gameplay is smooth, exciting and well executed. Graphically the game stands above other recent triple-A platforming titles we have seen.
In short. Buy this game! The price might seem steep but, it is 100% worthwhile. With enough love and support Skylar & Plux could break the boundaries of what a platformer is.

Ok, first review ever, so GO:
First Impression:
Nice graphics, witty dialogues, and perhaps a bit few combo possibilities.
So, then into details:
Graphics:
They are not as breathtaking as maybe Ori, but they are nice enough that you still enjoy looking at them even after some hours of playing. The advantage of the more simple 2D-style: they don't need much resources.
Gameplay:
As mentioned at the beginning, you don't have that many different combos, that you can use. This seems like a something bad, but except for people looking for a real challange, they suffice, as the enemies are not the smartest, even on hard. This leads to the next point, the difficulty. If you complete most of the quests and keep track of the items and plans you collected, you can finish of most of the enemies with one or at most two combos, even on hard. This game is more suited for a bit of casual gaming, whenever you don't want to tax yourself too hard.
Story:
I completed a complete playthrough with all hidden objects and all the best upgrades for Dust within ~15 h. As I took my time, you could probably finish the main story with some side-quests on the way in 8 h. This should give a rough estimate of the amount of story you can expect. The story itself is told mostly in dialogues, except for some sequences at the very beginning and the very end, overall with pretty decent voice-acting. Arguably the best thing of the game: the funny dialogues, especially the banter between dust, the hero, and fidget, the flying companion, which is afraid of heights.... What I personally really liked were the many more or less hidden tributes to other games, in the dialogues or the within the world itself. Can you find them all?
I won't write much about the content of the story, as I hate spoilers. Its not groundbreaking, but very solid. You may guess the twist, but nevertheless, you can sympathise well with the characters, and thats what matters to me.
So overall a neat game, for some funny casual gaming to get down after a tough day, or a tough gaming session. ;)
If you got this far, thanks for reading and cherio!

This did indeed do a good job conjuring some of the feel of 2001-era 3D platformers. Gameplay was solid, but somewhat more casual than I was expecting. This takes the 'adventure' genre somewhat literally, in that it's largely more about exploring and platforming and puzzles than it is about combat (practically every enemy dies in one hit, and there's so much healing going on that I only died a couple times the whole game, and that was mostly due to me jumping in lava).

Plux pretty much just hovers near your shoulder the whole game and doesn't do anything, but itsn't obnoxious, either. (So, not like Navi :P )

I got it at 40% off, and I'd say this game is definitely worth it at that price point. It has some interesting ideas but quickly goes off the rails and seems to have been in need of a good script editor.  Some of the jokes just aren't funny and they seemed to have been too enamoured by them so seemed reluctant to lose them, hence the need for an editor.  When the General appears and the Nerd's sidekick starts talking about multiverses I gave up watching, the script had lost its way.
The idea that the ET game made the Nerd who he is is an interesting one, as is the search for the landfill site, I also liked the idea that his endorsement of a really bad game would make it sell and thus he could be exploited, an insightful view of himself and game reviewers in general.
James is fun to watch playing the Nerd but he suffers from being surrounded by actors and thus goes from underacting to overacting, neither of which is bad but it is jarring when set against everyone else in the film.  There are some funny moments but too often the film becomes indulgent and wanders, for example 3 dream within dream sequences, each of which were ok but could have been handled better.
It's worth a watch if you want to support James, it's just not tightly scripted enough to keep my attention.

This game makes me sad. It's a ton of fun when it wants to function properly but... it's very much like a beta. Think Killing Floor but with dinosaurs instead of zed and in a large, objective-based, outdoor map.
The hit detection is awful. I've wailed away at dinos point blank for no damage only to finally start damaging them after I aimed above their heads. This is on top of having to aim at enemies that have an extremely narrow profile. Y'know you jumpjet up to a vantage point so you can provide fire support for you team mates with the snazzy, new sniper rifle you got only to be endlessly pounded by flying things that you can never spot. So you aim at the flyers only to not be able to hit them since they disappear into the bloom from a sun or your crosshairs are the same color as the f*king sky. Wonderful.
Oh and let's talk about buying things, hmm? In Killing Floor you have a short time to buy things and the shops appear at random locations but the map gives you fairly clear directions and usually, a lot of time. Not in Orion. To be fair you get a clear waypoint marker for shops and it's in the outdoors, so you can spot them. But the maps are MASSIVE. The game even gives you vehicles to traverse them, they are so massive. However, you only get about a minute to get to the shop and other players can actually shorten that time by pushing a button. Not to mention that people will frequently take off with vehicles simply leaving you in the dust.
And finally, players can damage other players. No, seriously. I don't know how many times I've been in a nice spot and had someone just throw genades at me. or use the gunship guns to blast me.
TL-DR: The final verdict is that Orion is a ton of fun but is ultimately ruined by glitches, bugs and poor design. Some of these problems can be fixed by simply forming your own groups. It's hard to recommend but for the one dollar price tag, maybe this is worth it to you.

Usual warnings about early access, non-implemented features, bugs and performance are particularly important here - read the early access explanation on the store page and decide whether you are willing to give the game a try in its current state.
I would still recommend the game - while it is undeniably rough around the edges right now, it is still the best airport management/tycoon game I have played in a long time. Basic features in the game work (although you'll have to play around with things to work around some of the issues with implementation that exist at the moment, most notably traffic), and there's definitely something here to have fun with even at this early stage. While the in game tutorial does not cover everything, and some things can be frustratingly obscure at first, a little patience and a bit of trial and error goes a long way towards making this game enjoyable in the long run.
More importantly however, the developers seem highly active, engaging with the community and providing patches on a regular basis to address bugs and other issues. As with all EA titles, make sure to report any bugs you come across - if all players did this, I suspect we will have a much better game sooner rather than later.
TLDR - Recommended for the massive potential the game has. Basic features are there, enough to have a bit of fun with the game in its current state. Be ready to accept bugs, quirks and a few frustrating things. Game is clearly at a very early stage - buy with this in mind, and you'll have a much better time enjoying what is already on offer.

An amazing title. Coming from someone that wasn't very fond of Hero Shooters until now, Paladins is a very addicting and captivating game. The gameplay is fast paced with a lot going on, but at the same time very fluid and fulfilling. Playing different champions feels like your playing an entirely different style of game, which means it's pretty difficult to get bored of Paladins. Unlike most team-gameplay in other games, Paladins gets it right, Even if the other team is way more skilled than you, if you use teamwork and class synergy (which not to mention, communication in-game is very easy) then your team can still pull out a victory. The characters are both memorable and charming, their quotes and personas add to the gameplay. I do very much believe that if you're able to enjoy Overwatch, TF2 or any other hero shooters, that you'll be able to enjoy Paladins. The game isn't very demanding either, so even your grandmother can enjoy it on her Windows 98! (not really but still.) I would complain about bugs, but this is a beta, and those are to be expected in a beta, and regardless, the bugs are very small and aren't very detrimental to the gameplay.

F.E.A.R. slow-mo'd its way onto my list of top FPS games, competing with Battlefront 2, Halo 2, Far Cry 3, and Republic Commando.
F.E.A.R. beautifully manages the thin red line between horror and first person shooting with atmospheric yet intense gunplay. Your opponents, the Replicant soldiers created by Armachan and the Armachan private army both have excellent AI. They behave very intelligently under the circumstances and coordinate well as squads.
The storyline engrossed me completely even though it wasn't deep. It was disturbing, dark, and thrilling as you put together the picture. Overall the game feels satisfying. There's nothing quite as satisfying as ambushing an enemy squad then while in slow-motion wipe them all out in less then a second (in game time).
Most surprisingly the graphics hold up better than its sequel, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin. Now nearly 10 years after its original release F.E.A.R.'s graphics are visually interesting and highly functional. The enemy units come in variety and all are fascinating to look at. The sequel's graphics while most advanced are simply dull and remind one of Call of Duty.
Ultimately, I recommend this to any member of the gaming community to play. Be wary of the sequels, they are unimpressive but fun at best. They're downright terrible if you want more of the original flavor.

On the surface, Dead Bits looks like your average licensed TV Show handheld shovel ware. But underneath that, is one of the biggest revolutions the medium has ever seen. Funny, smart, deep, timeless. Read on to find out why this stands as one of the finest licensed video games of all time, or indeed, one of the finest video games of all time. You play as Cory, the kid from the TV show who finds himself living in the White House. The gameplay is simple; you need to sneak around the various rooms and do various tasks, which often involve talking to someone or getting to a certain room. It sounds simple, but between the deep stat management systems, varied character patrol routes, and the amazing dialogue options, the gameplay is top-notch, making the likes of Metal Gear Solid pale in comparison (including on storytelling prowess, more on that later). The mini-games like the lock-picking are so deep, they could be sold as full games themselves. The graphics are life-like, the character portraits are so realistic you will think you are watching the show! I haven't seen such good graphics on a handheld game, ever. The audio is as good as a DS game can sound, it's all in there, from the sound effects to the catchy theme from the TV show. As an audio-visual experience, Dead Bits delivers the best on the DS. What truly shines however, is the dialogue and the smart humour in the game. The dialogue here is comical to kids, but truly hilarious to adults, which are more likely to get the subtler jokes. And yet, it's full of life lessons and themes that resonates to all of us, children and adults alike. It's like watching the best Pixar film of your life. The writing here may live on as a timeless example of comedy. What they have pulled off here may be one day looked back as "the Shakespeare of comedy". Overall, this game is a hidden masterpiece, one that will change the way video games are made. Just give it time. For now, you can be privileged enough to play this masterpiece while the rest of the world is still unaware of its implications and future impact on the medium. They will catch up, eventually.

I keep a positive approach to indie developers, especially if they already created something I enjoyed. My attitude here was "World of Goo was great. A second game from the same dev? A must have!". And perhaps because of expecting a similar quality of gameplay, I was ultimately underwhelmed.
The mentioned gameplay is as simple as it gets. Buy things -> burn them -> receive slightly more money than you spent on it -> buy more things -> repeat ad infinitum. Some items here and there react a bit more interestingly then others when burned, but in the case of most of them it's about what you'd expect - they catch fire, turn to ash, end.
There's no challenge, no timer, no optional objectives a la WoG's OCDs, nothing that really requires you to pay attention. It is definitely much more casual than WoG, though not necessarily more family friendly - some toys screaming (even if cartoonishly) when burned "alive" can be quite creepy. Which is good, as it helps stay awake during the game.
The game is short - which wouldn't be bad by itself, but it's short despite being already artificially dragged out by time delays between buying items and receiving them (from several second at first to up to about 4,5 minutes for more expensive items). Game takes about 3h to finish, whereas it would take perhaps 30 minutes without the waiting times - and it would be a considerably more enjoyable experience in that case. Between a 30 minutes of well-paced engaging fun and a 3h game in which I regularly alt-tab to keep myself busy while waiting for cooldowns to end, I'd take the former any day.
To give credit where credit is due, the game is visually pleasing + has a theme song I occasionally catch myself humming. There is definitely a good dose of creativity put into the aesthetics of Little Inferno. But though I don't regret playing it, I find it hard to recommend to anyone due to the ultimately dull and unrewarding gameplay.

A wonderful love letter to Ratchet and Clank, and Jak and Daxter.
That's what Right Nice and Grip Digital set out to do, and they did a splendid job. For a three hour experience you can sit back and enjoy more of what you love: platforming, collecting, puzzle-solving, enemy bashing, and upgrade nabbing. The visuals are dynamic and pleasant to the eye, with cell-shaded graphics adding a cartoony effect, like its predecessors.
The cons to the game are that it adds nothing new to the formula of 3d platforming or collect-a-thon, and it is amazingly short. The music I feel wasn't mixed very well wih the other sounds of the game, it felt louder than everything else. The transition to a different area on the hub world didn't feel natural. The characters were a little stiff. Also, there was a large frame-rate drop with battling the final boss each time I went through it.
But ultimately this doesn't take away from enjoying the game. In fact the last boss was the only frame rate issue I ever had. And the music was absolutely enjoyable to listen to. Also, there is so much to the lore and universe they have and can add, that I feel sequels and trilogies will pop up. Skylar and Plux have unlimited potential. Plus I really liked 100% the game in less than eight hours.

Well its a jekyl and hyde affair really with what could of been the best racing game ever, but ruined a bit by a couple of flaws.
What it gets right is the track realism, the variety of cars, the custom options, the career mode and there is plenty of challenge in there for all. You can customise your cars setup, tune it, and the realism of the cockpits and sounds seem to represent the real life cars. V6s, V8s V12s and turbos all sound different.
Unfortunately the things it gets wrong is the cars handling is a bit unresponsive with gamepads as there is some sort of controller input lag on this setup, but ive heard this isnt the case if using wheels.
The other annoying thing is the Computer cars AI is excessively aggressive at times, where they will deliberately swerve off their racing line to shunt you off the road when you attempting to overtake. The collision physics is all wrong and biased here too in favour of the computer cars, whereby a tiny contact will send your car shooting off like a rocket whilst the computer car barely gets affected.
Shame really, because is could of all been amazing but its let down by some flaws.
Overall would give a 7/10, but it could of been a 9 or 10 if the other issues were fixed.

The Witcher 2 is a fantastic game that I would recommend to anyone, especially when its often on sale for a very low price. Witcher 2 isnt open world like W3 and is a far more linear experience. The smaller areas the game takes place in are semi open and there are several sidequests in each area, although they arent amazing. Instead the main quest is far more prominent and offers the player important decisions which will drastically effect gameplay offering great replayability. Graphically Witcher 2 looks fantastic, the areas are all drastically different, the enviroments are extremely detailed and combat looks brilliant (monster apperance, effects from magic etc). Lastly the combat is a drastic improvement over Witcher I and is more challenging than W3, I found it to be highly enjoyable as I was forced to use different tactics for various enemies.
If you've played W3 you owe it to yourself to give this and Witcher I a look as well, and if you're new to the series entirely this is a perfect starting point (Witcher I's combat is a little dull by comparison).
It's also not required to play Witcher I or have read the novels on which this series is based to understand the plot (although you will appreciate some of the references).

As other reviewers have illuded, as  much as I have enjoyed games like Minecraft and Skyrim over the years, this game has been a nice alternative to the constant stress of exploring creeper-infested mines and caverns, or having to fight for your life forever threatened by orcs, goblins, trolls, zombies, and every other horrific imaginings. Airport CEO is a complex game. Its systems, even at this early juncture, are deep and sincere in their attempt to model real world airport operations and management. Like Prison Architect, its quirky graphical style belies a serious simulation of its subject matter.
While the depth and accuracy are great, they also make this arguably more of a niche game than Prison Architect. Airports are not prisons, and the air travel industry is a lot more obtuse than locking people up for murder. An example of this is how you construct your airport: you don't just hire a bunch of workers directly. You have to sign a contract with a construction firm and actually call them to summon a number of contractors to your airport. Want shops and restaurants in your airport? You'll need to build them in the terminal and then sign a lease with a franchise to operate each one. And don't even get me started on the baggage system (easily the most complex system of them all). But when it does all work, it's really a sight to behold.
For all the superficial similarity to Prison Architect and its ilk, this game right now, a day into Early Access, looks and plays like Prison Architect did after a year or two. And if it's that good now, imagine how good it'll be a year from now. The developers are committed and highly responsive. There have been multiple patches in the last 24 hours alone based on community feedback and bug reports. And to top it all off, it's less than $15. This is a no-brainer for anyone who falls into this niche (you will know it if you do), and for those who aren't sure, you probably should buy it anyway. If you might like a game like this, this is the game to find out.

I think this game is a nice mashup of turn-based (Gal Civ) and real-time (Sins) 4x space strategy. It holds up well as a representative of that genre in terms graphics and interface, but I'm guessing you're more interested in what sets it apart from the rest of the pack--for better or worse.
For Better:
1. The randomized tech tree system is an interesting twist on the usual tech tree. You don't know when you'll see a particular option again, so you really have to weigh each decision. There are occasional "rare" cards that show up, too, which are often related to anomolies you've discovered and researched with your science ships. I think all of this is well done.
2. You can assign leaders to command fleets, govern planets or sectors, man science ships or research teams, and lead armies. All of these leaders have their own traits and level up with experience. It literally puts a face on aspects that other games leave rather abstract or generic.
3. The ship designer lets you customize your ships if you feel like it. It's not as flexible as the designers in similar games, but it's better than nothing. However, I found it more convenient to just let the AI automatically upgrade my ships as new techs became available. In other words, it turned out not to be very useful (to me), but I still appreciate having the option.
4. The music is particularly good. Even after 60 hours of play, I never felt the desire to turn it off or listen to something else instead. Remarkable, really.
For Worse:
1. The developer obviously isn't a fan of micromanaging. Fine, but instead of allowing you to assign sectors or planets to AI, you're forced to. It's my game; I should be allowed to play it how I want, not how a designer thinks I should.
2. Upgrading your fleets take so long that you're better off just destroying or disbanding them and making new ones instead. This isn't realistic and feels wrong.
3. It's irritating during an intense battle to have to keep pausing the game to give new orders to a science vessel, construction ship, research team, or hire a new leader after one passes away. It'd be nice if you could somehow supress time so that you could focus on a battle rather than be constantly distracted with this stuff. It'd be nice if you could set your science and construction ships to automatically survey and build stations, respectively. While the system will let you queue up actions, this doesn't work if you don't currently have the resource (minerals, mostly) available. I'd rather it let me queue up anyway, and just perform the action if and when the resource becomes available.
In balance, though, I think the pros outweigh the cons, particularly if you're burned out on the classics of this genre. Half the fun (to me, at least) of these games is learning the ropes, and this one is sufficiently different to stay engaging for quite awhile.

Stellaris is a  great game. It draws elements from Civilization, Master of Orion, and Sins of a Solar Empire, without feeling like a clone of any one of those games. It is real time, but it almost feels turn-based because you can adjust the speed and pause at any time (and yes, you can continue to issue orders while paused.)
There is a bit of a learning curve, even if you are a master of the aforementioned games, so please do yourself a favor and click the "full tutorial" button when you start your first several games. There are a lot of nuances and advanced concepts, (such as genetically modifying races) that you are not going to figure out on your own - you need the instructions the first time or two.
There are a few bugs which need to be worked out, but the ones I encountered were all very minor and did not impact gameplay much (for example, I encountered a situation where the random name generators stopped working and I had to restart to fix it, and another situation where I had a strategic resource and it showed up in my resource bar, but when trying to construct something which required that resource, the game was telling me I did not possess the resource.)

For those of you that still haven't played this game, I strongly recommend you check it out. Of all of the games I have on Steam this is the game I most consistantly come back to. You play as Isaac a young boy who lives with his Christian mother, however one day your mother hears the voice of God telling her to kill her son as a sacrifice to prove her loyalty. The game definitely gives that creepy vibe of religious fanaticism. As far as gameplay it is very simply you move around with WASD and shoot your tears at enemies with the arrow keys. If is very simple but very elegant gameplay that takes very obviously after the original Legend of Zelda game. The difference is that Isaac is a rouge-like meaning that you play every run with permadeath, as soon as you die you have to restart and even cooler with the wide selection of items no two runs feel the same. You could get an absurdly powerful item such as brimstone or mom's knife to start off your run, conversely you might get something as awkward as lemon mishap. If you are a fan of randomly generated levels and runs that are different every time then Isaac is definitley worth checking out. Though just be forewarned of the messed up nature of the game. If you are alright with creepy, and downright ridiculous enemies, bosses and story then Isaac gives you a game with very solid gameplay that can easily give you countless hours of enjoyment that constantly leaves you with the feeling of wanting to play just one more run.

The first few hours are pretty great; exploring, getting all sorts of interesting pop ups from your scientist...the research system is innovative and I like it. Well that's about the good part...
After you run into some other empires, you'll soon learn that diplomacy is basically non existent. No really; don't expect much from it, since it's just (plain) mathematics, which most of the time you cannot influence enough...Factions that like you early on; those will be your friends. Factions that dislike you; this will not change much, not enough to become allies. Think you can do defensive alliance? Think you can join up to go to war to the same rival? Think you can actually trade for some energy/minerals? Well think again!
Allies suck either way; since the only thing they will do is follow you strongest fleet. Yeah really; that's ALL they will do, regardless of ANYTHING that is happening around them. Some enemy jumping into their home-system, just 1 jump away from them? Nope; not gonna defend it!
You thought there were interesting battles? Well perhaps in the future. But for now; you cannot do ANYTHING, you cannot tell your guys to hold a point (dont move), nor to attack the heavies first, nor...well you just cannot do anything.
And wait for the joy of battleships...see the AI is not smart enough to reduce speed when moving a sector...so your strongest ships will arrive after the rest of your fleet is already annihilated.
Colonies, sectors, planet management. I mean really; have Paradox not taken a look at any other 4X space games? Sectors suck so hard; the AI is just...well basically stupid. There are so many things missing; like the inability to transfer food from sector A to sector B. What use is a mining sector, if the minerals (surplus) cannot be transported from it?
What baffles me is how you create an galaxy with so little interaction. Not for a second does it feel alive. It is just conquer this enemy; conquer that enemy; alliances and federations are flawed and thus pointless. There are so many thing missing gameplay wise; I could write pages on stuff that seems so obvious, that Paradox must have known...and they still brought out this game and sold it for 40,- euros. That is just rather ♥♥♥♥♥♥; call it alpha access if that's what it is!

Garry’s Mod
Gameplay: Garry’s mod is a sandbox style game. In which you can make all sorts of things like cars, buildings, and practically anything. It is derived from Valve’s source game, Half-Life 2. But it can Also implement almost any game with the source engine like, Half-life, Team fortress 2, and Portal (Just to name a few.)
Violence: The game is derived from half-life 2 a bloody, violent, and gory mess of a game. There are multiple kinds of enemies and gun you can shoot, and yes there is blood, lots of blood. The enemies include but are not limited to (I will explain later,) zombies, soldiers, giant things that try to kill you, I am pretty sure you get the picture. On the gore side of things, you can disable corpses but when you shoot them they will ragdoll and flop until they disappear. The violence is realistic, and yes you can cut the zombies in half like in HL2.
Drugs: Yes and no, mainly no because they are not in the game its self it is in an addon.
Cussing: I have heard none in single player but in multiplayer the swearing can get intense.
Adult material: None that I have found in single player but people may have obscene tags and pictures.
Spirituality: Almost none, you mainly use devices to make stuff, but there is a no-clip feature that allows you to fly around. There is god-mode.
Online interactions: There is quite a lot, the game revolves around things called addons they are like DLC made available by the steam workshop. And there are multiple downloadable gamemodes, some of them being “Trouble in Terrorist Town, Stop it, Slender, Jailbreak, and more.”
Controls: Players that play many fps games will feel right at home, but will have to learn a couple of game mechanics.
My rating: For reasons above, and because of the game’s original gameplay I give it an 4.5/5. Recommended for ages 14 and up.

Really well designed game.
Since enemies only move with the beat as well the game almost ends up somewhere between a real time and turn based game. You can't move really fast but every beat requires an action to keep up your multiplier so you end up deciding your actions every half a second or so.
The game also has enemies designed that work well with the combat system. Their movements are predictable so you can plan around them. For example some slimes only jump between two squares, skeletons only move every other beat, dragons can only use their ranged attacks when you're to their side. This makes it feel like you're really improving since learning their pattern makes them much easier to deal with and lets you progress that much further in the game. There are also training rooms to help you practice fighting enemies once you've seen them before. All in all it really meshes with the rhythm mechanic.
Other than that some things worth mentioning. There are a few different characters with mechanics that can really change how the game plays. The music is pretty catchy (important for a music based game). The bosses are unique and music themed. The merchant sings with the music when you enter his room (this isn't really important but I liked the addition so I figured I'd mention it). Also the items in the game really help mix things especially the different weapons since they can have different attack patterns which will switch how you deal with enemies.
The game does have local coop too if you have someone you'd like to play with nearby. The dev said the beat movement nature of the game would make online coop impossible but local is pretty fun if you get the chance. The game is definitely worth a purchase it regularly goes on sale and it has quite a bit of replay value to it. I enjoy playing it every now and again even though I suck at it.

When I want to tell people about this game, usually I just show them trailers and gameplay footage. What you see is what you get, and it's pretty obvious that this game is unique and interesting, so I won't waste your time saying that.
There's two things that aren't immediately obvious about Necrodancer: first, this game is hard. There are games that require you to think fast and act with good timing, and games that require you to think logically and make good tactical and strategic decisions. This game requires BOTH, in a way I don't think I've seen anywhere else, so the parts of my brain needed to play well were sorely lacking in training, and I'd wager yours are too. It'll take time and patience to get used to how the game plays, simply because there's nothing else like this on the gaming market.
The second is that this game is HARD. Once you get past the initial "what the crap is going on?" stage... it's STILL really hard! It's really quite outstanding just how difficult this game is. If you play as Bard - the character who violates the "move on the beat" restriction - you'll see just how simple it is to get to the end and how short the whole game is. This really puts into perspective just how insanely hard it is to make it through a 12-floor dungeon when you have to move on beat. (15 if you get the expansion) Some of it is random chance, but luck is on your side; you'll rarely get screwed by a bad roll, only blessed by good fortune or not.
But if you don't mind dying and dying and dying and dying and dying and DYING, Necrodancer is well worth the $15 price tag. If nothing else, the positively ROCKIN music kept me going right from zone 1.

Skylar & Plux is one of those games that I can only describe as a love letter to the predecessors that inspired it; it is a beautiful platformer that clearly borrows elements from legendary series like Jak & Daxter, Ratchet & Clank, Banjo & Kazooie and Rayman, but does so in a way that feels like it pays homage to those games while at the same time constructing its own identity, rather than feeling like a cheap copy. In short, if you are someone who has enjoyed the aforementioned flagship titles, or just a person that enjoys 3D platformers in general, you will probably like this game. All that aside, lets take a close look at some of the game's most important elements.
Starting with the story, you take the role of Skylar, a humanoid character from a feline species, as she narrowly escapes from the clutches of CRT, a huge, evil robot that had imprisoned her and siphoned most of her memories for unknown reasons. Stealing a space pod with the help of her newly constructed, sentient robotic arm, Skylar crash lands on Clover Island, a beautiful seaside paradise that is under attack by CRT and his minions. There, she meets Plux, a talking, bird creature that wishes to escape the island and, seeing as their only chances of making it out alive are to defeat CRT, they join forces, utilizing Skylar's combat expertise and Plux's knowledge of the environment in order to take the fight to the enemy. While not an award winning scenario, I found the story to be quite entertaining, with a couple of interesting twists. Much of the game's lore can also be nuanced by talking with npc's that you rescue, adding some depth to the setting. To this end, I have to mention that some pieces of dialogue in this game are among the most hillarious I have ever heard, with highlights being the comedic exchanges between Plux, CRT and his underling, Bob.
Gameplay wise, as mentioned above, Skylar & Plux is a 3D platformer, with all the gaming tropes that the genre encompasses. Most of the game consists of Skylar traversing dangerous areas that require precission jumping in order to reach the end, while trying to locate all collectibles along the way. Of course, jumping is not all this title is about. Every area will require different strategies to be overcome, and that is where the various gadgets Skylar will find across her adventure come into play. From technology that slows down time, to a magnetic arm, all the way to the all-time favorite Jetpack, players are presented with a diverse array of gameplay mechanics and challenges in each level, keeping them from getting bored. Other than classic platforming, the game also has a few interesting puzzles, a couple of which will require some thinking to solve. As for the collectibles, the game tasks you with finding and freeing 51 Lua's, cute, puffy creatures imprisoned by CRT, whose cages can be found across all areas. Most of them are easy to spot, or hear, but there are a few that will test your perception skills. My only complaint regarding gameplay is the fact that there were some missed opportunities with the character of Plux. Throughout the game, he merely acts as a commentator and never really gets into the action. It would have been cool to include a few instances where I would have had to utilize him to get through a level, maybe some flying sections or something like that. Food for thought about a possible sequel.
In terms of graphics, in one word; Amazing. The visuals in this game are beautiful, and the same can be said for its art style. Everything is colorful and crystal clear, from the characters, all the way to the areas that Skylar and Plux will have to visit. Clover island is a majestic place composed of diverse environments, including lush beaches, mesmerizing desserts, imposing, snowy mountains, as well as mechanized areas, among others. There is an alluring, cartoony feel to the game that really works, fleshing out the world and pulling you into it.
Regarding audio, the game has a single main theme that is performed with different musical instruments, and in different ways, depending on the area you are visiting. It is quite enjoyable and never really bothered me in any way. The voice acting is also top notch, especially that of CRT and Bob.
As for controls, I played the whole game with a controller and had zero issues. Everything was impeccably responsive, which is vital when it comes to platform titles, so I would recommend using that instead of a keyboard and mouse, which I feel might not be very appropriate for a game like this. In any case, whatever works for you.
If there is one thing that people might find off-putting about Skylar and Plux, that would probably be its length. It took me around 5 hours to finish it 100%, including all of the achievements. Now, even though this aspect did not really bother me, I did find myself wishind it was a few hours longer, but only because I enjoyed it so much.
Before I conclude, I'd like to offer a few suggestions that it would be nice to see integrated in a possible sequel. First, it would be cool to see Plux utilized gameplay wise, as I mentioned before. Second, I'd like to have a more diverse array of collectibles to find, as well as an increased number of them. Finally, add secret areas to the game, places where players will need to overcome small, platforming challenges in order to gain something, a new gadget, a new ability, something along those lines.
All in all, I really liked Skylar and Plux. It reminded me of some of the greatest platformers I have ever played, and it is a breath of fresh air at a time when platformers are quite scarce, at least 3D ones. I had a lot of fun finding all of the collectibles and laughed quite a bit with some of the silly exchanges throughout the game. I am really looking forward to a sequel, since I'd like to follow these two characters in new adventures. For now, this is a great platformer that will give you a few hours of fun, as well as a nostalgia trip if you grew up during the PS2 and N64 era, like me.

Having been an AVGN fan for a while (and watching every episode), I just recently found out that the movie was on Steam, and on a dirt-cheap sale. So I rented it, expecting a B-movie really only intended for fans.
Firstly, I felt that the story was kind of mediocre. The overall idea for the plot was a solid basis, but then it gets muddled ad complicated amongst all the details. For what this movie set out to achive, it could have been WAY more straightforward, and that would've been fine. And the pacing feels a little off too.
I had similar feelings about the humor. About half of it hits, and the rest falls flat. For example, there's the track-and-field scene which pulls off some pretty funny innuendos, but then there's a flat-out boob-signing scene that's just plain weird. Numerous foruth-wall breaks poke fun at the film's campy nature and low budget. They gave me a chuckle at first, but they start becoming overused and... quite
I think my criticisms stem from the fact that this movie is a whole different beast than anything James Rolfe has done before. He's mainly stuck to short movies with short plots, and his web series where I think his humor fits tighter. This is decidedly not an AVGN episode; it feels like a whole different thing, and if ideas maybe got streched a little thin.
But then again, most of the soundtrack fit well and was pretty catchy. The acting was decent all-around. And most of the low-budget effects are right in plain sight. They're jarring yes, but they're also a large part of this film's charm; you're reminded that this was a passionate, fan-funded project just for them. For a second, you just feel like you're watching another video by James.
But then fanservice is a hit-or-miss too. There's a few very sneaky details that keen eyes (and ears) will appreciate, as well as notable well-done cameos. And then some are just in-your-face-you-can't-possibly-miss-this, which is not how you do it.
I can understand why a lot of people don't like the movie. Yet I got some decent enjoyment out of it anyways.
If you're not a huge Nerd fan, then skip it. If you are, it's maybe worth a rent, especially on sale. It's also a way you can support James Rolfe and Cinemassacre. But you'd also be fine just sticking to the AVGN episodes; you're not missing much.

Jumping off from The Witcher EE and right into The Witcher 2: AoK EE is a like a huge weight lifted off my shoulders. No more does the Witcher plod along with no sense of direction and clunky combat, Geralt has gradualted to next-gen. I feel kind of ashamed I haven't invested as much into these games earlier as they really are quite special and this game is espeically gorgeous to behold with it's visuals and combined soundtrack.
Where as the previous game felt loose, plodding, and directionless at times, the Witcher 2 thankfully tightens up the story and quests and this helps keeps the game moving and myself as a player invested in continuing on.
Many issues from the previous game have been adressed here and it's a blessing that CDProjectRed is a developer that actually takes feedback and improves their product. It shows here and I expect the same of Witcher 3 when I get to it.
The UI is improved, it's not perfect but a huge improvement from before. My only gripes are that you can no longer quickly switch between menus such as inventory, journal or map as you could before as you have to first exit out to the play screen and then go into the other menu instead of just, you know, switching menus. Potion brewing and bomb making is simplified now and thankfully doesn't feel like it takes up as much of your mental energy as it did in the first game. However you will need a blacksmith for making traps and throwing knives.
Speaking of, actual crafting of equipment is a thing in this game. You will need the crafting diagram for most better gear in the game and the necessary materials and someone to make it. In addition you can upgrade equipment as well. This all ups the ante over what was a rather static equipement system from before. Many new swords and dress await you now.
Combat has thankfully been focused more on action RPG mechanics now. You get a weak and strong attack for your swords with blocking, counter and dodge roll abilities. You mix it up with sign(magic) use and extra weapons such as throwing knives, bombs or traps. Same as before, steel sword for humans, silver for monsters, and it's makes more of a difference now than before. To note here though, I read in many places and I would agree that the in-game tuturial on the game's mechanics is lacking and unclear.
The only real gripe worthy change to mechanics was that potions are limited to use outside or before a battle only. While in theory this makes realistic sense... It just seems like a needless annoyance. The times you'll most often want a specific potion, you'll already be in combat and there isn't always a good indication ahead of time what you will need. Besides, sword oils are applied instantly in battle... So why again are potions not so? Just seems like a silly rule to follow.
Physical item limits are out, but now you get a weight limit typical of Bethesda RPGs. It's bothersome as it is in those games. Especially when you play as a loot ♥♥♥♥♥ like myself. Overwieght? Crawl back to an inn or shopkeep to deposit or sell things. Annoying, but I suppose it is preferable to the system from the previous game.
I do want to make a note about sound. It's not something that usually comes to mind when I play a game, but in the case of the Witcher 2 this game has some of the best use of surround sound effects I have heard in a game in some time. Most games I find it hard to distiguish actual direction with their sound effects, but whatever the Witcher 2 is doing, it's doing it right and it's a pleasure to hear.
Ah, dice poker is still here. ♥♥♥♥ it. Arm wrestling is a bit more fun, and the fist fighting is definitly more entertaining.
Also vendor prices are... a bit outragous. To put it lighty.
Okay, let's talk those sex scenes. The Witcher 2 is known for some great visuals and by now you've probably seen some of them. So... Yeah, I'm going to spoil here but that scene of Geralt and Triss in the elven baths is only good sex scene in the game. Everything else, at least from what I've seen is just a recycle of the generic brothel sex scenes. Honestly, I was disapointed that there were no other good, uniquely rendered scenes.
Now to be fair, there are two main paths in the game. The "Roche" path and the "Ioverth" path. I went with Ioverth on my playthrough as I thought it a more interesting choice but you only get acess to certain events on one route or the other. So this will likely necessitate a second playthrough just to experience things from the other route.
Overall, I enjoyed this game much more than the first. 8/10 for me.

I\'ve been going through the Witcher trilogy in the weirdest way possible. I played 3 first, then 1, then now I finished at 2. Anyway, this game is great. It\'s definitely not as great as Wild Hunt, but it\'s still good. Is it better than the Witcher 1? In terms of story, it\'s debatable in which story is better, but The Witcher 2 definitely improves from the first game in literally everything else. The gameplay is much smoother, the voice acting is much better, better graphics (obviously), the characters are better, and in my opinion the story in the Witcher 2 is about equal to the Witcher 1. I can\'t decide which is better. Both are pretty good stories, so that\'s enough for me.
My only gripes with the game is that the singleplayer is the shortest out of the trilogy, which is kind of disappointing, but at the same time it isn\'t because the story ended strongly and everything in the story was satisfying to me and they really didn\'t have to make unnecessarily long like The Witcher 3, but still. I completed the first game in around 50 hours. It took me ~80 hours to beat Witcher 3 (just the main story, excluding the side activities), and it took me around 28 hours to beat the campaign and the side activities. But it\'s fine. And plus, the enemy targeting system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. There were quite a few moments where I\'m looking at an enemy to hit, but the system is targeting someone else that I\'m not even looking at and it\'s kind of frustrating especially when you\'re fighting a group of people. Those are my only gripes. They were minor and they were addressed in the third game.
Tl;dr: This game is a great game. It has beautiful graphics. It has a deep and enthralling story and anyone who is interested in RPGs with good storylines should have this game by now.

Update after first week of release:
OK, Now I am changing my review to positive because there has been a lot of improvement this week. Around ten updates were promptly released by the devs and majority of the annoying and game changing bugs has been fixed as of now.
Some rapid feature implementation and improvement is going on, as well. Devs are listening to community and acting accordingly. There was a lot of criticism including mine about game manual and they already improved it. Auto maintenance of the facilities are implemented, and so on. Thinking of the featuers that are announced but not implemented yet; I can easily say that the huge potential is realizing slowly, but surely.
I am sure they are working hard in optimization. Still there is some way to go there. And it would be great if some sort of auto contracting or regular weekly scheduled flights could be implemented in the future. It is sometimes boring to sign contracts and arrange flights everyday. These are the two things that bug me in the current state of the game.
Airport CEO is how an early access game should be: Superb devs working really hard to improve and fix things, a great community offering very serious feedback, game already boasting hours of play and you already know what is to be implemented in future updates.
Go get it tycoon guys, Airport CEO must be in your collection.
My old review:
Well... So far, not so good.
There has been a big hype about Airport CEO and I think that the release has not met my expectations. I am not going to say this is a bad game. Concept is good, game design and art is very nice and has lots of potential. But man, too many annoying bugs. I mean very simple bugs here and there. Let me give few examples: Ramp agents not attending planes they can not find paths, luggage of the arriving passengers stuck on the baggage way. Things like that. Not game breaking bugs but annoying litte things that come together and make the game unplayable. I think these simple bugs could have been easily ironed out beforehand.
The game manual is also a weakness of the game. I had been stuck on many occasions on what to do to keep things working and find the solution by trial and error. A proper tutorial could be helpful.
And do not expect a very optimized performance from this game. My mid-end rig which performs satisfactorily in manygames suffers fps drops frequently. I think the game is not optimized well, yet.
And the good things: The Dev is very active and already pushed some updates in less than 24 hours to clean out some bugs. A very nice community is growing and many things are to be implemented in game. It has the potential to be the best airport management game.
Give it a little time, follow the uptades. If the Dev sorts the game out, then go for it.
And then I will happily update my review, as well.

After more than 140 hours game time I would like to share my opinions of the game so far.
First of all the game has fallen under alot of unjust criticism. I dont quite understand this. Maybe its because those that criticise so heavily are comparing the game to other paradox games that have had extensively more time to develop and have infinitely more dlc to pad out areas of the game that were lacking upon release (CK2, EU4, etc.). It is true that mid-late game is lacking on content but I do trust that this game will be the same as the above mentioned, paradox seem to have a formula they stick to and I for one am not complaining as they make the best strategy around.
Secondly, if the games mentioned above dont tickle your fancy, this most likely wont either. CK2, EU4 and Stellaris all follow a similar style of gameplay, just with a different background. This may turn some people off but it just makes picking this game up so easy for people who have had experience with any previous paradox games.
Following on from this, as per with paradox games, if your new to the developer there will be a very steep learning curve, one that will demand alot of time and could put alot of people off. If you are just looking for a game to sit down and play for half an hour, this is maybe not the best choice but it all depends on what your willing to give in order to enjoy the game.
To finish I would just like to say that this game has re-ignited my passion for gaming. This is the first game since the Witcher 3 came out, that I have sat down and played for 24 hours in a row and I barely felt it. I was and still am so engrossed in the game. This is my favorite game from paradox games so far and as a result i have completely neglected my girlfriend. So, so far 10/10, im expecting even greater things to come and I thank you for producing such a wonderfull game.

Colonizing planets and working tiles isn't fun, and warring is rock-paper-scissors with the additional caveat of "Do you have a bigger number next to your ships". The only reason for colonizing and working tiles is to colonize and work more tiles, and maybe war if you get strangled by borders. I have no interest in expanding my borders because they are not and will never be clear nor defined, but rather they are amorphous and often not even attatched.
Unlike EUIV, rather than having a hand in deciding how ♥♥♥♥ed you are when you begin, the game decides that for you by rolling dice. How well you advance through the early game and onwards is just a matter of "Did the game decide your starting planets and solar systems blow hard♥♥♥♥♥♥or not?"  As a matter of fact, rolling dice is involved in essentially everything in the game. Any goals or opportunities you have could easily be thwarted because the computer didn't roll dice good enough for you.
Diplomacy is essentially non-existant, as people will hate or not hate you for things as trivial as what traits and ethics you chose before starting. Even what you say to an alien race whilist first meeting them is pure flavor text. Traits and ethics do next to nothing besides minor buffs or debuffs that hardly matter in the long run. Along with this, what planet type you start on and what appearance you choose have no impact on any game mechanics.
As it stands, Stellaris is shallow and boring, but I'm sure Paradox would be happy to reach into our pockets to fix the issues the game has. However, the game is real-time rather than turn-based, which automatically makes it leagues more tolerable than Civ.

TL;DR: It's a new and overall great perspective on a familiar game many love, with it's issues, but it is an overall welcome addition to the Dungeon Defenders series.
Longer review:
I absolutely loved Dungeon Defenders 1. They got a lot of things right, and all into one accessible game. Now Dungeon Defenders Eternity came out, keeping in mind a lot of the issues that were in the original Dungeon Defenders.
They have largely smashed the hacker issue, due to server-side items. This requires an online connection, and I'm more than happy with that in return for limiting hackers.
They have have several notable changes to the class mechanics, some major, and some even controversial. In my view, the way to look at this is... this is not DD1. This is a familiar game, with a new perspective. Are the changes for the best? That's a matter of opinion. Personally, I find the changes refreshing.
They added on several new game mechanics, and fixed some annoying issues from DD1. Did they get every change right? Probably not. But overall, this is a new take on DD1 that I find a new great twist to a familiar game, and worth the one-time price tag for a still awesome game that now comes with much of the previous DLC content right along with the base game.
In the end, even with issues considered, I would certainly recommend this, what is in my opinion a wonderful game, to others.

A game of galactic empire where--playing on default settings--I was unable to find a single exoplanet to colonize.  (Looks like the game generated approximately 2 habitable exoplanets to split among 4 players.  None of them were in my half of the map.)
You can choose an ideology to guide your civilization, grant you special perks, and change how other civs react to you...but you select one based on how you choose to resolve events when colonizing planets.  Since I had no planets to colonize, I was apparently locked out of that entire branch of the game.
So far (14.4 hours played), I've had the game crash about 8 times.  The game autosaves, but doesn't seem to do so at the interval I specified in the game options.
Tooltips lie to me constantly.  The ship designer said I would unlock the next sensor tier at 10 sensor power; it actually unlocked at 8.  It said my ship design had 3 movement; it actually had 4.  The distance display (which I only figured out how to use by reading the wiki) told me it would take 3 turns to reach a particular point in space; it actually took 2.  The production queue told me the building would be finished in 2 turns; it actually took 1.  Colony morale showed a "coercion" penalty in its calculations that wasn't reflected in the total, and did you know that 9 / 8.8 = 88%?  Several techs that reduced the cost of various things failed to mention
they reduced the cost of, leading to hilarious tips like "-5% manufacturing cost, and also -5% manufacturing cost."
Terminology is poorly-chosen and inconsistently-used.  There's a split between "military" vs "civilian" manufacturing, but they really mean units vs buildings; colony ships and trade ships are "military" but buildings are "civilian" for manufacturing purposes even when they have the "military" subcategory.  Ship components are divided into 5 groups: engines, weapons, defenses, modules, and support--when a tech gives a bonus to "support modules", what do you think it applies to?  (Answer:  some, but not all, of the modules, and also some, but not all, of the support.)  Some effects stack with each other, and some replace earlier effects, and there's nothing to indicate which is which.
The UI is generically painful.  The tech tree is too zoomed-in to be useful, tooltips on the galactic map randomly fail to update when you move the mouse to a new gridspace, the building queue is way too tiny for all the building upgrades that get automatically added to it (and re-added every turn if you manually delete them), the borders of black holes are hard to guess, some galactic objects look very similar to each other, you can't see the name of the player who owns a ship even when you select it (only their crest)...
I'm not sure the designers understand the basic strategy of their own game.  If you add a bunch of items to any given production queue, it works on them one at a time, in order--working on them in parallel would be idiotic, right?  But then they encourage you to do exactly that with your military and civilian production!  You can force the game to do one at a time, but it's complicated--the UI was clearly not designed for it.  And then you can
that unlocks the ability to--wait for it--force an individual planet to devote 100% of its production to military (something you could already do anyway if you worked at it).
I was going to give the game one more chance tonight, but it crashed while trying to load my saved game.  Maybe I'll replay Endless Space instead.

40 hours in a single game and despite my federation covering about 50% of the galaxy with our combined borders, and every empire not within the federation being a vassal of either myself (mostly) or one of the other members, THERE WAS STILL NO VICTORY! I literally couldn't declare war on anybody and if I wanted to leave my federation to take over the other members, I'd need to wait a 10 year truce...
So often there are AI ships stuck in a system not moving anywhere, even when that empire is under immediate threat. If you click on the fleet, it will show that it is beginning to warp to another system, but then tries to warp to a different one, and it sits there flipflopping between the two. I managed to defeat my first major battle, despite me being severly underpowered, because I exploted this by attacking two systems on either side of the empires main fleet.
When you declare war, every other empire within your control (including allys), "look to you for wisdom". By that, they turn your highest "power" fleet into a deathball by following it with their entire army. This is so moronic that even if the enemies begin bombarding their planets, their main fleet will still follow you around like they are on a leash.
Now, this is helpful in some circumstances. You can take out some much more powerful enemies when you have a few empires worth of ships all attacking the same target, but come on, it would have made much more sense to split up and attack some different targets, especially in the end game when you outpower everything.
God forbid, if you decide to join a Federation with your Alliance. It works by giving each member a 5 year turn at being leader. They get to choose who to go to war with and what the demands will be in the case of victory. When it came my turn I found myself declaring war on 4 lesser empires just so we would still be at war for at least part of their turn, because in the 100 or so years that I was in a Federation, I think we declared war on two other empires, and had them declare war once on us. In all 3 circumstances, the AI leader would set the demands to liberate a few enemy planets. The problem with this is that the liberated planets still take a lot of work to befriend, so it's usually easier to just declare war on them and cede them like the AI should have done in the first place. Liberating planets is literally the dumbest move you could do in your war demands as it just prolongs an already severly drawn out game.

Binding of Isaac is one of the best games I've played on Steam. It has the right level of difficulty, an interesting base story, and a lot of secrets to uncover. Being able to play as a bunch of different characters, all with different stats and starting items, and random items every time you play through the game, makes the game extremely fun and random. Some runs will work, some won't and a lot does depend on luck, but even in a run where you haven't been particularly lucky you still have a chance to pull it off if you fit in a bit of skill.
This is one of the first games I played on Steam, and I didn't really enjoy it at first. I sucked at it, and couldn't even get to the first Mom fight. Eventually though, as I played the game more, I got better and learned how to deal with the various enemies. I learned advantages and disadvantages of picking up certain items, and which items were OP so I could hope for one of those. The wiki really helped a lot at the beginning to help me learn the items, of which there are over 100 each with different effects.
Though I believe it's intentional for some characters to be more difficult to play than others, it's not a feature I can fully appreciate. I like when all the characters in a game are balanced, which could have been very possible in BoI but some characters are still distinctly worse than others.
This game also takes a long while to get the hang of. At first, I played about 2 hours of this game then quit and didn't play again for almost a year. I was then reintroduced to the game, and I started playing it a lot more. It still took me another long time (maybe 40-50 hours) to beat mom for the first time, and then 100 more hours on top of that to beat ??? at the end of the game. It takes practice and patience to finally beat the game, but it's worth every minute of it.
The DLC for this game is definitely required. Wrath of the Lamb adds so much important content and it's not nearly as fun without it. There are significantly fewer items, less end-game content, less enemies, and a lot less fun to be had. Although, with or without the DLC, Binding of Isaac is easily worth the price you pay for it at any time. $8 is nothing compared to the amount of fun you will have playing this game.

Review is edited because this one wouldn't actually post:
But in all seriousness...
I bought this game for the Xbox360 when it first released, when I had heard it was released for the PC, I didn't hesitate to buy it again, at the full price. Yep, this game was valuable enough to me to BUY IT TWICE.
How this game, made by ONE person specifically for the Xbox360, gets a better PC port than most Triple A titles just goes to show the lack-luster effort devs with literally hundreds of millions of dollars at their disposal throw at trying to satisfy their customers. One guy was able to do it better than an entire team of hundreds of people.
This calls back to a time when games were made by gamers, for gamers - for enjoyment. Not by Publishers, for money - because f**k you. The game basically sells itself.
People look at cliches with a stigma of "It's bad" when really most stories are just variations of the "Seven Basic Plot Points". Without revealing too much you've got: Generally quiet, withdrawn protagonist with memory loss, with the comedic relief side-kick and a literal facist antagonist. If you haven't stopped reading this review by now, buy the game dammit.
As for the Genre, it's a heavy mix of Side-Scroller, Beat'Em Up, with some RPG leveling aspects in the background. This is a game you play for the gameplay and the story, not the genre itself, of which Dust: An Elysian Tale can't really figure out which category it's in.
Speaking of gameplay, it's more akin to well, Halo's difficulty curve - veteran Halo players will know that Legendary isn't that difficult once you figure out the technique. Enemies hit hard, and have more health the further you push it up. So people looking to be an unstoppable force should start the game on Normal, it's easy enough. The biggest jump between difficulties is that Checkpoints regenerate less and less health the harder the difficulty. 100, 50, 25, and 10 percent respectively from Easiest to Hardest. Once you find an item that regenerates your health, you just go AFK and wait for Dust to heal while you grab a snack or something. I mean you could use all that food you've collected/bought - but why would you? Gotta save that resource, of which you have no limit to the number of items you can hold, all the way to the end of the, by which time you've beaten it and went through like all 14 hours of the game without eating a damn thing while, considering the moves you can pull off, Dust has to be burning like 10000 calories an hour here.
Infact, that's probably my one critique, having to handicap yourself to make the game more difficult, even on the hardest difficulty. "BUT REACH IT SAYS YOU HAVEN'T BEAT THE GAME ON TOUGH OR HARDCORE." You got me skippy, I haven't... it's one of the few games for the Xbox360 I have to be completely finished for all achievements, back when it was released.
Other things I should probably address:
-"REACH, I SEE ANTHROS IN THE TRAILER AND THUMBNAILS UP ABOVE." It's the art style, honestly, I think anthropomorphic characters suit the design and direction better anyway. Pay no attention to it, the characters, save the talking sword, talk mostly normal save a few monologues. This isn't some spat-up Tumblr/Deviantart Anthro R34 garbage. Just by playing the game you can see the time and effort the creator dumped into making this game.
-"Reach, why are you posting this review so late in the day if you bought it all the way back when?" I rarely post steam reviews, and only for game I consider to be extraordinary. This was on the front page because of the Steam Summer Sale, 2016 and I went "Huh, I should post a review on that, it's a good game."
Ending notes:
-Buy it
-It's awesome
-Lots of fun
-Good story
-Great gameplay
-Feel the effort put into the game
-Find all the goodies and extras

Really well designed game.
Since enemies only move with the beat as well the game almost ends up somewhere between a real time and turn based game. You can't move really fast but every beat requires an action to keep up your multiplier so you end up deciding your actions every half a second or so.
The game also has enemies designed that work well with the combat system. Their movements are predictable so you can plan around them. For example some slimes only jump between two squares, skeletons only move every other beat, dragons can only use their ranged attacks when you're to their side. This makes it feel like you're really improving since learning their pattern makes them much easier to deal with and lets you progress that much further in the game. There are also training rooms to help you practice fighting enemies once you've seen them before. All in all it really meshes with the rhythm mechanic.
Other than that some things worth mentioning. There are a few different characters with mechanics that can really change how the game plays. The music is pretty catchy (important for a music based game). The bosses are unique and music themed. The merchant sings with the music when you enter his room (this isn't really important but I liked the addition so I figured I'd mention it). Also the items in the game really help mix things especially the different weapons since they can have different attack patterns which will switch how you deal with enemies.
The game does have local coop too if you have someone you'd like to play with nearby. The dev said the beat movement nature of the game would make online coop impossible but local is pretty fun if you get the chance. The game is definitely worth a purchase it regularly goes on sale and it has quite a bit of replay value to it. I enjoy playing it every now and again even though I suck at it.

This is a short game and the difficulty is fairly easy, especially if you choose not to explore too much and/or do not search for the "collectibles". I can see how some would expect and want a few more hours of gameplay, but as someone who is quite busy with a limited amount of time to play games I can appreciate a short, entertaining experience for a fair price.

Unfortunately some power-ups are clearly superior than others, meaning that you could be dominating in one playthrough and dying in the next, depending on your upgrades. Be warned that this game is hard, expect to die lots once you made it past basement. The inaccuracy of your tear attacks naturally makes this game more challenging since you have to rely on a bit of luck to hit your targets. As a result, your attacks can feel rather ineffective and it could get frustrating. Despite the utter randomness of everything, the awesome soundtrack, boss battles, and power-ups makes this game worth buying.
