2017 seems to be the year for the revival of 3D platformers, Yooka Laylee being the most prominent example.
While it wasn't as great as I expected it to be, it still made me yearn for more games like the classic Ratchet & Clank, Jak and Daxter, and Sly Cooper series.
For a game that has just four devs and a presumably smaller budget than Yooka Laylee, I vastly preferred Skylar and Plux. Sure, it was significantly shorter and only had one boss throughout the game but not once did I get frustrated with dated mechanics or awkward camera controls.
The camera feels snappy and never once screws you over, the platforming controls are tight and responsive, and the combat is satisfactory.
Its a shame that the game is so short, I beat it in just over two hours but still wanted more, I wanted more backstory for Skylar and Plux, more areas to unlock, more combat options than simply punching, spinning or ground pounding. More collectibles, more than one boss, weapons etc all of this would greatly improve the sequel if we get one.
Skylar and Plux themselves are... well they're okay. Skylar is a silent protagonist which is a shame, as having her banter with Plux would have been a delight, and Plux himself is a bit of a nuisance at times with some cringe-inducing attempts at humour.
Yet I still enjoyed the humour, it reminded me so much of some of the cringey moments in the likes of Ratchet & Clank that I beared with it. Maybe the devs could pull a Jak 2 and give Skylar a voice in the next entry, or at the very least add more humorous companions to meet.
Storywise its pretty basic but does the job, the big bad, CRT, has captured you at the start of the game and grafted a cybernetic arm onto you, at which point you manage to break out and escape, leading to your crash landing on Clover Island, home to Plux, who immediately joins you without question.
I mean, the damn opening cutscene had a freaking huge robot that I was hoping to fight but nope, it just throws you onto the island. The whole prologue felt rushed which was disappointing.
The game is riddled with clichés but it knows this and also mocks itself for it, something I admire. The banter that CRT throws your way at times is kinda funny but the amateur voice overs kind of drag it down, however for amateur work its still rather good.
Throughout my playthrough, the game ran smooth with next to no frame drops outside of clips showing the next area, which would absolutely tank the fps for some reason. Graphically, the game is packed with gorgeous colours, the Unreal 4 Engine being used to great effect.
In terms of music, my god its some amazing stuff, on par with Grant Kirkhope's work in Yooka Laylee, especially the whimsical track that plays in the first area, it just screams nostalgia and I loved it. The music combined with the first island had me feeling like I was playing parts of the original Jak and Daxter.
Considering its called Skylar & Plux, I went in hoping that we could at least use Plux in some way, even if its just for flying like Yooka does but all he does in this is talk and fly by your side, it would have been great if he could help in combat or by grabbing objects out of reach.
Finally, the one and only boss you fight in this is mediocre, usually in games like this I die at least once before I figure the mechanics out but it was so simple in this I beat him within two minutes.
At least one more type of collectible would be appreciated
Game is far too short, but again this is a budget game
Some of the voice acting can be bad at times
Combat is far too basic
Plux does nothing in this
Overall, for the current asking price and if you're a fan of 3D platformers then I recommend this. If a sequel does happen and has a bigger budget then hopefully they can vastly increase the size and length of the game and improve most of the aspects. A great game by an up and comming, tiny dev team, I hope we see more from them in the future.

Although it's a bit dated graphically, this is really an excellent horror FPS.  The weapons and gunplay in general are satisfying, and  enemy AI is quite good--far better in fact than what we've grown used to in SP FPSs, and it has an engrossing and haunting story that gradually reveals itself as the game progresses.  Levels do get a bit repetitive, though, which may hurt replayability.
It does have some cheesy jump scares at times, but the overall atmosphere is very tense and creepy, in no small part due to the surprisingly restrained but genuinely unnerving sightings of Alma, the psychic spectres of her former victims, vivid and disturbing hallucinations that the player experiences, and the poorly lit environs crawling with mercs and other, less human monsters that most of the game plays out in.
You'll definitely want to explore at least a bit, though, as a fair amount of narrative context is conveyed through voicemails, laptops, and overheard conversations that you'd miss if you're speed-running through the levels.  The plot, while good by FPS standards, is still incomplete and requires the completion of FEAR2 and FEAR3 to fully comprehend, which is disappointing since both of those games (story-wise) don't measure up to the original by a long shot.
If you like atmospheric, story-driven horror FPS with smart AI, look no further.  This is a new classic for good reason.
Oh, and the ending--so perfect.

This game was one of my personal most-hyped-for titles this year.  It looked like a fun mix of Ratchet & Clank and Jak & Daxter with maybe just a dash of Banjo-Kazooie and a faint hint of Metroid.  And it had a cat in it, which for a self-proclaimed crazy cat lady like myself is a bonus!  I wanted to love this game.  Which makes writing this review so hard for me.
First off, the camera.  The camera was too freakin' sensitive, always darting around if I barely touched my mouse (and sometimes when I wasn't touching my mouse AT ALL).  So many of my deaths could be contributed solely to the glitchy camera.  Oh, and the look sensitivity settings do nothing.  Trust me, I tried.  I can only assume this is because I was playing with a mouse instead of a controller.  Every other 3D platformer I have played on the PC I've been able to completely with a mouse/keyboard setup.  This is literally the only one that has fought me for not using a controller.  It's just a huge frustration that makes this casual game into a nightmarish heck to play through.
But let's say all of the camera issues magically disappeared.  Surely this game would become the grandest of all, right?  Ehhhhh....no.
First off, the titular duo.  Skylar and Plux.  Skylar's ok, if a bit of a flat character.  Then again, she does have amnesia, so she's not really GOING to have a major backstory.  Her design is very Samus-meets-Looney Tunes, which shouldn't work and to some people it won't but I thought it was fun.  She makes absolutely no sound, which is kinda weird.  But all in all, she's ok.  Plux, though...hoo boy, that Plux.  His design's cute, I'll give the devs that.  But his character is annoying.  He tries to be a funny sidekick, kind of like Kazooie or Clank.  But he falls so short with his weird references and butt jokes and constant Navi-style navigation.  And he never does anything but fly next to you.  Sure, within the context of the story its fine, because he's leading you around the island.  But gameplay-wise, he's just taking up visual space.  He never aids Skylar in combat or helps her fly over obstacles or anything.  He just flies around and makes jokes.  Oh, he also tries to tug at your heartstrings with his stories about his missing dad, but they feel more awkward than heartwarming.  This is coming from someone who usually feels bad for characters with missing dads, however flimsy their characterization may be; so if you couldn't make ME feel sympathy for your character then something went wrong.
Collectables.  You got your crystals and your floaty cloud people called the L'oa.  Both reset after you die.  The crystals resetting isn't so bad, but the L'oa resetting after you spent several minutes trying to get the camera to work with you while you jumped your way to them can be ragequit-inducing.  Of course, if you're unlike me and don't have camera issues, then this probably won't be a problem.  Still, worth mentioning.
Settings and soundtrack.  The settings felt like they were really big, but not with a lot of stuff occupying it.  Just felt very vanilla, which is a weird way to describe a 3D platformer's level design but I stand by it.  The soundtrack had some nice tropical/celtic vibes to it, but a lot of times it was just kind of ... there.  And they both blended into each other until I didn't really notice or pay attention to either.
Okay then, so that's all the negatives and neutrals I had with it.  Anything positive to say about it?  Well, besides Skylar's design, I really liked CRT.  His voice actor was the best in the whole game, and had just amazing delivery to his lines.  He got some genuine giggles out of me a couple of times.  Kudos to that guy.  I'm okay with it being short and casual (or at least, I'm sure it'd be casual if the camera worked right for me...I bring up that camera a lot, and I don't apologize), because sometimes being able to just pick something up and beat it in an hour or two is great.  And...ummm....well, its only $15.  In today's economy, that's a steal.
TL;DR: without the camera issues, I'd give this game a solid "meh" out of "wow."  Unfortunately, WITH those camera issues, I have to give it a "nope" out of "wow."  I am more than willing to edit this review and eat my words if they fix the camera, but until then...eh, just go play The Last Tinker or Yooka-Laylee or Poi or, heck, even Macbat 64.  Or just break out your old PS2.

You play as the silent protagonist Skylar. Equipped with a powerful mechanical arm, you must find away to save the island from the evil CRT with your talkative guide Plux at your side. The story is rather cliche, but even still, I didn’t mind it too much.
The gameplay is all about the platforming. You’ll spend a lot of time jumping, hovering, or swinging from one place to the next. Falling or being hit by enemies causes health damage, but you can easily heal this damage by collecting crystals that are found all over the place. If you do happen to run out of hearts, then you just have to restart at the previous checkpoint, so you don’t usually lose much progress since the checkpoints are fairly frequent.
As you play you unlock 3 different abilities that you’ll need to use to access different areas: a rocket jump, a time slow, and a magnetized glove. There are some puzzles to solve as well, but nothing that presents as much of a challenge.
Unlocking the three abilities, especially the time slowing ability, on top of increasing your total health pool does make the game significantly easier as you progress.
The game took me about 2.5 hours to complete, while finding most of the collectibles. There are still some other collectibles that I can go back and find though.
Skylar & Plux is a short game, but it’s cute, and it was fun while it lasted. If you enjoy casual 3D platformers with nice level design, and good platforming, then you’ll probably like Skylar & Plux: Adventure on Clover Island.

Gameplay:
Red alert 3 oversees an interesing  transition from RA2, incorporating numerous alternations to the gameplay that allows the game to be more tense as the designs shift more to what you will see in a serios RTS-- most prominently, ore becomes a confined resource which cannot be harvested exponentially by cramming your build order with harvesters. Units can be categorized into anti-infantry and anti-armor. Main battle tanks may be terrifyingly effective against armor yet at the same time they require five to six shots to kill some of the most cheapest infanty, which indeed is hard to grasp at first. As such, attacks emphasize on the cooperation of different units spamming only one type of unit would not bring you anywere. Micromanaging becomes vital through the concept of 'crushing levels' where infantry are subject to be crushed by incoming tanks while tanks are subject to be flattened by even bigger vehicles. Several secondary abilities and attack formations of the different factions also heavily rely on micromanaging.
The single player campaign is also incredibly entertaining. I loved the cutscenes shot in real person. The humorous plot is mildly funny and worth a laugh.
Graphics:
Absolutely brilliant special effects with breathtakingly beautiful water. Personally I prefer the rather vibrant hue in RA3 instead of  other CNC games or Starcraft. Antialiasing options lags the computer more than smoothing out the edges, however the game does not suffer from antialiasing issues much even without AA turned on.
Annoying bugs:
The pathfinding system is a total mess.
Sometimes units would take a full round trip around the building it just came out of before heading anywhere else.
Units getting stuck on the road for no reason.
Highly expensive naval fleet would randomly be stuck on the shoreline, becoming virtually worthless.
Units would line up and move single-filed, slowing each other down.
Nanocores of the Empire unable to deploy and stop en-route for no reason on certain maps
EA:
The experience for the game would be much smoother if it wasn't published by EA. RA3 had great multiplayer potential as with the introduction of the competitive aspects to the game. However, the servers in charge of hosting RA3 online closed down and there has only been a community supported server ever since, and the popularty of the RA3 community has been ever plummeting since. You won't find as much players nowadays as compared to when the gamespy servers were still online, and as a result matchmaking is almost impossible due to the tiny amount of players still playing the game.
Overall, the Red Alert 3 is a great game that could be great fun to play no matter by yourself or with others. However I certainly don't think that it is worth this price due to EA's unresponsible attitude towards this game. Buy it if you have some spare money to have fun with, but it is not on the must-have list.

this game would be awesome IF it wasn't for it needing soo many tweaks and fixes.
First of all is the targeting.  you virtually have no control over it.  sure you can hit the space bar to select the closest one to you, but too many times a bird would fly by and the dragon would act like the dogs from teh movie "Up" when they saw a squirle and immediately auto target the bird.  This is the game breaker for me. Too many times have i had a definate kill then all of a sudden a bird would fly by and my targeting would jsut switch and let teh enemy dragon get away.
Second, there are alot of balacing/Tech issues with the game.  The Server lags tremendously. too many times do you hit a skill button and it does nothing, in match making it puts you in with other players that are way higher developed than you.  For Example, when the more you play a particular weapon or dragon, the higher rank you get with it. it goes through the typic progression of no rank -> bronze -> silver -> gold -> diamond.  when you rank your dragon up it moves faster and gets more health and the weapons get shorter cool downs on the skills it gives you.  this is a huge advantage in games as either they can jsut out run you and get away or chase you down with you having no hope of escaping.
Thrid, is how oyu upgrade your dragons.  they go from I - IV and they get bonuses each time they upgrade.  you upgrade by getting 3 of a particular rank. you get dragons either by random chance by using crystals or you can buy the rank 1 for 2.99.  if you have a dragon you really like and want to get it to rank IV you either have to get really luckky with the random eggs OR you can by it for 81$ US.  Also as you lvl up you can start using Runes and to get runes you have to buy them with either crystals or using real money and even if you use real money the runes you get are totally random.  this is basically a pay to win game and if I am going to use real money i want a definate choice on what I spend my money on, not a random chance.
Lastly is the game type selection.  Instead of letting you choose the game type you want to play, the map is voted on and then for the next 30 min you HAVE to play that map.
This game is a huge let down because it has to the potential to be a great game, not only on the PC but console platforms too.  The game play is fun, but incredibly fustrating with all the issues it has that I mentioned above. I have been a huge fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd for almost a decade. I have watched every episode of his popular Yotube series many times over, and love the hell out of it. This movie was the combined effort of people like me - but not me personally because I'm a cheapskate - who love everything that James Rolfe does.
Starring a bunch of people you don't know, and a whole lot of cameos that you do know comes his first theatrical release... AVGN: The Movie.
I remember back in 2012 walking to the store with my best friend and being like Öh my god, I can't wait for his movie! It's going to be EPIC." Well, I did have to wait... a long time. Setbacks arrived, and ultimately delays were enivitable. What came out of all the hard work, and crowd-funded budget crunching is... well... James Rolfe made it. It's vulgar, it's juvenile, and it's The Nerd. But the most disappointing thing about this movie... is there is a whole lot less Nerd than I anticipated.
The plot centers around everyone's favourite nerd, who apparently has a job at the local Game Cops... clearly a pun on Game Stop. When a cameo enters the store, he goes on about the latest AVGN review. Then, another cameo walks in... get used to that in this movie. But, everyone in the store starts chanting for the man with a pocket pouch to review E.T. , because a game company called CockBurn Inc. (Yes... that's the name they went with apparently.) realizes that there is money to be made making crappy games instead of good ones... kind of like the plot of The Producers, except this is a video game, so the difference is clear... in that they ripped off no plot whatsoever... completely original story... well okay. The plot kinda sucks. Remember when I said that we all wanted a lot of game references, major cameos, Youtube star actors in similar fashion to Ashens and the Quest For the Gamechild? No? That's because that was implied. It's what we automatically think of when we thing "Angry Video Game Nerd Movie". He's gonna duke it out with E.T, right? Nah. He's gonna dig up  a bunch of games in the desert. You know, the famous Atari Landfill story. R I V E T I N G.   P L O T. So then they get in some trouble, some army dude thinks they are looking for aliens and almost fires the US National Guards most powerful weapon - the Matchbox army playset missile - and decides to go do it himself, because some random lady tells him not to. Don't worry, he gets his arm cut off soon enough. And then the other blown off.
So what about those actors we have no idea who they are? Well, the cast really is the "who dat" of budget cinema. We have our standard black sidekick who does nothing but be obnoxious, our attractive female double-agent and a soldier who doesn't wear any panties.  Who are they played by? Well, no point giving you their names, because no. No they were not in anything you know. Or in some cases, they weren't in anything at all.
The humour in this movie is sometimes a bit funny, but nothing memorable... unless outright stupid. And there are a couple of random, pointless gags in the movie, like the resident Chris Tucker impersonist saying the only thing that would survive the ultimate destruction of  Earth via the foreshadowing so heavy you ca barely see the set peice it's covering is... no joke -  bologna sandwiches. Why? never explained, never enlisted, never spoken of again. In the words of the Nostalgia Chick, that is what we call a "Big Lipped Aligator Moment."
The movie is just... disappointing. The effects are cheap, the jokes can be lame at times, and the nerd is not very angry. In fact he barely yells at all in this movie... and in fact, the E.T. review that accompanies the credits is... REALLY tame. I guess really if he made a full review, it would have overshadowed the movie itself, but as it stands, it's still a lackluster ending to a lackluster feeling,
But the thing about all of this is... this is an AVGN movie. If you were expecting a gigantic theatrical production, you clearly do not know the source material. Random vulgarity, non-sensical situations, and cheap production values are a tradition it virtuously upholds.
If you are a huge fan of AVGN, you owe it to yourself to see this film. Do I recommend paying admission price? No. As much as I love to support James in all of his endeavors, you are much better off just pirating it on putlocker or watchseries.

'90s nostalgia at it's finest. This is a PC port of the old PS1 game, no disks needed!
The controls are a bit limited, but I attribute that to the fact that this is a decades old game (holy crap, I feel old now) and the game was originally designed for a controller, so keyboard + mouse was not a consideration during the development of this game. Regardless, the controls feel fine and the only problem is this game's age and everything is done through menus unlike modern games. Overall, the controls are fine if you can learn the controls and learn how to play the game like you would have needed to when this game came out.
The story is an epic tale told in traditional JRPG fashion with memorable characters and many action-heavy in-engine cut scenes. This story, as with any good tales, has stood the test of time of it's lifetime as one of the more memorable RPG storylines in any game that I have played.
Overall the port runs fine on my system and I have had no major glitches or crashes, so this is a definite buy if you played the game on the PS1 and want to re-live the experience.

Good afternoon, dear readers! I would like to talk about a game like ABZU. The game is quite sensational and not just.
Pluses:
Music, landscapes, not difficult gameplay.
Disadvantages:
Price, no plot.
Let's start with the fact that it was done by a person who created such a game as Journey, and consequently, the setting of the game will be slightly strange, but at the same time bewitching. However, unlike Journey, the game also appeared on the PC, so anyone can try it out. Is it worth it? It is, and now I will explain why.
ABZU is an adventure game from the 3rd person in which you have to play for a diver and explore the underwater world. It sounds depressing, and from the part so it is. But there is something in this game that drags on a lot of time.
Graphics- One of the chips of this game. Do not be embarrassed that the game is made in a cartoon style. As experience shows, (for example Firewatch) the animation gives just the charm of the game. The underwater kingdom in ABZU looks just amazing, and if you also have a large screen, you will have something to see and really appreciate the picture. The transfer of colors, architecture, light, everything in the game is simply perfectly done, from which I want to explore every corner, the designers of the levels have enormous respect for such work.
The gameplay here is simple, we do not have to fight with the local inhabitants, and on the turn, the campaign of the game, we start in some sense to understand the fish, especially this is much closer to the end of the game when we get off the pier and along with the fish float down the stream to the portal. I also want to mention excellent music, which also fits perfectly into the game. The developers seemed to know at what point you will be in the right place and have tweaked music a second with your actions. Music by the way was performed by an orchestra, it is shown in the Steam game store.
Are there any downsides to the game? Perhaps there is. To the minuses, I would refer the ratio of price and duration. My game costs about $ 5 and it's expensive for a game where you just have to admire the scenery and music, and if you do not, the game can be played in 1 hour and 17 minutes, the proof is on YouTube. So there is no plot, because of what the player simply does not understand where he got, what he is doing and what is his ultimate goal.
The game is good and if you have a powerful enough PC, then I recommend this game to your collection, but I recommend taking it at a reasonable price.
Well, play, try, and I wish you to meet more good games!

I'd love to recommend this game right now but unfortunately the lack of polish and content in the mid to end game just doesn't allow that.  I will say it's a great base for a game and if Paradox supports the game with updates like they say they plan to then it very well has the potentially to one of, if not THE, best 4x space strategy game out there.
So I'll go through the game in order but first off I'd like to say at the time of writing this I've played the early game with 3 different civs.  Created about 5 civs and played 1 game until end game.  The one I played until end game was playing basically the Federation from Star Trek so was mostly peaceful unless attacked and such.  I've got all the achievements for the game pretty much other than bugged ones and end game ones.
Empire creation is nice.  There are good options and I really like the look of the animated portraits for the races.  They really provided a great number of options too which is wonderful.  They also provide a lot of options for banner symbols (though a few more background options and color choices would be appreciated, already mods out for these though).  They also provide some good choices for racial traits.  All in all it's a nice process with good options.
Early game is probably the most fun I've had in a 4x game mostly due to the science ship questing and surveying.  Now I could see this aspect getting stale after playing it numerous times but I'm not there yet.  Usually in a 4x game the early game tends to be a lot of hitting end turn, maybe moving one unit and generally just waiting for things to build up.  Here you tend to be juggling about 5 units from the start to survey and research, build mining and research posts and your fleet to clear out hostile aien space creatures.  Combine all that with the usual space 4x jobs of managing planet tiles, colonization and research and it does a great job of keeping you busy.
Mid game it feels like the game is done.  The exact problem other 4x games have in early game this game has in mid and late game; nothing happens, you just wait around for something to come along.  Now as stated before I was playing a peaceful cooperative sort of species so this someone led into this.  Once you have an alliance or federation and you've explored the planets you can up to the borders of those sueround you then the AI just sits back too.  Nobody declares war, there are no big events mid game to keep you busy, there's really nothing at all happening.  Now if you were playing a war civ then  maybe you could keep busy with declaring war but that can only be so exciting if the AI never initiates anything themselves.
End game can have some events to spice things up but they are very late and can miss entirely.  In my game I've had the unbiden spawn on the other side of the galaxy in the middle of the 2nd largest civ.  Due to diplomacy bug I can't get military access from them so I have no way to go after the unbiden.  The Unbiden are also growing very very slowly.  So them spawning has basically brought nothing to the game for me because my only options are to declare war against another civ which makes no sense for my empire or ditch my allies and join their alliance just to get access.  I've also been working on trying to tick off a fallen empire by researching sentient AIs but they refuse to declare war on me even though I've refused their demands and was sitting at like -400 or -500 relations.  My AI also hasn't rebelled yet though I've populated a couple planets with them.
So basically since early mid game I've had two very minor wars and other than that for the last 8 hours of play or something ridiculous (hard to estimate, I leave the game running at times) I've been doing nothing but upgrading buildings, colonizing planets as I research unlocks for new planets and otherwise just twiddling my thumbs.  It's been boring.  For the last 3 hours before quiting my campaign I've found myself watching movies with the game running in the background and just alt+tabbing to it when a notice sounds that research complete or a leader died grabs my attention.
The game also has a lot of bugs/unifinished aspects.  I've not had as bad of sector AI as some seem to have, mine build up tiles pretty well as long as I keep them supplied with resources.  They aren't perfect though and they really are lacking in dealing with slight out of the ordinary situations like robotic populations (they keep building farms for food that isn't needed).  The real annoying bug though is the regular locking up/freezing of the game since late mid game.  Basically the UI is still responsive but the game will basically pause and not respond for about 10 seconds every few minutes or so.
I think the problems are fixable and they've acknowledge some and pledged to work on them so fingers are crossed here.  But right now the game just isn't fun when it needs to be so can't recommend people buy.

I don't know why I like this game, but I do.
There are plenty of problems with it. The physics is off, there's plenty of rendering issues that make the engine feel very dated, there's not enough variety in crops, etc. I could nitpick for quite a long time about how I wish it were prettier and bigger. Because I do wish for those things. In particular don't expect a 'simulator' in the same sense that X-Plane is a flight sim; this has very arcade sensibilities. Nothing wrong with that but, given how little there is to really do, you'll start to crave more problems to deal with.
So, sloppy graphics, dull game play, lack of content - why did I click to recommend this?
First, don't get it if it's not on sale, there's a limit here. However, there's something sort of relaxing about such casual, basic work. Manging logistics really since you'll often not do much of the actual farming yourself but rather 'hire' workers. What will you be doing? If you're like me, probably this:
- Mowing; there are side missions to mow grass. It's fast and easy and gets you some solid cash.
- Package delivery, you use a forklift to take stuff around and have to worry about it sliding off the lift at a sharp turn or a big bump (you also need a good lift if you want to make the bigger runs in time).
- Hiring workers; you don't have to, you could do it all yourself, but any given field needs to be prepared, seeded, probably fertilized in some fashion, and harvested to start over again. Depending on what you plant and if you get tricky, you can do all this in 2 passes of a field. If you're not tricky it'll take 4.
- Driving a wagon; you can't hire someone for this which is why you'll be doing it all the time, driving a wagon up for the harvester to empty into and then taking it to storage until the prices are good for selling. If you tried to do everything yourself it would take all day to manage just a few fields.
So, goals... really just make money and get better equipment. Which is part of the problem, once I got the best harvester, the best tractor, could work with any fruit I wanted... that was it. Sooner or later I'd own the map and then what?
The game is 'idle fun' until that point, something to do while you're doing other things really, but it wont keep you going for hundreds of hours. It's certainly not for everyone either, so if you don't think you're going to like it, you probably wont, but if the idea amuses you, try it.
And if any devs are listening, take it further. More machines. More crop types and side missions. More things to go wrong: bad weather, insects, soil acidity, nitrogen loss - hell, teach me soil science as I play. Mechanic mini-game to fix busted engines? Hell, why not! Make working with animals more invloved too and don't forget long term goals. Make it a bit harder to stay out of debt, force you to compete with other farms, hire you to help with famine somewhere else. These are all just off the top of my head.
I know, it's not a game that appeals to everyone, it's not going to pull in game-of-the-year money, just my little wish-list of what could be.
For all its faluts it's still a recommendation, a light one but a recommendation.

Well under normal circumstances I guess I would recommend this game, but you are not here to hear the good things about this game, are you? Overall I think the witcher 2 is an okay game, but I want to talk about the things that I see as problems:
- The Save-System: you can't overwrite saves so managment of those is extremly clunky if you don't want to accidently delete something important.
- The dialogsystem: Sometimes it's not very easy to guess what Geralt might be saying, because everything is kept extremly short for example: "I don't believe you." became "You are lying, and now I'm killing you."
- The highlighting of the dialog system is a little bit misleading: yellow text is for quest's or things that advance the conversation, white is for trivia and other stuff that you can ask to get to know the world better, but sometimes there are dialog-parts that make the other person stop talking to you (starting a fight etc.) and in combination with the shortening of the text, it's not clear at the moment that this would happen.
- The choices of the game: Yeah they are in a grey area, but sometimes it's like asking me right or left. In the first game I could make my choices, after I understood what right and left were standing for, but here I had the feeling my choices were often a surprise box, and I have too open both boxes too know what I get. And too really get the bigger picture you had too go both of the bigger paths anyway.
- Can't drink potions: Well not in a fight, so if you played the first time you had to guess when to drink a potion and even then there are moments in the game you don't even get the chance to drink a potion because there is a dialogue before it.
- The story gets pretty political, so sometimes I had the feeling that I lost sight of my initial goal, like : What the hell am I even doing here?
- The Combat system: the concept of the fighting is pretty good when it works ,but it has a few flaws that are pretty annoying:
- The Lockon-System: Geralt automatically locks on the enemy you're looking at and if you don't have an enemy in your sight he still locks on and if you are pressing an attack button, he jumps straight at him even if he isn't even on screen, which can bring you in pretty bad situations, and with many enemies it is hard to lock on the person you want to hit.
- Enemies are invulnerable when the are dodging or switching weapons, even if your sword goes right through them, well you are not, you can even get backstabbed while you are dodging I mean literally midair, and you can take much damage while drawing your sword.
- Geralts different attack patterns: Geralt chooses his attack depending on the distance and position to the locked on enemy that means he might rollattack, spin around or just simply hit the enemy and that would be completely okay, if you could dodge while in animation, but you can't, and while Geralt takes his time spinning around with his sword, you are open to enemy attacks and depending on how many enemys that could pretty much mean instakill. (The spinning around, is the same button command which is used for the normal fast attack and the only trigger is the distance. 1 Spinattack is approximately 2.5 normal hits and most of the time you only have time for 1 normal hit.) In the combination with the not so good lock on system I often get the feeling of not being in full control of gerald.
- Quest-connectivity: There are a few instances where you really should do some quests before others, which I did not and noticed that something was missing in the quest so I had to backtrack to get the item I was missing to get the full experience , no way around I had to get this item on the long way. I mean Geralt can persuade, intimdate or hex people why can't I use that when it could really help.
- Restrictions of quests: I know that games need to have boundaries, but I got too often to the point where I wanted to do something but the game didn't let me. Like: If I just kill this person I'm going to change the outcome of this quest, but the game won't let me, or: can't I just investigate a little further, or ask this person this or that, those boundaries made me feel extremely limited and I just don't like that.
- Ressource-managment: You are collecting so much♥♥♥♥♥♥through the game, and you are not going to need most of it, but you don't know that so you scavange everything ,save all the money  and in the end you don't even need it...
Well that's it, don't get me wrong I kinda liked the game, but I had way too much "Did this really have to happen right know."-moments , you know this feeling as if the game was flipping you off.

I originally posted a similar review to this, but negative, only because of a bug I experienced where the game froze my computer. The review had only been up a day when it was commented on by a developer, who helped me fix the problem. I was very impressed by this display of care and decency. So on top of all the great things I have to say about this game, the developers are great people who listen to feedback! Now to the original review:
First off, the real star of the show: the soundtrack. I don't listen to electronic music by choice, I prefer rock and roll, but this soundtrack is one of my most played on Spotify. It is absoloute genius right down to the last gram, and it seronades the gameplay perfectly and makes you feel awesome as s**t the whole time. It still sends a shiver down my spine when I get to the last level of stage 4, hearing "Wight to Remain" come on. I really can't recommend this soundtrack enough.
The gameplay might start off basic to get you into the swing of things, but it becomes as intense as the soundtrack, with monsters coming at you from all sides. It's difficult, but when you pull of a combo, killing 5 enemies without pausing, it feels great. But then the other 90% of the time you'll fluff this and die really quickly XD. The difficulty jumps quite severely every time you unlock a new stage, but this is the benefit of the random generation: you don't get bored trying to learn the new attack patterns and getting used to the new stage. The negative reviews of this game seem to site extreme difficulty, but I think the key thing is whether or not you meld well with the concept of playing to the beat. If it's something that comes naturally to you, then you just groove to the music and you'll feel like a god. If you have to concentrate on the beat then you are gonna have a hard time.
I've recently been having a go at the All Stages mode, which is so much fun.
There is some ambiguity to the items etc. so you have to do some trial and error to find out what they do sometimes. One of my best runs was ended because I picked up a ring marked "???", which makes you die in one hit (FYI its the one with the brown band and grey tentacle skull on it. DON'T PICK THAT RING UP). Things like that might be frustrating, but its a system that promotes learning the hard way.
The story isn't really the focus of the game, but it's a bit whacky. Once you complete all 4 stages you do it again for story reasons with a different character. This is actually probably my one actual problem with the game: when you do the game a second time they change the soundtrack so it sounds all weird and I don't like it. Maybe you will, but I really like playing with Cadence so much that I haven't really explored the other characters. I was also informed by the developer that you can change this to the original soundtrack for all the characters.
This is a fantastic game, especially if you're into music, so please give it a try.

If there’s a phrase that can be associated with this game, “ Moving to the Beat ” would suit it perfectly. Crypt of The NecroDancer is a Hardcore Dungeon Crawler Roguelike Rhythm game, in which you do anything and everything while moving to the beat.
From the first glance, the game might seem like an easy indie game. But don’t let the visuals confuse you, because the game delivers its promise of being a Hardcore Dungeon Crawler Roguelike Rhythm game.
Author’s Note : This might be a bit unrelated, but it plays a big role down the line if you mess it up. When you first start the game, you’ll have to calibrate the heartbeat for a minute or so. Try and make sure you have 0 delays, because missing a beat in this game can be the difference between life and death. And playing the tutorial is mandatory, because It explains the controls and how the game works.
The gameplay is pretty simple, you make every action to the beat of the music. This includes interacting, attacking, picking up loot, everything flows to the beat of the music. You move square by square horizontally or vertically, so every beat you can move to another square, attack if there’s an enemy on that square, interact if there’s something to interact with on that square, etc.
This game can be supposedly completed in under 2 hours, but I have clocked in 100 hours (as of writing this) and I still haven’t been able to finish this game completely. I guess that’s a testament to how hard this game is.
The game isn’t necessarily hard it’s pretty in-depth actually, but it comes down to it being situational. As the name implies, this means that the difficulty comes down to your ability to react accordingly to each situation.  This is because dealing with an enemy needs you to attack in a specific move pattern. Each character is different in how you have to tackle enemies, but how you tackle them will be dependant on what your situation is.  Wether it be how much damage you can dish in a single beat, how much range your character can cover, or even the type of enemy you are facing are just some of the many ways in which you have to assess the situation.
But Timing is the actual difficulty of the game, since everything moves to the beat. Every action you make has to be in sync with the beat, hence why “ Moving to the beat “ is applicable to everything in the game. As the game progresses, the song and ultimately the beat will steadily becomes faster and faster. The enemies do have simple patterns, but the beat will still get to you and cause you to make dumb mistakes that might result in your death.
The best part of this game, is the characters. The character just doesn’t add a thoughtless gimmick, but it changes the whole game drastically. The best example to this is Monk, his gimmick is that if he picks up gold, he will instantly die. The problem is that every enemy in the game drops gold, and even bosses which didn’t, do now. This makes positioning key for Monk, as you cannot move to the same square that an enemy has died on. And since the only way to remove gold out of places is to blow it up with bombs, killing enemies strategically is advisable if not mandatory to lessen the clutter of insta-kill pennies of doom scattered on the level.
The soundtrack is pretty good, I guess. The songs are really good, but the thing that wore it down is that you’ll be hearing them often and sometimes too often. Thankfully, the base game provides 4 remixes of the base game soundtrack that you can pick and choose to which levels get which songs set.
This is one of the best and hardest games that I have ever played, although this game is pretty niche. Reccomending this game for the general audience would be hard, but I could easily recommend it to any fans of the Roguelike and Rhythm game genre.

F.E.A.R. ~ An almost forgotten relic from 2005.
If you managed to find this game because of curiosity, a recommendation from a friend, you're an old FPS die hard fan, or some other reason, this game may leave you satisfied.
The major strengths of F.E.A.R. consist of a suitable soundtrack in which the music matches with its appropriate scene. If you are isolated and cannot predict what is around a corner, there will be suspenseful music. Otherwise, a fierce firefight will make your blood pump faster and the music won't disappoint.
The A.I. for the enemies, specifically the Replica forces, will not bore you. They are unpredicatable and vicious for they only serve to complete the main antagonist of the game. In other words, the movement of the Replicas are well coordinated and they tend to flank. In harder difficulties, their attacks are more devastating thus forcing you to avoid confronting more than a couple of these soldiers. Each Replica unit is unique and I find most of their voices, interactions with their squad and the given environment, and the way they assess threats very realistic.
There are a ton of weapons , ranging from the usualy pistol and shotgun, to a futuristic particle weapon that can sear the flesh off a living being.
Thanks to "Slow-mo', the one ability in this game that makes a difference, F.E.A.R. allows you to see your inflicted destruction on targets in a "beautiful" way. This is what gives you the ultimate power over your enemies.
Although I do like this game, its existence is not without cons unfortunately. F.E.A.R. was heavily focused on action and left other parts of the game underdevelopd.
The plot is scarcely detailed and relies too much on listening to mundane laptops , voice mails, and some news reports. These are easily skipped and it's a waste of time to listen to them.
Overall, most of the characters are forgettable and they don't have that much interaction with each other.
Some of the transitions between suspense, horror, and action seem quite "choppy". In greater detail, if you leave an area after a fight, you're almost immediately pulled into a terrifying scene. This will make a lot of players more confused than scared.
As for the expansion packs, they are acceptable to play. Be warned though, that Extraction Point is more horror oriented, has more jumpscares, and the plot is even thinner. After playing it for a while, you will lose your interest if you favor action. On the other hand, Perseus Mandate seems like a ripoff of F.E.A.R. and its aforementioned expansion pack. There may be some new enemies, weapons, and 3 "bonus missions" that can test your skill but this game will leave you more upset if you're a loyal fan. In my case, the most hated part of the game for me was the music. It was good but it's not sutiable for a F.E.A.R. game!
Despite the criticism, I do recommend F.E.A.R. if you like to possess "slow-mo" and mow down enemies with any newly obtained gun. So far, the action is what keeps me playing F.E.A.R. every once in a while.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is an action-platformer indie title taking some inspiration from classic platformer RPGs, like Summon Night, Valkyrie Profile or Super Paper Mario. It follows the adventures of the amnesiac super-fighter Dust who everyone seems to know from somewhere, the wise old talking magic sword Ahrah, or more specifically, the Blade of Ahrah, and the hilarious flying nimbat Fidget, the protector of the Blade of Ahrah. You use either the mouse and keyboard or a controller (which, trust me, is the far better option) to control Dust and, to a lesser extent, the other two as they explore the Metroidvania world and fight endless monsters on a quest to recover Dust’s memories and stop the murderous General Gaius.
The first thing that will strike you about this game is its beauty. Every sprite, except for the Blade of Ahrah, is hand-drawn and scanned into the game, and whoever made these things is one of the best artists in the modern world. It’s like Rayman Origins and Muramasa: The Demon Blade combined, and it is, by far, one of the best-looking games I’ve ever seen. You know this is fantastic place when even the giant man-eating spiders are a work of art. Equally well-done is the soundtrack. Every song gives me chills to hear and fits its stage like a glove. For the most part, it’s completely orchestral, and adds to the overall effect of the game’s appearance. The voice acting for the main characters is generally fantastic, and the story, while slightly predictable and one-noted, is presented quite well and the climax at the end that everything leads up to is Lord of the Rings-level in epicness. Every area is incredibly atmospheric and varies from underground crystal caverns to mountains where you climb on enormous stone statues that have fallen form their perches, giving you a full range of the visual capabilities of this game. If anybody doesn’t believe that video games can be a form of art, this is the game that will single-handedly prove them wrong.
The combat is fluid and fulfilling, and the combo meter, while kind of useless, adds quite a bit to what would otherwise be a rather boring battle. Getting up that combo meter feels so satisfying, even if it adds almost nothing to the core game besides refilling some of Fidget’s power and completing a single sidequest. Oh, and it adds experience, but you’ll never really know the difference. Speaking of sidequests, there are quite a few here, and they make up about half the game’s length. They range from simple material quests to searching for survivors of an attack by soldiers to a cursed box owned by a paranoid creature who thinks its his mission in life to destroy all toothbrushes. Every one has a suitable reward and is actually quite fun, with the exception of the black sheep quest. There are five black sheep hidden in the dark, massive area of Cirromon Caverns, and if you miss a single one your first time through, may the great Pokémon in the sky have mercy on you.
Now, as I have shown, this game is a true work of art, but it isn’t perfect. The combat is fluid, but it requires almost no skill to win any of the battles. There are some special moves and combo attacks you can do, but it often ends up being way easier to just mash the buttons, and it actually ends up looking just as flashy and feeling almost as satisfying. The Dust Storm, especially when mixed with Fidget’s Fireball ability, is one of the most overpowered things in any video game ever, and makes every single battle or boss that would otherwise be a difficult fight into a complete cakewalk. This one ability combination will get you through the entire game with ease, no matter what difficulty you put it on. In fact, this is a pretty easy game, with most of the challenge coming from the unlockables, until you hit one of those weird difficulty spikes, like fighting Lady Tethrys or when you first enter the Sorrowing Meadows. The entire layout of the maps are often confusing, and you always end up forgetting where certain objects and unlockables are. The voice acting is usually spot-on, but then there are the occasional actors, usually playing children, who sound like they’re just trying way too hard. Most of the villains are dimensional and well-sided, with the odd exception of General Gaius himself, who never gives any reason for his murderous purge other than he doesn’t think the people he’s killing are worth much, though he seems to be very friendly to people he knows. It’s kind of weird, seeing a guy who’s so nice who is still most definitely the villain and not an antihero. It’s almost kind of jarring, and makes you question whether it was intended.
There are occasional glitches, like the time I got a combo of over 1500 and it still didn’t complete the sidequest, and the stage hazards are often devastating to Dust, trapping him in endless spike loops or striking you with poison when you don’t yet have an antidote. Such hazards can usually only be avoided through large amount of platforming, and let’s just say that Dust isn’t half as smooth in jumping as he is in fighting. One of the most annoying part of the game is the ridiculous knock back Dust takes whenever he’s attacked, especially with an explosion. It sends him halfway across the screen, off of platforms, far from battle, and sometimes into other screens entirely. Easily the worst part of the game though, are the enemies.
Almost all of them can fit into three categories: fast and annoying, slow and ridiculously powerful, and completely useless in every regard. Every enemy in every new area feels like a reskin of a previous one, and the game compensates for your overpowered-ness not by giving you more creative enemies with better AI, but by throwing enemies into areas where they should never be, resulting in a lot of cheap shots, and sending small armies of them for you to deal with at once. It gets tiring really fast. There are a few really cool original enemies, but they’re always very rare and almost never used to their full effect.
Ultimately, though, most of these are nitpicks. The combat, upgrades, exploration, characters and polish of the game are top-notch, and, while it may be a little short, it’s no worse for wear. At some points you’ll just let go of your controller and let your jaw drop in amazement of the beauty and atmosphere, and other times you’ll almost get emotional about some little subplot that you should hardly care about. Little things like notes from servants of a long-abandoned mansion really flesh the world out, and the three-way interaction of Dust, Fidget, and Ahrah alone makes the game worth buying.
Overall, Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game that gets almost everything right. It's one of those games that could easily get by an atmosphere alone, but it keeps going through excellent gameplay, working controls and an overall sense of fun. It’s a diamond with a few rough cuts, but no less beautiful and valuable. This is one game that’s certainly worth buying on any platform.
On the GameInformer scale of 1-10, with 7 being average, 10 being perfection, and 1 being the Ouya controller, increasing by increments of 0.25, Dust: An Elysian Tail, gets a 9.25 out of 10.

F.E.A.R. is an interesting game with heavy inspiration from horror movies like "The Ring" (Haven't you noticed that the scary girl from The Ring looks and acts almost identical to Alma?) And succeeds in almost everything it sets out to do. The gameplay is solid, the music is good, the graphics are very impresive at the time it was released, the level design is great, and the enemy AI is still superior to most games today. Not to mention the awesome weapons that you can find (The minigun is my faverite!).
Now for the parts of the game which aren't so good, the story in F.E.A.R. 1 was servicable, but in Extraction Point and Persus Mandate I didn't feel as though anything important happened. What dissapoints me the most however is the horror aspect of the game: F.E.A.R. isn't scary, it just isn't. There is never a moment in the game where you feel vunerable because of all of this elite weaponary you have on top of the slow-mo. It's really hard to genuinly scare someone after they just single-handedly destroyed two mechs with a rocket launcher. That isn't to say that the game doesn't have it's scary moments, but those scary moments only take up about 25% of the game.
Overall F.E.A.R. is a very good game, and and I did have fun blasting someone in the face with a shotgun in slow-motion. But if you want to play a game just for the horror aspect, you might want to pass on this one.

To be completely honest, it's weird for a game like this to actually be pretty scary. When you think about it, there are no real horror like enemies in the game. No weird monsters or mutated freaks. Just Replica Soldiers. But god the atmosphere in this game, along with the audio can be so thick that you can cut it with a knife. The environments are dark and sometimes in states of complete ruin. The noises you hear are just terrifying, and ugh, don't get me started on the late game stuff.
You can sorta put this game into two parts.
The first is the action part. Where you're shooting enemies and trying to stay alive. Whilst it's mostly standard shooting stuff, you have a feature called Reflex, witch pretty much acts like bullet time from Max Payne. And like Max Payne, it helps to elevate this game, and even the odds against your enemies. Plus they actually give you a story reason for having it!
The second part is exploration. This is where the game gets scary. When the music and ambiance ramp up, and that little comm symbol in the corner displays a flickering "Unknown signal". You know that you're in for some freaky stuff. This is where the FEAR shines. I was legit hesitant to move on because of how much I was scared and worried about what was to happen. Even if I knew that I was in no danger.
Now I mentioned that there are no "Monster" type enemies in the game, but that's kind of a lie. In certain segments, and parts near the end, you fight aparition like monsters. But like I said, they're kept for very specific parts and for a short while.
If the main game wasn't enough, however, it also comes with the two expansion packs, Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate, for absolutely free, adding another 5 hours each to an already 8 hour game.
Extraction point is a direct (But non canon) sequel to the first game, taking place where it left off. Due to events at the end of the first game, the area you were in has been devestated, and the supernatural anomolies which were mostly contained are running in full force.
This expansion I would almost say is even scarier than the main game, mostly for the fact that, like mentioned, the supernatural is now in full force. You'll be fighting some more creepier enemies, and going through a lot more scary♥♥♥♥♥♥than the main game. Along with the newly added weapons, this is the best out of the two expansions.
The main problem with the second, Perseus Mandate, is that it feel like more of the same. Non of the new weapons from Extraction point appear, and the only thing they add are a new enemy or two. It's still creepy, and still fun, but not as good as the other two parts. I'd suggest playing this one first if not for story reasons.
But overal, F.E.A.R is more than worth getting. The online feature doesn't work anymore but, it is still a great, and horrifying single player experience.

I'm about halfway through the game right now (interval 6 out of 11) and I don't see anything changing at all in the other half so I figured I may express my thoughts about this game right now. I'd describe the overall experience of the game to be pretty poor. It's incredibly linear, featuring corridor after corridor after corridor filled with office props and sick♥♥♥♥♥dynamic lighting. I've always heard about FEAR having stellar gameplay due to the gunplay mechanics and smart AI but here's how the gameplay usually goes: you walk through corridors, press some switch, walk some more and hear the occasional "kill the bad guy" on your comm link and then maybe you fight some enemy grunts and walk some more. There is a level where you're supposed to run after some annoying fat guy and it was literally corridors - turret - corridors - turret - corridors - two turrets - end of segment. I understand the reasoning behind your character running at an extremely slow speed with no sprinting as it sets a specific horror-ish pace for the game however the entire "horror" aspect of the story seems to be a couple of spooky things happening (which seem to completely go away mid-way through the game). Adding to that, there's no survival horror involved, you always have plenty of ammo and are always maxed out on health kits. That being said, you can still be killed in seconds in a firefight. Speaking of fights, I can't figure out why people are praising the AI so bad in FEAR, 90% of the enemies you encounter are grunts wielding the same guns as you and their behavior reminded me of the soldiers in the first Half-Life who would try to flank you or flush you out with nades and sometimes run away from the fight for their own sake. Usually you would just enable slow-mo and mow most of them down and then deal with the rest with the arsenal available to you. The game also completely lacks music at some points and it may take away some of the joy from shootouts.
Overall, FEAR is and should be mostly praised for its gameplay as its other aspects are downright horrible apart from the visuals (although they mostly consist of the same environments), if praised at all. In my opinion the gameplay could be improved so much if Monolith completely ditched the plot narrative, uninteresting story and cardboard characters. If you're attempting to create John Woo-styled gunplay mechanics then make the movement faster and add more "run and gun" options for people to play around with.
IMO: FEAR is still worth checking out for its dirt cheap price despite its flaws and problems.

With most horror games, they blow their load early and show you the scariest stuff in the first ten minutes. Over the course of the game, the player becomes desensitized to it, having to repeatedly encounter zombies and monsters across the span of 7-10 hours.
F.E.A.R. on the other hand is a game of build-up. It doesn’t start out especially scary, but as I kept playing it, it very gradually started to creep me out. I would hesitate to say that it outright scared me, because it takes a lot for a game to legitimately scare me. But as you creep around its desolate office complex, an unsettling feeling begins to seep in to your brain. It’s like being in a supermarket after hours - a place so obviously bustling with people and noise and life, now empty. You can’t shake the feeling that something’s wrong and you really, really shouldn’t be here. Everything’s too quiet and you feel a little vulnerable.
Eventually the tension mounts and the creepy atmosphere pays off. The end of the game could’ve had a bigger finale with some sort of climactic boss encounter, but ultimately it doesn’t need one. The ending is unforgettable even without a big scary monster to kill - and maybe that’s for the best. I’d complain that F.E.A.R. ends on something of a cliffhanger, but all the best horror movies do, and so too does F.E.A.R.

A fun callback to old PS2 platformers.
There's not a whole lot to say about it, if you liked Jak and Daxter and Ratchet and Clank, this will also be up your alley. It doesn't revive the genre or nything, but it has a couple of interesting quirks that make it more than a clone. The look is great, especilly the desert temple level, and the character design is on point too. The movement is just as good as you get in any of those older games (I particularly liked the rocket long jump, it felt very good), and it is a major plus that there aren't a whole lot of invisible walls or intangible platforms. I was able to get all sorts of places I clearly wasn't meant too, and I could stand on them and there was grass and trees on them, so I really applaud the level of detail. The story is nothing impressive, but it's still better than Ratchet: Deadlocked, so it's not a problem or anything. The combat is actually pretty fun once you get more gadgets, and I would really like to see something more done with that if another game comes out. The voice acting is fine, with CRT standing out but the rest are serviceable, though it would be nice if there was some voicing for Skylar, like grunts or something when she punches.
All in all, i liked it a lot and I recognize that much of that comes from nostalgia. If you loved PS2 platformers, you'll love this, and so will younger kids who are wanting something more than Skylanders. But if you're not already a fan of 3D runing and jumping and not much else, you might not see the charm.

Hey, hey, kids! How are you doing today? Are you having fun? No? Are you bored of the internet? Cat pictures and♥♥♥♥♥♥not enough for you? All these electronics all over the place just white noise getting in the way of your fun? I have an idea!
BURN IT ALL. EVERYTHING. HA HA HA. IT'LL BE TONS OF FUN. AND IT'LL KEEP YOU ALL NICE AND TOASTY-WARM. DO IT. BURN ALL OF YOUR TOYS. BURN IT ALL.
Oh? You can't? Well, why the ♥♥♥♥ not? It's easy, come on, anyone can do it. Here, I'll even get you started. Here's your own little personal, nonstop, high-definition, entertainment fireplace. Little Inferno! (Uproarious screams of feral children)
Little Inferno is the latest indie masterpiece from the geniuses behind World of Goo, over at Tomorrow Corporation. Originally a launch title for the Wii U's eShop, Little Inferno also found a nice home on PC and Mobile.
Like its predecessor, Little Inferno is incredibly unique. The art style is noticeably distinct, with a strong Tim Burton vibe. And that style seems to leak into every other aspect of the game in all of the best ways. Your only purpose in the game is to burn everything. Burn it all. Let it all burn. If that doesn't sound like fun to you, why, you may as well be at the bottom of the ocean.
Little Inferno will start you off with the meager instruction manual of the fireplace itself, which will burn pretty quick. But everything you burn will fade to dust, and from that dust will pop magical coins. Coins of a material far more valuable than gold, or silver. They're coins of love. Or maybe chocolate, but those would melt close to the fire.
Once you've gotten that far, the entirety of the game opens up to you. You'll be able to purchase a fine selection of perfectly burnable items from one of the many catalogs. Each one brings with it its own unique properties. If you burn batteries, they explode. If you burn wood or paper, it burns very bright and quick. And if you burn living things, why they let out the most delightful scream. But it's not until you've started combining things that the action really starts to heat up. Ba-dum-tss.
Little Inferno is a special game in that it's not one with concrete goals. There are no missions to complete, or collectibles to find. It's a simple game with a simple goal. Burning things. It's not quite a puzzle game, or a physics game, or a sandbox game. But it definitely features elements of all three.
Trivial "combo" challenges work as one of the little things to keep you busy, tasking you with solving little pun riddles by burning specific items together. For example, the "Springtime" combo requiring you to set fire to a pack of flower seeds and an alarm clock. Which explodes into a fun little mess of flowers and mechanical bits. Aside from that, the only real "goals" to the game are burning every object at least once.
But Little Inferno isn't one of those kinds of games. Little Inferno is about more that that. It's about bigger things. Simply burning everything, yeah, that's pretty fun. But the game's surprisingly strong story leaves the biggest impact. And it's done in such a subtle way. In addition to the many flammable objects that you'll be getting in your little mailbox, you'll get occasional letters from your neighbor and other characters. While at first innocent, charming, and mildly creepy, they'll slowly start to clue you in to a much bigger, much more chilling goings-on happening away from your fireplace.
It's not a very long game. Unless you attempt to solve every challenge, you should be done with it in hours. It's a lot like like lighting your house on fire. It goes out super fast unless you pour gasoline on it. Trust me. You wouldn't even need to call any firefighters or anything. If you're looking for the kind of game that you can sink tons of time into doing things that might seem "productive", this game is not it. But the developers clearly put a lot of love into every little object. Each one is unique in quite a few ways. Some of them have multiple pieces, or react to fire in fun ways. And some have properties that can interact with other objects. You can light a cat on fire and have it explode, filling your entire fireplace with cat poop. And then drop a nuke inside. What kind of sick person would NOT jump at the opportunity to nuke a fireplace full of cat poop?
Once you've burned through the game, Little Inferno's haunting and chilling feel will live on in your mind for quite a while. Everything from the zany pyromaniac action to the beautiful use of sound and music, and quirky art direction will leave an impression on you. It's definitely the kind of game that sticks with you for a while after. Burning inside you. Ba-dum-tss.
It's the most fun you can have that isn't lighting actual things on fire. And once you've finished playing it, you can just burn the game too. Burn your computer, your game systems, your phones, just burn everything. It'll be tons of fun.
Always remember, kids. If you're not the one setting things on fire, you're just the kindling.

Good afternoon, dear readers! I would like to talk about a game like ABZU. The game is quite sensational and not just.
Pluses:
Music, landscapes, not difficult gameplay.
Disadvantages:
Price, no plot.
Let's start with the fact that it was done by a person who created such a game as Journey, and consequently, the setting of the game will be slightly strange, but at the same time bewitching. However, unlike Journey, the game also appeared on the PC, so anyone can try it out. Is it worth it? It is, and now I will explain why.
ABZU is an adventure game from the 3rd person in which you have to play for a diver and explore the underwater world. It sounds depressing, and from the part so it is. But there is something in this game that drags on a lot of time.
Graphics- One of the chips of this game. Do not be embarrassed that the game is made in a cartoon style. As experience shows, (for example Firewatch) the animation gives just the charm of the game. The underwater kingdom in ABZU looks just amazing, and if you also have a large screen, you will have something to see and really appreciate the picture. The transfer of colors, architecture, light, everything in the game is simply perfectly done, from which I want to explore every corner, the designers of the levels have enormous respect for such work.
The gameplay here is simple, we do not have to fight with the local inhabitants, and on the turn, the campaign of the game, we start in some sense to understand the fish, especially this is much closer to the end of the game when we get off the pier and along with the fish float down the stream to the portal. I also want to mention excellent music, which also fits perfectly into the game. The developers seemed to know at what point you will be in the right place and have tweaked music a second with your actions. Music by the way was performed by an orchestra, it is shown in the Steam game store.
Are there any downsides to the game? Perhaps there is. To the minuses, I would refer the ratio of price and duration. My game costs about $ 5 and it's expensive for a game where you just have to admire the scenery and music, and if you do not, the game can be played in 1 hour and 17 minutes, the proof is on YouTube. So there is no plot, because of what the player simply does not understand where he got, what he is doing and what is his ultimate goal.
The game is good and if you have a powerful enough PC, then I recommend this game to your collection, but I recommend taking it at a reasonable price.
Well, play, try, and I wish you to meet more good games!

+ uses the updated version of the Sage engine, the one that debuted in Generals: the effects (especially the water effects) look stunning
+ has a similar script that Red Alert 2 had: they toned down the seriousness of the very first game and instead included some funny dialogues to help with the cheesy storyline
+ ambitious casting, perhaps the best in the entire series with Tim Curry, Peter Stormare, Jonathan Pryce and J.K. Simmons just to name a few
+ inclusion of offshore battlegrounds: almost every building can be built on water; this gives way to newer tactics
+ finally, a 3rd faction we can choose from: the Empire of the Rising Sun is an instant favourite thanks to the unit variation (plus George Takei!)
- ore fields were removed: we now have stationery ore mines that are nice but cutting of the enemy's' resources now is not as important or effective as it used to be
- campaign could have been a little longer: while there are 9 missions with each side completing the first 4-5 does not take very long
- the game desperately tries to show something new with the inclusion of the naval warfare: this is not necessarily a problem but throughout the campaign there's too much emphasis on it
- mediocre coop integration: while playing all 27 levels with a friend is pretty cool, playing solo is pretty difficult at times due to the dumbed-down A.I. that is not always helpful
To summarise: for me the number 2 will be the essential Red Alert title but this one was also pretty neat back in 2008. Running it on modern PCs can be a tad bit difficult - thanks to the uploaded guide available you can find some fixes for the game.

Let me start by saying that I consider myself a fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd, and of James Rolfe's body of work in general. I have seen every AVGN episode, most of them multiple times. This means I am used to the style and production values associated with the series, and had a good idea of what to expect going in. I tend to think this would not be the case for those unfamiliar with the Angry Video Game Nerd, and I would strongly recommend watching a few episodes on YouTube before buying this movie, so you have an idea of what you are getting into.
The easy way to describe Angry Video Game Nerd: The Movie would be as an almost two hour AVGN episode, and that's not entirely untrue. The movie features many of the tropes found in the episodes, along with references to running gags from the Angry Video Game Nerd series. However the pacing of the movie is significantly slower than the typical episode, a necessity given their 12 to 20 minutes run time, and there is a far smaller emphasis on games and more on a wacky road trip adventure.
Likewise, the Nerd (played by James Rolfe) spends most of the movie being relatively calm, which is in stark contrast to his over-the-top persona in the AVGN series, particularly the early episodes. The later episodes have shown a calmer Nerd, but it's more down to the fact that the character cannot realistically spend the entire two hours cursing and breaking things. Depending on what you like about the Angry Video Game Nerd series, these disparities may or may not be a deal breaker.
The premise of the film is simple enough. A fictional video game company, one I am fairly confident I cannot name without raising the ire of Steam's filters, has noticed that when James Rolfe (the Angry Video Game Nerd) reviews a product and talks about how bad it is, people buy the game to see for themselves. The company thus decides to make a sequel to the perceived worst game of all time, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial on the Atari 2600, and have the Angry Video Game Nerd review it to boost sales. The game in question is infamous for its part in the real-life video game crash of 1983, which very nearly destroyed the budding video game industry in North America.
The game underperformed so badly, that an urban legend persisted for over a decade claiming Atari had buried millions of copies of the game in a landfill  in Alamogordo, New Mexico (which is partially true.) Through a series of events I will not cover here for brevity, James Rolfe along with Cooper, his self-proclaimed manager, and Mandy, executive at the video game company creating the sequel, sets out to debunk the urban legend, with the Nerd claiming he will review E.T. should the game actually be found in the landfill.
The plot unfolds in an utterly ridiculous fashion, as one might expect from the Angry Video Game Nerd. The acting ranges from somewhat cringey to stupendously hammy. In this respect Mandy, played by Sarah Glendening, seems out of place for being relatively normal, at least compared to the performances by the rest of the cast. There are a lot of cameos and in-jokes, though these rely on your familiarty with AVGN and various other YouTubers. The music is okay, and pretty consistent with what you would hear in an Angry Video Game Nerd episode. The production values are somewhat higher, but still very consistent with the campy, intentionally low budget style of the series.
Overall the movie feels stretched thin and kind of adrfit, which occasional bits of a humor and amusement, but not enough to sustain interest for two hours. It's not terrible, but it's not terribly good either. I can't recommend this to anyone who is not already a fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd, and even then it's only a cautious recommendation.
