Well, here it is.  My review of Angry Video Game Nerd: The Movie.  I have seen many ******* movies in my time, some of them classics, some of them good, some of them bad, all of them movies, and this is one of them.  In this movie, you
watch Herb, which I suppose is supposed to be representative of The Angry Video Game Nerd.
His goal is to make it to a landfill and gather all of the pieces of a legendary artifact.  The problem is these pieces may or may not even be there, it's random.  Random like rolling a set of loaded dice onto a **** full of ******** **** with **** while you **** **** *****.
Most of the movie centers on a fictitious game known as EEETEE 2, which is the successor to the supposed worst game of all time, EEETEE, which is really just ET by another name, like when Color Dreams rereleased Menace Beach as Sunday Funday, but more likely for legal reasons, in case Spielberg actually had a pack of velociraptors on hand to send after anyone touching his precious intellectual property.  Because you know he does.
Gameplay is pretty much nonexistent.  You just hit "watch" and wait through a longass 2 hour cut scene.  I tried using the mouse, joystick, keyboard, but I never could get the game to be interactive.  See, there are controls, but they are not always obvious and only give you options like "pause" and "go back".  At least Big Rigs let you actually try to play the game.
There are a lot of bad reviews on this movie, and I can understand that.  It's a movie that probably has a very limited audience.  People are criticizing the acting and humor, and I don't think that's quite fair for a movie based on a series where there are characters like "*** Pickle" and "Supermechadeathchrist" gets into a battle with a demonic Super Mario Brothers 3.  There is this absurdity to AVGN that is definitely seen throughout the movie.  The premise is silly, the lines are full of cliches and homages, and I didn't find the acting all that bad personally, I think the characters were acted as they were written.  I've seen acting in movies much worse in movies that were much more well-received.  Watchmen, now that was some ********* acting there.  James Rolfe's admiration for Troma and B-movies is seen in  AVGN and Cinemassacre, and Lloyd Kauffman even has a cameo here.  There wasn't a chance of this movie winning any Oscars by any stretch.  There were details such as the use of toy cars in a lot of scenes that added something to the ridiculousness of the movie, like seeing the strings on the flying saucers in Plan 9 From Outer Space.
What it reminded me of, in a lot of ways, was Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back.  You know, that movie Kevin Smith did with his own side-characters that was really just a long montage of references to movies such as Star Wars, but revolved around a silly plot.  The character of Mandi actually made me think of Justice from that movie as I watched it.  Perhaps one complaint I could have is the same Cinema Sin that so many recent reboots fall into: putting in references to better movies, reminding you of how much better those movies were.  In this case, however, that effect is probably intentional.
One thing you cannot do while watching this movie is take anything too seriously.  In the series, the reviews were semi-serious but everything else just did whatever the **** it wanted.  This movie is a lot like the non-review segments of the episodes.
So was this movie good or bad?  I enjoyed it, because I like AVGN in the first place.  It was a fun, silly movie that didn't take anything seriously, and it played with a big part of gaming lore, the legend of the Atari landfill, a legend that was found to be true during the making of this movie.  So it's not great, but it also does not **** **** monkey ****.  If AVGN's non-review parts aren't enjoyable to you, you will hate this movie.  If you're a fan of AVGN, however, you'll probably enjoy it.  I did.

Stellaris is really my first venture into true 4x games. To be honest I have
so much apprehension to this genre it has always kept me away. I used to
watch my friends sink hundreds of hours in Crusader Kings, and Europa
Universalis 4 and they seemed to love it. I was always sitting in the back
thinking, “I don’t want to have to go back to school practically to learn a
video games mechanics and the finer points of the game before I can give
it a try.
So I picked up Stellaris the newest title by Paradox and as someone
who is new and was previously intimidated by 4x, I can say with confidence
the game is quite excellent and above all accessible! The game features
a great level of customization from everything about planet management
(buildings, policies, upgrades) to individual ship designs (weapons, power,
shielding) as well as empire customization (leader traits, government style,
military tech start, etc) The game allows for you to custom tailor your star
fairing race to a fine point. As well as the finer details of micromanagement
and creating sectors to manage planets under one “system/sector” so
that takes a bit of the stress off the individual micro of planets.
The game features a beautiful aesthetic barring performance issues at
this moment of writing it. Giant space battles and honestly when Civs start
growing and filling the map you are going to see a frame hit. I am running
a 980ti… so there are things left to be desired in terms of game performance
but I have heard they are hard at work fixing these optimization problems.
so I do have faith Paradox will work hard on fixing the issues that are affecting
the game currently. They also have given full mod support to the community
so expect some amazing mods and total conversions (BSG,MassEffect,Star
Wars,Star Trek, etc). Stellaris has a lot it got right and it made it fun for me
to learn and to challenge myself to manage my empire better.
The game features fun random events that can be great for your empire
or not so great. It also features a random tech tree so you really won't have
the same options a second time in the order you get them in say your first
game. Which I personally enjoy, take Civ5 for example with an incredibly
linear tech tree, having a random tech tree with “rare” tech etc spices things
up and encourages you to play differently and focus on what you need or
are going for rather than following the same path over and over again. It
adds variety and fun challenges to your empires rise and potential fall.
I could talk about the game all day to be honest but I think I will try to
keep this someone concise. Stellaris may be Paradox’s best 4x game yet.
I have a new genre to enjoy and sink massive hours into. This is an easy
recommend to veterans of 4x/Paradox games, and even a recommend
for those trying to get into this genre. It’s fun, accessible, and addictive!

I'm about halfway through the game right now (interval 6 out of 11) and I don't see anything changing at all in the other half so I figured I may express my thoughts about this game right now. I'd describe the overall experience of the game to be pretty poor. It's incredibly linear, featuring corridor after corridor after corridor filled with office props and sick♥♥♥♥♥dynamic lighting. I've always heard about FEAR having stellar gameplay due to the gunplay mechanics and smart AI but here's how the gameplay usually goes: you walk through corridors, press some switch, walk some more and hear the occasional "kill the bad guy" on your comm link and then maybe you fight some enemy grunts and walk some more. There is a level where you're supposed to run after some annoying fat guy and it was literally corridors - turret - corridors - turret - corridors - two turrets - end of segment. I understand the reasoning behind your character running at an extremely slow speed with no sprinting as it sets a specific horror-ish pace for the game however the entire "horror" aspect of the story seems to be a couple of spooky things happening (which seem to completely go away mid-way through the game). Adding to that, there's no survival horror involved, you always have plenty of ammo and are always maxed out on health kits. That being said, you can still be killed in seconds in a firefight. Speaking of fights, I can't figure out why people are praising the AI so bad in FEAR, 90% of the enemies you encounter are grunts wielding the same guns as you and their behavior reminded me of the soldiers in the first Half-Life who would try to flank you or flush you out with nades and sometimes run away from the fight for their own sake. Usually you would just enable slow-mo and mow most of them down and then deal with the rest with the arsenal available to you. The game also completely lacks music at some points and it may take away some of the joy from shootouts.
Overall, FEAR is and should be mostly praised for its gameplay as its other aspects are downright horrible apart from the visuals (although they mostly consist of the same environments), if praised at all. In my opinion the gameplay could be improved so much if Monolith completely ditched the plot narrative, uninteresting story and cardboard characters. If you're attempting to create John Woo-styled gunplay mechanics then make the movement faster and add more "run and gun" options for people to play around with.
IMO: FEAR is still worth checking out for its dirt cheap price despite its flaws and problems.

The Witcher 2 was a huge improvement over the first game. Combat felt better, the crafting system was nice, graphics were bonkers, and the skills/items/equipment were varied. This game has a lot of detail put into which made seeing new places for the first time quite fun. Although this game was a big jump forward, they were still held back by their complicated political storyline. The entire series is more political so I can't say it's bad just for that, just not my favorite narrative. So let's break this down...
Pros:
- Gorgeous graphics. This game was loaded with detailed skins and textures on even the most remote portions of the map. The devs definitely didn't skimp on graphics.
- Combat was much smoother, there was more to fighting than just "Steel or Silver sword?" Your spells and items made it so you could approach fights in different ways
- Crafting was a nice addition which allowed many more combinations of appropriate equipables
- Some of the Boss fights were awesome! I always like fighting huge monsters.
Cons:
- The story didn't feel like it had a beginning or an end. Like it was just a chapter of a book. It didn't work for me, made me feel bored and detached from what was going on. I didn't really care about any of the characters other than Triss or Geralt.
- Hitboxes were attrocious. Every fight I'll be rolling around dodging attacks like a hero but then out of nowhere I'll get blasted by a fireball or sword swing that was way off. Boss battles or fights against large creatures were the worst for this because their attacks were frustratingly difficult to dodge.
- Enemies that can block forever... I can't do that, why can they?
- Menus were VERY unresponsive and I had to wait a second or two before I could access meditation after I brought up my quick menu. A lot of you won't agree, but I hold responsivness in games very highly. Maybe that doesn't seem like a big problem but it's really annoying when you're playing a game that doesn't respond to button presses when you press them. Maybe if there was some fancy animation that was happening before I could press a button I'd wait, but there isn't, it's a clear open menu that doesn't respond quickly to input and that's not acceptable.
Don't bother with this game and just go straight to Witcher 3 unless you like to play all games in a series. I was very torn on whether or not to recommend this game but after sitting on my thoughts for a bit after finishing the game I realized it just wasn't that fun.

With most horror games, they blow their load early and show you the scariest stuff in the first ten minutes. Over the course of the game, the player becomes desensitized to it, having to repeatedly encounter zombies and monsters across the span of 7-10 hours.
F.E.A.R. on the other hand is a game of build-up. It doesn’t start out especially scary, but as I kept playing it, it very gradually started to creep me out. I would hesitate to say that it outright scared me, because it takes a lot for a game to legitimately scare me. But as you creep around its desolate office complex, an unsettling feeling begins to seep in to your brain. It’s like being in a supermarket after hours - a place so obviously bustling with people and noise and life, now empty. You can’t shake the feeling that something’s wrong and you really, really shouldn’t be here. Everything’s too quiet and you feel a little vulnerable.
Eventually the tension mounts and the creepy atmosphere pays off. The end of the game could’ve had a bigger finale with some sort of climactic boss encounter, but ultimately it doesn’t need one. The ending is unforgettable even without a big scary monster to kill - and maybe that’s for the best. I’d complain that F.E.A.R. ends on something of a cliffhanger, but all the best horror movies do, and so too does F.E.A.R.

I'd say it's worth about one playthrough, though not much else. for the price it's asking for, though, it aint too bad, though it's no steal either, and their are certainly better games to buy for the price, but if you're looking for just some dumb hack-n-slash action with metroidvania elements, I'd say you should at least check this out. hell, if only for the effort put into it.
It's not without it's flaws, though. No sir.
First off, like i said, it's only worth about one playthough. Reason being is that, sadly, there really just isn't much replay value. Unlike other metroidvanias and even some spectacle fighters, there's a reason to go back and unlock stuff, and try different weapons and magic and♥♥♥♥♥♥on different enemies, but here, you just kinda have one  sword, with two different types of attacks, and very limited combo potential. every secret you find is either money or a indie-game cameo. it doesn't help that it's actually kinda hard to level up to the point of being super OP, or at least in my experience. The game is designed to be balanced, which isn't always a bad thing, but when i play a hack n slash, or a metroidvania, or a spectacle fighter, the best part is always becoming stupidly powerful badass that obliterates all who get in my way, but with dust, he ain't like that.
And the gameplay in general is pretty mindless, also. like, even by hack 'n slash standards. most of the time you'll be mashing the attack button with doing a dust storm/fidget attack thrown in the middle.  even the 1-on-1 bosses are this way, minus the final boss who's kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥take. a good amount of the time, you'll probably not be doing interesting or intricate combos, paying attention to the enemies, or find very much variety in this game's combat, though I will say that for that first playthrough, it IS fun.
Outside of that, there's also the story. Right, so, let's open this can of worms with the main characters, Dust, Fidget, and Arah the talking sword. Dust is an mysterious, amnesiac, but all-around good hearted swordsman looking to find the best outcome possible and save the day from the racist furries.
BORING.
He's a character with no important flaws and his origin and background don't change that, every flaw he has was something he HAD, and doesn't play into the main story, so whatever flaws he had don't matter anymore. He's flat as a pancake, made only to be likable. Arah is his guide and... not much else, really. he's just as boring, if not more. And fidget is entirely pointless, she literally only serves to be something you either laugh at or go "D'AAAWWWWWWW" at. And the rest of the story is just... like, here's a sad moment, with a character i barely know anything about! why should i give a♥♥♥♥♥♥if you dad is dying, you fat egg child!? what have you done for me RECENTLY?But no, really, a bunch of characters barely get any development or screen time, yet we're supposed to care for them.
But outside of those flaws, this game would be straight up bad, if not for it's high points.
First off, the animation is pretty tight, although it's kinda weird to see dust and some monsters have super detailed animation, and all the other NPCs are animated with tweens (i think). also, despitre it's problems, the combat is genuinely fun for the first playthrough, which is actually kinda lengthy and you do explore varied areas with different enemies, so the levels always feel fresh and different. If you're willing to blow 15 bucks on an admirable little game, i'd say give it a shot, although it may be best to look into some of the gameplay a bit more before doing so, as this won't be everyone's cup of tea.

Skylar and Plux is a 2000 style 3D action platformer, very similar in style to Ratchet and Clank or Jak and Daxter. While it draws inspiration from these games it struggles to understand what it is that makes them great.
First of all, the game is short. It's priced at £12, it's not trying to hide the fact that it's short, but it is, so you should know that before you go in. I finished the game in under two hours and I imagine 100% would be between 4-5 hours. I think that the price is right for a game of its length, and when i read other reviews i was expecting it to be a fairly short game, but when i started playing I realised it would be over quicker than I had expected.
The level design is nice but way too big. In PS2 era games the levels were much tighter, puzzles had more purpose being an obstruction, when the levels open up too wide you lose the linear design, there's less challenge in getting to your objective when you can take slightly different routes, not a single path that's been designed for you.
The Combat is tricky to place. All three enemies take single hits, but the fighting seems slow and inaccurate. Your Move set is more similar to Jak and Daxter than Ratchet and Clank, but it isn't as fine tuned as you would expect. Attacks have a hidden recharge time that you can't properly guage when they are ready again because the animation has finished but you still have to wait before you spin again. And this is where the combat becomes tricky. One enemy is difficult to attack beacuse it fires too fast, so you can't easily dodge its rockets. The smaller enemy is hard to hit because of its size and erratic jumping, the only real challenge comes when you fight 20 at once. The Third enemy isn't difficult at all, as the game gives you a slow time gadget so you can then easily dodge it's stream of bullets.
The gadgets you unlock in each of the three areas of the game are easily the best part of the game. The first is a jetpack which gives you a passive glide ability and also a charge roll that propells you forward. The downside of this is the game finishes faster. Its other ability is ultimately pointless; a rocket jump ability that is only used twice in the game isn't useful at all. The slow time ability is fantastic for puzzles, it feels great using it to get around fast moving platforms, its downside though is that it makes combat laughably easy. The third is a magnet and again this makes the platforming great fun, but again the combat becomes tediously easy when you get in certain situations.
The Story of Ratchet and Clank was 'we should stop the bad guy, because thats what good people do'. The story in Skylar and Plux is a confusing mix of amnesia, heroism and daddy issues. First you're told that you, Skylar, have lost your memories and the only way to get them back is to get the three orbs on Clover Island and then you'll get your memory back. That alone is fine, but then you meet Plux who wants to help free all of the villagers other than it's a good thing to do, all the while he's talking about how his dad left him on Clover Island and will come back to get him. And in the short space of two hours Plux goes from 'my Dad will come back for me' to 'I know my dad won't come back for me and I'm OK with that'. We never learn about his dad, and we never see his dad, what was set up as a mystery is now just a coping tool for single parent kids. Oddly there is no mention of Plux's mother, she must be kept for the sequel.
And now that I have mentioned Plux I should warn you that he is the most annoying character you will meet. From his wierd frequent anal fixation to his annoying references (Miley Cyrus' wrecking ball being the worst) he is one of the worst parts of the game. He's actually not even needed for anything. While Ratchet needed Clank to use him as a jetpack, Plux isnt used for anything, he just follows around Skylar and keeps talking about his absent Dad. Skylar even has another companion already, a talking fist, who i didn't find that bad, and would have actually like to hear from more instead of a needless bird. Character design is also odd as there is no need for any of them to be animals. Clank was a robot so he could turn into a jetpack and do other stuff, Plux is a bird who you don't need to fly, so as a companion doesnt make much sense being a bird. Skylar confuses me as to why she is a giant cat, although apparently she was a thief so maybe she's a cat burglar, I don't even know anymore.
The Story and Voices are both very odd. For what strikes me as a young Kids game it's very odd hearing Plux telling the bad guy that he should go stick stuff up his butt (probably an actual line from the game I dont care or remember now). It's also odd hear him almost swear alot "what the funk" etc. It didn't offend me, it just left me feeling really odd knowing that it had been written for kids. The characters will also spoon feed you out of place references like an badly dull Tinder joke for example, not the kind of stuff you would expect a kid to get. None of the writing is good, it just makes you cringe just a little bit more with every butt or bad song lyric trown at you. The Voice acting isn't very good either. Most of the characters speak quite slowly, and it isn't really an issue but its just very odd and noticable, and a little annoying.

Curretly I do kind of like this game, but it has a huge amout of problems, specifically to do with the balenceing.
Now the game and each of its' maps are and always has been ruled by a select few dragon and weapon combinations that have the highest DPS and pretty much beat any other dragon/weapon in the game, as you can no doubt guess, this plays hell with the game balence, as if you meet one of these wonder combinations on a map it's suited to, then you've pretty much lost before the battle's begun. Wait you cry, what about support and other roles? I'm sorry to dissapoint you, but appart from 1 or 2 healing dragons and weapons which are hardly ever picked anyway, this game is deicded purely on who can dish out the most damage in the shortest amount of time, there's hardy any skill involved when facing an opposing dragon, just simply who is the highest level and who has the highest DPS build.
Now the matchmaker, if you could call it that, is also unbalenced. Unlike in most other MOBA's, there's no pregame lobby where everyone selects their dragon and weapon, no, instead you select the dragon, weapon and spells [pretty much the only spells anyone uses are the healing spell and the base teleport] you want before you jump into the game and the matchmaker throws a bunch of random people together, which combined with the fact that there can be multiple coppies of the same dragon/weapon on either team and the imbalenced combinations I mentioned above means that the game is pretty much decided before it even starts, which is very bad game design.
Now as I said above multiple maps with one map being in rotation at a time, the map to be put into rotation is selected by the comunity via an in-game poll. So, four very different maps, sounds extensive for a MOBA right?  However practically no one votees for the standard MOBA map called Towers And Titans and Nether gates hardly ever shows up in the map poll. So there are pretty much only two modes, Balistae ally which is pretty much a single corridor where three high damage balistae bolts are shot from each side every couple of minutes. The other most played mode is Chaos unleashed, wherein you collect gold to summon Chaos who helps you detroy some structures. Having only one map in rotation and knowing which map is in rotation creates some serious balence issues, people can simply pick one of the afformentioned wonder combinations that is suited to that specific map.
And know we get on to the Pay to Win aspect of the game. Now the game isn't pay to win as such, practically everything can be unlocked by playing for free, unfortunatly the vast majority of the very best stuff is placed at such a high amount of RNG and luck that it is just not practical to get them as a free to play player, so to get them, a little bit of money is called for.

I'm only about an hour in to this game but I had to stop and come on here to say something about this game. I love 3D platformers and I've played nearly every one I can find on Steam, Skylar and Plux is better than all of them. It look gorgeous, the controls are flawless, the levels are large with plent of hidden areas to find, you get new abilities as you play, combat is satisfying and neither too easy nor too difficult. I kept waiting for something to go wrong. To fall through the ground or get stuck behind the scenery or something but it never happened. The polish on this game is perfect so far. The only strike I have against it is the voice acting for the villain. He sounds like a high school jock in drama class. The lines for everyone are a bit cheesy, but his are delivered in a way that really grates on me. Of course, that's entirely subjective and some people will love him I'm sure. And I'm not saying it's poor acting or anything, just the wrong personality choice for the character I feel. But it can be easily forgiven since the rest of the game is so good.
Skylar and Plux is definitely in the vein of the first Jak and Daxter. At least that's the feel I got from it. But with touches of Ratchet and Clank and even some Banjo Kazooie. Still feels entirely like it's own game. It lovingly borrows and pays tribute to its predecessors rather than callously rips them off. Considering it's on sale right now too, it's the perfect time to drop the cash.

Skylar & Plux: Adventure On Clover Island would have been alright if the game had more than two hours worth of content.
The game took me roughly an hour and a half to complete the story mode with the only other gameplay being finding more caged villagers sprinkled around the small map. For the price of $15 I don't feel this game contains a worthwhile amount of content, it feels more like a demo than a full product.
Gameplay revolves around collecting gems, platforming and occassionally fighting enemies, all utilizing a variety of tools and gadgets to do so.
The combat is very basic and doesn't happen very often. There are a total of three enemies in the game and none of them are all that interesting to fight, especially the small minions as they blindly jump at you and will hurl themselves into death like lemmings. When these enemies do hit you it often feels cheap as they randomly swarm you.
Fighting them off is an endeavour, especially early in the game when you have no access to any sort of ranged fighting. You have a basic three hit combo attack and a jumping slam attack. It's basically the same setup as Ratchet & Clank. The downside is it's like only having the wrench instead of an arsenal of weapons.
Speaking of Ratchet & Clank, Skylar & Plux desperately wants to evoke emotions from that series. Everything from having the same attacks, currency systems, overall level design and movement system. They even went as far as to add a jetpack that functions in the exact same way that Clank's helicopter upgrade does. The only difference being that this version doesn't work as well with the maps.
The extra jetpack options like high jumping or boost jumping don't even work with the game as there are few to zero areas that even require their use. In fact the times I attempted to actually cross areas with them I just died because the game would rather you just double jump and glide across everything.
Adding onto this, there is no ledge hang feature so your character will often either bounce off or glide up ledges if you don't quite make them.
There are gadgets in the game and this is where the game shows the most promise. There is a swingshot lookalike and a dynamo but the other two gadgets are rather interesting. One has the ability to slow time and the other is a magnet can pick up objects to be thrown whether it be enemies or certain objects.
The magnet is your only ranged weapon in the game.
The thing is once you have the slow time gadget, you use it during every fight because it can just slow everything down so you never get hit. It makes the combat even easier and feels like cheating.
There are so many glitches in the game. There were points where I was able to bypass level areas left and right, along with moments where my character became stuck.
The worst one I encountered is that the game doesn't respawn the world if you die, unless you lose all of your lives. This means that in sections that have fall-away platforms you will respawn on the first ledge but there will be no platform there to jump on anymore so you are screwed. On top fo that there was a portion of the game where you outrun lava but if you die, the lava doesn't reset so you just spawn in it or underneath it. When you spawn underneath then it just doesn't hurt you and you can bypass the entire section.
I also had two cutscenes not initialize so I had to skip them entirely.
I was actually okay with that because the characters are some of the most annoying I have ever dealt with in a video game.
Plux (the bird) is the worst character I could imagine. He is the pinnacle of a "hello fellow kids" style character. Everything from his voice acting to the dialogue is done in the cringiest, late 90's way possible. Even if it were done on purpose it was still ear-drilling the entire game. The other characters are also kind of annoying, but nowhere close to the awfulness of Plux.
Skylar is fine, I don't really like her design but she doesn't talk so she can remain out of my hate book.
The storyline is extremely predictable and offers nothing engaging, especially being so short. I keep saying that but seriously this game is three hours at the most if you want to 100% everything in it. It's like playing the opening two worlds of Jak & Daxter.
Graphically the game looks alright, but there is a problem with the lighting that makes shaded areas look extremely dark and difficult to see. That needs to be fixed.
The music in the game is lovely as well as the presentation. To their credit I did feel like I was playing a game from the golden era of adventure platformers.
I get that this game was made by a first time team and former students, but the amount of content and quality of said content is not anywhere near what I consider acceptable for a consumer.
If you enjoy platformers, this one is mostly harmless, but incredibly short and easy. As a finished product though, it's nowhere close to what it needs to be.

It is eerily similar to Overwatch, so it's hard not to talk about OW when talking about Paladins.
With that said, if OW didn't exist, Paladins would be, hands down, the best multiplayer shooter in the neighborhood. And it's free-to-play, so that's saying a lot!
It's not as polished as OW, but most of the subtle differences in gameplay make it more suited to my tastes. It's slower, has WAY less one-hit-kill situations, the Ultimates are not as impactful in the team fights, and has way more hitscan weapons. The matches have way less crazy, over-the-top stuff going on than OW, but at the same time I rarely feel frustrated at cheap deaths or extremely lucky plays from my opponents.
Items seem like they could be this super deep and interesting system, but they're really not. Once the match starts you pretty much know what are the optimal items to buy. They do affect the strategy in hero picks, though. And the hero-picking is PERFECT. I wish OW had hero-picking in Competitive like Paladins does!
Speaking of Comp, the competitive scene in LatAm is pretty much non-existant, though, so unless you want to just hang around Casual mode and have fun, like I do, it is not worth the time investment.
Finally, the game is very much alive. Every other week it seems there's a new update, and since I started playing around a month ago they already added 2 brand new heroes.
Give this game a chance =)

Stellaris is really my first venture into true 4x games. To be honest I have
so much apprehension to this genre it has always kept me away. I used to
watch my friends sink hundreds of hours in Crusader Kings, and Europa
Universalis 4 and they seemed to love it. I was always sitting in the back
thinking, “I don’t want to have to go back to school practically to learn a
video games mechanics and the finer points of the game before I can give
it a try.
So I picked up Stellaris the newest title by Paradox and as someone
who is new and was previously intimidated by 4x, I can say with confidence
the game is quite excellent and above all accessible! The game features
a great level of customization from everything about planet management
(buildings, policies, upgrades) to individual ship designs (weapons, power,
shielding) as well as empire customization (leader traits, government style,
military tech start, etc) The game allows for you to custom tailor your star
fairing race to a fine point. As well as the finer details of micromanagement
and creating sectors to manage planets under one “system/sector” so
that takes a bit of the stress off the individual micro of planets.
The game features a beautiful aesthetic barring performance issues at
this moment of writing it. Giant space battles and honestly when Civs start
growing and filling the map you are going to see a frame hit. I am running
a 980ti… so there are things left to be desired in terms of game performance
but I have heard they are hard at work fixing these optimization problems.
so I do have faith Paradox will work hard on fixing the issues that are affecting
the game currently. They also have given full mod support to the community
so expect some amazing mods and total conversions (BSG,MassEffect,Star
Wars,Star Trek, etc). Stellaris has a lot it got right and it made it fun for me
to learn and to challenge myself to manage my empire better.
The game features fun random events that can be great for your empire
or not so great. It also features a random tech tree so you really won't have
the same options a second time in the order you get them in say your first
game. Which I personally enjoy, take Civ5 for example with an incredibly
linear tech tree, having a random tech tree with “rare” tech etc spices things
up and encourages you to play differently and focus on what you need or
are going for rather than following the same path over and over again. It
adds variety and fun challenges to your empires rise and potential fall.
I could talk about the game all day to be honest but I think I will try to
keep this someone concise. Stellaris may be Paradox’s best 4x game yet.
I have a new genre to enjoy and sink massive hours into. This is an easy
recommend to veterans of 4x/Paradox games, and even a recommend
for those trying to get into this genre. It’s fun, accessible, and addictive!

F.E.A.R. is a First Person Shooter Horror game.
You are the "Point Man" a person without any informations about, at least at the beginning.
You have a job, to catch a man called Paxton Fettel, a man that has more bounds with you than you might think at the beginning of the game. On your mission you often hear about a girl called Alma. Who is that? You even meet here several times in your paranormal visions. And the game is horror indeed. Often you are in levels where you are hunted by Fettels and Almas paranormal visions. Persons who die in front of you eyes and who die because of having their flesh removed from their bones. Thats totally normal. And that is not even all. You are always hunted by the dark... It can wait behind every corner. But who is Fettel and Alma actually? One thing is clear, you are bound with them but you cant tell how. That is your mission to find out.
The game has nice graphics especially for the fact its from 2005. I doubt that there was anything better looking back then, not even Far Cry from 2004 looked that great. If you ask me at least. Nearly everything is demolishable and the physics are great. What I really love is the bullet time that you can start anytime you want, but its limited and needs to recharge sometimes. You also have a flashlight but this one needs to recharge too. Dont waste your flashlight because you will need it. The play with the light and the dark is really amazing in this game.
I played the multiplayer once, it was ok and can make some fun.
BUT. The official multiplayer is done. There is F.E.A.R. Combat though, the multiplayer of F.E.A.R. that has been published by the community and is still supported. Works without problems. You should try it, its free. Just google for their website.
The Steam version also has both released addons for free!
Both are NOT considered canon by the official developers Monolith. Its fiction.
Means things that happened in them are not covered by FEAR 1, 2, 3.
Extraction Point tells the story what happened after the main game ending.
Its nice and it still had those Horror shocker. I really liked this addon.
Only downside is that for some reason its not supporting widescreen out of the box.
Weirdly the main game and Perseus Mandate does... However, you can easily edit a ini to get your desired widescreen resolutions, google it.
Perseus Mandate on the other hand wasnt really my taste.
You are a whole different character trying to uncover mission perseus.
The horror shockers in this addon are nearly non existent if you ask me.
Also its mostly about shooting yourself through corridors flooded with replicants.
I died very often because it was way too difficult, even on normal compared to the other games.
It was frustrating and a little bit boring, especially at the end.
Both addons were developed by another developer named Timegate Studios.
The maingame will take up to 10 hours to finish.
The addons each around 5 hours.
The Steam version comes only in English!
There are several language packs available as Steam guides and also in the web.
I also added a German UNCUT language pack for those who like to play the games in German.
Its in the guide section.
Also I want to say that F.E.A.R. and its addons suffer from FPS problems on most modern rigs.
This is due to the engine having problems with several HID devices like mouse, keyboard, controller.
All systems starting with Vista can have this problem. The fix is to disable several HID devices. Google it. This is actually really annoying. There are some more problems. EAX does not work on all modern systems starting with Vista. Some can still enable it with soundcard driver programs. Or use a tool called directsound to activate basic EAX support. I should note that Windows XP fixes actually both issues. Also the game itself is not able to activate soft shadows and anti aliasing at the same time. To do so you have to use Nvidia inspector and a online tutorial to add proper anti aliasing support. Just disable the ingame AA but leave soft shadows on. Works fine then. I dont know if there is a AMD way to do this.

Buy it. If you are thinking about it, buy it. Don't use any fancy renderers which add mouselook, jumping, crouching or many things which ruin the original game design, just use
(brings it as close to the original renderer and returns a few effects which later sourceports removed, like the game's naturally spooky darkness effect) and disable Y-Axis mouselook in options.
There, now you are ready to play a game which really has not aged a day. It is still visceral as hell, still satisfying, still difficult, addictive and challenging to the core and now you can play this game as it was intended. The mouselook, crouch, jumping and cleaner advanced renders all make the game feel older.
Yes, a few levels out of 30+ suck, but you get the double barrel shotgun. Every major part of this game holds up, the abstract and sinister level design, the weapons where every weapon has a use (even the pistol can be used as a low-ammo flashlight in dark areas), every single enemy is uniquely balanced with the weapons and level design to have strengths and weaknesses that you have to exploit, the sound design which feels visceral as hell and lets you get hints at enemies lurking around the corner or behind walls... the list just goes on in how many ways the game has held up.
Without being able to look up it is still more complex than most shooters today, with a very specific vibe where you get REALLY into it if you keep playing. You feel every shot, and it's pretty much the perfect game to feel good.

Honestly, I'm not sure why I'm even bothering to write a review of Dust: An Elysian Tail.
Everybody already knows that this game is awesome. Tens of thousands of reviews have been posted. I believe that everything that needs to be said about the game, has probably already been said. Furthermore, I can't make up a bunch of complaints and flat-out lie, just so I can be "Mr. Contrarian". If were to present an argument that Dust isn't really all that great, first I'd have to convince myself, and that isn't happening.
Why do I think Dust is great? It's mainly due to the controls and level-design. If you've played this game, then you're well-aware of the protagonist's abilities, particuarly his uh... tornado spin?(Press Y button while in mid-air*). This move homes in on enemies, and can even cause Dust to be launched miles into the air, if he's aiming for a flying enemy. A neat trick is using a Lightning storm, then following with the tornado, as enemies are lifted into the air by the electricity. There's a certain joy to be found in soaring through the sky, even when there isn't an incentive (such as treasure).
At the same time, Dust's ability to practically fly isn't a hindrance to the level-design. There are a few shortcuts, and maybe even a sequence break or two, but there's nothing that comes off as really awkward. Due to Dust's mobility, he doesn't really work in a pixel-precise-platformer. Thus, all of the platforms in this game - moving or otherwise - are wide enough. I'd say that on average, they're more than two "Dusts" in width.
Now hang on a second. How does one measure "Dusts"? In platformers, it's always important to consider the character and their relationship with the world. Take Super Mario Bros. 1 for example. The smallest block in SMB1 is only slightly wider than Mario. This gives players just enough time to react, but they don't have to constantly measure their jumps. Having to adjust your landing for every single jump not only affects the pacing of the game, but it also becomes tiring for the player. Another example is the first Sonic the Hedgehog game. Sonic is a faster character, so the platforms he lands on tend to be twice as wide as he is. There's more that could be said here, but it would all be irrelevant to this review of Dust: An Elysian Tail. In short, platforming in this game works, because the player has enough freedom to move around.
The combat also benefits from all of the mobility. There are many tools to play around, and even if they're at times unnecessary, they're still appreciated. If a player wants to tornado through all of the enemies while tossing storms everywhere, that's fine. They can just as easily stay on the ground, and decimate everything with the sword alone. Switching between multiple styles is seamless, and it works wonderfully.
Oh and if you haven't noticed this before. In the final area, if you perform an air-grab on the flying ships, the game pauses for a suitably epic second. The game doesn't do this for any of the other enemies (even the final boss), and that's really cool.
Other than that... Well, I'm afraid I don't have anything else to add. This is a superb game, but you already know that.

The final decision to not recommended Eternity reflects my personal experience about the original Dungeon Defenders and my personal preference of gaming.
There are a lot of negative reviews about Dungeon Defenders Eternity which are incorrect. Let's talk about the most false and improper negative reviews I've read. They include one or more of following statements:
It was clear to me that Eternity will have bugs, glitches and exploits like every other PC game but I never mocked about it like others because it was obvious that Trendy will work on fixes. A lot of users were complaining about the broken stat progression after Trendy has fixed an exploit which has given way overpowered gear. I appreciated the fix since I was still able to reach 2k and higher stats in order to beat the game easily. People were just too lazy to invest time to build a set and to upgrade their stuff. The game was still fine and I liked it a lot.
Then they released Content Update #1 and 'Nightmare' difficulty. I still was able to beat most content with gear which I've collected during the 'broken stat progression' but even on Deepers Well on Nightmare difficulty (the easiest - first map) were dropping stuff with stats way better than mine.
The hardest part of the game now is to reach the required Hero Level to be able to equip this stuff in order to get 4k+ points in multiple stats. Makes the whole game pointless - DD was about grinding - take it away and there are no goals anymore. You are able to reach up to 10k points in a
short time to cover huge maps with a single aura stack and a Buff Beam and you still beat the map without any further defenses.
'Nightmare' turns into 'Laughable easy'.
This depends on two questions. If you answer both with yes then go ahead and buy this game.
Do you like to play solo as in the community is extremely small?
Do you play more casually as in grinding XP and gold will be your only issue?

(Positives)
+ Movement around the environment was fun and smooth.
+ Combat was enjoyable and I liked that the spin attack had a delay on it and therefore forced me to use other attacks and not just spin around in combat.
+ I had to fight the camera in some instances when looking over ledges, but nothing too detrimental to the enjoyment of the game.
+ Collectables were fun to collect, but I wish they didn't respawn and instead were limited so I could make sure I'd collected them all as a fun side mini-game.
(Negatives)
- Animation of character movement could be a little bit slower as I felt I was moving around the map too fast.
(Positives)
+ Solid world design with some really nice-looking zones and nicely hidden areas.
+ Puzzles, they were nice to have and moved the levels along.
+ Platforming in this game was enjoyable
+ Tools given to you in each zone were fun to use especially
(Negatives)
- Puzzles were a little bit too easy.
- Some wasted space in the level design.
- I wish there were more fully fleshed out zones.
- Only 1 boss, which is a shame because it was well designed. I kept expecting one at the end of each zone.
- Only 3 types of enemies and they all died with 1 hit. (It should have been dogbots = 1 hit / rocketbots = 2 hits / machinegun bots = 3 hits) <-- would have added a little bit more complexity/challenge in my opinion.
(Positives)
+ Started off strong with CRT a fun bad guy.
+ Voice acting was in my opinion really good all round, but I was slightly confused why the elder had a very youthful voice, but the actress still did a good job.
(Negatives)
- Ending was just a little bit too cheesy for me.

-  All the other characters are voiced so why not Skylar? (I know protagonists of old were silent like Jak, but I feel she was the least interesting character. The Elder's voice would have suited her!)
- Too short! (I would have loved to spend more time on this island and another two or three zones would have made this even better!)
(Positives)
+ Graphics in some zones were really nice and made each level distinct.
+ Game ran smoothly for the large part except for in cutscenes, which were always choppy. I also had some problems in the volcano.
(Negatives)
- Those lava textures are just awful. They're just red and looked like a flat floor.
(Positives)
+ The soundtrack was really well made and gave each zone its own flavour.

For a great many people Final Fantasy VII may as well have been Final Fantasy I. This was the game that introduced me to the genre of JRPGs, with its classic spiky haired protagonists and oversized weaponry. More importantly, it also demonstrated, to a worldwide audience, the potential scale and spectacle that modern video games now provide almost effortlessly. At the time, this was something special.
Returning to the game now might intially highlight some out of date looks and casts a stark light on plotting that perhaps passes less muster to a more discerning, mature player. However, I think too much is made of these critisisms; the game, while aged (as happens to all of us) still has a charm to it's blocky low-poly models that elevate it above most games of that period (even ones that were arguably better looking at the time), and the high production values, cinematic camera shots, and incredible music score help promote a timeless quality that help retain playability. And the story, while suffering from a sometimes dodgy translation, touches upon big themes of identity, loss and the environmental cost of progress, while remaining accessible in a children's action/soap opera vibe. The story beats swing between comedy and seriousness a little unevenly (sometimes a more than a little, actually), but not unsuccessfully, and overall the plot is driven by appealling character relationships, and great action set pieces cut between quieter, more reflective moments.
The game is huge, opening out from an inital starting city into a whole world to explore, filled with lots of optional things to do which will keep you busy way past the more linear main story path. The combat system is interesting, featuring an active time battle system which merges turn based strategy with some time pressure. The magic system is fun, collecting materia, which acts as spells which attach to your weapons and armor, and level independently of your characters, providing flexibility. The game finds lots of ways to play with the systems it establishes.
The PC version has some weaknesses in that the backgrounds don't always merge as seemlessly with the video transitions and 3D foreground elements as well as on the original console versions, and the music suffers a bit too. Also, if you play with keyboard controls, some of mini-games have occasionally overly dexterous key mappings which might turn your delicate hands into twisted pretzels.
Despite the flaws above, if you haven't played Final Fantasy VII, the PC version remains a solid way to experience a true classic of gaming.

FFVIII was the first Final Fantasy game I ever played when it originally came out on the Playstation v1.  I loved the plot and the game as a whole.  The concept of SeeD (essentially mercenaries) and the Gardens (their Command Centers) was very interesting to me, as was their hidden/seemingly-lost origins.
Gameplay/Combat:
The world is fairly free-roaming and open, which is really nice and a particular favorite of mine. I loathe games where you can't have the freedom to move about as you wish.  This makes it very nice to grind and earn your money/EXP.
I really liked the combat system being a sort of real-time and turn-based system. Random load/ready times to take action for each participant, but you can change attackers (as most RPG's allow) or do nothing while the enemy team still takes action. It's also interesting that you have to draw all potential magic from a source other than one's self - Either Monsters or Draw Points, making magic a fairly limited item since you can't be sure of what you get except in battle where you can seemingly just keep drawing it from enemies as long as you're willing to take damage to do so.
Using magic to enhance the attributes they're assigned to is also a really interesting idea and can help make/break some combat situations.
Individual limit breaks, or each character's special skill/ability, was almost completely useless to me, personally.  I got Squall's to work any time I wanted, but the rest were hit and miss, usually miss. Dunno if it was my timing or what.
Interface/Graphics:
The interface wasn't bad, but bland and static.  For the time the game came out, the graphics weren't horrible, but they weren't great, either, and could have been enhanced.  The budget just didn't seem to be there for it.  When I compare this to games that came out about the same time ("Legend of Legaia", "Star Ocean: The Second Story",) I'm disappointed, though Star Ocean was very similar.
Plot:
The protagonist of the story, Squall Lionheart, irked me as a character.  I didn't really like him.  He's a cynical, emo brat and we're given no indication as to why that is or his history at all.  He just assumes everyone looks at for themselves and is a non-responsive♥♥♥♥♥the majority of the time.
Music:
Pretty good.  There's a fair amount of music and it's pretty nice most of the time and fits the situations.
There is no voice acting at all and, other than one song, no voice work of any sort.
Pretty good if you wanna go old school for a bit, but more for the RPG element than true enjoyment of the story.

Unfortunately this game doesn't offer much in the way of engagement. You swim here, swim there, swim towards this object and press the interact button, then swim some more. The only variation on this repeating cycle is that brief segment where you are swimming around big dangerous things trying not to get zapped. Getting zapped doesn't seem to do anything but LOOK painful. I never died or had to reset as a result. I jokingly called it a swimming simulator while playing, but by game's end, yeah that's about right. Steam says I played 4.2 hours, but I did leave it running while I did some work, so it may only be about 90 minutes without rushing.
It does feature gorgeous visuals and a very pretty soundtrack. The music was just a lil strange now and then, suddenly picking up tempo (which would normally imply incoming danger) while nothing special was happening. The visual style is super easy on the eyes, and has many extreeeemely pretty things to look it. But that seems to be all.
The game features a silent narrative, but I feel it's extremely weak. It mostly uses murals inside some architecture to try to tell some of the background story, but I wasn't able to decipher much from them. Then suddenly there's this big scary angry triangle and your shark friend swims into it all heroic like which blows it up and...it really doesn't seem to mean anything. A tiiiny bit of stuff is happening...but I don't have context to know why this shark sacrificing itself was at all important. It was almost funny because it seemed entirely unnecessary.
The biggest problem this game has by FAR is the incredibly bossy, insistent camera. This usually isn't a problem because you're usually free to swim where ever, but if you're trying to do something specific, it really likes to move itself such that trying to orient yourself becomes quite the pain. Swimming uses tank controls and feels sluggish to respond. There is acceleration to your turn, so you may be trying to just turn about 60 degrees, but because of the slow-feeling response and acceleration, you end up turning 100+. The game will try to flip you right side up if you turn yourself upside down. This is annoying when you're trying to swim straight up or straight down, which you must do a few times. It feels like the game is fighting with you.

For a game like this I really wish there was a way to publish a 'neutral' opinion as Stellaris is just...ok. Which is disappointing from the studio it is coming from and in comparison to Europa Universalis IV or Crusader Kings II.
The game is strongest early on when it is a full on space 4X game, the early exploration phase has some of the best moments a game like this has given me and is easily the most replayable part. There are great events, exciting discoveries and lots of really memorable encounters which set a great base for something to be built on. This early game, the research system, quest chains, planetary & ship development and the soundtrack are probably the great strengths of the game.
Currently, after the early stages the game really takes a nosedive. The transition to mid-game and expansion into the 'Grand Strategy' segments (which are admittedly significantly simplified compared to Paradox's other games) is not smooth. There is suddenly a real lack of things to do apart from conquering your neighbours, there are areas that obviously need to be filled by a espionage system and robust trade. Overall the game turns into a slog to expand your borders where you are constantly having to take the initiative within a mostly static galaxy full of predominantly passive AI that do not help create memorable characters of themselves.
There are also a number of significant bugs including broken event chains and some features not fully implemented, for example you can have an empire of slaves that will never rebel because that ability is currently turned off for them.
I am somewhat conflicted about Stellaris as I feel that after a few expansions and more time it will improve dramatically but at the moment it is probably not worth it for most people.

I can kind of see where the hate/disappointment comes from, but I guess that's the pattern with crowd-funded movies/games: They get so hyped to the point where people get excited beyond reason. After two years of it's release, I FINALLY got around to seeing it and I LOVED IT. I think the thing is people wanted it to be more of a nod to video games, but it ended up being more of a nod to films. It's one of those films that's really not meant to be taken seriously (especially since the opening includes the Nerd throwing a game into a trash can and the trash can explodes.)
I loved the film, and it does have a few moments with bad green-screen (mainly Cooper's introduction) but the rest of the green screen is REALLY well-done, and all of the moments that look bad were MEANT to look bad. It's a self-aware comedy, but not the kind of self-aware that the Scary Movies pull and looks at the audience, winks and says "Yes, this is stupid." AVGN The movie just lets the craziness happen, and I LOVE that about it. It's meant to be a fun comedy that never takes itself overly serious, and it's immersive in it's plot and story-telling.
The effects are also pretty good for a rather small budget. Yeah, there are moments where it's obvious it's a miniature or a guy in a suit or a dummy being thrown, but that just adds to the comedic charm, and speaking of comedy, the film does a good job of THAT, too. There were moments where I almost threw up from laughing so hard. There's even a moment in the audience reaction track (yes, I actually watch those. Shut up) where people were laughing so hard you couldn't even hear the next line of dialogue in the film.
In the end, I may have loved it, but it could just be another one those films that's truly appreciated by fans and film-makers, but I'll be up on the cinematic barricade of indie films with a musket defending this film like Jean Valjean. (Yes, that was a botched reference.)
(Besides, it's better than pretty much every YouTuber movie made by YouTube Red.)

After playing it for over an Hour, I quite like it!
It's not just an Overwatch copy, although there are similarites in MANY characters.
The formatting of the game is awesome and very enjoyable to play matches, which are very long compared to other Shooting Games.
Although, the game, I feel, is sometimes unneedily over complicated- Eg. Buying extras in the middle of matches.

---Edit---
I have read the Dev. Diary in full.
The differentiated FTL types added depth and flavour to both play styles and existing and created races. With the subsequent increase in homogenity, Stellaris is little different than any other Moo clone, let alone any of the Moo's themselves in terms of FTL.
The diversity of FTL was one of the reasons for my initial purchase--since the vast majority of 4x space empire games use a hyperlane paradigm.
If a product has specific features at the point of purchase, said features should be retained and not arbitrarily removed for the sake of design or ease of coding. Decreased variety/utility in a product, post purchase, is neither reasonable nor wise for the maintenance of consumer goodwill.
Given the product I purchased is now going to have features removed, with what I believe to be vastly inferior "replacements" added--per the Dev. Diary, I can no longer recommend Stellaris or any Paradox product (as the production house cannot be trusted to maintain the features of it's products post purchase).
---Edit end---
Stellaris is a nice, current, addition to the 4x sci-fi family of games. Stellaris is NOT Master of Orion (in any iteration) and I find significant differences in the degree of necessary micromanagement and diplomacy. The tech system is simple and clean, though, without an in game "visible" tree, what you research and when is left open to "chance/insipriation" rather than by focus. The odds of going down a given tech chain do increase with more techs in said chain, but, when new, knowing what chains are actually there is very much a "black box" (without looking at game files).
Diplomacy, thus far, is superior to many sandbox/4x games I have played todate. The AI, when operating on it's own, remains above average, both in their interactions with the player and between AI to AI. AI operations become more "questionable" in either an alliance or a federation--where their ability for independent action seems to have been labotimised.
Stellaris is highly modable and has scores of options for alteration. This allows for a nearly infinite replayability.
My greatest complaint with Stellaris is the fragile quest chains currently present. Though the quests/missions are well written, several of the longer chains can be very readily broken, and thus the quest being incompletable. This, I hope, will be addressed in future patches.
I have found multiplayer to be enjoyable, however, the speed of the game and the time required to complete a full game, currently makes pick-up games of Stellaris impossible. That is to say, unless you have a regular group for regular gaming sessions, you will NEVER finish a multi-player game of Stellaris. This, I find, is unfortunate. The scale of Stellaris is one of it's major selling points, but that same scale makes pick-up multiplayer matches untenable.
Thus far I highly recommend this title. We shall see what future patches and DLC afford.

Indie Rogue-Likes are a dime a dozen on Steam these days, but Necrodancer stands out by being both creative and really, really fun to play.
While it may not be the next Nuclear Throne in terms of depth, Necrodancer does have a few tricks up its sleeves to keep things interesting. A half dozen or so unlockable characters (all with their own unique twists and stipulations), a customizable item pool, and of course the traditional random level generation are here, but I often found the smaller things, like being able to dig through walls, more fun to mess around with. There's a lot of replay value as well, if you don't mind the challenge that is.
And speaking of challenge, it can be a surprisingly difficult game at times. Although there's just 4 levels (with 3 stages each), you'll know the ins and outs of every one of them before long because of how much experimenting the game wants you to do. Stuck on a level? Try using a new item, or looking for a specific room.
But let's be real here. The soundtrack is an incredibly crucial part of any good rhythm game, and Necrodancer knocks its music out of the park. This isn't a game OST pretending to be a dance album, it IS a dance album. Hands down, this game has some of the best beats I've heard in a while.
Everyone involved in this project has poured their heart and soul into it, and it really shows. If you like rhythm games, you absolutely
to try this one!

It’s amazing how one simple twist can make a game. Crypt of the NecroDancer succeeds at being challenging, fair, and most of all: fun. I was completely hooked since the second I started playing. What a wonderful experience.
The game is turn based, but its main mechanic is that turns pass on the beat of the music, and you can only move or attack if you do it on the beat. The game rewards you for following the beat with a coin multiplier, which is also important for damage and other stats if you have certain items.
It borrows elements from Spelunky and Binding of Isaac, but I think the greatest strength the game has is its enemy variety. There are dozens of enemy types, each with their own movement/attack patterns. You’ll have to learn their patterns to succeed. You’ll have to treat each death as a learning experience. It felt so rewarding to beat areas for the second time like it was nothing, where they were very challenging at first. And man, the bosses are just
. They’re creative, varied and funny. I love it when games take the time to make bosses great.
The only criticism I dare to give this game is about the bats. I don’t think they fit in this game because they move randomly. There is no way to predict where they’ll move next, which goes against everything else the game is about, which is
.
This is simply a brilliant game worth your time and money. It has tons of value if you’re up to a challenge, and its combat is beautifully designed. It’s also incredible how well the game teaches the player how to get better. The learning curve was really smooth, and I felt like I was getting better as a player every time I beat a level. I could not recommend this game more.

Let me start by saying that although I rated this game as a "No", I keep coming back to it beause of the cool features. THe reason it's a "No" is because once I have played it for a short while I realise that the game has the potential to be the best space faring strategy game of all time but for some reason the developers have stopped short of including all of the little things that would make it perfect (and these things are not ot be found in the DLC).
Nevertheless the greatest feature of this game is the ship designer and ultimately the only reason anyone plays it.
So a list of things that could and should be made better to creat a GalCiv that would stand the test of time...
Improve the imersive experience and the UI:
1. The experience. All the elements are there for this game to really capture the wonder and majesty of space exploration, colonization, diplomacy and battle, but unfortunately the only thing that's done well is battle with everything else second fiddle.
A. Let's start with Exploration: This is pretty vanilla. The Devs clearly have great imagination but for some reason don't apply it to making this element more fun and more significant. What I really want to be experiencing is wonder at discovering new life forms, anomolies and the like and not only that but having them make a real difference one way or the other. Sure you sometimes get a few bc and maybe a tech increase but what I'm suggesting is more: Quests and story arcs that can result in more bc, tech or other bonuses but not right away, only after the quests have been completed. Next, planets should have to be explored first before they can be colonized, to determine resources but also to spark more quests and bonuses and the like. What's on the planet should continue to have an effect, be it artefacts, subsentient beings or dangerous events.
B. Colonization. This is all good in principle, but wouldn't it be great if there was more to it? As mentioned explore the planet first and while I like the ideology idea, I'm more interested by the stories that prompt the choices when you colonize. It is a real shame that the story elements themselves are never again mentioned when dealing with the planet as they could add a fantasticly rich and imersive gameplay experience. Next, if the landmass was more relevant to the improvments and there was just more to do from the colony screen the experience would again be improved beyond measure. Imagine if there were options to export certain native resources, wildlife etc. or if there was more detail on the mix of races and tensions there. There are so many possibilities!
Next, perhaps different races are more suited to different atmospheric conditions or the like, a Class 10 planet to one species might be a Class 9 to another and this could be balanced by actually having a greater number of that race on the planet... something like that.
C. Diplomacy. This is where the devs have made some great improvements but its still very one dimensional. My greatest disatisfaction is that most of the treaty stuff is useless. It's worse than Civilization. Again, look to Paradox and specifically the latest  Europa Universalis or Crusader Kings for how diplomacy is ideally dealt with in a strategy game.
D. Battle. This is not bad and is the best part of the game. My biggest gripe here is actually UI related. For some unknown reason the pivot point of the camera has been changed from GalCiv2 to GalCiv3 and now it is difficult to maneuver and take in the whole battle from every angle you desire. The focus and pivot point should be the centre of the battlefield. The camera also breaks down in free mode at certain angles. The camera usablity nearly destroys the one thing that makes this game unique and great. This is a MUST FIX. Make the camera more user friendly or you undermine the point of the designing your own ships.
Next, is planetary invasion. This is again too simple. THere should be more tactical requirements. Cheaper transports but separate ground based military. Think Distant Worlds: Universe.
2. The UI. Stardock could really learn a thing or two from Paradox, who do this really well. Again I'm talking EU or CK here.  There are a few times where information is unavailable or it is squashed into a box too small for the content. This needs an overhaul.
My biggest gripe is that once you form a fleet the movement points of the fleet are not visible in the bottom left but they are when hovered over.
3. Improvements:
A. History!
Another big point for me is history. In the dim dark reesses of my memory I seem to recall there used to be a "notes" section for planets in GalCiv2. If there wasn't then there should have been. This simple feature (i.e. allowing notes to be made for each planet in the colony screen) would again drastically improve the game experience. Here players can record the history of the planet or reminders of strategy or the like. Ideally, a history log of each planet would be automatic but adding notes gives the player greater flexibility.
While I'm on this notes thing, imagine there was a record of each ship you ever commissioned as well. For some reason that makes the experience better for me, to be able to look back as say "Wow, the T.A.S. Victory was a mighty fine ship, destroying X number of ships before being destroyed at the Battle of So-And-So".
B. Great People. I know its a rip off from Civilization, but let's be honest so is a lot of the GalCiv idea. This is a concept that, if done better than Civilization does it could add a lot more depth to gameplay. This would need an overhaul
Anyway, Enough rambling. I doubt Stardock will ever see this or think to fix these issues as for most people games are about beating the game and winning but for me it's about the experience. I look at games as entertainment, not acheivement. I don't go to a movie just to say I've watched it or to beat it, and in the same way I don't play a game to beat it or win, but rather to enjoy the experience of playing.

Not flawless, but it's actually a great game to introduce your kid / little brother into 3D Platformer / Adventure genre. I hesitate to recommend it for hardcore 3D Platformer fans though due to mild difficulty :)
Skylar & Plux: Adventure on Clover Island is a homage to early 3d platformers. You control your feline hero and help her gather three relic parts to restore something that brings her memory back.
•	Game World and Graphics are top-notch: seriously, the character models / animations / level design is something you would expect from the AAA game.
•	Controls are very responsive (maybe except for jetpack jump) and controlling your character feels great. The jumping, which has often been an issue in the old 3d platformers is done surprisingly smoothly here. It presents a challenge, but you are fighting with the obstacles, and not controls.
•	Beautiful Sounds and Music: the Music fits the colorful game mood and enhances it.
•	More than anything, the game is fun to play. It gives a good mix of puzzles, jumping and destroying enemies, which makes the gameplay exciting, since you never get bored while playing.
•	Camera. It often feels that together with early 3d platformer feeling the developers decided to bring in the clumsy camera controls which was often an issue back then. If you want to look up – the camera often shifts right to your characters butt. Turning during jumping can also be a bit painful experience (although it’s somewhat mitigated because the gamepad has the button that centers the camera behind your character).
•	The plot is somewhat cheesy (which honestly is understandable), but the initial premise was that the cat character had memory removed and was trying to restore it. By the end of the game, this completely shifts and it seems like nobody cares about restoring the memory anymore. After completing the game, you still don’t know what happened to the character and how she ended up being where she is.
•	Not much Content / Low Difficulty: there are about 5 different enemies and one boss. The game itself can take about 3 hours to complete if you just want to run through it (to counter that: there are multiple optional health unlocks that can greatly prolong the experience; 100% completion will take much more time; the lack of enemies is also compensated by puzzles and good level design that requires lots of non-repetitive jumping with different approaches to getting past the obstacles).
Despite the flaws, the game is still fun, but not for typical hardcore gamers who are nostalgic about 3d platformers. The length of the game might be questionable, but the experience quality justifies it. It’s the game that I’d buy for my kid, because it is very colorful, well-polished and reasonably challenging. For veteran gamers with 3d nostalgia though – I hesitate recommend it and I leave this up to your discretion.

The game Skylar & Plux: Adventure on Clover Island by Publisher Grip Digital and developer Right Nice Games is, at its heart, a platformer. Its story is somewhat . . . lacking—although in due fairness most Mario games don’t have much of a plot beyond save the princess and Sonic fans tend to riot whenever SEGA tries to give one of the Sonic games a deep, convoluted story—though I will admit I occasionally enjoyed the banter between the characters Plux, CRT, and Bob. A disclaimer I would like to mention is that this game is short—as in I was able to complete the story and get over half of the collectibles within three hours short.
Skylar & Plux: Adventure on Clover Island consists of a tutorial level, three stages, a small hub world to connect the three stages, and a boss fight. You start with the ability to double jump, punch, and swing from grapple points and gain more abilities as you progress through the game. My impression of the tutorial level and first stage is . . . uninspired. Most (if not all) of the content in this part of the game felt like any platformer—which might not be a bad thing if you are a huge fan of platformers, but it left me with a feeling of ‘been there, done that.’
The second stage is where things start to get interesting. The ability you get from that stage is rather unconventional (the ability to make time move at less than half speed for up to 10 seconds) and saw such good use in the stage that I found myself wishing the ability saw more use outside of the second stage. The third stage is likewise interesting in its new ability and level design and, unlike the second ability, this ability sees some use outside of the stage in which it is introduced. The third ability is a magnet, which considering all of the enemies in this game are robots, is fairly useful.

ABZU is one of those games that I will come back to again and again. Like the great games of yore, ABZU captivates the imagination and compells the player to immerse (possibly submerge? ;) ) themselves into the experience. These kinds of experiences seem to be few and far between in these days of ultra-HD blockbuster fireworks that are, quite honestly, a dime a dozen it seems. In an age of passable movies and passable games ABZU shines as bright as the lapis and gold walls that are found in the temples, and has formed as strong a bond with me as I did with the Great White Shark.
On a side note, as someone with a debilitating fear of deep water I was half expecting all manner of jump-scares and deep-sea chase scenes or worse. Instead I was greeted with calmness, serenity, and an invitation to challenge stereotypes.
On behalf of people like me, thank you to everyone involved in making this game,
