Stellaris is really my first venture into true 4x games. To be honest I have
so much apprehension to this genre it has always kept me away. I used to
watch my friends sink hundreds of hours in Crusader Kings, and Europa
Universalis 4 and they seemed to love it. I was always sitting in the back
thinking, “I don’t want to have to go back to school practically to learn a
video games mechanics and the finer points of the game before I can give
it a try.
So I picked up Stellaris the newest title by Paradox and as someone
who is new and was previously intimidated by 4x, I can say with confidence
the game is quite excellent and above all accessible! The game features
a great level of customization from everything about planet management
(buildings, policies, upgrades) to individual ship designs (weapons, power,
shielding) as well as empire customization (leader traits, government style,
military tech start, etc) The game allows for you to custom tailor your star
fairing race to a fine point. As well as the finer details of micromanagement
and creating sectors to manage planets under one “system/sector” so
that takes a bit of the stress off the individual micro of planets.
The game features a beautiful aesthetic barring performance issues at
this moment of writing it. Giant space battles and honestly when Civs start
growing and filling the map you are going to see a frame hit. I am running
a 980ti… so there are things left to be desired in terms of game performance
but I have heard they are hard at work fixing these optimization problems.
so I do have faith Paradox will work hard on fixing the issues that are affecting
the game currently. They also have given full mod support to the community
so expect some amazing mods and total conversions (BSG,MassEffect,Star
Wars,Star Trek, etc). Stellaris has a lot it got right and it made it fun for me
to learn and to challenge myself to manage my empire better.
The game features fun random events that can be great for your empire
or not so great. It also features a random tech tree so you really won't have
the same options a second time in the order you get them in say your first
game. Which I personally enjoy, take Civ5 for example with an incredibly
linear tech tree, having a random tech tree with “rare” tech etc spices things
up and encourages you to play differently and focus on what you need or
are going for rather than following the same path over and over again. It
adds variety and fun challenges to your empires rise and potential fall.
I could talk about the game all day to be honest but I think I will try to
keep this someone concise. Stellaris may be Paradox’s best 4x game yet.
I have a new genre to enjoy and sink massive hours into. This is an easy
recommend to veterans of 4x/Paradox games, and even a recommend
for those trying to get into this genre. It’s fun, accessible, and addictive!

I don't have time to stop play every 20 to 30 minutes to figure something out (only to find out that the consensus is that whatever it is I am looking at is broken). I hate this reliance on DLC to "fix" issues. Basically it looks like the issues were created to begin with to force us to buy DLC!
Why am I capped at 5 star systems to manage? Why can't I have a larger range of options in the way I manage my sectors? Why do fleets act stupidly and charge into combat when they have the longer range? Why are strike craft/fighters only short ranged? Why do I have to look at each Population individually to determine their happiness?
The interface has serious issues. Things that should require a mouse click or two require 4 or 5! There aren't any resources except the community to tell me how to do things. Someone says "I coopted a primative society." How?!? Is there some technology that allows that? I don't know because the randomness of how techs come up is excruciating.
That all said I still play, because I want to figure this stuff out. Not because I am really enjoying it, but because I refuse to be defeated by another Paradox game.
One day Paradox you will create a game that is easily understood, enjoyable to play, and truly engrossing for all the right reasons, but not today. Curse you!

It’s amazing how one simple twist can make a game. Crypt of the NecroDancer succeeds at being challenging, fair, and most of all: fun. I was completely hooked since the second I started playing. What a wonderful experience.
The game is turn based, but its main mechanic is that turns pass on the beat of the music, and you can only move or attack if you do it on the beat. The game rewards you for following the beat with a coin multiplier, which is also important for damage and other stats if you have certain items.
It borrows elements from Spelunky and Binding of Isaac, but I think the greatest strength the game has is its enemy variety. There are dozens of enemy types, each with their own movement/attack patterns. You’ll have to learn their patterns to succeed. You’ll have to treat each death as a learning experience. It felt so rewarding to beat areas for the second time like it was nothing, where they were very challenging at first. And man, the bosses are just
. They’re creative, varied and funny. I love it when games take the time to make bosses great.
The only criticism I dare to give this game is about the bats. I don’t think they fit in this game because they move randomly. There is no way to predict where they’ll move next, which goes against everything else the game is about, which is
.
This is simply a brilliant game worth your time and money. It has tons of value if you’re up to a challenge, and its combat is beautifully designed. It’s also incredible how well the game teaches the player how to get better. The learning curve was really smooth, and I felt like I was getting better as a player every time I beat a level. I could not recommend this game more.

All things considered, Dust is a fantastic metroidvania-esque game. I heard that one guy did almost all of the work on the game by himself. I think the only thing was the voice acting and some of the sound effects.
Some of the best features:
Great mechanics
Tight controls
Superb voice acting for a game of this scope
Combat feels great all the way through the game. Simple at it's core, but plenty to play around with
A great length for the scope and price of this game. I think my first playthrough on Normal took around 10 hours if I remember correctly
Sound and visual feedback during combat is one of the best I've ever seen, at least for a game of this scope.
Some things that might put people off:
Animal characters. I like the decision, but it may not be everyone's cup of tea
Combat may seem repetetive if you do the same one or two combos over and over
"easy" in the sense that there's no real difficult puzzles and enemies. Some can be challenging the first few times though. It's a game that you're meant to run through though, so the enemy mechanics shouldn't need to be very deep. Still, may not be for everyone.
Story is okay. Nothing groundbreaking though. Voice acting makes up for it in my mind however.
Dialogue-heavy at parts, but all the dialogue is skippable, so it's fine if you just wanna play and not pay attention.
Overall:
Good:
+Gameplay/combat
+Length
+Voice Acting
Ok:
Story
Level Design
Meh:
-Animal characters (if it's not your thing, didn't bother me)
-Lengthy (skipable) dialogue

F.E.A.R is... well, let's just say it's different. It's like most shooters (at least from its time), but not. It combines a creepy atmosphere and super intense action to create the experience. I guess it's really not fair to compare it to other shooters because it is not like other shooters in the sense that this one has a story. It's a weird story and sometimes off, but a story nontheless. The greatest thing about this game is the slo-mo feature. Yup, you can slow down time all Matrix like. And yes, before you decide to question it, it is amazing. The AI, while stupid in some parts, is actually quite good. they work together instead of running past the same corner ten of their buddies were shot next to. for example, if you are up against two enemies, one will stay back while the other slowly approaches you and flanks you. The one who stayed put, will use suppressing fire to distract you, giving the other guy a minute to smack you in the back of the head with his own bullet. They also really like to use grenades, and have a pretty good arm too, so watch out for that. Even though the game is over five years old now, it still looks pretty decent. the blood and gore effects are stil gruesome, and the vaporization effects Alma (antagonist) uses on some helpless people during cutscenes is impressive. It's always fun to watch someone's skin get burned away by an angry ghost child. That's another thing worth mentioning; the horror in the game is cut down to mostly just jump scares and long, dark hallways. nothing really else outside of that. The action, however, is intense. especially when you come across the mechs. Oh, did I not mention that before? Well, now I did. Yes, giant metal monsters will be trying to blow your insignificant human body up into millions of tiny, bloody pieces. Conclusion: should you but this? To put it simply, yes. Even without multiplayer, it is still a fresh change from the mundane of shooters we have been forced to suffer with in recent years.

Dust is a simple 2D action platformer with an undeniably gorgeous aesthetic, great audio and smooth responsive gameplay.
The story is nice for what it is, using the easy amnesiac hero trope to help introduce the player to the world, which is made more enjoyable by your companion being adorable, the other companion acting as a guide with both characters offering dialogue and advice during in-between sections of story to keep you amused going forward. The NPCs offering side-quests are a mixed bag on what you're going to get, with some offering interesting dialogue and others being dull fetch quests.
Level design is well thought out with plenty of variety, although you do feel discouraged to explore areas on your first run through the game as many areas are locked behind talent abilities that you unlock later in the game, forcing you to revisit areas once you're overleveled trivialising the exploration in the first place.
Interacting combat with your companions is interesting as it emphasises your ability to chain together a combo by giving you an auto target ranged attack so that as you're being a swirling blade master of death between enemies, you can keep that combo-chain going to gain bonus experience and if you do happen to come across a larger enemy, you can parry incoming enemy blows with a well timed attack making you near immortal, even on the highest difficulty.
Overall I had plenty of fun during my play through, which is of a good length. Making it well worth picking up in a sale if you're interested in a simple 2D action platformer.

Metroidvania with a *beatiful* setting, furry characters, fast combat, fun and a decent challenge but certainly not 'Nintendo hard'
The backgrounds for this game are absolutely gorgeous. They have a handpainted look along the lines of Muramasa and Odin Sphere. Characters look good, but not quite as good as the backgrounds. The cast is very much furry, but not in a fetishy way. For me this was neutral, but if you're a furry I'd recommend this even more, and if you just can't stand furries you should probably avoid it.
Combat is very fluid. Sometimes almost too much so, aerial moves leave you soaring across the screen and can home in on nearby enemies. This can be great for boosting to secrets and shortcuts, but occassionaly can fling you away from the fight or even into an area you didn't mean to go. The combat isn't exactly hard, but do require different tactics for different enemies. Some are almost invlunerable till you parry them, others explode if you get near, etc. For most of the game it seemed like enemies couldn't do one-hit kills, the first blow that would take you to 0 HP took you to 1 HP instead. This seemed to stop being true about 2/3rds through (on Tough). Since you don't start with regen this is nice for letting you conserve healing items and if you play carefully reduces the need to level HP.
Gear is mostly a linear progression of improvement other than rings, which have some specialized bonuses (item find, extra XP, stat multipliers) you'll be choosing between. Levelling is straightforward too. You can choose between improved health, attack, defense or special attack, but they can't be more than 4 points apart from each other so no extreme specialization.

For the price tag, this is totally worth it.  Anyone with a negative review and dozens and dozens of hours played, ask yourself is $30 really not worth all those hours of fun?  I've barely scratched the surface and I definitely have gotten my money's worth.  My initial impressions were "meh, it's okay".  Then as I played more and more, and really started getting into the mid-game of my first campaign, the depth revealed itself.  Now I consider this a nearly epic game.
It is crazy complex, from diplomacy, trading interactions, technology paths and choices (very impactful), challenge, to combat... Which you cannot directly control, but you very much have control over it by designing your ships to counter your opponents through armour and weapon selections, and customization.
The more I play, the more fun it becomes and more addicting it is.  The depth is revealed.  I am a long-time civilization builder player, from the Civ series, to Master of Orion III, to Heroes of might and magic (all of them), to EUIV (completed a full iron campaign), to all Total war games.  This game might not be as epic as some of the games I've mentioned, but it is still really good, especially at this price point, and it is unique enough that it sets itself apart from other games in this genre.

While I don't regularly play this game as much as I did before, I still enjoy Dragons and Titans. Its gameplay is simplistic, and pretty much everything is well-designed, both in mechanics and art/figures. If you are feeling bored and trigger-happy, then this game might be good for you.
However, the gameplay doesn't involve much strategy. When you pick a game mode you just do a specific attack/defense pattern, and hope for the best. Secondly, the matchmaking system can be a nightmare very often. It just picks five random players for a team, so you frequently see copies of dragons on the same team. Or another case is when the opposing team has several powerful dragons, then your team is screwed. Thirdly, too many of the features require actual cash to be unlocked, like Acts and specific dragons or weapons.

While much of this game is the same as the first, there are a significant number of differences for me that make it worth getting, not the least of which is the level of Dev attention it is getting, which has fixed a number of starting problems, including many with the Summoner class (which stuck out for me as it is my class of choice).
The inclusion of most of the DLC content (the holiday packs and such don't seem to have made it) is something that stands out for me, especially given the price. This also means most new players will likely go for the DDE over DD1 (dungeon defenders eternity/one). New levels have been made and more to come, including one in the campaign (so far, I have not made it too far as I have been enjoying the social aspect, and testing out the classes), pets now come from eggs that hatch simply by having them on your person and you never know what you will get.
Also, gear now appears on your person in a physical way which is fun, especially when you get the full set of something. Mana is no longer the currency, coins are, which drop from creatures just like mana, and are used to upgrade your items. However you can no longer buy weapons or pets from the barkeep (as of yet). There IS an ingame cash shop, but the only thing in it is emotes for your characters at a dollar each. Dyes are also available now with the barkeep, as well as a new crafting system.
For crafting, recipes drop from mobs, and materials seem to only drop from chests (though I could easily be wrong, i tend to get caught up in the action). You can choose to join your own private tavern, or a public one with other people milling about. There are even more new features that I could mention but I am sure you could find more complete lists out there.
IN CONCLUSION:
I find this game to be quite a bit more fun than the original right now given it is easier to join people of my own level, there is more details on the games I am joining, I can host private if I really want to and only invite my own friends, and it has stopped me being booted out for not having that one awesome piece of gear or whatever other reason people saw fit.
The only downside I saw, no offline play, which I do hope comes later, but I understand why not if it doesn't.

I've been a great fan of airports since I was little and I will never forget my first airport tycoon game - the venerable Airport Inc. It was amazing for my younger self, with so many plane types, so many different contracts that included airlines, shops, fuel, turnover etc. etc. I loved negotiating, avoiding incidents, and so many different spots for your airport to be based in.
This game is much better. I've been following it for a long, long time, and it really amazed me. It's only Early Access now, but it offers you a lot more freedom than Airport Inc., has much better, really gorgeous graphics, involves the process of hiring your employees including construction workers, offers a lot more possibilities when it comes to directing flights and planning your stands (you can decide which ones will operate GA planes and which commercial ones), and it is more fun to plan your airport here. Sure, one might say that it doesn't have that many furniture types yet, and your terminals might seem a bit empty, but it is still EA, new stuff will come soon. They seem like a very decent studio that delivers what it promised, judging by the quality so far, and I'm convinced that this will be improved over time and will become truly amazing. It's great right now, and can only get better. There are not even that many bugs right now, which is pretty uncommon for EA titles.
1. The architect part. It's really fun to design your airport, although things like baggage claims should be available from the start. Those are one of the most basic things an airport needs.
2. Hiring employees. This really makes you feel like a CEO, especially hiring your directors who are essential.
3. Flight planner. A great feature that makes you really feel like a person in charge of an airport.
4.  Graphics. Simply gorgeous. Especially the menus. This looks better than RimWorld and Prison Architect in my opinion.
5. Intuitive GUI - it is easy to find everything, connect deks to your stands and set up queues.
6. It's quite bug-free for an EA titles. So far, mainly some issues with not being able to click something, works well after restarting the game. No big deal, nothing game-breaking.
7. In-game manuals are really helpful and contain a lot of information in a way that never seems overwhelming.
1. I guess I would like to see a historical mode like the one present in Airport Inc where you started in 1970 and experienced all the changes throughout the years from turboprops to modern airliners. But overall, it's just a nitpick.
It's really cheap for what it offers and I truly believe that this studio seems serious and this won't become another abandonware, as sadly is the case with a lot of EA titles. Support the devs and this amazing game!

What is Angry Video Game Nerd: The Movie?
It is a movie made by James Rolfe aka the Angry Video Game Nerd (AVGN) about the adventures of titular character when a fictional version of ET2 is to be released by a video game company that is deliberately made to suck even more than the original. The movie is done in a B-Movie style, with partially really obvious post-production effects, as often seen in the AVGN webisodes that can be seen on Cinemassacre or Youtube.
Now I had gotten the movie from another website where it included a big "Making Of" as bonus material, giving insight into the making of the movie, which is really worth watching. Unfortunately this seems to be missing on Steam, and actually I only own the movie here because it was in a movie bundle. So keep in mind that even though I can recommend the movie and therefor say "Yes" under the review, you do not get the best version here.
Note that the games in the story are completely made up, I might name them "ET" but in-story these are fictional games just clearly modeled after those real-life counterparts.
The story begins with the Nerd working at a video game store, when suddenly a copy of ET2 is given to him. Some undercover agent from the ET2 company gets in touch with him as well. Unfortunately this is also the biggest downside of the movie - the first 20 to 30 minutes are just boring to watch. After that, when the Nerd sets off into the desert of New Mexico to find a landfill of ET cartridges to hold an excavation there (which makes this movie a period piece as even before its release a real excavation was held there where indeed the cartridges were found). The military believes that the ET cartridges hold the secret to reach Area 51, and therefor tries to stop the Nerd and its friends, who set out to find one of the original creators of the game.
Between the paranoia of the military, the paranoia of the game creator and the hot desert, the viewer is left wondering if there is sexual tension or even a romance plot building up between the Nerd and the company spy, but in the end everything gets even bigger than expected, and unearthing the secrets behind the cartridge might have consequences not only for the Nerd and the miltary but the whole world...
Is the movie worth watching?
Well, if you like the AVGN or if you like B-Movies, absolutely! That is, if you can stand through the horribly boring beginning of the movie. I enjoyed most of the movie, although the false game names put me off from the suspension of disbelief I have otherwise for the Nerd web video series. However, the characters all have their distinctive attributes, although there is not much depth to be expected - what happens is Nerd humor, just on a bigger scale. If you want to take the movie seriously at any point, this is not for you. If you want to laugh at bad visual effects, paired with some cool gags and overall cheap atmosphere - go for this movie, it won't disappoint you!
Positive:
Nerd humor
Characters that all have a tick of their own
The movie becomes a gagfest enjoyable to Nerd fans
Cheap looking visual effects (Nerd style)
Negative:
First half hour is horrible
No real game titles (with one exception)
Cheap looking visual effects (that could have been more convincing)
If you don't like the AVGN humor or style, this is not for you
Steam version lacks bonus material
Specs:
The video gan be streamed in 360p, 540p, 720p and 1080p. The only language for both the video and audio is English. The only audio quality is 322 kbps, Surround 5.1 (tested only in 1080p resolution).
Recommended: As a movie, mostly. But the missing bonus material, especially the Making Of, is unforgivable.

I might've chuckled once or twice during the near two hours. I cringed through about half of the whole thing. I pushed through it only because I used to be an AVGN fan, but honestly I don't think I watched a film as unenjoyable as this ever before. Special shout out to the script for being a tragic mess. Plus, watching inside Steam's movie player is like consuming♥♥♥♥♥♥embodied in more♥♥♥♥♥♥
Was James Rolfe intentionally going for this effect? From what I observed during his blogging during production, I wouldn't say so. Rather, I think he's just outright mediocre at making cinema. He's talented at the AVGN web series, because it's off the cuff & casual, there's a real connection with his mates, and he's developed the right technical skills. But it just doesn't translate here at all.
This guy has bitten off
more than he could chew in production values―there's
many elements there were added in post. They look terrible, but not even in a funny kind of cheesy way. This film archieves what I'd like to call the 'uncanny valley' of CGI.
Before filming the thing though, it feels like it should've never left pre-production in this state. The story arcs are all over the place, and they attempt (& fail) to capitalise on jokes that must've only been funny to the writers because they wrote them while drunk and/or high. It kind of gives an impression of holding itself together, until about the midpoint, which from there on out, morphs into a gaint train wreck.
Perhaps I could've looked past that, if only the characters weren't so terrible―and that's this movies greatest weakness for me. So, they're all trope-based & lacking depth, not too suprised there. I guess I hoped to have developed some empathy for them at least, but the film didn't provide any real opportunity to do so. I can't say I blame all of the actors. Attempting to act for this thing would've been akin to polishing a turd. But in the end there's very little on screen chemistry, and much of the connections between characters feels forced.
If you just want to watch the review itself, skip to the credits. Don't hold your breath though. Even just watching this ending piece was a lackluster disappointment. After describing the gameplay, the Nerd proceeds to harp on about the game not being
bad, blah blah blah. Talk about anti-climatic. I'm not sure James could've given us bluer balls. Nothing entertaining here, just an attempt at some kind of enlightenment that falls flat on it's face.
The aforementioned rotten cherry on this rancid cake―Steam's desktop movie player―makes me not want to watch another video on Steam again, not unless Valve startes taking video streaming seriously. This film was released in anamorphic format (2.35:1) and I have a screen near that (21:9; 2.33:1). But instead of showing at native fullscreen res (1080p), Steam just puts a 16:9 pre-letterboxed (820p) stream in the middle of my screen, resulting in a 'black box' effect. Not to mention the constant screen tearing, it's pretty bad and my eyes are strained.
So in conclusion,

F.E.A.R is... well, let's just say it's different. It's like most shooters (at least from its time), but not. It combines a creepy atmosphere and super intense action to create the experience. I guess it's really not fair to compare it to other shooters because it is not like other shooters in the sense that this one has a story. It's a weird story and sometimes off, but a story nontheless. The greatest thing about this game is the slo-mo feature. Yup, you can slow down time all Matrix like. And yes, before you decide to question it, it is amazing. The AI, while stupid in some parts, is actually quite good. they work together instead of running past the same corner ten of their buddies were shot next to. for example, if you are up against two enemies, one will stay back while the other slowly approaches you and flanks you. The one who stayed put, will use suppressing fire to distract you, giving the other guy a minute to smack you in the back of the head with his own bullet. They also really like to use grenades, and have a pretty good arm too, so watch out for that. Even though the game is over five years old now, it still looks pretty decent. the blood and gore effects are stil gruesome, and the vaporization effects Alma (antagonist) uses on some helpless people during cutscenes is impressive. It's always fun to watch someone's skin get burned away by an angry ghost child. That's another thing worth mentioning; the horror in the game is cut down to mostly just jump scares and long, dark hallways. nothing really else outside of that. The action, however, is intense. especially when you come across the mechs. Oh, did I not mention that before? Well, now I did. Yes, giant metal monsters will be trying to blow your insignificant human body up into millions of tiny, bloody pieces. Conclusion: should you but this? To put it simply, yes. Even without multiplayer, it is still a fresh change from the mundane of shooters we have been forced to suffer with in recent years.

I just added FEAR in my steam library, altough i own the game since it's release. I completed the storyline (for the 10th, at least, time) and it's time for me to write a review. But now i think about it again, and i figure that this is the most irrelevant reason to play it  ;)
The protagonist is the "Point Man" (no real name) of F.E.A.R. (First Encounter Assault Recon),a secret unit of the US Government, specializing in dealing with paranormal threats. The mission is to take down Paxton Fettel, and his clone army, known as Replica.
It takes about 8-10 hours to complete the campaign (depending on the difficulty)
If you get this game, it wont be about the kickass graphics or its realistic gameplay, If you expect something like that, i bet you will be disappointed. However the atmospheric gameplay, created by the well-designed maps and the awesome light-shade effects, the enemy AI, which is far more advanced than even some today's FPS and the great storyline totally compensate the game's drawbacks.
Additionally, the multiplayer was awesome and made me spend many hours playing. When i found out that MP doesnt' work anymore i got sad.
+ Great graphics at the time of release
+ Atmospheric gameplay created by the lighting and shade effects, with the addition of even greater sound effets
+ Advanced enemy A.I. which can make the game challenging
+ Interesting storyline and plot similar to an action-horror movie. The well created cutscenes add to that.
+ Variety of weapons and grenades
- No multiplayer ( T.T )
- Some glitches may occur due to specific graphic combos.
- Usually repititive
Concluding, worth buying it since it's considered a classic!

You either already played the Witcher 2 or wanted to give it shot after discovering how amazing the Witcher 3 is. You might be surprised how different the previous chapters were in terms of gameplay and story telling. The Witcher 2 improved on its predecessor by vastly improving on the graphics, animations, dialogue but takes a hit when it comes to the role-playing elements. The second game requires you to have at least some knowledge of the world and lore of the series otherwise you can get really confused on the events that occur. Characters and enemies are thrown at you without much explanation about who they are and when it comes to monsters this makes it more difficult to deal with in battle.
On the topic of difficulty the combat system will leave you frustrated and scratching your head. Most of the essential skills can unlocked after the first tree of abilities are acquired making your initial journey more excruciating than necessary. Couple this with the fact that their isn't a side step option and your character free runs around enemies without locking on to them. This makes targeting very cumbersome and irritating as multiple enemies swarm you in confined areas. You also need to craft potions for combat but you cannot use them while engaged in battle. This makes it very annoying as you have to trial and error to figure out what type of potions you require for battle and drink them before engaging enemies.
The game is broken up into chapters that has our protagonist solve or deal with a main conflict. After it is solved or dealt with you move on to another section of the world and are not able to back track on anything you missed out on. This reduces the game's feeling of freedom where unlike in the Witcher 3 you could explore the world to your heart's content from one end to the other and discover vast amounts of adventure on the way. At times the world feels confined with invisible walls/blocked areas and a journal that doesn't always give you a general direction on where to go.
Seems like a lot of bad huh? Well to be honest, despite all these issues with the game, it's still a fantastic title. The graphics were amazing then and still hold up quite well today. If you delved into the lore from the Witcher 3 you'll find many familiar faces and acquire additional knowledge for their presence in the third game. The music is fantastic and the voice work is improved over the first game. The story is great although much of the information can be overwhelming without background knowledge.
Overall all I have to say is that if you liked the Witcher 3, you may be turned off by how "primitive" some of the mechanics of the second game are. You may find it confusing/difficult/frustating and ask yourself "why?" on occasions. Even still, you can generally get it at an amazing price for a couple of bucks and I highly recommend toughen it out through the first dozen levels to get your abilities and take in the great story, sight and sounds.

The quality of the game is a series of trade-offs.

The combat is simplistic and primitive; but innovative in a very humble way.

The world design is quite generic fantasy babble; but it has some neat pun based silly bosses.
There are a decent amount of unique areas and everything is randomized; but the map and enemy layout is inconsequential.
The primary downside to the game that is not balanced out by something, like with so many games now, is the difficulty.
The game has no problem with allowing chance to lock players into a deadly situation just because the enemy patterns synced up just right to be indomitable. The game has no problem with just spamming the player with enemies, which are almost impossible to survive because the player is locked to the beat and thus has a limited scope of what they can do at a time against multiple threats. Some enemies just outright have obnoxious attack patterns which require the player to literally stop everything and perform a specific chore to counter that one enemy; this being extremely problematic if that enemy has any help at the moment which the aforementioned issue of spamming enemies stacks onto. Finally, there are some enemies that literally just end the run if they show up because they are so strong and require you to do one specific thing to fight them; if you are in the wrong situation or do not have that enemy completely memorized then you just lose; because screw you for playing the game.
This all massively ramps up by the third area, which is where the game completely stops caring about being reasonable and expects you to trial-and-error master memorize everything if you want to progress.
Another issue is that because the attack and move buttons are the same, if the player has a weapon that hits more then just their directly adjacent tile; when the player goes to move to an open tile but something is in their weapon range in that direction they will be forced to attack it instead of moving. Which can cause legitimate problems and actual deaths. So having any weapons other then the basic one-tile-of-range dagger is also a bad thing because the way the game functions can lead to the extra range making the player attack things they don't want to, which keeps them standing still, which can get them hurt or killed. It is borderline impossible to account for in the heat of gameplay because of how awkward and unintuitive it is and thus it is just a problem that has to be accepted will hinder the player when using any weapon type except one.
The minibosses aren't very balanced either, at all. Some of them are trivial, some are average, and some are ridiculously overpowered and have an eighty percent chance to just end that run the moment they show up because they are literally that absurd to fight.
And the controls are quite bad. Everything is controlled by only four keys. So in a game that is meant to be rythme based and thus needs to be smooth, they thought it'd be clever to map over eight controls to four keys by requiring players to press awkward and unintuitive button combinations of those four keys to use things like healing items and spells. Not only did they make the controls bad for working with something that the player needs to do quickly if they're at low health or are in the actual spot to cast the spell and need to; they did it in a game where they have to do everything to the beat. Furthermore, the control remapping interface does not tell you what button combination does what in-game. So you have to look that up yourself. And the controller support doesn't acknowledge all the buttons on the controller, so the player can't even make use of them all which makes it harder to remap the bad controls into something playable if the player happens to prefer controllers. And using the analog stick causes the menus to flip out as well.
Although the game itself has a great concept, the game almost exclusively relies on artificial difficulty. If the bad and counter-intuitive controls aren't horrible enough, the difficulty of the enemies themselves is entirely based on unfairness. The game spams the player with enemies and ganks, the game makes the player fight enemies with tedious gimmicks that require the player to stop everything just to satisfy that gimmick, the game spams players with gimmick enemies which together cause mandatory damage; because their gimmicks line up in the exact way where the player can't avoid harm or they just can't respond to everything at once, the game spams the player with environmental hazards ontop of making them fight at the same time, the game spawns enemies with gimmicks that the player may not even be able to respond to in their current setting because there isn't enough space or time to do it.
The enemies themselves are almost all easy to fight, the game is difficult exclusively because it piles on enemies, hazards and blockages at once with no mercy or limitation. It expects the players to dance around it all exactly; exactly everytime to the most L33T degree in order to survive in the middle of a real time game where your movement is locked to a rythme. Even while knowing every gimmick and hazard, accounting for them all at once is absurdly difficult if not impossible. And beyond this, the game can line the player into a scenario where they fundamentally cannot survive no matter what they do. Because it is all randomly generated with no restriction, so it is possible for the player to get a game over because they were locked into an impossible situation.
The final zone boss and final boss are also just, the developers just throwing in as much difficulty as they possibly can to kill the player off. The final zone boss is absurdly spam-based and expects the players to fight multiple mini bosses while the invincible boss is spam rushing them, then players have to bait the invincible boss into performing a certain action while he rapidly spam rushes at the player the moment they are in his sight and he hits for over half the players health each time if it lands. Immediately afterwards players must then fight the final boss, which requires player to juggle an absurdly overbearing gimmick while fighting off constant waves of enemies who hinder the players ability to satisfy the gimmick. Until then the final boss shows up then the final boss must be fought while still juggling this gimmick and fighting constant waves of enemies and a mini boss spawns each time you even hit the final boss. It is just the developers making as much of a stupidly overpowered end to the game as they can so players can't finish the game and thus have to keep playing.
Everything about the game itself save for the controls is generally just fine. It's the completely arbitrary and meaningless sense of difficulty that the game has which makes it really hard to complement. Because there is no structure, limitation, or sense to any of it. Although during the first two biomes it isn't very significant, the final two are entirely steeped in it.
It's not like in most Rogue-likes where trial and error eventually leads to the player fairing better in surviving. From start to finish it is exclusively about the random generation of the game. Either surviving because the random generation didn't just game over the playthrough, or surviving because the random generation spawned enough good items for it to not matter.

tl;dr Might have been better off as a choose-your-own-adventure film than an RPG. Still worth getting when it's on sale though.
Positive:
The stroyline and quests are great. You're often put in a moral dilemma similar to the ones Geralt finds himself in throughout the book series. No decision feels 100% right which makes things more interesting and adds replay value because you want to go back and see what would've happened if you had done things differently.
The side quests are complex and add more depth to the story and characters. It's hardly ever "go here, fetch this item or kill this enemy, then come back and get your reward." There's always a puzzle or a twist to go along with it.
Negative:
The actual gameplay is pretty lack luster. Combat is a bit better than in Witcher 1, but still leaves a lot to be desired. Controls for traps/bombs feels laggy and unresponsive. The targeting system is really hard to control so sometimes when you've just rolled up to an enemy you want to attack, you end up running backwards through a gauntlet and trying to attack an enemy that wasn't even on your screen anymore. Or if you just defeated an enemy, Geralt will automatically choose a new one and immediately start attacking. This among other things make you feel like you're hardly in control.
Half the enemies can easily be taken out just by frantically clicking. Frantic clicking is also how you interact with a lot of objects, particularly in the prologue.
Sometimes there will be a cutscene where all of a sudden you have to click left or click right to avoid dying, as if the developers are just testing if you're still paying attention. Fist fights are pretty much the same, except you're pressing either W, A, S, or D every once in awhile instead of clicking.
Stealing and other crime has little to no consequences. You can walk into a shop, loot everything from all the boxes and chests, then sell it all to the vendor. You can slaughter all the buther's pigs and chickens out on the street and no one cares.
Also they're kind of pushing it when they call it "open world." There are open spaces, but there isn't a completely open and interconnected world.

I was reccomended to play ABZU by a friend and honestly, avoided it for a while because I was never a fan of water based games. Man, was that a silly choice. ABZU redefines the possibilities with which we can use a landscape. It makes a statement to show the beauty that an almost all-water environment can hold through the lens of the ocean, and explores all corners of that setting. You'll be exploring anywhere from brightly lit coral reefs to dark abysses.
The studio has achieved excellent level design. Each area doesn't feel claustrophobic as water levels are so often connotated, but feels really open like the ocean should without feeling like the area is so massive that you would get lost.
Admittedly, I got lost in a few of the areas, but never for long, and in those moments you still get a feeling of drifting exploration to keep you enthralled.
The creative director for ABZU was also the art director for Journey and it really shows. The world has the same whimsical feel and grandure. ABZU also follows journey in using a narrative concept called The Hero's Jouney from Joeseph Campbell's "The Hero With A Thousand Faces." Now this still makes the narrative compelling and draws us along an intriging narrative path, but it does feel a bit too much like Journey in the narrative.
Honestly, what I reccomend most about this game is the experience devoid of the narrative. The environment your player is in, the places you'll see, and the apotheosis segment of the journey at the end are truly incredible gameplay moments. The smooth and juicy feedback of the controls helps you stay immersed in these moments.
As a developer myself, I really reccomend this to level designers specificaly. Again, it just really nails the water environment on the head in a really effective way. Tech artist would also be bewildered by the schools of fish that really feel full of life. There was a talk on it during GDC 2017, so if you have access to the GDC vault, look up The Art of ABZU, excellent talk.
For the best playing experience, do a one session runthrough of this game on a day that you have time too. I got through it in 2 hours from my playtime on record, so it's a nice sitdown game. Don't have any distractions around either, if you are talking with a friend, have them be viewing the game with you. Just try to stay in the moment and really get everything you can out of this world.

Basically, Civillization V's hot one night stand with Spore's Space Age. Great combo of strategy and RTS as well as the 4x's of Empire building.
(Explore, Exploit, Expand, Exterminate)
Pros:
-Awesome race and empire creation
-Cool RP community
-Neat space combat AI and different interstellar travel and mechanics.
-Immersive strategy, diplomatic placements and choice in allies can save or break your empire.
-Cool ship customization and research progression, you feel like you're bettering an interstellar empire through your work.
Cons:
-The AI can suffer from Civ V syndrome, they won't budge in resource trade deals. Ever.
-Moderate learning curve (Not so much a con as a warning, you will get crushed in online games.)
-Slavery is OP (not even kidding, it's broken and very exploitative for aggressive empires)
-Slightly flimsy diplomacy, usually results in "I'll buy your love with credits, now let's be friends k?"
In summary, amazing 4x sci-fi strategy with a solid online community, would highly recommend.

I first played this game when I was around 11 years old. I hated it to be honest, the game was too confusing for me at the time and the system was weird, nothing like the almighty Final Fantasy 7 that I loved. Naturally, some years later I wanted to make a better judgement of it, and I did, and I absolutely loved it. Now that the game is on Steam, I can make a review with my memory completely freshened up after beating the game for the 3rd time, after many unfinished playthroughs.
Everything from this game seems to be way above and beyond of what gaming was at the time. The game is modern, it feels modern and even the system is unlike any other title. The way you build your characters is very unique in the sense that you can costumize every single detail and no character is like any other, the choices are also limited so you can't have a character doing absolutely everything while the others do nothing, which makes the concept of a party much more likely to happen.
Aeons or Summons have always been a big part in Final Fantasy games, but never like in FF8, not even in FF10 are Aeons as important as Guardian Forces in FF8, this makes the amazing GF cinematics in FF8 much more wanted, which for me was an issue in other games, they looked awesome, but physical attacks just cut it better in FF7, for example.
The characters all have a big role in the story (which will be the last part I'll talk about), and they're all well crafted, none of them are spot-fillers, they're there, they're unique in their personalities and traits and they're just not annoying. In other titles I've always felt there was this one character I didn't like, but I think it's the fact that in FF8, there's only 6 characters that makes it so much easier to like them all.
The side-quests are bad and few. And this is all I should say about this, but it won't be. The only ''side-quest'' you should be partaking in is the Card Quest, but unfortunately even to obtain all the cards you have to complete most of the other boring, dull, hard to find and hard to complete without guidance side-quests, this is the biggest flaw in the game in my opinion, the game barely gives any hints on how to find or complete most side-quests and you're forced to search the internet for most, such as the PuPu quest (after the 3rd occult fan, no more hints are given), or obtaining the Tonberry King GF (There's one mention of it in Trabia Garden, but one would only get so far to getting the GF by sheer persistence and guessing.
And before we move on to talk about my favourite part of the game, let's talk about how I love the draw system. Many people hate this system, some think it's unfair, some think it's boring, I personally think it can be whatever you want it to be. I have a system when I play that I get the magical and the defensive character do the drawing and have the offensive character do the killing. It works because it raises the stats equally and it's not boring at all, so I reach the middle of the game with all my characters balanced and even the ones outside the party get to have spare magic. And it's also super fun finding out magic from monsters.
Now, the story. The perfect, yet flawed story that makes me think this is the best game I've ever played (I've never have a game that I wanted to replay right after finishing it). The story is incoherent? Maybe. Maybe the story is confusing and has a lot of twists and weird happenings throughout the game. But it's all resolved in the end... Or is it? There are 2 theories to the story of this game that I love to discuss about, and they both make a lot of sense, but they're just theories, because the story allows for them to exist, the story isn't vague but it has this open space for creativity that's just right. I won't go into many details because of spoilers, but when certain things in the game come together and you start figuring out certain things, it just makes you go "wow...", and everything unfolds and makes sense in front of you, it's brilliant.
Also, Selphie is adorable.

I wouldn't recommend it for the moment, nor say people "don't buy it".
I personally find it much better than other Galactic 4x (endless space and Galactic Civilizations), so it deserves a thumb up, however it is far below other Paradox games, so it would deserve a thumb down.
As tons of people say the early game is awesome. The mid game is boring, if you get lucky enough to reach it. On my last playthrough, in Hard difficulty, everything was going fine. I was on track with other empires. Had some grand strategic movements in mind. A good army on par with others, with about 10 platform defense on the most important points of my Empire.
Good! Good!!
And then... A Fallen Empire declares war. That is something really bad for game balancing as they are completely overpowered compared to other Empires. The guy declares war for forcing me to abandon half of my Empire and sends me a 80K army in my face. I have 5K... And you can't expect to have much much more after 4 hours gameplay.
Game ruined... Have to start another game... Com'on... I play in Very hard since the first Hearts of Iron. I'm playing Ironman in Crusader Kings 2 where I'm twice Emperor and I can't even count how many Realms I have. I'm far from being a newbie in Paradox Games.
Such punitive events cannot happen in a Paradox Game. It would by like if in Hears of Iron you're playing Germany and you have a chance out of x that in 1938 just after the Anschluss EVERYONE declares a war on you (Russia, USA, Japan, France, UK, Poland, Tchekoslovakia, Italy, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Holland...). You can be as strong as you want, you just can't stand such things...
Apart from this kind of stuff the game is well done. Ultra stable. No bugs (for me at least). Very well polished. UI is great. But it feels so empty compared to others Paradox Game.
Don't get me wrong, it's much better than all others 4X / Grand strategy games, but Paradox kind of used me (us) to much better...
Superficial diplomacy. Non existent politics (Ministers? Parties? Government policies like drafting, economy scale, education etc in HOI?). Non existent economy / war economy (convoys? supply to troops (something like that...)). Personalities traits? I don't expect something as deep as Crusader Kings, but com'on... Each Character has 1 trait... No relation effect..
I mean... Paradox seems to me very lazy on this game.
I'm sure they will turn out to be a HUGE game within some years, but at this point... It is sooooooooo below other Paradox games. It's way below day 1 Crusader Kings. I'm a bit disappointed. But yet, it's a good compared to competition

F.E.A.R. is a pretty decent game, and one that I'm glad I played. It actually kinda reminds me of the original Half-Life a bit, just not quite as legendary as that game,
There are problems with this game. For one, it is NOT a horror game at all - there's barely anything remotely scary about it. There's a few potential jump scares, but that's it. On the other hand, the game does do a great job of setting a dark atmosphere for the player; it's scary in the same way that Half-Life was scary.
It's also a bit repetitve - sometimes I swore I had already been through certain places more than once. This is a fairly long game these days as well, at about 10 hours to complete, so this problem can be really annoying, depending on your tolerance level.
Another MAJOR thing you should be aware of if you think about buying this game: Logitech products cause it to massively drop frame rate for no reason sometimes. This is a well-documented issue, and it does have fixes; however, with my setup, the only thing that worked was to play for about 20 minutes before the frame rate really began to degrade, then unplug the mouse and plug it back in. Only took a second to do it each time, but was mildly annoying to have to put up with.
Overall I would recommend it - just don't expect horror from this one. Expect a shooter.

The quality of the game is a series of trade-offs.
The animation and art for the game itself isn't particularly impressive; but it has a phenomenal soundtrack.
The combat is simplistic and primitive; but innovative in a very humble way.
There are plenty of items and equipment to find and unlock; but they aren't very exciting nor is the unlock system itself.
The world design is quite generic fantasy babble; but it has some neat pun based silly bosses.
There are a decent amount of unique areas and everything is randomized; but the map and enemy layout is inconsequential.
The primary downside to the game that is not balanced out by something, like with so many games now, is the difficulty.
The game has no problem with allowing chance to lock players into a deadly situation just because the enemy patterns synced up just right to be indomitable. The game has no problem with just spamming the player with enemies, which are almost impossible to survive because the player is locked to the beat and thus has a limited scope of what they can do at a time against multiple threats. Some enemies just outright have obnoxious attack patterns which require the player to literally stop everything and perform a specific chore to counter that one enemy; this being extremely problematic if that enemy has any help at the moment which the aforementioned issue of spamming enemies stacks onto. Finally, there are some enemies that literally just end the run if they show up because they are so strong and require you to do one specific thing to fight them; if you are in the wrong situation or do not have that enemy completely memorized then you just lose; because screw you for playing the game.
This all massively ramps up by the third area, which is where the game completely stops caring about being reasonable and expects you to trial-and-error master memorize everything if you want to progress.
Another issue is that because the attack and move buttons are the same, if the player has a weapon that hits more then just their directly adjacent tile; when the player goes to move to an open tile but something is in their weapon range in that direction they will be forced to attack it instead of moving. Which can cause legitimate problems and actual deaths. So having any weapons other then the basic one-tile-of-range dagger is also a bad thing because the way the game functions can lead to the extra range making the player attack things they don't want to, which keeps them standing still, which can get them hurt or killed. It is borderline impossible to account for in the heat of gameplay because of how awkward and unintuitive it is and thus it is just a problem that has to be accepted will hinder the player when using any weapon type except one.
The minibosses aren't very balanced either, at all. Some of them are trivial, some are average, and some are ridiculously overpowered and have an eighty percent chance to just end that run the moment they show up because they are literally that absurd to fight.
And the controls are quite bad. Everything is controlled by only four keys. So in a game that is meant to be rythme based and thus needs to be smooth, they thought it'd be clever to map over eight controls to four keys by requiring players to press awkward and unintuitive button combinations of those four keys to use things like healing items and spells. Not only did they make the controls bad for working with something that the player needs to do quickly if they're at low health or are in the actual spot to cast the spell and need to; they did it in a game where they have to do everything to the beat. Furthermore, the control remapping interface does not tell you what button combination does what in-game. So you have to look that up yourself. And the controller support doesn't acknowledge all the buttons on the controller, so the player can't even make use of them all which makes it harder to remap the bad controls into something playable if the player happens to prefer controllers. And using the analog stick causes the menus to flip out as well.
Although the game itself has a great concept, the game almost exclusively relies on artificial difficulty. If the bad and counter-intuitive controls aren't horrible enough, the difficulty of the enemies themselves is entirely based on unfairness. The game spams the player with enemies and ganks, the game makes the player fight enemies with tedious gimmicks that require the player to stop everything just to satisfy that gimmick, the game spams players with gimmick enemies which together cause mandatory damage; because their gimmicks line up in the exact way where the player can't avoid harm or they just can't respond to everything at once, the game spams the player with environmental hazards ontop of making them fight at the same time, the game spawns enemies with gimmicks that the player may not even be able to respond to in their current setting because there isn't enough space or time to do it.
The enemies themselves are almost all easy to fight, the game is difficult exclusively because it piles on enemies, hazards and blockages at once with no mercy or limitation. It expects the players to dance around it all exactly; exactly everytime to the most L33T degree in order to survive in the middle of a real time game where your movement is locked to a rythme. Even while knowing every gimmick and hazard, accounting for them all at once is absurdly difficult if not impossible. And beyond this, the game can line the player into a scenario where they fundamentally cannot survive no matter what they do. Because it is all randomly generated with no restriction, so it is possible for the player to get a game over because they were locked into an impossible situation.
The final zone boss and final boss are also just, the developers just throwing in as much difficulty as they possibly can to kill the player off. The final zone boss is absurdly spam-based and expects the players to fight multiple mini bosses while the invincible boss is spam rushing them, then players have to bait the invincible boss into performing a certain action while he rapidly spam rushes at the player the moment they are in his sight and he hits for over half the players health each time if it lands. Immediately afterwards players must then fight the final boss, which requires player to juggle an absurdly overbearing gimmick while fighting off constant waves of enemies who hinder the players ability to satisfy the gimmick. Until then the final boss shows up then the final boss must be fought while still juggling this gimmick and fighting constant waves of enemies and a mini boss spawns each time you even hit the final boss. It is just the developers making as much of a stupidly overpowered end to the game as they can so players can't finish the game and thus have to keep playing.
Everything about the game itself save for the controls is generally just fine. It's the completely arbitrary and meaningless sense of difficulty that the game has which makes it really hard to complement. Because there is no structure, limitation, or sense to any of it. Although during the first two biomes it isn't very significant, the final two are entirely steeped in it.
It's not like in most Rogue-likes where trial and error eventually leads to the player fairing better in surviving. From start to finish it is exclusively about the random generation of the game. Either surviving because the random generation didn't just game over the playthrough, or surviving because the random generation spawned enough good items for it to not matter.

I picked up all three Witcher games on sale on STEAM in a bundle.
The Wither 2 continues the story from the first game, it also carries over some choices, money and equipment from the first game if you have a Witcher 1 save file on your system.
The Witcher 2 makes a lot of improvements over the first game, from controls, to game mechanics and to graphics. The UI is easier to use now, which is a huge plus.
There's still a number of problems with the game though. One of my biggest complaints is the game's quests and quest tracker. Most of the quests in the game are almost painfully ambiguous, they'll inform you of your end goal, but won't really give you a lot of details on how you need to complete these quests.
In the very beginning you'll find some contracts to kill monsters. Seems simple enough, but it really isn't. The game informs you that you'll need to "learn more" about these monsters before you can stop them and to read up in books. The game doesn't tell you where to find these books and the quest tracker has no indication of the location for these books. As it turns out, you can also just kill the same monster over and over again until you "learn" more about them.
Even after learning more about these monsters, the game simply hints at what you need to do. No further direction is given. This is incredibly frustrating and this is only an example. There are plenty of quests that tell you that you'll need to "Do 'A'", but won't tell you how to go about doing it or what you'll need. This has actually lead me to avoiding several quests simply because of the frustration of the crappy quest system.
Only to add insult to injury, I am constantly running into quest breaking bugs that either force me to re-load into an earlier part of the game or try to find a way around it. This doesn't make for a fun game. Another problem I have with the quests is a lot of them are simply repetitive, the game is just FULL of fetch quests that'll require you to walk from one end of the map, all the way to the other end. Without a fast travel option, this becomes annoying very fast. Granted, the maps aren't that big, but when you are constantly walking back and fourth like this, it feels like this mechanic was only put in to make the game longer.
Even at only 5 years old, the game shows it's age and a lot of times, it isn't very good. Graphically speaking, it's a nice looking game, although there's this weird glow from the light system that often times obscures the game in a annoying way.
And don't get me started on the random crashings.
I am still trying to enjoy this game, but it feels like every time I go to start a new quest I am bracing myself for what kind of garbage I'll have to do next and I always make sure to have a guide open on my phone.

What is there to say about Doom II that hasn't already been said?
I'm not entirely sure myself, but let's start off slow and easy.
Doom I and II will always be the best of the doom games, as they were the originals. Compared to the new Doom, it will be infinitely superior to some, but not all.
Doom II was for a different generation, a generation that valued patience and effort. Lets put it this way, imagine playing the new doom with only the arrow keys, the spacebar, and a couple other keys.
Sound good? Yeah, I don't like it either, thats because there was originally no mouselook. Which means tank controls.
This was for a generation that took it's time to finish the amazing levels this game contained, because they were forced to. They found satisfaction in the subtle fact that they had finally beaten that one map where monster closets open up on both sides, and you cant turn fast enough to fight both left and right, so they backtracked and funneled them through a hallway. It took strategy to beat this game, something the new Doom lacks entirely. Doom 2016 is about instant gratification, and that leaves no room for the feeling of accomplishment. What do you get? A nice first person animation of you brutally slamming an Imp's face into a wall, not to mention it goes by so quickly.
In the end, it's up to bethesda and ID software to determine how the games they make play and feel.
But I'm saddened that they encouraged the ideal of instant satisfaction over rinse and repeat strategy.

I was quite dissappointed by this game, having previously had great expectations thanks to a fabulous rating in reviews.  Dust is primarily a metroidvania, but the focus is taken away from the exploration and discovery that is a trademark of this genre.  Much more attention is given to combat, to some good effect.  There are a handful of combos, with both ground based and aerial move sets.  Unfortunately combat tends to follow a few basic formulas (example:  Parry, Perform Combo X, Repeat) all throughout the game, which eventually makes it fairly repetitive.  Bosses are laughably easy.
There is also a heavy focus on story, but this is lost due to the horribly cliche character tropes used.  The various furries that populate the Dust universe will shortly have you sighing with frustration as you click past their boring dialogue, rolling your eyes at yet another sword wielding main-character afflicted with amnesia.
There are a fair amount of treasures and secrets to find as you explore, in classic metroidvania style.  Sadly the actual level of reward for this explorartion is very low, being that most of your character's strength will be gained through killing monsters for experience and crafting new equipment.  The crafting system is very basic, and you will generally buy your ingredients rather than grind for them.
Final Summary?  Dust is not a terrible game... it's just not very good.  It certainly isn't worth the price tag.  Do yourself a favor and find a better title than this lack-luster offering.

I feel this game has gotten a bad rap.  Yes, it is the original game rehashed, but that was made clear prior to release.  Yes, it has new features, but more or less it plays like the original.  As an owner of the base games of both, this is the one that I prefer.
Graphics 7/10 - They choose a slightly different style for DDE and I personally liked the style of the original better.  The graphics don't seem as clear and crisp as the original.  They even have a warning about streaming textures....why can't I opt to download these?
Sound 10/10 - This game has some ridiculously addictive music.  I've caught myself humming along with bits of it.  A family member who played it breifly said the same thing.  Some sound effects could use a little more oomph but that's about the only downside I could say.
Gameplay 8/10 - I'd love to give this game a 10/10 here if not for one fact.  Load times.  Load times drag down the overall experience even when playing in a private lobby.  On the plus side, this game is FAR more accessable that it's predecesssor for finding gear for your characters.  Having the option of which stats that the game is comparing is a big deal for newbies especially.  The massive amounts of mana available on each map means your resources are not the limiting factor, it's more focused on your strategy.
Developer Support 10/10 - Let's face it folks, this is the game they are supporting more at this date and time.  DDE has gotten a lot of bad reviews and most of the constructive criticisms have been addressed.  It has gone from what felt like a beta release to a full release over the last few months.  Their continued support and patches will make this into an even better title.

Okay, before I go into details (this will mainly compare it with the original): is the game still fun with friends? Yes.
This remake/redo/whatever did improve and balance the gameplay, which was definitely needed. That is one major positive.
However, it threw away so many of the basic elements that made the original a great game. I am unable to stay in the same lobby with my friends between matches, instead it boots them to some random server. The original had it great, keeping us all in the same place, instead of making me reinvite and reconnect every time we start or fail a map/tavern.
By the same token, because the servers are now externally hosted (I understand - helps control hacking), my ping is so much higher. This isn't such a bad issue when there are not too many monsters, but later on, it is a real pain.
The microtransactions, well I don't really care too much about them: they're mainly just for taunts, which are not needed.
However the shop is so much less intuitive and instead of making everything easier, it became much the opposite. It tried to improve on sorting, which is good, but it still fails to have a filter for a certain type of armor. Considering you get set bonuses, it would be better to have this.
Also you don't get the bonuses from two weapons, instead everytime you swap your weapons, your towers get the current weapon's stats. This is fine for balance, except everytime I press "z" to swap weapons, my towers are half damaged. It would be easier just to have the one weapon so I can easily replace it when I get better ones, or have an option to have 1 or 2.
Yeah, just my rant.

Stellaris is a game that sadly fails to deliver much beyond its initial promise.
The gameplay and mechanics should be familiar to anyone who's played 4X strategy titles. Race design and ship design are extremely fun, even if their practical applications are minimal.
However, the game hits several major hangups:
1) Gameplay is extremely repetitive. The number of "anomalies" (read: subplot drivers) is very limited so the game tends to play the same regardless of how you built your empire. There are no real incentives for playing a pacifist or mercantile empire, and the game mechanics don't really inclue a "trade" system beyond the existing resources.
2) Diplomacy is pretty much nonfunctional. The system design resembles Total War in many ways, but other empires seem to reject completely reasonable proposals, even outright advantageous ones, while accepting completely ludicrous or exploitative proposals.
3) Multiplayer setup is maddening. Every time I try to get our group of four together to game I plan on at least 30 minutes of trying to work around the innumerable bugs and issues. For a game that prides itself on its multiplayer focus (being able to save multiplayer games and resume them later, etc.), this is unacceptable.
All in all, Stellaris feels like a letdown. I may have to check back on it in a year or two.

Dust is primarily a metroidvania, but the focus is taken away from the exploration and discovery that is a trademark of this genre.  Much more attention is given to combat, to some good effect.  There are a handful of combos, with both ground based and aerial move sets.  Unfortunately combat tends to follow a few basic formulas (example:  Parry, Perform Combo X, Repeat) all throughout the game, which eventually makes it fairly repetitive.  Bosses are laughably easy.
There is also a heavy focus on story, but this is lost due to the horribly cliche character tropes used.  The various furries that populate the Dust universe will shortly have you sighing with frustration as you click past their boring dialogue, rolling your eyes at yet another sword wielding main-character afflicted with amnesia.
There are a fair amount of treasures and secrets to find as you explore, in classic metroidvania style.  Sadly the actual level of reward for this explorartion is very low, being that most of your character's strength will be gained through killing monsters for experience and crafting new equipment.  The crafting system is very basic, and you will generally buy your ingredients rather than grind for them.
Final Summary?  Dust is not a terrible game... it's just not very good.  It certainly isn't worth the price tag.  Do yourself a favor and find a better title than this lack-luster offering.

Stellaris is a game that sadly fails to deliver much beyond its initial promise.
The gameplay and mechanics should be familiar to anyone who's played 4X strategy titles. Race design and ship design are extremely fun, even if their practical applications are minimal.
However, the game hits several major hangups:
1) Gameplay is extremely repetitive. The number of "anomalies" (read: subplot drivers) is very limited so the game tends to play the same regardless of how you built your empire. There are no real incentives for playing a pacifist or mercantile empire, and the game mechanics don't really inclue a "trade" system beyond the existing resources.
2) Diplomacy is pretty much nonfunctional. The system design resembles Total War in many ways, but other empires seem to reject completely reasonable proposals, even outright advantageous ones, while accepting completely ludicrous or exploitative proposals.
3) Multiplayer setup is maddening. Every time I try to get our group of four together to game I plan on at least 30 minutes of trying to work around the innumerable bugs and issues. For a game that prides itself on its multiplayer focus (being able to save multiplayer games and resume them later, etc.), this is unacceptable.
All in all, Stellaris feels like a letdown. I may have to check back on it in a year or two.

I adore this game. Ignore the Mixed rating. It's my favorite space trucking game and one of my favorite games period. It's not the fanciest-looking, but I think the clean little 3-D ship models and the space backgrounds look really nice.
You choose a role (prospector, fighter, trader, etc.) and build your ship with different modules (engines, navigation console, thrusters, hulls, all kinds of different weapons, etc.) and fly around mining, trading, cargo shuttling, or shooting pirates with your giant lasers/cannons/death rays/what have you. There's tons of items and ship parts and a big skill tree system that tangibly affects your combat, piloting, and trading capabilities.
Yes, it could probably use more story content, because there are a lot of small side quests (some are amusing, some are more your typical meh RPG fetch quest) but the overall story and NPCs are thin, and the bases/systems are very similar to one another. This is not a space
game.
But I've spent plenty of happy hours cruising around the map and leveling up to where I could afford the biggest lasers. I like the music too, so flying around listening to it and looking at the stars is relaxing. It probably is to me what Euro Truck Simulator is to other people.
I find the combat fun and satisfying. There are lots of ways to configure your ship so it fits your needs and style, and that affects your combat approach. Right now I'm flying a big armored death machine with four top-tier heavy lasers, so my frontal killing power is awesome and I have no worries if I get swarmed by pirates. But the side-to-side maneuvering isn't good at all compared to the light fighter I was trying out before this, so I can't jump into quick one-on-one dogfights. I love that I have to tinker, compromise, and upgrade.
Also, the character avatar creator has excellent eyebrow options. Better eyebrows than Dragon Age: Inquisition. 10/10 would choose eyebrows again.
I will say that the
(or one of the other community voice mods) is a must because the native flight-computer voice is not great.

I really wanted to enjoy this game; after all, I've enjoyed nearly every other Paradox release.  Unfortunately, a combination of game-killing bugs (defender warscore anyone?) that should have been fixed before release coupled with a glaring dearth of mid and end-game content have left me feeling like this was a game either rushed to release, or designed to serve as a money mill for future DLC that will eventually make it into what we all want it to be.
That's not to say that it doesn't have its moments.  The early game is stacked with memorable adventures, an eager pursuit of exploration, and seemingly boundless possibilities and paths that your fledgling space empire might take.  However, it doesn't take long for the aforementioned bugs, shockingly shallow diplomacy and governance systems, and an even-worse battle system to shake one's confidence in the long-term viability and enjoyability of your play through.  Once your empire starts finding its borders closed in by those surrounding, the lack of AI proactivity and the sheer absence of much to do leaves the player in the position of simply sitting and watching turns ticks by until something even slightly (and I do mean slightly) interesting occurs.
It is truly a shame that Paradox made the decision to strip much of the 'grand' out of this grand strategy title thereafter - leaving it as a title with a lot of potential, but very little to deliver.  Perhaps if this was a fresh entry into the genre from a new developer some of these issues would be easier to overlook, but coming from a shop with the reputation that Paradox has nurtured, it is hard not to wonder if they may be starting to lose some of the magic and creativity that has made previous titles so easy to love.
I, for one, will be looking forward to the modding community more than the product Paradox has delivered - here's hoping that they may save the day for an otherwise extraordinarily disappointing release.
