[SPOILERS (?) AHEAD]
Disclaimer: I got this game on a heavy discount, for next to nothing. Over half of the game time is due to a Steam Idler. Beat all 9 levels.
Dead Bits is a pixel-based FPS game, and its premise is that you're abducted by aliens to fight alien zombies. From the get go, you get the idea the game itself is going to be pretty off the wall in terms of content.
The vast majority of things in the game world (even water, your enemies and yourself) are made of small colored cubes. As a result, the game itself is very colorful, almost having a childlike vibe to it. Given the blocky aspect of things, there's no much visual detail. The look of the game is complimented by a semi physics-based system which you can only notice when you kill something - the body's blocks fall in such a way, and you can shoot them around as well.
The music compliments the game well. The vibrant colors make the music itself seem seamless, and the music starting up just as you pick up a new weapon and a bunch of enemies pop up as a result makes you feel like it truly is♥♥♥♥♥kicking time. That said, I detest dubstep, so the genre soured me on it as a whole.
The pros end here. Now, the cons. The game is riddled with bugs and unfair gameplay, rather than difficulty. There are so many holes in the levels' surfaces that you'll find yourself more often dying from falling off the map than being killed. If you land a jump too close to something (a wall, platform, etc) you aren't able to make your next jump unless you back off first. The game's level progression makes no sense - you go from trees to tunnels to sky ice levels to hell to something straight out of sci-fi. The game's 'weapon switching system' is virtually useless since in most levels you're only given one weapon to work with (if at all). The enemies themselves aren't much of a threat at all and you can easily just make them run circles around you. Aiming is worthless since you do the exact same amount of damage hitting a leg that you do hitting the head (20 dmg for machine gun, 150 for rifle, 50 for alien blaster, and I forget the damage of the metal bat, I think it's instant kill for the smaller enemies at least).
What secured the negative rating of this game for me were, unfortunately, the game breaking bugs. I came across three - for example, the hitboxes aren't reliable: you can shoot a zombie in the face with your rifle and it doesn't register a hit, and you can go through a healing block square in the middle and you don't get healed (dying unfairly as a consequence); in level 7, I noticed that if I didn't get the final 2 enemies to magically come to me (and I was horribly inconsistent with it), I would get locked where I was and fail the level due to running out of time; and finally, in level 8, the game would frequently lock me between enemy waves and not move onto the next.
I can't recommend for someone to actually pay for this broken mess, and I'm not sure I would anyway if the game was free. While it does start out well enough, it soon gets really frustrating...

This is a fun little puzzler made by the people who brought us World of Goo (one of my favorite puzzle games of all time). Once again they show a knack for taking simple gameplay and making it a more complete experience with fantastic art, sound design, writing, and general presentation. The fire looks great. The menus look great. The cutscenes look great. This game just looks and sounds fantastic. The story is super compelling, and the writing is fantastic. They manage to make you care more for a character you never once see than most AAA games with motion capture could ever hope to while being darkly funny all at the same time.
My only real complaint about this game is that it's very, very short. I beat it in about 2 hours. If you're being a completionist about it and trying to get all the combos, I could see that stretching to 3-4 hours, but not a minute more. It also has less replay value than World of Goo (imo), and less gameplay depth in general. I wouldn't pay the full 10 bucks for it, but the 50% off sale price I paid is more than fair and there's no reason you shouldn't buy  it if it's 5 bucks or less.

I finally managed to get the RTS games "of old", back when the genre was popular in order to get over this gap in my life of RTS games. Red Alert 3 has a few things that satisfy me:
Empire of the Rising Sun is pretty great; not as stupidly broken as GLA is considered in Generals, also has by far the most interesting units as well as the deployable buildings giving you a flexibility Allies and the Soviets do not have. They also have Gundam-like robots shooting lasers out of their eyes; seriously, that is a valid selling point of this.
The presence of secondary abilities could have went really wrong pretty easily, their implementation was spot-on in a way that it's pretty balanced and useful. Some units depend on their secondary, particularly Empire of the Rising Sun's which occupy dual roles (Sea/Sky Wings, Striker/Chopper VXs).
Factions in themselves area pretty balanced to the point where it's really depending on your playstyle what faction works the best for you. In my case Empire of the Rising Sun fits me because of usefulness of dual-role units and flexibility of building placement; nothing throws your opponent more off-course than hard rushing by placing Defender turrets right outside of his base's exit.
Campaign-wise you'll have a lot of fun and engaging time. I finished all campaigns in nearly 12 hours, but I played the game since when it got released in 2009, so you'll definitely spend upwards of 14 hours. Most difficult mission you'll encounter will be Empire's last mission.
The cutscenes using actual actors are another thing which worked for games like Act of War, C&C 3, Red Alert 3 and even C&C 4 (even if that game turned out to be garbage), sadly lost and really miss them.
Skirmish, like in any RTS game is on-point and fighting against hard AI is a doable battle, not visibly cheating like how Command and Conquer 3's AI.
I haven't had a shot at multiplayer yet, since I currently don't have anyone to play against, but expect it to be just like any C&C game.

It's probably the most convenient way to play the game these days, and that counts for something. And it really is worth playing; it's the black sheep of the Playstation FF games, but that makes it interesting. It's broken, has an even more ridiculous plot than usual, dungeons are very often literally copy-pasted together, and the ever-present card game brings the pace to a crawl. But, it also has a great cast, interesting changes to the typical FF ruleset, the card game is fun, and the settings are varied and beautiful while creating a more consistent universe than its immediate predecessor.
THAT SAID...
If you have a Playstation/PS2 hooked up to a CRT TV/XRGB-type scaler, or an emulator with a good CRT TV simulation mode, you will have a vastly better experience. The game is designed around the limitations of the Playstation, and the PC version makes no attempt to hide the "strings", such as they are.  The backgrounds are 320x240 scaled up with nearest neighbour scaling, while the characters are rendered for native resolution and filtered, and it creates a distracting mismatch - only exascerbated by "crowd scenes" where the crowds are baked into the backgrounds, designed to match up with low resolution Playstation models but completely out of place with the smooth, detailed characters.
It's actually kind of fascinating to get a the behind-the-curtain perspective on the game like this, it gives you an appreciation for the craft and cleverness of the developers - but it takes you out of the game, looks like crap, and that sucks.  Games designed for low resolutions should be played in low resolutions.
Also, by default, the music uses awful general MIDI versions of the soundtrack.  There are mods to fix this, but it's kind of unacceptable to put out a rerelease of a game praised for it's music with a general MIDI soundtrack in the year 2014.  My god, you don't have to fit it on 4 CDs anymore, you can distribute it with a recorded soundtrack!
I recommend it because it's good, but the presentation is awful.  Step up your game, Squeenix.

So I'm flying around my newbie ship in the starting system having a pretty good time with the game. I did the opening quests, rescued a few survivors, killed some pirate lieutenants, and mined a LOT of asteroids. You can never have too much money when you first start a game.
After mining, I loaded up on all the best kit available at the starting station -- whichi sn't very much. I put a light laser and autocannon on my ship, bought a new engine that even the item's description said was a bad engine, but it was still better than the civilian engine I was currently using. The rest of the kit I had on my ship was the stuff you start the game with. There just wasn't anything else to buy.
Now I choose to locate the Order faction recruiter who was located 3 jumps away. No problem. I make the jump to the first system right next door to the starting system -- and I'm immediately destroyed by a swarm of pirates. Yeah,  it's the standard jump gate ambush tactic that I really loathe.  By the time you've even oriented on the change of scenery and figured out which ship is actually yours, you're dead.
I tried just letting autopilot take me through the swarm on cruise -- but that doesn't work, either. First, there's usually a collision or two, slowing your ship down to a crawl. If you manage to get through that, the range on the pirate's weapons reaches halfway across the system, so you're still getting pummeled even if you run away.
Okay, forget that quest. I'll do it later. So I decide to jump to a different system, a high tech system right next door with a danger rating of 4. Oh good, maybe I can buy better weapons or even a better hull with more hardpoints. How dangerous can a danger rating of 4 be, anyway?
I jump through to the high tech system and -- yeah, you guessed it. Another pirate swarm. This time I managed to blow through them but ended up with no shields and only 35% of my structure remaining. I fly for a second or two and ended up in the middle of a second pirate swarm.
Because yeah, the pirates seem to know the moment you jump into the system and know exactly where you are. I don't even have time to open up my map to plot a course to a station. If I try to do that, I get killed. Again.
Hey, I don't want a game to be pathetically easy -- but when you can't even leave the starting system without getting obliterated mere seconds after jumping, that's not a challenge, that's developmental griefing. In essence, you've programmed the AI to mimic the worst kind of behavior of real people.
And I don't have any options. It's not like this happened mid-game and I have a bad spec or a lousy ship. It's not like I can improve my ship in any way, either, since the only station accessible is the station you start in.
I really should give this game a thumbs down. I really should. I hate griefers so much that I stopped playing multiplayer games altogether -- there's no sportsmanship, no sense of honor. Games are so stupidly competitive now that bad behavior is just part of the so-called "fun."
So when the AI is actually programmed to mimic griefers ambushing you at the jump gate ... reminds me of EVE Online , well, I should give it a bad review.
And no, I don't want to hear anyone defending multiplayer and how people behave -- and how not everyone is like that, blah blah. Yeah, I know not everyone is like that. But all it takes is a few. No point in calling me names, either, because that would just prove my point, now, wouldn't it.
At any rate, I'll still give this game a thumbs up because, aside from the pirate swarms at the jump gates, it's actually a fun little game. It would be nice if the devs toned down the ridiculous pirate swarms -- especially around the jump gates near the starting location -- but I doubt that will ever happen.

Stellaris is a game that sadly fails to deliver much beyond its initial promise.
The gameplay and mechanics should be familiar to anyone who's played 4X strategy titles. Race design and ship design are extremely fun, even if their practical applications are minimal.
However, the game hits several major hangups:
1) Gameplay is extremely repetitive. The number of "anomalies" (read: subplot drivers) is very limited so the game tends to play the same regardless of how you built your empire. There are no real incentives for playing a pacifist or mercantile empire, and the game mechanics don't really inclue a "trade" system beyond the existing resources.
2) Diplomacy is pretty much nonfunctional. The system design resembles Total War in many ways, but other empires seem to reject completely reasonable proposals, even outright advantageous ones, while accepting completely ludicrous or exploitative proposals.
3) Multiplayer setup is maddening. Every time I try to get our group of four together to game I plan on at least 30 minutes of trying to work around the innumerable bugs and issues. For a game that prides itself on its multiplayer focus (being able to save multiplayer games and resume them later, etc.), this is unacceptable.
All in all, Stellaris feels like a letdown. I may have to check back on it in a year or two.

It used an amazingly easy algorithm derived from the classic STRIPS planner, but surprisingly efficient. The AI opponents are tactically intelligent: the know when to ambush, when to flank, when to flee, and when to throw a grenade and flush you out, they can even take advantage of the environment or execute some simple team tactics which may amaze you for a moment, this is truely brilliant for a game made in 2005.
Enough said about the AI, the other elements are also great: guns are fun to shoot and really pack a punch, you can actually feel the impact of bullets when they land on the enemies or even on the environment; slow-mo feature is fun to use and the visual effect for slow-mo is really cool (for an 2005 game, of course); the levels are cleverly designed, they are complex enough for AI opponents to execute their tactics, as well as for you to take advantage of; the length of the game is just right(it takes me a little over 10 hours to beat on hardest difficulty setting); and, of course, everyone's favorite girl Alma will freak you out(well, not really if you played some real survival horror games, this is an FPS afterall).
The visual of the game is also amazing for a 2005 game. This game uses shadow volume just like Doom 3, which is hard to find in today's games, if you have ever saw how the shadows are like in Doom 3, you can expect the similar effect in FEAR. The colour tone and lighting is just right: a contrast between brightly lighted areas, and shadows lurking around them, and blood trails everywhere.For the horror parts, unlike Doom 3, this game takes advantage of some tricks  usually found in Japanese horror movies, it is better for you to see it yourself, they are neatly executed in the game.
Please try this game if you haven't yet, you will get much more than you expect.
Last, just a few warnings, there are two expensions come with the original game, they are not developed by Monolith Games(developer of the original), Extraction is okay, but definitely worse than the original; while Perseus Mandate is not worth your time, it is really bad. For the two sequels, if you like the original game, you can try FEAR 2, but don't expect the same level of quality from it; and please, by any means, avoid the third game.
Update: For those who experiencing low fps issues, there is a high chance that you are using Logitech G series mouse or keyboard, the game engine has a known compatibility issue with these devices. Just go into the device manager and disable all devices with "HID" in their names under "human interface devices" and you'll be fine.

I really wanted to enjoy this game; after all, I've enjoyed nearly every other Paradox release.  Unfortunately, a combination of game-killing bugs (defender warscore anyone?) that should have been fixed before release coupled with a glaring dearth of mid and end-game content have left me feeling like this was a game either rushed to release, or designed to serve as a money mill for future DLC that will eventually make it into what we all want it to be.
That's not to say that it doesn't have its moments.  The early game is stacked with memorable adventures, an eager pursuit of exploration, and seemingly boundless possibilities and paths that your fledgling space empire might take.  However, it doesn't take long for the aforementioned bugs, shockingly shallow diplomacy and governance systems, and an even-worse battle system to shake one's confidence in the long-term viability and enjoyability of your play through.  Once your empire starts finding its borders closed in by those surrounding, the lack of AI proactivity and the sheer absence of much to do leaves the player in the position of simply sitting and watching turns ticks by until something even slightly (and I do mean slightly) interesting occurs.
It is truly a shame that Paradox made the decision to strip much of the 'grand' out of this grand strategy title thereafter - leaving it as a title with a lot of potential, but very little to deliver.  Perhaps if this was a fresh entry into the genre from a new developer some of these issues would be easier to overlook, but coming from a shop with the reputation that Paradox has nurtured, it is hard not to wonder if they may be starting to lose some of the magic and creativity that has made previous titles so easy to love.
I, for one, will be looking forward to the modding community more than the product Paradox has delivered - here's hoping that they may save the day for an otherwise extraordinarily disappointing release.

Doom 2, the sequel to Doom, holds its own quite well and makes some good improvements from the first installment in the series. At first glance the sequel to Doom looks identical to its predecessor with the same graphics style, HUD, enemies ect take a closer look and it will show that there are a few new changes. The game has a runtime of 30 levels and almost feels longer than the original Doom possible because the game is whole and not split into episodes. This can hurt it however as some parts of the game seem to drag on as you wonder how close you really are to the finish line. There is one new weapon in Doom 2 and it is the super shotgun, and it lives up to its name as it obliterates enemies in your path. The inclusion of more than just one weapon would have helped increase the appeal however. The levels in the campaign are once again a mix of fun and very confusing, but with modern technology a guide is only a few clicks away. Overall Doom 2 feels somewhat like an addon for the original Doom but does show a few new tricks while still keeping the old ones.

F.E.A.R. is a game that holds a special place in my heart. One of my first horror games to the Xbox 360 when it was released back in 2006. What I remember is that I never dared to complete the game. But now, eight years later, I finally picked up the F.E.A.R. Collection to embark on a nostalgia trip. Before giving the full review I recommend buying each game individually and skip the colleciton. You save a few pennies by this.
F.E.A.R. is a very old school shooter; the days when shooters still was quite new and shiny compared to modern shooters of today. To be aged, the game is actually quite acceptable to today's standards. Even though the melee can be a little slow at times the reflex-system, or adrenaline system makes up to any flaws. What is better than to be able to slow down time for a few seconds to see the enemy flying backwards in a wave of gore? And the shooting in general feels very fluid; I would rate the shooting in F.E.A.R. to have much higher standard than your regular Call of Duty game out there. Just enough variation in the choice of weapons. But bare in mind you can only carry up to three weapons, so choose wisely.
Overall level design and atmosphere is the icing on the cake for F.E.A.R. They have managed to get in the perfect moments for something bizarre to happen. This game is indeed focusing alot on the scare factor and contain tons of scare tactics not for the player with a weak heart. To be honest the intimidation factor is not extremely high as in some modern horror titles. But it contains just enough horror for you to be paranoid around every corner. They did a fantastic job of designing the main antagonist Alma Wade. She will jump at you a dozen times. The only negative factor I can think of kind of ruining the atmosphere from time to time is the A.I. They can sometimes create some hilarious glitches and just be weird in general. But that's probably the price we must take to play an old game.
All in all this is a great experience. Not for the faint of heart. Old school classic shooter with very well designed scare and horror factors. The visuals are unexpectedly good for a game of this age and live way over some of today's shooters. I think all horror and shooter gamers will very likely love this series.

The original Doom revolutionized video games forever. Doom II is, comparatively, a much smaller deal. At a glance. However, it's additions provided critical tools for the modding community: the greatest weapon in any video game ever, the Super Shotgun. An expanded bestiary featuring horrific creatures like the Arch-Vile. Plus, a bunch of engine improvements and new textures. Since 1994, modders would use these new resources to create the single largest mod libraries for any game ever. Doom II is the closest to a truly endless game that anyone could fathom; there exist over two decades of high quality map packs and mods, and new content continues to be produced for Doom II on a daily basis.
Doom II is one of the greatest games of all time.

I'm mixed on this game. It has a lot of problems that, by rights, should mean it isn't fun. But I've still logged over 30 hours over two playthroughs, so something about it works...
There are three really big problems with this game in my opinion. First, the balancing is very, very poor. The first couple hours of the game are, by far and away, the most difficult. This is because your first few levelups, which take a long time to get, multiply your base stats more than tenfold, but enemies are balanced for your stats once you've leveled up a bit, so they are wildly overpowered to start with. You just cannot afford to get hit more than a few times at the beginning of the game, but you can shrug off small mistakes for the rest of the game, even during the final chapter.
Second, the fighting mechanic is shallow. The core of the game is fighting mobs of enemies, but all of the enemies have very similar attack patterns, and your moveset isn't very complex either. After a while, you get into a grove of comboing enemies using the same spacing tecniques, and all of the fights feel very similar to each other.
And third, in my opinion, the story isn't as good as it could have been. Avoiding spoilers, when Dust's identity is revealed, the story has a lot of opportunity to explore subtle themes and to paint the antagonists in a somewhat sympathetic light. Instead, in my interpretation, it doubles down on making Dust a designated hero who gets to kill the Bad Guys because he's the Good Guy.
For those flaws, though, the game is still a lot of fun to play. There's a lot of exploration in the game with plenty of very rewarding secrets hidden in each level. And the art is absolutely geogeous. Playing this game is fun, but there are other games I can play that are both fun and don't feel like they have rough edges.

It's hard to put 50+ hours into a game and then give it a thumbs down.
I've had some good times with the game but mostly it's been either a game that was so trivial to beat the AI (early patches), or maddening ones (patch 2.0).....all while playing normal difficulty. I'm glad the devs are constantly improving and evolving the game but I think it has a critical flaw in that it has simply too broad of a surface area on ways to play it, which can easily run the casual gamer into the ground...repeatedly. Ultimately it comes down to a "secret sauce" formula, as seen on countless fan sites, where you are going to lose unless you get a certain minimum amount of objectives done in the first 20 to 100 turns or else you're destined to lose.  In other words, the whole game is made in the first series of turns....and the rest is simply a process of going through the motions.
I've played Civ1 through 5, GalCiv2, Elemental, FE, etc.....and damn do I REALLY want to love galciv3 but it's just too screwy of a game that seems to be angling more for hardcore players. I think the game needs to be focused a bit more starting with the overwhelming state of the research tree.  Yep, i'm sure that's controvertial but it's WAY too broad.  As a player I get sick of clicking through 4 trees (sorry but it needs to be 3) and having 12+ different choices that only (for the most part) very incrementally change the game.  Research alone forces a player to micromanage, when that's a turn off for a LOT of people.
I could talk for ever and give example after example but it's just not worth my time.  GalCiv4 will need to start from scratch if it wants to win me and others back.  By and large it was too similar to GC2 to start with....but made worse by minutia and formulaic measures in order to win.

Final Fantasy VIII is a somewhat controversal entry in the Final Fantasy series. It is also my introduction to the franchise and the first Final Fantasy game I ever played.
And to be honest, it's easily one of my favorite FF games.
FFVIII was the first game in the series to mix reality and fantasy as well as science fiction elements. It featured a new (somewhat confusing) junctioning system, Guardian force summoning, and a new cast of human characters.
For all extents and purposes, it is a divisive title in the FF franchise. Yet it was the game that introduced me to what would become my favorite gaming franchise of all time.
Personally, I found the story to be a little weaker then some entries in the series. But it has a human element that was lacking in many of the previous games in the series. Based on the theme of love, FFVIII has a very human cast of characters and I found each one of them quite likeable in some regard. Main protagainst Squall is often portrayed as cold and shallow, but learns trust and respect throughout the course of the game. The supporting characters are all interesting in their own right. You will learn to care about them and relate to them over the course of the game as you help them in their struggles to defeat the Galbadian army and the Sorceress Edea.

This PC remaster includes the full game “Chocobo World” featured in the original PC port. It also includes 45 unlockable achievements and a magic booster feature.
Final Fantasy VIII has it's critics, but it is a welcome entry into the FF franchise. Featuring a beautiful and moving story, a cast of uniqe and human characters, and a exciting battle system. It is easily among my favorite Final Fantasy games.

I think this game was well made for it's time. It has its ups and downs but the pros seem to outweight the cons for me.
Firstly, graphics were pretty much "make everything as 3D as possible" and was a nice step up from simply having characters move around on a set background. One could easily tell from even simple places that they tried to put as much detail as possible into things.
The cutscenes were rather nice for their time and if you pay attention near the end of Disc 1 (the parade) you'll notice the dance being done is very similar to Michael Jackson's Thriller dance. Another moment of hilarious in hindsight is a phrase Selphie tried to get going. "Booyaka!", guess which WWE wrestler would make that his catchphrase a couple of years later?
The battle system was different and kept the game at a challenging level, almost everything (save for a few bosses with levelc caps) leveled up as you did. This could be good or bad depending on how skilled of a player you are. If you play it well enough you can pretty much level up quickly right after obtaining Siren (Life-RF skill yourself Zombies + Life/Full-Life and go fight some T-Rexuar).
While keeping a low level is generally advised to keep the game easy, going to over level 40 as early as disc 1 can prove helpful by getting some of the best skills in the game to junction to your characters making the rest of the game a cakeqalk (Junction either 100 Quakes or Ultima to Attack and say good-bye to difficulty~).
The music was excellent. Most of the music would fit the mood, although sometimes cheerful music would continue to play during times where it suddenly became very unfitting (nothing new there actually). The battle and boss music is what has always stuck out the most to me though, it always made me feel pumped and excited to keep playing the game.
The GFs were also another fun factor, some had really humorous attack animations (Tonberry, Cactuar, or the Brothers) while others could be downright frightening or strange (Eden, Doomtrain, or Diabolos (imagine a giant dark matter sphere crushing you into nothing!)). The junctions and abilities they give are incredibly helpful. However I tended to always need to make one of them forget SumMagic 10% to add a more needed ability such as HP-J or the coveted and rare Ability - x4 (Rosetta Stones are very hard to come by and unless you can find more than the one at Ultimecia's Castle, only the person with Bahamut will get the full benefit).
Overall, I think this game was great for it's time and while the Romance theme is a bit strong, the game managed to remain fun to me then and still does now. 8.5/10, would recommend to others.

A pretty good Paradox 4x strategy game, simpler than EU4. You can create pretty much anything from a race of run-of-the-mill humans to space♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ From hippie-dippy xenophile democracies, to hive mind hegemonic empires that expunge all xenos in their path. Ships can be heavily customized and from the very start, you choose which type of FTL and weapons you start with among a few types. Upon the surface of planets and in orbit, you can spread your dominion and destroy or enslave all those in your wake. It is by all accounts a good all-around space 4x, there are however issues.
Planetary armies are nigh irrelevant, larger ships take forever to build, and wars are consequently won after one side has had most of their fleet destroyed. In most other Paradox 4x games, there's often the possibility to rise from the ashes and put up another round or more of force against your enemy once you've lost but not here. Exceptionally weak stations in orbit of a planet are the only source of ship construction and can easily all be destroyed before you get more than a destroyer or two out. Without the ability to build a navy from a planetary surface or use ground-to-orbit weaponry, victory is pretty much completely based on fleet strength.
In time I'm sure patches and expansions will smooth out combat issues but for now, its a good concept that pretty much makes anything but genocidal hegemonic empires simply incapable of maintaining a serious presence on the galactic stage.

VoidExpanse seems to have been design primarily for trading-oriented people, but it simply does not have enough things to do to give the player a persistent galaxy to get lost in.

1)
I liked it.
2)
Nice, but not too many tracks.
3)
Quite basic, you just buy modules for your ship.
4)

You mostly get just small passive bonuses for upgrading skills. Skill upgrades seem to cost too much compared to how many skill points per level you get.
5)
Quite useful to from a system to another, but you cannot set the autopilot to a specific point in another system.
6)
You'll need a dedicated Freighter ship for this, but you can do a lot of trading in this game. However, there is no information hub on prices on other stations, so you have to get there and manually write down those prices to compare them.
7)
You retain your momentum, so it's a bit difficult (but realistic). Unfortunately, there are not many types of weapons nor special abilities.
8)
It's grindy, but it goes well with a trading approach to this game.
9) Mods support - There are quite a few good mods on the steam workshop that make the game more interesting.
10)
Few roaming around, but with a realistic behaviour (patrol ships chase down pirates, mining ships mine, trading ships go between stations).
11)
Really wonky. You need to either stay close to an object (and still) waiting for it to slowly attract stuff in your cargo. After a while it gets really annoying.
Very, very limited crafting, you can only craft some basic components.
Very few things to do.
Tedious Exploration
Tedious Tractor Beam
NO Crafting cool stuff
NO Great variety of weapons
NO Research
NO Fleets (although later in the story you can hire one ship).
NO building stations
NO conquering new systems
NO Wars/large engagements between factions
NO, NO, NO a lot of stuff that you would expect in a game like this.
Overall, the game seems that it's lacking all the elements to make it really great, and it feels more like an Early Access game with missing content than a fully realized game. The DLC felt really meh (it gives you missions with a factions that hates you from the start, so you have to do a lot of work before you can even get to their quest line) and adds too little (it could have been a free patch, although for a small developer I can see why it was not).
Hopefully, one day, there will be a VoidExpanse 2 or many more DLCs that will add all these missing features and will make this a really great game but, until then, I can only recommend picking this game up on a sale or if are really into trading because there aren't many things to do beyond some grinding.

F.E.A.R.: First Encounter Assault Recon is a first-person shooter psychological horror video game developed by Monolith Productions and published by Sierra Entertainment and the first game in the F.E.A.R. series. It was released on October 18, 2005.
F.E.A.R. puts you in the shoes of "The Point man", a secret special ops group of the U.S. government specialized in dealing with paranormal threats, When the game begins, the player witnesses a man named Paxton Fettel taking command of a battalion of telepathically controlled clone supersoldiers, seizing control of Armacham Technology Corporation (ATC) headquarters, and killing all its occupants. A strong atmospheric shooter, FEAR does so many things right, but fails in some categories drastically. While the shooting is top notch, dynamic lighting and a solid soundtrack makes this an enjoyable shooter, the lack of enemy variety and repetitive nature of the leves might turn off some players. You are equiped with a fairly diverse arsenal from the basic pistol to more advanced weapons like the Type-7 Particle weapon and many other. The bullet time is superb, the amount of enviromental destruction is here aswel, as particles and walls shatter after you shoot them. It's a briliant showcase of how a shooting something should behave. Not many games offer this level of detailt, to be honest, and this one is quite old. The story is quite nice, a bit generic with the whole *experiment gone wrong theme* and some of the plot elements are delivered via phone calls or debriefed during loadtimes. Nothing too over the top, it gets the job done and keeps the player interested. Overall this game has much to offer, and falls into the category of "old-school PC shooting games", reminescent of the goldern era of shooters (1994-2004) with health pick-ups, no cover system, just plain balls to the walls action. Lastly, I'd like to talk about the AI, which has received much praise, and it deserves it. Your enemies use tactics and commands to adapt to certain situations you put them into, responding adequately, making them feel more human than just lines of code. When you shoot them, they react in a realistic manner, thanks to some great physics in the game, overall they perform well enough.

Considering the popularity and quality of the first edition of Dungeon Defenders, I was surprised by the overwhelming number of negative reviews for what I'll call the *upgraded* Eternity edition. I should start by saying that my experience with the original was only about 2 hours playing the demo on Xbox 360. I was impressed but never got around to purchasing it. So I'm basically brand new to the franchise.
My friends and I have been playing some Sacntum 2 recently (and loving it), so we decided to give DD Eternity a shot. We almost didn't purchase Eternity due to the large number of negative reviews, but after canvasing the complaints most of them could be categorized as follows:
1) The UI is totally unintuitive (some say broken)
2) There aren't enough new features added over the original to really consider this a new version
3) It's online all the time
4) No single player or private modes
Let me address each of these:
1) The UI is totally unintuitive - Yah this isn't the greatest UI in the world, but it does actually work. It just takes some getting used to. But it definitely isn't broken, just suffers a bit from poor design. I wouldn't make your buying decision on this characteristic alone.
2) Not enough new features - I'm a totally new player to the franchise, so I can't speak to the evolution from the original to Eternity. But I can give my opinion on how I think the new version plays: It's fun as hell! There are quite a few classes to choose from each with their own flavor of play, tons and tons and tons of items, a variety of ways to build your characters, and the combat is smooth and easy to get used to after a few matches.
3) It's online all the time - This is true. It really boils down to personal preference. You don't have to interact with any other players, you'll just see them in the Tavern (Dungeon Defenders equivalent of a Lobby). I'm not in the habit of playing with strangers, but the online only component doesn't really bother me. They have their own online platform they are developing called Playverse which is a bit convoluted when you are trying to get a group with your friends, but it still works. We've gotten used to other platforms where you essentially invite a friend with a single click, or accept an invitation with a single click. Playverse makes you have to do like three clicks the first time to accept a friend invite, after which the invites work much easier.
4) No single player or private modes - So this game came out about a month or so ago as of this writing. I have  a feeling that the game may have launched without single player/private modes, but has since been patched to allow it. Here's the bottom line: you can absolutely play single player or private mode with up to 4 of your friends. If it's just two of you in a private match it's totally fine - you won't get any strangers added to your game. I've played several matches solo and won handily, so the difficulty must scale with more players.
Overall I would definitely recommend this game. It has a few rough edges, but these are things that can easily be improved with some patches going forward. The game is not broken as others are claiming. It plays beautifully and is a lot of fun to play either by yourself or with friends. After playing for a few hours now I felt obligated to come and write a positive review to offset the huge number of negative reviews.

But here is the problem; none of it is quite as good as with The Witcher 3. If you have never played The Witcher 3 you wouldn't know all the tiny things you're missing when you're playing The Witcher 2. But if you already have, you got to admit that in comparison The Witcher 2 feels rather small, clunky, limiting and occasionally claustrophobically one dimensional. This is not exactly fault of the game itself, but because the sequel happens to be probably the best game ever made.
So do yourself a favour and don't do like I did. Don't go straight to The Witcher 3, but play this one (and even the first one if you can stomach the outdated experience) first or it will be very hard to come back. Personally I've found the story itself intriguing and craving more for the world of The Witcher. Right now, being used to the best coming back to something almost as good isn't quite cutting it anymore.

Regardless, this game is easily worth the money.

UPDATE: After several patches and developer diaries from Paradox I feel this game is just getting better. If you played this on release and found it a little lacking, it is well worth coming back and having another go now, and same thing in a few months time after the next two patches.
This game does have a few things that Paradox needs to work on, and I think they knew this before it was released. Problems with diplomacy, mid game content, and how some features work prevent this game from being a smash hit straight out of the box.
That being said, I've played almost nothing else since it was released, and it's smashed all sale records for Paradox, which is usually used to niche titles released for niche audiences.
On the one hand I wish I had seen the game with the fixes and extra features they are adding over the next few months, on the other hand I'd have been severely annoyed if this game was delayed, so they can't win.
Overall if you're into sci-fi and you're into strategy this will be a perfect game for you, and if you've always liked the sound of Paradox's games but felt CKII or EUIV weren't accessible enough, this is their most accessible game yet.

I have to admit that this game isn't my usual cup of tea.
Technically, the game is not good.  The physics are terrible, the missions are extraordinarily repetitive, and there doesn't seem to be any real challenge to it.  What it succeeds at, though, is being a farm simulator.  It's not about physics.  It's not about missions.  It's not about challenge.  It's about farming.  Not life or death, but the mechanics and details of growing and harvesting crops.
This is a 'zen' game that I'd play to relax and not think (once I got the hang of the process and equipment).  It's not a tense or pressure-filled game.  It's rolling along in a tractor, fertilizing a field, mowing a lawn, and towing a trailer.
For that, I'd recommend it.  If you're looking for something deeper and more challenging, keep moving.

Call of Duty: Black Ops is not your typical Call of Duty. It stands out from the others and is very unique. For the majority of the campaign, you play as Alex Mason. You are being interrogated and the whole campaign is based around your character's flashbacks and his, well..."imaginations." What makes this Call of Duty so your unique from the others is that it's not all about shooting people. Sure, you do that a lot in the game, but it's really not just that. Also, in this Call of Duty, I actually felt really engaged with the characters in this one. I felt like I was actually in a black op mission. At the same time, I felt like I wasn't Alex Mason. I felt like I was my own character for some reason. For an example, if I find a gun that is meant for me, it's like, "Yeah, this is MY gun." It's hard to explain, but hopefully you get what I mean. The customization in this game is awesome. This game is pretty much were Call of Duty games from 2012 got the idea of putting buyable customizations in their multiplayer experience. Anyways, this is just a great game. There is a pretty big twist at the end of the campaign and I found it really enjoyable. The soundtrack, voice acting, action scenes, sound effects, guns, etc. were just fantastic. Some bad things about this game were the ending (they could of ended it a bit better, it felt kind of like, "Oh, that's the end?"), the graphics (I don't judge a game by it's graphics. This game didn't have bad graphics, but they honestly weren't that good for it's time [2010]), and some glitches of course. Another thing that is kind of arguable is the price on the Steam version. This game is not worth $40 anymore. You can probably buy it for $10 for the Xbox 360 or PlayStation 3. I think it should at least be $20 on Steam, but you know how Activision labels their prices on Steam for Call of Duty. Anyways, just get this game when it's on sale. I think the lowest I've seen it on sale is $20, which is when I bought it on Steam. This is to me a must-buy for shooter fans.

A pretty good Paradox 4x strategy game, simpler than EU4. You can create pretty much anything from a race of run-of-the-mill humans to space♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ From hippie-dippy xenophile democracies, to hive mind hegemonic empires that expunge all xenos in their path. Ships can be heavily customized and from the very start, you choose which type of FTL and weapons you start with among a few types. Upon the surface of planets and in orbit, you can spread your dominion and destroy or enslave all those in your wake. It is by all accounts a good all-around space 4x, there are however issues.
Planetary armies are nigh irrelevant, larger ships take forever to build, and wars are consequently won after one side has had most of their fleet destroyed. In most other Paradox 4x games, there's often the possibility to rise from the ashes and put up another round or more of force against your enemy once you've lost but not here. Exceptionally weak stations in orbit of a planet are the only source of ship construction and can easily all be destroyed before you get more than a destroyer or two out. Without the ability to build a navy from a planetary surface or use ground-to-orbit weaponry, victory is pretty much completely based on fleet strength.
In time I'm sure patches and expansions will smooth out combat issues but for now, its a good concept that pretty much makes anything but genocidal hegemonic empires simply incapable of maintaining a serious presence on the galactic stage.

FIRST ISSUE RESOLVED: For those using wirelss devices under Windows, you DO NOT need to disable the devices. You just need to disable everything under HID Compliant  Devices in the device manager. You do not need to disable HID Compliant Devices under mouse, keyboards, or input devices.
SECOND ISSUE RESOLVED: The game will occationally give you a "server disconnected" message when trying to load a save game. Some times the save data becomes corrupt for seemingly no logical reason (likely a bug in the save function or incompatibility issue with newer versions of Windows). MAKE SURE you use both regular and quick saves. Using both will minimize the chance of having to start over.

I love FEAR. It's one of my favorite games of all time actually. A lot of people will tell you that the first is better than all the sequals, and in some respects they are correct. The problem I see is that people go back and play FEAR thinking it's this masterpiece and get dissapointed by it's dated graphics and odd level design. The gameplay still shines though, hot damn is it still fun. Most shooters of that era are almost all the same when it comes to gameplay, but I think this game really stood out with it's "tactical" esque game mechanics. I don't know what the develpers were thinking when they took the "lean" feature out of the sequals. This feels like an old tactical shooter, aside from the crazy melee (you jump kicks and the like) and the usual "slo-mo" feauture.
Oh, the whole "horror" thing. Huh. You know, big Horror game fans may be a bit dissapointed. There are a few jump scares, and a few awesome atmospheric moments that really lead to a lot of tension, but I would consider this an "Action/Horror" sort of deal. The plot is actually really good, especially for a shooter from this time. There's lots of hints throughout the leverls about what led up to the events you are now walking into and what happened to the people there. Alma is an awesome villain, and has a great, well written backstory. Fettel is intriging as well, but at times can be a bit "campy".
My only issue though is with the length of the game. I sped through it seems, and was kind of dissapointed by the the last act of the game. The multiplayer also doesn't exist anymore, so don't expect any.
I'd say buy it, if it's on sale. I myself loved it, but can recognize why others might not.

What more can I say it's a Final Fantasy game. You either love them or hate them, Even after 10+ years this gem seems to satisfy my need for not only nostalgia but lust for a decent RPG, Yes the story might not be the greatest, that's for you to decide, And the Dialogue might be a bit dated considering it's age. After all this is about personal preference.
If you like
Epic FMV's (even after 10+ years and with SquareEnix updating the FMV's to 720p they look as amazing as they did the first time i saw the opening cinematic)
A simplified Battle system, (Final Fantasy 7 had materia, In FF8 you draw the magical essence from the enemy or from draw points, The game get's more difficult or easier depending on your level)
SIdequests, (Triple Triad, PuPu, Odin, Tonberry, Cactuar to name but a few)
Music. (Ok so this is a sore point due to the fact the game doesn't have the PS Music files it has the ones from the previous incarnation of this game that was ported over. They're midi files. Still a remarkable score like most final fantasy games. Eyes on me might not be as breath taking as One winged Angel was on FF7, But nonetheless an Amazing Score for anyone who appreciates JPRG Soundtracks)
Final Note. If you like RPG's and have already played this game I don't really need to convince you to buy this. But if you haven't and have never picked up this or any other final fantasy rpg's and would like to try them, They're dirt cheap in regards to what they were when they came out, I remember my PS copy being around £35 and original pc copies of this game used to retail on Ebay up to £120.
Just get the game play through it, if you dislike it you have wasted £7, This alongside FF7 will give you thousands of hours of fun and gameplay. And once you have completed the game you can choose to do a low level playthrough, No magic. Inital Equipment. The possibilites are near infinite.

This is an excellent title by Square Enix and in my personal opinion, one of the best Final Fantasy games I have ever played! To define and enhance the defition of a(n) RPG is what Square Enix set out to do in 1997 and not only did they succeed but they re-shaped the entire existence of a Role Playing Game! When it comes to negativity about the game there isn't much I can say however it gets quite grindy at certain parts of the story and if you're planning to enter the game blind then you should know that sometimes it leaves you with no idea of where to go and you may have to search for up to 1/2 an hour to check out every single place on the map you may need to go to.Personally I love the FF franchise and of course this game, therefore I would strongly advise you get the game and if you're sitting on a fence, check it out rather I hope this helps someone decide whether or not they should buy FFVII and thx for reading! :)

The most unusual aspect of Farming Simulator 2013 is the complete lack of competition. In a single-player career, there is only you, the farm, and the AI townspeople who wander around but can’t be interacted with. Even in multiplayer, all players work together on a single farm. In both modes, the game will not fail you for slow production or even no production at all. As a result the gameplay is incredibly peaceful, though possibly a bit daunting for newcomers to the series. Admittedly, the act of virtual farming doesn’t sound like it would require a complex series of steps to perform, given that most of your job involves jumping in a tractor, attaching a tool, and slowly driving in straight lines. However, there are subtleties that are under-mentioned or completely undocumented that require some practice to master. AI-controlled workers can be hired for most tasks, and watching how they perform can teach you techniques to use when you get behind the wheel.

FFVII was the first real JRPG I ever played when it was released in 1997. I must admit - that although the graphics (which were state of the art for its time) now look pretty dated - this is still one of my favorite games. From the somewhat silly and nonsensical rantings of its characters, to the weirdly exotic variety of creatures you encounter. It serves to remind you that while the overall story is quite serious, the game is not above making things more than a little interesting in terms of comic relief.
Probably one of the greatest assets the FF series has (and VII implements this very well) is its Active Time Battle System. This makes you think on your feet, and makes sure you know your inventory and spells well in advance.
In short, however, I would definitely recommend this game for those looking for a certified classic.

I actually enjoy FF8. I'm not enjoying this edition of the PC port.
Why is that? You should never lose a game because the controls are awkward. And yet, FF8's re-release seems to succeed in this regard.
If you use a gamepad, the game still displays the keyboard controls in-game. So if you're trying to input codes in the stupid train mini-game (which is a fine example of how Square tried to innovate by sucking the fun out of the game, but I digress), you're struggling to remember what the default X, C, S, and V (Seriously, Square Enix? No WASD? No space bar? No Enter key? Did you just pick a bunch of keys at random?) map to on the gamepad, and this is fatal when you're trying to enter 4-digit codes. At least the original PC port allowed you to use a gamepad seriously, displaying the buttons instead of the keys-- by contrast, this revisit is a joke. FF7 didn't have this problem, of course, because they used keywords for each button regardless of how you mapped the buttons. Awkward at first, but then, you weren't confused by the time you were doing squats in Wall Market or rifle drills in Junon. That they didn't put forth the same effort for FF8 is unacceptable, as they decided to always show a disclaimer about seizure risk before the game is launched, and always show the keyboard map every single damned time the game starts like FF7. Who designed this port, anyway? A barrel of monkeys?
So, gamepad users, here's a workaround for this annoying feature: Map the keyboard keys to numbers representing the buttons on your gamepad. Hopefully the game will now display those numbers instead of the default keys. You'll still need the keyboard to get past the insanely annoying key map reminder.
To add insult to injury, the keyboard and gamepad button maps don't line up in the config screen, which makes one wonder if they really hired monkeys to develop it.
I'd much rather find my old FF8 discs and play that instead...

Freedom, group of mercinaries who are interested in escaping void expanse. And of corse, the Fanatics (my favorite story wise). The fanatics are a group of people who worship the antagonist as their gods. But you learn what their leader really thinks.
Each story has it's own ending that makes you feel like all the work was worth it.
Once again (because I can't say this enough) It is quite a breathtaking story that is worth your time and money, to follow.

ABZU is an extremely well painted work of art. You don't so much play ABZU as you do just explore the game. You are pulled along a fairly linear path through the story, being able to explore side areas and giant open spaces that are strung together. This leaves a feeling of openness without making you feel lost or confused as to where to go next. You end up just thinking "Okay, I know where to go when I am done, but I am going to have a look around first". With that, the level design is very well crafted by making you feel emotions just by moving from one place to another. Coming through a narrow cave to wide open ocean can shock you and make you feel vulnerable and put off guard. The soundtrack is amazing and creeps up on you in a way that makes you not take notice until you are already surrounded by it. The story is very well crafted and delivered in such a way that not a single word is needed.

As you can tell I highly recommend this game and it is a great experience. My only complaint is I would not recommend this game at full price ($20 USD as of this review). I played through the entire story and gained 8 out of 12 achievements in less than two hours. This one is one you put on your wishlist and wait for a sale.

F.E.A.R is a brilliant game and work of art. Cant remember a shooter that was more involving, intriguing, viceral or scary than this game. The combat is just spectacular.. AI is good, they take cover, try to outflank, throw grenades and will work together to take you down. You will literally feel the heat of the gun battle.. with contineous fire, the area get's smokey, dusty and the surrounding gets destroyed in an intense fight. The bullet time turns the hectic action into a beautiful battle sequence and
Once the dust settles, you are ready to press on...  always wondering whats going to happen next. You know your objectives but their is a variable, a big ♥♥♥♥ing supernatural.. variable that will keep you guessing and  the atmosphere is always tense, and their is a sense of something very sinister in the air.Throughout the game you are haunted by disturbing visions that are geniunely scary and mysterious. But you continue eagerly, you are in persuit of a sinister maniac and you want answers to the visions you see, put all the pieces together.  The sound design is exemplorary and the best I have heard. Brilliant from begining to end. Though the game lacks in variety of enviroments it makes up for it in the mood it sets and  the story it tells. The constant tension will turn into fright when you least expect. Their is no cliches here. Nothing forced, no shock value, gore for the sake of it. The game is molded to scare you pschologically and it succeeds. Though your tough guy with big guns and bullet time, you will tread carefully... like a girl :)
As the the story draws to it's climax, your heart will pound harder and you will press on without a break or blink. Once the final cutscene plays, it is not an ending  to relax upon and will leave you in awe. Expect the experience to stay with you..  even after the credits roll.

This cult game is a must-play for any fan of shooters. Scratch that, any gamer whatsoever.
F.E.A.R. is a fast-paced, frantic first person shooter developed by Monolith. It tells the story of a silent protagonist known as Point Man who was recently transferred to the top secret First Encounter Assault Recon division because of his inhuman reflexes. The division deals with paranormal threats to the USA, and Point Man is quickly sent on a mission to execute Paxton Fettel, a military experiment gone haywire. But, it turns out there's more to the story when a strange black-haired girl starts showing up out of nowhere.
The game itself is fantastic. It's got everything; the action, the thrilling story, fine-tuned mechanics, smart AI, great level design etc. One of F.E.A.R.'s main trumps is the action that can sometimes prove to be too fast for the player to enjoy; because of that, Monolith gave the player a limited slow-motion ability which proved to be the most well-executed slow motion in gaming to date. The enemies aren't diverse, there are about 5 types you'll encounter, but the artificial intelligence is amazing. Each squadmember knows his role, whether that be flanking, covering, storming in, sniping or otherwise. The story unfolds at a relatively slow pace, but that isn't a problem, as the game knows how to keep you interested. The general atmosphere is another one of F.E.A.R.'s high points; by combining bloody scenes and ambiental music, Monolith managed to create a genuinely creepy experience I'd be happy to go back to in a year or so.

I'm rewriting my review for F.E.A.R. because I do not felt I went into detail enough with it. Previously, it was just:
"Production values are inconsistent and pacing and narrative can be a little off and uninteresting at times, but for the most part Fear is an enjoyable shooter with satisfying gunplay."
I still stand by this, but I didn't really explain it. I'm going to do so now, and this review will be pretty long, but I feel compelled to say something more than that for a title that deserves more than that.
The Fear series is a mixed bag. You have the highly praised original, one well praised expansion pack, one mediocre expansion pack, one well praised sequel, one fair expansion pack that should have been free, and one tremendously mediocre shooter that contains none of the elements that made MONOLITH'S game style enjoyable.
I myself do not follow the non-canon timeline, so for me it's Fear, Fear 2 and then I might also play Extraction Point and Reborn for the fun of it.
The first game in the series was an example of something big. Something that was revolutionary on a *small* scale. This is where the production values thing comes in. The first Fear has fantastic lighting that seems like a more refined take on id Tech 4's "everything shadowed is unrealistically pitch black". The refined quality makes it more believable and interesting. It was about two years ahead of its time. Models though - particularly characters - are firmly cemented in the year of its release, if not seemingly earlier, where games from 2004 like Half-Life 2 and Halo 2 excelled in this aspect but were nowhere near Fear in the lighting department (the former of which wouldn't be until a 2007 update). This juxtaposed with the lighting gives us moments where Pointman's fantastic shadow also shows us his low-poly looking head, or his body and the enemy bodies seeming far more dated than the areas around them. Meanwhile, textures are still fantastic for the time.
These are the "inconsistent" production values. They seep into the sound as well, but just barely. This does not detract from the gameplay, but I feel is important to highlight when it is a game praised for its good looks aiding in the creation of the atmosphere.
Said atmosphere is great. You'll fight a plethora of enemies in some tense moments, some situations more explosive and dangerous than others, some more quiet and with a vibe of survival horror.
A great strength of Fear is its weapon pallette. Almost everything is fun to shoot. There's a rocket launcher that's relatively standard and an SMG that isn't too great, but they're made up for incredibly by the Penetrator and the ASP Rifle. They're also well varied, as a staple of the series (at least until the third game) was the mixing of weapons with sci-fi elements and modern day weapons. Great gunplay. Can't really describe it, you'd have to play it for yourself.
A great downside (and easily the biggest) of Fear is the way the game progresses, in regards to maps and narrative. The story starts out fairly active and then becomes much less involved. You'll go through what feels like filler trying to reach an objective that is one of the main things holding your interest in playing for hours in a campaign. It eventually comes back around, but they could have made it much better in this regard. Worse than that, and the source of many "filler" moments, is that the majority of Fear is *literally* a "corridor shooter". A handful of levels are just a series of office cubicles and crawlspaces. Ocassionally something will occur or be there to change things up, but shortly afterwards you go straight back into the office cubicles and crawlspaces. The shooting is still plenty fun, but it becomes monotonous very quickly, particularly at moments when you're just fighting soldiers. It's not bad enough to ruin the game, but it does hurt the game. This is one of the things that was made much better (in my opinion) in Fear 2, along with pacing, though that game had its own downsides as well. It's also popular to hate for...I really have no idea why, as someone who enjoyed the first game greatly and Extraction Point as well before the sequel was even released. I digress.
Most FPS games I feel are well played in two long sessions - the first half, a break, and then the second half - because the majority of FPS games since the invention of the FPS take about 6 to 12 hours to complete on average. With Fear, it's totally different. This is a game I highly recommend, but recommend broken up into chunks.
Overall, it's something I'd consider just about required gaming for shooter enthusiasts - PC or console (as it was ported, along with the expansions) - because it's ultimately a satisfying game, and it's also a remnant from a moment in the past where shooters of all forms were reaching some sort of strange peak, just before a great regression to simplistic gameplay.

Crypt of the NecroDancer is a roguelike about rhythm and precission. I really tried to like the game, but I couldn't. I am a fan of both rhythm mechanics and roguelikes, but this just didn't fit in. Quite a few people mention things such as high level players picking you off in pvp at the early stages, however that's just not true. You can literally pick up the game, start playing and be competitive from the first match till your last - here is why.
You start with 3 random dragons which may or may not be high level dragons (each dragon has 4 levels, and with each level you get stat increases such as higher speed or lower mana consumption).
Like with most MOBA's, you start each match with just the basic attack unlocked, and as you harvest minions / gold you earn EXP, and when you lvl up you gain an experience point which you use to lvl up current abilities or unlock new ones. You have 4 abilities in total, and two spells which you may change before each match. As you lvl up, you unlock more spells - so yes, higher level players do have access to more spells, but that just makes sense - if it wasn't that way, what would be the incentive to lvl up in the first place?
Now - when you join a pvp match EVERYONE starts with the basic abilities of their chosen dragons. Yes, those that have played with a specific dragon for a long while will have mastered his dragon (bronze, silver, gold and I think platinum), and they will receive health and speed bonusses for each lvl), however this rarely causes you to be outmatched in a way that is unforgivable.
I just started a new game, and from the first match I played till now I have ALWAYS been competitive. In most matches I can easily obtain a highest score with dragons I haven't even mastered yet - and that's while playing against those that have. So it's just utter garbage that you're cannon fodder for experienced players.
Sure, if you're in an inexperienced group you might get wasted every now and again by a better team, but that's just logical, and not due to an unfair advantage.
I agree that we need more maps. More maps would make the game feel less repetitive. And perhaps even a few additional game modes (dungeons / raids perhaps?). Oh, and there are not enough support type dragons in my opinion that specializes in buffing / debuffing other dragons. I mean, they have 2 healing dragons, and then one that heals and steals mana, but not in such a way to be a healer - more of a support healer. So perhaps a few more dragons that offer support for their team members rather than just focussing on attack.
We also need more players - I think new blood is always good for a game.
So in short - I'm enjoying the game and find most pvp matches challenging (other than Ballista Alley which is usually over in just a few minutes).

Dead Bits Review - Raymond KT
Considering the entire game was developed by one man, Dead Bits is a pretty impressive effort. Unfortunately, the game is lacking in almost every aspect when compared to its competition with the exception of its toe-tapping, head-bobbing dubstep soundtrack. If you're curious what's possible with the Unity engine and you like dubstep, it might be worth a look, and if you do, make sure to add on the soundtrack for a buck. Otherwise, stay clear. The combat is incredibly boring. There is nothing on the flat platforms for neither the player nor enemies to use as cover or anything else really, so all you can do is just move backwards while shooting them, and try not to fall off the platform (which is a bad design for the the game in first person view, and probably exist only, so the player will be forced to restart the game more often, and thus extending the play time)

Trendy does what they want and cares nothing for their customers & fans.  Long story short: This is a game that's being marketed as "definitive" that's in an early beta phase, at best.  There's rollbacks and lag issues for their online-only servers (there's no offline mode), a complete lack of meaningful loot progression, horrible UI issues (it looks like it was made to fit in mobile, and there's annoyances like item stats not being on dedicated lines so it's hard to compare items), and there's a HUUUUGGEEE list of features that existed in DD1 that don't in DDE.
Things missing:
1) Nightmare mode, hardcore mode, mixed mode, and pure strategy mode.
2) Full Single Player functionality - They added single player after the community outcry, and have been slowly adding in more and more functionality, but it's not quite there yet
3) Private taverns - You're stuck in a communal tavern with 15 other people happily making tons of noise.  If you dislike hearing Slice 'n' Dices attack dummies or simply don't want to read a 13y/o's curse-heavy ranting, or simply want to decorate your own private tavern, then you're out of luck.
4) No achievements/awards/trophies - With the conversion over to public tavern, all the joys of trophies in private taverns are gone.  There's nothing to work towards, and no reason to beat any maps besides the ones that give loot.
5) Challenge rewards - Currently, challenges provide ZERO experience and loot.  Upon completion, they DO give artifacts, which are permanent stat boosters, but these artifacts are not stackable and offer completely negligible increases (we're talking adding 8hps to a character with 10-20k life, and 1-2 to fire resist when you have 950).
6) Loot despawning priorities - In DD1, loot has prioritization on what disappears first.  In DDE, it doesn't.  And there's FAR fewer items allowed on the ground (online server reasons?).  Currently, instead of the ~200 items allowed in DD1 on bigger maps, there's 35 allowed in DDE, and because there's no loot despawn prioritization, that means stuff often disappears before it hits the ground.  Loot only appears near you, and even when it does that upgrade that just dropped might disappear before you can get to it while the 50g item you can buy from the tavernkeeper sticks around for 10 minutes.
7) Meaningful progression and incentive to do hard maps - Everyone does insane ramparts.  Why?  Because it drops far better loot than any of the DLC or later maps like CD, and it's one of the easiest maps in the game.  Of course, this means that once you get the gear from ramparts, there's nothing else to do, so the playerbase has dropped by half every 1.5-2 weeks since release.
8) Tower/Character balance - DD1 didn't have great balance, but it at least didn't have completely broken classes.  Huntress traps are so bad that no one uses them, summoner pets are broken (either useless or so OP they break their own animation with how fast they shoot), towers get over-nerfed for no reason and in an odd manner (including nerfs to huntress traps no one uses), and some classes are flat-out bad now (barbarian is HORRIBLE).
9) Itemization - Some great items from DD1 are missing (treadmill pets, costumes that change gameplay mechanics, meaningful & unique weapons), and the itemization in general is just inferior.  Weapons are all very similar and no longer have speed stats, so they all basically feel the same (outside of huntress, who has a few weps that are clearly superior, especially with the removal of speed stats).  Monk weapons all have horrible ranged damage so ranged monk dps isn't viable, barbarian swords are junk (speed stat issue again causing problems, to say nothing of barbarian stat scaling itself), apprentice weapons are all similar and junky enough that apprentice DPS isn't really a thing, etc.
10) Rewards for the challenges/campaign maps/survivals - There's no rewards for any of these, including beating CD.  You get... nothing.  no seahorses, no pets, no specific weapons dropping from specific bosses... nothing unique.  everything that drops drops everywhere, and while some campaign maps like aquanos will reward you after beating a boss, the rewards are completely random... you can get a few accessories and nothing else.
11) A whole MESS of maps, costumes, pets, items, and other fun things that simply don't exist in DDE.  Too many to count or list here.
12) a workable armor set system - DDE has a few extra slots for armor and 9 different sets instead of 4.  I'm too lazy to do the math, but instead of sets being fairly viable for everyone, at any level, they're now basically inaccessible to most of the community, since the chances of you having the same 1 (out of 9) type of item for all 7 slots that's decent enough to wear is nigh impossible.
13) A balanced upgrading system - The new system is percentage-based, and it's FAR harder to get money for those upgrades.  You'll have to spend a LOT of time playing Vacuum Simulator, since smashing the "E" key and picking up everything to sell it later is the only decent way to get money.  But even that aside, the percentage-based system (10% of base stats per upgrade, and 20% of base damage per) completely breaks itemization.  I won't go into detail, but suffice to say this breaks endgame items and throws items (and thus, characters) completely out of balance.
14) Kick system - If you like playing public games, accept that about half the players you encounter will simply afk the second they join the game, and there's nothing you can do about it.  At all.  And that's if you're lucky... if you're not they can actively ruin your experience by selling your towers, and again, there's nothing you can do about it.
Basically, I could go on for paragraphs on content that's in DD1 that was simply left out or is plain better (UI, loot despawn code, loot progression, trophies, map rewards, etc etc etc), but here's what it all boils down to:  you are NOT getting a definitive version of DDE.  You're buying what everyone playing agrees is a beta product.  I didn't even list out the major bugs & exploits in the game, and there's a LOT.  So while this game has a few improvements (more active play options with amulets, a conceptually better survival mode), none of it is balanced yet and there's so many bugs and issues in the game that you shouldn't give Trendy money for a "definitive edition" when it's nowhere near that state.  Some people might still like the game and play it, but no one can argue with the fact that this is a works-in-progress, so ask yourself if you want to reward a company that essentially spits on their best customers by re-releasing a title like this in such a misleading fashion.
At best, hold on to your money until the game is what they say it is, and frankly, I don't think it ever will be.  The core of DDE is so busted that even when they DO tack on NM, it's certainly not going to FIX anything... it'll just magnify the problems that already exist and aren't being addressed.

So first I should note that I am a long-time Paradox game player.  I'm used to the foibles and nuances of their games, as well as their development process.

I endorse their games knowing that they will only get better with time, and they aren't afraid to overhaul major game mechanics if they aren't quite right, almost all for free. It's a unique style of development, more like an MMO.
If you just want a perfect experience right now, play the game and just forget about it, then this may not be the game for you, yet. You can wait and get a more evolved version of the game later. As for me, I will enjoy the richness of the current experience, and watch as the community and developer together explore and evolve a fantastic and unique game.

Before I get into this review: I have seen all the banal comparisons to
levelled at this game. Seeing as how I have never played
, and probably never will, you can expect an unbiased opinion in that respect. Also, I have altered the content of this review to bring it more in line with my change of opinion, which used to be negative.
is a free-to-play 1st person shooter featuring a colourful cast of characters, each with their own unique abilities and playstyles. Cooperation and sensible team composition are essential to victory in the three game modes on offer: Siege, Payload, and most recently Onslaught.
At its best,
is wonderful. When a team comes together, blasts away the enemy, and clinches a climactic victory, the results can be glorious. Bridging the gap somewhat between a twitch shooter and a MOBA,
is surprisingly accessible, with a satisfying amount of depth for customisation of character builds and tactics. There were times when I would spend upwards of six hours a day playing
; it can be that addictive. It used to be one of my favourite multiplayer games ever, almost on the same level as
.
Of course, the operative words here are "used to".
It was around the Open Beta Patch 42 that things started to go wrong. The stability of the game's network began to degrade, leading to some noticable server-side lag that negatively affected gameplay. Not too bad, that can be fixed in the next patch, right?
Nope.
With each new patch,
has become more and more broken. Matchmaking is hopelessly lopsided, leading to unbearable games in which one team is blatantly more skilled than the other (besides parties). Character balance is all over the place, especially after the introduction of so-called 'legendary cards', and Hi-Rez seem to be dedicated to meddling with characters who did not need anything doing to them. The in-game economy, once one of the most fair and accessible economies I've seen in a F2P game, has been twisted so that the grind is slowed to a crawl, making the purchase of premium currency with real money all the more tantilising (and don't get me started on the stupidly overpriced premium loot chests).
This is the third version of my review of this game, and I think it will be the last version. HI-REZ have messed about with the game in unnecessary and even harmful ways. Gone are the days of finely balanced shooting action and one of the fairest F2P economies in modern gaming; now we are left with a pale shade of what the game once was, and could be again if HI-REZ would just pull their heads out of their collective backsides. Character balance is worse than ever, and glaring issues are being ignored in favour of crowbarring in more and more methods of monetisation, diluting the experience for those who don't want to stump up the green to get some nonsense premium currency in order to actually make some progress.
I still want to love the game, but
is, sadly, another victim of the modern gaming industry.
