Overall: Hesitant dislike.  Kinda fun, kinda meh, lots of grinding, very empty; overall lands on the negative end, if only barely.
It's a somewhat fun game, but spread too thin.  In the end I had some fun, but many game sessions felt unwholesome because of all the padding and time-wasting that diluted the experience.  It's also begging for content, so I'd recommend checking out lots of mods to enrich the experience; I now regret playing the game in its original form.
TL;DR: It's kinda fun, but a very thin and grindy experience.  If you're looking for a time waster, it'll be fine for that; if not, it will feel very frustratingly slow and underwhelming.  I still feel an awful, kinda gross, unsatisfied sensation, even after beating it.  Like the time was very poorly spent.  :(  So keep that in mind when considering a purchase!
There's very little story, and very few actual missions beyond the random ones the base leaders give you (and those are insubstantial).  Most of your time is spent traveling, whether on unsatisfying fetch or delivery quests, or traveling across half the galaxy to reach your quest again after a death.  The last few quests I did had a ton of travel from one corner of the galaxy to the other; very boring, even in the alien areas where the enemies were actually dangerous.  I did a medium sized galaxy and I recommend you try a small, simply to drop that travel time padding.
Combat is somewhat fun, but it does feel awkward.  You're fighting foes who have the computer's good aim, but you need to aim manually and this makes many of the weapons awkward and impractical to use.  You need to figure out how to move with your weapon to land even a fraction of the hits, and enemies don't appear to be limited in ammo like you are.  I also figured out early on that energy weapons are the way to go -- instead of a limit of 20 shots, you turn your entire fuel tank into ammo, and you just need a powerful generator to keep your energy levels stocked.  If I remember right, for solid ammo, the game is extremely stingy with refill items for some reason, so you'll have to return to base constantly to stock up again; this is bad for longer missions, mining ventures, etc.
The skill tree is almost entirely made of tiny stat upgrades, making you turn or strafe or cruise slightly faster, or do slightly more damage with a weapon type.  A few skills unlock better equipment, and one skill (persuade) adds dialog options in quests, and the rest are tiny, incremental stat boosts; very sterile.  For that reason the skill tree feels very unexciting... yes you make your ship work better, but with my level in the 60s it was only about 25-50% better in a select few areas.  And I had to focus in those areas to do it.  The game begs for that tree to be stuffed with new abilities in combat, mining, and quests, differences in *kind* instead of just differences in scale.
Also it's a little frustrating that the starting classes are not even -- some simply have way more free skill points assigned at the start of the game.  You should play the class that has the most skills you like, but also the most skills total that you plan on taking... and that means doing some google searching.
That's one example of how the game feels like it lacks balance, polish, and content.
Did I enjoy it?  Yea, it was
.  But man was it a slow grind, and I feel like a different game might have done a better job.  I walked away from this game multiple times because I felt crappy after playing it, because the experience had been so grindy and empty.  It's an awful feeling.
What's impressive is the good parts were just good enough to leave me nostalgic, and I returned to finish the story.  It actually feels like they were planning a bigger game, ran out of time/budget, released what they had with plans for later expansions, but then had to abandon it when the negative reviews rolled in.  And that's tragic, because there's a lot of potential here, but overall the experience is diluted, grindy, and unsatisfying.  :(
Last of all, multiplayer: I played briefly with friends, but we drifted away from the game because if felt so empty, and didn't lend itself to non-combat playstyles.  Players who primarily wanted to trade or mine, for example, felt very disused.  I hear the game cuts you off after a few missions (you can only continue in single player), but we didn't get that far, so I can't say whether that's still the case.  Maybe worth a look, especially with mods?

This is the first time I have ever reviewed a title on Steam. Having played video games mostly on consoles as a child I have not really had a huge amount of expeince of PC/Mac gaming growing up. However that has now all changed as I edge ever nearer 30 and now have a top end iMac. I will be looking at the Mac version of the game but honestly it doesn't matter which version of tghis game you have as it is just glorious.
Dean Dodrill has single handedly created a passion project that, along with help from others with the sound and playtesting, is one of the true masterworks of indie gaming of the past 10 years. From the sublime visuals to the game engine that runs as smooth as silk with not a hint of slowdown in any part this is a game that oozes the care and attention that many video games of today sorely lack. With a story of both discovery and redemption this game urges you into it's game world and won't let you go until you have seen all that is on offer in the game. The controls are responsive with it's Metroidvania cues very apparent, this is a game that just feels great to play when mowing down enemies or tackling the few tricky platforms or puzzles that take place.
One thing I want to massively complement is the way that thios title, that started out as a Xbox 360 XBLA title is the way in which the title has been ported to PC/Mac/Linux. It has more options than almost any 2D title I have ever seen with all resolutions covered, a multitude of option to help with performance and even little things like a colour blindness option. This seems to also be true of the PS4 version which I have heard was also a superb port as well.
Are there any faults? There are but they are small and minimal. There was a few text boxes in the inventory screen that had the text not wrapped around correctly when you read some of the completed tasks you have done and the game on the lower difficulties is pretty easy. That is fixed by playing the game on the higher difficulties though, the game will test you harder on those. The only other thing that may hold you back is the art style, that is a very subjective thing and honestly if you have a problem with that then I can understand but i feel you are really missi9ng out.
In the end though, most people should of heard of this game and better still many have played it, I may of been late into getting this but by no means does it lack any impact it has now as it did the 4-5 years ago when it first came out. Seriously buy this game and just enjoy a really well crafted and enjoyable game expereince. One we really need more of.

I got F.E.A.R as part of the Humble WB bundle (the one with the Arkham games) and decided to go through them again since I hadn’t tried the 2 expansions before. For some reason, Steam bundled the first game along with the 2 standalone expansions Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate together into a massive 17 gigabyte installation. This is weird since the 2 expansions are so similar to the base game (in graphics and gameplay) that they probably should have just shared most of the same data files and shrunk the size considerably. The three games have different Steam entries too, so once F.E.A.R is installed, just choose to “install” Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate and it will pretty much instantly install them.
You play the part of an unnamed First Encounter Assault Recon soldier, though they refer to you a few times as the point man for the team. Your squad has about 4-5 people but you get separated from them right away so there’s no squad based gameplay. Your primary mission in the game is to take down Paxton Fettel, a psychic commander created by the Armacham private military contractor. Psychic commanders are supposed to control “replica soldiers” who are basically genetically engineered clone soldiers. Fettel went insane for some reason and his replica forces are tearing the place up. As the story progresses you find hints about Armacham projects called Perseus and Origin, which are somehow related to Fettel’s creation. Throughout the game you also see visions of a little girl who appears out of nowhere and vanishes when you get close. There are a lot of “dream sequence” type hallucinations where you learn about Alma, the little girl, and what they did to her at Armacham.
Fear is a first person shooter with a slow motion “power” that you can activate with the push of a button. It’s explained in the story as your character having off the chart reflexes, and you can use it to give yourself an advantage in battle. In reality though, it’s not as useful as you might think. You’re not actually moving faster in slow-mo, it’s mostly just to give you more time to aim your shots (you can’t dodge bullets like Neo). Reloading and aim correction from weapon recoil still slow you down. The thing that really sets Fear apart from other games at the time was its advanced enemy AI. The replica soldiers actually behave like real human players a lot of the time. They throw grenades if you’re under cover and they try to circle around you. Most importantly though, they don’t sit still in combat, making it a little harder for you to flank them. Fear uses a health/armor system where you have both a health number and an armor number and constantly find armors lying around in the levels. You can carry up to 10 med kits which you use manually by pressing a button. You can carry up to 3 weapons and can switch them around by taking the stuff your enemies drop.
Pros:
+Excellent enemy combat AI
+A bunch of scares thrown in when Alma pops up or hallucinations occur
+Immersive storyline
Cons:
-The game’s graphics are pretty dated now. I don’t think you can get more than 1280 x 1024 resolution. And it’s a large download for such an old game.
-No real “boss fights” which are usually fun in first person shooters
-The enemies have great aim. It seems like they can hit you no matter how far away they are.
Mini reviews for the 2 standalone expansions:
*FEAR Extraction Point:
This is a non-canon continuation of the story. That means that it if you play the sequels, FEAR 2 & 3 will ignore what happens in the FEAR Extraction Point story. The game is standalone, which means you don’t keep all the upgrades and gear that you found in the base game. There really isn’t anything new in Extraction Point except maybe 1 or 2 weapons that you only use for a few minutes.
*FEAR Perseus Mandate:
A few new weapons appear which actually make it into the sequel FEAR 2. So even if the story isn’t “official” they were clearly paying attention to this game.  This one has some pretty mean new enemies including a difficult boss fight. Definitely better than Extraction Point. Perseus Mandate’s story is separate from the original game. You play a different person in a different FEAR squad, though there are a lot of references to events in the base game happening at the same time.
Overall I’d give FEAR a thumbs up if you can handle the large download and don’t mind some poor (by today’s standards) graphics. You cannot just download the base game; you automatically download all three at the same time (FEAR + Extraction Point + Perseus Mandate). If you could pick and choose, I’d recommend you skip Extraction Point. The experience is better if you play in the dark.

Excellent FPS game that still holds up to this day. The atmosphere, the lighting, the physics, the gameplay and the level design all come together to make this a solid classic. I feel especially the dynamic lighting deserve extra praise; there is something wonderful about jumping from the sight of your own shadow. There are a few jump-scares thrown into the mix, but I would say the horror element of the game comes from the creepy atmosphere.
The plot is relatively thin, but it works. It delivers what little there is of story and it is consistent within its own universe. Mostly it succeeds in moving the player forwards so you can enjoy the gameplay, the differing ways to approach a fight and still give you a bit of a chill even though you are a soldier with superhuman reflexes.
Favorite part of the game is in Extraction Point, where, after having fought your way through countless enemies, a whole squad of them run away at the sight of you, with only a lone soldier covering their retreat. THAT is attention to detail and how you make the player feel like a badass.
In short, if you like classic shooters like Half Life or No-One Lives Forever, you will love this. If you want to see what the fuzz is about; this game is nine years old at the time of writing, I recently played through it, and I would argue that it looks better than modern games. It certainly plays better.

Normally, I get bored of rogue-like games after playing them for a while. Not sure what it is, but it gets repetitive, even with the procedurally generated levels, which are meant to give you a new stage every time you play, yet somehow it always feels like the same exact experience, and not in a good way.
That being said, however, I did hear about this game some time ago, after one of my favorite YouTubers, FamilyJules7x, had apparently been releasing videos of songs related to this game. I didn't check them out, and still haven't (although now I might), but after seeing those pop up in my subscriptions, suddenly I kept seeing the game EVERYWHERE. There was rarely a moment where I wasn't made aware of the game's presence on the market.
So, giving in to my curiosity, I found the game on Steam and added it to my wishlist until I could make the time and money to buy it. I finally picked it up during a sale and got it for $3. I cannot recall if I saw the trailer. If I did, I don't think I took much interest in it.
Needless to say, the gameplay took me by surprise. 10 minutes in turned into what seemed like damn near 4 ♥♥♥♥ING HOURS. Holy God, this game is addicting beyond anything I've played. The art style during the cutscenes is amazingly done, and the character sprites are very charming to look at. Half the time I fail to get past even the most basic enemies and bosses because I'm so invested in keeping the beat with that ridiculously catchy and amazing soundtrack. I expect nothing less from Mr. Danny Baranowsky himself. I'll probably be buying it in the near future. I was also delighted to hear Jules' additions to the game.
BRIEF SHAMELESS PROMOTION: Check out FamilyJules7x on YouTube. Killer guitarist.
All in all, I've completely fallen in love with this game. I'm definitely gonna be grinding to see how much further I can get. I'm glad I decided to check this game out, and I highly recommend it to anyone who's looking for a new spin on rogue-likes, or just wants an all-around fun game.

Final Fantasy VIII is one of my favorite entries in the series. And it holds up incredibly well for a game released in 1999. Visuals don't look that great on modern HD screens, but everything else is as good as it was in the original release.
Characters are involving and exciting, and they all take part in a mature and complex storyline to stop a sorceress from the future from compressing time. But they are not base archetypes or generic "heroes" found in many games.
The main protagonist is Squall Leonheart, a recently graduated member of SeeD, an elite mercenary force. He starts as an introverted, grumpy and cold teenager who pushes away those who would otherwise be considered his friends and doesn't seem to really care about anything or anyone else but himself. You'll probably hate his guts until halfway through the game when you find out why he is the way he is. Squall begins to change when he falls in love with Rinoa Heartilly, a cheerful member of a resistance group from Timber, and also Squall's employer on his first mission as a graduated SeeD. As you progress through the game, you see Squall rethink his choices in life and accept the support and friendship of his comrades which in turn makes him step up into his role as a leader - something he never asked for.
You travel all around the world in your journey, and the locations you visit range from the the peaceful harbour city of Balamb to the busy capital of the Galbadian empire. You ride trains and drive a Garden, you take part in an elaborate assassination plot during a parade. Hell, you even go to space! Sadly you don't have access to a submarine this time around, but the Ragnarok makes up for it pretty well - it's probably the coolest airship of the series!
Character customization is done through Junctions - you basically join a Guardian Force (summons in previous games) with one of your characters to have access to specific abilities and in-battle commands. Bigger, more beautiful and far more complicated, The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a terrific game, but beware, you might find yourself missing certain details and plots if you haven’t read the books.
We continue our adventures as Geralt of Rivia, the famous monster slayer, this time, we face new difficulties as a mysterious group of people has started killing kings, we find ourselves struggling to clear our name after being framed for one of these murders. Following clues, finding key people and killing monsters will be the foundations for this new quest for the Witcher. More and complicated political issues and alliances are part of the story this time, as we have to take sides, each side leading to new missions and characters.
The Witcher 2 is a totally different game if we compare it to the original title, controls have been changed making gameplay more difficult to get used to, as we must learn how to use every new control and key. Bombs, traps and daggers were incorporated to make gameplay more varied, we still have the use of signs and our well-known steel and silver swords.
On this occasion, signs feel more significant, they have a different touch, this time signs make you feel they are important to use depending on the battle we are having or the danger we are facing, they are concise and powerful to use, they deliver powerful blows and do a great deal of damage, even more if you level up the power and use of stamina.
Bombs, traps and daggers are a great new addition, but in my case, I stuck only to bombs as they are more reliable and have more variation, poisonous, shrapnel, explosive, you name it, we have many different bombs for different situations, they are created the same way potions are created, by meditating, just get the right ingredients and the formula and you are all set.
The new system includes quickslots, very helpful in fighting situations, here you can select which kind of secondary attack you wish to use, bombs, traps and daggers are the only options.
Meditating is still tactical, as you may know, the witcher games are not the typical hack ‘n’ slash game, before going into any battle against monsters or humans, meditating is important and a must for you have to drink the right potion and brew what you need for battle, this characteristic has been improved as well, we no longer need a fire to meditate, just any place with no danger around will suffice. Leveling up will give us points we can spent on the skill tree where we have four paths, each of these paths have multiple options we can improve, so choosing correctly is up to you.
Depending on the development of your skill tree Geralt will start showing more fighting moves, the power of signs will increase, toxicity tolerance will improve and also a new addition has been introduced, the adrenaline rush, a perk that will deliver a killing move as an in-game cinematic.
TW2 offers more variety regarding armors and swords, the previous title was very limited and the creation of new swords was narrowed to some few silver and steel swords, even worst for armor sets, here we get to find new and better armor sets with many different perks and characteristics, the same for swords, blacksmiths are more common and ingredients for the creation of new tools are plentiful.
TW2 is a beautiful game, it is a gigantic step taken if we compare it to the original witcher, gameplay changed so did graphics and effects, it feels smoother and more defined. While the graphics are one of a kind here, the game also offers a great detail in weather effects and it adds a more consistency regarding the climate as well as day and night cycles. The engine really shines every time many of these aspects interact whether in battle or just when searching for clues related to any of the many missions and side-quests. There are little details in all sort of vegetation, the skies show multiple effects depending on the levels and sometimes in the distance the firmament is shown full of stars. More importantly, the engine is very keen to show off the diversity in the main cities we visit. Especially Upper Aedirn, a fantastic city built by dwarves, every stone, from a little stone to the biggest of the constructions the city is of a great design, it really captures the atmosphere of a place that has seen countless battles, magnificent.
The series has always been very serious regarding sound and voice acting, and this time is not an exception, voice actors did a great job on every aspect of the acting, characters are believable and demonstrate different kind of accents during the story, we even get to listen to more of the elves’ language, superb work, nothing negative here.
As for sound, TW2 is solid, we can feel the atmosphere on any landscape’s sound, nature, monsters etc. Everything is unique and deserves attention while the music adds intention and action to every battle, mission and interaction. Outstanding.
Perhaps what makes this game difficult to get used to is the amount of characters, their personal views, politics and different story lines and past events that make the lore of the witcher a deep abyss of details, it might be complicated for people not familiar with the books, at least, on my first play through, I felt lost in the middle of the politics, unlike the original witcher, TW2 shows a more mature and adult view of the world. I would mention not to pick this one without a little bit of knowledge related to the lore, I strongly recommend the books to get a better insight of the witcher world and politics, after that, the series starts to be easier to understand and at the same time it helps appreciate even more the different aspects of the game, the kingdoms, lands and peoples, wars and history.
As I said before, The Witcher 2 is a more mature game, a more adult-oriented title that will not disappoint at all, it has the depth regarding stories and lore, and it shows a more complex game style, definitely a must for RPG lovers and fans of the books.

*might contain minor spoilers*
Almost 5 years after the release, I finally played Witcher 2.
You play as an imprisoned witcher, Geralt of Rivia, who is accused of murdering a king. The game begins with compelling flashbacks in which you storm a castle, and it shows how the murder happened. Through the game, you are chasing the real killer as well as try to recover your memories about the Wild Hunt and Yennifer. You meet interesting characters (some from the 1st Witcher game), and in one point have to choose who will you follow. This changes the story quite a bit (mainly different location in chapter 2), so the game can be enjoyed in the 2nd replay.
The game has prologue, 3 chapters and an epilogue, with different maps you cannot return to when you finish the chapter.
I don't think you must play Witcher 1 to enjoy it (I didn't finish it for instance).
Pros and cons:
+ The game still looks very pretty.
+ Good voice acting and quality mature dialog (even non clickable npcs ramble when you run by).
+ Intriguing main story, the world is rich (although you might get lost with all the different names).
+ You can 'steal' anything and nobody will attack you.
+ You can sleep with a number of women (there's a cut scene with boobies and booties).
+ Sweet soundtrack that fits nicely.
+ Not black and white: monsters aren't necessarily bad. You also have a choice to kill or spare     some people which effects the political map of the world.
+ You can skip dialogue and cut scenes.
+ Some of the quests are very interesting...
- ...but some are classic monster slaying type. Either eradicate xxx or you fight through monsters to get to the place, find item etc.
- Walking back and forth can be a chore sometimes.
- You must meditate to drink potions.
- If you are trying to collect materials for crafting weapon/armor, the local shop will have good alternative relatively cheap, which makes crafting undervalued.
I cannot really comment about fighting difficulty as I played on easy (focused on the story), but for me, the fighting mechanics were better than in Witcher 1.
The game has a few puzzles, but I also cannot comment on difficulty as I was mostly too lazy and just googled correct sequences.
All in all, it is a great game which can be bought really cheap on sales. If you haven't played Wild Hunt yet, I think these ~40 hours into Witcher world can be well spent before throwing yourself in the latest installment of the Witcher saga.

Get Ploughing While The Sun Shines !
Though I am not usually someone who would play this game I purchased it for when I look after my nephew who is tractor mad and to my surprise this sim title has for me turned out to be gold compared to another farming sim I tried first and which was sadly just rubbish.
Farming Simulator 2013 for me in its latest patched Titanium edition is both very simple but at the same time very engrossing with something always in need of your attention in the game so you don't feel like you are waiting it out for a crop to grow especially since this sim does not advance by seasons but can be played in real time speed and with a whole plethera of options covering crop growing speed and many many other things.
The other thing that really helps the game is the graphics which portray a very nicely balanced view in any camera mode and lends itself well to the overall feel of the sim whether your ploughing or collecting hens eggs.
As for activities and things you can do there is a lot more to the game than simply growing corn in a field as this sim features  the typical farm animals to care for and that form part of the farms income like the cows for instance which can be milked and the milk sold to the local milk supplier.
When it comes to crops the choice is large and varied and can for your farm become more than just wheat to sell as you can not only harvest base items like wheat but you can then collect the hay left behind and use that in bales for feeding etc.
One of the other things I am impressed by in this sim is the vehicles which are not only nicely modelled but seem to be able to mimick most things in the real world including needing front weights if you are taking an oversized plough out on your tractor.
The one thing I would say negatively about this title is the default keys mapping which really should be one of the things you sort out when you get going as the default key setup is not too clever and not very intuitive either but once sorted it helps the game play become smooth and easier.
Also of note this title has a huge amount of community of players behind it who have made over 300 mods which cover everything from new maps to a pressure washer for cleaning your vehicles and so there is always something you find to add to your farm.
Although this review has not gone too deelpy into the sim and is just a general overview I would still say to anyone who has an interest in this type of gaming to buy this title and find all the great things about it as you develope your farm and feilds.

As an sightseeing tour Abzu was quite interesting, but don't come expecting gameplay, and any talk of it's "story" should be taken with a pinch of salt.
I like the environments. Great care has been taken to recreate the ocean floor in ways that captivate the players emotions and sense of imagination. My favourite part was the undersea city that was filled with prehistoric animals, like the amonite and the elasmosaur. (Pity I didn't find any megalodon.)
The thing that keeps me from reccomending Abzu isn't the price or it's appeal to relaxation as opposed to challenge, it's the story.
It's your standard three act affair with a set up, where you have fun frollicking among the sealife and learn about the ancient race of sea-dwelling humanoids; a second act where it is implied that these menacing floating pyramid things with glowing red eyes have done something to the ocean; (exactly what is never shown or explained) and a third act inwhich you are appointed somekind of robot-fish messiah and overthrow the tyranny of the angery pyramids by slamming into them and replacing them with coral phalusses.
This wouldn't have been so bad if I could at least understand what the conflict was about, but Abzu is too busy trying to wow me with it's interactive schools of fish to concern itself with coherent storytelling.
You get pretty much what you see in the trailers, so if you think it's pretty and you enjoyed swimming around with the whale in Rayman 2, then it might be worth your time if it's on sale.
At full price, I wouldn't bother.

This was one of the first games I got on steam. Some friends told me that it was not worth its full price and I should just wait for the discount but I didnt listen to them. This game is completely worth its price. Its only five dollars without the DLC and eight dollars with the DLC making it extremely cheap. This game requires very little power so I could play it on my terrible laptop. When I first started playing this game I was so bad at it and I wondered how anyone could ever beat it. But if you play this game for the first few rounds you will start to want to play more and more and beat what you got last game. The first ten times you beat the game, even if its with the same character, you get something new. Then you can beat it with all the other characters. Every character has their good parts and bad parts. Character choice is also a crucial decision even in the late game making you really have to figure out who you like to pay as. Some poeple say that this game is very small and that is true but you have to remember that this actually started out as a flash game. ocne youve beat the game a lot it starts to feel a bit repetative but to give you an example of what I mean by a lot, I have played over 200 hours of this game and only in the past 2 hours or so did I start to feel it getting boring. But that means that I got about 25 hours of gameplay for every dollar I spent. This is a great game if you like roguelike games. Every run is either a bit or completely different from the others depending on what items you choose to pick up. This isnt a multiplayer game but its fun to play around friends to see peoples different strategys. I really enjoyed this game and all my friends hate me because I played to much of it. 9.5/10

The pinnacle of JRPGs for many players, this game has aged like wine in many regards and like milk in others.
The graphics have aged poorly, and the early-PS1 blockiness and untextured polygons of the characters may turn off some people, though they are charming in their own way. The pre-rendered backgrounds still look decent, and battle models are much less blocky than their overworld counterparts.
The story has aged very well, and provides a strong narrative with many emotional moments and memorable locales, and all of the main characters have strong character arcs and growth throughout the story, even if they are not in the forefront at times.
The battle system is good, never feeling too frantic or too slow, and abilities and strides a nice line between turn-based and real-time. Difficulty is pretty well-tuned throughout the game, there were not many situations where it felt that grinding levels and equipment was necessary (Although if one wants to take on some of the post-game optional bosses, they will need to grind quite a bit).
The soundtrack is immaculate, and almost every track in the game is memorable in their own way.
Not really my thing, but still a hell of a lot better than the first one.

Never before has a game invoke  such a wide range of emotions from me. And no, I don't mean the story, I mean the actual game itself. There were times where it made me want to smash my controller, and other times  when I couldn't put it down. Because of this, comparing it to the other games in the franshise, and giving it a definitive rating is hard.
Positives:
* (see negatives and neutral)
+ Stunning graphics, even by today's standards this game looks great
+  Difficulty, definetely a skill based game *
+ Fluid, fun combat *
+ Interesting story, with a diverse cast of well written and voice acted characters, and many important descisions to make
+ Roughly 20-30 hour story, depending on how many side quest you do
+ Definetely replayable
+ Sets up Witcher 3 well
Negatives:
- * Despite changing the combat from Witcher 1 significantly there is no significant tutorial on the new system, making the first few hours pretty rage inducing.
- potions can no longer be drank on the fly
- significantly fewer side quests than Witcher 1
Neutral:
> * significant changes to the combat. The combat is  good (once you get used to it), but I really liked Witcher 1's system and was sad to see it go
> Shorter than the other games in the series by a significant margin (Witcher 1 took almost 40 hours to finish) this took only 26, which is still long enough for me, but i'm sure it annoyed some.
Verdict: For every step forward Witcher 2 makes over it's predecessor, it takes a step back or makes a seemingly necessary change. So in the end , I'd certainly still give it a recommendation, but unfortunately, I can't say that it's better than Witcher 1 overall.

Let's just get this out of the way, this is not CKII in space! Don't expect to have some dynamic family tree you need to manage with complex laws governing the nuances of land ownership. Though there does exist a leader tree it's rather simplistic at best, but don't let this deter you as the depth of this game is offered in different places. It's a 4X sci-fi game so with regards to basic game play elements there's nothing new here. However it's well worth mentioning where others in the genre fall short Stellaris seems to deliver. Of course it's not a perfectly polished game, but the core is here and it's a very solid one indeed!
The best way I can describe the feel of Stellaris it's like a combination of Endless Space and Stardrive. Yes both games had major flaws, but take those out combine the two and you have Stellaris; a solid game with hidden depth. The music, story, and atmosphere do a great job of painting the picture of a vast galaxy full of once was and current civilizations. I'm a huge advocate for having a solid musical score in my games (It's one of the reasons I've played guild wars 2 since launch). Stellaris' music is solid, nothing outstanding nor out of context. It's an original piece of grand sci-fi that suits the game. Some reviews claim the writing is lackluster, but personally I actually enjoyed reading the dialog. It's laced with just enough subtle humor to keep a smile on my face.
Obviously it's worth touching on some of the cons. First and foremost is the sound design. Like many others have noted the sound clips used for space battles are very tinny and just overall poor quality. Sometimes you zoom in on a fleet battle and it simply feels like toy ships flying around zapping each other with their toy ray guns. The A.I. is also rather suspect here as well. Though their diplomatic behavior is logical their handling of fleets during times of war is rather questionable at best. The good news is that not only have the developers acknowledged the A.I. flaws and plan to fix them, but the game has full mod support. Within the next month or two one should expect to see plenty of sound mods.
Overall I think this is a great 4x sci-fi game, one that has brought me back to the genre for another "just 5 more minutes" type of session that usually ends up being far longer than intended.

F.E.A.R. or First Encounter Assault Recon, is a psychological horror first person shooter, amazingly well designed and one of the few games that always made me feel uneasy while playing it. This game will make you jump out of your chair, and always when you least expect it.
You play as the Point Man of the First Encounter Assault Recon, a secret United States organization that investigates and deals with paranormal phenomena. You get called into action after you are informed that Paxton Vettel, a Psychic Commander has seized the headquarters of Armachan Technologies and killed everyone there. His reasons are unknown at first, and it's up to you to discover why. He controls an army of clones, and you have to fight and investigate your way through the mess that was created.
The story is more than meets the eye. It is not predictable, and it is told to you in subtle ways. You have to explore your surroundings, listen to voice recordings and pay attention to certain laptops to find out what is going on and the reasons behind the disturbing events. The way the story is told is brilliant, because each player will fill in certain gaps in any way they want, and experience the game in a very personal way. The overall story line however, is well crafted and some points in the plot are completely unpredictable.
F.E.A.R. is a horror experience like no other. The mood is everything in this game, and the way the lighting, sound, hallucinations and Alma (more on her later) combine to the feeling of isolation and fear, it's almost certain this game will make the hair in the back of your neck stand up, you will never take a hallway, a room or even an open setting for granted. You will never feel safe in this game, both from enemies and from hallucinations, it will creep you out. It takes elements of Japanese horror, where the mood, sound and shadows create the bulk of the atmosphere, and in this type of game, less is certainly more.
Alma is part of why this game will scare you at times. It is hard to imagine that the apparition of a little girl can be scary, but in this case it is extremely effective. Every single time Alma shows herself, in badly lit areas combined with the game's excellent sound effects, it WILL leave you breathless. These moments are tense and completely unexpected. Forget everything you know about creepy games. F.E.A.R. rewrites what a creepy game is all about. The best way to see why Alma is a character that is often quoted as one of the creepiest ones in gaming, is to play this game and see for yourself.
The game's visuals are still quite good, despite this being a game with quite a few years. The textures and lighting effects are well done, and feel realistic. The most impressive aspect about the visuals are the particle effects, which really come alive in slow motion. The game offers you the option to engage firefights in a slow motion type of way, called Reflex Booster in the game, allowing you to slow down time and make easy some complicated situations. It is usefull against several enemies who attack you at once, and you will need this gameplay aspect, the AI in this game is probably the most intelligent I have ever faced in a video game. Enemies will call for backup, try to pin you down with supressive fire while another one flanks you, use the environment to create cover and even ignore orders not to get in harm's way. They are really challenging, and it's a big part of why this game as aged so well, nothing comes close on modern first person shooters. There is a good variety of weapons as well, some of them extremely rewarding to use. The one thing all have in common, is that no weapon feels too weak, they all have their use even later in the game. Finding out which ones to take with you is part of the experience, as the game limits the amount you can carry, 3 is the maximum. Firefights can be brutal. Depending on which weapon you use, you will see body parts flying and blood spilling quite a lot, it is not for the faint of heart.
F.E.AR. is a must buy. It manages to be an amazing horror/creepy game and a superb first person shooter with a very good story. It will scare you and make you feel helpless at times, but it is an experience you will never forget.
The Good
-Creepy Atmosphere
-Amazing story
-Visuals, Sound and Particle system
-Alma is the creepiest little girl ever put into video games
-Enemy AI is brilliant
-Good selection of weapons
The Bad
-Game might feel a little short to some, takes about 13 hours to finish without rushing
-Could have used a little more variety in the environments

This was one of the first games I got on steam. Some friends told me that it was not worth its full price and I should just wait for the discount but I didnt listen to them. This game is completely worth its price. Its only five dollars without the DLC and eight dollars with the DLC making it extremely cheap. This game requires very little power so I could play it on my terrible laptop. When I first started playing this game I was so bad at it and I wondered how anyone could ever beat it. But if you play this game for the first few rounds you will start to want to play more and more and beat what you got last game. The first ten times you beat the game, even if its with the same character, you get something new. Then you can beat it with all the other characters. Every character has their good parts and bad parts. Character choice is also a crucial decision even in the late game making you really have to figure out who you like to pay as. Some poeple say that this game is very small and that is true but you have to remember that this actually started out as a flash game. ocne youve beat the game a lot it starts to feel a bit repetative but to give you an example of what I mean by a lot, I have played over 200 hours of this game and only in the past 2 hours or so did I start to feel it getting boring. But that means that I got about 25 hours of gameplay for every dollar I spent. This is a great game if you like roguelike games. Every run is either a bit or completely different from the others depending on what items you choose to pick up. I give this game a 7/10.
As far as MOBAs go, Dragons and Titans is a boiled-down MOBA that is GREAT for beginners. I have a friend who never plays them, and she actually gave DaT a try and loves it. There are no items to deal with in the game, and experience is granted by killing enemies and collecting gold. Potions that drop on the map restore your health, and there are numerous spells you can use in-game (similar to other MOBAs). There are various ways to play and the map cycles every half hour. There's even a single-player campaign to unlock new dragons, and you can upgrade dragons and weapons over time. Dragons are also really well-designed and are really cool. I have a total of five, right now due to weekly rewards and the single-player campaign, not to mention the three you get for free for playing through the tutorial stages.
The downside? It is a boiled-down MOBA. Experienced MOBA players might find the game a bit dull, overall (especially if you're coming from DOTA). I played LoL for a while, and I currently play SMITE, but Dragons and Titans is stilll a fun game to play with friends. It just doesn't take nearly as much skill, in comparison.
Another downside is that much of the content is locked behind what they are calling the Titan Pass, a $20 pass that gives you access to a bunch of extra stuff (like the other three single-player campaigns). Granted, if you're THAT into the game that you're willing to pay that's great. But I feel it is a bit much for someone who only plays casually.
Lastly, queue times for PVP games can be rather long due to a small population of players. I had a PVP queue last at least 5 minutes a few days ago, for example (I've never waited more than a minute and a half in SMITE).
Overall, Dragons and Titans is a great MOBA for beginners, and shouldn't be counted out just because it started out browser-based, or because of the boiled-down features. Give it a shot - the darned thing is free. If you don't like it, uninstall. If you do, though, keep playing and I hope to see you in the sky someday.

Dungeon Defenders Eternity - For those new to the franchise, a fresh slate, this game is really not bad. I would dare to say fun.
Unfortunately, I am not new to the franchise. I - Long ago, I was very much into the original Dungeon Defenders. A game that focused on teamwork, strategy and growth. Before I can review the game let me explain what this game is. Dungeon Defenders Eternity Is a combined game of Dungeon Defenders, and all its DLC. It includes rebalancing of loot, minions, bosses and characters. They have added a few new items, as well as crafting and cosmetic upgrades to the game's customization. In addition, it is a client-side game hosted by Play Verse with a separate friends list and party system not linked with steam.
This description is a description of what the final version of this "definitive" game is supposed to be. However, currently, it is missing several things as well as added some annoying things which I will list.
-Not All DLC, Game-modes and Difficulties have been added
-Characters are not by any means balance (Squire is a requirement, and Summoner has no building use)
-Loot was bugged, spawning Epicly overpowered stats. A patch has come and nerfed all loot, messing up everything further
-Chance of getting decent loot is absurdly unlikely. Long Long hours of grinding is necessary. (No feeling of growth)
-Play Verse is tacky, and not well optimised
-Matchmaking is buggy and constantly doesn't let you join games.
-Private Taverns have been changed to public, achievements no longer visible
-Cosmetics cool but unnecessary
-Crafting, not really crafting. No real gameplay. Just play enough till your able to craft the item you want.
-A few maps are unplayable due to unbalanced gear.
These are just some of the issues with Dungeon Defenders Eternity. If you want to see more, I would recommend you check out the Forums.
Dungeon Defenders Eternity claims to be a "Definitive" version, meaning complete, perfected, fixed. Instead, we have scraps of features to be added to Dungeon Defenders 2, portions of Dungeon Defenders 1 and a whole lot of bugs. For the sake of the sequel I want to recommend this game, but I can't because it feels like a beta. It really would not give justice to the original in any way. Dungeon Defenders Eternity is a hollowed out version of the original. This game is getting patched but nothing more than quick fixes. The reason for this is because they don't care about this game. It is a quick cash operation to help fund the sequel. The shame is 90% of the people who bought this game were the people who would have bought Dungeon Defenders 2. If you have never played the original, for the sake of saving money, it might be worth a buy. If you have played the original, do not get this. It will leave you full of disappointment, and disgust for Trendy.

Never before has a game invoke  such a wide range of emotions from me. And no, I don't mean the story, I mean the actual game itself. There were times where it made me want to smash my controller, and other times  when I couldn't put it down. Because of this, comparing it to the other games in the franshise, and giving it a definitive rating is hard.
Positives:
* (see negatives and neutral)
+ Stunning graphics, even by today's standards this game looks great
+  Difficulty, definetely a skill based game *
+ Fluid, fun combat *
+ Interesting story, with a diverse cast of well written and voice acted characters, and many important descisions to make
+ Roughly 20-30 hour story, depending on how many side quest you do
+ Definetely replayable
+ Sets up Witcher 3 well
Negatives:
- * Despite changing the combat from Witcher 1 significantly there is no significant tutorial on the new system, making the first few hours pretty rage inducing.
- potions can no longer be drank on the fly
- significantly fewer side quests than Witcher 1
Neutral:
> * significant changes to the combat. The combat is  good (once you get used to it), but I really liked Witcher 1's system and was sad to see it go
> Shorter than the other games in the series by a significant margin (Witcher 1 took almost 40 hours to finish) this took only 26, which is still long enough for me, but i'm sure it annoyed some.
Verdict: For every step forward Witcher 2 makes over it's predecessor, it takes a step back or makes a seemingly necessary change. So in the end , I'd certainly still give it a recommendation, but unfortunately, I can't say that it's better than Witcher 1 overall.

This is a piece of work which not only transcends the medium of interactive software, but equally transcends the idea of art itself. Great art asks the question "What does it mean to be human?" but Abzû goes beyond this. It not only asks "What does it mean to exist?" but also asks "What is the relationship between consciousness and existence?" In Abzû, you play as The Diver, exploring an ocean with serves as a representation for the sea of knowledge. The Diver is a creature of the air and the earth, seemingly out of place in this aquatic wonderland. She occasionally breaks the surface for glimpses back at the lands above—her native land which serves as a metaphor for the imagination. She has many meaningful interactions with the many fish (as a highly influential member of The Oceanography Society, I am happy to say the fish AI is highly detailed and accurate) which remind us of the many individual facets of knowledge (both earthly and otherwise) which exist within the greater sea and help us throughout this beautiful, existential journey. The Diver, being a metaphor for the higher consciousness, swims not only through the sea of knowledge, but also surfaces for bouts of imagination, reminding us that we must hold within our consciousness a balance between both of these great principles. As the consciousness explores the beauties of knowledge and the mysteries of imagination, we are reminded of the symbiotic relationship between existence and consciousness, which we now realize are inseparable from knowledge and imagination. To know is to be, and to think is to create.

Stellaris is only an unenthusiastic recommendation from me. The game is competent, but uninspired. I don't regret buying it, and maybe it'll have a chance to come great with a bunch of patches and the obligatory DLC, but the game does nothing to overcome the mid to end game grind typical of the genre.
I've played 25 hours of Stellaris and restarted three or four times. Each time I expanded for around 6-10 hours or so with little in the way of competition, then started a completely unnecessary war out of sheer boredom. After either winning or stalemating the war, I looked around and observed that at the same rate I had at least another 6-10 hours of the same before hitting anything approximating a win condition. At this point I deleted my save game and started again.
The game’s big selling point, the supposed ‘stories’ that mix things up and make every game different, weren’t particularly obvious to me. My first game did result in an event where my civilization immediately spawned a 'splinter group' (basically, pirates). This ended up nerfing my start, but other than that I hunted them down and killed them, ending that particular story line. Every other game has largely followed the same trajectory, minus the initial rebellion.
Mostly, the same half dozen mini-missions (research anomalies) appear in regular rotation - ancient graffiti, ruined ancient organic star ship, ancient comet crashing into a planet, etc. Meh.
The other civilizations are all generic, and I regret my impulse preorder purchase to get a few more ‘cosmetic’ options for the other races in the galaxy (different portraits). These portraits don’t spend enough time on my screen for them to even register.
As far as emergent events are concerned numerous games do it far better. Spore’s end-game for one. Not to mention related procedurally generated SF ARPGs such as SPAZ and Space Rangers 2, where you can genuinely feel the life of the galaxy going on around you. In Stellaris, unfortunately, the universe feels almost entirely static and empty.
To finish on a few specifics, 75% of the gameplay seems to be micromanaging scout ships exploring and constructors building mines and research outposts, even into the late mid-game. There are no unit automation options, such as Civ's autoexplore and autoimprove, which is probably intentional since eliminating these two options would obviously also eliminate 75% of the gameplay.
Ship design feels like an add-on. Basically, research bigger ship size, maximise ship design for dps, research for a bigger ship size again… rinse and repeat.
Ultimately, playing on a sparse star field has little of the charm of Civ's changing geographies. In the absence of the buzz associated with discovering new coastlines, mountain ranges, swamps, rivers and cities, a space 4X really needs to offer something else. Stellaris promised to add that interest with its emergent storytelling. Sadly, with the game in its current empty state I’m not seeing it at the moment.

Occasionally you'll find yourself laughing, other times you'll sit in amazement at how "the Nerd" can get his frown to look so cartoonishly fake, while still being real.  The movie has several nods to older video games.
The budget is low (which I personally loved) which may distract or anger some viewers.  The story is fairly consistent with being inconsistent.  Towards the end it's made even more evident that the director just wanted to throw in as many cheesy and low budget special effects as possible, probably blew the wad on the last 15 minutes alone.

The Binding of Isaac: Wrath of the
Lamb, henceforth refered to as "BOY" for convenience and amusement. Let me say from the get go that if you intend to buy this game, get the DLC as well: it adds a significant amount of variety to the gameplay.
But before getting ahead of myself, BOY is a pretty standard twin-stick bomberman-arena'ed randomized-stuff shooter of sorts. Notice how I purposefully avoided using the word "rogue-like", since while it does share rogue-like elements it is not fair to call this a roguelike at all: being a rogue-like implies startegy, and BOY can only manage to give you choice... when it's having a good day.
BOY features a boy who is deprived of everything by a fundamentalist-religious mother and somewhat borrows minimalistically from the religious tale of Isaac's sacrifice for the purpose of premise. In reality, you are a boy wandering through the most amazingly large basement full of spiders, aborted babies and embodiments of sin.
Gameplay, as a twin-stick shooter, features the main character litterally crying tears against the nightmarish things that were locked in the basement. There's treasure that more often than not are stat sticks, increasing max health, damage, tear range or tear flux. There's treasure that passively grants abilities, such as a poor dead cat that when you get hit spawns friendly flies that will attack the enemies or irritable bowl beans that cause surrounding enemies to become poisoned if you get hurt. There's also treasure that is actively used, with an interesting twist on how to refill charges based on number of rooms visited; this is arguably the most "strategic" BOY gets, and even then you still have to get lucky with what treasures you'll find in your run.
Some of the boss fights feel a little unfair, even if you know them like you would yourself, however. Between the last fight in the game (on either path) which requires an insane amount of luck with the items you got while reaching it to have a minimal chance of winning and every random pot shot of green blobs that some enemies and bosses much enjoy spewing, passing through the "bullet hell" genre of unlikely dodges with nearly no reaction time allowed, some boss fights are pure and simply not really balanced, in my opinion. I for one especially hate Gurdy (or some such name, I can't remember it off the top of my head), the abortion that ♥♥♥♥♥ itself on the floor and charges at you; if you're not in a good spot when he starts charging, it can get messy really quick. And when you get two Gurdys in the same room? Yeah, absolutely not cool.
Now seems about a good time as any to mention that a lot of the developer's views and disturbed mind come across a subliminally conveyed message against religion and nihillistic views on life that gets more obvious the more you play the game and unlock endings. To illustrate, at one point you have to fight your mother and the next boss is your mother's heart, which can't mean anything other than symbolically killing your mother no matter how you see it.
So, what do I think of the game? If you don't think about it too deeply, as well you shouldn't for your own sake, BOY is just another twin stick shooter. The reason it got famous was because of the developer's previous title Super Meat Boy (see why I wanted to stick with BOY instead of BoI at the beggining?), and the amount of astronomical fame it brought as a game that was initially absolutely free to play over the Internet. But do I like twin-stick shooters? No, I really don't. I will concede that it was entertaining to some degree, and it was always fun to unlock some new item or deeper location, and pretty much the only reason I kept playing it was for the 100% clear. Which I have got, significantly sooner than I'd hope and sooner than I expected to get the achievements for "no damage taken on depth X". Incidentally, it bugs me that Steam decided to award me the "100% achievement achievement" and the "clear the womb taking no damage" (you heard it right: you're inside your mother's sexual organs, because of this twistedly sick nihilistic prick that is the developer) in the wrong order; Golden God would look cool as the most recent achievement when browsing on my games list, a naked Isaac smiling like he couldn't be prouder doesn't look anywhere near as cool or even something you'd want to see.
Bottom line, should you buy it? Sure, if you like twin-stick shooters go ahead. Keep in mind the frustration of randomness not being kind to you. Do I recommend you buy it? Nope. It's on the cheap side, granted, but you'll waste more time playing the game than you'd like in hindsight, and leaving it unfinished will feel like a huge waste.

Really cool and immersive game! RPG-based, with tons of space ready for exploring and tech customization. It has a very neat progression and quest system, with multiple dialogue options and a very well optimised character-class system, each with its own unique abilities and set of skills/perks, which allow for a diverse gameplay.
The UI is immersive, all the while keeping in theme with the arcade nature of the game. Also for the customization options, there's plenty of that, as the game offers a wide variety of ship upgrades, as well as useful consumables and other features, like mining lasers for extracting ore from asteroids. Furthermore, the tutorial is very explanatory, and there are details and descriptions following almost any action you make, that are sure to satisfy the lore-hungry gamers out there.
Last but not least, there's also a combat system which is well designed and that (at least on the lower levels, before you "master the stars") will be sure to introduce you to the thrills of space warfare, which will add to the exciting gameplay.
All around, i think this is a great game for fans of space exploration (like me). Albeit it's an arcade-ish game, it's fun and enjoyable to play. So, a big thumbs-up from me, and hopefully, from you guys too! :)

With my new style of reviewing games, I guess I should write a more 'professional' review about F.E.A.R. as well.
I'll try to keep things simple. The reason why I love FEAR so much and it's one of my top 5 games of all time is because it knows what it wants to do and does an amazing job at that: being an amazing action shooter with some creepy supernatural elements in between.
Good:
-Graphics, sound and the like: FEAR still looks pretty nice despite being nearly nine years old today and the sound design is as solid as ever. God, I love the gunfire in this game, it really sounds threatening. And don't get me started on the delicious Voice Acting by the Replica Soliders, that sounds extremely menacing.
-Gunplay and combatt in general: the game perfectly balances between being a realistic and tactical FPS and being not too supa dupa serious guise. Even the 'normal' weapons like the SMG or shotgun still feel great because you really feel like they pack a punch, especially the shotgun, that destroys anything that comes in your way. And then you still have the more fancy weapons, like the repeating cannon, the nail gun (god, nailing enemies to walls never gets old for me) and the particle gun, or as I like to call it, the skeleton gun (because it vaporizes (is that even a word?) any foe you hit with it, leaving nothing but some dust and bones). Melee feels great too and it's really satisfying to give a Replica Soldier a slowmo kungu kick to the face. Said slowmotion works great and is necessary if you want to survive, because..
-The AI: everybody has heard of FEAR's great AI by now. And while it's also the combination of good level design and intelligent scripting, the Replica Forces you'll encounter in the game really feel like smart and dangerous opponents that will destroy you if you don't use your wits, especially on higher difficulty, where it becomes 'kill or be killed'. These guys will, thanks to their awesome voice acting, insanely well co-ordinated teamwork and despite being clones still having personality, always carry a very special place in my heart.
-The horror: FEAR is inspired by japanese horror and it shows. Surrealistic and disturbing imagery, darkness and silence to drive you slowly insane, 'did I just see anything or was it just my imagination', all that. The game does have a few 'jumpscares' but nothing in the likes of 'spooky face appears with loud noise'.
-The story: FEAR tells it story through clever use of voicemail messages, date on laptops and the like. You'll really want to find out the truth behind project origin near the end of the game.
-TECHNOLOGY: objects that don't just stand there and get bullet holes when you shoot/melee/blow them up, the ability to see your legs, reflections in puddles of water, FEAR's got it all. Suck it, Bioshock Infinite, this nine year old game beats you here without any effort.
Bad:
-Dislikeable characters: some characters in FEAR (TALKING TO YOU, NORTON) aren't really likeable and you'd wish they'd just shut up so you can go and slowmokungfukick some more cloned soldiers. It's not really an issue, though, and more a matter of having something I dislike so people don't call me a fanboy that can't give negative criticism.
-Linear and repetitive scenery sometimes: you'll be fighting a lot of the times in the same type of buildings, though I didn't mind too much and this problem gets solved near the end of the game. There's still plenty of variation to make it bearable.
Overal, I give FEAR a 9/10. The same score I give to its two expansion packs, Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate, who are in my opinion the true 'sequels' to this amazing game and add some interesting weaponry, areas and enemies while keeping the amazing formula that makes FEAR so damn great.

DOOM II is a great game in its own right, being the basis for a lot of the newer mods in the DOOM community due to the other features it includes over the first DOOM. I will, however, say that it's not as great as I expected, being a sequel to the first DOOM.
There's things I love about it, such as the Super Shotgun, which is one of the best and satisfying weapons in any of these games, and the new enemies, providing a bigger challenge than before. However, the level design is what erks me here. More of the levels this time around don't feel as satisfying to go through and feel more tedious than before. Levels like The Gauntlet seemed like they should have been shorter than they were planned, and upon further playthrough, make me dread coming to them. They tried to go for a more open-world-like design in the levels, having you go to different separate buildings that lead you to nothing except a room full of enemies, and it becomes a waste of time if you haven't memorized them.
Overall, the level design isn't the greatest compared to the first game, but in its own right, it's still a great game.

After playing 2 hours, I must say that this was money well spent. I didn't experience any connection problems like many others have reported. Even with my crappy internet connection, it is a matter of seconds to exchange parts, so it seems like that issue has been fixed. Also, someone said that this game wouldn't have an options menu, which is simply not true. You can adjust resolution and graphics settings.
The game has some minor issues though. The GUI is a bit suboptimal. For example the red flashing button after you changed a component first made me think that I couldn't fit that part into the tank, while it was only meant to indicate which button is selected. Also, the menu navigation is a bit unclear. But tbh, this is complaining on a higher level.
While the environment is nearly completely destructible, many buildings leave a frame, meaning you can't drive through them. A pity, that would have been a really fun feature, just waltzing through some factory, living quarter or what have you.
Contentwise, the game offers 14 missions. I'm already at mission 8. But the 360 drills make up for that. You can also have custom sp missions, and then there's still the multiplayer.
This game is definitely not "pushing the  boundaries with modern graphics and exceptionally deep gameplay". For example the outline effect that indicates how well you hit, is rather cheap. But what Infinite Tanks does offer is solid craftmanship. The graphics do look nice, and the game is fun to play.
Also, the "Incredible realism" thing is a bit euphemistic. It's an arcady shooter game, not a simulation. Which is exactly what makes this game fun to play. It's rather easy to get into, but becoming good takes time and practice.
So, all in all, 5€ is effing cheap. I mean - seriously - the worst part of the game is the developers description on this store page ;) If you're even remotely interested in this game, go ahead and give it a try.

Crypt of the NecroDancer has one of the most unique concepts I've seen in my many years of playing games: it's a rogue-like dungeon crawler and a rhythm game all rolled into one. Your movements must match the beat of the game's music (which is phenomenal, by the way), and defeating/avoiding enemies requires knowing how they move to the music. It's got all the procedurally-generated levels and wide assortment of items (i.e. replay value) you've come to expect from a rogue-like, but now it's got a quite challenging (and musical) twist! And if the intrinsic replay value isn't enough, you can even use songs from your own music library as the BGM! That adds a whole layer of customization which allows you to create a list of songs that you enjoy/suits the pace at which you play.
If you like rhythm games or rogue-likes (or perhaps you like both?), this is absolutely worth your while.

This is probably the first time I've ever seen a game sequel be just as competent as it's predecessor, without really raising or lowering the bar.
I like DOOM. I like it a lot. And with all the hype behind the new DOOM 2016, I just couldn't help myself but throw some more hours into beating its sequel: Hell on Earth.
Because DOOM 2016 would beat my poor little laptop to death.
DOOM II takes place right after DOOM I, where Doomguy gets back from Mars to see earth covered with demons, and decides to take care of the problem the same way he did previously- by killing every demon that stands in his way. Like Carmack said, the story in games aren't important. While I may disagree with that statement, I do agree that an action-based should focus more on keeping you in the action as much as it can. And DOOM I and II both succeed in that, in my opinion.
With making a sequel, there's often the question of what will be added on to the new entry. With DOOM II there is a wide variety of new levels that are much more intuitively-designed than the first game, along with a new onslaught of enemies to face, including one of my least favorite enemies ever: The Pain Elementals. F*** those guys. Seriously. F*** those guys.
Surprisingly, as far as new content goes, besides the new enemies and levels, all you're given for new weapons is the super shotgun, which quickly became my favorite weapon. It uses two shotgun shells per round, and does extra damage as opposed to the standard shotgun. The game is challenging with all this new stuff, and I found myself in the DOOM-daze, where all I can think about over the week is playing more DOOM and getting more and more sucked in with every playthrough.
This is a very addicting game, but one flaw I saw throughout it (besides the lack of story) would be how the game really feels like an expansion to the original DOOM. It may have the run-time of a full game, but the textures, mixtures of old enemies with the new ones, and same arsenal as the first game, makes the game feel like more of DOOM I. I personally believe a game should accel from the foundation of the first game, but whether you disagree or agree with me is entirely your choice.
I won't deny that I love this game still. Just as much as the first DOOM. It's fast-paced, looks great, sounds great, and is addicting from start to finish. But since a lot of it does feel like the first game just bleeding into a sequel, I'm giving it the exact same score I'd give DOOM. A 7/10.

So I originally bought this because back in the day I played Seek and Destroy for the PS2 which looks quite similar to this; £3.99 was also a small price to pay compared to other games. I can see that this was ported from iOS and I wouldn't say it's a paticularly bad port from what I've played so far .
When the game first launched the servers were awful and my requests were always timing out. I am pleased to say that the servers (for the most part) are very good. Multiplayer games run very smoothly for me (unless someone has an awful ping) . The requests to get rewards after completing missions still take a decent amount of time but it's no longer game-breaking.
One thing I wish was a little bit smoother was tank customization. The customization is basically the core selling point of this game and it's probably the most tedious thing to do ; it's because every time you make a change to your tank it has to communicate with the server to deduct funds and manage your inventory of parts. It can probably take up to 5 seconds to remove each part which can be really annoying when you're moving parts around multiple tanks. I would say that they may be able to fix this by having a system that lets you make a bunch of changes and then you can confirm them all with a push of a button so the time spent communicating with the server is reduced.
because it's a good, quirky little game. There seems to be a large amount of customization that can be applied to your tanks - as well as there being 4 classes of tanks Scout, Light , Medium and Heavy. You can customize pretty much everything on the tank - the body, tracks, engine , turret etc and you can apply various boosts to your tank (Not microtransaction stat boosts, just modules that you earn after completing missions).
I've played through the whole campaign and it was 'meh'.  The story is pretty cringe and is comparable to something that I would come up with when I used to play with my toy soldiers. About as cliche as you can be with a rogue AI and nukes - but that's ok. I doubt it's really the selling point of this game. The destruction is decent ; your shots will take a couple of good chunks out of buildings and will blow up small props like cars and helicopters in game. I do not believe that there is destruction to the extent of buildings falling down like red faction. The campaign is pretty much a necessary evil to work through because it gives you lots of XP so you can level up and gain new parts for your tank.
The graphics are fine ; when I was comparing this to a PS2 game this was not what I meant. They're nothing groundbreaking but they get the job done. Though the average graphics connoisseur would probably not be impressed.
One thing that I didn't really like about the gameplay is that generally you'll do a lot better with a heavy tank or a tank destroyer rather than a scout or light tank. It's mainly because a light tank only takes around 1 or 2 well-placed shells to bring them down most of the time (when using a heavy or medium tank).
I think another reason as well is that the position of your tank doesn't matter too much in this game as long as the shell penetrates ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°). If you're in a light tank you'll probably lose to a 1v1 with a heavy/medium tank if you're both on full health. Even if you angle your tank against an incoming shell, it doesn't negate all that much damage. Equally, when you land a good hit on a tank (a 90 degree shot on the side or back) the damage does not change that much.
I did five shots in the test range on the heavy tank. I shot the tank 90 degrees in the front, 90 degrees on the side and 90 degrees on the back. For the front I got either 370 or 369 damage for my results. The side I got 407 or 406 damage from my results from the back I got 462 or 463 damage for my results.
So assuming that the 90 degree shot on the front of 370 damage is my 'base damage' the shot on the side yielded a 10% damage increase. My shot on the back of the tank of 462 damage yielded a damage increase of around 25% (rounding up). Whilst these damage increases do make aiming for these areas worthwhile (especially for heavy tanks with large damage outputs) it does not make the light tank viable in anyway. The gun on the light tank does not output enough damage compared to other tanks to make it worthwhile from a number's perspective ; which is a shame because I really like running light/medium tanks to try and flank. (I am not saying this just to cover up that I'm crap at the game. : D )
In terms of performance I imagine this could run on a toaster, at low settings at 720p. I'm current running this on Ultra 2560x1440 and I'm getting 100+ frames most of the time (R9 390, i7-4790K No OC).
Bottom line is I think it's a good game with deep customization and maybe a lot of replay value in the multiplayer. If you're thinking of buying this I'd would recommend it for £3.99 . I don't think this a game that I'll be hardcoring and playing a lot but I'll come back to it every once in a while. (Like those clan members that sit up on the hills in the arctic map in top tier tank destroyers and completely own you. Damn. I couldn't do anything against them. D:)
Apologies if any information is incorrect / not present because I have only played this for a little while.

At first, this game took me a while to get into due to the strange magic and stat system as well as the general world of the game, but I ended up surprising myself by how likable it ended up being.
In this game, you can gather magic spells from enemies via battle command, and then recast the spells, or equip them onto your stats to make them increase. This felt like a very weird system, having to gather and collect spells just to cast them later, as well as how slow you'd gather the spells. I later learned that the higher your magic stat, the faster your magic gathering would become, and I also learned that magic generally wouldn't be used a lot in normal combat anyways, so you'd rarely touch your huge pile of magic spells unless a boss or healing.
What really makes me like this system is equipping the spells to your stats, since the more magic you have of that type you're attaching to a specific stat (maximum 100 stack of any spell), the higher boost that stat would recieve. It also takes into account what kind of magic is being placed onto the stat, so placing something like... haste onto your speed stat would give it a massive boost. Casting spells equipped to your stats would cause that stat to lower, due to a smaller stack being there now, so you might end up finding a use for many spells you'd never even give the chance in other FF games.
I've personally only played FF4, 5, 6, and 7 (as well as this game), but I find this manages to be my second favourite, even beating out games I have a nostalgic feeling for. A well-written and interesting story, wonderful soundtrack (even though I think this port has a different one, but I haven't heard the original), and a cast of characters I ended up warming up to the same as the protagonist. If you haven't played this, I strongly recommend you give it a try if you're into "turn-based" RPGs, since it was a wonderful experience for only $12.
