Honestly, if there was a neutral option I'd use it. However, there isn't, and I decided to lean against recommending this game, if only because I feel that, while not bad, the game is certainly highly overrated already.
You can read some 12,000 reviews raving about how awesome this is, so let me summarize here why I'm not recommending this game to all my friends like 96% of the other reviewers would have me do:
- Gameplay: standard action platformer, really. You gain some extra abilities as you progress; however, they are almost all direct upgrades to a special skill you can perform. To my knowledge, there are no sidegrades (at least none that you get in the first 11 or so hours - I haven't finished the game yet), and all your core abilities and attacks remain the same. The enemies get harder, of course, but since your stats increase too, I haven't felt much of a difficulty curve. There are select few special enemies that can be interesting to fight, but they are found seldom and between each notable encounter, you're going to have to kill hundreds upon hundreds of grunts, super grunts, tough grunts, grunty grunts...
- More on gameplay, but regarding the platformer aspect: it really isn't the focus of the game. As such, while there are some instances of interesting level design, most of it just functions as terrain for the fighting. ...And now you see my problem: since the fighting (at least on non-hard difficulties) basically involves repeating a perma-stunlock combination of moves over and over until everything on-screen dies, there isn't much to do in this game.
- The story: ah yes, the story. It's what ties the game together; what makes plowing through waves of grunts worth it, to get to the boss battle and get a cutscene and get on with the story. Unfortunately, the story, as far as I have seen it, is highly cliche. I can't really comment on the entire main plotline, since I haven't finished the game, but here's what I have seen:
- - - You start in some sacred clearing in a random forest, with amnesia. What an original plot device! I'm sure the game won't be about the main character trying to regain their memories while getting mixed up in a quest they don't understand helping people they don't know, which is actually very much tied into what the character did before losing their memories, only to emerge changed and a better person than they were before!
- - - Oh wait, that's exactly what happens.
- On the same note as the story, the sidequests are all extremely cliche. You know the usual model of the protagonist just going around, having everyone unload all of their worries on him, and then going to find various monster loot, misplaced keys, and random trivialities that really have no consequence whatsoever in the bigger picture? Yeah, that's exactly how every single sidequest in this game is like. Back when Zelda et al. did it 20 years ago, it was fine, not only because the technology of the time didn't allow anything too complex, but also because a) this particular format hadn't been beated to death yet, and b) there wasn't really much precedent for better quests, so there was nothing to take example from. But this is a 2013 game, it can do better! Or, apparently, not.
- This was made by a single person. While some people talk about how this has let them put their all into the game, unhampered by a marketing department or disagreements in the team, etc., in my opinion this also has a downside: there is a limit to the creativity of a single person, and I really feel like a second or third pair of eyes helping develop the game could have only made it better, and a lot of the aforementioned problems stem from this.
CONCLUSION: this game is alright. I got it at something like 90% off, and more or less enjoyed the 10 or so hours I put into it. It's definitely not one of those horrible indie games that seem to be built solely for marketing (and screaming "Look! I play games like Counter Strike, Left 4 Dead, Battlefield, Team Fortress 2, Half Life 2, and the like.
These are first person shooters that: require reaction time, make you feel empowered, require strategy, manage your supplies, and make the threat of occasional death fun.
F.E.A.R. is all of these, similar to many other FPS games, in my opinion, especially Half Life 2.  The game features a slow-mo, and gives you a lot of supplies and health.  The AI is smart enough to occasionally flank properly, and pop up unexpectedly.  When you die (likely due to a grenade or explosion, as nothing else seems to kill me), you feel like you deserved it.
The story too, nicely compliments the game.  It's a simple story that lightly waves away why there are so many enemies, and while you are able to pay attention to the story and pick up the intersting nuances, it does not detract from main draw of F.E.A.R., the gameplay.
If you are not an FPS fan, this is a fantastic example of the FPS genre, and liking this game or not would make an excellent metric to compare to other FPS games.

A good concept ruined by poor execution.
All dragons, while unique in appearance are all very similiar. Each dragon only has two attacks, and almost all of them have a standard breath attack. So really dragons only have one attack that is different from another dragon. The way they tried to fix this, was with weapons. Equipping a weapon will give your dragon two more attacks depending on the weapon you equipped. The problem is, this doesn't make things more unique, it makes them more stale.
Say you and another dragon have the same weapon equipped. Well now you and that dragon only have one unique move between each other, and he's a completely different dragon. This is made even worse by the fact that there is no item shop in game. Dragons scale with levels, thats it. So while you might do good damage to an enemy DPS, theres nothing you can do to help you damage against a Tank, or if you need more HP to survive, theres no way to get it.
Speaking of "no way to get it", thats what I have to tell you bout a dragon you might want to buy. You see, you don't just buy the one you want, oh no, you have to get lucky and play whats basically a slot machine and hope you get lucky. Oh you got the one you want you say? Well guess what, dragons actually have different levels outside of the game that make them stronger. So while you may have gotten that awesome Gemtalon I, he's nowhere near as strong or awesome as Gemtalon III.
Its a watered down moba, aiming to cash in on the popularity of dragons by locking them all behind a slot machine and hoping you spend a bunch of money to get one, before you realize the game isn't deep enough to warrant spending money.

Ultimately this was not rewarding for me. If there was a demo, I'd have quickly dismissed this without buying the entire game. Clearly the rhythm mechanic of pushing up/down/left/right is of interest to many, given the number of positive reviews, but it's nonetheless lost on me.
I enjoy rogue-like games, in the Dead Cells sense...and I enjoy the fun of learn, die, repeat. But the learning in this game consists of dancing around and into monsters with particular movement patterns in order to hit without being hit back. Movement is inherently limited by this design, and I found no "aha" moments where some particular pattern or combination was particularly fun to execute.
Contrast this with other rogue-likes where one is rewarded, especially in the beginning, with new and interesting tactics and options to explore and find a playstyle that fits and rewards the player for their own creativity.
Sadly, such is not the case for this game, due to the nature of the limited mobility and incessant pulsing beat that feels as if it is playing you.
Would very much like my money back so I can risk it on something else in the rogue-like genre.

Now... I might be blinded by nostalgia, but I'm about 100% certain I'm not when I say this: Final Fantasy VIII is one of the BEST Final Fantasy Titles out there. The music (although in the original PC format which is said to be lower quality) is to die for, gorgeous and immersive Nobuo Uematsu makes you dive into the world and its conflicts with just the feeling of the music. From intense fighting music like 'Force Your Way' to the calm and majestic sounds of 'Blue Fields' and 'Find Your Way' the music throws you into the perfect mood for which segment of game you're on. Futuristic colorful city? Expect some electronic sounding wacky music that makes you feel upbeat but on edge, venturing into this unknown area. Going into a cave? Get ready for some calm music that makes you think: Where am I...? while also giving you hope to keep going.
Now onto another part of Final Fantasy, the combat, yes its turn based and has limit breaks, but all new mechanics are added in, Input Commands, Guardian Forces, A limit break system that goes on your HP instead of a bar, the Magic and Draw system are all changed and new, other than that you have your ATB and turns just like the usual pre-Final Fantasy XI. The input commands are similar to those of Super Mario RPG but only work with 2 of the 11 playable characters one who is temporary and the protaganist, Squall, during your swing you hit the 'Trigger' to fire his weapon, a Gunblade, to deal 1.5x damage, a simple rythm to get down and not too complicated, you can ofc put this on auto to make the game do it for you. Guardian Forces are the new summons, instead of using them as a spell they're their own action like 'Summon' from FF VII, they take a bit to come out and during the summoning time you will see the Guardian Force's (hereby refered to as GF) name go over the character who is summoning it, the GF will absorb any and all damage that is sent to the character at this time, shielding them for awhile. This also means they can be KO'd just like your party members, so it dosen't mean you can just spam them in fights you shouldn't of gone into and win, you'll just be drawing it out. I will discuss the intricate/menu workings of GF further down, this for now is the combat basics.
Next up the Limit Break system, Instead of having a bar like that of FF VII that fills up by accumalated damage, needing a higher amount for stronger attacks and the like, FF VIII goes by a roll depending on how low your HP is in contrast to your Max HP, so a low HP character is much more likely, if not certain, to get a Limit Break while a full health character will have little to no chance to get one. This allows for you to play a 'high risk high reward' style of play if you wish, keep your characters at low and do more damage, or keep them healthy and have no fear of being killed. The choice is yours, and finding that perfect combo and times to let yourself get low and when to be max HP. Now there are also Inputs on Limit Breaks as well, Squall's Renzokuken will have you pull the trigger on each attack, much like his basic attack, then usually follow up with a high powered attack, Zell's Duel will have you doing quick inputs with the "Up, Down, Left, Right, Select, Decline, Menu, Talk" buttons, giving you a limited time to get in as many inputs as you can or do a combo that finishes in a mighty blow, Irvine's Shoot lets you choose ammo from your inventory then give him special or normal shots from his shotgun to blast the enemies away. Each limit has strength's and weakness and some require no effort or items out of combat to learn, or even just walking around to teach them, overall the Limit System is very fun, although exploitable, but it dosen't take away from the game at all.
Now for the contradictory stuff that make a lot of people turned off about VIII, the Draw system.
In this Final Fantasy Magic costs no MP, since there is no MP. Instead you 'Draw' the power of spells from either places of power or from Monsters and Magitek-esque machinery, this allows you to 'Stock' your magic into a seperate inventory for each character, allowing up to 100 of one type at a time, you can then 'Cast' your magic when you need to, either by using the enemies magic reserves or your own, if you use your own it depletes 1 from your 'Stock' every cast. You can also move Magic from character to character, meaning if you want your mage to have some more Meteor instead of your hard hitting attacker you can move it over to them and easily rearrange your magic menus. Yes at first this system is very awkward to new players, its a huge change from the Materia of VII or the Magic/Jobs of V, but it also opens up another realm of oppurtonities: Junctioning.
Now for the number one thing no one ever understands about this game and they put it down. Junction. So I will try my best to explain this so you can fully enjoy the experience of this game.
Junction is when you take the GF you acquire and put their powers on a character, This allows them to use abilities such as Magic, Draw, or Summon their Guardian Force(s) they have junctioned, any character can have as many GFs as you want, there is no limit, want to put every one on one guy? Sure. Want to space them out so you have an even playing field across your characters? Go ahead. But! Each Guardian Force has a set of abilities, some that increase their stats, some that increase yours, and some that give you new abilities. When you Force Junction a Guardian Force they will give you the ability to Junction Magic onto your stats, meaning if you have Ifrit Junctioned you can now Junction magic to Strength, increasing it and making your attacks stronger, now the more magic you have of that type, and the more it corresponds with the stat, the higher bonus it gives, meaning 1 stack of Meteor will not give as much strength as 100 Stacks of Fire. Both are offensive, but since they do not have that stack to them they do not give the full effect. Now there is tons of junctions of Magic, From changing your Strength, HP, and Magic, to making your Weapon have Fire damage and allowing you to Absorb Poison and Frost damage and turn it into HP. The downside to this: If you use the magic you have junctioned to your character you decrease its influence on the Stat, meaning if i have Meteor Junctioned to magic at 100 stacks and it gives me a ton of magic damage, but I use Meteor to attack every turn, it will decrease in power due to me Losing stacks on the stat. So its a system where you have to Decide: Do I junction my strong magic here and not use it in combat, making my weaker spells up to par but keeping me from massive damage, or use the stronger magic and put a weaker spell on the stat, making it a ton weaker than it could be. Also, you can literally Junction Magic to any Stat, Hit chance, speed, SPR, VIT, Evade, all of that once you get the proper abilities for it. One other thing, just by having magic junctioned it will NOT decrease in its amount, meaning if I have Ultima attached to STR and Attack, I will not be taking a stack from Ultima, I will just be doing a Physical attack influenced by the Spell.
I hope I explained that correctly. And you might be wondering, Whats the point?
Well, Monsters level up with you, meaning they'll always be on par with your characters, no matter where you go, so you need the extra Stats to combat them, which is where the Magic System comes in, and the Junction System, Stronger enemies means stronger magic so yes, there is reason to level up still, since Firaga on STR is a helluva lot better then Fire on STR.
Now to the main part, the Story.

Pros:
1. Great ship designer. Actually, I would say that this is the best ship designer around. It has an even better UI for building than Gal Civ 2.
2. Somewhat unique tech trees for each race. However, I found Gal Civ 2's trees were far more unique than these trees.
3. Fairly easy to grasp gameplay. And, the graphics are pretty good.
Cons:
1. AI cheats. Even on the low difficulties, the AI still rampantly cheats. They did this because the devs were incapable of actually programming more competent AI during their "grand AI update." Nope, instead they just gave the AI tons of bonuses that varied based on the difficulty level.
2. Combat is still rock - paper - scissors. Chaff stops missiles, shields stop beams, and armor stops cannons. However, chaff does nothing against beams or cannons. The same with the other defense types as well. This was a gripe with Gal Civ 2 as well. However, the devs decided to give enhancement modules that gave certain bonuses to specific weapon or defense types. Which imbalanced the game even more and made this combat system even more focused on 1 weapon vs 1 defense type. Which, brings me to my next point...
3. Weapon balance is terrible: The devs tried to differentiate between weapon types even more. However, the rule of thumb is that missiles have the most threat but are also the largest, beams are middle of the road with 100% accuracy but also with insane upkeep costs that can't be reduced via tech, and cannons are the smallest weapons and rival missiles in actual combat power compared to missiles when massed together, except they are the most costly to build. So, the best weapons, hands down, are still missiles. The game has no balance.
4. Threat system is borked. The devs added threat modifiers to weapons and weapon enhancements. This is used to dictate how "powerful" your fleets are viewed by the other races. However, it's all completely borked as it's not balanced at all. The rule of thumb is, go missiles (despite not being actually more powerful) if you want to have the highest threat. However, it's really meaningless as the AI cheats so much that they spam tons of ships extremely easy.
There's many more cons that I could go through, but I view these four issues as the major issues with this game.
Edit:  Just tried patch 2.0 to see if it fixed any of the issues listed above.  The definitive answer is "no".  AI still spamming ships out much faster than the player even on the easiest difficulties, combat is still rock-paper-scissors, weapon balance is still completely terrible, and threat system is still borked as well.  To add to that, they included an administration system that punishes players that like to build lots of star bases.  This was to combat people who spam tons of economic starbases around their planets for overlaping bonuses.  However, instead of taking the logical way and just disallow overlaping bonuses, they decided to add administrators that punish everyone.
This game is done.  There are faaaar better space 4x options out there that have faaaar less bugs and stupid features implemented.  Hell, even its predecessor, Gal Civ 2 is a far more superior game than this tripe.

One of my favorite games of all time. Something about this game just draws you right into it. I never liked the Final Fantasy series as a kid and didn't find the appeal but one of my friends persuaded me to try FF7, and I reluctantly did, but never regretted it. Don't be fooled, even though this game is nearly 20 years old now, it is huge and has tons of content. There's a reason it took 3 discs on the original Playstation version.
All of the main characters draw their own unique story and make you want to help their cause. The game starts out slow and easy, at first I didn't think it was going to be good, but once you get out of the starting area and unlock the world map, you'll quickly find why this game is so good. The areas, characters, and soundtrack all work together in a perfect way to deliver a very impactful story.
As for the graphics and other technical details of the game, you have to remember that this game came out in 1997. Keeping that in mind, this game still looks and sounds amazing. The port to PC works great and has never crashed on me or had any issues. I do recommend a controller as that's just how the game was designed to be played, but even with a keyboard and mouse you can complete everything just fine. Using a controller adds to the nostalgic and original feel of the game, which boosts the experience though.
100% recommended to anyone who is into old or classic games and like RPGs or to anyone who likes the other games in the Final Fantasy series. The story does not have any stale points and keeps you wanting to complete it all the way through! If you're planning to get the remake for Playstation 4, I recommend trying the original before or after you play that one so you can get a better feel for what FF7 is about.

I really hesitated on this one as I no longer trust the developer. I loved GCiv II but the final expansion was never completed, almost all AI persnalities were broken (2 worked), the tech tree was broken etc. Most people never realized this simply because they didn't get very in depth into it. Hardcore fans did though, and ended up having to overhaul/fix the entire game, tech etc. through modding. Unfortunately, the AI was still severely lacking in differences/depth since only 2 were useable and the community was unable to fix that.
That said I loved the previous one, and wanted this one bad but didn't get it until now (on sale 73% off with all DLC). It's pretty much everything the second was, but with active development. I see a lot of reviews saying it's not as good, but I have a realistic memory of the previous and this is an upgrade. Plus with active development for the period it's had basic things like tech trees work and were not abanoned entirely. This is better than Galciv II.
The big negative for me is the game crashes, a lot. I'm on a gaming rig i7 etc. etc. and usually ignore the "I have a new computer and this game crashes a lot" type of reviews as generally anyone that says "new" rather than their specs doesn't really know better. I never really have issues when people make such comments. This time it's different, there are a lot of crashes. Hopefully that gets fixed, but for now as I don't play multiplayer it just means I'll have to make sure autosave is set frequently. It doesn't destroy the game, just makes it a little frustrating for me anyways. With frequent saves and an SSD it shouldn't be a huge issue, but should definitely be addressed.
TL;DR
Thoughts
-Developer has a history of not completing what they start, this made me wary of even purchasing the game I really wanted. Rather than wary, I am now a little worried with the crashes.
-This dev has a very poor history with their AI. I haven't gottten far enough in to judge it yet.
-Haven't tried Stellaris, initial looks are that it's an incomplete game, so I can't compare it. Very limited in genre competition though.
Pros
-Upgraded Galactic Civ II in active development, which in itself is a great game. 100% worth getting but only when the entire bundle is heavily on sale.
-Much more content than the new MOO.
-Much more of a playable game state than Endless Space 2.
Cons
-Frequent crashes (not so bad with SSD and frequent saves if you stick with single player).
-Every update is DLC, crashes really need to be addressed though. The history of the company really makes me uncomfortable on this one. The DLC total is very steep, who knows how far they'll go with it.
-If you do get it and want to stop being forced to build ships, there's a hard to notice little checkbox at the bottom of shipyards saying "Don't notify me when queue is empty." (Interface is very unintuitive in general)
Overall I reccomend it due to the lack of competition in genre, and because at heart it is a good game. The price is way too steep on anything less than a 70% off bundle though.

The most important things:
Is Stellaris fun? Yes.
I like 4X games, should I buy it? Yes.
I haven’t played many 4X games, should I buy it? Probably not.
Ok, now lets begin.
This is a review by and for someone who has a lot of hours logged in 4X games. If you don't already like 4X games or know what I mean by 4X, then Stellaris is possibly not for you and there are better entry points to the genera. I suggest starting with the Civilization series before coming back. As a 4X game Stellaris is a mixed bag. It adds some things to the genera, but it also flat fails on some things the genera mastered a long time ago.
The Good:
What Stellaris does well is Tone, Theme, and Story(s). An area where this genera far far too frequently just phones it in. This is where Stellaris shines. Leaders and Ethics add a great deal of imaginary frosting to the everyday tasks of expanding your space empire. The event chains and the stories they tell were entertaining. The late-game crises and fallen empires were genuinely terrifying when they first popped up. It was a very refreshing experience, and I hope future 4X games step up to this challenge.
Mechanically I like the sector system, but want to see it more limited (like restricting a sector to the same planet limit as your core worlds). I like the random tech system. The basic game mechanics are nothing to write home about, but acceptable. There are some balance issues, but there will be patches.
The Bad:
While Stellaris does well with Tone, Theme, and Story, where it fails is that the vast majority of these things have only a token impact on the game mechanics. So you’ve chosen to be a militant atheist and your neighbor is a religious zealot. They hate you. Thematically great. Mechanically they were going to hate you anyway because you decided that you wanted some of your other neighbors stuff, because that’s the only reasonable way to expand. Everyone always hates you.
I love the leadership system for the fun little game of managing my cohort of cronies. Mechanically the bonuses they provide are only OK. And excepting survey vessels, if you don’t hire a leader for the entire game, nothing bad will happen.
And finally, the game is slow. Very slow. I’m that type of guy that built a custom map in Sins of a Solar Empire with 5 max size galaxies. I don’t mind a grind so long as i’m having fun, but Stellaris is REALLY a grind. I have something like 40 hours in Stellaris at this point and all that is all ONE GAME. And I’ve only got only perhaps 1/5 of the galaxy under my control and some fallen neighbors who could totally steamroller me. Not even close to winning yet.
The Ugly:
The interface and visual design (no joke intended) commit some major faux pas for a game of this genera. Notably by making you scroll through your overlay rather than keeping information nice and compact, clutter up icons in the play field, and have no reasonable find or filter functions. 4X games are in no small part information management games because there are so many things going on in them. And while the interface is well suited to an early game, by even the middle of the game i’m finding myself spending way too much time paused and scanning the screen for an icon or scrolling through a list of 40 items where the window only displays 3 or 4 at once. The interface looks great, but it simply is not good enough for a 4X management game. That the interface needs to be tight is something other 4X titles learned and mastered a long time ago. And this is my biggest gripe because it’s the itch that never goes away, and only gets worse over time.
Overall I’m enjoying the game, but will be looking for mods to help alleviate what problems I came across. At this point it is not going on my best games list, but there are definitely some sweet things I want future 4X games to take away from Stellaris.

In RA:3 there's 3 playable factions,the Allies,The Empire of the Rising Sun,and the Soviets. Each faction has it's own powerful commander-like unit. The allies have Tanya,a demolitions specialist that can one shot most ground infantry and can sneak inside vehicles or buildings to one shot them from the inside with C4.Tanya can also use her special belt to warp back in time to regain lost health.The Reds have Natasha,the greatest sniper in the Soviet Army,and she uses her sniper rifle to line enemies up and shoot through them all at the same time.She can also paint vehicles or buildings with a laser and have a bomber come by and one-shot them. The Empire of the Rising Sun has Yuriko Omega,a badass psychic in a schoolgirl outfit who can use her powers to instantly take a unit out of the fight permanently.She can also use her AoE attack and instantly kill units around her. Every faction has their own unique units and almost all of them are super fun to play around with. The allies have these helicopters that can each freeze one enemy unit and keep them there indefinitly stuck in cryostasis until the helicopter is destroyed.Each faction feels unique and varied and this makes the game incredibly more interesting and fun to play.
In case you didn't know,before games used incredible CGI cutscences they used FMV (Full Motion Video). These were played with real actors and personally I think they look way better than the cutscenes of today but that's besides the point. The FMV scenes in RA:3 are superbly done and add so much to the atmosphere of the game,making it feel significantly more real. These scenes actually make you understand the characters and the situations better and that helps out the gameplay and the story both.
Each faction has a singleplayer-only set of general powers. These powers can sometimeseffect battles greatly. Undertale, “the friendly RPG where no one has to die.” When a game makes you feel bad for killing monsters and makes you consider not killing any more, then it definitely does something right!
Story
The story goes that both monsters and human once ruled over earth, living together, until war broke out between the two races. The humans defeated the monsters and drove them to the depths of Mt. Ebott, trapped with a magic spell. You appear on a bed of golden flowers, and are greeted by a flower, and taught about friendliness pellets. Afterwards, you can choose to massacre every monster you meet, or choose to show mercy to your opponents. Your actions of killing or mercy will shape the way the game progresses, as well as how others view you. The dialogues, and even the music of the game will become happier or distorted based on your killings or acts of mercy. With that said, there are a few endings that can be achieved within the game, some being more satisfying than others; some feeling like you are cutting onions, and some just for the cold hearted. What makes these outcomes to impactful, and sometimes sad, is the way the monsters react to the player’s actions, and sometimes questioning your actions and making you feel like a monster for the things you do. This is also true when you do immoral things like take more than one candy from a bowl of candy that says “take one please”.
Gameplay
Gameplay is very easy to catch on to, and is like one of those old time rpg games like Earthbound. Your goal is simple, but complex, just get through the game(through any means necessary). Your initial goal, or why you are there are not stated, but you can assume you fell down the mountain (as seen in the opening). Your real goal is to play the game as you like, exploring this unique world of monsters and see what it has to offer. While you explore the world, you will have numerous random encounters with monsters, in which you are a heart that must avoid monster’s attacks, and will die if you take too much damage (causing you to restart at your last save). Pretty easy to understand and play, but a bit difficult to master, as some of the later encounters will be a lot more difficult to dodge seamlessly, and may prove to require a bit more thought and endurance to overcome, rather than just one lucky turn. The game itself is not too difficult, in that it does not have any difficult puzzles to do, and no grinding is required to win the game, as the game can be beaten without killing a single thing.
Visuals/Audio
The visuals are all a bit old timey, but that does not take away from the experience. As for the audio, there are a wide variety of songs that make the game very fun while in combat scenarios. The beginning music was a bit new to me, as I did not think it would have the old retro type of music, but it surprisingly worked well and was not monotonous, and seemed to match the backdrops, and battles very well.
Characters
Why would I include a characters section in a review? The answer is, because they are such an integral part of the game, otherwise it would be like any other rpg, with the exception of the option to spare your opponents. The characters are what make this game so memorable. It’s not the fact these characters are super likeable, since you may end up disliking or even hating some of them, but the fact these characters will end up growing on you in the end. Without such a unique and hilarious cast of characters, the player would not feel any real motivation to spare them, or any remorse if the player decides to kill any of them. They are in all respects to this game, the driving force that makes it so popular and why it causes many (if not all) it’s players to shed tears.
Verdict: 9/10

This is, to my mind, the best Command & Conquer game out there. Some complain about the blatant fanservice with respect to the use of well-edowed female actrices in the hammy videos, while others believe that Red Alert 3 has gone too far with respect to the silliness inherent in the series (i.e. the use of war bears by the Soviets and the mecha-inspired units in the army of the Empire of the Rising Sun). To me, all that stuff is simply silly fluff that shouldn't be taken seriously.
What should be taken seriously is the gameplay. The game is a refined version of the Command & Conquer style of real-time strategy game: a simple economy (you build powerplants to power your structures and harvest ore to get money to buy more buildings and units) with an emphasis on the spectacle of battle. Units are fragile, so expect many of them to be destroyed more or less as soon  as you encounter enemy forces. Hard counters are used, which means that some units, for example, have no defences against air units, or are weak against certain types of infantry, and so forth. This means that reconaissance is as important if not more so as in other RTS games.
Red Alert 3 is more micro-heavy than most of the other games in the series. Each and every unit has a toggable special ability (hotkey F), and use of these special abilities will prove essential in most battles. Combined with the speed at which units move and their fragile nature, this means that games can get very hectic, very fast. It's for this reason that I mostly avoid multiplayer: I know that I won't be good enough to compete anyway. Instead, I stick to singleplayer and it's loads of fun.
The game has three factions and each of them gets their own campaign, with each campaign consisting of nine missions each. The different factions are the Allies, the Soviets, and a new third faction especially developed for this game, namely the Empire of the Rising Sun (essentially Japan). The Allies emphasize their air power, while the Soviets field relatively sturdy ground troops and can spit out a lot of units. The Empire is a high-tech faction with specialized units (remember: F is your friend!) and probably the most difficult to play by newcomers. The leaders of each of these factions are played by well-known actors: Vincent Pryce, Tim Curry, and George Takei, respectively.
I've put many hours into the disc version of the game before buying it anew on Steam and do not regret a single minute that I spent playing the game. The campaign is entertaining and can also be played fully in co-op mode. If you don't have any friends, an AI will take over. The AI sometimes really helps out during missions, but more often than not simply forms a distraction that the enemy AI will occupy itself with while you build your base and reinforce your army. If the campaign is not your cup of tea, you can always play skirmishes against the computer or go online (there is a replacement out there for GameSpy, so the online component does still work, thanks to the fans).

If ever there were a game I wished you could give a thumbs sideways to, it's this one. I'm not recommending it mainly to counteract its current "very positive" status. Because many of those reviews are ssimilarly hesitant.
I like it. It's good. But like many people, I was hoping for more grand strategy in space. What I got was in many ways Endless Space but tweaked. It's really, on the whole, quite a simple game. If you've played any 4X game, you understand 95% of the systems in Stellaris. And it is a 4X game, not a grand strategy game, and a not particularly complex 4X game at that.
There are no dyanstic mechanics, the variations in races aren't nearly enough, superficially or mechanically, as they diverge.  Diplomacy isn't fully fleshed out, federations and alliances are far too limited. There are maaaaaaaaaaaaaany bugs. Alien races all seem to contact you telling you they're establishing embassies with themselves when they mean with you, events are constantly filled with placeholder text and missing entities.
I won't go too in-depth on all the problems or even LIST all the problems, as that woudl take a while - it is a big game after all. But to further elaborate on one of the big ones: you can form alliances and federations with other races. This is the most basic thing they could do, really. Alliances are just, "Hey, we've got each others' backs, so step off." That's it. Nothing else to them. In fact, they actually LIMIT your diplomatic options with alliance members.
Federations are the next step. They're the UN. Except there are no resolutions to pass. The president rotates. They can declare war and design a new federation ship. And that boils down to, "Oh, I'm the president. WE'RE AT WAR WITH MY NEIGHBOR; I WANT THEIR♥♥♥♥♥♥"
There is no way to change rules and regulations for federations. You can't be a peaceful or warlike one, forbidding instigation of conflict or demanding contribution to a federation fleet, for example. You can't change the rulership style. There's so much potential, but it ends up so frustratignly limited. Your federation ends up being whatever the rotating president at the time wants it to be. This works a bit better in multiplayer, I'm sure, but♥♥♥♥♥♥ who has the time for that. Not me. I play singleplayer. I have a job.
In addition, bugs and missing features aside, some of the features that do exist are just silly. You need to occupy a planet to get someone to cede it. Sort of makes sense in theory, but... why? Isn't bombarding it from orbit kinda enough? Especially if the enemy is desperate for peace?
On the whole, it's a disappointing game, but not unfun, and it's a solid base. With modding support and, hopefully, Paradox's general tendency to provide big, worthwhile updates, fixes, and DLC, it will be worth buying and playing for many many hours a year from now or so.
As it is now, don't make my mistake. Be patient; wait for fixes and more content and more mods. Play or replay Endless Space. That's what it makes me want to do right now.

Honestly, if there was a neutral option I'd use it. However, there isn't, and I decided to lean against recommending this game, if only because I feel that, while not bad, the game is certainly highly overrated already.
You can read some 12,000 reviews raving about how awesome this is, so let me summarize here why I'm not recommending this game to all my friends like 96% of the other reviewers would have me do:
- Gameplay: standard action platformer, really. You gain some extra abilities as you progress; however, they are almost all direct upgrades to a special skill you can perform. To my knowledge, there are no sidegrades (at least none that you get in the first 11 or so hours - I haven't finished the game yet), and all your core abilities and attacks remain the same. The enemies get harder, of course, but since your stats increase too, I haven't felt much of a difficulty curve. There are select few special enemies that can be interesting to fight, but they are found seldom and between each notable encounter, you're going to have to kill hundreds upon hundreds of grunts, super grunts, tough grunts, grunty grunts...
- More on gameplay, but regarding the platformer aspect: it really isn't the focus of the game. As such, while there are some instances of interesting level design, most of it just functions as terrain for the fighting. ...And now you see my problem: since the fighting (at least on non-hard difficulties) basically involves repeating a perma-stunlock combination of moves over and over until everything on-screen dies, there isn't much to do in this game.
- The story: ah yes, the story. It's what ties the game together; what makes plowing through waves of grunts worth it, to get to the boss battle and get a cutscene and get on with the story. Unfortunately, the story, as far as I have seen it, is highly cliche. I can't really comment on the entire main plotline, since I haven't finished the game, but here's what I have seen:
- - - You start in some sacred clearing in a random forest, with amnesia. What an original plot device! I'm sure the game won't be about the main character trying to regain their memories while getting mixed up in a quest they don't understand helping people they don't know, which is actually very much tied into what the character did before losing their memories, only to emerge changed and a better person than they were before!
- - - Oh wait, that's exactly what happens.
- On the same note as the story, the sidequests are all extremely cliche. You know the usual model of the protagonist just going around, having everyone unload all of their worries on him, and then going to find various monster loot, misplaced keys, and random trivialities that really have no consequence whatsoever in the bigger picture? Yeah, that's exactly how every single sidequest in this game is like. Back when Zelda et al. did it 20 years ago, it was fine, not only because the technology of the time didn't allow anything too complex, but also because a) this particular format hadn't been beated to death yet, and b) there wasn't really much precedent for better quests, so there was nothing to take example from. But this is a 2013 game, it can do better! Or, apparently, not.
- This was made by a single person. While some people talk about how this has let them put their all into the game, unhampered by a marketing department or disagreements in the team, etc., in my opinion this also has a downside: there is a limit to the creativity of a single person, and I really feel like a second or third pair of eyes helping develop the game could have only made it better, and a lot of the aforementioned problems stem from this.
CONCLUSION: this game is alright. I got it at something like 90% off, and more or less enjoyed the 10 or so hours I put into it. It's definitely not one of those horrible indie games that seem to be built solely for marketing (and screaming "Look! I'm a new and innovative indie game, unhampered by the conventions of the gaming industry, and I'm definitely not a poorly-executed cash-grabbing attempt!") and not actual entertainment. But if it's not on sale, I still think it's not worth the money.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a story-driven, side-scrolling hack and slash.  The unconventional cartoon art and the lack of complexity in combat mechanics may drive away the average gamer.  I was certainly filled with skepticism as I began the title, but was quickly drawn into the comedic drama inside this lively and vivid world.
The game had an old metroid feel as I traversed through different frames of the 2D world in all four directions.  And in true metroid fashion, there are places that are unreachable without movement power-ups acquired in later stages of the game. The world, is split up into different zones, both optional side-quest zones and mandatory main-quest zones.  Each zone had its own personalities, colors, and feel.
The unique characters in some zones, which to my surprise had fantastic voice acting, brought life to the game.  Sure, they were fantasy cartoon creatures, but they felt human.  Even as I followed the linear quest line tied to problems in the fantasy world that I cannot possibly relate to, I felt connected to the characters' struggles, feelings and values.
There are little things that the game delivered well and others that could be improved upon, but the big thing that this game delivered is the main moral issue presented in the story.  The drawn out dialogues allow the player to emotionally invest in key characters in both the "good" and "evil" side.  Even though the ending made a clear distinction of good and evil, the parity in my mind was not so decisive.  I questioned my own morals and imagined what kind of background the "evil" side had, to drive their radical actions.
Overall, this game was a pleasure to play. I apologize to the creators for not going through all of the content, as I skipped most of the side-quests.  This short installment of Dust's adventure is simple, indulging, and was a pleasant surprise.

FEAR is a decent old school shooter with a good plot, impressive atmospheric effects, a satisfying weapon arsenal, and a decent implementation of bullet time into gameplay. On the downside, the levels are the most linear I've ever played. The first door you can open is usually the one you need to go to. While the game seems to suggest stealth, the reality is you can only stealth kill the first enemy you see--the others instantly go on alert. The enemies were also pretty forgettable except for Alma herself, though the "bosses" you face in the game and the two expansions are invariably suits of powered armor. Don't expect Crysis-level detail from the engine. FEAR was already a bit dated when it came out. On my computer it was clunky but playable. I don't want to make this review sound wholly negative--I grew up on old school shooters and this is one of the best. Just wait for a sale--$9.99 is a bit pricey at the moment.

I've played this game for like 10 hours now the first day I purchased it. Clearly I must like it.
You have a good reason to like it too. This game reminds me of EVE Online only in an arcade format. There is a single player mode and a multiplayer mode.
In this game you are a space adventurer struggling to deal with the aftermath of a disasterous war where your part of space is cut of after the Federation (no relation to Star Trek) destroys a stargate leading back to the heart of intersteller civilization, surrounded by a scant number of merchants, fellow stranded space adventurers, and aliens and pirates who want to kill you.
This is a sandbox game. Yes you are given quests to do to earn currency, but you get to do what you want. You buy better ships for combat, exploration and mining, making sure you got the best weapons and devices snapped on. You loot destroyed enemies, or you get looted if they destroy you. There are three play modes, the first one (I'm familiar with) is you respawn after you die but you lose your loot. The last one is permadeath where you really do need balls of iron, because when you die, you die.
You get to play in a faction, each one has advantages. There are six if memory serves. The single player mode stores a galaxy you can set the size of with a slider. I haven't tried multiplayer only because I just got the game. When I play multiplayer, I'll update my review.  Even if I hate multiplayer it won't change my recommendation because the single player mode is worth the money paid alone, with or without the discount.
The ships you get to play range from small fighters to large warships but they cost money and, if you are an EVE Online player like me, you really need to fly only what you can afford to lose. While the hulls are limited to what you can slap on for hardpoints, there is room for some customization at the device part and some hardpoints allow either a beam or a ballistic weapon.
You get to customize your character you play, gender, hairstyle, skin color, eye type, nose type, mouth type, accessory...it's limited but I'm sure the devs will add more choices...yes, that was a hint.
There's a class and skill tree where you can tailor your character's development as the character earns levels. You get to choose a class, miner, combat, etc, with some of the basic skill points aready filled on, and then as you level you earn skill points where you can allocate to parts of the skill tree, like efficiency in energy usage for firing weapons and shield operation, or tracking weapon turret time. If you played EVE Online this is going to be familar to you.
The ships move similarly like EVE Online's propulsion physics, meaning there's no Newtonian mechanics here. You coast to a stop after you end propulsion, of which there are two, RCS thrusters and main engine. In this game you move directionally using the W A S and D key and laterally using Q and E. Ships use a form of fuel which is converted to energy that is then used to power weapons, defense systems, gadgets and so on.
The game may crash in singleplayer mode from time to time but because it autosaves when you go from system to system, or dock, it's not a big inconvienence.
Recommendation? This is a beautifully visual game where every control and menu makes sense being where they should be. It does not require a killer graphics card and even old laptops can play it with the tweaking of the graphics controls. Buy it. It's a fun space romp in a desolate galaxy where anything can happen.

I love Dungeon Defenders, it's an amazing RPG/Tower Defence game that I would reccomend to any person who enjoys strategy games. I was extremely excited when I heard about Eternity coming out, but when I got it, I felt slightly disappointed. The reason for this is that this game didn't really have much to offer. Of course, I do enjoy the new items and mechanics, extra maps, and having every character availible without having to buy DLC is always nice. But I feel like this game should have been just downloadable content, rather than a game on its own. One thing I don't really like is how you join maps. I would much rather select a group to join from a list then wait in a queue. That's one reason that I feel this game should just be DLC. The option of a queue would be nice to have, but I wouldn't want to have to be in a queue every time. I would prefer to just have the option, along with being able to join games like the original Dungeon Defenders. But the biggest complaint I have, is that this game has absolutely no tutorial whatsoever. Playing the game for the first time, I had no idea how any of the new mechanics worked, and I hadn't played the original in so long, I needed to refreshe my memory. Eternity lacks that though. I consider myself a veteran Dungeon Defenders player, and even I was confused at first. I would hate to have somebody completely new to this game be totally lost, as it doesn't even explain the mechanics of the game that were in the original Dungeon Defenders. I understand this this is meant to be an expansion, but it needs to explain how the new things added to the game works. Despite these flaws though, Dungeon Defenders Eternity is a great game for those who have already played Dungeon Defenders and want a little bit more, or newcomers willing to do a bit of research about the game. Any strategy lover should play this game.

In modern parlance Paladins would be described as a free-to-play "hero shooter" - that is to say, an objective based, co-op only, first-person shooter where, rather than your avatar being largely defined by the gun you pick or the items and abilities you equip, they're already fully formed characters with their own unique, pre-defined abilities and specific roles.
There are several modes to play, but the main thrust of the game is Siege mode, which sees two teams of five charge to the centre of a map and try to hold an objective zone. While there's a lot of nuance to the mechanics and conditions of play, the fundamentals are this - capturing an objective zone to spawn a payload earns your team one point; escorting the payload to the enemy base earns you another point; but if the opposing team manages to successfully prevent the payload from reaching their base within a set time, then they earn the point. First to four points wins the match.
Characters, or "champions", technically fall into one of four different roles - front line; "tanks" made to take punishment and hold the objective - damage; made to dish out said punishment - support; primarily focused on healing - and flank; who are all about being sneaky-sneaky and harassing the enemy from behind. I say "technically", because, even though that's how they're labelled in-game, most champions can bleed into a couple of roles to varying degrees.
One important thing to note is you can't change champions once the match has started. So if you're part of a terrible group of players who wouldn't know how to create a decent team composition to save their life, then you're kinda screwed and more or less have to endure a horribly unbalanced game where a team lacks any real cohesion and synergy. But to help with this to some degree are loadouts and items.
Every champion has a deck of sixteen cards that are unique to them, and during your time outside of matches, you can construct your own loadout based on five of these cards which boosts the effectiveness of their abilities. Items are like temporary versions of cards that can be acquired mid game but are only applied for the duration of the match and bought with credits earned during play. And finally, there are Legendary cards, with each champion having three of these but needing to commit to one for the whole match. These are cards which apply a massive bonus to one of your abilities and can make your champ highly specialised in one aspect of performance or another. But this is where you have to be really careful, as choosing the wrong cards or items could make or break how a match goes.
This is actually one of the most ingenious features of the game, I think, as it allows for a lot of strategy and means the player with the best aim or reflexes won't necessarily be the victor. In fact, one of the things I love so much about the game is how accessible it is to so many different skill levels and styles of play. If you just want to do the shooty pew-pew thing, there's plenty of characters that'll have you covered there. Maybe your aim isn't so good but you have a keen sense of timing and situational awareness, in which case healer might be the role for you. Or maybe you just like being a stonkin' great big tank throwing your weight around at the centre of it all. There's a little something for just about everyone.
But the real star of the show here is the ever increasing cast of colourful, creative characters that somehow manage to all play massively differently from one another. Both the design and artwork really shines through, and is topped off with great animation and largely top-notch voice acting. There's an abundance of detail in every aspect of them, whether it's some little nicks and scuffs on the side of a firearm, or even the motions as they actually fire and are reloaded, or just the way a character moves around and performs each of their abilities, or even how they idle. There's a real sense of love and attention that's very clear to see, and that extends to every aspect of the presentation both throughout the UI and within each of the many maps as well. And, if anything, this only seems to be getting better as more and more interesting and creative content is being released with admirable and impressive regularity.
As well as all the artwork (I don't think enough credit goes to the card art in particular, while I'm at it) I think special mention has to go to the audio as well. Sound is very important in this game as every single champion has their own noises, from the sounds of their abilities being activated, to their main weapon being fired, to the stomps of their feet. If you listen out to what's going on around you then there's an awful lot of information to be found just by keeping your ears open. At any given moment you'll likely be able to tell exactly who's firing, roughly what direction they're in, and probably even how far away they are. A lot of players probably aren't even consciously aware of it, but it's always there and making a huge difference, more so than just about any other game I can immediately think of.
It's not all roses, though, as the game does have its fair share of problems. Personally, I think the damage feedback is desperately in need of improvement. Having the very outer edge of the screen momentarily turn a faint red hardly seems adequate in the heat of combat, and at this point I've lost track of the number of times I've died without even knowing I was being attacked in the first place. But a bigger issue than that is the matchmaking.
I wouldn't go so far as to say it's broken, but I'm only a few more bad games away from calling it that. It feels like it's becoming increasingly hard to get games with consistantly matched players of equal skill, and 4-0 stomps are becoming more of a thing lately - which are never fun, no matter what side of them you're on. The rating system, on the other hand, I think at this point I can call broken. In Competitive mode, both your individual champions and your overall account ratings are awarded or docked points based on whether you win or lose, and then (presumably) used to calculate further matchmaking as it attempts to queue you up with players of equal skill. The trouble with this system is, it seems so focused on the bottom line win or lose result and has little bearing on personal preformance. As a result, you could play the best game of your life, but if you were teamed up with bad players, or someone on your team was disconnected or there were heavy lag issues, the game doesn't really care and will still deduct you for it. It's really not fun when you feel as though you're being punished regardless of your own ability or contribution, and as it stands right now, my own personal rating for both my account and many of my champions are in the toilet despite my consistant above average performances. And the worse thing is, that effect only seems to be confounded with time, as it takes multiple wins to make up the points for a single loss.
Also, due to recent changes, the grind for new players seems a little rough going. Cards need to be unlocked through a random loot chest system or bought with "essense" from duplicate cards, which could take a while and doesn't exactly encourage new player experimentation. Although, to its credit, it's nowhere near being pay-to-win, and I think Hi-Rez are generally pretty reasonable, and maybe even generous, with its current financial model.
I mentioned the build version at the start because this is a game that's constantly changing. It's worth pointing out this was a very different game a year ago compared to what it is today, and some or all of what I've written could be completely irrelevent a year from now, for better or worse. But if it does change, I really hope it will be for good, and that I'll still be playing it and loving it just as much then as I do now.

I can't tell you how many times I have played Final Fantasy VII. It is perhaps my favorite Final Fantasy ever, and I know many will agree with me. There is a reason why they made several other games and a movie based on the Final Fantasy VII universe.
- Cut-scenes still look good
- Game-play still great
- Story still holds up (it still excites me even though I know what will happen)
- Oh my God, the music
- The materia system is so incredible. It is so fun and rewarding to experiment with different materia combinations. It is by far my favorite magic/equip system of all Final Fantasies
- Plenty of side-quests, side-stories, mini-games, and collectables
- Some extremely challenging boss-fights
- Plenty of little glitches (none that are game breaking from what I know)
- All those polygons (old graphics)
- Turn based battle system - don't get me wrong, I really enjoy the system to this day. However, many magic/skill animations (especially summons) take a lot of time, are unskippable and ruin the flow of battle.
- Damage cap at 9999
- It can be difficult for new players
I understand that it can be difficult to convince someone to buy Final Fantasy VII. For me, it's main selling point is the nostalgia. If you have no emotional ties to this game, it's basically an old game with a dated turn-based battling system. However, if you are willing to give Final Fantasy VII a shot, you will not regret it. The story is captivating, the battles are exciting, the world is vast, and the materia system is magnificent. I guarantee over 30 hours of old-school goodness.

Very fun game, even though it hasn't aged well.
Final Fantasy VII was one of the first RPG's I've played (next to Super Mario RPG), so nostalgia has a big factor in this. I feel like there are better Final fantasys out there, such as VI, IX and XIII, however, this one is great too.
To get the negatives out of the way - the story is very convoluted. In order for me to truly understand it's plot, I had to read several forums to understand it all. Not saying the story is bad at all, it's really great, but super confusing and at several points left me feeling like I had no clue what happened or how any of that made sense. Additionally, the character development in this game is weaker than other games. Some characters develop wonderfully, but there are points where it feels like entire personalities change.
Negatives aside, there's a lot to love with this game. The story is addicting and and epic (confusing points aside), the side quests are truly one of a kind (you get to breed and race chocobos!), the materia system is fun (but a little too simple), and the characters are for the most part enjoyable and understandable. The main villain Sephiroth is okay, he's not as cool as Kefka from VI, but felt like at times there just wasn't enough proper motivation developed with him. And Cloud is okay too, but I honestly prefer Lightning from XIII than Cloud, who were both pretty much the same character from the start.
If you're looking for a starting place for the Final Fantasy games, start with this or IX.
If you're new and want to know what the fuss is all about, the steam port is fantastic.
If you want to see what JRPG's had the biggest impact on the genre, play this or VI.
If you want to satiate the nostalgia urge inside of you and relive the glory days of playing VII for the first time, all I can say is I wanted the same, and I leave very, very satisfied.

This game is everything it has been advertised to be.  It is a fantastic space strategy simulation.  The perfect mix of RPG elements into a strategy game brings out so many hidden gems to slobber over that I can hardly do them justice with a simple description.
As an avid Sci-Fi reader, what impresses me the most is how well read the Paradox Interactive team must be.  The Sci-Fi tropes from all the classic novels, all the best of so many different worlds and minds are spread lightly across the top like salt on some perfectly fried french fries.
-Robots and a possible AI revolution.
-Uplift Species from mere planetbound life to sentience and the ability to travel beyond the stars.  As your true companions or as your genetically engineered slaves.
-Find planets of pre-spaceflight aliens and observe from orbit or become more "intrusive" in your scientific pursuit of studying alien culture.
-Grow Clone Armies in vats to fight your wars for you.
-Build a Slave Center and brainwash your alien slaves to fight as your invasion army.
-Be a friend to all and create a United Federation of Species to share knowledge and explore.
-Re-engineer your own species to adapt to new worlds, or terraform the worlds to suit your own needs.  Why not do both?
-Send you science ships to the far reaches of the galaxy and explore strange new worlds.
-Build massive fleets of your own design and pit them against your rivals.  Or simply use the auto-build feature.
There is so much to see and do I can't fathom the scale of it, and i've barely brushed the surface.  It will take me several hundred hours of playtime to really say I know the game well.

60 hours in and I only now feel ready to write a review. This is a great game; it has a clear tutorial when you start so if you are new to grand strategy or Paradox games, which I was, you still pick up the general gist of the game and how to play. The best thing about this game was every time I thought I had cracked it and was now the best Stellaris player of all time there was something new to throw a spanner into my Galactic ambitions!
Play this on the ironman mode, you can earn the achivements (if that is your thing) but most importantly it is more fun knowing you can't just go back and undo a bad decision; the excitment and thrill of knowing every decision has consequences adds so much to this game.
The mistake I made was going to big to quickly, try starting out with a smaller sized Galaxy if you are new to these games so you can get a better sense of the game and don't have to restart so often.
I do think the diplomacy could have a few extra options and depth but on a whole is still pretty good, I aslo think a vassal should pay tribute each month and there be an option to form union with them which isn't absorbing them into your Empire but perhaps becoming a council with them which has no happiness penalties and the more empires you add into your Galactic council of xenos the more difficult the bureaucracy becomes as when going to war or making diplomatic decisions you all have a vote.
The game feels different throughout early to mid to late game with some great and interesting side missions and random happenings to throw you of course, help you or even to give you something else to do. I did have to start again a few times with different customisation options before I could get into mid game in a strong position so don't be disheartened if the same happens to you as well. There is a vast range of customisable races; how they look, how they function, what their ethics are, what type of ships they use, how they travel through space, what they are called, how they react to the way you will play.
So this isn't too long I will end now by recommending this game even if you are new to grand strategy like I was (I have always loved strategy games but not really played grand strategy like this)

Pros:
- Extremely impressive combat AI
- Combat in general with the AI
- Good atmosphere most of the time
- Fairly good pacing
- Interesting plot
Cons:
- While the levels were put together well and offer a good spatial complexity, there is an attenuated theme and texture variety.
- Too much ammo (personal pet peeve :)
- Limited enemy selection. Aside from the basic replica soldier with different skins and HP/armor (skins look good), there are about 5 other enemy types: heavy soldiers, mechs, flying mechanical things that shoot lasers, stealth kung fu commandos, and ghosts. Minus the regular replica soldiers, all the other enemies numbers, individually, are in the single digits, save the ghosts, but youll only see them once.
- More environmental interaction would be preferable personally. You are basically limited to opening and closing doors, breaking things like glass, and pushing the button that advances the story.
I played this game through when it was released, but never got the expansions or sequals. I got the bundle of all of them on sale, and am glad I played through the original again. Being almost 10 years now since I originally played it, I can now really appreciate how good the AI actually is. FEAR's AI was revolutionary at the time, and remains as a high standard that few FPS games get to (mention some if you can, Id like to know of more games with impressive AI like this).
As the player, you are as vulnerable to bullets as the enemies, and more so on higher difficulty levels. To be good at countering the AI, a person cannot approach the enemies as they would a normal FPS, meaning you cannot charge into combat and hop around a lot, or jump out into the open with guns blazing, with a little adadadadadadadadad dancing here and there. Try that, and even on medium, youll get torn to pieces.
You also cannot wait for the soldiers to come to you; if you do, youll be waiting a loooong time. You must actively engage the majority of them as they use cover to wait for you.
Cover and leaning around corners is essential, especially on hard difficulty, and without question necessary on extreme difficulty. Expose your body for more than just a second (and sometimes not even), and youll take damage. Stay uncovered and in LOS to multiple enemies, and youre sure to die.
"Reflex Time", or bullet time, is slow mo that can be activated for short periods at will. It is not really necessary to use it unless playing extreme difficulty, but is a lot of fun at times, allowing you set up some impressive moves.
The combat AI and battles with it is where this game shines, and remains truly impressive, even a decade later. While there are some shortcomings to FEAR, the stellar AI mitigates much of their effect.
Highly recommended.

TL: DR version: get it because it is an amazing indie game made by one single person.  And the soundtrack.  Get the soundtrack as well.
The "I have time to read a short story" version:
What a beautiful game!  I got it through the Humble Bundle a long while back, and it was totally worth it.  There are some things that would annoy me usually, like some of the voice acting and a couple of the battle sequences.  However, I'm able to overlook anything like that simply because IT WAS DONE BY ONE PERSON.  ONE. FREAKING. PERSON.
He did such an amazing job programming and drawing the whole thing, absolutely a labour of love.  The backgrounds were gorgeous and varied, nothing was really repeated from one area to the next (ok, the spikes and the ground icicles are the same concept, as in ouchies to bump into) and enemies that move the same yet have different powers.
The story is decent, maybe a little cliched at times but has an interesting concept to it.  Dust can be funny, especially when speaking to the fourth-wall-breaking Figet (who is really quite funny).  Ahrah gets a little snarky as well at one cold, snowy point that made me laugh.
There are a bunch of side-quests to do that rely on your getting specific special moves throughout the game (a lot of revisiting), and it is a hoot when you get to see all of the "hidden buddies" in the Sanctuary.  Getting to them was challenging, sometimes rage-inducing (stupid final colour gem at the very end of the game....grrrr...) but worth finding.
The soundtrack is fantastic, and I listen to it often.  You actually end up finding the Hyperducks (the music composers) in the game!  They included "vintage" versions of some of the themes, which translates to "if they were for an arcade game" sound which is fun.
This game was incredible from start to finish.  I hope that there will be some kind of sequel later on, because...well...play it to find out!

I have to say that personally I loved VoidExpanse, a open world space exploration sandbox game.  If you want to be a billionaire miner...  dust off that monocle, if you want to be a pirate hunter, than arg matey, have at it.  If you want to fight off the hostile aliens Independence day style, get that cigar out and be ready to smoke it... The game is a top down shooter, you can move your ship using the W,A,S,D, or you can use the arrows keys, nothing too uncommon with that.
to bring your ship to a complete stop, very useful for trying to pull in containers, mine asteroids  or port with the various space stations.  The combat is a combination of frustration and exhilaration, you'll be frustrated as the limitations of the game's combat system and the gliding nature of your ship, it can take quite a bit of getting used to before you master. Questing, experience, and levels, you can acquire quests while docked in a space station, numerous quest exist, delivery, rescue, destroy, etc etc etc.  These quest will grant you experience, although quests aren't the only way to get experience, you'll get it from just about every action in the game, from mining ore, to fighting ships, you even get experience for selling certain ores.   The experience is used to level up, each level will grant you points, which you can use on skills..  Skills are the life blood of your character, they allow you to shape and alter how you'll play the game.
Many different skill combinations exist, it's best to thoroughly inspect and decide what skills best fit your play style, loads of different combinations exist, will you be a smooth talker who gets his way with non violence, or will you decide to let your lasers, missiles or chain guns do the talking for you, the possibilities are endless.  Going right along with skill customization will be your ship, you can outfit your ship with numerous different parts, want to travel further without having to return for fuel... buy yourself a new fuel tank, want to mine more ore before having to return to port and sell... get  yourself a bigger hull.  Feeling tired of getting picked on and assaulted by pirate ships.. upgrade those weapon systems and wreck pirates.  So many combinations of ship parts exist, from your lowly civilian parts to high tech military grade items.  What kind of ship will you build?
