VoidExpanse is a Top-Down, Open World Space RPG with a branching story line. With the ability to define how big your universe may grow, this game can take you quite some time to fully explore. As an added bonus, since the universe is procedurally generated, you will never experience the same universe twice in a row.
The game has a beautiful backdrop which can make each system look and feel somewhat unique. The character portraits being randomized for non-key NPCs also add a refreshing new feel to each replay of the game. The ships have enough detail and varietie for this style of art to make them visually appealing as well. The sounds are fairly standard, but they work fine for this game.
There are many different character options to choose from at the start of the game. You customize your character portrait as well as your starting Class. Starting Classes just give you a head start down their related Skill Trees, however as you play, it is completely feasible that you could max out every Skill Tree.
Skill trees are the games way of locking you out of content that would otherwise make you too powerful to start with. Luckily, early on it is easy to gain levels so you can quickly unlock better ships and weapons that you may need to progress. This system does have a bit of a drawback though. When playing through one of the factions, I was told I had to destroy enemy space stations using a custom missile that I was issued. This is where a major issue occurred for me. Since this was my second play through, I had opted to play as a miner/trader who operated a freighter. My freighter was only a middle tier ship that had medium pulse lasers. My ship wasn’t designed to fight and didn’t even have a bay that could support a missile let alone a level 3 one. It was simply equipped to defend against a single attacker or a few lower class attackers while making its escape. I had almost maxed out my energy weapons, Industry (mining), Social (trade skills) and my Piloting (to enhance cargo space and speed) skills. This meant I had not focused anything on the other weapon types or heavier hulls. I had bought myself a very heavy beam only Death Bringer ship for making runs into the Alien space and the heavy pulse weapons for it… but didn’t have the skills to fly it yet, was still working on that. At this point I knew I was either screwed or I was in for one heavy grind. I needed to be able to get enough skill points to unlock level 3 Missiles, heavier hulls and the money to buy the ship and everything I needed to equip it properly. I had to do tedious filler missions given by the random stations while doing mining runs to raise the experience and money required. Days later, I finally had my heavy ship loaded to the teeth with everything including my missile. This made blowing up those Alien space stations even more satisfying because of the effort I had to put in to it.
As mentioned, there are plenty of customization options for this game. There are quite a few different ships to choose from, each with its own loadout slots and statistics. It would be nice if there were a few omni-slot ships that let you customize it exactly how you want, but using the ones already in game works. There is an even wider assortment of weapons to choose from plus the critical ship systems and subsystems that can also be customized. The numbers of configurations you can make are almost limitless. This, along with the aforementioned procedural generation of the selectable size universe helps to make each replay unique. One feature I like is the fact that your character isn’t a miracle worker. If you find yourself a better weapon floating in the debris of the ship you just vaporized, you can’t just slap it on to your ship and fly off merrily on your way. You have to get to a space station and dock with it in order to adjust critical components of your ship. Really the only thing your pilot can do while out and about is to reload the consumable things such as hull repair or shield energy. This is a rather good decision on the Developers part as it adds realism to the game. It actually makes it a little more exciting to know that if you don’t survive the trip back to the nearest space station, your new found prize will be lost when you explode.
Why might you want to replay the game? Well after the introductory area, there are three factions all looking to take you in as a recruit. Once you determine which faction you want to join you can seek out their recruitment officer. The recruitment officer of course doesn’t let just anyone join, you must prove yourself worthy of their cause. This is where the story lines diverge. Once you are in a faction you will have to stick with that choice until the end of the game. The end mission will be changed to suit the faction you are a member of, be it to blow the aliens out of their part of the galaxy, find a way back home, or finding a way to pacify alien hostility.
Unfortunately, once you finish the starting area and do all the efforts required to join a faction, when you are really ready to get going, the game hits the home stretch and ends shortly after. This game relies on the fact you have to do the generic missions, hunt enemy (or if you are a jerk, friendly ships) and mine in order to gain experience and money. This works great early on but becomes a very heavy and barely rewarding grind in the later portion of the game. The deeper into the Alien territories you go, the heavier their resistance becomes. You will quickly find yourself swarmed with ships at a far higher level than you. Another issue I had is if you take a jump gate then look at your map too long, you will find a swarm of pirates zoning in behind you and almost killing you before you can move. Death is also unforgiving and what it takes from you is based on what difficulty setting you took at the beginning of the game when generating your universe.
Another thing that pads out gameplay is travel time. Often you will find the mission provider and the mission system are separated by a vast distance. You then need to fly there with the assistance of Jump gates to link systems together… but unfortunately there is not usually a direct route. You will have to pass through each system that separates you and your destination dealing with any hostiles that may decide to attack you. You also need to watch your fuel levels or you will find yourself having to limp home at a low speed.
Overall, there is plenty to do in VoidExpanse. It is a fun enough game that you might find yourself replaying it just to see how the story ends for each of the factions.

Even though the movie has been finished for a while, it finally made its way to Steam and has given me a reason to go watch it. Before I bought this movie, I saw a few reviews of the movie on Steam saying how disappointing it was and how bad it was. How exactly? James Rolfe and Cinemassacre did an excellent job with this movie and you could tell a lot of hard work and effort was put into this movie.
Plot: I'm gonna try to make this as spoiler free as possible. Basically the plot in a nutshell is that the Angry Video Game Nerd works at a knock-off of GameStop and there's a game company that's making the sequel to E.T. (the worst video game ever created). Because the new game is coming out, everyone is assuming that the AVGN is gonna review the game. But surprise surprise, he ♥♥♥♥ing hates that game and refuses to review it. However his friend, the Super Rad Video Game Dude, says if they can't find any of the original cartridges in New Mexico where they supposedly burried them, then he doesn't have to review the game.
What I liked about the movie: At first, I honstly thought the movie wasn't gonna be that great because it was a indie movie, it surprised me how well made it was. Yes there are certain scenes in the movie where you're like: "Oh wow. Gotta love that greenscreen," and "Is that a toy alien ship?", but it does work out really well on what it's trying to show. is a hybrid sort of RPG/Strategy with bits of Simulation mixed in that takes place in a sci-fi space environment.  The level of different options available right from the start would qualify it as a sort of open world or sandbox style even, on a fringe sort of level, but nonetheless it certainly would qualify as such.
I've had a lot of fun leveling up.  The skills seem very worthwhile to get, and it's hard to decide on what I would like to work on next.  Level requirements of future upgrades can help in determining the order I want to go in though.
I love the way the star systems are put together.  The combat is fairly easy so far, which I like.  Once I got some levels up, and better customized my ships.  Took time to get used to the ships too, but I am now able to use them fairly well, out of what I've tried thusfar.
I enjoy the graphics and the music is nice as well.  I find it relaxing, and it doesn't get on my nerves like some games can tend to do after playing a while.
Exploration has been a good thing too.  I'm still unsure how to progress, and which quests are more important for moving the story along.  They do seem to have symbols next to them in the journal.  Some of the "filler" quests are obvious, but they are good for the money and experience as well.
I would like a little bit more variety as far as weapons and ship selection.  Maybe more can come about in the future?  There might be more I haven't seen yet as well.
I think there are not enough types of quests.  You start to see the same "filler" ones appear again and again as you visit various star systems and base planets.
I wish I were able to keep track of where things were in my storage areas in different star systems.  It's something I've had a difficult time retracing, especially in a medium to large sized system.
I have seen a couple of small grammatical errors already, but they aren't too glaring, or anything so bad I cannot easily interpret what is being said, so I will sort of give a pass in that case.
Doesn't destroy the flow of the game, and I know I make my own from time to time, so not a huge deal.  I did notice a couple though.
I'd definitely rather have several saves to utilize, and not a single one that autosaves often.  I like going back and trying different things, so having a single save per game is sort of a killjoy for me, personally.
So, I started my first game as a prospector, and got a few missions at the base it starts you at.  I destroyed a ship and got some crates, and I was pretty happy about that!  I venture a little further out, and I see several red marks on my radar, so I figure I would investigate.
I was toasted pretty quickly, so I lost some stuff, which was a letdown, but I had it on normal, as I wanted to get used to the basics of the game, so not a huge deal...  Just had to pay some money to get my ship back in working order, and off I went again on a different mission.
Luckily, this one was a straight shot with nothing in the way, and I finished it with no problems.  Level up!  Picked my traits, then while choosing what I wanted to level, I noticed I had some nice skills in my tree for mining...  So of course, the idea popped in my head, and I got a little tool in the shop to mine stuff from the asteroids, and started doing that.  Was getting decent experience from going out and back again, but I didn't  have much cargo room.  Still the experience plus the profit was a nice little side job to work on getting better parts, and so that became my focus for a little bit.  I'm glad there are different options like this for somebody to do based on where they are strong or weak after starting attributes.
A little over ten hours in now, and I've had a lot of fun leveling up so far, and the selection of various skills has really augmented my gameplay experience.  Some are pretty important, and others are more related to ones playstyle.  I don't sense a hard cap for level, but maybe there is at some point.  So far it's not very tough to level.
I wish there were more variety in what you can buy, and the variety of random filler quests could use a little bit extra quests, instead of running into many similar quests that you quickly begin to recognize.  I've run into the same ones many times, and I'd like to see more down the road.
Despite having more cons than pros, the strength of the pros, and also the fact that I grouped some of the pros into multiple parts gives them an edge.  I am really enjoying this game!  I will probably continue on as neutral, and see where that takes me.  Maybe that has something to do with why I cannot figure out how to move along with the story.
Anyway, so far I highly recommend the game.  I enjoy the RPG system, and the other elements work well in conjunction with the overall gameplay experience.

Without a doubt one my favorite Final Fantasy games; FF8 sports an interesting leveling system unique to the series where the enemies level in power and skill based on your level.  This makes it so every location you visit, regardless of its original level, a challenge every time.  But this does not mean that you need to be on even ground with the monsters you are fighting due the interesting, and very strategic, Junction system.  This system allows you to use magic, and your summoned creatures to not only tip the field of battle but to completely throw it off and allow you to dish out massive damage, while at the same time turning you into a damage sponge.
Off the top of my head, I believe, the game has about 16 summon creatures called Guardian Forces.  These GFs work as an augmentation device, as noted above, but also serve a number of other useful positions.  With a GF attached you will be able to equip your normal system, items, summoning, and the most important being draw.  I’ll talk about that in a moment though.
And although the GF can equip these basic skills, at first, there is a medley of other things that it can equip as well, which would include stat buffs outside of the magic junctions, special attacks, enemy avoidance, the ability to turn enemies into trading cards, and many others.  Most of these skills are learned through fighting battles while other, more powerful ones, can be purchased at pet shops or can be found later in the game.
Now we move onto the magic system.  Again, it is interesting, different, and happily strategic.  There seems to be a little more strategy in this normal FF title than there seems to be in your average tactics game, but I digress.  Players do not have the ability to outright use magic, instead, they Draw magic from specific draw points or from any enemy in combat (tedious but preferred) and storing it for your junctions or using it.  I normally just kept them for the junctions since most bosses have something that will dump the scale in your favor (You can use and take whatever they can use).
A little added piece would be to always draw everything you can from every boss you find.  This will often give you powerful magic and hidden GFs.
Now above I mentioned that you could turn enemies into trading cards and this doubtlessly raised an eyebrow or two.  This is for the card game Triple Triad, a game found in this particular world.  Now normally I avoid these mini-games like the plague but this one actually has a useful purpose.  Aside from a few achievement unlocks, a good number of the many cards in the game will give you items if you use one of the GFs special abilities to convert cards into items or powerful magic.  The game itself is also pretty fun as the matches are quick and the rules and play-style change as you go to different places.  Also the rules and play-style of other areas will dynamically switch with others.
The story is interesting, it has evolving characters, aside from the obligatory emo lead character that Japanese games seem to love so much, and it will keep you invested and engaged along with some side missions and story tied secret bosses thrown in for a bit of fun on the side.
The big reason to play this game is for the strategy involved in it and how it will hook you just from the into movie.  And although it is a little dated for today, and some of the characters and story elements are sort of stale and overused in the genre, it really doesn’t pull too much on the overall impact of the game.  Final Fantasy 8 is still an 8/10.
It’s a really good game and should be a part of any RPG fans library.

I was instantly absorbed. I'm sure younger people won't get why so many older people go on about FF7, it isn't a matter of it being timeless exactly, though I still love the story. I think it's a matter of if you grew up playing video games in the 90's, this was just something else. There really had never been something quite like FF7. It wasn't a kids game, it was an over the top action title, it was serious and dark (relative to the era again). It had/has amazing music, a deep story and narrative, one of the most classic villains in gaming, one of the first and most powerful death scenes in gaming and had a great battle system. Again though, this was all for its time (Except for the soundtrack, it's still wonderful). By todays standards I'm not sure it compares so well, especially since RPG's have really changed in a lot of core ways, from combat to dialogue, it just doesn't work the way RPGs today do. It requires time, a lot of it, investment and interest. If you're the kind of gamer who just clicks through unspoken dialogue you should probably pass, if you play games in a hurry and don't walk around searching areas and talking to random NPCs, you should probably pass yet again. You get into FF7 to get into a story the way book worms get into a book, this is an investment on your end. You should celebrate the characters triumpths and mourn their losses. I'm sure that sounds silly to many, but that was the era of gaming this was a part of. We weren't CoD junkies who lived for point and click gratification, we wanted stories, and not the stories that our parents had, these were OUR stories, these were the new stories of our childhoods, we just didn't know it yet.

From the other reviews (at least, those that weren't inexplicably hung up on the gender and skin color of the default human faction leader), I expected Stellaris to be just Yet Another 4X, and a rather
one at that, but I'm addicted to the genre, so I bought it anyway. While it is by no means perfect, I was pleasantly surprised.
At its core, Stellaris is a solid and competent 4X game. There aren't really any big surprises, or groundbreaking game mechanics, but there are plenty of subtle differences which give Stellaris a unique feel. For instance, you can group individual systems within your empire into AI-controlled sectors, which the AI does a pretty good job of balancing, so you avoid the all-too-common situation where your empire is starving because each system individually decided to maximize its score by producing high-dollar strategic resources instead of food. Another example is how the diplomacy system requires you to define victory conditions in advance when declaring war, and how all members of an alliance vote over any decision that affects the alliance as a whole, such as a treaty or a war declaration. I also like the scavenging mechanic, where you can earn significant amounts of research credit by harvesting the debris of a defeated fleet.
But the most important innovation, to my mind, is the randomized research: where other games have a static research tree where each research topic is unlocked as soon as its prerequisites have been researched, Stellaris divides research into three fields (physics, engineering and society), and when you complete a research topic within one of these fields, you get a small and partly randomized selection of new topics to choose from. The topics you
choose may pop up again as soon as you complete the one you did—or they might not show up for another fifty years. This helps keep the game less predicable and increases replay value.
Now for the bad. Other reviews have lauded the game's interface, but frankly, I find it chaotic and wasteful of screen space. In addition, the game does not always auto-pause when you enter a UI screen or open a notification. You can easily become overwhelmed by the latter, especially in a war, where a couple of fleets rampaging in tandem through an enemy system while a science ship is scavenging the remains of the previous one could easily result in dozens of notifications per minute: one per fleet per battle plus one per debris field harvested. I've also had the misfortune, while playing as a democracy, of having a string of chancellors die after only a few months in office, because they were all roughly the same age when the game started; you can hand-pick administrators and military leaders, but politicians are controlled by the game. Finally, the 2D art, such as leader portraits or planetary landscapes, is frankly not very good (but bonus points for animated portraits).
On the whole, Stellaris is well worth the money, and it will be interesting to see what improvements and add-ons Paradox come up with over the next few years.

This early impression (given its a paradox title) is aimed specificly at fans of EU IV (as I am) wondering whether they should get stellaris. Please bear in mind that this is no full review of stellaris.
The game starts out much more like a civilization game than an EU game. You start with a singular solar system, scout you surroundings, meet enemies and neighbors, build mines to collect resources and send out colonists to expand your empire. Sounds familiar? You also develop technologies along a tech tree, have random events and kill pirates (think barbarians). Even the classification of your race (spiritual, industrious, militaristic, pacifistic ...) reminds me strongly of civ IVs classification of leaders.
Now, I am not saying this is civ in space. However playing stellaris to me has a lot more in common with said titles as any paradox title I know. It starts out pretty simple and straight forward. You start on your own and for the first years you are pretty much expanding without much trouble. After all, your competitors are more or less on your level of power, technology and resources. The amount of micro management grows proportionately to your empires size, which means after a while you'll be busy managing all those planets. Eventually you'll get into conflict with a neighbor who, depending on your play style, may have little more or less military power than you.
The point is, that this is a pretty fair game. Everyone starts the race more or less equal and your success largely depends on your system mastery. Even the fact that success is a thing (I dare you to define success in EU IV) makes a massive difference. There are traditional win states such as "have the largest empire" or "kill everyone else".
EU IV in contrast is a completely unfair game. Whether you start as mighty France or little Albania (if you're insane), the game is never balanced. Some nations are doomed from the beginning and making it to the year 1821 for them is a major achievement. Other nations might strive for world domination.
I like stellaris and I'm sure I'll get my money's worth out of it. But for me something is lost in the balanced race to supremacy. EU can be impenetrable with its interface and its complex systems. It can be cry out loud harsh when apparently out of nowhere an alliance rises against you. But setting my own goals, playing as a super power or a tiny monastery fighting against the odds is what keeps EU interesting to me. I don't see how stellaris can do the same.
I hope these impressions help to set expectations for the game correctly. I will update this text if I find that I was wrong or have further remarks.

Garry's mod has been a game I've stuck with for quite some time. I've had several pleasant experiences with this game, spent many days in servers hanging out with friends and companions and enjoying the diversity of the game modes and different modules you can experience in the workshop and the server lists. Garry's mod though isn't inherently entertaining. You have to be prepared to download plenty of server content and add-on content to enjoy it. It doesn't have a story, but with a little love and coding practice, you can make one for it yourself.
PROS:
*A wide, diverse range of game modes and experiences that tend to be unique to each player due to the unpredictable and spontaneous nature of each server.
*Open source, built for the sole purpose of having programmers and designers to go in and modify/create their own masterpieces.
*Good compatability between modules and scripts that would usually break the game if conflicted.
CONS:
*Get ready to download. This game relies almost entirely on your ability to download assets and workshop content to enjoy what it has to offer.
*Unpredictable servers could lead to miserable experiences with toxic staff/players
*YOU WILL NEED ASSESTS FROM SEVERAL ORANGE BOX GAMES INCLUDING CS:GO. You can either get these resources through paying for the games in Steam, or through some other method that I don't condone as I think developers should be paid for their works. (That and CS:GO is essentially a staple anyways.)

X4 space empire games are really hit and miss, and getting a good "feel" for galatuic empire building while not drowning someone in info or drugery is a delicate balance.
Stellaris has some very well thought out features that aid you in feeling like you have "just enough" control over your empire to run it without having to over micromanage (there is some micromanagement, but its not constant and not always something you need to do).
A good example of this is research.  Your empire comes up with projects and you are presented with options for research from three main scientific branches: engineering, physics, and sociology.  You dont get to look down a tech tree, you have to pick major research projects from what your scientists etc come up with and steer tech that way. These picks are enfluenced by your peoples traits.  Like militarists come up with more weapons tech to research than say frontier clinics and diplomatic philosophy for helping newly colonized planets).  if you pass on something it will likely come up again, but how likely is it that plasma dichargers are going to be pushed again by your say pascifist scientists in the next 10 years.
I enjoy the look of this game, and the UI (some have said they have difficulty with it, but honestly its probably just new to them and the tutorials fault for being so light weight...which isnt a bad thing tutorials can be a turn off in games like this if they are heavy handed).  The art is cool, and the varierty of species and other visuals is really nice.  I love how the game creates random species so you dont just run into the same cookie cutter races in all your games.  Ideals and ethos can change for a species and empire aswell, so you can directly help to shape/change other empires and species.  I won a war against a religious crusading race and as part of the treaty to end the war freed the closest two star systems from their empire and got pacifists of that empire and species as neighbors.  Not everyone wanted the war species wide.  I like that I didnt have to genecide them and return them to the stone age.  Even though I could have.
Story telling is a thing in this game, and events can be empire threatening (or saving).  These challenges and plot goals unfold to keep you on your toes and provide you with choices that can change the face of your empire.
Combat is interesting and isnt quite rock paper scissors like some other reviews claim that I have read.  More that diversity is your friend and becomng tacticaly inflexible as a race is dangerous.  There are counters to all the tech I have seen thus far, and your ability to adapt to what you face with what you have is huge (you might not get say point defense for countering missile boat enemies for a while or you might get it right away.  Dont assume a time frame (although most basic tech will be presented to you in the early game, but sometimes its not something you have time to research at that time).
The game does have a learning curve but its totaly doable, and its actually fun to learn as you go.  If you have questions about how stuff works they have a wiki and you can find all kinds of guides all ready for this game.
Bugs:  I have found basicaly one so far in 32 hours of play, and I am not actually sure its a bug.  I had an underground empire generated under a planet I colonized but its profile was a futurama joke about "filthy neutrals".  There was a note in the description stating that this profile was to be replaced by a full functional one, but they must have missed it before release.  So all I could do was say hi or declare war against them.  As it turns out some of them fled to the surface as outcastes and I got myslef a free new species to my growing empire that was good at ground combat.
All in all I have loved how this game plays, and I look forward to Paradox polishing it up (small things like being able to retrofit an orbital defense platfrom left behind from a previous border threat etc. ).

VoidExpanse is a interesting space game with RPG nad open world elements thrown into the mix. For a open world game like this, you would want there to be a lot to explore and stuff to find. VoidExpanse does that, with the open world freedom that this game delivers it really gives you a lot of freedom to explore.
This game seems to have all the right elements that a open world, RPG game should reallly have. Massive areas to explore at your own free will, there is no limitation or blocked off sections to limit the open world experience of this game. There is so much to explore, the amount of quests there are in this game is sure to keep you playing for hours upon hours. There is a extensive and impressive upgrading system in this game, which also ties in with the huge amount of researching that can also help you along whilst you play this game. The fighting in this game is pretty basic, with simple mechanics that you will have gained, weapons, armour, and sheilds. The sheilds and some of the weapons use a yellow energy bar, weapons such as lazers will require you to use energy to shoot. The bigger and more powerful lazers in the game will require more energy, and therefore you may have to wait for your energy to recharge after battling a few enemies. On the other hand, you can use weapons such as missiles and guns which use there own supply of ammo. Although I found that you would run out of ammo for missiles rather quickly, and would have to dock at a nearby station in order to restock your rockets. There does seem to be a multiplayer mode built into the game, although it seems that you can't bring your ship from single player into other servers to play multiplayer. This isn't much of a problem, as playign the game single player doesn't really limit or change much when you have a couple of others helping you in multiplayer servers. At first this game doesn't really seem to be a grind, you are happily just accepting quests, completeing more and leveling up as you play along. But it does seem that after a while of playing this game, it just becomes more of a grind to level up to gain skill points that you want. The missions do start to get boring, as they seem to repeat themselves with recon missions and exploring astroids and such.
The overworld itself looks very space like, with all of these galaxies that you can see in the background as you drive your ship throughout the world. The background images are quite dull and some of them really nicely constrast with the dark background. Each area you visit doesn't feel the same as before, there is a rather nice variety of different colours and backgrounds throughout the game. The graphics of each of the ships that you can get are rather nice looking, some of them have a nice light at the back of the ship which sort of glows behind you slightly as you fly around space.
+ Open world
+ Different types of weapons
+ Single player & Multiplayer story mode
+ Nice graphics
+ Trading cards & achievements

This game is an extremely enjoyable platformer with RPG elements and beautiful eastern-style visuals. A lot of love and care has gone into crafting a fantastical world populated by a myriad of anthropomorphic creatures and beings, who are brought to life through a wonderful combination of visualised emotions and superb voice acting. The cream on the proverbial cake is the music, which often changes to suit the "mood" of the level or situation and can be very emotive.
You explore this world as Dust, a humanoid wolf warrior, accompanied by his trusty (and sometimes annoying) sidekick, Fidget. Puzzles are simple but enjoyable. Dust can execute a variety of attacks, earn XP and gold, find and equip items and assist the various denizens (read: complete quests) that occupy this strange but exciting world.
As you level up you earn gems (skill points), which you can use to increase various stats (health, attack, defense, Fidget). Gold can be spent at shops to buy items and materials, which in turn can be used to craft items. Items conists of consumables (usually to regain health), equipables for stat increases (such as rings), and augments to enhance your weapon or Fidget.
Combat is smooth and fluid; the game utilises a "combo" system with colourful numbers popping up all over the screen, but without cluttering or obscuring your vision. There are a variety of enemies with different abilities to defeat, including boss fights. However, if you want a challenge, the game must be played on the hardest difficulty.
The story is well written and compelling. There are moments both happy and sad, serious and light-hearted. As the story progesses Dust learns more about himself, and the player learns more about the world he lives in. The often cruel nature of the story is juxtaposed with both humour and bright, colourful visuals.
This game is absolutely fantastic and I highly recommend it.

is a top down open world space sandbox game. You play as someone from the Far Colonies who flees from a farm world on a civilian spacecraft, but who that character really is, is up to you. The plot of the game relies on the fact that the Far Colonies are abandoned, after a hostile alien race is discovered. Therefore, it is up to you to fight this threat, if you choose to do so that is. One thing that surprised was the fact that even though this is a simple, yet good looking 2D game, ti has a very detailed video options menu and separate audio sliders, which is a big plus in my book.
Before being thrown into the procedurally generated universe of VoidExpanse you’re able to create your own character. The game offers a good variety of options such as, hairstyles, accessories and other facial characteristics to customize your character portrait You also have the option to choose one of 9 different classes such as Prospector, Trader, Rogue and Adventurer, each one having their own unique starting bonuses and preassigned skills.
Upon entering the game, if you go on the Character tab you can see your character experience points and skills. Here, you can also access the following categories: piloting, combat, social, industry and engeneering. Each one of these categories has its own unique skill tree which is also affected by the profession you choose during your character creation. That said, I’d recommend you to take your time and examine these and determine which kind of role you want to play. You can be a pirate, a trader, a miner, how you embrance this open universe is entirely up to you. Different skills will have very different applications, some will allow you to persuade certain characters and avoid conflict, others will improve your piloting and mining skills, while others are just required in order to use better gear.
Right next to Character tab, you also have the System Map which is very easy to navigate. It allows you to see the various planets on your current system, asteroids, enemies, space stations as well as jumpgates. It also allows you to set your own navigation points which you can use as destinations for your autopilot. Beware though, your autopilot isn’t smarth enough to avoid pirates and other dangers so make sure you’re actually paying attention to the game while you’re taking advantage of this very helpful feature.
Next up, if you go on the Star System Map, you can see different systems connected by jumpgates and also see each factions territory. If you go to the Factions tab you can see what kind of relations each faction has with one another. There are a total of 6 different factions, including the neutral faction. Each one of these systems has their own characteristics and some might have special events such as gas clouds or debris from past conflicts. Here you can also see each system tech and danger level. The higher the tech level of a system, the better items you can find there and the danger level of a system will affect how difficult are the enemies there.
Of course, as with any space sandbox game, you also have your lovely inventory. Here you can check what items you currently have and see what different modules you have equiped. Still, the only items that you can equip outside a space station are consumables, such as mines and repair kits. Modules such as an engine, generator and shield require you to be inside a space station. It is also on the inventory window that you can check your cargo, this is where you’ll hold various types of goods such as ores and food.
Once you enter a space station you’ll be able to refuel, repair and check various sections of the station. On the hangar you can change your ship parts and on the shop you can buy and sell items. The type of items that are for sale on the shop vary depending on the type of station you’re in. If you’re on a military station you’ll get access to more military gear and if you’re in an outpost you’ll get access to more ships. However, the type of items you’ll find in these shops also depends on the Tech level of the system. Finally, you can also go to the station decks. Here you’ll find people from various factions and their reactions towards you will depend on your reputation with that faction. Most importantly, you can take missions and talk with them. You can ask them about the various different factions, about events and locations, thus gaining some background information on the events that are taking place or that previously took place.
If you pick up a quest you can check it on your Journal. Here you can also see failed and completed quests. Any progress made within a certain quest will also be shown here as well as the dialogue and story behind it.
The overall gameplay is really fun. You move your ship with W, A, S, D, Q and E and you aim with your mouse. Combat is in real time and hip movement and maneuverability is really important here, because weapons on ships have an arc of fire and so, you should try to keep yourself out of the enemy range. This allows for some sort of agile combat that requires you to keep both your ship moving and your weapons aimed towards the opponent at the same time.
Flying around on your spaceship and fighting enemies requires you to keep an eye on some key things. Your ship has several meters such as energy, shield and structure, as well as fuel which is pretty self-explanatory. The shield bar obviously represents what percentage of shield you currently have on your ship, if this reaches 0 you’ll start taking structural damage and if you manage to not get hit during a certain time, your shield will eventually recharge. The energy meter on the other hand acts as if it is your stamina bar. Firing weapons and mining, for example, uses energy so you can’t just spam your weapons and have to time your shots correctly. That said, you’re also required to be at a full stop when mining, and the same goes for when you’re looting a container dropped by an enemy.
Combat and movement aside, the game pretty much plays as you want to play it. You can attack friendly vessels, you can hunt down pirates or any other faction or you can just make your fortune by mining asteroids and selling the ore at a nearby space station. You can help characters and join a faction and help them achieve their ultimate goal, or you can just ignore everyone and just do your own thing.
I HIGHLY recommend this game to fans of spacefaring, space sandbox and space sims. If you enjoyed games like SPAZ or Space Rangers I’m sure you’ll have a great time with VoidExpanse!

Locoland is a retro indie game about the world of steam trains from wonderland and our opponent who has stolen our most precious diamond, The Golden Gear. The game is a combination of Tower Defence/Strategy Tactics. You always need to analyse the situation with the opponent and take the best way to get through the mission.
So I'll descrive you the first three missions. You start the mission with a locomotive + two gun trains and you need to be fast with your decisions. In the war of trains you need two things - the factory and repair building which usually is near the starting point. At first you need to build your gun trains from the money you start the game with. The locomotives are also important cause they power the trains. After you have some army you can go into some battles to destroy the opponent or just some of his trains. In every battle you can lose your trains so the repair building helps you with war damages. The factory is building trains at the same time so you can therefore connect them into repaired group or attack the opponent from other side. You need to remember - your opponent is building trains at the same time and he can attack you as well. Besides destroying the opponents army you have to destroy the factory/repair building in the opponent's base (if he owns that).
The game is therefore about who is the strongest on the map. There are 20 mission points and every one is different. The money you have in the game is a static number for every mission. I discovered one way to earn extra money - you can destroy the passenger train which is neutral in the game and sometimes drops the money. You need to know that some of the missions doesn't have factory and repair building :) After every mission you're calculated with the points earned in the battles.
To summarize, it's a enjoyable game which will lead you to many thinking hours on how to pass that train and complete the mission's objectives :)
What could be better and fixed in the game:
* in the game you are introduced into the storyline but there's no tutorial to get to know the controls - they're listed in options
* sometimes it's hard to see the trains when they're behind the environment. It would be great to see border of the hidden train
* if you create a lot of trains, highlighted is only the selected one so it's hard to discover the connected/unconnected trains when there's many of them
* the game uses the maximum resolution of 1024x768. I'd recommend creating windowed mode for that small res
* i have only 23 FPS while the GPU's usage is about 10%.. weird?
* alt+tab makes the game unplayable
* if you own double monitor - moving the mouse outside the game window gives the same effect like with alt+tab; but also when you get out of game, your opened windows are confused :)

What is F.E.A.R.?
--
F.E.A.R. is a classic first person psycho-horror shooter, with a fluid bullet time mechanic, and a number of phenomenal jump-scares.
--
--
Who would most enjoy F.E.A.R.?
--
The game is a bit dated now, but it has aged decently. It's not a particularly action packed FPS, though it's far from dry in that department. Where the game really shines, however, is in keeping the player constantly wondering what might happen next. It's packed full of ambient tension, and just enough jump-scares to keep you constantly on the edge of your seat. It's a fairly challenging game, definitely not for the light of heart, but if you're looking for a rush, and can get over the dated engine, F.E.A.R. is definitely for you.
--
--
Over-all: 70%
A solid game. Worth playing through for sure, especially if you plan on playing the later titles in the series. F.E.A.R. holds its own as a ground-breaking title in the psycho-horror genre.
--
Mechanics: 3/5
The mechanics aren't perfect, but they serve the needs of the game. Mobility is slightly cramped compared to most modern shooters, but the fluidity of the bullet time experience definitely compensates in this regard. Despite the clunkiness, it's not enough of a weakness to distract from the fantastic immersive experience the game provides.
--
Experience: 5/5
The greatest strength in F.E.A.R. is it's ability to pull the player into the game. Despite the dated audio and visuals, the game still manages to immerse the player to a degree I haven't experienced in a long time. The audio mixing, though dated, and overly simple, is fantastically orchestrated. Ambient static, strategically placed, and dissonent instrumentation instill a very desirable sense of paranoia. Headphones are definitely recommended. Some of the dialogue gets a tad redundant and obnoxious, but can definitely be overlooked, given the phenomenal work done in the other departments. The visuals are painful at times, especially during cutscenes, but during the actual gameplay, with the bullet time effects at play, and the visual interruptions that are part of the psycho-horror theme, you almost completely forget all of this. The game is visually dated, for sure, but still manages an incredible depth of immersion, adding tremendously to the experience.
--
Balance: 3/5
The fight blance is pretty poor over-all. Some fights are far too difficult, especially if you've run low on ammunition or health kits due to a string of accidents. That being said, this does add to the tension at times, which is great, as long as it doesn't become frustrating. The AI is good enough. It's simple by today's standards, but it's not dumb enough to be noticably distracting, and that's more than enough in this case.
--
Longevity: 3/5
The game itself is 21 missions long, each ranging between 15 and 45 minutes (though you could probably speed run some of them very quickly). There is no immediate replay value, but if you give yourself a few months or years to forget the specifics of the game, it's likely you'll enjoy a second play-through at that point.
--
--
Expansions:
--
Extraction Point: Extraction point is a decent expansion. I would not recommend it, however, as it distracts from the fantastic finale' F.E.A.R. leaves you at, which, incidentally, is where F.E.A.R. 2 picks up. That being said, it's not bad enough to suggest not playing, if you're really interested in the series, beyond just the experience. There are some great, fights in the expansion, and while the over-all quality is slightly lower than the base game, in my opinion, it still provides a few new twists and plenty of lore to keep you entertained. The finale' of Extraction point does a poor job of explaining itself, and is slightly baffling, but the adventure there is possibly worth it.
--
Perseus Mandate: Perseus Mandate is over-all, a terrible expansion. It plays more like a poor action FPS game than a psycho-horror, and drags on far longer than I wish I had the patience for. I would only recommend this expansion to players who find themselves fascinated by the lore of F.E.A.R.. It provides a bit of extra insight in this department, which is nice (though distracting from the experience of the series). There are several intersting gun battles, but almost no jump-scares, or tension at all, for that matter. If you're on the fence about this expansion, I'd suggest against it.

Locoland is a cute real time arcade action puzzle game from Buka Entertainment.  This game is cute, different, innovative and imaginative.
Graphics while cute and visually appealing are restricted to 4:3 perspective with 3 selectable resolutions 640x480, 800x600 and 1024x768.  The art work is cartoon like with surreal colours and shading and would be at home in any children's story book.
Game sounds are atmospheric but can be hard on the ears at higher volumes.  The music is a variety of sequenced loop samples with arrangements hovering between circus music and new-age or pop.  Some of the sound loops clip between loops giving pops or distortion.
The user interface and menu system are usable, but are a little on the rough and ready side.  Some text story are grammer bad with spilling orrers (sic).
Game play starts off simple with missions becoming more complex and fast paced as the game progresses.  The user gets a factory which can build locomotive engines, Gun carriages, Mortar carriages and Missile carriages.  There is also a repair facility where damaged trains can be repaired by driving through.  Enemy AI gets similar facilities.  The player needs to clear obstacles, navigate complex train track lay-outs and eliminate enemy trains and facilities.  While repetitive (like tetris, galaxian, space invaders or pac-man) the game keeps the player hooked with escalating pace and complexity with plenty of challenge and demanding spot decisions under pressure.
Over all Locoland is a fun to play arcade game (with good re-play value) which is family friendly and should appeal to casual and arcade gamers of all ages.

Don't let Locoland's (originally Steamland) dated graphics deceive you, this classic RTS's gameplay holds up very well for a 12 year old relic only now making its way to Steam.  The charming steampunk setting and cute story will entertain you through tough as nails gameplay that is sure to satisfy the most dedicated strategy enthusiast.
Take note that I am generally not one for strategy games, so my opinion may be a bit noobish compared to a genre aficionado.  That said, the gameplay consists of classic strategy fair with the added twist of unit movement being relegated to set rail paths. Keeping this mechanic in mind, you must capture and construct buildings, build your force (in this case trains), complete a variety of objectives, and maneuver your trains in and out of on-rail battles against enemy units that are altogether unforgiving.  Make no mistake, the game is hard, super hard.  Although getting a hang of the controls and hotkeys helps immensely, this isn't a casual title in any sense of the word.
My biggest complaint is a lack of tutorial.  I spent a TON of time figuring out how things worked and what exactly I needed to do, but perhaps I've been spoiled by the casualness of newer games, even hardcore titles give more instruction than we receive here.  But to its credit, Locoland is from an era when hand holding and player swaddling wasn't a thought in the developer's mind.  Learning to play the game was as much of the gameplay as anything else.
Despite my frustrations, Locoland is a very fun strategy game.  I only wish we were given more graphical options, perhaps windowed mode, but considering its age I imagine it would be difficult to implement or that it's simply not possible.  Either way, strategy fans take heed, you'll want to check this one out.  If you often find yourself reminiscing on the gaming days of old, this is your chance to relive a unique and challenging RTS at a very reasonable price.
Bottom Line: Recommended for strategy game enthusiasts looking for something unique and challenging, although a bit dated.

Whilst an older game, it holds up well despite a lower resolution than you would expect to see these days (something that I found pleasing in a nostalgic way). The gameplay is solid, each unit is unique and can be utilised to render different attack and defence patterns. Enemy AI is about what you would expect from an RTS, challenging but predictable.
The art style is interesting and for the most part very effective, although in some instances can make elements on screen a little hard to pick out. That being said, it suits the game well and immerses you into unit management nicely.
Well worth a play if you are an RTS fan looking for something a little different in that genre, or just an indie game fan that enjoys a smaller, less frantic game from time to time.

Locoland:
~~~~~~~~
A happy and peaceful civilization of hard working robots with an extensive railroad network, enjoying robotic life as best they can.  Cherishing the ancient “Golden Gear” relic as their ancestors have, unfortunately the evil Khon-Kaa-Doo has other things in mind. On a beautiful night, he sent his troops to steal the relic. From now on, your mission is to get it back!
An interesting strategy game involving trains as your main units. Building wagons containing canons, artillery, missiles and more to destroy the enemy’s forces. Make sure to build plenty of engines to pull or push your trains into the enemy territory. No good building an arsenal and being as slow as a snail!! This game is all about the manoeuvrability of your trains and how efficiently to attack the opposing forces.
You really need to study the movements of the enemy trains in this game to beat each map. I personally enjoy the diversity of the train tracks; each map has a different layout. Day, night and weather condition the like of storms or Volcano showers will keep you on your toes.
In terms of graphics, they are cute and fun. Good control commands and easy to master. The music fits well with the game but I must admit the sound of the whistle every time you move your trains is a bit much.
You have 3 types of difficulty; easy, normal and hard. I would suggest starting on the easy level to get the feel of the game.  I must admit this game is growing on me but please rectify the whistle!
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	20 levels to fight
-	Cute graphics
-	Good command system
-	Trading cards
-	Good price
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~~
-	No achievements
-	Annoying whistle
Overall this is a fun strategy game with a touch of novelty!

My first ever memory of being grounded, came from this game.
Back when I was just a little girl, my family got our first computer through my father's job. Every evening around my bedtime, my dad would retire to "work" on it in his office, and I was told by my mom not to disturb him. Overcome with curiosity, I snuck out of bed one night to go and see what kind of work he was doing, only to find him playing this game instead. I was afraid he would scold me, but instead, he lifted me up on his lap, set me in front of the keyboard and said "Lass, the world needs us. Let's save it"
It became our regular thing. I would sneak out of bed without mom knowing and sit up with dad while we played Doom II until it was time for dad to go to bed. At first I just watched him, then he started to teach me what he was doing as he played. Not many days later, I got to try it for myself, and under his wing, I managed to complete the game with some assistance. It was such a thrill for me as just a little child, and I had so much fun doing it.
Eventually my mom caught us; my dad, who was supposed to complete his reports for his work, was instead playing a game filled with horrible monsters and gore with his young daughter, and me; a 7 year old girl up at 11 in the evening on a school night.
She was not happy.
I got grounded and I didn't see her talk to dad at all for at least a week. Still, it is one of my favorite memories from growing up.
20 years later, I still return to this game, again and again. While a bit outdated graphically, Doom II is still nothing but a pleasure after all these years, and I can do nothing but recommend it. My now 55 year old dad also still play it, and has nothing but positive things to say about it.
Mom still doesn't recommend it.

Lets take the rose tinted nostalgia glasses off for a moment and really address the issue most negative reviews try to bring up about GalCiv3.  "This is a pale comparison to GalCiv2".  Gal Civ 3 is better in 95% of the game than Gal Civ 2 was.  Its bigger, looks better, has the massive majority of the same mechanics, and offers some new things as well.  I was playing GC2 literally up until the point that GC3 became available to me so I have a pretty good frame of comparison for the two.  GC2 was an amazing game, 10 years ago that is.  I haven't noticed any bugs, never had any crashes, and often play very long games on the most massive of maps.  Is the game perfect?  Absolutely not.  There are a few frustrating mechanics, the UI isn't as intuitive as it could be.  I felt like the star base mechanic wasn't fully realized.  Do these small problems make it worse than GC2?  Absolutely not.  Play 10 hours of GC2 and you will be able to jump into GC3 and know exactly what to do.  Its an upgrade of almost the same game.  Its weird when a bunch of 26 year olds can't understand why a game doesn't engage them the same way it did when they were 16.  Well you've changed a lot since then, your mind doesn't allow that same kind of wonderment due to the endless amounts of stimulation.  There are a lot of reasons people look back on the past as being better than it really was.
GC3 is a great 4x space game and a pretty big improvement over GC2, despite what nostalgia laced fan boys might want you to believe.

- The mechanics, visual style, audio design, and story arc are all obviously inspired by Journey.  But that isn't a bad thing, and ABZU does have some of its own thing going on to set it apart.
- Aside from VR games, I don't think I've played many games that give such an enormous sense of scale.  Ocean and dive depth, whale size, and other things I won't spoil left a strong impression on me because of how _huge_ they felt.
- Man does this game ever look good at times.  Striking.
- The camera and movement controls are sometimes pretty janky and immersion-breaking.  But that's my only real complaint.

60 hours in and I only now feel ready to write a review. This is a great game; it has a clear tutorial when you start so if you are new to grand strategy or Paradox games, which I was, you still pick up the general gist of the game and how to play. The best thing about this game was every time I thought I had cracked it and was now the best Stellaris player of all time there was something new to throw a spanner into my Galactic ambitions!
Play this on the ironman mode, you can earn the achivements (if that is your thing) but most importantly it is more fun knowing you can't just go back and undo a bad decision; the excitment and thrill of knowing every decision has consequences adds so much to this game.
The mistake I made was going to big to quickly, try starting out with a smaller sized Galaxy if you are new to these games so you can get a better sense of the game and don't have to restart so often.
I do think the diplomacy could have a few extra options and depth but on a whole is still pretty good, I aslo think a vassal should pay tribute each month and there be an option to form union with them which isn't absorbing them into your Empire but perhaps becoming a council with them which has no happiness penalties and the more empires you add into your Galactic council of xenos the more difficult the bureaucracy becomes as when going to war or making diplomatic decisions you all have a vote.
The game feels different throughout early to mid to late game with some great and interesting side missions and random happenings to throw you of course, help you or even to give you something else to do. I did have to start again a few times with different customisation options before I could get into mid game in a strong position so don't be disheartened if the same happens to you as well. There is a vast range of customisable races; how they look, how they function, what their ethics are, what type of ships they use, how they travel through space, what they are called, how they react to the way you will play.
So this isn't too long I will end now by recommending this game even if you are new to grand strategy like I was (I have always loved strategy games but not really played grand strategy like this)

From the other reviews (at least, those that weren't inexplicably hung up on the gender and skin color of the default human faction leader), I expected Stellaris to be just Yet Another 4X, and a rather
one at that, but I'm addicted to the genre, so I bought it anyway. While it is by no means perfect, I was pleasantly surprised.
At its core, Stellaris is a solid and competent 4X game. There aren't really any big surprises, or groundbreaking game mechanics, but there are plenty of subtle differences which give Stellaris a unique feel. For instance, you can group individual systems within your empire into AI-controlled sectors, which the AI does a pretty good job of balancing, so you avoid the all-too-common situation where your empire is starving because each system individually decided to maximize its score by producing high-dollar strategic resources instead of food. Another example is how the diplomacy system requires you to define victory conditions in advance when declaring war, and how all members of an alliance vote over any decision that affects the alliance as a whole, such as a treaty or a war declaration. I also like the scavenging mechanic, where you can earn significant amounts of research credit by harvesting the debris of a defeated fleet.
But the most important innovation, to my mind, is the randomized research: where other games have a static research tree where each research topic is unlocked as soon as its prerequisites have been researched, Stellaris divides research into three fields (physics, engineering and society), and when you complete a research topic within one of these fields, you get a small and partly randomized selection of new topics to choose from. The topics you
choose may pop up again as soon as you complete the one you did—or they might not show up for another fifty years. This helps keep the game less predicable and increases replay value.
Now for the bad. Other reviews have lauded the game's interface, but frankly, I find it chaotic and wasteful of screen space. In addition, the game does not always auto-pause when you enter a UI screen or open a notification. You can easily become overwhelmed by the latter, especially in a war, where a couple of fleets rampaging in tandem through an enemy system while a science ship is scavenging the remains of the previous one could easily result in dozens of notifications per minute: one per fleet per battle plus one per debris field harvested. I've also had the misfortune, while playing as a democracy, of having a string of chancellors die after only a few months in office, because they were all roughly the same age when the game started; you can hand-pick administrators and military leaders, but politicians are controlled by the game. Finally, the 2D art, such as leader portraits or planetary landscapes, is frankly not very good (but bonus points for animated portraits).
On the whole, Stellaris is well worth the money, and it will be interesting to see what improvements and add-ons Paradox come up with over the next few years.

This early impression (given its a paradox title) is aimed specificly at fans of EU IV (as I am) wondering whether they should get stellaris. Please bear in mind that this is no full review of stellaris.
The game starts out much more like a civilization game than an EU game. You start with a singular solar system, scout you surroundings, meet enemies and neighbors, build mines to collect resources and send out colonists to expand your empire. Sounds familiar? You also develop technologies along a tech tree, have random events and kill pirates (think barbarians). Even the classification of your race (spiritual, industrious, militaristic, pacifistic ...) reminds me strongly of civ IVs classification of leaders.
Now, I am not saying this is civ in space. However playing stellaris to me has a lot more in common with said titles as any paradox title I know. It starts out pretty simple and straight forward. You start on your own and for the first years you are pretty much expanding without much trouble. After all, your competitors are more or less on your level of power, technology and resources. The amount of micro management grows proportionately to your empires size, which means after a while you'll be busy managing all those planets. Eventually you'll get into conflict with a neighbor who, depending on your play style, may have little more or less military power than you.
The point is, that this is a pretty fair game. Everyone starts the race more or less equal and your success largely depends on your system mastery. Even the fact that success is a thing (I dare you to define success in EU IV) makes a massive difference. There are traditional win states such as "have the largest empire" or "kill everyone else".
EU IV in contrast is a completely unfair game. Whether you start as mighty France or little Albania (if you're insane), the game is never balanced. Some nations are doomed from the beginning and making it to the year 1821 for them is a major achievement. Other nations might strive for world domination.
I like stellaris and I'm sure I'll get my money's worth out of it. But for me something is lost in the balanced race to supremacy. EU can be impenetrable with its interface and its complex systems. It can be cry out loud harsh when apparently out of nowhere an alliance rises against you. But setting my own goals, playing as a super power or a tiny monastery fighting against the odds is what keeps EU interesting to me. I don't see how stellaris can do the same.
I hope these impressions help to set expectations for the game correctly. I will update this text if I find that I was wrong or have further remarks.

This is simply one of the best single-player shooters available today.
The enemies are smart and react quickly, and the way the levels are designed allows for interesting encounters with them. Every weapon, from the high-capacity, accurate pistol to the heavier cannons you'll find in the mid and late game, are powerful, distinct, and serve a purpose while being incredibly fun to shoot.
Most levels are simply warehouses and office complexes, but most modern shooters are drenched in gray anyway so you might not even notice the fairly bland environments. That doesn't mean FEAR is devoid of style though. Sharp shadows, lots of smoke, sparks, and other particles, and a fondness for fire and blood give FEAR a distinct art style that other shooters, especially its sequels, lack.
There is a story to be had for those who really want to engage in it. There is a cannibal, mad science experiments, psychics, and a clone army. Players that don't care about the plot can skip -some- cutscenes and ignore the answering machine messages (the FEAR equivalent of System Shock 2's audio logs), and be apathetic to the dialog.
Despit its name, FEAR is not a scary game. It tries to have some spooks here and there but its strength is in its unparalleled gunplay. Each expansion gets progressively duller and there is no option to not install them. Extraction Point is worth playing if you enjoyed the base game.

An interesting 2d top down space sandbox with elements resembling single ship space pirates and zombies, Eve, and a little system shock 2, replete with that new-car indie smell.
You generate a galaxy, pick what class's skill package you want to start with, and are dropped in the starting system and offered a tutorial.
There are a variety of ship types and weapon types to choose from, various techs to find, and a number of factions of varying difficulty to join.
How you gain experience and money is up to you;
You can visit stations and talk to npcs to try and get odd jobs,
go around hacking old alien ruins floating around for stuff to sell/turn in for science points,
go around fragging pirates randomly,
trading goods between stations,
or hunting down valuable resources hidden in asteroids.
The combat has been harkened in other reviews to be like "Ice skating motorcycle duels" and that's KINDA true. It's more remenicent of 2d top down naval battles, where each of your weapons have their own arcs and you have a radar you can use to fight things off screen with guided weaponry, and you're sliding along space trying to avoid getting shot up too hard. It's ok.
My only gripe is that it's easy to get in over your head, and dying isn't the end, and the game is very grindy.
See, the game constantly autosaves, and you aren't allowed to make your own saves. The game is effectively ironman, so if you die then you die. You get deducted a small amount of money and are respawned inside the nearest friendly station.
This may sound like a good thing, except for your super expensive investiture of a ship being completely gone for good as well as its contents. You have to buy up the (thankfully free) civilian junk and start from scratch. It's a lot like EVE in this way.
Which has the major downside of runing into the grind wall that the game seems to be.  You get such a small trickle of money for the effort that you put into the game that it often is faster to just start a new galaxy and start from scratch rather than grind from a civ ship back up to where you died.
There's also a few interesting mods on the workshop, most are russian with (mostly) english translation.
Annoying crash that's been happening for well over half a year isn't fixed yet. Please put some time and effort into this devs,. it's very frustrating to lose progress like this.

Do you enjoy dungeon crawlers? Do you enjoy rhythm games with great music? Do you enjoy frustration? Do you enjoy vowing to never play a game again only to find yourself playing it half an hour later?

All in all I highly recommend this game because it is worth every penny.

FEAR, and its two expansions, in one neat bundle. I'd recommend them for three reasons.
First reason: The games are more tactical shooter than any modern FPS. The "high difficulty" setting in FEAR is all right, but in the two expansions, it's much harder. Why am I mentioning this? The AI in FEAR is smart, and will not hesitate to shoot you. Unlike most "modern" shooters, the AI in this will try to flank and attempt some form of attack on the player. The bullettime ability makes the AI a lot easier to manage, but running out of it means you'll be killed by a group of three.
Second reason: It's the only cinematic shooter on the market. The amount of dust and destruction to the enviroments, along with the slow motion, gives FEAR unique movie-style moments. Unlike other shooters (COD and BF series namely) that try to make it SEEM cinematic with skyboxes and pathetic story time, FEAR is all about shooting and making the shooting look good.
Third reason: It's creepy at times. FEAR isn't exactly scary, but it does have some scares.
Just remember, FEAR: Perseus Mandate is the only one that will function properly on modern PCs. The original FEAR and the first expansion require some tweaking to function properly.

The game is very enjoyable. I played it for several hours now and I want to see more. It reminds me of Wing Commander Privateer and X3: Reunion. What I like about VoidExpanse:
- Simplicity: Limiting to 2 dimensions, a simple control scheme. It works and feels right.
- Graphics: Thruster exhaust and explosions are a joy to look at. Most of the scenery looks nice as well.
- Combat: I really enjoy combat in this game. It is a good mix of skill and having the better hardware. It might be too easy, but I don't mind that.
There are a few points on which VoidExpanse could do better:
- Ship design: I was never proud to own a ship because of its looks. Ships are like cars. When you look at them you should think "I want to fly that thing!".
- Dialogues: This is by far the weakest link in the game. The dialogues are so shallow you won't feel the slightest empathy for the characters in the game. They're also quite hard to follow because they're spammed on the screen without any non-verbal communication.
- Stations: Every station looks the same on the inside, and most of the actions on the station are performed through some user interface. It would be nice to see more of the station interior and to have more variety in station interiors.
- Ship components and materials: They look very abstract, having only a coloured icon to represent them. It would be nice to have at least a real picture of the thing.

Skipping all the balance issues, bugs, game flow and variety of activity(or that lack of it) issues , I just want to talk about A.I.
I never have a clue how can it be so hard to write a decent algorithm for optimizing a planet. Basicaly you just clutter buildings of the same type(so easy for OOP languages given the class hierarchy), and try to make buildings with more adjacency bounus more surrounded. For smaller planets you build special buildings that gives global benefits, such as shadow temple. When I first come to the game I felt the computer can do it so much better than a human player, the size of the planet hardly ever exceeds 15, you'll never get a combonatorial explosion. But apperently not so when they wrote the thing. I highly doubt the developers ever played the game themselve.
Since no human player ever bother to make detailed calculation to decide building sequence,or exactly how much should a planet specialize, we just make very simple rules, such as "one or two farm and one happiness building per planet and then build starbases around planets", "build astroid mines around the most specialized planets" .  It's rumored that the computer will observe how humans play and learn from them, but I've never seen any of these basic and frequently needed and deployed tactics picked up by the A.I.   Of course, this is sorta high-end , less cost-efficient to actuallize than to talk♥♥♥♥♥♥about.
The recent patch finally weans the a.i off that stupid zero ship maintainance bounus( which basically made this game's early launch tragic) but really that's it. A player 20 hr into the game can easily specialize a precursor world to produce some 300-500 research close to mid game, but I hardly ever see that achieved by a.i. , it probably wont even adapt it's research queue to make precursor world more productive, nor would they prioritize ceasing and protecting these powerhouse worlds in war or the anticipation thereof.
The a.i. also doesn't seem to show trace of any mechanism to decide what to do actively(what to prioitize, how to realize; what to anticipate, how to prepare.etc.).These are just left to  very unpolished and unpractical characterization, i.e. declare war on different ideology,  I'm a dregin so I'm going to war even if I got a really bad start in the colonization phase, or just mechanically protesting if ppl are bring forces near border.
In summary, I feel like playing with plants, not intelligence.

A step up from the first game, this one improves on nearly everything, from the story, graphics, characters and especially combat.
The story, I have to say, had me quite a bit more invested, once again, in the world itself rather than the ultimate goal (The Kingslayer). Replayability is mention, as to get a full experience of the game, you need to go down two paths, basically two playthroughs. I have to say I was far more invested on Iorveth's path than Roche's, even though I was consistently split between the two paths, once again. Choices are not clear cut.
Stealth sections are introduced, but I felt like they were average. Geralt doesn't move carefully enough when you move, so you're likely to be caught when Geralt stumbles further than you push the analog stick or keyboard.
Combat is much better, as your signs have obvious effects and it's more difficult for your enemies to hit you (provided you use the OP Quen sign). At the same time, when you get hit, it's not obvious, and enemies do a lot of damage, so you're always on your toes, even by the end (should your Quen go down). It's easier to make bombs and potions, though I found myself using bombs far more than potions.
Inventory has both been improved and stepped back with the weight limit. Removing the weight limit with a mod is a must, as it freed me up to move around without any drawbacks, given the sheer amount of containers and loot in the world. However, there are far more weapons and armor to collect and craft as you progress.
Character development isn't much different, though I found with just one perk per level I could barely get anything really good unless I focused soley on one of the skill trees. Once again, a mod fixed that.
I have to say that I was a little worried with the inclusion of a dragon throughout the plot, but by the end I was so happy with how they handled it. I won't spoil anything, but one of Geralt's lines in one of the endings sums up exactly how I feel about dragons in fantasy RPGs, which is ignored by nearly every other game out there with dragons (even my favourite RPG up to this point - Skyrim).
Great game, with great story, great graphics, more old and new interesting and realistic characters, fun combat, with some strange choices that don't impact it at all if you have access to mods. If you like Fantasy RPGs, you'll love this game.
