Definitely one of my favorite Final Fantasy's, especially considering how much weight it had in my decision between getting a PS1 or an N64 back when those were current. As one of the first 3d oriented games from Square though, it felt revolutionary seeing what were once 2d anime sprites as 3d models. Although the graphics aged quickly, low-poly block-people that the characters were, the strength of these characters and the narrative surrounding them had people clamoring for a remake with graphics that could do justice by them.
Now, roughly 20 years after the original release, Square is finally opting to remake this classic, albeit with news of voice-acting, adjusted minigames, and being released in installments a la Final Fantasy XIII. Hearing that, I figured I'd replay the original to see how much of what I remembered was really amazing and how much was just nostalgia.
Roughly 80 hours later, I find myself largely happy but still harboring mixed feelings. I still love the flexibility of the Materia-slot system in this game and how it allows you to move around mastered abilities between characters, along with the balancing act that comes with choosing weapons according to not only strength and accuracy but how quickly it helps you master the abilities of these Materia.
Plus, I still love the core story surrounding Cloud, Sephiroth, Tifa, Aerith, and the life of the planet.
But there's plenty of stuff I realized I don't particularly like too. In retrospect, almost half the characters lack depth and relatability, namely Yuffie and Cait Sith. While they, along with others including Cid, Vincent, and Red XIII all have some moment to shine in the spotlight, it becomes so one-off that it can feel a bit disjointed from the story.

Putting aside the graphical improvements over the last two decades though, it's hard not to see how RPG mechanics and games overall have improved. Though I really enjoy turn-based combat, I can understand adapting the ATB system to something closer to the action RPG style of FFXII. Plus, FFVII originally released on a set of 3 CD's, which is a great reminder of how limited the game is by the spatial and quality limits of the time. With how much more content games are capable of now, why keep things like the overworld exploration or different towns markets as limited as they were before? Who knows how much planned content needed to be cut in order for it to even fit on just 3 CD's? Even if these things are improved, I'd still be perfectly happy so long as the core narrative and fundamental mechanics remain faithful to that of the original.
That being said though, I've already mentioned that the story could be improved on as well, such as adding greater depth and empathy into the other characters in the cast. Not only that, but I think the ending could be improved on as well.
If all these things are improved upon, or at least changed, it's no surprise that some doubt that the remake will truly be faithful to the original. Ultimately though, FFVII was great for its time, but greatly limited by it as well. There's no telling how much was cut in order to fit it on the PS1, or how close the final product was to what the designers envisioned. I can only take comfort in knowing that the original creators are on board for the remake, and in the enjoyment I got from playing it again.

Combining Master of Orion with Europa Universalis, that just has to be the one of the greatest game ideas ever.
At the beginning, the game feels awesome. The races are well designed, and researchable technologies are more or less scientifically realistic. The 3 different FTL technologies give a nice strategic depth to the game, which can also be at times frustrating.
The game lacks diplomatic relation mechanisms. It is hard to see or understand why some races attack you.  Even playing passively your neighbors randomly declare war on you. Trying to gain an ally is often hindered by missing a few positive relation points with no way to gain further points. Often I ended up as a strong lonely nation that gets beaten down by strong alliances. If I finally manage to gain an alliance friend, I get a declaration of war by some other alliance further away that somehow manages to pass through occupied space to invade my planets. I am sure this can be understood after a certain amount of play time, still the different map overviews in EU4 were a lot easier to analyze. Here are none.
Further the AI tends to create many small fleets. Fighting 2 nations with different FTLs at the same time, each of them having 5-6 perfectly micromanaged fleets, while you are trying to send your 2-3 larger fleets defending your empire is rather annoying. Not to mention, bigger fights even bring the best PCs to its knees with 2-3 FPS. The CPU just can’t keep up.
The early game has been nicely polished and gives a positive playing experience. The further you get into the game, the more unfinished elements appear. The game just got released to early and seems unfinished. I am sure Paradox will release several DLCs and patches making this raw diamond into a great game, but just not yet

I'm gonna keep this pretty short.
If you like space 4X games, this game is for you. Just don't fall for the same trap that most of these negative reviews have in comparing a brand new title with games that have years of content update, expansions, and/or dlc behind them. I've been in on the ground floor for an awful lot of 4X game releases, and Stellaris has outperformed them on nearly every point, and in the ones it hasn't, I can point to a half dozen titles that its got the same features.
I'm fairly sure most of the negative reviews are from people coming from either other paradox games expecting this to be grand strategy and not 4X, or people who hear the hype but don't play 4X, or people that have been playing games that have been around for ages with lots of expansions, like Sins or GalCiv. (Yes, I count Galciv as being around for years, its been in EA for ages, and it was terrible at first imo, just like Civ5 was).
--------------
Does it have bugs? Yes of course. Its brand new, and it didnt have an Early Access period. Personally I count that as a good thing.
Are the bugs annoying? I don't really think so. Much like with Bethesda games, I find most of them to be amusing more than anything else when taken with a grain of salt.
Are there showstopper bugs? I've only found one, and that one hasnt repeated itself since the first hotfix, and I've never met anyone else who had it, so I'd honestly have to say 'no'.
And here I am with almost 100 hours played now. Its a fantastic new entry into the scifi 4X genre. (And don't let anyone try and tell you its Grand Strategy. This is Master of Orion / Endless Space on steroids, pure and simple.)

Overwhelmingly overrated. Even though the game looked a bit infantile from the screenshots, I decided to give it a shot anyway, hoping it would prove me wrong utilising an interesting plot, innovative mechanics, cool ideas, or a great atmosphere. To tell the truth - the 96% of positive reviews were the deciding factor. And I've never been so dissapointed with a Steam game so far. I really tried to like this game, but the more I played, the more it felt like just an another cute side-scrolling action game. I mean, it is ok, I'd say even very good for an under 18 y/o, but the community rating just doesn't do it justice.
Especially, the sweet graphics and furry characters (the annoying sidekick included) make it unbearably cute to swallow for adults (unless you have some sort of a weird furry fetish, I guess). The gameplay proves to be a nice way to unwind for about 30mins to recharge mental batteries, not thinking too much and just mashing the buttons, but easily gets repetitive after a longer time. The story so far seems to be pretty simple and easy to follow for the young ones, but pretty boring for older audences. And... nothing spectacular to keep you hooked on, it's pretty much all the same as in any other game of this genre.
And although this game looked like a game for children from the very beginning, I bought it hoping for a magical, dense atmosphere like in 'Child of Light' or 'Ori and the Blind Forest'. Sadly, this one doesn't get further than what is shown on the screenshots: a simple, cute-looking, quick-paced action slasher for kids. So if you are planning to buy it for your 12 year-old, I can recommend it. If you want to play it yourself - don't get fooled by the raving community reviews.

text:
FEAR is a first person shooter with light horror elements. The story evolves around a member of First Encounter Assault Recon (which has to be one of the most forced acronyms on video game history) who is pursuing a guy called Paxton Fettel who is being a huge ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and commanding cloned super soldiers to kill people through telepathic abilities.
FEAR really plays like 'Hollywood Shootout: The Game'. Everything that is shot seems to break, or take a ridiculous amount of damage, and the player has the ability to use slow motion. This really feels awesome, and makes every shoot out feel badass.
Also helping the gunplay is the AI. The AI is willing to flank, retreat, throw grenades, and even just push your position. What most modern game AI can't seem to do on hard, these guys can breeze through on normal difficulty. This game is at least challenging which is a great change from most games of today. You also tend to only take on squads of 3-4 at a time, and this really works. The combat is challenging without relying on having a bunch of dudes bum-rush you.
Weapons all feel good. You've got the standard assault rifle, SMG and pistol. The shotgun is gutsy as hell and will tear things up. You also get the penetrator, which is like a slow, powerful assault rifle, a burst firing scoped rifle, a particle rifle which can strip the flesh from most enemies in one hit (basically acting as a sniper rifle), an automatic cannon, and a burst firing rocket launcher. Some of these later weapons don't have a lot of ammo around, which is a shame as they are fun as hell to use.
My biggest gripe about this game is the horror. It's honestly not scary, it's just annoying. A little girl staring at you is only a little spooky to begin with. Eventually I found myself just wanting to skip the flashbacks and wanting to kill guys again. The game is also quite repetitive with it's environments, but the firefights are so good that I honestly wasn't too bothered by it.
The base game is easily worth $10. I'd give it an 8/10.

A game that not only is horrifying but fun to play.
This is hard to describe, but everytime I pulled the trigger, I felt the weight of the gun, unlike in Call of Duty or Battlefield.  The enemy A.I., especially on the higher difficulties, is extremely refined and intelligent, usually attempting to seek cover whenever possible, get clear of grenades and other explosives, and attempt flanking maneuvers or adopt new tactics if I am too much to handle.
In terms of horror, the game relies on its atmosphere, situation, and classic tropes, like the creepy little girl.  While the game's story is scary, the expansion pack, Extraction Point, cranks it up a notch.
Overall 10/10
Please note a few things if you care about the story:  Both Expansion Packs are technically considered noncanon with the release of F.E.A.R. 2 and F.E.A.R. 3.  However, Extraction Point is itself a good finish for the main story.  Perseus Mandate is more of sidestory and does not have much to do with the overall plot.
Should you want to get the next games, be aware of a few things: You do not have to get the DLC for F.E.A.R. 2, because it is technically rendered noncanon by F.E.A.R. 3.  F.E.A.R. 2 can be considered just as horrifying, but it does have more action elements, which is hit and miss.  With F.E.A.R. 3 there is Co-op play, but it does tend to make the game less scary and more like L4D or Dead Space 3 Co-op.

The patch of 01/04/2014 which introduced an auto-aim really did dumb down the key strategic aspect of the game and  in my opinion this was one of the stronger points of the game. It no longer requires any skill at all to play which is painfully obvious after playing one match after another with 1-3 of your 4 teammates where always going afk, and pulling out a win albeit unlikely is still possible.
By reducing the competitiveness of PvP to the extreme that they have, and not only with auto-aim but with matchmaking as well they made this feel like a "grade school level" type of moba where even basic levels of tactics, strategy, and intelligence are obsolete as Teamplay and individual skills no longer exists.
The developers of this game boasts that this is a fast pace game and in fact it once was, today however the number of users using 1 hit kill hacks or speedhacks has made the community who do still play legit feel unmotivated during gameplay which is likely why there are now so many afkers on both sides in every match. While this can still be a fun game to play especially when both team are actually competing at their best, this however is becoming a rare sight.
To give you some prospective, out of 30 matches I played today only 6 of them where interesting or engaging battles with all 10 players participating the others where mediocre 1 sided bouts often lasting under 60 seconds due to large amounts of afk'ing going on right from the start of the match, and at lest 4 of them had 1 or more hackers in it.
In short the game itself is very fun and recommended,  it's the community's lack of interest or motivation to participate in the matches they chose to join that is in my opinion dragging this game down. And I believe that is ultimately cause by a horrible lack of competitiveness that the developers have now brought to the game.
With that said I wouldn't recommend this game to all the competitive players of a moba genre, though I would recommend it to the more casual players,  first timers, and  perhaps the younger crowd of players just looking for a good time

I've seen a lot of negative reviews about this game, but please read this before you read those negatives ones.
This game, although not advertised as early access, certainly feels early access.
First of all:
-The download "client" (I say it with quotation marks, because it's very poorly made), looks terrible and for me the download percentage bar, went down, but the number went up. The amount of bytes in the negatives.. Which I found amusing. :)
Anyway, into the game.
The game starts off with a good looking menu. You press Play. Instantly transported to the tavern, where literally everyone and their mothers are hanging out. You don't get to choose your class straight away, unless you look into the defenders forge deep enough, to find at the bottom of the character list, that you can choose between the four main classes. The tavern shop, is incredibly messy. I didn't know what was what, and where to go for whatever item I wanted to purchase.
This game IS TOTALLY MULTIPLAYER CURRENTLY. No singleplayer. Frustrating to say the least. But you can host a private game however. The mana graphics have changed so they all look exactly the same... (makes it worse really). The chests are buggy to open, take a lot longer than the original DD. Standard weapons do a lot more damage too. Other than, not much difference.
This game has MASSIVE potential, it just needs to be refined a lot more. It's extremely messy and all over the place. I do love the loot you can get now, you can get jewellery and temporary boosts and potions and whatnot. Also, I do love the fact armour shows up on your character now. PLUS!!
Other than that, it's a bit of state at the minute. If you wish to purchase and experience it... be my guest. :) But I wouldn't recommend it, EVEN though this is a positive review. This is positive because of the sheer potential this game could have if done properly and is refined more.

8/10: One of the best Final Fantasy's, with a compelling story and interesting combat and skill mechanics. Still, it's a port of the original PS1 title, so despite the surprisingly well-rendered backgrounds, things like the in-game graphics and certain plot points have not aged so well and underline the limitations of the time.
Definitely one of my favorite Final Fantasy's, especially considering how much weight it had in my decision between getting a PS1 or an N64 back when those were current. As one of the first 3d oriented games from Square though, it felt revolutionary seeing what were once 2d anime sprites as 3d models. Although the graphics aged quickly, low-poly block-people that the characters were, the strength of these characters and the narrative surrounding them had people clamoring for a remake with graphics that could do justice by them.
Now, roughly 20 years after the original release, Square is finally opting to remake this classic, albeit with news of voice-acting, adjusted minigames, and being released in installments a la Final Fantasy XIII. Hearing that, I figured I'd replay the original to see how much of what I remembered was really amazing and how much was just nostalgia.
Roughly 80 hours later, I find myself largely happy but still harboring mixed feelings. I still love the flexibility of the Materia-slot system in this game and how it allows you to move around mastered abilities between characters, along with the balancing act that comes with choosing weapons according to not only strength and accuracy but how quickly it helps you master the abilities of these Materia.
Plus, I still love the core story surrounding Cloud, Sephiroth, Tifa, Aerith, and the life of the planet.
But there's plenty of stuff I realized I don't particularly like too. In retrospect, almost half the characters lack depth and relatability, namely Yuffie and Cait Sith. While they, along with others including Cid, Vincent, and Red XIII all have some moment to shine in the spotlight, it becomes so one-off that it can feel a bit disjointed from the story.

Putting aside the graphical improvements over the last two decades though, it's hard not to see how RPG mechanics and games overall have improved. Though I really enjoy turn-based combat, I can understand adapting the ATB system to something closer to the action RPG style of FFXII. Plus, FFVII originally released on a set of 3 CD's, which is a great reminder of how limited the game is by the spatial and quality limits of the time. With how much more content games are capable of now, why keep things like the overworld exploration or different towns markets as limited as they were before? Who knows how much planned content needed to be cut in order for it to even fit on just 3 CD's? Even if these things are improved, I'd still be perfectly happy so long as the core narrative and fundamental mechanics remain faithful to that of the original.
That being said though, I've already mentioned that the story could be improved on as well, such as adding greater depth and empathy into the other characters in the cast. Not only that, but I think the ending could be improved on as well.
If all these things are improved upon, or at least changed, it's no surprise that some doubt that the remake will truly be faithful to the original. Ultimately though, FFVII was great for its time, but greatly limited by it as well. There's no telling how much was cut in order to fit it on the PS1, or how close the final product was to what the designers envisioned. I can only take comfort in knowing that the original creators are on board for the remake, and in the enjoyment I got from playing it again.

I enjoyed my time with this game. This is not the best metroidvania out there, but it's good enough to warrant a look.
Pros:
+ Art is nice to look at, at least in most cases.
+ Story is nothing to write home about, but there are a couple interesting plot twists, and it does sort of keep you guessing.
+ Furries! For someone who grew up on Disney Afternoon cartoons, this feels really nostalgic.
+ Many throwbacks to classic games.
+ Many throwbacks to indie games.
+ Combat is fluent and it's deeper than in most metroidvanias out there (still pretty shallow though)
+ Controls are responsive.
+ Music is good. I did listen to OST for a while.
+ Fidget is dangerously cute.
Cons:
- Ending feels a bit abrupt, and there are plot threads that are left unaddressed. I think in an interview, developer admitted that due to time constraints he had to cut about third to a half of a game.
- Jumping can feel floaty. Thankfully, there isn't much precision platforming required.
- Animation quality in cutscenes is less than stellar, but it's tolerable.
- Endgame is a bit rushed.
All in all, it's a decent entry into metroidvania genre, and I do recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind an occasional cringe-inducing animation in cutscenes (there aren't many cutscenes anyway).
In any case, this game is an outstanding achievement for something developed almost single-handedly (music was outsourced). So thumbs up from me.

Studio known for it's historical grand strategy games decides to shake up the 4X-genre. Release is surprisingly smooth, a lot of content is left out or is just too shallow to be interesting (such as diplomacy and internal politics) which makes mid game and especially late game repetitive and quite bland. There aren't really much interaction between game mechanics and with previously mentioned issues, this stomps emergent storytelling - which in my opinion is the best spice in Paradox GSG games. Every now and then Stellaris feels like it's from different developer, but smooth and logical gameplay remind the game is crafted by Paradox with love. Looking past the disappointment, Stellaris is filled with creativity and great ideas and it's early game is most refreshing 4X in years. While mid and late parts of the game feel sloppy, they have their unexplainable charm. Stellaris should've been named: "Sci-fi Tropes: The Game".
Freedom in creating your own species and empires is astounding and gives huge replayability. There is difference if you're playing xenophile, pacifist birds or if you're on a militaristic crusade through the galaxy. The game even properly manages to handle multispecies Empires. Stellaris has a sturdy foundation for Paradox to build a classic, a new milestone for the space 4X-genre.
Paradox has already published their plans with next upcoming patches, which will (hopefully) flesh out the game. On basis of their plans and current state of the game, Stellaris was released a few months too early.
+ Engaging early game, exploration and expanding
+ Audiovisually best 4X there is (soundtrack is superb)
+ Mods only not supported, but encouraged
+ Innovative, stands out in a stale genre of space opera strategy games
+ Really a lot of customization
+ Flawless multiplayer
- Diplomacy is simple, boring and almost useless
- Internal politics are nominally there, population system is just a faded shadow of Victoria II's one
- No trade mechanics, resources are almost meaningless
- Wars are tedious.
- Not really a lot of ways to interact with other empires.
At the moment (1.0.3 version) my score: 72/100. For me it was worth the money, but wouldn't recommend it unconditionally. Would suggest to wait for first bigger updates "Asimov" and "Heinlein".

Story: The story is pretty classic. You are Squall, an elite mercenary and member of Seed. The game starts out with you completing your final test to be a full fledge Seed. Shortly after you get your first assignment and you move out. From helping a small resistance, to fighting of a witch, to saving the world this game has it all.
Appearance: FF7 may have been a revolution in going from 2D to 3D but this game improved upon that. With a more “realistic” 3D models this game is amazing. The world is huge and beautiful. Following the story you will see maybe half of what there is to see in the world. There is a few items/events that you can permanently miss which is sad but the amount of content and re-playability is amazing.
Game play: This is a classic retake on the final fantasy game play. You have a four party system typically consisting of Squall and three others. You can choose from up to six permanent characters and five temporary characters. Its still maintains the turn based battle system with a few added bonus's. Over world and in world exploration is easy and reminiscent of most final fantasy games.
You have an overworld that you traverse to go from town to town. Over time you gain different vehicles each having its own pros and cons.
You are able to use a controller with this game. I was able to use both a corded xbox 360 controller and a PS3 controller. It was more difficult to use the PS3 controller but it was well worth the effort. Of course you can use a keyboard but its not really advised.
Achievements: The achievements for this show an improvement over the FF7 achievements. Its nearly impossible to complete the game with all achievements in one go. Most of the achievements are simple and self explanatory but there is one or two that will make for a challenge.
Bottom Line: The game averages for about $12. On sale it has been as low as $5. Even for full price its worth picking up for some nostalgia but at the same time I would wait for the next sale to pick it up. The game is a lot of fun even though nothing has changed in 15 years but its worth picking up.

Combining Master of Orion with Europa Universalis, that just has to be the one of the greatest game ideas ever.
At the beginning, the game feels awesome. The races are well designed, and researchable technologies are more or less scientifically realistic. The 3 different FTL technologies give a nice strategic depth to the game, which can also be at times frustrating.
The game lacks diplomatic relation mechanisms. It is hard to see or understand why some races attack you.  Even playing passively your neighbors randomly declare war on you. Trying to gain an ally is often hindered by missing a few positive relation points with no way to gain further points. Often I ended up as a strong lonely nation that gets beaten down by strong alliances. If I finally manage to gain an alliance friend, I get a declaration of war by some other alliance further away that somehow manages to pass through occupied space to invade my planets. I am sure this can be understood after a certain amount of play time, still the different map overviews in EU4 were a lot easier to analyze. Here are none.
Further the AI tends to create many small fleets. Fighting 2 nations with different FTLs at the same time, each of them having 5-6 perfectly micromanaged fleets, while you are trying to send your 2-3 larger fleets defending your empire is rather annoying. Not to mention, bigger fights even bring the best PCs to its knees with 2-3 FPS. The CPU just can’t keep up.
The early game has been nicely polished and gives a positive playing experience. The further you get into the game, the more unfinished elements appear. The game just got released to early and seems unfinished. I am sure Paradox will release several DLCs and patches making this raw diamond into a great game, but just not yet

Quite interesting platformer with a lot of action, puzzles and exploration. Even quests and dialogues to give it a RPG flavor. It's a beautiful looking game and the controls are responsive enough to have a lot of fun. The ennemies were rather easy to kill, even bosses, so I'm glad I decided to turn the difficulty level up to be more challenged. Despite the cartoonish graphics and story à la Walt Disney, there is something a bit dark about the story. It's not as cute as you might think.
I would not recommend this game to very young children, they are not the target audience at all. Dust is very fast and powerful and rarely gets hit while he kills dozens of ennemies, but a few hits taken and he will die quickly. While some parts are very hack & slash and rather easy even at the hardest difficulty level, the real obstacle is coming from some areas more difficult to navigate by their tricky - but fun - design.
I find it hard to understand why I liked this game so much, because while I think everything was good I would not give a near perfect rate to any aspect of this game - story, gameplay, levels design, controls, graphics, variety, etc, but there is something special about Dust: An Elysian Tail. I did not particularly enjoy the leveling and stats system, disliked the crafting system and components collecting, I ended up with way too much money and items.
Overall it's an impressive indie game, developed pretty much by a single guy from what I understand. I strongly recommend it to all platformers fans out there because it's a lot of fun.

This game might not be perfect, but it certainly is an overlooked gem. I have a somewhat strange fascination with rogue-likes/lites. I also quite enjoy a nice space exploration game. I quite like this game and I keep coming back. Not all games get the formula right, but I think this one does. Some people might say that this game is too easy. I wouldln't know, I find it just right. I am playing it on Normal difficulty though so your mileage may vary.
Graphically, it looks decent enough. It's 3D models and particle effects are quite beautiful with lovely backdrops. I would say though that perhaps the backdrops are a bit too colourful. Most of space is empty and black, and I find it hard to believe that you'd see this other huge galaxy in the distance. Sure it would still be millions of light years away, but isn't very realistic. That isn't to say that I don't appreciate them, I do. It makes it seem a bit less bleak than space normally would be.
The music holds up, and gives your ears something to listen to although I didn't much care for the music at the start screen. I like the sound design. Although, the ships don't actually have that much difference in engines and the various other effects are the same if you have a Level 1 or Level 3 Laser.
In my current run, I find that Laser Energy weapons are by far the best and easiest to aim. A lot of it comes down to the ship though. There are various types of those. I haven't tried Multiplayer yet, but when I do, I will be sure to comment on it.
The story is the same, but the destinations are procedurally generated. There are various types of missions. Rescue, Mining, Delivering Packages, Intel, a few mini-games in hacking Enerak terminals.
I discovered that running out of fuel wasn't the end of the world, but you travelled a lot slower, even whilst cruising. Without fuel, your ship is severely exposed and crippled. You have no energy for weapons or shields, but you can still live to fight another day.
Is it a perfect game? No. I found a few glitches mostly to do with the autosaving message (it is a bit offscreen, I am playing at 4K. I also found that sometimes when you dock with the autopilot or not, the ship circles around the object a bit swirling closer and closer in and then eventually docking.
Overally, I really like this game. There is something about exploring space, fighting pirates, mining, and buying parts for your ship to upgrade it. If you enjoy rogue-likes/-lites then you'll enjoy this.

Dragons and Titans used to be an awesome game. After several buffs and nerfs, the game wasn't any longer fun to play.
Things that I used to like about D&T that changed:
The possibilty to invite up to 5 friends to form a team.
Having to use all different dragons in a match.
The old controls system without auto-aim.
Anything before the Titan Pass.
D&T couldn't afford itself after the yearly Titan Pass, for it didn't create any beneficial profit.
What D&T should of change is:
Starting with the Titan Pass (Same price for a month is more than enough).
Remove all Runes (stones collected within the matches), since this allows players to easily use hacks and sometimes stay low profile, and as well helps to keep the abilities of the dragons balanced.
Remove the use of repeated dragons in a match.
Weekly updates, including at least 1 weapon or 1 dragon.
At least 3 Moderators per chat (since not all are always able to be online).
Weekly developer or admin visits so players notice the interest of the D&T team towards them.
And last but not least, team XP in matches, instead of individual (This will give players a more pleasent and friendly match, since it will encourage all to assist for a common cause).
Some new ideas:
Replacing the collection of stones for Gold pieces to buy some upgrade for their weapons/dragons with a prior limit set, within the match. The upgrades could either have just a few levels but several type that does not mess the balance in match, such as ''Returning to hoard ability cooldown'', ''Short protective shield for teammates'', ''Dashing a small distance'', and stuff like that.
Anyways, there are many things that can be changed to make the game not just as good as it used to be, but greater. Lets not forget the improvements keep players interested, but every change must to be properly debated between D&T team, in order to avoid colliding every feature or element in the game.
At the end, there is far too much that can be improved in Dragons and Titans, but the income must to be well thought, that way the D&T team will always feel excited to work with such awesome game. The concept that this game handled is very insteresting and satifying, specially to those who love dragons. But if anyone wants the players to return to this game, a lot has to be done and responsabilities to be assumed.
Thanks D&T for so many fun moments and to allow me to meet some of the coolest and easy going people to play with.

Before I say anything else, let me be clear about one thing.  This game IS good for someone who is new to MOBAs.  Playing around on it can be fun, and you can have a good time just pounding on the computers if you want.  I like the way that you can mix the activatable abilities of your dragon by swapping in different weapons.  It's a feature I haven't seen in the other MOBAs I have played.  The weapons usually don't provide abilities that are broken with any specific dragons, so the balancing on it isn't too bad.
However, if you are familiar with MOBAs, you'll only really play this one when you don't have access to your favorites.  The monetization of this game leaves a lot to be desired.  I get that they are trying to make money off of their product, but they didn't have to make it into some sort of CCG for dragons and weapons.  It's nice that they provide a daily login bonus, and that every 5 days you get another free (random) dragon, but the amount of gems that it takes to get the booster pack of dragons or weapons is pretty high, and you don't even have the option of picking out a specific one of either.  They love to point out how many gems you would have earned after each match if you had just been willing to spend the money on a Titan Pass, too, which I find to be very annoying.
All in all, this game shows a lot of potential, but it's just not living up to it for those of us who are already familiar with MOBAs.

Did you like the original Dungeon Defenders game?
Do you primarily use a desktop computer to game?
If so, then steer clear of this shoddy re-release!
Although the development team claims that this is primarily a PC game, the game itself claims otherwise. With shoddier controls, a forced always-online multiplayer tavern, mantdatory waiting period before starting a match (even a private match), and a new 'playverse' interface which feels optimized for touchscreens (likely because it was), this re-release seems to offer very little in the way of enhanced content over the original title.
The good:
-You can stream the game's levels as you need them
-New item types & revamped stats
-You can play the game on your iphone & your android & your pc & probably your OUYA too
The bad:
-Touchscreen interface is clunky when using a mouse or gamepad
-Character management is horrid
-Character skins were converted to items, cluttering your stash with needless junk
-Always-online means you need 100% connectivity to play even singleplayer
-80% of the options are gone, such as replaying a level without going back to the tavern
Final thoughts:
Maybe this game will get better before release, but I doubt it. These issues are part of their cross-platform design experience.
2/10, buy the original instead.
EDIT: Changed my rating from 4/10 to 2/10 on my discovery that if you lose internet connection for even half a second, your session is terminated. In singleplayer. Yup.

Well, here's some points:
I love good Pixelart...I really do, but this mostly isn't good one.
The artists are using the same colour for too many pixels on many images, making it look very very old fashioned. Some look good but too many don't
If you wanna see really good Pixelart go check out Stardew Valley, Nuclear Throne, or Starbound, they all have their own take on Pixelart and they all look gorgeous. Sadly, CotND doesn't.
The game forces you to make quick decisions.
There is not a single time you can have a break, except for maybe switching between two tiles in an empty room.
For a game that mostly has a puzzle take on Roguelikes this isn't good, since you barely can concentrate and are gonna panic move a lot which just leads to unnecessary frustration.
If you wanna see difficult, but non-frustrating games check out the Dark Souls series, Nuclear Throne, Super Meat Boy, Geometry Dash, The Witness...and many many more, there seriously is a lot of them!
The tutorial doesn't show you how to use items and how the gold multiplier works, enemy health and strength aren't shown, so you either have to remember or guess. Items in the shop aren't explained, so you never know what you're buying, neither are alternative gamemodes.
The game really needs to get a little more polished.
Let's compare to other Roguelikes.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth has a huge amount of different and unique items, enemies, playable characters and gamemodes, also a lot of them you have to unlock through certain actions.
Rogue Legacy has a big Skilltree, many character traits and a fluent progress system.
Faster than Light has a huge learning curve, and also a big amount of upgrades and unlockables.
Nuclear Throne got at least a decent amount of weapons, playable characters, character perks and secrets, but therefore it still beats CotND in almost every other cathegory and takes long enough to play through anyways, due to its difficulty.
So where's any of that in CotND? At least one thing should be worked out deeply.
other Roguelikes got great OST too.
Okhlos: Omega for example got way better one in my opinion and even other Roguelikes like The binding of Isaac, Dead Cells or Nuclear Throne can keep up with CotND
To Masterpiece Soundtracks like the ones of Dear Esther, Clannad, Rabi-Ribi or the Final Fantasy games it's not comparable at all and unlike them this is a music game!
There's simply better ones. Point. Ones where you don't have to solve a puzzle while keeping the Rhythm, ones where you're not feeling like a metronome after 5 minutes.
Check out Geometry Dash, Osu, DDR or Final Fantasy Theatrhythm...and guess what: Osu and DDR and Geometry Dash let you add your own music too.
In addition it's one of those games with a horrible DLC policy, I mean, the soundtrack (split among multiple DLC's) costs more than the actual game, who did get that idea?

Introduction
and this edition is no exception. It has much more equipment and a better appearance.  Many may know it for its glitchy physics but in truth this is the most realistic farming simulator on steam and on the gaming market. If you are interested in the world of agriculture or just love machines then this is definitely the game for you.
Gameplay
Farming Simulator 2013 is, as i say again, by far the best farming simulator out there to date. With the expection of very bouncy and unrealistic physics, it is the most realistic agricultural simulator that you can find. The graphics could do with an upgrade to compete with other simulation games such as Euro Truck Simulator 2 but none the less the equipment you can buy is still fairly detailed.
When you first jump into the game you are given a very large, yet abandoned farm. You are given a few older tractors to start off with and some basic implements to put on the back. Things start off slow but it doesn't take long before you can be running a highly profitable business. In the begining you are expected to work the fields by planting grain crops such as wheat, barley or canola. The smallest leap into new areas of farming is to simply buy yourself a mower and plant grass instead. As you get further into the game you can explore new areas of farming from turning silage into biogas to growing potatoes and harvesting them with some colossal machinery.
Farming Simulator 2013 has a large variety of real life tractors, implements and other agricultural equipment which look fairly good. If you feel that this selection is not large enough for you and you need more equipment then there is a large and very active modding community for this game with most mods being very simple to install. You can find some of the best mods
on GIANTS own website.
Conclusion
Farming Simulator is very addictive. Before long you will be wracking up many hours of gameplay. The quantity of areas to explore can lead you into hundreds of hours of gaming pleasure and when you've explored all of that there's still the modding community to rely on. If you like farming or big machines i can almost guarentee that you'll love this game.

I'm gonna keep this pretty short.
If you like space 4X games, this game is for you. Just don't fall for the same trap that most of these negative reviews have in comparing a brand new title with games that have years of content update, expansions, and/or dlc behind them. I've been in on the ground floor for an awful lot of 4X game releases, and Stellaris has outperformed them on nearly every point, and in the ones it hasn't, I can point to a half dozen titles that its got the same features.
I'm fairly sure most of the negative reviews are from people coming from either other paradox games expecting this to be grand strategy and not 4X, or people who hear the hype but don't play 4X, or people that have been playing games that have been around for ages with lots of expansions, like Sins or GalCiv. (Yes, I count Galciv as being around for years, its been in EA for ages, and it was terrible at first imo, just like Civ5 was).
--------------
Does it have bugs? Yes of course. Its brand new, and it didnt have an Early Access period. Personally I count that as a good thing.
Are the bugs annoying? I don't really think so. Much like with Bethesda games, I find most of them to be amusing more than anything else when taken with a grain of salt.
Are there showstopper bugs? I've only found one, and that one hasnt repeated itself since the first hotfix, and I've never met anyone else who had it, so I'd honestly have to say 'no'.
And here I am with almost 100 hours played now. Its a fantastic new entry into the scifi 4X genre. (And don't let anyone try and tell you its Grand Strategy. This is Master of Orion / Endless Space on steroids, pure and simple.)
This os a good Farming simulator 2013 investment.

text:
The story has an excellent premise, as evinced by the extensive efforts of Square Enix to milk the universe of all its worth (spin-offs include
and even a movie,
among others). You start with Cloud Strife (employed as a mercenary) and long-time friend Tifa Lockheart as members of eco-terrorist group AVALANCHE, under the command of Barrett Wallace. The underlying belief of the group is that the planet's life energy is being consumed by Shinra Corporation's reactors, slowly but surely destroying the planet. The group organise attacks against the reactors in the belief they are saving the planet. These events are eventually dwarfed by a new threat to the planet: Sephiroth.
The game has done well over the years thanks to a whole plethora of reasons that help make it come alive, and it often stays alive in the minds of gamers long after players have experienced it. The engaging story, of which I have only touched upon here, is littered with so many twists and turns and shocking discoveries that you'll likely be dizzy with awesomeness by the end of it.
Gameplay is much the same as previous titles, using the standard random encounter mechanic we all know and love to initiate fights with monsters or people. Equipment is limited to one weapon and one armor at a time, but these can have various materia slots. Materia is crystallised Mako, or lifestream energy, and is the source of many abilities and enhancements characters can make use of in the game, not the least of which is magic spells, summons, auto-abilities and stat boosts. Materia can be levelled, and once mastered can spawn a duplicate materia, allowing much customisation and experimentation.
The game really is an emotional rollercoaster. The characters are a lot more fully realised than many of those in previous titles in the series - Barrett's concern for Marlene, Tifa's concern for Cloud ... even some of the Turks inspire our empathy at times (eg, Reno and Rude deciding they are 'off-duty' in regard to orders to search for Cloud, after working together briefly). Cloud's cross-dressing scene is good for a laugh. People are killed. Truths are learnt. A good game is a game that holds our attention, and that is what FFVII and its characters do as we strive to know more about what is happening and why. Indeed, the shock death of one of our own team members definitely added to the game's infamy. Most of you already know who I'm talking about. And perhaps because of this, Sephiroth is often lauded as one of, if not
, greatest game villain of all time. I know my own feelings are a mix of admiration and hate when I think of him.
The art style was a leap ahead in its time, but in today's world of newest releases it does have a dated feel to it, with chunky 3D graphics on par with much of the earliest games to implement 3D graphics. On the PC version little has changed, although it has been criticised for its lower quality graphics, installation and framerate problems. I did not experience any problems personally, and have come to not expect vast improvements in framerate from FF re-releases.
Some would say the PS version is more impressive - I myself cannot say as I never got around to playing that version. It does seem as though Square Enix has only done the bare minimum to get the game to work on PC - a trait shared by many FF PC ports, much to the disgust of expectant PC FF fans.
The music is excellent, but many of its most loved tracks have been reworked for
and it is these versions I enjoy the most, especially
As it happens, the FFVII version is also composer Nobuo Uematsu's favourite from the soundtrack, and his favourite battle theme from any Final Fantasy game.
Some cons I believe are worth noting:
- Cheap final boss fight, impossible to lose
- A minority might find the plot very confusing to grasp as more facts are brought to light
I would have listed the game's linear nature, but this isn't so bad when you consider it as a trade-off for good story. Also to make up for this are the game's various mini games, helping to beef up an already impressive game. There is a barrel pushing game in the Sector 5 Church, a 'squats' mini game at the Wall Market, a sneaking game in the Shinra Building, in addition to various mini games that can be played at the Gold Saucer, including G Bike, the Fort Condor strategy minigame, and of course the chocobo racing game, among others. Some of these are easy while others can be hard.

Taking cues from Japanese horror films as well John Woo action films, FEAR creates a beautiful hybrid between the two genres. The game puts you in control of a member of F.E.A.R. (First Encounter Assault Recon) a SWAT team of sorts that specializes in dealing with the paranormal.
The game consists of basic first person shooter mechanics, but the game's real curve ball was bullet-time (or slow mo) à la Max Payne. Combining that with its amazing graphics (which still hold up fairly well) and particle effects, as well as spooky atmosphere-- all which made the game stand out amoung the other shooters at the time.
Think the slow motion made the game to easy? Think again, F.E.A.R features some of the most amazing AI ever programed into a game. Enemy squads would work to flank you, and if you hid somewhere too long you would most likely find yourself face to face with an enemy hand grenade. Killed one enemy? The remaining squad would notify its members via radio and strategize accordingly.
The game wasn’t just a pretty and intelligent, but extremely atmospheric thanks to its level and sound design. Dispersed between the intense gun fights you would find yourself in dark spooky hallways encountering Alma, a creepy ghost girl heaily inspired by The Ring. Sometimes she would appear in the corner of your eye, other times she would outright startle you, and then there would be moments where you would find a corpse with its flesh melted off and hear a girlish giggle in the distance.  Shooters that try to be scary often fail miserably, but it was with great skill that Monolith actually pulled off balancing horror and action in FEAR.
The game was followed by a number of expansion packs as well as a couple of sequels (each worse than the last) which failed to capture the magic of the first game. Monolith later revisted similiar terrirtory with its equally excellent “Condemned” a first person horror game that focused more on hand to hand combat. Both games are worth your money and time.

This is one of my favorite games. While F.E.A.R. 2 is very obviously creepy, what sets the first F.E.A.R. game apart is how incredibly normal it is. Then slowly, inconsistencies start piling up, and the feeling that develops isn't one of horror, but that somewhere, something went wrong.
Gameplay-wise, you can expect a shooter that feels like a lot of shooters from 2005. It plays a little like Half-Life 2, without the weapon variety or physics. It's not so generic as to be boring, but it's  nothing to write home about. In a way, that generic quality drives the something-out-of-place vibe brought about by horror elements, but admittedly makes replays not as fun.
If you're looking for a Dead Space or Amnesia-like experience, you might be disappointed. But if you want a solid shooter with constant eerie undertones, I couldn't recommend a better game.

This movie was made with a $500,000 budget, which for movie making standards, is pocket change. The tone, storytelling, and overall quality isn't much different from your typical Cinemassacre video. You're literally watching a feature length nerd episode. Kind of like the R.O.B the robot episode, but bigger. The movie tries to be a lot of different things, and you can tell that everyone who worked on it had a great time.
Lots of practical effects were used. In fact, about 90% of the effects are practical. Some look good, some look pretty obvious, like when miniatures are used.
Oh and that music, the music is just incredible. Bear Mccreary, composer for the Walking Dead TV series did an amazing job on the soundtrack. From epic orchestral versions of the AVGN theme to fast paced car chace music with some 8-bit sounds mixed in. Even if you don't think the movie is pleasant to look at, there's no denying that it all sounds great.
One of my major gripes is the acting. For the most part, the acting is on par with a television sitcom. Not bad, but not great. But a lot of the extras just plain suck. For example, there's one scene where a group of people are running for their lives. They're doing the cheesiest fake run in front of a green screen and have the biggest smiles on their faces as their letting out half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥screams.
Overall, if you're a fan of the Nerds work, you should enjoy this. If you aren't a fan of him, you probably won't like it.
For those just going in, remember that it's just like a Nerd episode, but bigger. Don't expect Citizen Kane.

The Binding of Isaac is one of the best games I have ever played.  It is a roguelike game with endless replayability and a brutal difficulty that can get a bit frustrating at times, but it doesn't feel unfair.  What really makes this game unique, however, is the leveling system.  Rather than using a conventional leveling system with experience points, items are located in various rooms on each floor, some giving a small stat boost, and some giving an effect that forces you to change your play style drastically.  You don't know what items you will get from run to run, so this mechanic keeps things fresh every time you play.
Plus you play as a naked kid running around a basement who kills his insane mom with his tears.  What's not to like?
Point breakdown:
Gameplay: 9/10
Graphics/Aesthetics: 7/10
Difficulty: 10/10
Replayability: 10/10
Music: 8/10
Story: 8/10
Overall: 9/10, Highly Recommended

My first experience almost made me want to rage quit the game. You click play and you're dumped into a tavern with 20 other people. WTF? Then I go look for a way to get my friends in. Eh... nope. Escape-menu? Nothing. After 20 minutes of Googling, I finally found that if either press F11 or go to a menu where you get a mouse cursor, and then click the icon in the top-right that looks like a ball of wool, you'll get a sidebar menu that looks worse than Games for Windows Live. Seriously, it's horrendous. But, this is the thing you have to use to add friends to your friends list (because you can't invite Steam friends straight into a game, like with Dungeon Defenders 1), and then you need to form a party using friends from your friends list. Only then can you start a game with your friends.
The gameplay so far has redeemed the poor user experience with the friends list. All classes from DD1 are there, though they have been altered a bit. The summoner no longer has its own unit count, but shares defense points with the rest. You can still equip two pets like before. Pets also grant you a special ability, which you can activate with the X key and which has a short recharge timer. There are a few more gear slots and item sets are now clearly indicated. There are consumables which give you more options while you play, such as regeneration amulets or taunt-totems.
Loot is now assigned to each player, like in Diablo III. This is also the case for mana from treasure chests. So everything you see on the ground, you can pick up!
They introduced coins as a currency for in the shop and for upgrading items. I suppose this is to make a distinction between the stuff you use to build towers and what you use to enhance your characters. So far it feels right.
TL;DR; Social features are messed up. Remember: open a menu (Escape or i) then ball of wool in the top-right corner. Besides that, it's a decent game that looks to be an improvement over DD1.

At the time of this writing I've only played Bit Shifter for 2.5 hours, but I've already seen enough to know that I'll be putting a lot of time into this little gem. In fact the only reason I'm not playing at the moment is because I feel compelled to tell all of my fellow gamers about it.
Bit Shifter is an Early Access game, and having been bitten badly by an early access game once before in which the devs just walked away from it unfinished without having done much at all with it, I was somewhat hesitant about signing up for another one. But the price is low enough that I decided to give early access another try. I'm glad I did. Bit Shifter has the feel of an already finished, well polished game, and therefore I can only assume that they've introduced it as an early access game out of an abundance of caution. Thus far I have not encountered any bugs or even as much as a hiccup. In my experience, that's pretty unusual even for finished AAA games from big name studios. Admittedly I've only been playing for 2.5 hours, and there's still plenty of room for a bug to show up somewhere, but I take pride in writing honest and factual reviews, and if any significant problems pop up, I won't hesitate to amend my review, though to be fair I always notify the devs and give them a reasonable amount of time to fix it before writing it up. Essentially, the more hours past 2.5 I get without amending the review, the safer you can feel about the game and the game devs’ willingness to fix problems.
Let's get down to the nitty gritty of what this game is about, and what makes it fun. Bit Shifter takes place in a cartoon world representing a computer. Even the clouds floating by overhead are circuit boards! If the game is nothing else, it is one giant Easter egg packed full to bursting with more Easter eggs, many of which are puns or word play on their original meaning.
The computer world you play in is under attack by viruses (viri?), and the defence of the computer world is up to you and a gigantic armada of flying saucers similar to yours except...   a rather explosive event right at the beginning wipes out the Armada...  soooo... the defence of your computer world is up to you alone. Your job is a difficult one. Not only must you destroy the viruses, but you must do so before they spread far enough to enter your world's body of water which is named (what else could it be?) the Bit Stream.
Fortunately you don't have to fight the viruses entirely alone. Your flying saucer, named (wait for it...) Scandisk can carry tiny soldiers called "Bits". How many Bits can your ship carry? How many would it take in order to take a byte out of a virus in a computer world? Eight bits make a byte, so eight! Obviously. So you fly over to the virus and do what Scandisk was notorious for. Drop bits!
Learning how to use Scandisk and its weaponry, and the world around you could not be easier. It's built right into the story line. The first few maps are dedicated to it, and you are given enough time at the introduction of each new button/key press or concept to become proficient at it without waiting so long to introduce new concepts that it becomes boring. It's a tour d'force on how to teach new users how to play a game, so much so that it would be wise for developers even at the largest studios to take note of and learn from it.
The game also boasts a broad range of difficulty settings beginning with a setting that a crippled snail could defeat, on up to a difficulty level which would challenge any professional gamer well versed in flight sims or outer space combat games. This is proving to be very useful to me not only because I'm a crippled snail, but also because I'm learning how to use a new controller (a Steam Controller) which is much more sensitive than my old one. As I become more proficient with the new controller I'll be able to increase the difficulty, even in the middle of a level during an intense fire fight if I want more of a challenge.
I've only scratched the surface with this review. I'll close by saying that it's really amazing to me that this is an early access game put together by a two man indy development team, especially at its price point. It is excellent value for money not only because of its almost infinite replay value, but also for reasons too numerous to list. It's obvious that this game is a labour of love for its two very talented developers; else it could not be what it is.
Happy Gamming!

I read all of the bad reviews of Dungeon Defenders Eternity, then waited a few days and bought it anyway. We have two accounts at my house and have been playing two person games. Overall we are enjoying it very much but there is a lot of confusion. Some things that should be simple take an internet search to figure out. Because the game is new, there is not a lot of information on the internet. Simple things like inviting friends, creating a party, and hatching eggs are just different enough to cause problems. My biggest issue is initial load time. One computer may be ready to play almost immediately while the other wants to reload a lot of graphic files. So far it seems almost random one whether a computer want to reload graphic files. We have learned to start the game, then go gather our drinks and snacks while the graphics load, then come back to play the game. With a weekend of play we only had one instance where a party member was dropped as the dungeon was loading. No time warps as far as we can tell.
Over all we had a lot of fun with the updated version of a favorite game. Everyone gets their own chests so building is faster and much more even. Experience is divided evenly among characters. No more worrying about the knight and mage towers giving most of the experience to those characters. I do wish that the inventory system was easier to use. There is still a lot of junk items to go through and sell. I need to experiment with the item filters in the Options menu and see if I can filter out the items without losing the income I get from selling them.

Ok so I DID NOT play the original Witcher game and I found that it really didn't affect my overall enjoyment and understanding of the game.
My god has this game not story and narrative overload! There is a lot of lore and backstory to the world and the characters. From side characters like Triss, Zoltan and Roache, you meet so many characters with interesting stories and lore behind them that you can't help but make sure you know every detail about their lives! For the first time in ages in a video game, I wanted the conversations to keep going (which, to me, is an outstanding feat). You play as Geralt of Rivia again; a witcher who is framed for the assassination of a king as is on a quest to rid his name of false accusations. At first, seems like a pretty straight forward story but it soon takes many different side stories, background quests and just overall outstanding lore. I don't want to get too much more into the story but trust me; it's detailed! My only real complaint about the story is sometimes it can get a little hard to follow and the characters you meet are drip-feeded quite quickly (it is a much shorter game after all, just look at my playtime) however a quick read of the detailed glossary always made sure I knew what was going on and why. There seems to be only one really major decision during act 1 of the game that truly affects the game but then again, I cannot judge too much as I haven't played through twice (which apparently is the way to play it which can increase play time by about another 30-40 hours).
I had strongly mixed feelings about this gameplay system. One thing that is
noticeable is the restricted movement system. To be honest, it is not that bad but it can kind of feel generic and weird at times (seeing as you can't jump either). Exploration is encouraged with plenty of side quests to be discovered and areas to explore and secrets to discover. Inventory management is far from perfect but it's efficient enough that I didn't get
frustrated at it. Combat is definately interesting and a mixed bag. At first, it feels so restrictive and clunky with awkward aiming and slow casted spells. In fact, the control scheme for me on a mouse and keyboard got so irritating that I ended up using a controller. However once you level up Geralt and his abilities the combat becomes much more fun and engaging but still not fluent. As you journey around the zones you'll pick up crafting items to help craft oils and other alchemy items. Now this might sound tedious
its quite fun and rewarding and also really neccessary. Overall, the fighting is not perfect but still quite fun and I enjoyed most of the fights (minus some annoying boss fights). There is also plenty of items to craft too (armour, swords, etc).
My god this game is still beautiful after how many years?! The lighting and detail in the areas is an absolute joy to observe! I am playing this on high and ultra settings (FXAA) at a constant 75 FPS and it is still an absolute joy to soak in all the details and colour. The character models and items look authentic too however, they do suffer from odd animations during conversations (but this isn't a huge deal breaker0. The voice acting is overall pretty well done with some convincing performances.
Overall the Witcher 2 is one of my all time favourite RPG's. Deep crafting, combat, skills and story kept me coming back week after week. The only thing that got me to stop playing was that I moved to the Witcher 3 (review coming soon)! I highly reccommend this 'forgotten' gem as it truly is a master piece in game design.

From what I have seen so far the game is wonderful. You can micro manage down the most minute detail of every decision or set automatic orders. For example you can order your ships to automatically do a thing and only notify you when they encounter something that needs your attention. You can also do this for ships, space stations, and even planets. You can create such a large universe that games can last up to hours order even days. Thankfully it has a save game, even for the multiplayer which I have never seen before.
Now for the problems. It just loves to crash. My drivers are all up to date. I deleted the entire game and reinstalled. I have no mods. I have even tried it on three completely different computers. I just don't understand how people are playing this game? On one computer I simply start the tutorial and it crashes when I press OK on the intro screen. On the other I play a single player and it lasts anywhere from 10 minutes to 1 hour then crash. Often the save games are kind enough to save three turns before the crash. Of course once you launch the save game it crashes again after three turns but you keep loading hoping if you do something different this time you can get your game back. Sometimes you do and sometimes your hours of game play are gone forever.
I am not asking for my money back because I believe this game has promise. I loved previous Galactic Civ games so I plan to shelve this one until I see a patch.
*** Update ***
I have an update. I still have the same three machines that this game would not run on. However I upgraded my 2011 ASUS-G73 to Windows 10 and now the game seems to run fine on it. It has been about six months since I last tried the game so I don't know if it was my OS upgrade or a recent patch to the game that fixed it. That is the machine I intended to play the game on so I am now happy enough to flip my rating from negative to positive if I can.
